en: *Huayan Xuantan Huijuan Ji*, Scroll One, compiled by the Bhikṣu Puri of Zaiwang Temple on Mount Cang.
In order to elucidate this entire *Xuantan*, it is opened with a preliminary analysis in two sections: first, a general explanation of the title; second, a sequential [exegesis].

The initial section of the difficult-to-explain text is further divided into two parts: first, the individual explanation of the title of the *Dharma* (the Sūtra), because the titles of the Sūtra, the Commentary (*śāstra*), the Outline (*pīn*), and the Sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) are distinct;
second, the general explanation of the title of the [author] of the Outline, because there is no difference regarding the person among the Commentary, the Outline, and the Sub-commentary.

Now, for the first part: in general, the exposition does not exceed four stages, namely: first, the outline; second, the Sūtra; third, the Commentary; and fourth, the Sub-commentary. The reason it is thus is as follows.
Those who wish to understand the general outline of this sutra commentary cannot do so without a topical outline (ko);

therefore, the outline is presented first. Although the general outline is known, the meaning remains difficult to comprehend within the text; therefore, the main scripture (the *sūtra* itself) is cited next. Although the main text is visible, how can one know its meaning without a commentary? Therefore, the commentary is explained next.
Although the commentary’s explanations are clear, they are often general and concise; therefore, the text of the *Chao* (the sub-commentary) is used to supplement them and make them complete.
Since these four types [of exegesis] are logically appropriate in this way: first, the Buddha spoke the sūtra; based on the sūtra, commentaries (*śāstra*) were composed;
based on the commentaries, topical outlines (*kośa*) were established; and following the outlines, word-by-word sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*) were produced.

Now, in explaining the title, we shall follow the sequence of their arising to demonstrate that they exist through gradual development. Hereafter, we will explain the text by addressing difficulties as they arise, without overstepping the sequence of the exposition.
As is customary, the titles of the Dharma differ, and there are four such titles divided into four sections: first, the title of the sutra;
second, the title of the commentary; third, the topical outline; and fourth, the sub-commentary.
Regarding the first, the title of the sutra, it is the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*; these seven characters are indeed inexhaustible.

The general definition and categories of the term *sūtra* are extremely vast; although they will be explained extensively below, it is first appropriate to provide a brief presentation before entering the text.

This shall be analyzed by way of seven gates, in accordance with the seven characters of the title: (1) clarifying the purpose of its arrival; (2) the correspondence between the Chinese and Sanskrit translations;
(3) listing the correspondences according to the title; (4) identifying the essential substance of the name; (5) [the fifth]; (6) [the sixth]; (7) [the seventh].
1. Explaining the analysis [of the six perfections]; 2. Distinguishing their various names; 3. Resolving obstacles and difficulties. First, regarding the intent of the introduction:

The *Avataṃsaka* Great Teaching is the ultimate discourse on the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). When my Buddha, the World-Honored One, first attained perfect enlightenment, he observed that all sentient beings universally possess the virtues of their inherent nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*);
yet, because they are shrouded by delusion, they are unable to realize them. Thereupon, in accordance with this nature, he suddenly expounded [this teaching].
This sutra clarifies that the natural radiance of each person’s own fundamental ground is no different from that of the Buddha, so that all may together realize it.

Second, regarding the correspondence between the Chinese and Sanskrit terms: since the Buddha appeared in the Western Heaven (India) and his teachings flowed to the Eastern Land (China), there would have been no means for understanding them had they not been translated;
therefore, those who lecture and study must first clarify this to manifest the arrival of the teaching.
Naturally, there are both general and specific translations. As for the general translation:
the Sanskrit *Mahāvaipulya-buddha-kaṇḍa-prabhāsa-sūtra* is rendered in the language of Tang as *Dafangguangjuezhezhuangyanjing* (The Great Vaipulya Sutra of the Flower Ornament of the Awakened One).
As for the specific translation: *mahā* means "great," *vaipulya* means "vast/extended," and *buddha* means "awakened."
*Kaṇḍa* means "cloud," *vibhūṣaṇa* means "ornamentation," and *sūtra* means "discourse. Among these, "Awakened One" (*buddha*) refers to the Buddha;
the Sanskrit phonetics are preserved in abbreviated form to inspire faith.

Furthermore, the two characters for "various ornaments" (*vibhūṣaṇa*) are omitted to avoid prolixity, and the title is established using these seven characters. III. Regarding the correspondence based on the title, there are seven characters. One.
The titles are categorized into ten matters arranged in five pairs: first, the pair of teaching and meaning;

within the teaching, the single character "able" (*neng*) is the teaching that expresses, while the six characters "great" (*da*) and so forth are the meanings expressed. Second, within the aforementioned meanings, the pair of phenomenon (*dharma*) and metaphor (*dṛṣṭānta*);

here, "great" and so forth are the phenomena, and "Lotus" (*huá*) and "Adornment" (*yán*) are the metaphors. Third, within the aforementioned phenomena, the pair of person (*pudgala*) and phenomenon (*dharma*); namely:
"Mahāvaipulya" (Great Extensiveness) refers to the Dharma that is realized; "Buddha" refers to the person who realizes it. It is also termed the "confrontation of object and wisdom.

Within the four categories above, this selects and upholds one pair: the character "Great" (mahā) performs the function of selection, while the characters "Vaipulya" perform the function of maintenance.
Specifically, "Great" distinguishes the Great from the Small, the Real from the Provisional, and the Result from the Cause; it is also the essence.
Using either the pair [of characters] or the pair of essence and characteristics, we borrow the character "flower" (hua) from among the five to serve as a metaphor for its cause;
that is, the pair of cause and effect. Since the Buddha is the fruit, the single character "flower" alone serves as a metaphor for the cause.
If the two characters "Huayan" (Flower Adornment) are combined, they likewise serve as a metaphor for the aforementioned four characters. Fourth, the naming of the essence and meaning:

"Great" (Mahā) is named according to its essential nature, with "eternal pervasiveness" as its meaning. Being eternal means it cannot be altered across the three periods of time; being pervasive means there is nothing outside the ten directions of empty space.

Thus, it takes the true reality (*dharmatā*)—which is both entirely existent and entirely empty—as its essence. It is then designated by the term "Dharma" (*dharma*), which signifies "guiding and maintaining.

Because it simultaneously maintains both nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it guides and gives rise to sentient beings' understanding. Therefore, it is defined by the six aspects (*ṣaḍ-lakṣaṇa*) and the ten mysteries (*daśa-guhya*).

Its essence is vast because it derives its name from its function; its meaning is that of "encompassing" and "pervasive. "Encompassing" means broad containment, while "pervasive" means broad penetration.
Thus, its essence consists of the mutual inclusion and interpenetration of the defiled and pure, the dependent and the primary.

As for the Buddha, he is named after his person; his meaning is that of "awakening" and "illumination. "Illumination" clarifies the profound depths of the myriad dharmas, while "awakening" realizes the heavy darkness of the great night.

The "darkness" (昏) takes as its essence the cloud-like body of the ten non-obstructed bodies; the "flower" (華) derives its name from analogy and has the meaning of manifesting fruits and adorning the body.
Manifesting fruits signifies the perfect completion of the myriad practices, while adorning the body signifies the full possession of all virtues.
Its essence consists of the mutual pervasion and integration of practice and vow, while it receives the name "adornment" through its functional efficacy, serving as a resource for adornment.
"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the substance and function of the vast [Dharma], which adorns the Buddha-bodies of Reality (*dharmakāya*) and Response (*nirmāṇakāya*).

It takes unobstructed great wisdom as its essence; it is called a "sūtra" (*sūtra*) by virtue of its capacity to express [the meaning], and its "meaning" consists in its function of upholding and maintaining.

Taking the inexhaustible nature and characteristics and the boundless gathering of sentient beings as its scope, it takes the body, name, phrase, and sentence as its essence. (This concludes the explanation of sections five and six.)

Regarding this analysis, there are four permutations of combination and separation that apply to all three interpretations—namely, the locative (*adhikaraṇa*), the agentive (*kartṛ*), and the possessive (*svāmin*).
First, "Mahāyāna" (Great Vehicle) refers to the Dharma realized therein. This applies to both the locative and agentive interpretations:

because the Mahāyāna possesses the essence, characteristics, and functions [of that Dharma], and because the Mahāyāna of the Vaipulya (Extensive Scriptures) possesses the essence of those characteristics and functions.

Therefore, from the perspective of the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent designation), "Great" (*mahā*) refers to the meaning of sequential dissemination (*caryā-vistara*), while "Vaipulya" (*fangguang*) refers to the Great itself;
thus, the essence and function are mutually identical. From the perspective of the *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound), this refers to the meaning of perfect interpenetration.

Regarding the Buddha of the *Avataṃsaka*, who is the person capable of realizing it, both interpretations apply: "the Flower of the Buddha" distinguishes it from the practices of the causal stage, while "the Buddha of the Flower" distinguishes it from the fruition of other vehicles.
Because this is not a Buddha of other vehicles, it is also based on the primary term [in a *tatpuruṣa* compound].

If one understands the characteristics of the integration of the "holding the function" (*karmadhāraya*) and the "vast and great" (*vaipulya*), then the Buddha of the Three Great Vaipulya [Sūtras]—the *Avataṃsaka*—can be known as that which distinguishes the Buddha from the provisional or Hinayana Buddhas;

and the "Vast and Great" of the *Avataṃsaka* Buddha can be known as that which distinguishes the Dharma obtained at the stage of a cause from [other teachings]. Thus, the characteristics can be understood. Fourth.

The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra of the Mahāvaipulya Buddha* distinguishes itself from sūtras such as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*; "the *Mahāvaipulya Buddha-avataṃsaka-sūtra*" distinguishes it from that which is explained in the śāstras.
This is an example of a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound). Regarding the practitioner who upholds [the text]: the phrasing follows the meaning, and the meaning follows the phrasing;
thus, the expression and the underlying principle are perfectly integrated. Furthermore, when the aforementioned teaching is viewed in relation to its meaning, and the person in relation to...
Regarding the term "Dharma," it may be understood that both the *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) and *bahuvrīhi* (exocentric) analyses are applicable. Sixth, to distinguish its alternative names:

as stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it is called the "Sūtra of One Hundred Thousand [Verses]," which is designated by way of its numerical extent, because this sūtra originally consists of one hundred thousand stanzas.
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is called the "Sūtra of Miscellaneous Flowers" (*Kusuma-vicitra*), which is designated by way of a metaphor. In the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*... [text continues].
It is titled the *Mahā-acintya-vimokṣa-sūtra*. This is designated as such because it refers to the Dharma itself.

Furthermore, both the "Chapter on Manifestation" (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*) and the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*) each possess ten titles, as fully shown in the subsequent illustrations. Qingliang [Zhiyan] stated: "The first three are alternative names that are mostly general and concise;
the ten titles of the latter two chapters are mostly derived from specific names and are restricted to their respective chapters. Therefore, this present translation [adopts the former].

Since this [title] consists of seven characters as its name, it simultaneously designates both the person and the Dharma, and equally presents both the Dharma and the analogy. It encompasses both substance and function, and includes both the fruit and the cause;

thus, its principles are exhaustive and its meaning is perfect, and for this reason, it is placed at the beginning of the sutra. Regarding the seventh point, the explanation that resolves potential objections:
A questioner asks, "The three characters 'Mahāvaipulya' (Great, Vast, and Extensive) appear frequently in other sutras, such as the *Triśaraṇasamgraha-sūtra* and the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*."
In sutras such as the *Ratnakaraṇḍa* and the *Awakening of Faith*, there are more than ten sections that contain the term "Great Vaipulya" (*mahāvaipulya*).
Are these identical to or different from this sutra? If they are identical, why is only this sutra designated as the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*)?

If they are different, what are their characteristics? Guifeng replied: "If one assigns them according to the three greatnesses (*san da*), they are identical; however, their explanations of the meaning differ."

Regarding the differences according to their respective schools: while the *Awakening of Great Perfect Enlightenment* (Yuánjué dà) assigns [the dharmadhātu] solely to the essence (*tǐ*), asserting that its self-substance is eternally pervasive;
this sutra holds that whether it be the characteristics (*xiàng*) or the functions (*yòng*), all are identical to the true nature (*zhēnxìng*) and thus eternally pervasive.

Furthermore, in that [other] school, the "directions" (*fāng*) are assigned only to the characteristics as that which sustains the self-nature and gives rise to understanding through its patterns; here, however, both nature and characteristics are maintained together, fully embodying the ten mysteries (*shí xuánmén*).
Each and every mark serves as a model that gives rise to understanding in sentient beings;
furthermore, while its vastness cannot be equated with the essence itself, this [function] is precisely the activity of the marks of virtue. Thus, the Postscript states:

"The true essence is merged within the realm of myriad transformations, while the marks of virtue are manifested at the gate of profound mystery; their functions arise in profusion yet remain eternally as they are. Therefore.
This differs from other sutras. Having finished explaining the title of the sutra, we next explain the title of the commentary (*śāstra*).
Regarding the title *Da fangguang fo huayan jing shu*, Scroll One, together with the preface: first, we provide a structural analysis; second, we provide an explanation.
In the first part, we first take the two characters "together with the preface" (*bing xu*) and relate them to what precedes.
The eleven characters beginning with "Great" (*mahā*) constitute the first pair, that of the "enabler" (*nirdeśaka*) and the "enabled" (*nirdiṣṭa*).
Second, taking the first two characters in relation to the nine characters beginning with "Great," they form the third pair, that of the "recorder" (*vaktṛ*) and the "recorded" (*vācya*).

Furthermore, taking the character "Volume" (*juan*) in relation to the eight preceding characters, they form the fourth pair, that of the "basis" (*āśraya*) and the "dependent" (*āśrita*); here, "Volume" is the basis and the eight characters are the dependent. This is the first section of the Commentary.
Regarding the seven characters above as the "explanatory" (*nengshi*) and the [preceding] seven characters as the "explained" (*suoshi*), there are two modes of interpretation.
First, the explanation of the meaning; second, the sixfold analysis. Regarding the first, the explanation of the meaning: the seven characters of the sutra title have been explained as above.

As for the term *shu* (commentary), it means to loosen, to resolve, to open, and to penetrate. That is to say, where the principles and meanings within the sutra are profound and abstruse, one "loosens" them by means of the *shu*.
It is called a *shu* (commentary) because it elucidates the essential meaning of the scriptures, resolves doubts, opens up what is obscure, and brings about thorough understanding;

furthermore, it carries the sense of "organizing" or "arranging. As Lu Tong said: "A person has hair, which they comb and arrange every morning; yet though one possesses a mind, why does one not do the same?
This work now organizes and arranges the textual meanings within the scripture. As for the term *juan* (fascicle): [The remainder of the text follows.]

"Unfurling and rolling up" constitutes the meaning: when unfurled, one reads it; when rolled up, one reflects upon it. Because there is no obstruction in unfolding and rolling up [the text], it is called a "scroll" (*juan*).
"First" (*di yi*) refers to the sequence (*dici*); "one" (*yi*) is the ultimate of numbers and the very beginning. This commentary consists of twenty scrolls;
the number is now recorded so that the order does not become confused, hence it says "first. Regarding the phrase "together with the preface" (*bing xu*): "together" (*bing*) means "inclusive."
"Yě" (also) and "yě" (to reach). "Xù" (sequence/order) means a thread; it is like a cocoon finding its thread—once the thread is exhausted, the silk of the entire cocoon is revealed.
Just as a window-lattice finds its sequence—once the sequence is exhausted, the intent of the entire lattice is revealed.

Furthermore, the *Erya* states that the east and west walls are called "xù" (because they serve to order and distinguish the interior from the exterior). By observing the walls, one understands how they distinguish the depth of the residence; by observing the "xù," one [understands... the [meaning].
To know the author’s intent, furthermore, "preface" (*xu*) means to introduce;
it refers to describing the general purport of the sutra and commentary at the beginning of the text, so that students may suddenly perceive its great principles. Thus, it is called a "preface.

Having finished the explanation of the meaning above, the subsequent "sixfold combination of explanations" (*liuhe shi*)—the single character "commentary" (*shu*) in relation to the preceding seven characters—is the basis for the subject and object of the explanation.

Regarding the term "Commentary" (*shu*), there are three interpretations: first, it may be interpreted as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative compound) that encompasses both the general and the specific, because this refers to the commentary on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and excludes treatises (*śāstra*) and the like;

alternatively, it may be interpreted as a *tatpuruṣa* that distinguishes the general from the specific, because the character "commentary" (*shu*) applies generally [to all works], while the characters "of the Sūtra" (*jing-zhi*) specifically refer to the two volumes.

Regarding the first three characters, "of the Sūtra, Volume One," there are three explanations. First, a *tatpuruṣa* interpretation based on the general and the specific, where the character "volume" (*juan*)...
This is the first [title] as a whole; this is the first [title] for the individual fascicle. There are twenty individual fascicles, and the "first" is the sole initial one among them.

Within the whole, there is the first of the individual fascicles. Regarding the two aspects of essence (*tǐ*) and function (*yòng*): the word "fascicle" (*juàn*) denotes the essence, while "first" denotes the function. By taking the essence as the function, the fascicle is itself the first.
Thirdly, by explaining "fascicle" through the method of attributive apposition (*dài shù shì*), the fascicle is the phenomenon (*fǎ*) and "first" is the number; thus, the phenomenon is the fascicle.

1. Because it brings forth the first number, [the title is established]. 2. Third, looking at the character "juan" (卷) in relation to the eight characters above, it is the scroll of the paper-surface (*pattraka*) which serves as the support;
this name is manifested from the commentary (*vṛtti*), which is the supported, thus forming a *tatpuruṣa* compound: "The Scroll of the Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha. 3.
Fourth, looking at the two characters "first" (第一) in relation to the nine characters above, they are that which records, derived from what is recorded.

The title *Zhāngmíng* (Manifesting the Name) is also an *adhikaraṇasamāsa* (dependent determinative compound). Furthermore, the two characters "with preface" (*yǒngxù*) are interpreted as a *vyadhikaraṇasamāsa* (non-co-locative determinative compound) in relation to the preceding main title.
The explanation of the title of the *Śāstra* is now complete.
Third, the explanation of the section title: *Dàfāngguǎng Fóhuáyánjīng Shū Kēwén Juàn Dìyī* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Great Vaipulya, Sectioned Text, Volume One). Explanation.
Regarding this section title, first is the initial listing of correspondences, followed by the subsequent explanation of the meaning. As for the initial listing of correspondences:

the eight characters above serve as the "object of the analysis" (*ko*), while the five characters below serve as the "agent of the analysis. The character "scroll" (*juan*) is the agent relative to what precedes it, serving as the basis upon which it depends;

the character "first" (*di yi*) is the agent relative to what precedes it, serving as that which records it—both may be understood as before. Regarding the subsequent explanation of the meaning, there are four parts, the first being the brief [overview].

I. Explaining the Names and Meanings (1) II. Ancient and Modern Debates (2) III. Categorization by Meaning (3) IV. Discernment through the Sixfold Exegesis (4) First, regarding the brief explanation of the names and meanings:

the eight characters of the "subject" (*ko*) have already been explained as before. As for the five characters of the "agent" (*neng-ko*), the three characters of the first fascicle do not differ in meaning from the previous subject-text.
Now, the two characters of the "explanatory text" (*ke-wen*) shall be briefly explained; first, let us explain them.

Following the explanation of the characters of the *ke* (sections), we shall now explain the meaning of the term *ke*. This has two senses: first, explaining according to its semantic meaning; second, explaining according to its graphic form.
Regarding the explanation according to its semantic meaning, various interpretations differ; here, I shall briefly demonstrate them.

One says that "ke" has the sense of "limitation" (*fenqi*), because it establishes boundaries for both the text and its meaning. Another says that "ke" has the sense of "categorizing and gathering" (*leiju*).
Whether regarding the words or the meaning, they are subsumed according to their respective categories.
One explanation states that "section" (*ko*) means "to cut" or "to determine," for it cuts off and establishes the measure, distinguishing right from wrong.

Another explanation states that "section" is defined as "opening up" or "passage," because when one sees the section headings, the meaning is opened up and made accessible. Yet another explanation states that "section" means "abridgment and collection," because...

Because few words encompass many meanings, one explanation states that "kē" (科) signifies "sequence. If there were no topical divisions (*kē*), the textual principles would necessarily become disordered and confused;
since the headings and judgments already establish a sequence, the six interpretations above all rely on the semantic definition.

Second, regarding the form of the characters: the shape of the character *kē* consists of the radical "grain" (*hé*) with the phonetic "bowl" (*dǒu") attached; its textual meaning is like "dividing grain" (*hé-kē*).

The pattern resembles grain in a *dou* measure; by obtaining the *dou*, one knows the number. When the pattern attains its classification (*ko*), the meaning becomes clear. Later commentators on "syllables" (*mon*) hold that syllable is identical to the character (*ji*).

However, when the position has not yet shifted, it is called a "name" (*myō*); once the position has shifted, the name is termed a "pattern" (*mon*). This is because the pattern serves as the basis for names and phrases.
Here, the term "pattern" is used because it encompasses both names and phrases. Second, the ancient and modern views are contrasted and analyzed through this structural classification (*kohan*).

The meaning of this [classification] originally derives from Buddhist scriptures; they may be called "chapters" (*pin*), "sections" (*zhang*), or "divisions" (*fen*), all of which are alternative names for structural units, such as the thirty-nine chapters of the present sutra.
If we speak in terms of historical traces, in this land [of China], Dao’an is regarded as the beginning;
it was at his request that the Wei Emperor (some say the Qin ruler) invited various virtuous masters into the palace to lecture on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.

A question was posed: "I have heard that the Buddha-dharma is profound and its ultimate principles are mysterious and abstruse. Yet, observing what has been discussed thus far, there appears to be no systematic order at all. Why is this?

When the virtuous ones could not respond, Dao’an, who was then in Xiangyang, heard of this and subsequently categorized the various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras of China into three divisions (tripiṭaka).
At that time, the entire court disapproved; it was only later, during the Tang dynasty, that the Tripiṭaka Master [Xuanzang] translated them accordingly.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* composed by the Bodhisattva Bandhuprabha divides the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* into three sections:
the Section on the Causes and Conditions for the Arising of the Teaching, the Section on the Exposition of the Holy Teaching, and the Section on Practicing in Accordance with the Teaching;

from that time until now, this division into three sections—neither overly elaborate nor too concise—has been followed by both the ancients and the moderns. Subsequently, various masters have each provided their own [divisions], some more and some less.
There is no need for further elaboration on these three types of classification. Generally, there are two categories of structural analysis (*ko-p'an*):

first, the threefold classification; second, the fourfold classification. Regarding the threefold classification: first is the textual classification (*wen-ko*), which analyzes according to the text itself;
second is the topical classification (*yi-ko*), which divides according to the meaning (*yi*); and third is the combined textual-topical classification, which considers both together.
Because they are categorized according to both the phrasing and the meaning, there are four gates of meaning:

first, categorizing by following the meaning from the phrasing (*vyañjana*), which means that this classification is based on the meaning expressed (*abhidheya-artha*) and does not restrict itself to the literal wording;

second, categorizing by following the phrasing from the meaning, which means that this classification is based on the textual sections of the expressive phrasing (*vācaka-vyañjana*) and does not restrict itself to the meaning expressed; third, the mutual conformity of categories of meaning.

Section One: Regarding the categorization according to the titles, although there are differences between persons (*pudgala*) and dharmas, they are treated as a single section because they serve as the titles.

Within the main text itself, although there are differences between the introductory passages and the main body of the text, these are likewise combined into one category because they constitute the main text.

Section Four: Distinguishing Differences in Categorization; for instance, although the titles regarding persons and dharmas may be identical, they are distinguished based on their respective headings.
Because persons and dharmas are distinct, they are divided into two. Within the main text, the sequence and the commentary are also differentiated and cannot be treated as the same;

they must be separated. Regarding the "selection and examination" (*liao-jian*) of the four or six types of commentaries on the text: the two characters "ke-wen" (text-division) refer to the structure of the text and its function.
"Ke" (division) is the text itself, interpreted as a *karmadhāraya* compound. The remainder may be inferred accordingly. This concludes the explanation of the title of the commentary.

Fourth, the explanation of the title of the *Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning according to the Sub-commentary* (*Da fangguang fo huayan jing su shu yan yi chao*), Volume One, including the preface.
This also has two parts: first, the listing of correspondences; second, the explanation. Regarding the first, the listing of correspondences:

(1) The "Explication of the Meaning" (*yan yi*) and the two characters "according to the sub-commentary" (*su shu*)—along with the preceding seven characters—constitute the "explicandum," namely the sub-commentary (*su shu*) such as the *Sui yan chao*.

The four characters "néngshì" (能釋) and "chāo" (鈔) correspond to the two characters "suíshū" (隨疏): "néngshì" refers to the explanatory text as the means of expression (*nèngquán wén*) that follows what it follows (*suísuǒsuí duì*).

Third, the two characters "yǎnyì" (演義) refer to the commentator’s (*chāojiā*) expression of the meaning explained by the sub-commentator (*shūjiā*); this is the correspondence between the expressive (*nèngyǎn*) and the expressed (*suǒyǎn*).
Fourth, the two characters "suíshū" correspond to the two characters "yǎnyì," forming the pair "following the text and expounding the meaning" (*suíwén yǎnyì*).

Regarding the four characters "five upper" (五上), "use" (用) constitutes their function and "copy" (鈔) constitutes their essence; this is one pair of essence and function. Regarding the character "six volumes" (六卷), it is the supported in relation to what precedes it, and "supported" (能依) is the support; this is another pair. Regarding the first [character], it is the recorded in relation to what precedes it, and "recorder" (能記) is the record;

this is another pair. Furthermore, regarding the two characters "with preface" (并序), they are the "preface" (序) in relation to the title above; this is the pair of the "prefacer" (能序) and the "prefaced" (所序). As for the subsequent "explanation" (解釋): The five characters "five upper" constitute the function, while "copy" constitutes the essence; this forms the pair of essence and function. The term "six volumes," in relation to what precedes it, is the supported, and [the preceding] is the support; this forms another pair. The first [character], in relation to what precedes it, is the recorded, and [the preceding] is the recorder;

this forms another pair. Furthermore, the two characters "with preface" are the preface in relation to the title above; this forms the pair of the preface-giver and the preface-received. As for the subsequent "explanation":

There are three parts: first, the explanation of the meaning; second, the sixfold classification; and third, the questions and answers. Regarding the first, the explanation of the meaning: "sui" (following) means to accord with, which is the sense of non-contradiction;
"shu" (commentary) refers to the explanatory text, meaning it does not contradict the text of the sūtra; "yan" (elaboration) means to flow forth and open up the meaning;
"yi" (meaning/principle) refers to the doctrinal principles that are explicated by the sūtra and its commentary; and "chao" (abridgment/extract) means to extract and abridge what was incomplete.

The meaning of this [title] summarizes the following intent: by following the original commentary (*shu*) and adding words of explanation, it causes the profound meaning of the sutra and its commentary to flow forth and be opened up.
This work abridges what is redundant, supplements what is missing, corrects what is erroneous, and extracts the essentials;

therefore, it is called the *Suishu Yanyi Chao* (Commentary on the Meaning Following the Commentary). Other meanings should be understood accordingly. Regarding the "two-fold combination" (*lianghe*) method of explanation: first, the direct correspondence...

The *nominative-locative* (upapada) compound is used because the name is established by taking the "explanatory" (*vyākhyā*) from the commentary that explains [the sūtra], and the "subject" (*kartṛ*) from the sūtra that is explained.

Regarding the second pair, "according to the name" (*anuvyākhyāna*) means following the commentary; "following the name" (*anuvyākhyāna*) thus follows the basis of the holder, employing both the *agentive* (*kartṛ*) and *objective* (*karman*) interpretations respectively.
Regarding the third pair, "expounding" (*vyākhyāna*) refers to the act of expounding the meaning; "that which is expounded" (*vyākhyeya*) refers to the object.

The name "Yanyi" (Explication of the Meaning) is so called because it expounds upon the two commentaries; this is also the case for the fourth pair, which provides a divergent interpretation because it differs from the *Suwen* (Following the Text).

Regarding the fifth pair, one may apply either a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound or a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound with a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*), because both functions share the same substratum, namely the body of the *Chao* (Excerpts).
Alternatively, it may be understood as a general and specific *tatpuruṣa*, wherein the character "chao" applies universally to all [the texts].

The *Chao* (Commentary) distinguishes itself by elaborating upon the meanings of the *Shu* (Sub-commentary); thus, the remaining three pairs of explanations may be inferred according to the preceding principles. Question:
Why does the *Shu* correspond to the *lun* (treatise) and the *Chao* correspond to the meaning (*yi*), yet they cannot be mutually interchanged? Answer:

The *Shu* concerns the expressive medium (*neng-quan*), whereas the *Chao* merely follows along with the meaning (*yi*) as the expressed content (*suo-quan*). Since the *Chao* must expound and chant [the meaning], it corresponds to the meaning.

Question: It is not for the sake of mutual correspondence. According to the conventions of the commentaries (*śāstra*) by various masters, the word "commentary" (*shū*) should be placed beneath the title of the scripture, and below that word "commentary," the number of the sub-commentary (*chō*) should be established. Why is it not done so here? Answer:

Because within the title of the sub-commentary itself, the word "commentary" already exists, which serves as a reference to the title of the commentary. If the word "commentary" were added once more above, [it would be redundant].
In the title, there are two characters for "commentary" (shū); as the text repeats them, it lacks the ingenuity required for establishing a formal name.

Now, with only the single character "commentary," the subtlety of the name being established through its dual correspondence with the two titles above and below is truly present here. This concludes the explanation of the title of the *Śāstra-ṭīkā*.
The preceding four sections, which provided separate explanations of the title of the *Dharma*, are now complete.

Next, regarding the general explanation of the title, "Commentary on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan at Mount Qingliang’s Great Huayan Monastery," this title is divided into two parts:
the first seven characters refer to the locus (*āśraya*), and the last five characters refer to the person who relies upon it (*āśrita*).
Within the locus, furthermore, the first three characters are the general designation for the locus itself, while the following four characters [specify its particularity].
Regarding the reason for citing both names for the distinct designations of this site, there are two intentions:

first, to cite the mountain so that those from afar may know it, and to cite the monastery so that those nearby may know it; second, because Empress Wu extensively propagated the *Mahāvaipulya* (Huayan) scriptures, she frequently changed the names of Huayan monasteries, and as Xianshou resided there, the name was applied to his dwelling; therefore, the mountain is cited here now to distinguish it [from others].
Regarding this, it is said that the Clear and Cool Mountain (Qingliang Shan) is precisely the Five Terraces (Wutai) of the Yanmen Commandery in Daizhou.
Because ice accumulates year after year and flying snow solidifies even in summer, with never a scorching heat, it is called the Clear and Cool Mountain.
Its peaks rise steeply and are devoid of trees, resembling terraces built of piled earth; thus it is also called the Five Terraces. This is what is referred to in the present sutra.
In the northeast there is a place named Mount Qingliang (*Śītavana*). Furthermore, the *Ratnagarbha-dhāraṇī-sūtra* states:
"After my parinirvāṇa, in the northeastern region of Jambudvīpa, there will be a country named Mahācīna.
In the center of that country is a mountain called the Five Peaks (*Pañcaśīrṣa*), where the youth Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta wanders and resides for the sake of all [beings]."
Regarding the Bodhisattva assembly preaching the Dharma therein, it is further stated in the *Dàcǎo* (Great Digest):
"By departing from [the trigrams] Kǎn and Qián, and attaining the central principle of Kūn and Lién, the eight trigrams are universally assigned to Mount Qīngliáng.
Since Wǔtái is situated near the west, the Eastern Terrace lies between the two trigrams Lién and Kǎn; the Northern Terrace lies between the two trigrams Kǎn and Qián; and the Western Terrace..."
Between the two trigrams Qian and Kun lies the Southern Terrace; between the two trigrams Li and Kan lies the Central Terrace.
Thus, the Central Terrace occupies the most central position among the four trigrams—Li, Kan, Qian, and Kun—and embodies the principle of the Middle Way.
It is further said that this mountain ranges over seven hundred li across several provinces, bordering Mount Heng to the left, connecting Mengjin to the right, and facing northward.
At this remote frontier, the southern reaches embrace the winding waters of the Fen River; it harbors the sun and moon and stores the clouds and dragons.
Though the accumulated snow brings bitter cold, ten thousand species of famous flowers flourish; though the freezing winds are fierce and violent, a thousand varieties of auspicious grasses thrive.

It is even said that when white clouds gather and spread, they surpass the clarity of the Yangtze River for ten thousand *li*, and when the bright sun is about to rise, one beholds a great ocean three feet deep.
Regarding what is called the Great Huayan Monastery, it is the ancient Dafu Lingjiu. According to the *Gantong zhuan*, when Nanshan asked a celestial deity, [the deity] replied:
"Thirty li southeast of Mount Wutai, there currently exists the Dafu Lingjiu Monastery;
the ruins of its two halls still remain. To the south is a flower garden about two *qǐng* in area, which displays its splendor throughout the four seasons."
No one has investigated this thoroughly; some say it was established by Emperor Ming of the Han, while others claim it was built by Emperor Wen of Wei—these accounts differ.
How is this so? Tian replied: "Both emperors were responsible for its creation. During the time of King Mu of Zhou, the Buddha-dharma already existed.
This mountain is numinous and extraordinary, being the dwelling place of Mañjuśrī. King Mu of Zhou constructed a monastery there to make offerings."

King Aśoka likewise established stupas there. At the beginning of the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, the monk Kāśyapa Mātanga, possessing the divine eye, also saw that there were stupas there.
He requested the Emperor to establish a monastery; because the shape of the mountain resembled Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa), it was named Dafu Lingjiu. "Fu" means vast faith.
The Emperor, believing in the principles of the Buddha, established the monastery and encouraged others [to do so]; the flower garden was located before and behind the monastery.
The Sovereign subsequently renamed it Da Huayuan Temple. The *Zhulin ji* states:
"From the beginning of spring until the end of autumn, various extraordinary flowers bloom in succession, their radiance dazzling the eyes of men. On all four sides, there are groves of trees;
because the flowers are so wondrous, they cannot be transplanted elsewhere, nor can they grow once moved outside the grove. This continued until the time of Empress Wu Zetian.
While the Tripitaka Master from Khotan was translating the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he saw that the Bodhisattva resided on Mount Qingliang;

consequently, the name was changed to the "Great Avataṃsaka" [Sūtra]. As for the "Si" (Temple/Office), it refers to a department. The Son of Heaven established nine departments to appoint the Nine Ministers: first, the Taichang Si, which presides over rites and music;
second, the Zongzheng Si, which presides over the kinship relations of the six classes of relatives and the ancestral order of *shaomu*; third, the Dali Si, which presides over criminal justice.

1. The Yù (Prison) oversees the four *Guānglùsì* (Court of Imperial Entertainers), primarily managing culinary provisions; 2. The Wǔ (Five) oversees the *Sīnóngsì* (Ministry of Agriculture), primarily managing granaries and stores; 3. The Liù (Six) oversees the *Dàfǔsì* (Grand Treasury), primarily managing the standardization of prices; 4.

The Qī (Seven) oversees the *Tàipúsì* (Court of the Imperial Stables), primarily managing carriages and litters; 5. The Bā (Eight) oversees the *Wèiwěisì* (Court of the Imperial Guard), primarily managing weapons and equipment;

6. The Jiǔ (Nine) oversees the *Hónglúsì* (Court of State Ceremonial), primarily managing foreign guests. All envoys from foreign regions are accommodated within this court during the reign of Emperor Míng of the Hàn dynasty.
At that time, the Emperor [Huan of the Later Han] received the two masters, Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna, who were Tripitaka masters newly arrived in this land;
he had them descend at the An Commandery. Thereafter, the monasteries where the monks resided were named after it.

Next, regarding the person who relies [on the Dharma], the two characters "Shamen" (Sāman) are the general designation for a son of the Śākya. In the Sanskrit language, it is fully called *śramaṇa*, which here means "one who has stilled evil."

The *Yingjing* (Corresponding Sūtra) states: "Among all dharmas, causes and conditions are empty and without a master; because one quiets the mind and realizes the fundamental source, one is called a śramaṇa.
Furthermore, there are four types of śramaṇas: first, the śramaṇa who excels in the Path; second, the śramaṇa who lives by the Path;

third, the śramaṇa who demonstrates the Path; and fourth, the śramaṇa who defiles the Path. Their meanings are as explained in a separate chapter. However, the Master of the present commentary, based on...

Speaking from the perspective of the fundamental, he is the *vīrya-mārga-śramaṇa* (the śramaṇa of the supreme path); discussing it from the perspective of the traces, he is the *darśana-mārga-śramaṇa* (the śramaṇa who demonstrates the path).
The two characters "Chéngguān" are the master’s honorary title: "Chéng" signifies concentration (*samādhi*), and "Guān" signifies wisdom (*prajñā*).

This represents that the Upādhyāya cultivated both concentration and wisdom in tandem; as recorded in the *Miaojue Ta Ji* (Record of the Miaojue Stūpa), his Dharma name was Chéngguān and his courtesy name was Dà.

Tanyi’s secular surname was Xiahou, and he was a native of Kuaiji in Yuezhou. A spiritual being conceived within the Dharma-realm, he was born into the lineage of Emperor Yu according to the conditions of his time, as naturally as a pearl is cleaved from its shell.

Possessing profound insight that reached into neighboring rooms, even in his childhood he would hasten to the courtyard when his father taught him the "Poem of the Sixth Month," which begins with the lines, "It is truly awe-inspiring;
one must be reverent. Whenever he played as a child, he would gather sand to build stupas, or else he would offer admonitions.
"Regarding this, you gather sand; how can you avoid being stained by dust and defilement? He then bowed respectfully and replied, "Sand has no inherent nature;
it is gathered from the True (zhen). How could the True be stained? My former habits have been awakened.

At the age of nine, he took the Master Tizhen of Bolin Monastery in his native prefecture as his preceptor. After one year had passed, his understanding of the Tripiṭaka was thorough. By the time he reached ten...
Having received the grace of ordination, he donned the robes of a farmer and contemplated the profound principles of the Way;
he then lectured on fourteen sutras, including the *Prajñāpāramitā*, *Nirvāṇa*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Vimalakīrti*, and *Awakening of Faith*;

and nine treatises, including the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha*, *Yogācārabhūmi*, *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, *Abhidharmakośa*, *Madhyamakaśāstra*, *Śataśāstra*, *Hetuvidyā*, and *Tattvasaṃgraha*. Upon reaching the age for full ordination, he entered the gate of the Great Master Tanyue.

Later, while residing at Nanshan, he lectured on the Vinaya-piṭaka. Furthermore, he paid homage to Chan Master Changzhao, received the Bodhisattva precepts, and from beginning to end fulfilled his ten vows.
His physical appearance did not violate the outward marks of a śramaṇa; his mind did not contravene the regulations of the Tathāgata;
his sitting was never turned away from the sūtras of the Dharma-realm; and his nature remained unstained by the obstructions of worldly passions.
His feet did not tread the dust of a nun’s temple; his ribs did not touch the couch of a layman; his eyes did not gaze upon colors that were improper;
his tongue did not taste delicacies served after noon; his hands did not let go of the perfectly clear pearl; and he never stayed overnight apart from his robes and bowl.
Thus he attended the Great Master Wuming, received his seal of approval, and attained the free and sovereign enjoyment of profound stillness.
He then said: "Illumination clarifies the obscure, and the Dharma penetrates delusion. Thus, a thousand gates reflect one another and ten thousand phenomena are harmonized;
vast and all-encompassing, it contains every artifice within the entire *dharmadhātu*. Only the Great *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra relies upon this.

Having heard and received the profound purport from the Venerable Daocun at the Eastern Capital, I attained sudden awakening through my sharp faculties. After two cycles [of study], I was able to expound it. Daocun said: 'The *dharmadhātu* is complete.'"

It is with you. ▲ Upon arriving at his residence, he examined the text of the "Chapter on Dwelling" and observed that Mañjuśrī’s contemplation of the five peaks was such that one would not travel even ten thousand *li* to entrust one's life to it (the *Dachao* states:

"Although the journey was five thousand *li*, the round trip amounted to ten thousand; at that time, rebellious bandits disrupted the regular order and the blades of war rose up like thorns, yet he traveled without hesitation, hence the phrase 'entrusting one's life'").
He took refuge in this sacred realm for a succession of ten years, hanging his staff at the mountain gate of the Great Avataṃsaka Monastery. True.

At the earnest request of his companions to propagate [the teachings], he then reflected that the sages of the Five Stages dwell within the realm of the Buddha and have realized True Suchness (*tathatā*) in their minds;
yet, through their subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), they give rise to conventional minds to study worldly understanding.

Thus, he turned back to examine the *Shi* and *Li*, the transmitted classics, the prophetic diagrams, the *Daode jing*, allegories, the Four Categories, the Ten Wings, the various schools of thought tracing back to the *Zhouyi*, the writings of the Masters, and the Chinese classics.

The ancient teachings of Xia, the Sanskrit scripts of Central India, the various divergent doctrines, the four Vedas and five sciences, the esoteric and exoteric ritual manuals, and the calligraphic styles of the two kings—all were brilliantly clarified and dissolved like ice.
Thereupon, within the Prajñā Hall, he inaugurated a maṇḍala and engaged in leisurely contemplation, praying for divine protection;
in a dream, a golden image emerged, towering and majestic like a mountain, its *ūrṇā-kośa* (tuft of hair) as full as the moon.
Standing upright in mid-air while still within his sleep, he held [the brush] to his face; upon awakening, after a long time, he finally let the great pen fall, as if by divine inspiration.
In this month, he established an *amogha-pūjā* (unobstructed offering) to celebrate it.

Just as the memorial was completed and about to be promulgated, he suddenly dreamed that he had become a dragon’s head, resting its neck upon the Southern Terrace while its tail coiled around the Northern Terrace, its scales and mane shining through the sky with a brilliance surpassing the bright sun.
In an instant, he manifested as many dragons through his vigorous spiritual power and departed, a portent of the future dissemination [of the teachings].

Subsequently, he composed the *Sui shu yan yi chao* (Commentary on the Meaning Following the Commentary) in forty fascicles, the *Sui wen shou jing* (Hand Mirror Following the Text) in one hundred fascicles, the *Huayan gangyao* (Essentials of the Avatamsaka) in three fascicles, the *Fajie guan xuanjing* (Mysterious Mirror of the Contemplation of the Dharma Realm) in one fascicle, the *San sheng yuanrong guan* (Contemplation on the Perfect Interfusion of the Three Sages) in one fascicle, and the *Huayan yuan*... [text fragment].
The *Jue si fen zhong guan deng lun guan mai* (A Treatise on the Pulse of the Fourfold Contemplation and Madhyamaka) in thirty-odd fascicles;

the *Qi chu jiu hui hua zang shi jie tu xin jing shuo wen* (The Heart-Mirror Exposition of the Diagram of the Flower Treasury World in Seven Locations and Nine Assemblies) in ten fascicles; the *Da jing liao yi bei yao* (Essentials of the Definitive Meaning of the Great Sūtra) in three fascicles;

and the *Qi sheng jiang dan jie dui yu jiang jing tan lun wen jian yi jia shu shi biao jian zhang zong* (Collected Essays, Poems, Petitions, and Memorials for Imperial Lectures on the Festival of the Seven Sages’ Births).
In more than eighty fascicles, he later received an imperial edict from Emperor Dezong to translate the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (Hua-yen) supplement presented by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā.
Once the translation was completed, the Emperor requested that he lecture upon it. After the lecture, the Emperor remarked, "Truly profound these words;

subtle yet manifest," and subsequently bestowed upon him purple robes and a square cassock, while also honoring him with the title of Professor Upādhyāya. By imperial decree, he composed [the following]:

The ten scrolls of the commentary were presented during the festival celebrating the Sage’s birth; the Emperor granted him a palanquin to escort him into the inner palace, where they discussed the Dharma.

The Emperor commanded that the new sutras be extensively expounded, the essential purport of which was: "How great is the True Realm! It is the source from which the myriad dharmas arise... (and so forth).

At that time, the Emperor sat in silent, profound stillness like the ocean-seal samādhi, his great awakening radiant and clear. He cautioned his ministers, saying: "The words of my Teacher are elegant and concise."
"Your mastery is profound and rich; you have fanned the true wind within the Heaven of the First Principle (*paramārtha*). You are able to cool my imperial heart with the Holy Dharma;

I shall therefore confer upon you the title 'Master of the Cool Grove' (*Qīngliáng Guōshī*). At that time, the high ministers of both the inner and outer courts all received the Eight Precepts from him as their teacher.
Later, he responded to Emperor Shunzong’s inquiry on the meaning of the scriptures at Xingtang Monastery.

He constructed the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-vimāna*) and the Flower Garland (*Avataṃsaka*) Pavilion, and modeled the *Avataṃsaka* illustrations depicting the sequence of the Dharma-realm Assembly (*Dharmadhātu-saṃnipāta*).

Subsequently, in response to Emperor Xianzong’s request for a golden seal as the "Emperor of the Dharma-realm" (*Fajie Di*), he was promoted to State Preceptor (*Guoshi*) with authority over all monastics under heaven.

Emperors Muzong and Jingzong, moved by his immense merit, both conferred upon him the title of Great Illumination State Preceptor (*Da Zhao Guoshi*). This occurred in the twenty-sixth year of the Kaiyuan era, the Wu year.

Born in the Year of the Tiger (738), he left the household life in the Wuzi year (748) during the reign of Emperor Xuanzong. In the Dingyou year of the Zhide era (767) under Emperor Suzong, he received the mind-seal precepts.

In the Wushen year of the Dali era (768) under Emperor Daizong, he was summoned by imperial decree to enter the palace to serve as the "Great Virtuous One for Polishing the Text" while the Tripitaka Master Bianzheng translated the scriptures.
In the Jiazi year of the first year of the Xingyuan era (764), he composed a commentary; [the text continues] in the Ding... year of the Zhenyuan era.
In the year of the Hare (Mao), his work was completed; in the Bingzi year of the Zhenyuan era, he was granted the purple robe for translating scriptures;

in the Jiyi year, he was conferred the title of National Teacher of Qingliang; in the fifth year of Yuanyou of Emperor Xianzong’s reign, the Gengyin year, he was granted the seal of the Head of the Sangha (Sengtong);
and in the Xinchou year of the Dahuang era of Emperor Wenzong, the Emperor transmitted the Mind-Seal to him. This continued until the third month of spring in the Jiwu year of the Kaicheng era.

On the morning of the sixth day, he issued an imperial decree appointing his foremost disciples—the head seats of the Three Teachings, including the Great Master Baoyin Hai'an—to receive the transmission of the Dharma and entrustments;
having completed these, he passed away. Throughout nine successive dynasties, he served as the gate-teacher for seven emperors (Daizong, Dezong, Shunzong, Xianzong, Muzong, Jingzong, and Wenzong).
His secular age was one hundred and two, his monastic seniority eighty-three, and his stature nine chi and four cun.
His hands hung down past his knees; his eyes emitted light at night and did not blink during the day. His speech was refined and elegant, and his conduct served as a model for others.

He was learned in the nine schools of thought and possessed the talent of two scribes. Of his writings that have been transmitted to the present day, there are more than four hundred fascicles in total.

He maintained the practice of eating only once a day throughout his life. He lectured on the *Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* fifty times from beginning to end and presided over ten *asaṃvara* (unrestricted) great assemblies.
There were thirty-eight disciples who served as teachers for others, with Hai-an Jiguang at their head;
they received a thousand students in total. Only Sengrui of the Eastern Capital and Zongmi of Mount Gui alone attained its profound mysteries;
the rest came with empty hearts and departed with full bellies. After twenty-one days had passed, his countenance became increasingly radiant and refined.

The solemnity of his person was the power of his own realization on Mount Yue. On the twenty-seventh day of that month, he reverently received the final instructions and his entire remains were enshrined in a stone chamber on Mount Zhongnan.
The Emperor suspended court affairs, and high officials wore white mourning garments; the rest may be inferred from this.
During the first year of mourning, a Buddhist monk from the Western Regions saw two messengers walking along the Pamir Mountains.
He stepped upon the empty ground and, having halted [the procession] with a mantra, interrogated him, saying: "I am the deity of the Mañjuśrī Hall in North India.
I came to the Eastern Land to obtain the great tooth of the Avataṃsaka Bodhisattva for veneration. When he reached the stone chamber and opened it to verify this, there was indeed no great tooth;
instead, there were thirty-nine [teeth], brilliant as frost. He then cremated the sacred remains and obtained the *śarīra*.
The seeds are several thousand in number, bright, white, and lustrous; the tongue is red like a lotus and cannot be altered by fire (the preceding portion is an excerpt from the text).
Furthermore, the accounts recorded in the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan* (Great Tang Biographies of Eminent Monks) by the monastic head Zan Ning contain many errors and should not be cited at length.
This [work] is a compilation by the author; having gathered and recorded various texts, he has composed these chapters and sentences to explain them.

Because it is based upon [the original], it is called a *zhuàn* (compilation); the phrase "based upon" (*yǒuběn*) in the original text means "to recount" (*shù*). This likely refers to the meaning of "recounting rather than creating.

The *Yueli* states: "Those who know the essence of ritual and music are able to create; those who recognize the patterns of ritual and music are able to recount. The creator is called a sage; the recorder is called enlightened.
The above is an analytical explanation. As for a synthetic interpretation: "Clear" (*qīng*).
Regarding the name "Qingliangshan Dahuayan Monastery," it may be explained through the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) or *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) compounds, or as a combination of both.

First, if the mountain possesses the quality of "coolness" (*qingliang*) and the monastery was revived there by means of the *Avataṃsaka* (*huayan*), then the names are respectively interpreted as *karmadhāraya* (appositional) and *bahuvrīhi* (possessive).
Alternatively, since the sutra reveals that the dwelling place of the Bodhisattva is at Qingliang, and the monastery is situated upon that mountain, [the name is derived accordingly].
Regarding those who take "Huayan" as their name, these are "adjunct-releasing" (linjin shi) compounds;
furthermore, both "the śramaṇa of Da Huayan Temple on Mount Qingliang" and "Da Huayan Temple" itself are "possessive" (yizhu) compounds, consisting of both general and specific terms.
"The śramaṇa of Da Huayan Temple on Mount Qingliang" refers to the śramaṇa Chengguan; "the śramaṇa Chengguan" refers to the one who composed the *Chengguan*.
Observing the two commentaries, it appears that both contain individual titles for each section within the *Wenke* (Outline of Questions), *Sushu* (Sub-commentary), and *Caoshu* (Explanatory Notes).
Why, then, do you now explain only one title? Answer: Although there are three titles, they refer to no different person;
therefore, by explaining them in one place, the other two are clarified comprehensively without the need for redundant or confusing elaboration. The explanation of the title is concluded.

Regarding the subsequent difficult points in the commentary on the text, we first explain the preface to the *Chao*. The phrase "The Sage transmitted his instructions to mirror the profound ultimate of the One Mind" reveals that the Tathāgata preached the sutras. This explanation is divided into three parts: first, listing the correspondences; second, interpreting the text; and third, clarifying the five teachings. Regarding the first two sections of the ten items in the preface: 1. The title of the work. 2. The author of the work. 3. The purpose for which the work was composed. 4. The reason for composing the work. 5. The name of the person who requested the composition. 6. The place where the work was composed. 7. The date of composition. 8. The number of fascicles. 9. The source from which the work was derived. 10. The lineage of transmission. First, regarding the title of the work: it is called the *Commentary on the Meaning of the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* (*Weimojie jing yishu chao*). "Vimalakīrti" is the name of the person; "nirdeśa" means "explanation" or "instruction"; "sūtra" refers to the scripture; "yi" means "meaning"; "shu" means "commentary"; and "chao" means "extract" or "abridgment. Thus, the title signifies an abridged commentary on the meaning of the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*. Second, regarding the author of the work: he is the Great Master Zhiyi of the Tiantai school. "Tiantai" is the name of the mountain; "Great Master" is a respectful title for one who has attained the Way; "Zhiyi" is his personal name. He is called a "Great Master" because he was a man of great virtue and wisdom who served as a teacher to the world. Third, regarding the purpose for which the work was composed: it is to clarify the profound and subtle meaning of the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, so that practitioners may understand its essential principles and thereby attain liberation from birth and death.

Fourth, regarding the reason for composing the work: although the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* is a profound teaching, its meaning is vast and difficult to fathom. Fearing that later generations might find it hard to penetrate, the Master composed this commentary to provide a guide for their study and practice. Fifth, regarding the person who requested the composition: it was the monk Huiguan, a disciple of the Master, who respectfully entreated him to write this work. Sixth, regarding the place where the work was composed: it was written at Mount Tiantai, a place of serene seclusion and spiritual cultivation. Seventh, regarding the date of composition: it was completed during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. Eighth, regarding the number of fascicles: the work consists of ten fascicles. Ninth, regarding the source from which the work was derived: the Master relied upon the original text of the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* and various commentaries by past sages to extract the essential meanings. Tenth, regarding the lineage of transmission: the Master received the Dharma directly from the Buddha through the lineage of patriarchs, ensuring that the true essence of the teaching was preserved and passed down. Thus concludes the explanation of the first two items of the ten matters in the preface.

1. The pair of "person" and "dharma": "this person" refers to the Most Holy One (the Buddha), while all else is dharma. 2. The pair of "dharma" and "meaning": "the promulgation of the teachings" is dharma;

"the single mind and so forth" is meaning. 3. The pair of "general" and "particular": "the single mind" is general; "the profound ultimate" is particular. 4. The pair of "dharma" and "analogy": the character for "mirror" is the analogy;
the promulgation of the teachings is the dharma. 5. The pair of "discernment" and "retention": the character for "most" (*zhi*) can discern the holy one.
"Characters" (*zi*) are able to sustain [the meaning]; "to eliminate" (*xiao*) refers to the written text; "to reach" (*zhi*) means the ultimate; "sage" (*sheng*) means correctness.

Although those from the stage of seeing the Path onward are called "sages," only upon reaching the fruit of Buddhahood are they termed "Supreme Sages. "To hang down" (*chui*) means to spread; "proclamation" (*gao*) refers to the canonical proclamations.

As the *Book of Documents* says, "Canons, Narratives, Instructions, and Proclamations"—these are all specific designations for the scriptural proclamations. "Mirror" (*jing*) is a metaphor for the aforementioned word "proclamation"; "Dharma" (*fa*) refers to the canon.
The *Gao* (Proclamation) clearly demonstrates that the one mind reflects the subtle and profound ultimate; it is like the "Qin mirror," which is so luminous that it illuminates the human heart.

Thus, Zhu Kai’s poem states: "In the Western Kingdoms there is the Qin mirror, its radiance rare in this world; it reveals the liver and gall of those who look into it, and when examining objects, it penetrates the most obscure and minute.
We now take precisely this as our basis; hence the subsequent commentary says: "Using the holy teachings as a bright mirror for illumination."
Seeing that one’s own mind and others are neither two nor three—this so-called "one" is the solid, numinous clarity; this is called the "mystery" (*xuan*), meaning profound and subtle;

and the "ultimate" (*ji*), meaning the most supreme limit. The intent is to say: our Buddha, the World-Honored One, disseminated the teachings like a bright mirror to clearly discern the naturally abiding principle of profound mystery and ultimate supremacy within the single mind.
Regarding the clarification of the five and three teachings: first is the *Hīnayāna* (Small Teaching).

"Ultimate" (*zhì*) refers to the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); "sage" (*shèng*) refers to the wisdom of the emptiness of persons. Having severed the fetters beneath the Bodhi tree and attained Buddhahood, he is called the Ultimate Sage (*zhìshèng*).
"To bestow" (*chuí*) means to establish or to lead; it refers to the provisional establishment of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) teachings to lead those of the two vehicles.

"Scriptures" (*gào*) refers to the *Āgamas*, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, and others. "One mind" (*yīxīn*) is a provisional designation for "one mind," meaning that external dharmas are [mistakenly] held to exist substantially due to the mind.

Transformation is not entirely mind (meaning that although mundane and supramundane phenomena—whether defiled or pure—are produced by the mind and induced by karma, they undergo change and movement and are therefore not identical to the mind itself). Second, regarding the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*):
"Reaching" refers to the principle of the two-fold emptiness; "Sage" refers to the wisdom of the two-fold emptiness.

One who attains perfect enlightenment at the peak of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven is called a "Supreme Sage. "To descend" means to teach or to awaken. From within fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), subsequent wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) flows forth.

Having attained subsequently-attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), one gives rise to great compassion and proclaims [the Dharma] for the sake of sentient beings, causing those of the two vehicles to realize *vijñapti-mātratā*.
Thus, the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, *Laṅkāvatāra*, and other sūtras speak of "one mind," which refers to the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*). However, there are three categories:

first, when both the aspect (*nimitta*) and the seeing (*darśana*) exist together, it is called "one mind"; second, when the aspect is subsumed back into the seeing, it is called "one mind"; third, when the object (*grāhya*) is subsumed...

"Returning to the King" refers to the name "Ultimate Profundity of One-Mindedness": "Profound" (*xuan*) signifies fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), and "Ultimate" (*ji*) signifies the principle of the two-fold emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Third, the "Final Teaching" (*zhōngjiào*): "Ultimate" (*zhì*) refers to the principle of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-parāvṛtti*), and "Sage" (*shèng*) refers to the wisdom of initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*);

the non-duality of the initial and the original is called "Ultimate Sage. "To bestow" (*chuí*) means to grant or to manifest. Because the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) manifests the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*dharmatā-dharma*), it is called a "Decree" (*gào*), which is the Dharma itself.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and other scriptures speak of "one mind. This refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is named "one mind. This also has two aspects:
first, subsuming the branches back into the root (subsuming the first seven consciousnesses into the eighth); second, subsuming both the defiled and the pure into the *tathāgatagarbha*.

"Quiescence and illumination" refers to naming the union of the true and the false as "one mind"; "pointing to the mystery" refers to naming the non-duality of the true and the false as "one mind. Each of these is exclusively...

This constitutes one meaning. That which is called the "Ultimate Mystery" (xuánjí) refers to the two types of awakening: original awakening (*ādikṣānti-bodhi*) and initial awakening (*prathama-bodhi*).

Regarding the four sudden teachings (*sudden-vehicle teachings*): "Ultimate" (*zhì*) refers to the principle that transcends all principles; "Sage" (*shèng*) refers to the wisdom that transcends all wisdom. Because there is neither Buddha nor non-Buddha, it is named the "Ultimate Sage. "Transmitting" (*chuí*) means to pass on or to manifest.

The "Single Transmission of the Mind-Seal" (*xīnyìn*) manifests the principle of absolute transcendence (*juédài*). Therefore, "proclamation" (*gào*) refers to the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

The *Yi* (Benefit) and other sutras state that "one mind" refers to the merging and cessation of defilement and purity; this is called one mind. Ultimate wisdom that transcends all dependencies is termed "mysterious transcendence," and the principle that transcends all dependencies is termed "the ultimate.
The fivefold Perfect Teaching (*pañca-paryāya-yāna*) refers to the ultimate, which is the principle of non-obstruction, and the sage, which is non-obstructive wisdom.
The "ten bodies" are the unobstructed clouds of bodies, termed the "ultimate sage. "To hang down" (*chui*) means to spread, to bestow, and to settle; it signifies universal penetration.
The discourse on the "Directions" (*fang*) is spread throughout the Dharma-realm because it establishes the fourfold meaning of the Dharma-realm.
This is precisely what the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* refers to when it speaks of "the one mind," which is the unobstructed one mind. This also has three aspects:

the mutual inclusion of phenomena (*shì*), the mutual identity of phenomena (*shì*), and the inexhaustible net of Indra (*dìwǎng*). (The above five teachings encompass ten kinds of one mind, as explained in the *Xingyuan Chao* and other texts. It is called "the profound ultimate" (*xuánjí*).
This also refers to the wisdom and principle that are free from obstruction.
Regarding the Great Master’s extensive elucidation of the profound subtleties of these illuminating words, it is the Bodhisattva who composed the treatise. The commentary is divided into four parts:

first, the enumeration of correspondences; second, the explanation of the text; third, the classification according to the three teachings; and fourth, the reconciliation of other ritual protocols. These two lines constitute the introduction.
The text also consists of ten items in five pairs: 1. The pair of person and dharma: "a person" refers to the Great Being (Mahāsattva), while "the propagation and elucidation" refers to the Dharma.

2. The pair of sūtra and śāstra: some say this is the pair of root and branch; "subtle words" refers to the sūtra, while "propagation and elucidation" constitutes the śāstra. 3. The pair of teaching and meaning:

"subtle words" refers to the teaching, while "profound significance" refers to the meaning. 4. The pair of dharma and metaphor: "propagation and elucidation" is the Dharma, while the character "candle" (zhù) is the metaphor.

Regarding the five points concerning the selection (*viveka*) and maintenance (*dhāraṇa*) of the "Great" (*mahat*): first, as for the capacity to select and the capacity to maintain, the term "person" (*puruṣa*) refers to those capable of these two functions. Second, regarding the explanation of the text:

"person" (*puruṣa*) generally denotes human beings, yet there are four distinct types—ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), superior persons (*uttama-puruṣa*), great persons (*mahā-puruṣa*), and the unsurpassed person (*anuttara-puruṣa*).

Ordinary beings are merely called "persons"; those of the Two Vehicles are called "superior persons"; Bodhisattvas are called "great persons"; and Buddhas are titled "unsurpassed persons. Here, by selecting [the Bodhisattva] over the other three, they are termed "Great."

The scholar, following the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, explains that there are ten meanings of a "Great Being" (*mahāsattva*): first, relying on the Mahāyāna teachings; second, giving rise to great faith; third, formulating great vows;
fourth, fully practicing the great deeds; fifth, traversing the great stages; sixth, giving rise to great wisdom; seventh, severing great delusions;
eighth, perfectly realizing the Great Principle; ninth, attaining the great fruit; and tenth, delivering great sentient beings. This is the general characteristic.

As for the term "Mahāsattva" (Great Being), it is said that one is so named because they rely on the Great Teaching (*mahāśāsana*), generate the Great Resolve (*mahācitta*), practice the Great Conduct (*mahācaryā*), and realize the Great Fruit (*mahāphala*). Question:

If a Mahāsattva refers exclusively to a Bodhisattva, how can this be reconciled with the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) teachings? Answer: Many treatises of the Lesser Vehicle were composed by Bodhisattvas;
for example, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu—who concealed his solitary brilliance within the *Abhidharmakośa*—composed five hundred treatises on the Lesser Vehicle, among others.
"Is it so? "Yes. "Hong" means to propagate; "chuan" means to expound. "Expound" refers specifically to the various treatises composed by Bodhisattvas.
"Illuminating" is a metaphor for the aforementioned propagation and exposition of these treatises. As a sutra says: "For example, a treasure in the darkness cannot be seen without a lamp;
though the Buddha-dharma exists, if no one explains it, even those with wisdom cannot understand it. Among the sutras of the Dharma, there are no [treatises] by Bodhisattvas."
One cannot perceive its profound subtlety; it is like a treasure in the dark that cannot be seen or grasped without a lamp or candle.

"Subtle words" refers to the scriptures of the imperial edicts bestowed from above; "profound subtlety" means "profound" (*you*) signifies depth, and "subtlety" (*zhi*) signifies the ultimate intent—the meaning elucidated within those aforementioned subtle words.
The intention is that the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva composed this treatise to propagate and expound [the teachings].
This fully illuminates the profound and subtle purports within the Buddha’s sutras.

Regarding the classification of the teachings of the Three and Five [Periods], the "Small Teaching" refers to the profound purports of the six consciousnesses, the three poisons, the seventy-five dharmas, and so forth, as elucidated by great masters such as Vasubandhu and Vasumitra in their commentaries on the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, and the sūtras on dependent origination and the *Āgamas*. This is the Initial Teaching.

This refers to the great bodhisattvas such as Asanga and Vasubandhu, who propagated and elucidated the treatises on Yogācāra and Vijñaptimātra, explaining the profound subtleties of the eight consciousnesses, the ten suchnesses,

and the hundred dharmas within sutras such as the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and the *Laṅkāvatāra*. Regarding the final and sudden teachings, it refers to the great bodhisattvas such as Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna,
who propagated and elucidated the treatises on the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, explaining the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Nirvāṇa* [sutras].

The subtle profundities of the dharmas of defilement and purity— such as the two gates, three greatnesses, and nine characteristics found in the *Banneng* (Vajracchedikā) and other sūtras— are elucidated in the Perfect Teaching (*Yuanjiao*). Furthermore,
the great beings such as Vasubandhu and Nāgārjuna extensively propagated the treatises on the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the *Acintyastava*, and others,
explaining the subtle profundities of the six aspects (*liu xiang*) and ten mysteries (*shi xuan*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
Although this Commentary has forgotten its own conceptual attachments within the realm of the expressed meaning, it nonetheless flows vast and expansive across the ocean of words and principles;

this is to resolve potential obstacles. As for these obstacles: [the text states] "Principle is fundamentally wordless" (referring back to the preceding sections on the bestowing of instructions and their broad elucidation), and "Meaning transcends all boundaries" (referring back to the preceding sections on the single mind and the profound, mysterious ultimate).
The Greatly Awakened Benevolent One and the various Bodhisattvas have, by forgetting discriminative mental states, realized the fruit of truth. Now, furthermore...
Is it appropriate to say that the distinction between the sutras and the treatises lies in their methods of elucidating the meaning? This interpretation—

though the wording of the character "although" (雖) appears to concede the first clause while refuting the second— intends to convey that although Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, within the single true Dharma-realm,

have no mental attachment to the boundaries of the expressed and the expressed meaning, this does not hinder their manifestation through non-conditioned compassion (*nirālamba-karuṇā*) for the sake of living beings.
Those who have not yet awakened find that vast and profuse textual meanings arise like the depth and breadth of the ocean.
The two subsequent lines of the *Chao* (Excerpts) are intended to clarify this point. Question:

Since one has already forgotten the mind within the realm of the expressed meaning (*zhēnzhǐ*), why not forget words to accord with the Way (*dào*), instead of being overwhelmed by textual meanings? Therefore, it is said here: [the meaning is that] the Way...
Fundamentally there is no speech, yet it is not non-speech; how then can the principle be transmitted? Fundamentally there are no forms, yet they are not non-forms; how then can they be manifested?
