Question: If there is no time of cessation, and it is not said that there is a subsequent time, can this be called "eternal"? Question: Since a single sound is expounded all at once, what is the necessity for three periods? Answer:
Although it is possible to expound [the teaching] all at once, it serves to manifest the shallow and deep levels of the Dharma. Question:

If the manifestation of the three stages is sufficient within the seven-day period—specifically the first week—what is the necessity for the ninth week and the five years thereafter? Answer: The three-week period...
Since Śrāvakas such as Śāriputra were unable to manifest the uncommon teaching, it was necessary for them to ask questions at a later time;

yet, if the timing were not perfectly harmonious, how could this accord with the intent of the Sūtra? The answer is that it is precisely because they were harmonized across different times that this assembly was convened.
Regarding the phrase "The Commentary further divides [the teaching] into three periods," the *Sheng Yama-pin Shu* (Commentary on the Chapter on Ascending to the Yāma Heaven) states:

"When [the teaching] follows the proper time, those who hear it are delighted and submit; when it moves [the audience] at the proper time, those who see it revere and follow. Regarding the two preceding sections of the Commentary, they concern the place and the time;
since both are divided into ten [categories], it is said that they provide an "extensive analysis."

Regarding the phrase "those who receive [the teaching] at the inconceivable ocean-like assembly" (*asamkhyeya-sāgara-parṣad*): the first clause refers to that which can transmit the teaching (*neng-bei jiao*), while the commentary categorizes this as "that which is received by the capacity [of the audience]" (*suo-bei ji*).
This is because the "capacity" (*neng*) is used here to designate the "object" (*suo*). As for the second clause, "the assembly" (*hui*) refers to the meaning of gathering;
when many people collect together in one place, it is called an "assembly. Other meanings are as explained in the *Shu-chao*. Question: According to the listing of the various assemblies below...
In the first assembly, there were forty-two groups, or forty-five groups (the forty-nine including those born together, ordinary beings, and the thirty-nine on the lion throne;

plus one group from within the Bodhi tree, the boundless bodhisattvas within the palace, and the newly assembled group from between the eyebrows—totaling forty-five groups). Altogether across the nine assemblies, the total number of groups is one hundred and seventy-five.
Since these can be clearly enumerated, why is it said they are "inconceivable"? The answer is: precisely because of these very groups.

Regarding the phrase "difficult to conceive," the sub-commentary (*śāstra*) states: "These various assemblies may be considered collectively as a single assembly of those belonging to the One Vehicle;
or they may be divided into two, because there are both real assemblies and manifested assemblies; or they may be three, consisting of humans, devas, and asuras;
or they may be four, consisting of Buddhas, bodhisattvas, humans, and non-humans; or five, by distinguishing devas from non-humans; or six, with the addition of..."
Because of animals; or because of the seven divisions of the desire and form realms; or because of the eight divisions as there are both this realm and other realms for Bodhisattvas;
or nine because there are principal and attendant [beings] in other directions; or ten by adding the śrāvakas; or one hundred and seventy-five by adding what was previously mentioned;
or immeasurable and boundless because of the various categories of meaning and types of lands—each of these may be considered in terms of *kṣetra* (buddha-fields).

Because the number of assemblies is as vast as the atoms [of the universe], and because it is like the examples given above regarding the emergence of the Bodhisattvas' hair-light from the new collection, each and every assembly is without limit.

This is still based on their distinct characteristics; however, if they are integrated and absorbed, each single assembly contains all one hundred and seventy-five assemblies, for they exist mutually within one another as an assembly of the Dharma-realm’s dependent origination. Above...

Furthermore, if we consider a single world-system—let alone those that extend throughout the ten directions and across the infinite, inexhaustible nets of Indra within the atoms of various classes of lands—the assembly gathered at the Flower Adornment Sea is truly boundless; from this, one can clearly perceive its inconceivability.

"Macro" (hóng) means "great," which refers to the phenomenal dharma-realm (*shifenjiejie*); "vast" (kuò) means "empty," which refers to the noumenal dharma-realm (*lifenjiejie*); "profound" (yōu) means "deep," which refers to the latter two dharma-realms. Since these four dharma-realms constitute the teachings and doctrines that can be manifested, the preceding [passage] points to their ultimate purport within the realm of the mysterious and subtle. As for the commentary’s reference to Samantabhadra and others: [The text continues: "Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, by virtue of his great vow-power, universally manifests the ocean of all Buddha-lands. Because he has attained the power of the Dharma-realm, he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. He is able to manifest the Buddhas of the ten directions within a single pore; he is able to manifest the lands of the ten directions within a single atom. He is able to manifest the kalpas of the ten directions within a single moment; he is able to manifest the sentient beings of the ten directions within a single body. He is able to manifest the dharmas of the ten directions within a single word; he is able to manifest the practices of the ten directions within a single thought. He is able to manifest the fruits of the ten directions within a single attainment; he is able to manifest the adornments of the ten directions within a single ornament. Thus, he manifests all things without exception. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of phenomena" (*shishi wuai*). It is because he has fully realized the principle of the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena (*shishi wuai*) that he is able to manifest such inconceivable transformations. Furthermore, it is because he has fully realized the principle of the non-obstruction of phenomena with noumena (*shili wuai*) that he is able to manifest the noumenal essence within all phenomena. Moreover, it is because he has fully realized the principle of the non-obstruction of noumena with phenomena (*lishi wuai*) that he is able to manifest all phenomena within the noumenal essence. And it is because he has fully realized the principle of the non-obstruction of noumena with noumena (*lilil wuai*) that he is able to manifest the noumenal essence within the noumenal essence. Therefore, he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of noumena. It is because he has fully realized the principle of the mutual non-obstruction of the fourfold dharma-realm (*sifajie xiangji wuai*) that he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of the fourfold dharma-realm. It is because he has fully realized the principle of the unobstructed interpenetration of the three mysteries (*sanmi wuai*) that he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of the three mysteries. It is because he has fully realized the principle of the unobstructed interpenetration of the three bodies (*sanshen wuai*) that he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of the three bodies. It is because he has fully realized the principle of the unobstructed interpenetration of the three wisdoms (*sanhui wuai*) that he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of the three wisdoms. It is because he has fully realized the principle of the unobstructed interpenetration of the three virtues (*sandao wuai*) that he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of the three virtues. It is because he has fully realized the principle of the unobstructed interpenetration of the three natures (*sanshen wuai*) that he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of the three natures. It is because he has fully realized the principle of the unobstructed interpenetration of the three truths (*sandi wuai*) that he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of the three truths. It is because he has fully realized the principle of the unobstructed interpenetration of the three realms (*sanjie wuai*) that he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of the three realms. It is because he has fully realized the principle of the unobstructed interpenetration of the three times (*sanyi wuai*) that he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of the three times. It is because he has fully realized the principle of the unobstructed interpenetration of the three worlds (*sanyou wuai*) that he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of the three worlds. It is because he has fully realized the principle of the unobstructed interpenetration of the three vehicles (*sanche wuai*) that he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of the three vehicles. It is because he has fully realized the principle of the unobstructed interpenetration of the three bodies of the Buddha (*fosanshen wuai*) that he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of the three bodies of the Buddha. It is because he has fully realized the principle of the unobstructed interpenetration of the three bodies of the patriarchs (*zuzusanshen wuai*) that he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of the three bodies of the patriarchs. It is because he has fully realized the principle of the unobstructed interpenetration of the three bodies of the masters (*shizhusanshen wuai*) that he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of the three bodies of the masters. It is because he has fully realized the principle of the unobstructed interpenetration of the three bodies of the disciples (*tongxuesanshen wuai*) that he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of the three bodies of the disciples. It is because he has fully realized the principle of the unobstructed interpenetration of the three bodies of the practitioners (*xiuxingsanshen wuai*) that he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of the three bodies of the practitioners. It is because he has fully realized the principle of the unobstructed interpenetration of the three bodies of the devotees (*zhongshengsanshen wuai*) that he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of the three bodies of the devotees. It is because he has fully realized the principle of the unobstructed interpenetration of the three bodies of the Buddhas of the ten directions (*shifangfosanshen wuai*) that he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of the three bodies of the Buddhas of the ten directions. It is because he has fully realized the principle of the unobstructed interpenetration of the three bodies of the patriarchs of the ten directions (*shifangzuzusanshen wuai*) that he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of the three bodies of the patriarchs of the ten directions. It is because he has fully realized the principle of the unobstructed interpenetration of the three bodies of the masters of the ten directions (*shifangshizhusanshen wuai*) that he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. This is called the "unobstructed interpenetration of the three bodies of the masters of the ten directions. It is because he has fully realized the principle of the unobstructed interpenetration of the three bodies of the disciples of the ten directions (*shifangtongxuesanshen wuai*) that he is able to manifest all things without obstruction. Question: When preaching the Dharma, do you not intend it to reach those such as Samantabhadra? Answer: The *Chuxian shu* (Commentary on the Manifestation) states:
"That which is called the 'perfect faculty' does not discriminate between ordinary beings and sages; since the Dharma is taken as the teacher, how could it not be that which is reached? Question:

Since the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says, "That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma," would it not follow that Vairocana himself is also one who is reached [by the teaching]? Answer: Vairocana is taken as the teaching itself.
The primary [subject] does not refer to the Buddhas of the ten directions who are questioned, because they are of the same category as Vairocana and thus are not the ones being questioned;
nor does it refer to Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī, for since their path is perfected and they have attained the supreme fruit, how could they be the ones being answered?

Now, considering this from the perspective of the provisional gate (*jimen*), they are the ones being addressed. As the Sūtra says: "Only those who practice as Samantabhadra can enter. This is simply because [the teaching] is excellent.

Regarding the phrase "the wealth and so forth accomplished for the sake of those to be benefited": while [the names of] Samantabhadra and others are somewhat obscure as being among those to be benefited, they are all indeed included therein.

This should be understood as having a mutual relationship of inclusion and omission with the "roots" (faculties) to be benefited mentioned below; for now, we shall simply speak of the assembly gathered at that time. As for the phrase "the number [of them] is as vast as the atoms of many lands":
this may mean either that the number of Bodhisattvas is vast, or that the number of those of superior virtue is vast; thus, it encompasses both meanings.
Regarding the categories of Reality (shin) and Response (ō), Expediency (gon) and Reality (jitsu): "Reality" refers to the true body of the assembly in the ocean [of the Dharma-realm];

"Response" refers to the various types of bodies manifested in response within that ocean-like assembly; "Expediency" refers to the skillful manifestation of the Buddha-fruit as various types of bodies.

Alternatively, "Expediency" corresponds to the aforementioned "Response," and "Reality" corresponds to the aforementioned "Reality. The analogies for mantra are manifold: "Response" corresponds to the aforementioned profound and vast characteristics.
"Seizing the explanation" means that the true [nature] is identical to the responsive [manifestation], and so forth;

furthermore, because there are various categories such as cause and effect, or origin and trace, the statement is "even more inconceivable. It is "even more inconceivable" because the ocean of fruition transcends thought, and these bodhisattvas have already lost even subtle thoughts.
Moreover, it has already thoroughly penetrated the ocean of fruition, yet it does not abandon the gate of the causal stage.

2. the Vajradhara spirits; 3. the body-protecting spirits; 4. the foot-traveling spirits; 5. the altar-of-enlightenment spirits; 6. the city-ruling spirits; 7. the earth-ruling spirits.
8. Lord of Devas; 9. Lord of Mountain Devas; 10. Lord of Forest Devas; 11. Lord of Medicinal Herbs (the above correspond respectively to the ten stages of abiding);
12. Lord of Crops; 13. Lord of Rivers; 14. Lord of the Ocean; 15. Lord of Water;
16. Lord of Fire; 17. Lord of Wind; 18. Lord of Space; 19. Lord of the Directions; 20. Lord of Night.
The Lord of Day (the above ten lines); twenty-first, the Asura King; twenty-second, the Garuḍa King;
twenty-third, the Kiṃnara King; twenty-fourth, the Mahoraga King; twenty-fifth, the Yakṣa King; twenty-sixth, the Nāga King;
twenty-seventh, the Kumbhāṇḍa King; twenty-eighth, the Gandharva King.
19. Human king for twenty-nine months; 20. Heavenly king for thirty days (the above correspond to the ten dedications);
31. King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; 32. King of the Yāma Heaven; 33. King of the Tuṣita Heaven; 34.
King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; 35. King of the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven; 36. King of the Mahābrahmā Heaven.
37. The King of the Heaven of the Thirty-three Light-Sounds; 38. The King of the Heaven of Universal Purity; 39. The King of the Heaven of Vast Results; 40.
The Great Sovereign King (these correspond to the ten stages). 41. The Assembly of the Lion Throne (corresponds to the stage of Equal Enlightenment); 42.

The Assembly of the Space Between the Eyebrows (corresponds to the stage of Sublime Enlightenment). Regarding the phrase "all as numerous as the atoms of a world-system," the Sūtra says: "There are..."
Vajradharas as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field. [The Commentary] explains that this illustrates the light from the Buddha’s mouth which summons [the assembly];

subsequently, it clarifies the extensive manifestation of signs described in the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Multitude," wherein the Buddha’s mouth and its many teeth emit rays of light as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field, illuminating worlds as numerous as the atoms within ten billion Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, and [reaching] the assemblies of Bodhisattvas—one by one Bodhisattva—within those oceans of worlds.
Each of these Bodhisattvas was accompanied by a retinue of Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of worlds.
Within every single pore of the bodies of those Bodhisattvas, there appeared ten world-atom numbers of jewel-lights;

within each of these lights, there further appeared Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of ten worlds (this is the successive manifestation of light from the pores). These Bodhisattvas...
Within every single atom of all the oceans of established realms throughout the entire Dharma-realm (this refers to pervading the atoms of all lands),
there are as many vast buddha-lands as there are atoms in a buddha-field (this refers to the basis of activity). Within each of these vast buddha-lands,
there are the Buddhas of the three periods of time, whom these bodhisattvas are all able to approach, serve, and make offerings to (this is the primary activity).
Since they have already made offerings to all Buddhas of the three periods of time, it is said that these encompass the three temporal dimensions.
Such meanings as these are beyond the contemplation of even great-stage Bodhisattvas; how much less can they be fathomed by ordinary minds?

It may be said that their meaning is profound and difficult to believe, their contemplation difficult to understand, their teaching difficult to expound, and their number extremely difficult to measure. Therefore, they are collectively described as "inconceivable."
Regarding the phrase "the oceanic assembly":

the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* states that each individual utterance pervades the entire realm of sentient beings (this is the meaning of "perfect," or *yuan*), yet its phonetic resonance remains ever-undisturbed and unconfused (this is the meaning of "sound," or *yin*).

If the sound did not pervade, it would not be perfect; if the sound were not uniform in its pervasion, it would not be perfect. Thus, the perfection of the sound lies in its universal penetration while maintaining its distinct character. This is what is meant by the *Commentary* stating that the "perfect sound" is vast and far-reaching, encompassing the ten lands and instantaneously reaching all.

If one loses its melodic cadence, then it is a circle but not a sound; now, without destroying the melody, it is equal and pervasive, and while pervasive it is unmoving, yet its cadence differs—this is the Tathāgata’s perfect sound (pradakṣiṇa-svara), which is not the realm of mental consciousness or discursive thought.
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states that "the text of the sūtra" refers to the very basis upon which the sūtra is expounded.

This is because vocal sounds constitute the basis of the sūtra’s teaching, yet they are not the teaching itself, as the teaching adapts freely to the capacities of sentient beings. Regarding the term "distant," it means that whether heard from afar or near, and regardless of the size [of the assembly], [the sound reaches all].
The *Śāstra* lists twenty [sections] of the sūtra; these are fully enumerated within the "Chapter on the Array of Flowers" (*Puṣpakūṭa-parivarta*), namely: the Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), etc.

The world of transformed forms (the shape of folding and unfolding as one comes and goes); the world of rivers and streams with swirling currents (where water flows and spreads in deep riverbeds and ocean abysses);
the shape of wheel-rims and the shape of altars and cleared grounds (an altar is earth piled up; a cleared ground is earth excavated); the shape of forests and the shape of towers and pavilions;
the shape of the *śīlā-dhvaja* (this refers to "fine jade," meaning a banner made of jade); the universal square shape, the shape of the *garbha*-dhātu, the shape of the lotus, and the *kharaka*.
Regarding "form" (which here is rendered as *zhú*; the *Huáinán zǐ* states that *zhú* and *tún* refer to a vessel made by splitting bamboo that can hold grain):

the forms of sentient beings, the forms of the Buddha’s marks, the form of the circular halo, the form of clouds, the form of nets, the form of gateways (the inner gates), the form of Mount Sumeru, and the form of ornaments.

As for the statement that there are ten buddha-fields for each [form], it is because within the sūtra, for each of these aforementioned forms, ten fields as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field are individually established.
Regarding the statement that there are worlds such as the "Revolving Form" (Pradakṣiṇāvarta) world, numbering as many as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields:

since the Sūtra lists twenty distinct types of worlds, why does the Commentary (Śāstra) speak only of "ten fields"? The Sub-commentary (Cāo) answers: "The ten are cited to manifest their inexhaustibility.
Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the Perfect Sound (Paripūrṇasvara) shall be explained extensively below," this refers to the ten [qualities] within the "Emergence" (Samudgama) Chapter.
The analogy of the proclamation at the end of a kalpa illustrates that the Tathāgata’s voice in preaching the Dharma has no master;
the analogy of the two echoes following conditions illustrates that the Tathāgata’s voice is without arising or ceasing—or, alternatively, that it is without demonstration;

the analogy of the celestial drum awakening beings illustrates that the Tathāgata’s voice is without interruption; and the analogy of the wondrous voices of the four heavenly maidens illustrates... [the same].

1. The Tathāgata’s voice accords with the faculties, faith, and understanding; this is illustrated by the five Brahma-voices and various similes. 2. The Tathāgata’s voice is divided according to the occasion;

this is illustrated by the simile of the six kinds of water having a single taste. 3. The Tathāgata’s voice is free from crookedness; this is illustrated by the simile of rain falling to nourish and flourish growth.

4. The Tathāgata’s voice accords with inclinations and desires; this is illustrated by the simile of gradual descent and maturation. 5. The Tathāgata’s voice is without delay; this is illustrated by the simile of gradual descent and maturation.

1. "Swift Sound" (the ninth): It descends [upon all] and is difficult to conceive; it is illustrated by the analogy of the Tathāgata’s voice, for although there are distinctions, they share a single nature.

2. "Pervasive" (the tenth): It descends upon various [beings]; it is illustrated by the analogy of the Tathāgata’s voice being universal—or as some say, his voice according to the species [of beings].

Furthermore, that text contains six phrases of analytical discrimination: namely, it is not limited (the ninth), not non-limiting (the fourth and fifth meanings), not primary (the first), and not... [the second].

"Without a master" (the sixth [point]) is neither "indicated" (the second and third meanings) nor "unindicated" (the seventh, eighth, thirteenth, and fifteenth meanings). The first pair reveals the Middle Way by affirming both aspects regarding their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*);
the second pair reveals the Middle Way by negating both regarding their essence (*svabhāva*); and the final pair reveals the Middle Way by negating both regarding their function (*vṛtti*).
The scriptural text is extremely extensive and cannot be cited in full; those who require it should consult the source. [From] *Chao-yi-yin*.
Regarding that which possesses all sounds within it, according to the *Brahmāyu Sūtra*, there are eight kinds of voice: first, the most excellent sound, like that of the kalaviṅka bird;
second, the easily understood sound, because its words and phrases are distinct and clear; third, the gentle sound, because it is free from coarseness or harshness;
fourth, the harmonious sound, because both high and low pitches are perfectly balanced; fifth, the venerable and wise sound... [text continues].
Because he is free from fear in battle, his voice is not mistaken; because there is no error, it is the seventh [quality], the profound and wondrous voice, as sound issues forth from the navel wheel;
because his voice is not feminine, it is the eighth, being masculine and resonant. However, this is explained merely by way of a single characteristic;
in reality, each of the ten preceding metaphors for the voice possesses all [qualities], which is precisely the meaning of the "perfect voice" (*brahmasvara*). — *Chao* (Excerpts)
The phrase "The Buddha utters a single wondrous sound" and so forth refers to the verse from the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs. The commentary (*shù*) and sub-commentary (*chão*) explain:

The first phrase indicates that there is only a single wondrous sound, which is the single *brahmā*-voice of India; the second phrase means it is heard everywhere because it accords with the nature of reality (the term "hearing" [wén] refers to sounds reaching in all four directions);
the third phrase means that because principle is interfused, the one possesses all; the fourth phrase means that from each and every one of those sounds, many [teachings] rain down.

Because the rain of Dharma—comprising the Four Truths, Dependent Origination, the Six Perfections, and other such teachings—is entirely replete [with it], the second phrase explains that each individual teaching is profound and vast in its phrasing;
because this single sound universally accords with the various dispositions of sentient beings, the third phrase follows from the preceding;
because this sound individually pervades all places, the fourth phrase follows; and because what is taught in each instance manifests the purity of intrinsic nature, the final phrase concludes.
Because of this principle, the Master of the Commentary states that the primary and attendant [teachings] are layered upon one another, resonating universally throughout the ten directions;

whereas other sutras provide specific teachings according to the capacities of beings and thus lack this layering that extends to the ten directions. Therefore, it is only this sutra that proclaims a ritual of universal pervasiveness. Question: Regarding all seven categories, it says...
Question: Since the exposition of the ritual (*vidhi*) is universally pervasive, why is this specific section alone entitled "Exposition of the Ritual"? Answer:

Because these six sections definitively establish that the [teacher's] body, location, time, assembly, and voice all pervade the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it is only here that one attains this title of "Ritual Exposition," characterized by the successive layers of principal and attendant elements.

While the preceding sections speak of them individually, this section receives the general name; in reality, however, all six preceding sections are also expositions of the ritual. Alternatively, the above was based on... [text truncated].
Regarding the ritual for the preaching of the Dharma by a single Buddha as described in the *Zhaina*, this specifically constitutes the general ritual for preaching the Dharma throughout all regions.
In the commentary (*chao*), the section specifically demonstrating the ritual for preaching is divided into two parts according to the oral outline (*kē*).
First, the formal explanation of this commentary (three parts):
first, the general heading;
second, the detailed explanation (two parts).
First, the explanation of the primary [teaching] with its attendants (the characteristics);
second, the explanation of the infinite interpenetration (two parts).
First, the discussion of infinite interpenetration through mutual relation (referred to as "adjacent").
III. Subsequent Mutual Pervasiveness of the Successive Layers (3):
First, the Successive Layers with this Buddha as the Principal (2):
First, Manifesting the Successive Layers by Reference to the Second Assembly (3).
First, the brief indication (consists of two parts);
second, the detailed explanation.
First, the arrangement of the principal and satellites, as well as their distance and proximity (which serves as a negation).
2. Explaining the double pervasiveness of the dharma and the analogy (2).
First, suppressing one layer to the east (3).
First, the dharma (If this...).
2. Two Similes (thus);
3. Three Syntheses (the meaning should be);
2. Manifesting the Remaining Layers (two).
First the Dharma (thus),
then the simile (like a person);
three fetters (one is taught).
2. All assemblies are manifested as mutually inclusive (thus); 3.
Those Buddhas act as the central figures in mutual inclusion (the ten directions);
4. This and that are viewed in mutual inclusion (thus).
The "three fetters" (saṃyojana) refer to [the preceding];
thus it is said that "two" apply generally to what precedes.

(However,) the *Chao* states that this is a general explanation, which interprets the term "in unison" (*qíchàng*) and also explains the specific characters within the topical outline (*kē*). ▲ *Chao*.
Regarding the "brief three phrases," these are all formulated with the speaker as the principal (*pradhāna*) and the witnesses as the associates (*sahāya*), rather than with the listeners.

Regarding the principal, there must be only one; regarding the associates, many are required. Although both those on the path of cause and those on the path of fruit may function as either principal or associate, the roles of principal and associate do not overlap.
Therefore, the sub-commentary below states: "Principals do not see principals; associates do not see associates; the principal sees the associates."
When the companions and their leaders see one another, they do so; if they do not see one another, each pervades the entire Dharma-realm.

When they see one another, they equally pervade the entire Dharma-realm together. As for what is called "singing in unison," this is also based on the principle that they mutually serve as leaders and companions;
because they simultaneously pervade the Dharma-realm, they are able to sing in unison throughout the ten directions. Regarding the "fruition leader" and the "fruition companion":

Question: If the leader of the assembly and the companions chant together, and the *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya] states that this is the Buddha’s teaching while the rest is the Bodhisattvas’ teaching, does this not imply that Vairocana and the Buddhas of the ten directions all taught it?
Answer: The "Chapter on Generating the Mind" (*Cittotpāda-parivarta*) states that the Buddhas of the ten directions share the same name, Dharmamati, and provides testimony, saying:
"We Buddhas also speak thus. Since the Buddhas have indeed spoken it, [it is established as the Buddha's word].
Does this Buddha not speak at all? Therefore, we know that it is merely in terms of what is signified, as previously clarified.
Regarding the terms "primary cause" (*hetu*) and "secondary cause" (*sahakāri-hetu*), according to the *Huìjiě* and *Zhǐxuán*, the speaker is taken as the primary and the listener as the secondary.

Why, then, in this context, is the assembly of the ocean-like gathering (*sāgara-parṣad*) not designated as the secondary, while only the Dharma-wisdom Bodhisattvas of the ten directions are so designated?
Because of this principle, when those preaching here in this direction are the primary speakers, those preaching in the ten directions serve as their companions by providing testimony;
and when those preaching in the ten directions are the primary speakers, the Bodhisattvas here in this direction serve as their companions by providing testimony.

Therefore, it is said that the primary and the companions sing in unison. However, those in the ocean-like assembly and so forth may only serve as the audience; they cannot be regarded as the primary speakers.
Regarding the companions, within the primary cause and its accompanying fruits, only Samantabhadra and others are mentioned, while the rest of the ocean-like assembly is not.

Furthermore, the *Zhi Xuan* states: "The text is composed by way of correspondence; the word 'sudden' (*dùn*) in the preceding phrase refers exclusively to the speaker, whereas the word 'simultaneous' (*qí*) in this phrase also refers to the speaker.
'Sudden' and 'simultaneous' mean pervading the ten directions all at once, rather than through gradual succession."
In the preceding sentence, the term "zhong" (middle/central) refers to being "sudden" (*dun*); here, it also refers to being "simultaneous" (*qi*).

If the subsequent [subject] were able to precede the prior [object], there would be the fault of non-correspondence. Now, examining this interpretation closely, it seems it does not capture the intent of the commentary.

The first instance of the word "ji" (extreme/pervasive) already clarifies that [the light] pervades the ten directions; for the word "qi" (simultaneous) to now also designate this pervasion would constitute a redundancy.

Because one understands the errors of Fan [Zhen], it is known that the former [treatise] distinguishes between the gradual and the sudden based on the horizontal and vertical [dimensions], while this [treatise] distinguishes between the "extreme" and the "equal" based on the subject and the object.

Let the wise examine these words: if the fruit is the principal and the cause is the attendant, then when the ten directions are viewed in relation to one another, one may speak of "layer upon layer" (*chóngchóng*). Now, however, Vairocana is the principal and Samantabhadra [is the attendant].
Question: If they act as companions, how can there be a layering [of realms] extending throughout the ten directions? Answer: This is one layer of Samantabhadra acting as a companion to Akṣobhya;
in this manner, when viewed from the perspective of the ten directions, there is also the sense of layering.

Question: If the fruit and the cause, the principal and the companion, sing in unison, why is it that in the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* the marks of excellence (lakṣaṇa) are taught as the fruit while the cause is not mentioned for the others?

Question: Since the fruit is explained within the chapter on the cause, yet it is not explicitly stated, how can one claim that the meaning of the Buddha’s teaching is identical [to that of the Bodhisattva]?

Furthermore, since the Bodhisattva also speaks of two chapters, is this not intended to manifest the subtle and the transcendent? Thus, even if the Buddha speaks, does it not conflict with the Bodhisattva speaking the same? Question:
For example, when the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are taught, both the Buddha and Vajragarbha speak of them; would this not lead to confusion? Answer: [This is not so.]...
In the "Chapter on Samantabhadra Samādhi," it is said that the Buddhas of the ten directions praise Samantabhadra with one voice;
could this unison also be disordered? Since many voices do not intermingle, how could two people singing together constitute disorder?
If even the simultaneous responses of various bodhisattvas to the myriad classes of beings are not disordered, how much less so would this [unison] be disordered?

Regarding the phrase "such as Dharmamati and others": [The questioner] asks, "If the Buddhas of the ten directions bear witness to Dharmamati’s preaching of the Dharma, why is it that there is also a cause and its principal, as well as an effect and its associates?
This is the answer. [The questioner] asks, "In that case, those Buddhas of the ten directions should lack the meaning of being 'associates' (parivāra).

Even if this were so, the following provides the answer. [The questioner] asks, "Since the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) must be perfectly integrated to constitute 'perfection' (pūrṇatā), why is this proposition now missing?"
Answer: In truth, [the Buddha] is indeed possessed of both [aspects], yet here we rely on the unchanging distinction between the honorable and the humble to accord with ritual propriety.
This is like how, although the true and the deluded penetrate each other, one simply speaks of "realizing the Buddha-mind through the ordinary mind," and so forth. [The *Shu*] states:

"To the east of this world" refers to the world of Abhirati (Sukhāvatī), where Akṣobhya Tathāgata (translated here as "Immovable") resides; thus, it should be understood that he is the presiding lord.
First, regarding the "companion," it refers to *sūtra*. ▲ In the *Commentary*, concerning the multiple enumerations of the Buddhas of the Dharma-realm:

above, this was discussed solely in terms of the Buddhas of the ten directions, thus consisting of only ten layers. Here, however, when the Buddhas of the entire Dharma-realm are compared with one another, there are infinite layers within the Dharma-realm;
reflect upon this. ▲ In the *Commentary*, the passage beginning with "like ten people" serves as a direct analogy for the principal fruit and its companions.
It may also serve as a simultaneous metaphor for the primary cause and its attendant causes below, yet it does not metaphorically represent the primary fruit and its attendant fruits.

[Question]: Regarding the statement in the *Chao* (Commentary), "The Buddha is the primary [cause] and the Bodhisattvas are the attendants, and it is likewise," one might ask: since the primary cause and attendant causes have a mutual relationship with one another, it is appropriate to say "likewise" (*tathaiva*).
However, the primary fruit and attendant fruits lack such a mutual relationship; why, then, is it illustrated by saying "likewise"? [Answer]: All... [text continues].
The Bodhisattva who expounds the Dharma not only looks to his original Buddha as a companion, but further becomes a companion to other Buddhas;
because there are thus inexhaustible layers of such associations, it is said that "it is likewise. This is an instance where the words are general while the meaning is specific.
Regarding the three meanings inherent in the *Chao* (Commentary), these summarize the preceding three phrases to constitute the three meanings.
The second commentary states: "Vairocana" refers to a single Buddha; this is discussed in terms of mutual pervasion within the layers of reality (*dharmadhātu*).

Furthermore, regarding the three phrases, it is the phrase concerning the fruit as the principal and the cause as its attendants that constitutes the pervasion. The commentary further explains that "the Hall of Universal Light" in the locus of Vairocana refers to the site where the second assembly was preached.
Regarding this, there are three interpretations: first, the hall is composed of jewels, and its light shines everywhere.

Therefore, because the second Buddha emits universal light therein, and the third Buddha preaches the Dharma-gate of Universal Dharma within the palace with the light of wisdom illuminating the world, these names are established.
Regarding the first meaning, it is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound); regarding the latter two, they are *bahuvrīhi* (possessive compounds).

As for "the eastern direction" and so forth, the Sūtra lists the ten directions: in the east is Mañjuśrī, as stated in the text; in the south is the world of Wondrous Color (*Vicitra-varṇa*), where Bodhirāja resides.
To the west is the Bodhisattva Vasumukha from the world Padmavarṇa; to the north is the Bodhisattva Ratnamukha from the world Campakavarṇa;
to the northeast is the Bodhisattva Guṇamukha from the world Utpalavarṇa; to the southeast is the Bodhisattva Kanakākṣimukha;
to the southwest is the Bodhisattva Ratnavaśitāmukha; to the northwest is the Bodhisattva Vajravarṇa from the world Dharmamukha; and below...
The Wisdom-Head Bodhisattva comes from above the Crystal-Colored [Buddha-field], and the Worthy-Head Bodhisattva comes from the Equal-Colored [Buddha-field];

in this manner, they all come from beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions to the Universal Radiance Hall. This constitutes the arrangement of the principal and attendant Buddhas according to their distance.
*Commentary:* If this principal Buddha faces east toward one world-system, this briefly demonstrates the suppression of one layer to the east.
Regarding these characteristics, there is the method, the analogy, and the application; this is the explanation by way of the Dharma.

For example, when the Buddha first sat in the Hall of Universal Radiance, Mañjuśrī came from ten Buddha-lands away. Now, as the Buddha faces east and has pervaded one world-system, he suppresses the first level of attendant lands;
this corresponds to Mañjuśrī coming from beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms within nine Buddha-lands. Nevertheless, through the relationship of principal and attendant...
Because it pervades all, Mañjuśrī returns beyond the dust-motes of ten *kṣetras*. ▲ In the commentary, "Like the vast empty sky," this metaphor has two meanings:
first, it is a brief illustration that the distances between the primary and attendant lands above are eternally fixed;

thus it says, "the moon is like the principal Buddha, and the constellations are like the attendants. Second, it is a brief illustration that the principal and attendants are undifferentiated yet pervasive; thus it says, "one."
In a single body of water, both the distant and the near appear simultaneously;

that is to say, as the stars and moon appear in this one stream at such distances, if those same stars and moon were moved closer to another stream to the east, they would likewise appear at those same distances there.
Thus we know that while the objects being moved do not move from their original realm, the first layer of principal and attendant deities moves further on.
In the Eastern region, although this analogy possesses the sense of being undivided yet pervasive, it lacks the principle of being layered upon one another;
therefore, it is described as "abbreviated. The meaning of the *Chao* (Commentary) should be understood as corresponding to what follows immediately below.
The Commentary states: Thus, following the section on the presiding Buddha, the remaining layers are revealed. First, the ten layers of the East are clarified.

When the Buddha first sat in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantābhāsā*), Mañjuśrī came from beyond the lands as numerous as the atoms of ten buddha-fields. Now, as the presiding Buddha pervades the East, this is precisely the dwelling place of Mañjuśrī.
The golden ground, as before, extends eastward for a distance of ten buddha-fields of atoms; to its west lies the lotus ground.

It was said that Puṣpavarṇa should have come from beyond twenty world-systems as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field, yet this is not so; he has come from beyond only ten world-systems as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field.
As for the statement that the Lord Buddha [of that realm] is at the extreme limit of the eastern direction and so forth:

if one goes ten world-systems as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field to the east of Suvarṇavarṇa, then Suvarṇavarṇa would consequently be located ten world-systems as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field to the west. Thus it is said.

The passage "Ultimately, one does not see Mañjuśrī" refutes erroneous interpretations. An erroneous interpretation states: "Since the Lord Buddha is already at the extreme limit of the East, Mañjuśrī should have come from the West toward the Buddha;
this [text] now refutes that. The underlying intent is that Mañjuśrī has also come from beyond lands as numerous as the atoms of ten *kṣetra*s in the East to approach the Lord Buddha.
Furthermore, an erroneous interpretation states: "It cannot be that Mañjuśrī has not come from the West."
Having passed to the east of the Buddha, he then returns from east to west to approach the presiding Buddha;

therefore, it is now denied that he sees Mañjuśrī and the others. Regarding these two sections of the text, there is an interpretation that the first denial means the Buddha does not pass beyond Mañjuśrī toward the east, while the subsequent denial means Mañjuśrī does not pass beyond the Buddha toward the west. However, this does not equal the former interpretation.
Other erroneous interpretations may be refuted by analogy with this. In the *Chao*, the passage beginning "Thus, the Principal Buddha is at the extreme west" explains the ten layers of the West;
by analogy with this, it should be understood that the same applies to all ten directions.
The Commentary states: Suppose a person uses ten coins as a base;

for the sake of a rough approximation, one first lays eleven coins on the ground facing east, with ten coins each in the other directions, totaling one hundred and one. The correspondence between the dharma and the metaphor is exact:

each coin represents a mental state (*citta*), while the edges of the coins at the location of the "Lord of the Realm" (the central mind) are like gold and so forth, representing the opening of the surrounding companions.
The distance between the *yuanbao* coins and so forth is like ten *kṣetra-rajas* (dust-motes of a world-system).

Regarding the statement that "the first coin is in the center," this means that the relative scale of the principal and its attendants (*sāpattya*)—both their distance and proximity—is the same for all.
As for the second coin being pressed upon the first coin, this second coin, in relation to the coin below it, occupies one-tenth of the total space occupied by the *yuanbao*.

Because it is shifted one part toward the east, it is said that the ground of the "eastern edge" is opened; thus, the *yuánbǎo* (original treasure) and others are also at the ground of the eastern edge.

This is a metaphor for the principal Buddha being near the eastern boundary, while the attendant lands (*bānchà*) are each separated by as many worlds as there are atoms in ten worlds, yet each is also near the eastern boundary. This sequence is like ten coins placed one atop another.
In all these cases, there is a reason for using the single character "Yuan" (元) as a metaphor for a Buddha-field as numerous as the atoms within a single Buddha-field;

this refers to the principle of "layer upon layer" (*chong-chong*). Furthermore, if the Lord Buddha were to reach the location of the Golden-Colored World, the principle that the Lotus-Colored World occupies the position of the Sahā world would not hold.

2. The objection regarding the absence of textual evidence within its own section: This means that within the section of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there is actually no text concerning entry into the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
3. The objection regarding internal contradiction with one's own words: This means that since the words of this very sūtra state "Saddharmapuṇḍarīka," how can it [refer to another]?
This refers to the question: "Does this mean that one returns to the *Avataṃsaka*? Regarding the fourfold challenge concerning the circular sublation of the distinct:

if the *Avataṃsaka* speaks only of the ultimate (the One), then it may be so for the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*); however, how can it be so when it also includes the Distinct [Teaching] (*biejiao*)? (For they hold that the *Avataṃsaka* teaches the Perfect while simultaneously including the Distinct.

According to the *Huìjiě*, all of these are addressed to resolve the difficulty. To first address the initial challenge: if the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* does not return to the *Avataṃsaka* but instead returns separately to its own Dharma...
Regarding the "Flower" (Huā), it corresponds to the Buddha’s wisdom in two ways: first, by initially seeing my body, one enters the Buddha’s wisdom; this is the *Avataṃsaka*.
Now, I likewise cause [beings] to hear this sutra and enter the Buddha’s wisdom; this is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Thus, there are two aspects to the Buddha’s wisdom.
As for resolving the second objection: is it not the case that causing [beings] to enter the Buddha’s wisdom right now is precisely the textual passage of this very section?

Furthermore, in the "Chapter on Resolute Belief," when [the son] first sees his father seated upon a lion throne—as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*—and later recognizes him as his natural father—as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—is this father not, in fact, the father from the past?
This too conforms to the scriptural text; thus, it resolves the third objection, for since it is based on this sūtra, it is indeed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Since its final entry into the Buddha-wisdom is no different from its initial entry, is it not the case that the *Lotus Sūtra* is the very scripture that subsumes the branches back into the essence of the *Avataṃsaka*?
It is clear that your own words are consistent from beginning to end; thus, your attempt to resolve the fourth objection is merely a failure to understand the doctrines of other schools.
Furthermore, your exclusive claim regarding the distinct [teachings] is a matter of your own school’s internal interpretation, arising solely from you.

Within our own school, it is not appropriate to conflate the *Avataṃsaka* with other individual [teachings], for to do so would lose the fundamental principle of "perfect interfusion and complete virtue.
Now, to raise this as a difficulty—is it not truly lamentable? Question: The meanings clarified above are all visible;
however, the sutra merely speaks of "entering the Buddha-wisdom. How can you then say that one returns to the *Avataṃsaka*? Answer: This...

This illustrates the relationship between the expressed meaning (*vācya*) and the expressive word (*vācaka*). As stated above, that which is called the "One Buddha Vehicle" (*ekabuddhayāna*) is precisely the *Avataṃsaka*.

This is for the same reason: since the *Avataṃsaka* primarily expresses the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and the Dharma-realm is itself the One Vehicle, and the One Vehicle is itself the Buddha-wisdom (*buddhajñāna*), now returning to the expressed meaning—the Buddha-wisdom—is precisely returning to the expressive word—the *Avataṃsaka*. Thus it is.
If one were to provide an exegesis of the four characters "subsuming the branches back into the root" (*zhōng shè mò guī běn*):

that which is capable of subsuming is the *Lotus Sūtra*; "the branches" refers to its subsuming of other sūtras. That which performs the subsuming is called "subsumption" (*shè*). Subsuming the branches is precisely the act of returning; thus, "subsuming the branches back into the root" means returning the branches to the root.

One should understand that the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is taken as the root, based on the agentive function of the substratum (*āśraya*) and the objective function of the object (*karman*). Furthermore, it is that which is subsumed.

That which is the ultimate destination of the branches is called the "return that subsumes the branches"; this "return that subsumes the branches" is itself the root, and is thus termed the "return to the root by subsuming the branches.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that the *Avataṃsaka* is the root while others are as explained below, this refers to what is taught in the section on the "subsumption of the teachings" and within the section on the "root of the teachings."

The intent of this composition is as follows: regarding those [ten] profound gates (*gambhīra-dvāra*) established by him, the characteristics of virtue (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*) are exclusively pure, while their functional activity (*karma-prayoga*) permeates both the defiled and the pure.

Therefore, when he describes their essence (*tattva*), it encompasses both the noumenal and the phenomenal; however, when he describes their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they are "characterless yet acting as characteristics" (and thus do not apply universally).

When he describes their function (*prayoga*), there is indeed mutual inclusion (*anyonya-anupraveśa*) and mutual manifestation (*anyonya-nirmāṇa*), yet these do not apply to the characteristics themselves. For this reason, the Master of the Commentary refutes [that interpretation].

Answer: It does not negate them. While both the Greatness of Characteristics and the Greatness of Function each clarify the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena, it is only the Greatness of Essence that negates them.

The equality of name, phenomenon, characteristic, and function is collectively elucidated as the principle; only when these two are unimpeded can they be considered profoundly mysterious.

The Commentary: The first phrase, "Fundamentally," serves as a general heading; the subsequent section, beginning with "Serene," provides a detailed explanation.

"Serene and empty-still" means being free from words; "profoundly mysterious and tranquil" means being free from marks. "Mysterious beyond the mysterious" indicates that there are no marks, yet these do not obstruct marks;
"external" refers to what is manifested. "Stillness beyond stillness" indicates there are no words, yet these do not obstruct words; "not a manifestation of form" refers to what is manifested.

"Characteristics are identical to the absence of characteristics" is contained within words. Regarding the phrase "words are identical to the departure from words," the *Zuanyao shu* (Commentary on the Essential Compendium) states:

First, the flesh eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*): within the physical mass of flesh there is pure form; seeing forms that are obstructed by barriers is called the flesh eye (the eye based upon flesh is named the flesh eye).
Second, the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*): extending from the vicinity of the flesh eye, one draws forth the pure divine eye to see what is obstructed.

The flesh eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*): This refers to the physical eye of a Buddha, which—relying on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*—is able to see countless worlds among humans; it is not merely the unobstructed pure divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) that sees the subtle forms of all devas. Excluding the seeing of celestial realms, the ability to see human affairs and so forth is called the flesh eye.
3. The wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*): Because it illuminates ultimate truth by means of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). 4. The Dharma eye (*dharma-cakṣus*):

Because it preaches the Dharma and delivers sentient beings by means of subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). 5. The Buddha eye (*buddha-cakṣus*): These four eyes are collectively present within a Buddha.
It is called the Buddha-eye (*buddhanetra*), and seeing the Buddha-nature in its perfect consummation is termed the Buddha-eye. Regarding the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), Guifeng said:

first, the unimpeded analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), which refers to the intrinsic nature of all phenomena; second, the unimpeded analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), which refers to the meanings upon those phenomena;
third, the unimpeded analytical knowledge of language (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), which refers to acquiring the local dialects and using their terminology to preach for others.

Therefore, regarding the four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), because one joyfully expounds inexhaustibly upon the various meanings and words according to the preferences of others based on the three aforementioned types of knowledge, one who first begins their training can gradually attain Buddhahood in the ninth stage and reach ultimate perfection. [Commentary]:

Now, the sub-commentary poses the following question: If it is established that [the two truths] are not different, how can the meaning of the "unhindered" be achieved? If one says they are not identical, then what of the principle and the phenomenon?
If one asks what is meant by "non-obstruction" (anāvaraṇa) in each individual case: if they were merely not different, there would be nothing to be harmonized;
if they were merely not one, non-obstruction could not be established. Now, because these two meanings exist simultaneously, the sense of non-obstruction is established.
The *Shu* (Commentary) clarifies that "the characteristics do not obstruct the essence" because the characteristics and the true essence possess the meaning of being neither identical nor different.
Furthermore, the *Shu* clarifies that "function is not separate from the essence" because it likewise possesses the meaning of being neither identical nor different. Question:

Since the three greats (the essence, characteristics, and function) are mutually present, why is the meaning of the mutual presence of characteristics and function not explicitly stated? Answer: In principle, the three... [are indeed mutually present].

The principle that the Great [Three]—essence (*tǐ*), characteristic (*xiàng*), and function (*yòng*)—are mutually present in their interpenetration is clarified here by means of the mutual presence of essence and function, as well as the mutual presence of essence and characteristic;

this is done because these accord with the principle of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*lǐshì wú'ài*). As for the meaning of the non-obstruction between characteristics and functions, it applies universally to all phenomena (*shìshì*), and thus it is omitted here without further elaboration.

"the True is called Principle (*li*), etc. refers to the two dharmas of the True and the False, which are explained through three pairs: Principle and Delusion (*moha*).

Regarding the statement that "the subject and object of obstruction correspond to birth and the Buddha, while the subject and object of transformation correspond to sentient beings," all those from the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) downward are termed "sentient beings.

This is because the eighth consciousness serves as the substance (*ātman*) of their rebirth; at this stage, it has not yet been transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). Question: Why are "birth" and "Buddha" characterized as the false and the true, respectively?

Answer: Master Sengzhao [states]: "The Buddha is the True, and sentient beings are the False. The *Minglun* (Treatise on Names) states: "Reality arises from detachment; thus the Buddha is called 'Real. Delusion arises from attachment; thus birth is called 'False.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* also says: 'Birth exists because of delusion; because of birth there is extinction. Birth and extinction are called false; the extinction of delusion is called Real.
Regarding the three pairs above—birth and death versus nirvāṇa, and the flow of transmigration versus the cessation of return—all of them mutually penetrate one another."

This meaning is a specific interpretation within the "Gate of the Unimpeded Interpenetration of Principle and Phenomena" (Lishi Wunai Men). Regarding the phrase in the *Commentary* (Chao), "The True encompasses the False from the root to the branches":
the preceding three pairs establish that the True is always the source and the False is always the branch. The statement "like waves and moisture" uses a metaphor to clarify this;

waves represent the False and moisture represents the True, and their mutual penetration can be understood thereby. Regarding the phrase in the *Commentary*, "Now it says 'thus'": this introduces the following question.
The combined explanation states: "Ordinary beings and sages mutually encompass one another; why then is it not so here? This is the answer. It is because of two reasons:

the non-destruction of characteristics and being beneficial. Regarding "the non-destruction of characteristics," this is explained in terms of the meaning of cultivation and realization, as it does not destroy the characteristics of a sage.
If a practitioner were to destroy the characteristics of a sage, what would they have to hope for? As for "being beneficial," regarding...
The two meanings of "arising" (birth) are each explained from one perspective. Question: In the previous explanation, true and false were taken as the Buddha and arising;

why now do you speak of ordinary beings and sages? Answer: This is because one wishes to clarify that true and false pervade both Buddhas and ordinary beings, and that there is a mutual relationship of breadth and narrowness between them.
Therefore, the previous statement that "Buddhas and arising" refers to the true being narrow and the false being broad applies to everything from the Stage of Equal Enlightenment downward.

Because they arise, it is said here that "ordinary" (*pṛthagjana*) is narrow while "sage" (*ārya*) is broad, since those who have attained the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) in the Three Vehicles are all sages.
Question: Why can those above the Path of Vision in the Three Vehicles be called "True" (*tattva*)? Answer: Because both see the Principle (*tattva*).

Since the former [distinction] was already established based on the Principle being the True, how could a sage who sees the Principle not be the True itself? Alternatively, "sage" may refer specifically to the Ultimate Sage (*uttamārya*) alone.
The term "Buddha" generally refers to those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), yet this is intended to manifest that [the state] is inconceivable;

it does not, however, preclude those from the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) downward from being for the sake of sentient beings. This means that if even the delusions of those prior to the stages can be immediately identified with the Real, how much more so for those at the Stage of Equal Enlightenment and below?
Both interpretations are valid. Question: If one follows the former interpretation, why say that the Sages have no afflictions (*kleśa*)? Answer: Only... [text ends].

Because they are free from discrimination, they are not the same as ordinary people. [The *Chao* (Commentary) states: "That which is beneficial to ordinary people causes them not to deceive themselves;
it also prevents them from being arrogant toward others. To say that it causes people to have false understandings means that they would instead sink into delusion and return to confusion.
Question: If ordinary people see the Buddha, would this not be an unwarranted intrusion into the ranks of the sages? It would also lead to mistakenly showing reverence to coarse individuals.
If one realizes that the Buddha is precisely the ordinary person, then one knows that his virtuous functions are sovereign and his advancing or retreating is without obstruction.
Since this responsibility is equal [for both], how can it be resolved? The answer is: this is intended to block false interpretations and to skillfully transform the faculties [of beings].

Now, to harbor such erroneous attachments again—how could this be considered correct understanding? The above is a brief commentary on the two phrases of the *Śāstra*. Thus far, only "arising" has been discussed.
The Buddha’s first pair is the principle of mutual penetration; the second pair is delusion, and the third pair is birth-and-death and nirvana—these are explained according to the above.
*Commentary:* Although the preceding and following sections have briefly explained the meaning of the phrase "the interpenetration of the true and the false," the meaning is not yet exhaustive;
therefore, there is the word "ran" (however/then). "Ran" is a term indicating incompleteness, which first clarifies the sense of mutual penetration.

As for the reason why there are four, it is said that while in principle five or six may indeed combine, four is taken as the correct number. Now, the reasons for establishing these four are: first, because [the false] does not depart from the one mind;

second, because the true and the false are mutually dependent; third, because they do not possess two distinct substances; and fourth, because the true and the false manifest their characteristics [in relation to one another].
It is gathered here because, for these four reasons, there is mutual penetration (*jiaochè*).
The *Chao* (Excerpts) states that the following section clarifies the characteristics of this mutual penetration through six propositions: first, false emptiness and true existence;

The basis for both dependent and perfected [natures] includes both birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and afflictions (*kleśa*), whereas the imagined [nature] includes either the basis or the afflictions, because it possesses both types of grasping (*grāha*).

here, they are fully correlated with the two truths according to both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*). Regarding the phrase "even if pure":

In the previous discussion on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), it was stated that the pure portion (*viśuddha-bhāga*) of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) accords with the ultimate, while its defiled portion (*kliṣṭa-bhāga*) is delusion.
Now, if conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is considered delusion, would the pure dependent phenomena of the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) also be delusion?

Regarding the section "As in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*," the six phrases of the preceding emptiness and existence are assigned according to their respective categories based on the gates [of the three natures], though they do not follow a sequential order but rather follow the meaning. first, the phrase "delusive emptiness and true existence" is explained in contrast to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); second, by means of the defiled portion (*kliṣṭa-bhāga*).

The fourth phrase (that both the true and the deluded are existent) is stated based on the other [schools] regarding the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) and the pure portion; this is according to the teaching on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

If one speaks of the two truths from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), then both the true and the false are empty; yet the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) could be said to be empty, whereas the ultimate could not be said to be empty.

*Commentary:* If we consider how both the True and the False pervade the two truths, the sixth phrase (the "double affirmation") has two interpretations: first, ...

It is said that when both the real and the false are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they are both empty; when both the real and the false are the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they are both existent.
Second, it is said that both phenomena—the real and the conventional—pervade both the real and the false, being both empty and existent.

This is because, according to the "Chapter on the One Vehicle," all dharmas possess both the meanings and functions of emptiness and existence; depending on the occasion, they may be applied either singly or in combination.

When both [existence and non-existence] are preserved and simultaneously negated, one may take whichever [aspect] one prefers; this is like the three natures (*trisvabhāva*): the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) has existence in terms of mental construction but emptiness in terms of reality;

the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) has existence in terms of its characteristics but emptiness in terms of its intrinsic nature; the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) has existence in terms of its nature but emptiness in terms of its characteristics.

All other cases should be understood according to this principle. Therefore, both the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional—comprehend both the meanings of emptiness and existence; thus, both interpretations are valid. *Commentary:* If one considers it from the perspective that all things encountered are the Middle Way:
The above section concerned the Middle Way in which both truths coexist; this present section concerns the Middle Way in which both truths are simultaneously transcended.
Since the Middle Way is free from the two extremes of emptiness and existence, it is the fifth proposition—that both the real and the delusive are neither empty nor existent (the "double negation").
