It cannot be known by consciousness, nor is it the domain of the mind; its nature is fundamentally pure, revealing it to all sentient beings.
The Buddha-wisdom is precisely the wisdom of the Buddha’s own domain. As the Sūtra says: "The wisdom of all Buddhas is sovereign, unimpeded throughout the three periods of time.
Such a realm of wisdom is equal to empty space. It is also called the two wisdoms of the provisional and the ultimate, as well as the fundamental and the subsequently attained.
The two wisdoms are also the two wisdoms of principle and means (*pramāṇa*), as well as the two awakenings of the beginning and the fundamental.
Regarding the passage "the preceding and succeeding penetrate each other" in the *Chao*, there are two intended meanings. First, it follows from the above to clarify the meaning of the text:

since it was previously stated that "one sees the Buddha-mind within the ordinary mind," there is a fear that people might mistakenly cling to the notion that their own minds are already identical to the Buddha-mind and thus need not be cultivated.
Because this is practice, the text here presents the conduct of dual cultivation. The *Chao* (Commentary) also states, from the second section below, that it directly reveals the meaning of the text:

those who study the Southern School and lose its intent, and those who study the Three Treatises (*Sanlun*) and do not grasp their intent, claim that by relying on the nature of fundamental wisdom (*benzhi*), the body itself is Buddha;
what need is there to cultivate myriad practices? Since the Sixth Patriarch said, "The mirror is fundamentally self-illuminating," [the text refutes this].
Not brushing and not polishing does not mean one lacks understanding; it is simply relying on natural spontaneity (*t'ien-chên*) without needing to exert effort.
Those who are mired in this view are especially numerous in recent times. This is the "lazy Chan" that neither cultivates nor abandons, where one has not yet mastered any of the Dharma-gates.
It is the deluded meditation of those who maintain silence while losing the essence of the Northern School, or those whose study of the doctrinal teachings remains unpenetrated.

Furthermore, those who do not consult virtuous friends nor listen to the sūtras and śāstras, yet practice with a wholesome mind alone, are attached to the teachings which state that the expedient means for cultivation must necessarily give rise to formal practices;
they seek outside their own minds for the superior conditions of the *paratantra* (dependent) Tathāgata to accomplish their own merit. This is merely the wild wisdom of following the literal text.

To say that both [positions] are biased attachments: regarding the statement in the *Commentary* (鈔) that "the nature of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is inherently complete," the *Awakening of Faith* (起信論) states that "the nature is spontaneously replete with all merits," meaning that its own essence possesses the significance of great wisdom and luminosity, and so forth.
Regarding the statement in the *Commentary* on "having nothing to seek" that "I therefore seek," this refers to the *Mahāvaipulya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (大方等陀羅尼經).
In the midst [of this assembly], the Buddha spoke to Ghoṣadatta concerning the past causes and conditions of the Bodhisattva Puṣpaketu, saying:
"In the past, there was a bodhisattva named Agrasena who entered a city to beg for alms. At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Gaṅgā who asked the mendicant, 'From where have you come?
He replied, 'I have come from the True. He asked again, 'What is meant by the True?'"

He replied, "Because it has the characteristic of quiescent extinction (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*), it is called 'reality' (*tattva*). Question: "Within this characteristic of quiescent extinction, is there anything to be sought, or is there nothing to be sought?
He replied, "There is nothing to be sought. Question: "Since there is nothing to be sought, for what purpose do you seek?
He replied, "Precisely because there is nothing to be sought, I therefore seek it therein. Furthermore, he asked: "In what place does the Bodhisattva seek?"

Answer: To seek within the six *pāramitās* and, having heard the *Gaṅgā*, sell one’s body to make offerings—this is to seek that which is not sought, wherein both conceptualization and its opposite are extinguished;
thus, though seeking all day long, there is nothing sought.

The phrase "the mind as a mirror" below criticizes the prior Chan school for its doctrine of neither wiping nor polishing. Furthermore, the phrase "principle does not obstruct phenomena" below [addresses] both.
This constitutes the two types of cultivation.

Regarding the phrase "according to the transformations of phenomena," Guishan’s commentary states: "In both pairs, the first phrase clarifies the basis, while the second phrase correctly elucidates the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*).
Although the dependent origination of the one and the many might appear to be redundant, this is because it refers exclusively to non-obstruction."
Question: Why does the *Chao* (Commentary) judge all [the preceding statements] as being "the reason why" (*suo yi*)? Answer: Because the two upper lines encompass the two lower lines;
both are the cause (*yin*) through which fundamental nature and principle are harmoniously integrated.

The *Chao* (Commentary) also divides [the section] into two parts for two reasons: first, because looking upward, the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai*) is also divided into two;
second, because looking downward, within the "Delineation of Meanings" (*yi-fen-chi*), the "Universal Inclusivity" (*zhou-bian han-rong*) is also divided into two.

As for the reason why the *Chao* provides a general inquiry with the phrase "Why, from the level of phenomena and phenomena... (*shi-shi xia zong zheng suo yi*) and answers it generally with the single sentence "Because phenomena are fused by means of principle" (*yi li rong shi gu*), [it is as follows].

This concerns the cause of the "gate" (dvāra). Regarding the first phrase, there is a formal explanation of two meanings. The first meaning constitutes the cause of the alternative formulation (*paryāya-hetu*):
"one" refers to principle (*li*), while "many" refers to phenomena (*shi*). Thus, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) can be understood. If one speaks of phenomena, it is by way of contrast;
now, from "by means of this," it is explained in accordance with the truth. From the phrase "the principle is already pervasive and harmonious," it refers to these very phenomena.
Because the principle within those phenomena is neither identical nor different, all phenomena are likewise integrated as neither identical nor different.
As for the statement "the rest will be clarified below," this is because the boundaries of the principles (*arthagati*) fully clarify the ten causes.
Regarding the commentary on the phrase "therefore one attains the ten bodies," the subsequent section states: "The commentary says 'mutual identity' (xiāngjí) and 'mutual functioning' (xiāngzuò).

This is because the Master of the *Kanding ji* sought to harmonize the two profound gateways of mutual identity and mutual functioning; since their meanings are not distinct and both ultimately converge upon this single gateway, the section heading and the commentary use the terms 'identity' and 'functioning' interchangeably."
Regarding the note on the difference between "ancient" and "modern" names: "Ancient" refers to the name used by Zhixiang;
"modern" refers to Xianshou’s revision of it as "broad and narrow," which will be understood naturally below. Regarding the note on the "eighth stage and so forth":

the *Shuchao* (Commentary on the Subcommentary) explains that because the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*) does not differentiate between one's own body and the bodies of others, one abides in the principle of equality and is free from partiality.
To speak of it separately: it is not merely that the illumination and the object illuminated are of one identical nature, but rather that both the subject and object of illumination have vanished.

This Bodhisattva’s knowledge is the subsequent conventional wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-saṃvṛti-jñāna*). The ten bodies that are the objects of this knowledge are all the essence of the perfect enlightenment of Vairocana.

Although the realms of the three worlds and five destinies, the inexhaustible lands, and the karma and afflictions that give rise to those bodies and lands are now referred to as "retribution," [they are in fact the essence of the Buddha].

Taking only that which can induce the four paths and four fruits, the self-realization of dependent origination, the wondrous fruition of the three stages of worthiness and ten bhūmis, mundane and supramundane wisdom, and all teachings, principles, practices, and fruits—wherein principle is empty and phenomena are empty—these, in sequence, constitute the essence of the ten bodies.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* subsumes these into three categories: the first three belong to the defiled portion, the next six to the pure portion, and the final one [to the non-dual].
The two non-dual divisions are such that the lands and bodies are combined and apply to both the pure and the defiled; for now, they are categorized as defiled according to one class of beings.

Next, the six [categories] are generally classified as the pure divisions of the three vehicles. Among these, the first four consist of humans, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas, differing only in terms of cause and fruit.
The next one is the realizing wisdom (*pramāṇa*), and the final one is the realized principle (*tattva*). Question: Regarding the ten internal [categories]...
Question: What is the difference between the principle and wisdom within the ten bodies (*daśakāya*) and this principle and wisdom? Answer: They differ in terms of breadth and narrowness.

That is to say, the principle and wisdom within the external ten bodies encompass the wisdom that distinguishes the five teachings and three vehicles, as well as the principles of all phenomena—including teaching, principle, practice, and fruit—therefore they are broad.
The principle and wisdom within the internal ten bodies pertain only to the specific vehicle [in question].
Question: Since it possesses the principle of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and the unimpeded wisdom, why is it described as "narrow"?
Answer: It is called "conventional" (*sāṃvṛta*) in contrast to the aforementioned ultimate true wisdom and true object;
however, if one speaks directly of the body of Vairocana, how could the true and the conventional be so restricted?

Since the meaning of "Ya-ge" (space) is unconditioned and boundless, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* asks why it is said that space merely exists as a provisional designation based on consciousness (*vijñāna*).

It has never been heard stated that the name "space" exists according to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), nor that there are such things as the characteristics of space. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* also says:
"When one person gives rise to the truth and returns to the source, the empty spaces of the ten directions all vanish. Why then rely on such a false construct?

Question: Is the meaning of "absence of substance" the Buddha-body? Answer: The Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) clarifies that because the nature and substance of this matter are inconceivable, it can constitute the Buddha-body.
Regarding the phrase "knowing all sentient beings," first it clarifies the reason for manifesting marks (laksana), which is because it accords with the capacities of beings;
alternatively, it is the intent behind manifesting marks, as the intention is to gather in and save sentient beings. The phrase "is able to" and below separately reveals [this point].

Briefly summarized, there are four points regarding the question: within the *dharmakāya*, there are the *dharmatākāya*, the *jñānakāya*, and the *ākāśakāya*. Since these three are all devoid of form or substance, how can one speak of "acting"?

If we consider it from the perspective of self-realization through wisdom, when one realizes the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they naturally manifest, causing one to suddenly perceive one's own body within empty space;
this is the meaning of "acting. If we consider it from the perspective of the capacity of sentient beings (*tatkāla-pratibhāsa*), it clarifies the Bodhisattva.
To cause sentient beings to accord with principle and wisdom, merging them indistinguishably with empty space—this is the meaning of "forming" (作).

From the perspective of this meaning of "relying upon" (依止), it is termed a "body" (身). Question: When forming sentient beings, are they like defiled sentient beings who possess suffering and affliction?
Answer: It is like a worldly game; because there is no injury or agitation, although four instances are cited here, by principle there should be ten, which are now complete.
Regarding the statement that "one hundred bodies" refers to one's own body being the very body of the Bodhisattva:

if one considers one's own body as an eighth-stage Bodhisattva in distinction from all other Bodhisattvas, there are then one hundred and ten bodies. In the *Chao*, the term "unbroken characteristics" (*buhuai xiang*) pertains to the sequential unfolding (*xingbu*) of the path;

the two characters "characteristics" (*xiang*) and "action" (*zuo*) pertain to the perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*). Only when these two meanings are mutually unimpeded can the profound mystery be established.

[The *Chao* (Commentary)] states: "The six stages, etc.," is explained in full as presented later in the section on the stages of attainment (*di-wei*). [The *Chao*] continues: "Although there is 'immediacy' (*ji*)," etc.
Regarding "entering the mind" and "taking up the broad and the narrow": "entering" refers to the cause (*hetu*), while "the broad and the narrow" refers to the thesis (*pakṣa*).

Because the thesis is revealed by means of the cause, here the entry of the great body and the great land into a speck of dust or a pore of hair represents the broad and the narrow of distinct entities (*bhinnasvabhāva*). In the lower section of the Jin translation, the entry of the minute within the vast represents the broad and the narrow of identical entities (*tatsvabhāva*).
The statement that "within the ultimate large there is a small aspect" indicates that phenomena lack a fixed nature (*aniyata-svabhāva*); this is the meaning of the cause.

The commentary states that from "all appear simultaneously and clearly" onwards, the eight mysteries are all elucidated by means of metaphors. Now, the metaphor of the mustard seed and the jar illustrates the principle as stated in the Sūtra:
"Within a single minute pore, unspeakably many lands enter in succession;
the pore can contain all those lands, yet the lands cannot pervade the pore. Here, the hair is like a beryl jar, and the lands are like mustard seeds. This is the principle.
The analogy can be understood.

In the commentary, it states that "one [container] can contain many"; even when taking one among the contained [elements] as the container, it is still "one containing many," which is why it is called "mutual inclusion" (*xiāng róng*).
Furthermore, in the commentary, the passage beginning with "This is the Tathāgata... distinguishes the source of the analogy.
Based on this analogy, since there has been no such precedent from antiquity as the "bundle of arrows" metaphor, I shall now indicate its source.
The Sūtra states: "At that time, while the World-Honored One was in samādhi, he emitted a light from between his eyebrows named 'Great Manifestation.
All those bodhisattvas who had not yet realized the tenth bhūmi, upon encountering this light, all..."
One sees within the tips of all hairs and inside every minute atom (*paramāṇu*) in the sky immeasurable Buddha-fields, like mustard seeds contained within a crystal jar,

such that all observers see them clearly (the intent being to capture the state of distinct, orderly differentiation without confusion). One version reads "white mustard seeds," which refers to the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*,
in the section on the "Inconceivable Realm of the Buddhas" (*Tathāgatagocarānupraviṣṭajñānābhijñāparivarta*), where it says they are placed in white [jars].
The remainder of the text regarding *sarṣapa* (mustard seed) is identical [to the previous entry]. Regarding *vaidūrya*, the *Yiqiejing yinyi* (Phonetic Meanings of All Scriptures) states:
"In full, it is called *vaiḍūrya*; this is translated as 'Not-Far Mountain' (*Bùyuǎnshān*).

This means that in the Western Regions there is a mountain not far from the city of Vārāṇasī, and since this gem is produced there, it is named after it. Tripitaka Master Yìjìng translated it as "green-colored gem," and further stated:

"Blue. ▲ The commentary states that "it is also a real quality (*dravya*) arising from dependent origination" in order to distinguish it from functional activity (*kāritra*). In reality, this category also extends to functional activity;
however, because one is here distinguishing it from the functional activity of humans and devas, it is said to be "not made by humans or devas. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 54, states:
"The devas of the form and formless realms transform their bodies into ten billion [forms], yet they can all stand together upon the tip of a single hair."
The power of meditative concentration (samādhi) acts according to the mind; this [section] now specifically excludes that [view].

It is merely a semblance and not the reality, for it never states that True Suchness (tathatā) possesses inexhaustible virtues and so forth. *Commentary*: Because the name of the scripture following the "Eight Phases" (aṣṭalakṣaṇa) is "Subtle," this "Subtle Gate" (sūkṣma-mukha) is established.
This refers to the text of the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*). The scripture says: "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva..."
Bodhisattvas have ten kinds of extremely subtle modes of progression. What are these ten? They are:
manifesting the initial arousal of the bodhicitta up to the stage of consecration (abhiṣeka) while dwelling in the mother’s womb;
dwelling in Tuṣita heaven while in the mother’s womb; manifesting birth while in the mother’s womb; and manifesting childhood while in the mother’s womb.
While in the mother’s womb, he manifested dwelling in a royal palace; while in the mother’s womb, he manifested the renunciation of the household life;
while in the mother’s womb, he manifested the practice of asceticism; while in the mother’s womb, he manifested proceeding to the site of enlightenment and attaining perfect awakening;
while in the mother’s womb, he manifested turning the wheel of Dharma; and while in the mother’s womb, he manifested entering parinirvāṇa.
Within the mother’s womb, he manifests the great subtle, which refers to all the practices of bodhisattvas and the immeasurable gateways of the sovereign spiritual powers of all Tathāgatas.
The commentary states: "Within the mother’s womb, whether manifesting as a single phase (*eka-lakṣaṇa*) or eight phases (*aṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*), he is fully endowed with the myriad virtues.
Just as it is with the single phase, so it is with every phase; yet this also applies universally."

Regarding the "virtuous marks" (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*) and "karmic functions" (*karma-vyāpāra*), this citation here serves merely to verify the virtuous marks. As for the statement that it "can contain the subtle and minute":

it is because things such as a single hair, a single speck of dust, or a single mark—which are difficult to perceive and are subtle—such as a minute atom being neither large nor a world-system (*kṣetra*) being small, can be contained within it.
The *Commentary* states that "one phenomenon encompassing inexhaustible phenomena" refers to the completeness of its own gate.
This is because the ten pairs of entities and phenomena, such as teaching and meaning, include all things without exception;

furthermore, regarding the nine subsequent sections, since this section stands at the beginning in the sequence of enumeration, the phenomena possessed by those nine sections are all fully contained within this section.

This is because the following sections explain the reason for this comprehensive inclusion; if one were to possess only the meanings of their respective individual sections, [the totality would not be achieved].
Because it establishes the general [principle]. ▲ The *Chao* (Excerpts) states that the tides do not exceed their limits:

fifty-two sūtras explain that within the four continents there are twenty-five thousand rivers that flow into the ocean; furthermore, there are eight billion palaces of nāga kings, each with its own waters that flow into the great ocean and surge forth at specific times.
Therefore, the tides do not miss their appointed time. Moreover, according to the *Wu* (Five [Treatises]):
In the ocean of the eleven sūtras, there are four great treasures that can absorb all waters; therefore, the waters of the sea neither increase nor decrease.
First is named Sūryagarbha (Sun-Treasury); second is named Ardratā-vigata (Free from Moisture); third is named Jvālārcis (Flame-Light); and fourth is named Aśeṣa-kṣaya (Exhaustion Without Remainder).
If these four treasures did not exist, everything from the four continents up to the Peak of Existence would be completely submerged and swept away.
According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the fiery vapors of the Avīci Hell are capable of swallowing and dissolving the waters of the great ocean;
the "Wojiao Stone" (the Stone that Consumes Water) mentioned in Confucian teachings does not fully capture this principle.
The excerpt from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* refers to the sixth of the ten merits in the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gao-gui-de-wang," which uses the metaphor of refining gold with a vajra.
Having cultivated all samādhis, they may now be understood through this analogy.
Regarding the "thousand lights equal to space," the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) states: "It is like a hundred thousand lamps illuminating a single room;
their light is perfect, complete, undestroyed, and unmixed. This is precisely what is being illustrated by the metaphor of that which is emitted.
Regarding the mutual functioning as conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*) through the gate of the interdependence of characteristics:

the meaning is that within all phenomena, the aspect of being capable of establishing [an effect] is termed "condition," while the aspect of being established by that power is termed "arising. Thus, the powers and functions interpenetrate one another.

Therefore, what follows below correctly clarifies their mutual inclusion (*anyonya-anupraveśa*); this is precisely the profound gate (*gambhīra-dvāra*). As for the statement "this is called mutual containment" (*anyonya-saṃgraha*), it refers to...

Regarding "the subtle and minute [realms] mutually containing one another yet being different," while above it was stated that "one contains many" as a single case of mutual containment, here it refers to the mutual containment of the one and the many.
As for the *Commentary* (Chao), it may also be used as a metaphor for mutual identity (*xiāngjí*);

however, since mutual identity also carries the meaning of mutual inclusion (*xiāngrù*), it takes mutual identity as its primary gateway. In this current metaphor, although mutual identity is likewise implied, it takes mutual inclusion as its primary gateway.

Regarding the phrase "the manifest and the hidden are both established," the Sūtra says: "For example, the people of Jambudvīpa see the form of the lunar disk as small, yet it does not diminish;
those dwelling within the moon see its form as large, yet it does not increase. The commentary explains: when one sees it as large, the large is manifest and the small is hidden;
when one sees it as small, the small is manifest and the large is hidden, yet there is no increase or decrease. The former [case] is the secret.
The secret [teachings] and the manifest are both established; all other categories of phenomena may be understood by analogy with this.
Regarding the "moon in the eighth or ninth night" in the *Yao* (Commentary), the lower *Shu* (Sub-commentary) states: "Moon" means "deficient," because it possesses deficiency.
It is composed of *sphatika* (rock crystal) and is capable of cooling and illuminating. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states that its city is square.
It is exactly one thousand nine hundred and sixty *li* in circumference, and its height and depth are likewise.

The king’s throne is twenty *li* [in diameter]; from a distance it appears round, but in reality it is square (the sun is the same in this regard). The *Abhidharmakośa* states that when the sun is near, the moon’s disk appears deficient because it is covered by the sun’s shadow.

This is because the sun moves slightly faster and the moon moves slightly slower, resulting in a difference in their orbital degrees. When the lunar period is nearly exhausted, the moon gradually approaches the solar disk; the sun’s light is so brilliant and radiant that it outshines the moon’s disk, causing it to become invisible.
This refers to the analogy of the moon, which, when contrasted with the sun or separated by Mount Sumeru such that it is not illuminated, manifests its full form;
yet when eclipsed, it appears as a reflection reduced to eight or nine-tenths of its size. To say this is unlike the "waning moon" (the new moon) is based on the *Chuxue ji*, which states:
"Hui" is the name for the end of the month; "hui" means ash. When fire dies, it becomes ash; likewise, when the moonlight is exhausted, it is called "hui."
Regarding "resembling it," the *Hongjue zhiyun* states: "Obscurity (*hui*) means darkness. Regarding "the moon's appearance" (*wang*), the *Chuxue ji* states:
"'Appearance' (*wang*) is the name for the full moon; it is when the sun and moon face each other. However, this metaphor has two aspects:

the concealment and manifestation from above, which refers to the concealment and manifestation of distinct entities (*yiti*). As in the passage beginning with "In the east," it first contrasts distinct entities.

Regarding the phrase "the entryway of the East," the subsequent section clarifies their identity-in-essence (*tongti*). Alternatively, it may merely serve as a metaphor for their concealment and manifestation, encompassing both the meanings of identity and difference.
In the commentary’s repeated interreflections, although all eight [entries] employ metaphors here, from the perspective of the gates themselves, this alone [is used].
The first gate receives its name from a metaphor; if established according to the actual phenomena (*dharma*), it should be called the "Gate of the Repeated Manifestation of the Inexhaustible.
The *Chao* (Commentary) likewise uses a metaphor to illustrate a metaphor below.

Because the principle of repeated manifestation is profound and difficult to fathom, and because the metaphor of the Indra’s Net (*Indrajāla*) does not manifest its form in the world, a proximate matter is used to illustrate this remote meaning.

The commentary states: "Moment-to-moment perfect interfusion" means that moments and eons are perfectly interfused; here, as we follow the text for the sake of correspondence, it says "moment-to-moment.

Although both moments and eons possess meanings such as mutual identity and mutual inclusion, what distinguishes this from other gates is that the others concern the phenomena upon which [time] relies (*āśrita-dharma*), whereas this concerns the time itself which relies [upon them].
Since the phenomena relied upon are already mutually interfused, the time which relies upon them is likewise so.
This is also a case of mutual integration.

Regarding the statement in the *Chao* (Commentary) that "the ten types [of teachings] explain the three periods of time," it should rather be stated as "using the three periods of time to explain the ten types.

In the passage from the *Chao* stating that "the present explains equality," the sub-commentary (*Shu*) below says: "Because the present is immediately visible in its phenomena, it is treated only in contrast to what precedes it."
Regarding the statement that "the present is established later while the future is said to be inexhaustible," the sub-commentary (*xia shu*) states:

"Because the future is a phenomenon that continues to arise, the 'future of the future' is termed 'inexhaustible'. Regarding the statement that "the three periods of time are spoken of as a single moment," the sub-commentary states:
"The single moment of the present belongs to the past; the future belongs to the future; [and] the past [belongs to the past]."

Thus, the three times are inherently complete. As for the statement that the characteristics of the three times are mutually causal: within these three times, the present has the past and future as its causes;

within the present, there are the past and future; the past has the present and future as its causes; within the past, there are the present and future; and the future has the past and present as its causes;
within the future, there are the past and present. Since the effect emerges from the cause and is not distinct from the cause, there are thus nine times.

This is to distinguish the single thought-moment as the totality. Regarding the phrase "a dream of a single night spanning several lifetimes," examples include the dreams of Huangliang and Nankuo, as well as the accounts of the Western Regions recluses found in the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks), which may be verified here.
As for the mention of Zhuangzi, it refers to the *Inner Chapters*, which state: "Once, Zhuang Zhou dreamed he was a butterfly, fluttering about."
The phrase "soaring like a butterfly" expresses his own metaphor for the fulfillment of his will; he was unaware of [the span of] Zhou.
Regarding the term "sleeping lightly," the commentary on the *Mao Shi* states that it refers to sleeping without removing one's robes or cap.

Regarding the phrase "the dharma-gates are layered and so forth": whenever one single dharma is mentioned, it is immediately all inexhaustible dharma-gates, because they arise from the void like clouds, suddenly layering upon one another and pervading the entirety of space.
Regarding the phrase "The Sub-commentary quotes the Sūtra below," this refers to the *Parināmanā-parivarta*.

Although there is no explicit textual passage [in that chapter], the present meaning is derived from the "Chapter on Ascending to the Tuṣita Palace. This section contains three passages of sūtra text that encompass four meanings.
Specifically, the first passage consists of ten phrases that clarify how many causes produce many fruits. The Sūtra says: "A hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas... and so forth.
The assembly of bodhisattvas dwelling in Tuṣita have produced [this merit] from that which arises from transcending the dharmas of the triple world;
from that which arises from conduct free from all afflictions; from that which arises from a mind that is all-pervasive and unimpeded; from that which arises from profound methods of skillful means;
from that which arises from an immeasurable and vast mind; and from that which arises from firm and pure conduct that increases inconceivable goodness.

The mind that manifests the offering to the Buddha—accomplished through the inconceivable skillful transformations arising from the faculties and sealed by the dharma-gate of the unconditioned (which is the "many causes")—surpasses all the offering implements of the devas (which is the "many fruits").
Commentary: The above illustrates how many causes produce many fruits. If one takes the former...
When many causes each produce individual articles of offering, this corresponds to the fourth phrase: "many causes producing a single effect" (which is the intended meaning of the present *Chao*).
However, within the *Chao*, for the sake of the argument, it cites the second phrase: "a single cause producing a single effect. That text states:
"All robes produced by the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*"; here, we cite these flowers as being produced from the *anutpattika-dharma*.

That which is produced from patience is precisely what is induced by its meaning; furthermore, the addition of the word "equal" (*sama*) serves as a cause for multiplicity, so that the citations in the sub-commentary (*śāstra*) below may be understood as following this pattern.

As for the *Chao* (Commentary), it is not that there is something else specifically indicated by relying on this [text], unlike the *Lotus Sūtra* where the robe symbolizes patience and the chamber symbolizes compassion; rather, here a single matter is used to symbolize a single meaning. Furthermore...

Because there is something signified that is distinct from the signifier, it is now clarified that a single phenomenon is simultaneously the person, the dharma, the basis, and the primary, possessing inexhaustible virtues.
Regarding the phrase "Zhixiang" (Ultimate Similarity) in the *Chao* (Commentary):
this refers to Zhixiang Temple on Mount Zhongnan, where the Tang dynasty Dharma Master Zhiyan [studied] the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The Second Patriarch received the transmission from Master Dushun, an emanation of Mañjuśrī.

Having mastered the mind [of the teaching], he composed his own commentary, which was compiled into one fascicle establishing the Ten Mysterious Gates (*daśa-guhya-dvāra*). Xianshou (Fazang) was a disciple of this school;
therefore, within the doctrinal systems of the Huayan school, the categories of "pure" and "mixed" were established. It was only upon reaching the *Tanxuan ji* that these were subsequently revised.

Regarding the "Gate of Broadness and Narrowness," it is said that there are two intentions; the following section clarifies the meaning of these revisions. Within the first intention, there are again two further points:

first, it addresses the confusion regarding the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*dharmatā-dharma*), establishing a hypothetical scenario to cite the opponent's defense, which also conflates the discussion by treating it solely from the perspective of phenomena;
second, it concedes that the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena (*dharma-dharma-anāvaraṇa*) may be established, yet subsequently refutes its conflation [with the previous point].

He immediately enters. ▲ In the *Jiaochao* (Commentary), regarding the distinction between the "Ultimate Aspect" (*zhixiang*) and "Practice" (*xing*), Qingliang’s intention in presenting the Ultimate Aspect should be illustrated by the following objection:

First, if it is argued that [the Ultimate Aspect] is "broad" because phenomena are pervasive according to principle, yet "narrow" because it does not destroy the characteristics of phenomena, this would also conflate the non-obstruction of phenomena and principle.
The answer is that we take what can accord with principle and clarify its non-obstruction with the unbroken characteristics.

Question: How can there be no confusion between the obstacle [of phenomena] and the non-obstruction of principle and phenomenon? If that were so, even the "Phenomena Reaching Principle" (Zhixiang) would include the capacity to accord with principle, as it clarifies non-obstruction.

Furthermore, if one asks whether the phenomena that accord with principle are themselves pervasive throughout all principles such that no other phenomena exist—because their characteristics are not destroyed—then since there *are* other phenomena, the distinction between these two gates would also fail to establish the Non-obstruction of Phenomenon and Phenomenon (Shishi Wuai). Answer: This is precisely what is meant by "pervasiveness."

If narrowness and width are identical, how can there be a distinction between the two gates? If that were so, then even at the level of ultimate characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they would be both pure and mixed;

how then could there be a distinction between the two gates? Second, if it is like the Diamond Ring Mountains—which are immeasurable in number—yet all can be accommodated within a single hair-tip, such that this vastness and narrowness do not obstruct one another, then this is the meaning of the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena (*shishi wuai*).

When [the hair] is formed, it again exists within the hair as the various mountain-phenomena; this is the meaning of "entering through the gate. If the hair is identical to the mountain-phenomena, then the hair is identical to the gate. Answer:
Although there is the sense of identity and entry, we take [this teaching] because it demonstrates the non-obstruction between the broad and the narrow.

If that were so, although there is the sense of identity and entry, we take [this teaching] because it demonstrates the non-obstruction between the pure and the mixed. If one follows the reasoning explained previously, the principle would be the same; now, however, I shall explain it according to the interpretation of Master Xianshou.
If the "characteristic of reaching all phenomena" (*sarvadharma-prāpti-lakṣaṇa*) were explained solely in terms of practice (*caryā*), its meaning would seem limited;
thus, Guishan remarked that his treatment of "purity and impurity" in relation to the ten thousand practices differs slightly from that of Xianshou.

Now, because the "Gate of Principal and Retinue" (*pramukha-parivāra-mukha*) was already discussed within the "Universal Ritual," and because we wish to establish the ten meanings, it is presented again here; thus, the teachings of the ancient masters are not neglected.
The meaning of this is that because the subtle principle is without fixed form, the above has distinguished between the ancient and modern regarding what is adopted or rejected.
The subsequent commentary on the text compares the blossoming of flowers: the myriad practices are in full bloom, which is likened to flowers opening upon brocade.
Although threads of five colors—blue, yellow, and so forth—are interwoven to produce the brocade, the colors of the flowers upon it are each distinct; this serves as a metaphor.
This refers to the pure and the mixed.
The *Chao* (Commentary) generally clarifies that "high" refers to the provisional (*upāya*) and "deep" refers to the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*); yet these may be mutually interpenetrating.

Furthermore, because it is deep, the provisional cannot fathom its height; and because the Lesser Vehicle is beyond hearing, the *Preface to the New Sūtra* states: "The One Ultimate proclaims the high."

Riding upon this, I shall now explain it according to the established principles of the text. Because the Dharma-gate is lofty and remote, although they have heard of it through expedient means, they do not believe it;
because the Dharma-gate is profound and subtle, although the Śrāvakas are present in the assembly, they do not hear it.

This is why these aspects of loftiness and profundity are distinguished and do not interpenetrate. Furthermore, the *Shu-yao* (Excerpts) poses the following question at the beginning of this section: "Since this major section has already clarified..."
Why are the former two not considered "beneficial"? This is the answer to that question. Regarding the term "admonishing by way of contrast":

for those who have not yet entered the provisional teachings of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha), one does not cause them to enter those, but rather causes them to give rise to faith and understanding in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). For those who have already entered [the provisional], one turns them back to cause them to enter the Perfect;
this constitutes being "beneficial. [From] the *Chao* (Commentary): "Taihua leaning against the heavens" refers to Taihua, which is two of the Five Peaks (*wuyue*).
Taishan is the Eastern Peak; "Tai" signifies that all things are in harmonious accord (*tai*) in the eastern direction.
Huashan is the Western Peak; "Hua" means "to obtain. This signifies that all things, having reached maturity, can be obtained.
As for Min and Eo brushing against the Han, Min and Eo are likewise the names of two mountains; "Han" refers to the Heavenly River (the Milky Way), which leans toward heaven and brushes across it.
The Han people all say that this refers to its loftiness. As for what is cited from the *Analects*, it is from the ninth chapter, "Zihan," where Yan Yuan exclaims:
"I look up at it and it seems ever higher; I drill into it and it seems ever firmer; I gaze at it and it is before me, yet suddenly it is behind me.
This refers to the sublime Way of the Master. Now, by borrowing the opening phrase, he praises the loftiness of this sutra.
The *Chao* (Commentary), citing the "Chapter on the Appearance," states that the sub-commentary (*xiàshū*) explains: the text first employs a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*).
The phrase "even if" (*shèyǒu*) appears to be a hypothetical assumption when compared to Maitreya’s praise of Sudhana.

It suggests that while other bodhisattvas require hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayuta* eons to fulfill their bodhisattva practices and vows, Sudhana is now able to purify the Buddha-lands in a single lifetime.
Regarding "lands" (*kṣetra*) and so forth, this is an instance of employing provisional means to manifest the ultimate reality; it is not a mere hypothesis.

As for the term *nayuta*, one hundred thousand is a *koṭi* (hundred million), ten *koṭis* is a *lakṣa* (ten million), ten *lakṣas* is a *koṭi* (in this context, ten million), and ten *koṭis* is a *nayuta*.
The *Kanding ji* states that the ninth numerical position corresponds to ten million times ten million. Regarding the "Dharma-gate of Great Majestic Virtue" (*mahā-tejas-dharmaparyāya*):
The *Jingxin lu* states: "This is precisely the one true mind. Question: If this Bodhisattva truly exists, in what stage does he reside? The sub-commentary (*shu*) answers:
"In principle, he corresponds to the Three Sages (*sanxian*), because upon entering the realization of the holy ones, he must believe in the Perfect [Teaching].

If considered according to the Path of Teaching (*jiaodao*), even after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, he has not yet entered the Mysterious [Ultimate]. The sub-commentary below states: "If considered according to the Path of Teaching, the three [stages] are provisionally established..."
If it is taught that since the Way is not yet true, the principle of attaining Buddhahood is likewise not true, then because the teaching is unreal, the mind harbors deluded thoughts;
to practice while carrying these deluded thoughts for many kalpas is but a laborious exertion in vain, ultimately failing to achieve the fruit of Buddhahood.

If, however, one refers to the realization of the Way, then after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* of cultivation, one must have already attained realization; since the provisional cultivation has already been profound.
After entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), one is then able to enter into reality and only then realize that deluded thoughts are fundamentally empty;

this is why ordinary beings can suddenly believe [this teaching], as their seeds have been formed by past causes and the permeation of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*). If they do not believe now, how could they hear it in the future?
Regarding the statement "if one obtains hearing," the following provides an explanatory interpretation: "being born into the family of the Tathāgata" refers to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
It says that realizing and attaining true suchness (tathatā) is called being born into the family of the Buddhas. Regarding the word "etcetera" (ādi), it refers to other passages which state:

"In accordance with the realm of all Tathāgatas, fully endowed with all the dharmas of Bodhisattvas, abiding in the realm of all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), and even penetrating deeply into the immeasurable realms of the Tathāgata," and so forth.
The *Jiaoshi* states: "Regarding 'the fish ascending the Dragon Gate,' the *Lüshi Chunqiu* says: 'Before the Dragon Gate was opened, the Yellow River overflowed greatly to the east of Mengmen;
this was called the Great Flood. Yu excavated the Dragon Gate, whereupon it began to flow south.
This is the present-day Longmen County in Jiangzhou. The commentary on the *Shangshu* states that Dragon Gate Mountain lies on the western border of Hedong Commandery."
The mountain is five thousand *ren* (one *ren* being seven feet) high and has three tiers;
its waters flow downward, and every year during the warmth of spring, crimson carp gather at the foot of this mountain and swim upstream.
Those who possess the destined lot ascend past the Dragon Gate, where heavenly fire spontaneously burns their tails and sheds their scales, enabling them to drive thunder and ride the lightning.
To rise upon the clouds and bring forth rain is to achieve transformation as a dragon (such as the capacity of one who enters the Avataṃsaka Sūtra).

If one fails to ascend, they will naturally have their foreheads marked with vermilion and shall not be permitted to ascend again, left to dry their gills beneath the Dragon Gate (as is the case with these so-called "provisional bodhisattvas").
Thus, the poem by Xie Xuanyi says: "Folding my wings, I hope to raise my head; riding the current, I fear my gills will be scorched"—this is precisely that meaning.

The profundity of this commentary is unfathomable; immediately following [the previous section], at the beginning of the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" within the assembly where the Tathāgata enters the *bimbi-samādhi*, the great multitude of Bodhisattvas all beheld various adorned realms in three locations—the Jeta Grove, the palace, and the void—and furthermore heard inconceivable dharmas and so forth.
This is because the great Śrāvakas neither saw nor heard them.

This is what is meant by "an auspicious assembly. The *Yi* says, "Success (*heng*) is the meeting of the auspicious," and it is further said that "an auspicious assembly is sufficient to accord with ritual propriety.
Here, the term is borrowed to designate the assembly where the Tathāgata preached the sutra.
Regarding the passage beginning "The *Śāstra* [states] that they all realize the True Dharma," the sub-commentary (*Ṭīkā*) below says:

"Now, these Śrāvakas are all Bodhisattvas; because he wishes to manifest the profound Dharma, he relies upon them as Śrāvakas. Therefore, the virtues praised herein contain both their original status (*mūla*) and their manifested traces (*vyañjana*). I shall now explain this by means of two gates:

first, regarding the traces, we examine the ten phrases from the perspective of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), all of which are the virtues of a Śrāvaka. First, they have attained direct realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the four [noble truths].

Because they have truly and well awakened to it (this refers precisely to the first of the three types of clear realization [abhisamaya] regarding the objects of perception in the *Abhidharmakośa*, while also encompassing the latter two);

second, because both have realized the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), having entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and already attained realization through wisdom that is free from artifice;
and third, because they have deeply penetrated the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), as their awakening has reached its ultimate limit. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
1. We enter equally into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), for there is no duality in principle regarding the three animals crossing the river;

2. We have forever emerged from the ocean of existence, for our rebirth has been exhausted; yet, because we lack great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), we ourselves have forever emerged [from it] (like the deer and the antelope escaping the enclosure);

3. Regarding the reliance on the Buddha’s qualities: these are the conditioned and unconditioned virtues (the *sopadhiśeṣa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa* nirvāṇas), which are attained by relying upon the Buddha.
Having attained one's own benefit, one is freed from the six fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);

this refers to the exhaustion of the "fetters of existence" (*bhava-saṃyojana*), namely the nine fetters (attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, doubt, view-grasping, adherence to precepts and rituals, envy, and stinginess) and the ten latent tendencies (the ten root afflictions which are difficult to resolve and thus called "fetters," and which enslave the mind and are thus called "tendencies").

Because these are abandoned in their active manifestation, one dwells in the seventh stage, the state of non-obstruction; because the seeds of the afflictive obstructions have perished, the eighth is that the mind is tranquil, just like...

1. "Space" refers to the mind being well-liberated (because it is free from the obstacles to meditative concentration, and because the mind associated with it has attained freedom from bondage). It is quiescent like space. 2–9.

"Permanently severing doubt and delusion" refers to wisdom being well-liberated (because it is free from the obstacles to the nature [of reality], and because it is free from the essence of ignorance, craving, and so forth).

One has no doubt regarding the Buddha (because by realizing these two, one attains the two kinds of merit: conditioned and unconditioned). 10. "Deeply believing in and entering the ocean of the Buddha's wisdom."

This clarifies that those not fixed in their nature can all turn their minds to enter the Buddha-wisdom (as the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Śāriputra, since even you have entered this sūtra through faith, how much more so the other śrāvakas;
the sūtra is itself the Buddha’s wisdom"). Second, regarding the praise directed at bodhisattvas based on their fundamental nature, it clarifies that these are all provisional:

first, they awaken to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and second, they are already fully equipped with skillful means (*upāya*) and are thus well able to enter the boundless limit (*ananta-paryanta*). (From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*)

1. Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is the reality and the realization of that reality is the limit; for all things that possess reality but lack a limit [are not ultimate]. 2. Because the truth of the threefold and twofold emptiness exhausts its source. 3.

Because one who possesses great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is able to enter [the world] without being defiled, thereby emerging forever [from saṃsāra]. 4. Because by relying on the ten powers (*daśabala*) and so forth, one is free from the views of the Lesser Vehicle.

5. Because by being neither interrupted nor simultaneous, one is then able to be free [from attachment]. 6. Because having already purified the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), there is no obstruction of duality.
Eighth, because they are eternally tranquil and realize that the eight bases are fundamentally empty;

ninth, because although they have not yet attained the unique qualities of a Buddha, they harbor no doubt regarding them (as stated in the "Chapter on Generating the Mind," where a bodhisattva harbors no doubt regarding the ten powers of a Buddha even though they have not yet attained them);

tenth, because they enter through the realization and faith in the knowledge of all modes (from the first stage upward, all rely upon the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom). Question: Since they already possess these virtues of the Fundamental Gate, how can they be deaf and blind?

The answer in the lower commentary states: "In all cases, the fundamental is set aside to follow the traces, so as to manifest the profound and mysterious depth of the unique cause and fruit of the One Vehicle.
Regarding "Jetavana" (Śītavana), the Chinese translation is "Victory over Battle" (*zhànshèng*); it was established by King Prasenajit for his crown prince.

Because the King achieved victory in battle when his son was first born, he named him [Jeta]. Because Sudatta purchased the Prince’s grove to offer it to the Buddha, the Prince’s gift of the grove became known by that name;
it signifies that by relying on a virtuous friend, one emerges victorious over the armies of Māra and the ordinary disciples.

*Śāriputra* (translated here as "Son of the Śāri" or "Son of the Śāri-heron"; the Dharma Master of the Mahāyāna says this refers to the hundred-tongued bird, also called the *śārikā*). *Yìcǎo* (Excerpts): [The text continues with the commentary].

In spring, the mother of the oriole has eyes as clear and sharp as those of that bird; thus he was named after his mother. His full name is Śāriputra, which means "Son of Śāri. According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, he is foremost in possessing inexhaustible wisdom and resolving all doubts. Mahāmaudgalyāyana (translated here as "Bean-Eater" or "Cai-shu-shi"):

In ancient times, there was a seer who lived in the mountains and ate beans; his mother was of that lineage, hence this clan name. According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, he is foremost in supernatural powers, being able to fly lightly and reach the ten directions. Mahākāśyapa (translated here as "Great Drinker of Light"):

His original clan was that of the Seers, and the light from the body of the Venerable One so outshone the sun and moon that they were eclipsed by it. According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, he was a man of great wealth in Rājagṛha.

The elder was named Kāvi; his wife was named Dhanā; their son was named Piṇḍola-bharadvāja; and his wife was named Bhadrā. Their household was a thousand times more prosperous than that of King Bimbisāra, such that none among the sixteen great kingdoms could rival them as neighbors.

"Piṇḍola" is the name of Kāśyapa; because he was born after his father prayed before this tree, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Fu-fa-zang-chuan) states: "After the parinirvāṇa of Vipaśyin Buddha, the golden image at his stupa became worn and damaged. A poor woman obtained a gold bead and requested a smith to plate it with thin gold. The master-artisan joyfully polished and refined it until the Buddha’s image was complete.

He then made a vow to become her husband for ninety-one kalpas, remaining in celestial and human realms with bodies always golden in color and constantly experiencing happiness. Finally, they became the husband and wife of Kāśyapa, fearing that [the former artisan] might incur the punishment of the King of Victory."

Subtracting one plow, only nine hundred and ninety pairs of oxen are used for the golden plow. It is further said that in his household, even the lowest quality woolen cloth (*kambala*) is worth a hundred thousand taels of gold; when driven ten feet into the ground with a nail, the cloth does not tear or break, remaining no different from its original state.

There are sixty treasuries of gold grain, each treasury containing three hundred and forty *hu*. It is also said that *Kṣubhyatā* gold lies at the bottom of turbid water, its brilliance penetrating through to the surface;

in the dark, it extinguishes the darkness. The bodily radiance of Kāśyapa surpasses this gold, illuminating an area of one *yojana*. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Among those who practice the eleven *dhūta* ascetic practices within the Buddha-dharma, Mahākāśyapa is foremost. He is called "Great" (*Mahā-*) to distinguish him from other Kāśyapas. Revata.

[The Buddha] often [spoke of this as] the "Star Chamber" (*tārakā-śālā*), because it is the place where one makes offerings to the living; thus it is also called the "Conjoined Harmony. Regarding the wisdom attained through awakening, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:

This person was staying overnight in an empty pavilion when he saw two ghosts contending over a corpse, both claiming, "I brought this here first! The two ghosts spoke together and asked him to divide it. The man truly saw a small ghost bringing it. When questioned by the ghosts, he thought to himself:

"If I say I brought it, that one will surely be harmed since he did not get it. I would rather die speaking the truth than perish with a lie. He then answered according to reality: "The small saint (*kṣudra-ārya*) brought it. Upon hearing this, the great ghost seized the small one by his hands and feet and devoured him, while the ghost who had obtained the corpse then took possession of the body.
