Then, turning his body and head like the circular movement of an elephant king, he looked back at those who were vessels for the Dharma. No [part of his body] remained unturned.
Because it is light and agile, its manifestation directs [the mind] toward the objective without omission or concealment;
thus it is said: "O Bhikṣu, may I likewise obtain all that you possess—such a physical body, such a voice, such marks and signs, and such sovereignty.
Regarding the ten kinds of tireless minds, the first is accumulation.
1. To have a mind free from weariness regarding all roots of goodness; 2. To serve and make offerings to all Buddhas while transcending dualistic views;
3. To seek all Buddha-dharmas; 4. To practice all pāramitās; 5. To accomplish all bodhisattva samādhis; 6.
To enter successively into all three periods of time; 7. To universally adorn and purify the buddha-fields of the ten directions; 8. To teach.
9. To tame and transform all sentient beings through emanations; 10. To accomplish the bodhisattva practices throughout all lands and all eons;

and for the sake of maturing all sentient beings, to practice as many perfections as there are atoms in all Buddha-lands to achieve the ten powers of a Tathāgata—thus, in this sequence, one acts for the sake of bringing all to maturity.
The realm of sentient beings accomplishes all the powers of the Tathāgata (the nine sections below all contain the phrase "with a mind free from weariness").

The sub-commentary explains: "The Dharma-gates are inexhaustible and sentient beings are boundless; if one practices while grasping at signs, weariness will arise after many lifetimes. If one becomes weary, one falls back into the two vehicles.
If one practices without craving or views, there will be no weariness. Being free from weariness leads to the fruit of Buddhahood."
"If even distant objects are not [obstructed], how much less so my own body? Thus it is said that the attainment of samādhi is named "Unimpeded Eye" (*anāvaraṇa-cakṣus*).
The commentary provides three meanings: first, because it can see while free from obstructions; second, because there is no hindrance to what is seen; third, because it possesses manifold functions.

That is to say, within this Unimpeded Eye, there are manifold functions such as the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*). Although...

Because this capacity is possessed while being devoid of the characteristics of seeing, it is called *samādhi*. Since one attains this *samādhi*, the following section specifically clarifies that there are four functions of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*):
first, "seeing everything" is the function of the divine eye; second, "and also hearing" is the function of the divine ear;
third, "also able to observe" is the function of knowing others' minds; fourth, "also able to recollect" is the function of recollecting past lives. (End of Sub-commentary)
It is said that because the Single Eye possesses these four functions, it is called "unimpeded. Regarding the tenfold turning of the wheel of Dharma:
first, it is fully endowed with the pure wisdom of the four fearlessnesses; second, it gives birth to the four analytical eloquences (*pratisaṃvid*) in accordance with the sounds of speech;

third, it is well able to expound and clarify the characteristics of the four noble truths; fourth, it accords with the unimpeded liberation of all Buddhas; fifth, it is able to cause sentient beings...
1. Attaining birth with a mind of pure faith; 2. Words that are never in vain; 3. Being able to uproot all sufferings; 4. Being sustained by the power of great compassionate vows; 5.
Following the emergence of sounds that pervade all worlds; 6. Preaching the Dharma without interruption for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; 7.

Giving rise to the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and samādhis; 8. [The tenth item is indicated by the character "ten" at the end.]
All those who preach the Dharma do so in ten ways: first, by teaching that all phenomena arise from conditions; second, by teaching that all are like illusions; third, by being free from conflict;
fourth, by being boundless; fifth, by having no dependence; sixth, by being like a vajra; seventh, by being entirely suchness;
eighth, by being entirely quiescent; ninth, by being entirely transcendent; and tenth, by abiding in the single meaning.
The Innate Accomplishment (in each of the nine [preceding] cases, the phrase "all dharmas" is stated): as for the ten eloquences (*pratibhāna*), they are: first, non-conceptual eloquence;
second, effortless eloquence; third, unattached eloquence; fourth, eloquence that thoroughly understands reality; fifth, unobstructed eloquence; sixth, eloquence through the Buddha’s empowerment;
seventh, eloquence through self-awakening; eighth, eloquence skillful in the discrimination of words and phrases; ninth, eloquence of true speech; tenth, eloquence that accords with...
"Causing the minds of all sentient beings to rejoice" (the phrase "possessing eloquence" [辯才] applies to all nine items above). The *Zhenyuan Shu* states:

"The meanings of the supernormal power of the spiritual realm (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*), the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-jñāna*), and so forth, are contained within the summary. The *Xuanji* states: "The current *Chao* contains six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). The first four are understandable;

furthermore, the 'exhaustion of outflows' mentioned below at that point refers to the supernormal power of the spiritual realm (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*). Thus, by expanding the six into ten, the six become ten."

There are ten supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): regarding the divine eye, it is divided into two based on the present and the future (the divine eye power [1] and [2] extending through all kalpas to the end of the future);
regarding the divine ear, it is divided into five based on sounds and linguistic expressions (the unobstructed, pure divine ear [5] and [7] the excellent discrimination of all speech);

regarding the power of psychic transformation (*ṛddhi*), it is divided into six based on karmic function and the physical body (the bodiless, non-active movement to all lands [6] and [8] entering into countless physical bodies); and [9] the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

The total of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) is divided into ninety-nine [categories] (the ten knowledges of all phenomena encompassing the cessation-samādhi of all phenomena).
One and three are not divided (one being the knowledge of others' minds, and three being the knowledge of past abodes). Thus, six become ten.

Based on the *Jixuan* (Collected Mysteries), if one intends toward quiescent illumination, then the application of the non-dual samādhi is manifested through many gates below. Since this is so, the examples of the inexhaustible many gates follow accordingly.

Now, as for the "ten thousand bodhicittas," this refers to the four immeasurable minds (great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity) and the six pāramitās (generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom).
These ten [categories] mutually support one another to become a hundred; the hundreds mutually support one another to become a thousand;
and the thousands mutually support one another to become ten thousand—thus, ten thousand is ten times one thousand. As for the "ten thousand samādhis," the first is the Great Universal Radiance.
1. The two sublime lights of samādhi; 2. The great samādhi; 3. Successively traveling through all lands; 4. Purifying the conduct of body and mind;
5. Knowing the treasury of past adornments; 6. The treasury of the light of wisdom; 7. Fully knowing the Buddha-adornments of all worlds;
8. The diverse bodies of sentient beings; 9. Sovereignty over the dharma-realm; 10. The absence of...
The Obstructing Wheel (the eight lower stages all contain the words of the Great Samādhi) likewise consists of ten that mutually support one another to become a hundred, a thousand, and ten thousand;
it is the same for the ten thousand *pāramitās*, which can be understood as being explained in terms of the ten perfections. At that time, Mañjuśrī [bestows] the Dharma of Superior Progress below;
this also has two parts: first, he instructs and exhorts those above, clarifying only the great mind without weariness, and now he causes them to dwell extensively.

Regarding the practice of vows and advancement, this explains the universal cultivation of speech for the sake of accomplishment; below, it clarifies how benefits are obtained through successive stages. Question:
To which of the three preceding positions do these six thousand bhikṣus belong? Answer: There are three explanations.

First, according to the commentary below, it is said that the three types of capacities in the final assembly [the *Bhikṣu-parivarta*] are distinct from the first two assemblies (the *Bhikṣu-parivarta* and the *Sarva-yāna-parivarta*). Since they have not yet long resided in faith, they still...

Because they are indeterminate, Sudhana’s faith can ultimately lead to realization; therefore, although the six thousand stages are situated within the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*), they are subsumed under the stage of "seeing and hearing" (*darśana-śravaṇa*).
Question: If this is so, how can one attain the ten supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) that follow the stages? Answer:

Because the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) subsumes the faculties and establishes the Great Resolve (*mahācitta*), it takes the beginning to encompass the end. Second, in terms of meaning, these correspond to the stage of "practice and understanding" (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) and "universal birth" (*sarvatra-janman*).
Because it encompasses the dharmas of the five stages, one attains the ten supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth.

If one were merely at the stage of the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*), one would be identical to those in the provisional teachings who turn from the Small Vehicle to enter the Great; practicing sequentially starting from the ten levels of faith, how could this be called "surpassing the provisional"?
Question: If that is so, how should one reconcile this with what is stated in the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) below? Answer: The sub-commentary below [addresses] the former two...

Because the capacity for awakening does not require passing through successive encounters with spiritual friends, it is indicated that [the practitioner] has not long resided in faith; whereas Sudhana’s universal pilgrimage indicates that he has reached the ultimate mind.
This is based on one sense of the symbolic teaching (*dharmaparyāya*), which does not violate the sequential order; thus, it corresponds to the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).
However, because this stage of faith universally encompasses all five stages, it differs from other schools. It is only because it instantaneously possesses all dharmas that it is so designated.
The realization of the Way (*mārga-siddhi*) is not the fixed stage of the ten levels of faith;

therefore, the *Shu-chao* explains that by possessing the ten universal practices, one achieves all Buddha-dharmas, which is precisely the "realization of the Way. Third, it says this is "the birth of entry into realization.

Since the previous *Chao* already stated that the "threefold birth of entry into realization" corresponds to the latter two lines [of the verse], are these two lines not, in fact, the two stages of sudden realization that transcend the provisional? If...
If one takes only the sudden realization (*tun-cheng*) from the commentary as two phrases, there is the fault that the upper and lower phrases are not symmetrical;
this is because the first two phrases already encompass both benefits. Therefore, we know that this section is cited collectively as proof for the arising of entry (*zheng-ru sheng*).

Question: According to this, [the sudden realization] alone universally encompasses the five stages (*wu-wei*). As for the "ten penetrations" (*shi-tong*), these refer to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*deng-jue-wei*).

Therefore, how can there be no meaning of "realization and entry"? The answer is: although his unimpeded eye encompasses only the five stages, within the section on the superior progression (*viśeṣa-gati*), it says:
"Abiding in the conduct of Samantabhadra; having abided in the conduct of Samantabhadra, one enters the ocean of great vows;
and having accomplished the great vows, the mind becomes pure," and so forth. Is this not identical to Sudhana’s [attainment] at the stage of Samantabhadra?

Is it that one suddenly realizes the meaning of the Dharma-realm within the body? Although these three explanations each rely on a particular principle and may be accepted or rejected according to one's inclination, according to the intent of the present *Chao*, the latter interpretation is superior.
Regarding the phrase "Qiming of the Eastern Temple" and so forth: the *Mao Shi* states, "In the east is Qiming," and the *Erya* states, "The bright star is called Qiming.
The commentary notes that this refers to the planet Venus (*Taibai*). When it appears in the east at dawn, it is Qiming; when it appears in the west at dusk, it is Taibai.
Based on this, Qiming is simply the name for the bright star in the eastern direction. Now, [this refers to] the Shunfucheng [Temple].

Furthermore, because it specifically awakens the luminous wisdom of Sudhana, it is called "Awakening the Light" (*Qiming*). It signifies that the luminous wisdom is first awakened and the mind of faith is established.
As for "temple" (*miao*), it refers to appearance; it is the place where the physical form of one's ancestors resides.
Since the stupa within now contains the physical form of the World-Honored One, it is called a "temple. Because the temple is located to the east of Bhadra City, it is called the "Eastern Temple."
The second phrase refers to wisdom illuminating the non-dual aspect, as fully explained in the *Śāstra* (Commentary).

Regarding the *Śāstra*’s exhortation to "arouse the mind" and so forth, this refers to the six thousand [eons] of the "unbroken aspect," which correspond to the stage of arousing the mind (*cittotpāda*). The subsequent *Vṛtti* (Sub-commentary) states:

"As it is said in the 'Chapter on Arousing the Mind' (*Cittotpāda-parivarta*). Since this specifically points to the "Chapter on Arousing the Mind," even though this is the initial resolve (*prathama-citta*), it already encompasses the entire stages [of the path].
Ultimately, this is different from the initial resolve of those in the three vehicles. Regarding "Fucheng" (City of Blessings):
because the people dwelling in that city possess much merit and virtue, it is called Fucheng. The city represents the prevention of wrongdoing;

that is, all sentient beings emerge from within the Single True Dharma-realm. Because the people dwelling within this True Realm possess blessings, they are able to shield themselves against and prevent transgressions and faults. To the east is...

It represents the head of all directions and the first appearance of the dawn; it symbolizes the initial entry into the Way through the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) by manifesting the portion of merit that accords with goodness.
Furthermore, it symbolizes the fundamental basis for entering the stage of merit and wisdom (*puṇya-jñāna*). *Śāla* means "lofty and far-reaching" because its forest trees stand tall and dense;
it symbolizes the future arising of the adornments of the myriad practices (*sādhana*) to subdue and overcome [obstacles]. It also represents the foundation established by the Buddhas of the past.
Regarding the Great Stūpa of Words upon which all Buddhas equally rely—the true nature of the fundamental awakening of the *dharmadhātu*—it is the place for returning to truth.
In Sanskrit it is called *stūpa*, which here means "highly manifest. Formerly it was called *taba*; its meaning is "the place for returning to the source.
Tripitaka Master Jikyo said: "This city is in South India; the great stūpa is to the east of the city."
Regarding the stupa of an ancient Buddha, this stupa already existed during the Buddha’s lifetime; the Tripitaka Master personally visited its site, where the stupa was immense.
While musical performances were offered from the eastern side, they could not be heard from the western side.
Even now, the people residing here frequently sing the "Song of Sudhana. The inhabitants of this city all possess the roots of goodness conducive to liberation. III.
The worthy one is fit to be a vessel for the Way. Regarding the passage on Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: previously he was called a Bodhisattva;
here he is called a "Kumāra" (youth) to signify his initial entry into the Buddha-dharma, and also to reveal that one cannot enter it without the practice of a youth.
The *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states: "A child of fifteen years is called a 'tóng' (youth); 'tóng' means solitary. From the age of seven until ten..."
The reason those five years are all designated as "childhood" is that the *taihe* (Great Harmony) has not yet dispersed.

Thus, when the sutras refer to great bodhisattvas such as Mañjuśrī, Sudhana, Ratnakūṭa, and Ratnacandra as "children," it does not mean they are merely young in age. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"For instance, Mañjuśrī possesses the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and so forth, fully embodying all the deeds of a Buddha."

Regarding the dwelling on the stage of *kumārabhūmi* (translated here as "Child" or "Youth"): it is said that if a bodhisattva, from the first generation of the mind of awakening, abandons desire until reaching *bodhi*, this is called being a "Child.

Furthermore, another interpretation states that because one internally realizes the true and eternal while remaining free from grasping—just as a worldly child is unstained by sensory forms—it is called the "stage of the Child.
As for the phrase "five hundred upāsakas," etc., [this is explained] in the sub-commentary below.

The statement that each group consists of five hundred signifies that the realization and entry into the five stages are common to the fourfold assembly; together, they constitute the two thousand practices of Samantabhadra.
As for the statement that Sudhana is "one," it refers to the manifestation of wealth at the very moment of his birth, which is a sign of goodness; thus he is named Sudhana.
While the Lesser Sage (Śāriputra) was honored as "Emptiness-born" because his room was empty, the Great Being (Mañjuśrī) was noble as "Virtue-born" because he possessed abundant Dharma-wealth.

Furthermore, "a mind that accords with principle" is called *śubha* (virtue); "the inexhaustible accumulation of merit" is called *dhana* (wealth). Regarding the statement that it distinguishes [this] from other *paryāya* (contemplations) and so forth:

it is because one knows this [person] is not of the common sort and has uniquely attracted the compassionate regard (*saṃgraha*) of the Sage; thus, the name "Sudhana" (Good Wealth) was established based on this. Regarding the statement that it causes one to "recollect" and so forth: it is to prevent self-deprecation.
Regarding the statement "teaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate": it means that for others who do not possess these faculties, [the teaching] would not be suitable.
It is fitting to further elaborate upon these previous words by speaking in verse. The verse says:

"The three realms of existence are its city walls, pride is its ramparts, The various destinies are its gates, and the waters of craving are its moat. The wheel of vows and great compassion is its hub, faith is its axle, and patient endurance is its pinion;
Adorned with the jewels of merit, may I be carried by this vehicle. Now, regarding the meaning of this passage:

Furthermore, those who previously went to the City of Blessings did so because their faculties were still subtle, they had not yet resolved their minds [on enlightenment], and because Great Compassion was profound;

now that Meghashiri has departed and Sudhana goes to seek him, it is because his capacity has gradually become superior, he has already resolved his mind, and it serves to manifest the gravity of the Dharma.
Finally, Samantabhadra does not come to Sudhana and Sudhana does not go to him, thereby manifesting that at the stage where the Dharma-realm is perfected, there is no coming or going.

Regarding the phrase "because it has come": the *Chao* states that "wisdom illuminates the non-dual aspect" means that when practice is perfected and ultimate, clear awakening resides within one's breast.
This illumination of the preceding practices and so forth is solely the single, perfect wisdom; there are no further distinctions such as priority or posteriority, clarity or obscurity.

It is like a mirror when dust is cleared away and it becomes bright—how could there be any distinction between prior and subsequent, or clarity and obscurity? The *Chao* quotes the Sūtra, saying: "At this time..."

Because both [the views of] inferior faith and understanding are severed, one does not see the present body; yet because the reflection back upon oneself has not shifted from the state of faith, one extends the right hand.
Furthermore, not seeing is true seeing, for it is simply the realization that one’s own mind is empty *prajñā*.

Thus, the statement "passing beyond one hundred and ten *yojanas*" symbolizes that each of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is fully endowed with all the qualities of the stages.

Because of their merit, the characteristics of the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) are not distinct from those of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); therefore, the three stages of worthiness are not separately opened up.

If one considers the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) as the further advancement of the tenth stage, then the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) are opened up. To say that they "transcend" means they thoroughly transcend the preceding positions;

because initial faith encompasses the ultimate fruit, it is said to "extend afar"; because the practice of compliance is accomplished, it is said to be the "right hand. However, this is a transcendence.
Regarding the fault of exceeding the *yojana* in measure: by measuring the crown of the head, it signifies inclusion;

furthermore, by placing the Universal Dharma (*samantadharma*) upon the crown of the heart, faith reaches its ultimate limit, and thus these words are spoken. Below, the Dharma-gate is shown through instruction: this involves citing the loss to reveal the attainment, consisting of nine phrases.
Of these, the first seven lack the cause, while the first lacks the root of practice and the second lacks the inferiority of mind due to seeking the Lesser Vehicle.
There are nine obstacles: first, sorrow and regret regarding birth and death; second, the lack of one of the three [protective] powers; third, the failure to advance in the four [virtuous] practices;

fourth, stagnation in a single good deed; fifth, not seeking extensively; sixth, failing to give rise to the non-abiding vows; and finally, the deficiency of conditions for the latter two. These nine types take the first as their root;
if the first is lacking, all eight of the others are likewise deficient. Although these eight are mentioned, the underlying intent lies in [the first].
To begin with, the primary intent of this sutra is to provide an indirect exposition (*paryudāsa*) that praises initial faith;
the phrase "cannot be fully understood" and what follows below further demonstrate that if faith is lacking, one cannot achieve the beneficial results. There are fifteen phrases;

the first five concern the objects of knowledge—the principles and phenomena—which comprise the four dharmas of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit. The first phrase refers to the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

The second phrase concerns the principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); the third phrase concerns the teaching; the fourth phrase concerns practice; and the fifth phrase concerns the fruit. The final ten phrases concern the scope of the knower;

this can be understood by reflecting upon them. In the *Commentary*, it says that "faith and wisdom are non-dual," meaning that the faith produced through cultivation and the ultimate wisdom of perfection are non-dual.
If one takes the Immovable Wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) as the beginning, then it refers to the text itself.

The Buddha of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* is named Acala (Immovable), which represents original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*). The name "Initial Awakening" refers to subsequent awakening (*paścāt-awakening*).
Because the subsequent merges with the original, they are likewise non-dual.

Regarding the phrase in the Commentary, "entrusting stages to Sudhana and others": Sudhana is the subject who entrusts himself, while the various stages and the various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) are the objects to whom he entrusts himself.
Regarding the "Provisional Stations" (*āśraya*), if explained according to their specific divisions, they consist of five aspects: 1.

From Mañjuśrī down to Gopā, forty-one persons represent the aspect of practicing by relying on provisional stations; 2. From Māyā downward, eleven persons represent the aspect of entering reality by converging conditions;
3. Maitreya alone represents the aspect of accomplishing causes by encompassing virtues; 4. The second meeting with Mañjuśrī [represents the final aspect].
The name "Wisdom Illuminating the Non-dual Aspect" refers to the five views; the name "Samantabhadra" manifests the aspect of the vastness of the cause. Now, regarding the general clarification:

the first phrase, beginning with the vision of Mañjuśrī, pertains to the stage prior to the ten faiths (*śraddhā*), while the latter phrase, culminating in the vision of Samantabhadra, signifies the perfection of the cause.

As for the term "seeking in the south," the Master of the Commentary (*ṭīkākāra*) states that those who serve as spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) mostly reside in the south, whereas on the stages themselves there is no fixed direction; after the stages, they appear in all directions.
Second, as for why the south is so called, there are five meanings in antiquity: the first pertains to the physical fact, while the remaining four pertain to its symbolic significance.

First, taking one direction as an example, the virtuous friends already present in a single quarter are themselves immeasurable, let alone those in the other nine directions. Second, it clarifies the meaning of illumination: it symbolizes abandoning darkness and turning toward wisdom.
The brightness of the south allows all things to see one another; that the sages face south is derived from this principle. Third...
Third is the meaning of "center," as it is free from the deviance of the two extremes—the eastern and western—and accords with the central, true path of reality.
Fourth is the meaning of "birth," for the south presides over yang and the growth of all things; it signifies the increase of the practices of Sudhana. Fifth is the meaning of "conformity":
turning one's back to the left and facing toward the right constitutes conformity. This is because the local custom of the Western Regions is such that cities, gardens, and residences all face east.

"From the east to the south, following the turning of the sun and moon" (now beginning with the arousal of the mind [bodhicitta] to the east of Fucheng, then proceeding southward to seek further, turning left toward the north and then right) is because it manifests Sudhana’s accordance with the teachings and principles.
On the grounds (*bhūmi*), one realizes the truth directly, free from the marks of realization;

yet, regarding the unimpeded presence or absence of subsequent activity on the grounds, here too—according to the general meaning—it is said that he "seeks to the south. Thus, the Preface to the New Sutra [states]: [text follows].
The phrase "Yunming zheng wei nanfang jin nan yi" (Cloud-Ming is precisely the limit of the south) means that it is based on the perfection [of virtue], as explained below in the *Shao* (Commentary).
Regarding "De-yun" (Virtue-Cloud), this refers to the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) of the first stage (*bhūmi*). The sub-commentary (*Shu*) states: "Possessing virtues like clouds.
Thus, clouds have four meanings, which correspond respectively [to the four virtues]: 1) universality; 2) moisture; 3) shelter; and 4) pouring rain.
Regarding the virtues of meditative concentration, merit, compassion, and wisdom, it is said that reaching Gopā means surpassing the thirty-eight individuals in the intermediate stages.
Specifically, reaching Maitreyī corresponds to the ten abodes (*bhūmi*); from the bhikṣu Sudarśana to the non-Buddhist Sarvagāmin corresponds to the ten practices (*caryā*);
from the merchant Dhūpa to the earth goddess Sthāvarā corresponds to the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*); and from the night goddess Vasanti... [and so forth].
Regarding Gopā: she is associated with the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Since Gopā was the Buddha’s consort, "Gopā" means "guardian of the great earth.
As a laywoman, she served as her parents’ guardian; as a princess, she guarded the royal domain.

Now, as his consort, she is named after her master (*adhipati-nirdeśa*), signifying that the ten stages are perfected and there is no ground she does not protect. Furthermore, the Crown Prince had three consorts: one—
The first is named Gopā, the second Yaśodharā, and the third Manuṣyā; because she represents the ultimate state of the causal stage, the first is selected here.
Regarding "Māyā" and those who follow: she is the Mother of the Buddha. Her full name is Mahāmāyā, which translates as "Great Illusion.
Because she understood all phenomena to be like an illusion, she attained the liberation of great vow-illusion-wisdom (*mahāpraṇidhāna-māyājñāna*).
The gates of liberation are the general characteristics for entering reality by gathering conditions; the subsequent nine [deities] are the specific characteristics. Namely:
the goddess Devī Prabhāketu attains illusory wisdom and the power of mindfulness; the youth Viśvabhadra attains illusory wisdom and mastery of all arts;
the youth Akṣayamati attains illusory wisdom and the alphabet; and the laywoman Bhadrottamā attains illusory wisdom and the liberation of non-reliance.
The Elder attained the Illusion-like Wisdom of Non-attachment; the Elder Wondrous Moon attained the Illusion-like Wisdom of Unsurpassed Radiance of Knowledge;
the Elder Unconquerable Lord attained the Illusion-like Wisdom of the Inexhaustible Mark; the Brahmin Most Quiescent attained the Illusion-like Wisdom of Sincere Vow-Speech;
and Guṇākara attained the Illusion-like Wisdom of Returning Knowledge to the Gateway of Illusion. Thus, including the previous five, there are ten in total, making eleven people in all.
To bring together the conditions for entering the true mark (*dharmatā*), this section now provides a general exposition that also includes Maitreya and the vision of Mañjuśrī;
both of these aspects constitute the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). The *Commentary* states: "Below, it is the same as the transformation-bodies of Samantabhadra," and further:
"Below, it compares the ocean of lands entered. Regarding the phrase "the lands within a single pore," this summarizes the equality and universal pervasiveness [of the dharmadhātu].
(Thus he proceeds; the following is the summary: "nor does he [proceed] equally in every thought-moment throughout all realms.

Regarding the phrase "thus he proceeds," the preceding scripture states that when Sudhana takes a single step within a pore of a Buddha-field, he passes through as many worlds as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Even if he were to proceed in this manner for all future eons, he would still not be able to know [the full extent].

Regarding the phrase "the sequence of oceans of lands within a single pore," and so forth, the statement that they do not vanish from this land and so on is because the phenomena of vanishing and appearing are identical to the *dharmatā*.
Thus, there is vanishing yet no vanishing, and appearing yet no appearing; for within the true *dharmatā*, there is neither emergence nor disappearance.
This is because, through the non-obstruction of phenomenon and principle, this and that are mutually identical; it is precisely within the phenomenon [that this is realized].
The characteristic of non-obstruction regarding phenomena consists of three points: first, this land is that land, and one land is many lands;
second, this step is that step, and one step is many steps; third, one thought-moment is immeasurable kalpas.
Furthermore, because these characteristics of "this" and "that" are vividly present, the secret and the manifest are both established; thus, these various times and places mutually interpenetrate.
Because in the ancient [state of] the Indra’s Net, the multilayered [realms] are simultaneously and fully present, all being immovable.

Regarding the phrase "At this time" in the *Chao* (Commentary): the first part clarifies that the stage is fulfilled and equal to the Buddha; the initial phrase indicates that one has spontaneously attained it, while the remainder is equal to what was stated above.

First, the causes are perfected; next, the fruits are fulfilled. The section on "one body" below specifically reveals the characteristics of equality. The sub-commentary (*Shu*) states: "This is the meaning."
When one attains equal enlightenment by virtue of being equal to the Buddha, the causal stage is already perfected and there is nothing further to be cultivated;

therefore, it is said to be "equal" without further seeking. Thus, the practice of cause and effect is fully accomplished in a single lifetime through sequential development, and it is not merely that the initial and final stages of principle-contemplation are perfectly integrated.
The *Śāstra* analyzes the subtle dust; here, "dust" (*rajas*) serves as a metaphor for emotional thoughts (*citta-vikalpa*), while the "sūtra" serves as a metaphor for Buddha-wisdom (*buddha-jñāna*).

Since within each particle of dust analyzed in this metaphorical sūtra, the Dharma corresponds to every thought-moment, the resultant wisdom (*phala-jñāna*) is thus manifested from the causal stage of sentient beings' emotional dust.

Therefore, the commentary states: "This section reveals the benefit of attaining the resultant fruit through the causes. The *Preface to the New Sūtra* states: "Within emotional dust there is the sūtra of wisdom."
The ocean has no exterior.
Regarding the passage from the "Chapter on Manifestation" (*Prakaraṇa*) and others, the meaning of that chapter concerns the mental karma (*manas-karman*).

As for the statement in the Great Sūtra, "the Buddha’s wisdom is boundless and his intrinsic virtue is perfected," the phrase "its measure equals the three thousandfold world system" means that because wisdom accords with reality (*tathatā*), it is said to be "three."

Regarding the "thousandfold world-system," the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "The four great continents, the sun and moon, Mount Sumeru, the six heavens of the desire realm, and the Brahma worlds—each of these one thousand is called a small thousandfold world-system.
A thousand times this small thousandfold world-system is called a medium thousandfold world-system. A thousand times this [medium system] is the great thousandfold world-system;
all of these undergo formation and destruction simultaneously. As for the phrase "within a single speck of dust," it refers to being covered by a single delusion.
Because they are real, two [cases] are small; because they contain the great, three [cases] are large; because they possess many, all objects are likewise so.
This is because there is not a single sentient being who does not possess Buddha-wisdom. There is one wise person who, by citing the sutras below, benefits sentient beings.
"Buddha-wisdom" below serves to combine and reveal the cause. As for the combination of delusive thoughts with objects, the Buddhas combine them with the wise person, causing him to... [proceed].
"Attaining fruition as a benefit" is also a passage from the Sūtra that demonstrates below how fruition is attained in every thought-moment;

it is precisely the section on the manifestation of Bodhi within that chapter. The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) below states: "This clarifies that [fruition] is universally present in all minds, constantly attained in every thought-moment without boundaries.
Regarding this inquiry and its explanation, it says: "There are two meanings for 'not being separate': first, sentient beings..."
Because the body and mind are what the Buddha has realized, this reveals the cause.

Second, because they are entirely identical to the nature of bodhi, if one accords with this nature of bodhi in every thought-moment, then in every thought-moment one accomplishes bodhi; this constitutes the benefit of realizing the fruit.
Regarding the benefit of accomplishing practice and vows, a questioner asks: "Other teachings all state that one vows to deliver infinite sentient beings;

why does this sutra alone [not mention it]? Does it not also accomplish such benefit? The answer is: Although their vow to exhaust all sentient beings is the same as the present one, it lacks the meaning of fulfilling practice in every single dust-mote (*rajas*).
Therefore, they differ. This is because those [other teachings] do not take all dust-motes as their basis.
Within all those lands, one undergoes miraculous birth throughout the exhaustion of kalpas in order to fulfill their vows.
If this is so, how could the vows in other teachings be in vain? The answer is: not so; it is simply that within those various lands, one practices and undergoes miraculous births.

Now, because we are speaking in terms of every atom being in accord with the nature (*dharmatā*), one attains [this state] throughout all the atoms of all lands. Reflecting upon these words, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states: [The text continues: "As for what is said in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*..."
In the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the section on "Correct Exposition" (*samyag-deśanā*), there are ten kinds of great vows that form an inexhaustible connection;
among these ten kinds of inexhaustibility, only one is cited here. Although the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) is indeed inexhaustible, this anticipates and addresses a potential objection:
if the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible, why does a bodhisattva make a vow to bring that realm of sentient beings to its end?
This is the answer. "Universally opening" refers to the arousal of the ten great vows with the desire to exhaust the realm of sentient beings, which is itself inexhaustible.

The citation regarding the "eternal and constant" is from the *Xianshou Zhigui* (The Essential Return of the Worthy Head), specifically the passage beginning with "There is not a single land... and continuing through the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
In the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, it says: "O Son of the Buddha, I do not see a single Buddha-land wherein the Tathāgata does not teach these ten stages.
Regarding the statement that there are some who teach them and some who do not: this is a summary of the two preceding points;

since they are both constant and universal across time and place, it is said that each accords with principle. As the *Avatamsaka-sūtra* (Chapter on Manifestation) states: "It accords with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)."
Because the Tathāgata’s manifestation is preached as inconceivable, the *Xiàxià Shū* (Lower-Lower Commentary) on my ocean of Dharma states:
"First, by way of reductio ad absurdum, it is shown that there is nothing he cannot relinquish. If there is not even a single passage that he does not relinquish, how much more so an entire section?
This is because a single passage is the 'one' that is identical to all, just like a single drop of water from the ocean."

Regarding the metaphor of "the light of wisdom eclipsing [other lights]": this refers to the dharma by way of a simile. The actual simile should be expressed as "the light of the sun eclipsing other luminaries.
As for the term *gǎorì* (the bright rising sun): when the sun is beneath the wood, it is called *yǎorì*;
when the sun is within the wood, it is called *dōng*; and when the sun is above the wood, it is called *gǎo*. This conveys the meaning of ascending brilliance. It is said to be "resplendent" (*lì*).
"Adhering and Illuminating" refers to the *Hexagram Li* (The Clinging) in the *Zhouyi*. Its *tuan* says: "Li means clinging. The sun and moon cling to heaven;

the hundred grains and plants and trees cling to the earth. The commentary states: "Clinging (*li*) is like adhering (*zhu*). It means that the sun and moon adhere to heaven, attaining what is appropriate for their adherence.
I am now merely employing its underlying meaning to say that this scripture is like the bright sun shining below.
Question: It was stated above that "the brilliance of wisdom outshines [all else]," using the bright sun as a metaphor for wisdom; why then is it compared to a scripture here? Answer:

This refers to the realm of the wisdom expounded by this very scripture, which outshines the wisdom of other scriptures. Thus, in the passage beginning with "Great Brilliance," the teaching and its metaphor are explained in conjunction.
Question: When this scripture was being taught, no other scriptures yet existed; how then can it be said that "this scripture extensively elucidates all [others]"?
The *Dian wu hui* (Mirror of the Non-Brilliance) provides two interpretations: first, it is said that this is explained in reference to a later period;

hence the commentary states, "Seeking this profound principle and then consulting other sutras, it does not concern the chronological sequence of their preaching. Second, it is said that even from the perspective of the time of preaching, it can outshine all other vehicles.
Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Manifestation" [outshines] the provisional-name Bodhisattvas, while the "Dharmadhātu Chapter" [outshines] those who abide [in the provisional].
Since the persons who rely [upon the teaching], such as the śrāvakas and others, have already been deprived of the teaching upon which they rely, it is evident that they have been deprived.

Regarding the metaphor of the "lofty and supreme, difficult to equal" in the *Jiyao*: this also refers to the dharma-terms; the metaphor used to illustrate the subject should be called the "metaphor of the mountain king eclipsing.
The previous metaphor illustrated its brilliance, while this metaphor illustrates its loftiness. Since it is both lofty and brilliant, there is nothing like this sutra.

Sumeru is also called Sumeru; this is translated as "Wondrously High" (Miaogao). There are ten meanings to its "wondrousness": 1. **The Wondrousness of Substance**: It means it is composed of the four precious substances.

2. **The Wondrousness of Form**: It means it has eight sides and four terraces. 3. **The Wondrousness of Color**: It means the four primary colors—gold in the north, silver in the east, lapis lazuli in the south, and crystal in the west.

All vegetation, birds, beasts, and other objects take on the same color as the place where they are located; this remains constant and unchanging. 4. **The Wondrousness of Virtue**: It means that the fierce winds from the eight directions cannot move it.
1. Wondrousness of the retinue (referring to the seven golden mountains that encircle it in seven layers and the seven seas of fragrant water with their "seal-impression" whirlpools);

2. Wondrousness of the support (only devas dwell upon it, while those who have attained supernatural powers may reside there); 3. Wondrousness of activity (without leaving its original location, it sustains the four continents, eclipsing the sun and moon to create day and night); 4. Wondrousness of the production of fruits (referring to the pārijāta tree, which can benefit the assembly of devas);

5. Wondrousness of being the foremost (it was the very first to be formed among the lands of the four continents); 6. Wondrousness of firmness (it is situated at the outermost edge of the Cakravāḍa mountain range).
Regarding the term "subsequently destroyed": it is said that its height is eighty-four thousand *yojanas*, and its depth below the water is likewise.

Its base rests upon the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanamaṇḍala*), and its summit borders the realm of space. Its dimensions in length and breadth are equal to its height; because it stands alone above the other nine mountains, it is called "Wondrous High" (*Sumeru*).

As for the "various peaks," these refer to the remaining nine great mountains: (1) the Snowy Mountain (*Himavat*), (2) the Fragrant Mountain (*Gandhamādana*), (3) Mount Vidiśa, (4) the Mountain of the Immortals (*Ṛṣigiri*), and so forth.

[The nine mountains are: (1) Yugandhara, (2) Īṣādhara, (3) Kālaparvata, (4) Cakravāḍa, and (5–9) the five [inner] mountains such as Nimindhara. These are now listed according to their heights, which can be understood from the Dharma [treatises].
Regarding the "seven golden [mountains]" and so forth, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "Sumeru stands in the center;

next is Yugandhara (meaning 'Holding the Pair,' so named because its two ridges on the summit can support [the heavens], and Yakṣas dwell there]; Īṣādhara... (so named because it supports the pole of Indra's chariot). (Note: The original text fragment ends with "Īṣādhara" and its Chinese gloss "this means...")

Yugandhara (Holding-Axis Mountain): Its peaks rise high like the axle of a chariot, for its summit holds [the world]. Khadiraka (Acacia Mountain): The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā* states that this is the name of a tree in the West;

the precious trees on the mountain resemble that tree in shape. Sudarśana (Good-to-See): This means "well-seen"; those who see it call it good, as it is the dwelling place of the five-fold supernatural sages (*pañcābhijña-rṣi*).

Aśvakarṇa (Horse-Ear Mountain): This means "horse-ear," for its shape resembles that [of a horse's ear] and it produces all kinds of fruits. Vinataka (Elephant-Trunk Mountain): This means "elephant-trunk," because its shape resembles that. Nimi... [text ends]

Mount Nimindhara (the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā* states that "nimin" is the name of a fish; because its snout is pointed, the shape of the mountain resembles it; the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra-śabdārtha-vyākhyāna* explains that this means "Holding-the-Borders Mountain," the dwelling place of the powerful Nāga deity).

Outside the great continents and other regions lies the Cakravāḍa Iron Rim Mountain. The seven preceding mountains are composed of gold (these seven mountains are thus called the "Seven Golden Mountains").

Regarding Mount Sumeru, all four precious substances [gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal] enter the water to a depth of eighty thousand [yojanas], and their wondrous heights above [the water] are likewise [eighty thousand]. [The seven golden...]

When submerged in water, it is equal to Mount Sumeru; when emerging from the water, it is not so. The remaining eight mountains each decrease by half in width, yet all are equal in height to their respective measurements.

(This means that Yugandhara emerges from the water at forty thousand [yojanas], down to Cakravāḍa, which emerges at three hundred and twelve yojanas; their widths are each equal to their heights of emergence, without distinction.

Regarding the term *peilǒu* (培塿): the first character is pronounced *pú* (蒲口切) and the second *lángdǒu* (郎斗切); it refers to a small mound. Question: The *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*) also says, "like Mount Sumeru."
Is this not a contradiction? The answer is that those [other teachings] are based on refuting the Small Vehicle to reveal the Great Assembly, showing that provisional means return to the Real;

they are difficult to believe and difficult to understand, and no other sutras can compare to them. This [present teaching], however, serves as the foundation for all doctrines, being perfectly consummate, unique, and supreme.
Since each relies upon its own specific principle, there is no contradiction between them.
Regarding the phrase "five hundred years," it should properly read "six hundred years. Some say that he appeared three hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa and lived for seven hundred years;
if this were so, he would likewise have entered the dragon palace only after six hundred years. The *New Commentary on the Sūtra* states:
"The Great Master concealed his traces six hundred years later before appearing in the Five Regions, and only after twelve hundred years did he [finally] emerge."

The *Preface to the Exploration of the Profound* (*Tanchuanxuanji*) in the tradition of the Eastern Continent (referring to the period from the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa until the fourteenth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, totaling one thousand two hundred years) also states:
"Vairocana first fashioned [the world] through the Sea-Seal Samādhi; twenty-one days later, Nāgārjuna arose.

Finally, looking down upon the palace of the dragon, six hundred years later he manifested his teachings. Regarding this Nāgārjuna, it is also called Longmen (Dragon-Fury) or Longmeng (Dragon-Vigorous).
Both characters are the Chinese translation for the word *vṛkṣa* (tree).

Tripitaka Master Yi Jing, who was proficient in both Chinese and Sanskrit, stated that *ārya* means "holy" (*shèng*), *nāga* means "dragon" (*lóng*) or "elephant" (*xiàng*), and *vṛkṣana* is translated as "fierce" (*měng*).

According to a separate biography, his mother gave birth to him beneath a tree, and because he perfected the Way in a dragon palace, he was called Nāgārjuna; thus, both characters are direct translations [of the components of his name].
Tiantai said: "The tree is the birth-body (nirmāṇakāya), while the dragon is the dharma-body (dharmakāya); it is from this [perspective] that we proceed. [Note:

Regarding the events, they are as recorded in the *Biographies* (*Biezhuan*) and the *Compilation of Spiritual Records* (*Zuānlíngjì*). While the *Biographies* contain only the account of entering the Dragon Palace, the *Compilation of Spiritual Records* contains the account of searching for and obtaining the sutra;
therefore, both are cited here together as evidence, as will be seen below in the translation of the biography.
This is fully cited within the *Gantong* (Manifestation of Response).
The *Chao* (Commentary) specifically adopts the version translated by Jue Xian—whose Sanskrit name is Buddhavarman—as this master’s translation dates to the Eastern Jin dynasty;
hence it is specifically adopted. Therefore, the topical outline states: "The fundamental reasons for its extensive propagation," which includes other aspects as well.
This is because the Jin edition of the sutra was translated after Zhiyan personally traveled to the Western Regions to receive the dhyāna methods from Buddhasena;
he subsequently invited Buddhayaśas to return to China to translate this scripture. Huiyan and Huiguan polished the phrasing, Fayue acted as the scribe, and the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta followed.
Later, during the first year of the Yonglong era of the Great Tang, the Jin edition was revised and supplemented where it had been omitted.
Wen-shi-cha-nan-t'o (文實叉難陀), which is translated as "Delightful in Study," translated the Tang scriptures in the first year of the Zhengsheng era.
Regarding the phrase "and others" (等), it includes the various masters who co-translated these works, namely Yi-jing (義淨), Hong-jing (弘景), Yuan-ce (圓測), Shen-ying (神英), and so forth.

Regarding the "Divine Continent of Daxia" (*Shenzhou Daxia*) mentioned in the sub-commentary (*Xiaochao*), it also states that the territory east of the Pamir Mountains (*Congling*), spanning several thousand *li*, is called the "Red Prefecture" (*Chixian*).
This Divine Continent is precisely the land of the Tang Dynasty’s Central China. The *Yishu Shuyao Yiyuan Chao* states:
"As for the term 'Divine Continent,' it refers to this eastern land; prior to the time of the ancient Emperor Shun, there were no inhabitants."
It is called a "Divine Continent" (Shenzhou) because it is the dwelling place of spirits and deities. The term "Daxia" preserves the dynastic name from the era of the Three Dynasties.

Regarding the "single word and single phrase," this refers to a single verse from the *Puyan Jing* (Universal Eye Sutra) held by Haiyun, specifically the verse spoken by Bodhisattva Juelin beginning with "If a person wishes to thoroughly understand...
The "single light" refers to the three tiers of the hell-dwelling deva.
The light of sudden and perfect [enlightenment] is as extensively explained below.

Regarding the phrase "How fortunate that the Image Dharma, etc.," the *Lunyu Shu* (Commentary on the Analects) states: "When one ought to lose something in a matter but instead gains it, it is called 'fortune' (*xing*).
One's life is situated in the lower [stages], where one ought to lose; yet looking back from the lower, one gains it. The meaning of "self-joy" (*zi-xing*) may be understood by analogy with this.

Regarding the statement that "knowing speech does not diminish the True Dharma" and so forth: the World-Honored One specifically prophesied that the True Dharma (saddharma) would last for one thousand years—possessing both teaching (śāsana), practice (pratipatti), and the realization of the fruits of attainment (phalaprāpti);

the Semblance Dharma (pratirūpaka-dharma) would last for one thousand years—possessing both teaching and practice, but lacking the realization of the fruits; and the Final Dharma (paścima-dharma) would last for ten thousand years—possessing teaching, but lacking both practice and the realization of the fruits.

Furthermore, because of the ordination of women, the True Dharma was reduced by half. Regarding this, there are two explanations: the first states that although the Eight Respectful Precepts (gurudharma) were taught...
The True Dharma does not diminish because it is not practiced; rather, it diminishes when that practice is absent.

Second, if the Eight Respects were not taught, there would be no practitioners at all when the True Dharma was about to perish; however, since there are practitioners, the True Dharma remains established. (The Sarvāstivāda school is cited above; the Mahāsāṃghika school speaks below.
Here, we rely on the latter interpretation. (The Eight Respects will be fully demonstrated later. Regarding the Master’s [Daoshi’s] *Niepan jing shu* (Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra), etc.:
He was born on the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-sixth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty.
He entered *parinirvāṇa* on the fifteenth day of the second month in the fifty-second year of King Mu of the Zhou dynasty, the *Ren-shen* year.

From that time until the first year of the Zhihe era of the Great Yuan dynasty, in the *Wu-chen* year, a total of two thousand two hundred and seventy-seven years have passed; this coincides precisely with the period of the Final Dharma (*mofa*). [At this time,] the [scriptures] were translated...
To hear such inconceivable sutras is itself a cause for celebration.
Regarding the citations from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-māsasamaya-vibhaṅga* and other texts, the *Vajra-kanjō-ki* states: "The former is superior and the latter is inferior;
'liberation' refers to the realization of the noble fruits of the Three Vehicles, while 'meditative concentration' refers to their practice, namely the outflow-free [wisdom]."
The "outflows" (*āsrava*) refer to the various matters and principles of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, which are generally understood by those who have heard much;

these include the sudden and gradual, the partial and the perfect, emptiness and existence (the former three must necessarily possess the latter, whereas the latter do not necessarily possess the former).

"Stūpas and temples" refers to those who do not seek the ultimate Way but instead prefer conditioned phenomena, using external assets and wealth to cultivate worldly meritorious deeds and the like. "Contention" clarifies the state of the Buddha-dharma.
Within these [teachings], there is much contention; for example, in India, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna were divided like those drinking from separate halves of a river.

Within the Mahāyāna, the *Xing* (Nature) and *Xiang* (Characteristics) schools differ; within the Hīnayāna, the twenty sub-sects vary, each factioning with their own views and regarding others as wrong.
This situation has not been avoided even here in this land, where there are disputes between the *Xiang* and *Xing* schools, and between the Southern and Northern Schools.
When Chan practitioners and lecturers hold conflicting views and their respective factions refuse to concede to one another, it is called "contention.

As for what is called "firm," it refers to people following established traditions with such determination that they do not abandon them; however, this is spoken of only in terms of prevailing trends and does not mean there is no mutual connection.
For instance, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, King Aśoka constructed stupas during the first century—how could this be restricted solely to the fourth period? Furthermore, regarding the Bodhi...
The *Sanzang jing* states: "In the final five hundred years of the Dharma, immeasurable virtuous people will practice dhyāna and attain liberation;
how could there be only one or two?
The *Chao* [commentary] notes that "the Sage and Enlightened Son of Heaven currently reigning" refers to Emperor Dezong of the Tang. The inscription on the stupa records the first year of Xingyuan.
The year Jiazi was when the commentary (*shu*) was begun; the year Dingmao of the Zhenyuan era was when the work was completed. Both are reign titles of Emperor Dezong.
Since the Zhenyuan era lasted twenty-one years, it was only in the year Bingzi of the Zhenyuan era that he translated the new scriptures.

He subsequently composed the commentary on these new scriptures, which is also titled the *Xinjing shu* (Commentary on the New Scriptures), likewise produced during the Zhenyuan era. Regarding the phrase "pagodas standing in rows facing one another," this refers to the Sanskrit...

According to the *Yujia chiduoluo* (瑜伽掣多羅), in the Western Regions there are no separate flagpoles; rather, flags are suspended from the tops of the pillars supporting the inverted bowl (*pratimaṇḍala*) of the stūpa.
What is currently called a *kṣa* (刹) is a corruption and abbreviation of this term. This is also explained in the *Xuanyan* (玄贊). Furthermore, the *Yaoyao lan* (要覽) states:
"The Sanskrit term is *laśca* (剌瑟致), which here means 'pole. It is now abbreviated as *kṣa*, referring to the flagstaff. Thus it is said.
Regarding the term *xiāngwàng* (相望): when the initial tone is *wúfàng* (無放), the *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as "standing outside and looking for someone's return.
When pronounced with the final tone (*yàofàng* [要放]), the *Shuowen Jiezi* explains it as "the full moon facing the sun. Here, we take the latter pronunciation.

As for the phrase "the resonance of the bell and the *brahman*," *brahman* refers to *brahmā*. The first fascicle of the *Yao-lan* (要覽) states: "In the language of India it is called *bhāṇaka*; in the language of China it is..."
When cessation and abandonment have been achieved through external objects, one then dwells in tranquility; this is the practice for the sake of the Dharma.
Furthermore, it is said that because the devas hear the *brahman*-mind, they rejoice; therefore, one must perform this rite. The Fayuan states:
"Now, *bhāṣya* (chanting) is the sound of praise and recitation. It should be made clear yet not weak, majestic yet not fierce, flowing yet not excessive, and concentrated."
When heard from afar, it is vast and profound yet dignified and elegant; when observed closely, it is composed and harmonious yet solemn. This is its general character.
Formerly, when the Prince of Chen-si of the Wei dynasty, Cao Zijiàn, was traveling at Mount You-shan, he suddenly heard the sound of Brahma-heaven music in the air—clear, resonant, and plaintive.
Its melody moved his heart; after listening alone for a long time, he then transcribed it.
Its sections were transcribed as *brahman* chants, with texts composed and melodies fashioned to be passed down as a model for future generations; this marks the beginning of the *brahman* sound.
For those who study in leisure at their academies, this single phrase from Master Zhao’s *Wuming lun* (Treatise on the Namelessness of Nirvana) illuminates the light.

Yáo’s commentary states: "Sì" (肆) means "to display. Zhōu Kǒng says: "There is an interpretation that this refers to the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, though I have not yet dared to definitively determine it;
it likely refers to the *Zhōulǐ* (Rites of Zhou). Within the school, books and histories are displayed like goods displayed in a marketplace.
Today, however, the sacred teachings are displayed as something extraordinary. The *Yāoyǎn* states: "In the Later Han, Zhāng Kǎi, styled Gōngchāo, was followed by students wherever he resided."
For the sake of the marketplace, the present section on training rules is now called the "Marketplace" (Sì). Regarding the phrase "probing the mysteries of the profound gate" (tànzé xuánmén):
the character *tàn* is pronounced *táihán* (thai-han); "to probe" means to test and extract its meaning. The character *zé* is pronounced *shìzé* (shi-ze);
Liu Xian’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* states that *zé* is a term for the ultimate depth and obscurity. The "profound gate" (*xuánmén*) can thus be understood.
Someone asked: "This place is located at Mount Ling; why is Qingliang Mountain called Mount Ling? The answer was:
"In antiquity, there was the Dafu Lingjiu Temple here because the shape of the mountain resembled a vulture (*gṛdhrakūṭa*).

The Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*) in the Western Regions is also colloquially referred to as 'Lingshan' (Spiritual Mountain), and this mountain is likewise abbreviated as 'Lingshan. Alternatively, it may be because the spiritual responses of this mountain are manifold."

Therefore, it is called "Numinous Mountain" (Lingshan). [The] Commentary states: Although the Great Sage (Mahāsattva) pervades all below, the text here cites the general title to specifically honor his virtue;
thus, his personal name is not specified. As when one recites the name in this mountain, one simply says "Great Sage Bodhisattva. [The] Commentary further states:
"Ten thousand sages provide profound assistance on the five peaks," which refers to the passage in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-vinaya* concerning Mañjuśrī and the ten thousand [sages].

Regarding the statement that "the Bodhisattva dwells within the Five Peaks of Qingliang" and so forth, concerning the period of one hundred *ji* (or *qī*), the *Nanshan Gantong Zhuan* records that there was once a celestial being named Lu Xuanchang who visited Master Xuan.
When the Master asked him about the matters of Mañjuśrī at Mount Qingliang, he replied: "Mañjuśrī is the ancestral teacher of all Buddhas; he appears in response to conditions to benefit beings."

These transformations differ from the achievements of great sages and are not within the ordinary realm; there is no need for laborious evaluation, yet one knows they mostly occur within the Qingliang and Wutai mountains.
Often people see them, and one cannot help but believe it. Furthermore, during the time of King Mu of Zhou, the Buddha-dharma already existed;
this mountain is wondrous and extraordinary, the dwelling place of Mañjuśrī, where King Mu built [a temple] therein.

The temple offerings for King Aśoka were also based on the establishment of stupas; as these instances are not limited to one, it is said that "a hundred [stupas] transmit their blessings," and so forth.
Regarding the term "Dàfú" (Great Faith) and others, this refers to the stupa established by Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty.
"Dàfú" means "vast faith," as has already been explained in the preceding title. As for the phrase "a single lowly monk," the *Fǎ* commentary on the *Zhōuyī* states: "Jiè."
"Even a minute fragment" is a handle for self-humbling virtue. Regarding the phrase "I here feel shame for many lifetimes," there are two interpretations.

1. The greatness of nature (*mahātmya*); 2. the greatness of superior resolve (*adhimukti*); 3. the greatness of superior intention (*adhyāśaya*); 4. the greatness of the provisions (*saṃbhāra*); 5. the greatness of time (*kāla*); 6.

the greatness of perfect realization (*abhisamaya*). As stated in the seventh chapter of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, regarding the greatness of the fruit (*phala-mahātmya*), the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (XI) explains seven kinds of greatness:

The lower section of the sutra states: "The *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) pervades all places. Below this, a question is raised regarding its third phrase:
"Since it should have the meaning of 'permanence,' how does it prove the meaning of 'pervasiveness'? The answer is: "What fault is there in [its] pervading throughout time?

Alternatively, it may simply be cited here because the first half of the reason is convenient for the context. Regarding the statement "the *dharmatā* is without action," the following passage from the *Samantamukha-parivarta* (Chapter on the Universal Gateway) is cited above.
The first half is the original text; the second half is an explanatory citation. It says: "The nature of all Buddhas is likewise pure by nature;
this fundamental nature is neither existence nor non-existence. The commentary explains: Because it is unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*), it has no prior limit;
because it is immutable, it has no subsequent limit; because it is like space, it is like the middle limit. Since it is thus with respect to the three limits, it is eternal.
The commentary states that "both" and "self-nature" (svabhāva) encompass the two preceding meanings; this explains the two characters "self" (自) and "uphold" (持) in the sub-commentary (*śū*).

Regarding the two meanings of the "True Dharma" (saddharma), there are both general and specific senses. Specifically, "True" (正) means being without partiality, and "Dharma" (法) means being a model or norm. Generally, both [terms] share the meaning of "upholding self-nature.
As for the phrase "innumerable qualities of self-nature," this is mentioned to illustrate how the general [term] reflects the specific; thus, it is said to be "without partiality."
The counterfeit does not exclusively reject the small, whereas the non-counterfeit rejects the external;

therefore, when it is said that the Buddha commands those who abide in the True Dharma to provide dual testimony for the two aforementioned meanings, it is necessary to rely solely on the first half [of the verse] as the testimony.

The Commentary likewise has two meanings; however, because the wording in the subsequent sub-commentary is abbreviated, it mentions "pervasive" (*zhou*) as having the meaning of "partial" (*pian*) without mentioning the meaning of "encompassing" (*bao*).

Nevertheless, since these two meanings—encompassing and pervasive—must mutually require one another within the "substance and greatness" (*ti-da*) discussed previously, they are combined into one, and the meaning of "constant" (*chang*) is brought forth to complete the two meanings.
Now, when using the term "conforming to substance" (*chengti*), it should likewise possess both constancy and pervasiveness.

Regarding the two meanings, if one speaks according to the conventional application of the meaning of "permanence," it is implicit; furthermore, since this is discussed based on manifest characteristics, the "encompassing" and the "pervasive" are distinguished as two separate meanings.
In terms of ultimate reality and practical function, "greatness" also implies non-interruption, and "permanence" likewise reflects the other, which is why it is said to be "like empty space.
This is from the text of the *Myōgon-hin* (Chapter on Wondrous Adornment); the full passage states: "For example, just as empty space contains all forms."
"Without making any distinctions regarding all objects" — the sub-commentary states that this contains a metaphor, for there is nothing it does not encompass;
thus it "pervades everything. This is from the text of the *Prādurbhāva-parivarta* (Chapter on Manifestation). It says in full:

"For example, just as empty space pervades all places, whether material or non-material. The sub-commentary explains: "The metaphor of empty space pervading everywhere is used here to illustrate [the nature of] phenomena by means of the emptiness of things."

In the preceding discussion on the emptiness of principle (*li-kōng*), both the meanings of "essence" (*tǐ*) and "pervasion" (*biàn*) were taken as the referents. Now, this [discussion] concerns the function that is identical to that essence;

thus, it likewise refers to the essence as possessing both the meanings of "encompassing" and "pervading. Regarding the essence mentioned above, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* cites "true suchness without nature" (*wú-xìng zhēn-rú*) as its essence.

In this present scripture, "the principle of non-obstruction" (*wú-ài-zhàng lǐ*) is cited as the essence. Within the characteristics (*xiàng*), the innumerable virtuous qualities of nature (*xìng-dé*) are enumerated.
Within the principle of "identical shadows yet distinct functions," a single atom encompasses boundless worlds, and at any given moment, it pervades the inexhaustible Dharma-realm.
When the particular and the identical shadows are raised together, their identity and distinction are unimpeded; these are all the Three Greats (san-da) of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao).

Furthermore, these Three Greats are mutually unimpeded when viewed in relation to one another, and they collectively constitute the realized Dharma-realm of non-obstruction. [The *Chao* (Commentary)] designates this as the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (miaojue).

These three truths are fused into the wondrous Three Awakenings; they are unimpeded as awakening, and may also both be understood as such because the three truths are that which is awakened to, and both the awakening and that which is awakened to are profoundly wondrous.
Regarding the phrase "eliciting the fruit" and so forth, the subsequent commentary states:
"The flower has two meanings: first, the flower of plants and trees, which metaphorically represents the causes of the myriad practices; second, the flower that adorns the body."
The metaphors of gold, jade, and so forth refer to the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the marks of excellence (*lakṣaṇa*), as these exist only simultaneously with the fruit [of Buddhahood].
Therefore, in the cited proof, the supernormal powers and the marks of excellence are used as evidence.
[From the] *Śrī-mahāvaipulya*... although the nature of the *Mahāvaipulya-dharma* is fundamentally pure, if it is not [perfected by] the myriad practices (*sahasra-pratipatti*)...
There is no way for it to be manifested; just as a mirror, though inherently bright, cannot manifest its clarity unless it is polished and refined.
To speak of a person who has attained the fruit of Buddhahood: an ordinary person is not a Buddha, for one becomes a Buddha through the merit of the myriad practices.

This is like a gem that is not yet an image; it must be carved and polished to become an image. Thus, "adornment" refers to the originally existent Dharma, while "attainment" refers to the person produced by cultivation—these are two distinct meanings.

Regarding the phrase "also adorning the fundamental essence," it means that all practices which adorn [the Buddha] accord with the fundamental essence of the *Mahāvaipulya*, because they are cultivated in accordance with the original nature (*prakṛti*).
This is because, just as when an image is adorned, the gold that constitutes its fundamental essence remains non-dual.

Regarding the phrase "by means of practice," it means that one becomes a person who attains the fruit of Buddhahood by taking the myriad practices as the cause; yet the cause is not identical to the fruit, for there is a distinction between cause and fruit.
Because they are distinct, it is like a skilled artisan who can create an image; the artisan is not the image because their substance is different.
Thus, that which adorns and that which is adorned are not different, yet that which accomplishes and that which is accomplished are not identical—this constitutes the meaning of "two.

Furthermore, the preceding statement that "that which polishes is not that which is polished" is a metaphor for the practice adorning the fundamental substance; yet since the practice is itself the fundamental substance, the two—the image and the adornment—are the golden substance itself.
The analogy [of the ornament] and that which is adorned are non-dual (the two characters "adorned" [飾] and "method" [法] both possess the dual meanings of being neither identical nor different).
Since the vessel cannot exist apart from the jade, the practice that completes the person is identical to the person; therefore, they are non-dual. The skillful artisan is not the image;

the analogy [of the artisan] can accomplish [the image], whereas [the image] is not that which is accomplished, and thus they are dual (the two characters "completing the person" [成人] also possess the dual meanings of being neither one nor two). However, the preceding analysis of the text has been based on a single aspect; as for how it applies [to the ultimate], [it is as follows].
The Dharma also has a "new" meaning, because it distinguishes the mind and its objects based on meanings such as being originally neither internal nor external;
the Buddha also has a "fundamental" meaning, because within the ocean of the Buddha-fruit, the benefit of beings has been eternally perfected from the beginning.

Furthermore, the practices that adorn this [Buddhahood] also have a fundamental meaning, as they consist of practicing generosity and other perfections in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*); practices that do not flow from the Truth (*tattva*) do not accord with it.
Because they are real, they also possess the sense of being new; since these are established by persons, according to this principle, the first four lines of the analogy are as follows:

the first line concerns the original existence and cultivated arising of dharmas; the second line concerns the cultivated arising and original existence of persons; the third line concerns the original existence and cultivation of practices;
and the fourth line concerns the cultivated arising and original existence of practices. Only when these four lines are perfectly integrated does it constitute true adornment.
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, there are only two [categories]," which refers to the middle two phrases. The first phrase, "surging spring," is that which is subsumed;
"the one who possesses the flavor of meaning" is that which encompasses the middle [category]. Question: Why does it not say "the one who possesses the flavor of the encompassed meaning"? Answer:

To manifest that the two meanings mutually interpenetrate and include one another—since the inclusion also includes the meaning, and the penetration also penetrates the capacity [of the practitioner]—it is said that "constancy" (常) thus applies universally.

The first three [categories] are all encompassed by the term "constant" (*nitya*); thus, the phrase "as explained in another passage" refers to the Preface to Ci'en's *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra).
That sub-commentary (*chao*) states: "'Guǐ' (track/standard) means a model or scale;
