Regarding the phrase "later, at the assembly, he will repay the Buddha's kindness" (*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*), the *Śū* (Commentary) states:
"The stage of causes has reached its ultimate limit. The *Cào* (Sub-commentary) states: "Having already perfected the virtues of a Buddha, he advances [to the next stage]."
Because they share the same rank as the Buddha. ▲ The *Chao* (Commentary) states in its sub-commentary (*shu*) below the Akaniṣṭha heaven: "The fruit-stage is manifested. The *Chao* further states:

"Manifesting the tenfold retributive rewards and transforming myriad classes of beings manifests and represents the fruit-stage; falling within the number of Buddhas, it is called 'the highest and greatest body among all worlds.
Regarding the measurement of the body in the Akaniṣṭha heaven, the *Jibei lu* (Urgent Record) states: "The body-measurement of the Akaniṣṭha heaven is ten thousand [yojanas]."

Six thousand *yojanas*. (The *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states: "In the Form Realm heavens, the first four increase by half a *yojana* each; above these, they double successively; only the Cloudless [heaven] is reduced by three.

This refers to the seventeen heavens of the Form Realm. In the first four heavens, each is half a *yojana*; reaching the fourth heaven, it is two *yojanas*. "Above these, they double successively" means: the fifth is four, the sixth is eight, the seventh is sixteen, the eighth is thirty-two, and the ninth is sixty-four. The tenth totals one hundred and twenty-eight;
because the Cloudless Heaven (*Anabhraka*) is intended to complete the number, three are subtracted, resulting in one hundred and twenty-five. The eleventh has two hundred and five.)

The tenth [level] is twelve thousand; the eleventh is fifteen thousand; the twelfth is twenty thousand; the thirteenth is twenty-five thousand; the fourteenth is thirty-two thousand; the fifteenth is forty thousand; the sixteenth is eighty thousand; and the seventeenth is sixteen thousand.
(Since the seventeenth is the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, the height of the body is sixteen thousand yojanas. The body size of Maheśvara is thirty-two thousand yojanas;
because the body size of the Mahāmaheśvara Heavenly King for a Bodhisattva of the Tenth Ground is doubled, it is said to be the most supreme and vast.

The *Śāstra* (鈔) states that "the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment" (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta-prajñā*) refers to the moment when initial enlightenment (*ādikṣānti-bodhi*) reaches the source of the mind and accords with original enlightenment (*mūlabodhi*).
It further notes that this is the path of non-interruption (*anantarya-mārga*). The *Śāstra* explains that it signifies the correspondence between the initial and the original.

Regarding the statement that "ignorance is suddenly exhausted and is called the 'knowledge of all modes' (*sarvākārajñatā*)," the *Vṛtti* (疏) explains: "When ignorance is suddenly exhausted, one clearly illuminates all phenomena; this is what is named [the knowledge of all modes]."
The knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is also the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), which is the fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*mūla-nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

This explains that, having spontaneously fulfilled the practice for one's own benefit, one truly attains Buddhahood; it does not specify a location. Regarding the phrase "it exists spontaneously," the *Cao* (Excerpts) states:

"That section [of the commentary] says 'the virtue of benefiting others is manifested. The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "It does not depend on effort; it is the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*)."
He then explains the aforementioned "other-retribution" (it-bao). Regarding the "present-life benefit" (*xianbao*), the *Commentary on the Daśabhūmika-śāstra* states:
"Within this very body, the merits of the two-fold adornment for one's own benefit are perfected.

This clarifies that the stage where the causes are perfected is precisely the retribution of self-benefit. According to the principle, this actual body of self-retribution has no fixed location or spatial dimension.
"Sunken and hidden" refers to the fulfillment of the cause resulting in the perfection of the fruit. Regarding "subsequent retribution for the benefit of others," that commentary states:
"Because one gives rise to the retribution for benefiting others based upon the retribution for self-benefit, it is called 'subsequent retribution.

This means that based upon the actual retribution for self-benefit manifested by the prior fulfillment of the cause, one gives rise to the subsequent retribution for benefiting others; furthermore, because it extends to the furthest reaches of the future, it is so named."
Regarding the later statement that [the Tathāgata] "is born from the locus of Maheśvara’s wisdom," the *Qingliang shi* (Commentary by Qingliang) provides two interpretations:

First, because Maheśvara possesses mastery over wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā*). This refers to his mastery over wisdom within his body of karmic retribution (*vipākakāya*). As the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* (Chapter on the Worthy Head, *Bhadramukha*) states:

"When Maheśvara, who possesses mastery over wisdom, acts as a great ocean dragon king and causes rain to fall, he is able to distinguish and count every single drop; he discerns them all within a single thought-moment. Furthermore, the *Śatapuṇyavyūha-sūtra* says: "Just as when the receptacle world is about to be formed, a great [rain] falls in the fourth dhyāna..."

Rain falls for five intermediate kalpas without ceasing, pervading the trichiliocosm and reaching as far as the Brahma-world; such raindrops the Great Sovereign Heavenly King (*Maheśvara*) is able to know in their entirety, and thus his wisdom becomes ever more vast. Yet, why is this heaven designated as a "station of wisdom"?

Because the lower heavens have less meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) are more prevalent, whereas within the fourth dhyāna, concentration and wisdom are equal. Since this is the ultimate limit within the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*), it is called the Heaven of Sovereignty over Wisdom.

Second, because the wisdom of retribution is perfected, it constitutes the seed-wisdom (*sarvajñatā*): (referring to the period before becoming a Buddha, it is subsumed under the tenth stage [bhūmi]; because the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) is already complete while residing in that heaven, it is said that "the wisdom of retribution is fulfilled. Thereafter...)

Because he attained great enlightenment in that celestial realm and was fully endowed with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*), it is considered a locus of wisdom. However, regarding the attainment of Buddhahood, the treatises generally explain that there are three aspects: first, manifesting the real through the provisional by appearing in Jambudvīpa, thereby pervading the entire dharma-realm;

second, manifesting the real through the retributive body by attaining enlightenment in Akaniṣṭha, whereby it immediately pervades the dharma-realm; and third, manifesting the real from the perspective of ultimate reality, wherein the sublime state transcends the three periods of time such that its timing, location, and physical characteristics cannot be fixed. Here, we follow the middle sense.

The *Shu* (Commentary) states that the ten kings of the underworld manifest the distinctions of the ten stages (*bhūmi*). The *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sutra) explains that a Bodhisattva of the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*) is an Iron Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*) who rules over one Jambudvīpa;
one of the ten abodes (*vihāra*) is a Copper Wheel-turning King who rules over two continents; one of the ten practices (*caryā*) is a Silver Wheel-turning King who rules over three continents;

one of the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) is a Gold Wheel-turning King who rules over the four continents; and [the Bodhisattva of] the first stage (*bhūmi*) is a [Gold Wheel-turning King] who rules over the four continents... [and so on].

As a King of the Floating Heaven, he rules over a hundred buddha-lands; as a King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he rules over a thousand buddha-lands; as a King of the Yāma Heaven, he rules over ten thousand buddha-lands;
as a King of the Tuṣita Heaven, he rules over one hundred million buddha-lands; as a King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, he rules over ten billion buddha-lands;
as a King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, he rules over one hundred billion buddha-lands; and at the seventh stage, he rules over the first dhyāna.
The King of the Eighth Stage rules over ten trillion buddha-fields; the King of the Second Dhyāna rules over one hundred million billion buddha-fields;
the King of the Ninth Stage rules over ten thousand koṭis of asaṃkhyeya buddha-fields; the King of the Tenth Stage Bodhisattva rules over unspeakably unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields;
and the King of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-realm rules over immeasurable buddha-fields—thus it is said.
In that sutra, there are thirteen Dharma masters; including those who believe in the fourteenth and the Buddha as the fifteenth, there are fifteen in total.

However, because this [text] clarifies only the ten stages (*bhūmi*), it refers to them as the "Ten Kings. [Question]: Regarding these Heavenly Kings mentioned here, they are merely Bodhisattvas acting as such.
How is it that they receive the rank of Buddha? [Answer]: It is precisely those Bodhisattvas who transform [into Buddhas].
Being the Buddha-body is the tenth layer of the *parabhogika* (other-enjoyment) manifestation. It indicates that the true Buddha who has attained enlightenment is without fixed location;
because there are those to be transformed in that particular heaven, he is currently present there. Thus, one should know that the body of the Heavenly King is of two kinds:
first, the actual perfected Buddha who manifests as a Heavenly King; and second, the transformation of that Heavenly King’s body into the tenth kind of *parabhogika-buddha*.
The body itself is the transformer; "clouds" refers to manifesting the attainment of *bodhi* within that very body (this is the interpretation of Xianshou).
Second, the Bodhisattva of the tenth stage, though not yet a Buddha, assumes this celestial king as a result of his retributive merit (*vipākaphala*);

since he is the one being transformed, it is said that the tenth stage is metaphorically assigned to this king. Otherwise, who would be the one being transformed? (This is the interpretation of Qingliang).
The present statement, "manifesting the attainment of Bodhi," adopts the first meaning.

Regarding the *Tiāngōng Chāo* (Commentary on the Heavenly Palace), Jizhao states that according to the *Cí'ēn Zhuàn* (Biography of Ci'en), it refers to Tiāngōng Monastery in Luozhou; this must be the commentary composed by the Dharma Master of that monastery.
As I have not yet seen the original text, I do not venture to provide a detailed determination. "The four wisdoms are perfected" refers to the previously explained Mahesvara.

This is the second meaning of Śūra’s "Abode of Wisdom" (*jñānasthāna*). However, according to the *Xuanxian xingzhuang chao* (Excerpts on the Life of Xuanxian), there are five distinct interpretations:
First, it is said that those of the Two Vehicles take the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) as the true Buddha and do not believe there is any other holy personage;

yet, they do believe that the Fourth Dhyāna is the place where holy persons are born. [The teaching] intends to make them understand that the eight phases [of a Buddha's life] are not the reality in that realm.
1. It is shown that [the formless realm] is established; 2. it is because it is not reached by the three calamities; 3.

it is because the substance of the desire realm and the form realm is coarse and exists, whereas the formless realm has no material substance at all, and since non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is free from both existence and non-existence, it accords with the Middle Way;
4. it is because Maheśvara has three eyes on his face, which symbolizes and verifies the nirvāṇa of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

In the fifth cloud [of the *Wu-yun*], it is said that in the lower realms wisdom (*prajñā*) is predominant while meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is scarce; in the upper realms meditative concentration is predominant while wisdom is scarce; and in the [realm of] manifestation, meditative concentration and wisdom are equal.

Regarding the passage in the *Chao* (the *Jingde chuandeng lu*) stating that one attains Buddhahood in the True Reward Land (*samyak-sambodhi*), various interpretations of this section of the text differ. Alternatively...
The *Tian-gong chao* (Heavenly Palace Extract) provides a supplementary response to the previous points in order to synthesize and explain the *Vijñaptimātratā*.

Now, examining the major headings (*dàkē*) of the *Chao*, it states: "First, synthesizing the *Awakening of Faith* and *Vijñaptimātratā*. This is precisely the text for the synthesis and explanation within the major headings. It belongs to the supplementary sections of the *Tian-gong chao*;
thus, it was mistakenly attributed to the *Wénshū chao* (Mañjuśrī Extract). Alternatively, the term "Tian-gong chao" may also refer to the wording [of that text].

Regarding the remaining meaning (as discussed at length): the present text uses two characters that represent two dots, which [correspond to] the five characters "four wisdoms perfected" (*catur-jñāna-pariniṣpanna*).
These five characters are connected with the following term "Vijñaptimātra" (Consciousness-only); however, this is the wording of the current manuscript and is not the correct interpretation.

Since it provides no supplementary meaning, what is the purpose of citing it? Furthermore, on what basis do the five characters immediately following arise? They lack any connection or affiliation. Therefore, I shall now examine the passage immediately below.
These five characters are from the *Tiangong chao* (Heavenly Palace Draft), the second response concerning the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

What follows is the Master of the Commentary’s exegesis reconciling the meaning of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* with the *Mahāyānaśraddhotpāda-śāstra* for the sake of Xianshou. However, there is a question: "Within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, [the land] is taken as the Reward Land (*vipākaphala-bhūmi*);
now, in explaining the *Śraddhotpāda*, why is it called the 'Other Reward' (*tādbhāgya-vipāka*)? This is the reconciliation. There are three sections as follows:
The *Kōyō* states that "the realization of the true reward through consciousness-only" refers to what is said in the seventh fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*:
"It is said that those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who seek the fruit of Buddhahood must, after [rebirth in] the realm of form, induce the outflow-free [state];

they will necessarily be born in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), in the palace of Maheśvara, where they attain enlightenment. The commentary on this states: "For those of sudden enlightenment who are ordinary beings, upon reaching the eighth stage..."
Having been born into the fourth dhyāna and attained a superior body, one then receives a transformation body (*pariṇāmika-kāya*);
thus, the "Palace of Maheśvara" refers to the Pure Land of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, where the *svasaṃbhoga-kāya* first arises and realizes [enlightenment].
Based on this, it is the actual *saṃbhoga-kāya*. (From the *Chao*: Regarding the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, in order to introduce the following question, since that...)
Question: For the masters who maintain that all is representation-only (vijñaptimātra), what constitutes the "true retribution" (bhūtāvasthāna)? Answer:
They take those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) who attain Buddhahood by severing the fetters through the thirty-four moments of mind beneath the Bodhi tree as the true retribution.

Now, the Vijñaptimātra school provisionally designates this as the true retribution in order to attract and guide those of the two vehicles, so that they may realize their own grasping is not ultimate truth.

The commentary now extracts the meaning of these two texts: either the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra* constitute the pair, or the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* constitute the pair.
To claim that the *Xianshou* (Fazang) and the *Tiankong* (Dushun) constitute the pair is incorrect;

the *Tiankong* is merely an explanation of the supplementary passages of the *Xianshou*, and thus shares with it the status of being a single text. It is said that the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* generally states "attainment."
Because his body is the most supreme and vast among all worlds, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* classifies this as the "Bodhisattva’s Fulfillment," which is the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).

The commentary states: "Because it is the greatest among forms and shapes, it is called 'vast' (*mahat*). My current interpretation is that this merely refers to the karmic retribution encompassed by the tenth stage (the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"To repay causes is called 'retribution' (*vipāka*"); because one receives the fruit once the causes are established, it is termed 'encompassment'). This demonstrates the manifestation of attaining Bodhi, but it is not the actual fruit-Buddha.
He manifests as the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) of that [heaven]; as this sutra says, because he predominantly gathers the reward, he acts as the king of that heaven.
It is not necessary to establish a fixed rule regarding his attainment of Buddhahood in that realm; thus it is said that this is explained in terms of gathering the reward.

Furthermore, even if he were to dwell in that heaven with his wisdom already perfected, and were to attain Bodhi there and become fully endowed with the Knowledge of All Modes (sarvākārajñatā), this would still occur within the tenth [stage].
The body that encompasses the retribution of the stages is attained [therein]. The critique states: Regarding the above explanation of Akaniṣṭha, there are differences among the three masters.

Xianshou [Zhiyan] considers it the *itabao* (retribution of others); Cien [Xuanzang] considers it the *shibao* (true retribution); and Qingliang [Fazang] considers it the retribution encompassed by the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
The same applies to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. By analogy, the *Awakening of Faith* should also be understood in this way.
The commentary on the ten matters of merit consists of those taught in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* (Chapter 24): first, the merit of making offerings; second, the merit of turning the wheel of Dharma;
third, the merit of receiving and upholding [the teachings]; fourth, the merit of practicing for the benefit of both self and others; fifth, the merit of bringing sentient beings to maturity;
sixth, the merit of serving [the Buddha]; seventh, the merit of purifying the buddha-field; and eighth, the merit of never being separated [from the Buddha].
The ninth is the merit of benefiting others; the tenth is the merit of attaining perfect enlightenment. According to this [schema], it corresponds to the seventh merit.

Regarding the phrase "all are entirely equal": because all transformations manifested by the Buddhas are purely untainted (*anāsrava*) and all accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), they are said to be equal.
The statement "it is not only I now" means that these are the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of all Buddhas, just as the lights of many lamps do not obstruct one another.
Sentient beings each perceive [this] differently according to their own dispositions.
The *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* (translated here as *The Sutra of Aṅgulimāla*, meaning "Finger-Garland") consists of four fascicles;
in the first fascicle, it is explained that to the north of Śrāvastī there was a village named Sona, where lived a poor Brahmin woman named Bhadrā.
A daughter was born to him named Sarvalokābhyudgata; she lost her father at the age of twelve, yet she was intelligent, wise, and eloquent.
Furthermore, in another village named Varahasī, there lived an old resident Brahmin teacher named Maṇibhadra (the following is an excerpt of his intent).
Sarvalokābhyudgata studied under him, and the teacher received [instruction from] the King.
He requested that she remain to guard his wife. The wife was young and her mind was overcome by passion; she pressured him, but he would not consent in this world.
The wife then hanged herself to destroy herself. The wife said, "In this world you have forcibly oppressed me.
The master said, "You have already committed evil; you must kill a thousand people to extinguish your sin. He then killed a thousand people and returned to see his master, who marveled at him.
Furthermore, he intended to kill another thousand people, taking one finger from each to fashion a garland for his head; he was short by only one person.
His mother went to deliver food to him, intending to kill her as well. When the World-Honored One appeared before him, he abandoned his mother and rushed toward the Buddha.

He was subdued by the Buddha, and the profound and wondrous details were extensively revealed as described therein. As for the words "not speaking" and "adorned and purified Flower Treasury," etc., there are five [points].
Duan Huìjiào should explain all of this.

Regarding the phrase "the *Chao* [commentary] encompasses the *Fanwang* [Sūtra], etc.," the "etc. includes the *Renwang jing*. The "Chapter on Receiving and Maintaining" (*Shouchi pin*) of the *Renwang jing* states:
"At that time, Candraprabha thought in his heart and spoke with his mouth, seeing Śākyamuni Buddha manifest immeasurable supernatural powers..."
He sees the Buddha Ratnapūrṇa upon the thousand-petaled lotus pedestal, who is the master of the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of all Buddhas (this must be Vairocana;
according to older translations, he is rendered as *Ratnapūrṇa*, where *pūrṇa* carries the meaning of "pure").

He further sees the Buddhas above each of the thousand petals of the world-lotus, each of whom is preaching the Prajñāpāramitā (this is identical to the verse from the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* cited in the *Shu-chao*, though the specific teachings they proclaim differ). It is said that [the teaching] extends around the thousand petals.

Furthermore, he manifests one thousand Śākyamunis; within each of the one thousand petals, there is one Great Trichiliocosm, presided over by a single transformation body of a thousand *zhang* in height.
In total, there are one thousand such transformation bodies of Śākyamuni, each a thousand *zhang* tall.
Within each Great Trichiliocosm, there are ten billion Jambudvīpas, and in each Jambudvīpa, there is a Śākyamuni who is a minor transformation body.
Thus, there are a thousand billion Śākyamunis. As for the statement regarding the source, Vairocana:

because the second layer of his *paranirmita-vipākaja* [retribution] is the source of the thousand great transformations and the one thousand billion minor transformations, it is called "also" (*yi*) and not otherwise.
The phrase "downward" (*xia*) refers to a general selection according to the text; this sutra’s "narrating downward" (*shu xia*) refers to a specific selection by way of illustration.
The *Daśadharmaka-parivarta* states: "This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva possesses a lotus flower whose petals are vast, extending to the limits of the ten directions, adorned with unspeakably many leaves.
This refers to the lotus flower of a Bodhisattva at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), because Samantabhadra occupies that very stage of Equal Enlightenment;
thus, it is said that the flower of a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage is equal [to this].
The "Ten Stages" chapter merely describes its magnitude without specifying the number of petals.
The Sūtra states that the name of its final samādhi is "Receiving the Position of All-Knowledge. When this samādhi manifests, a great lotus flower suddenly appears;
the flower is of vast extent, equal in measure to one million triple-thousand great thousandfold world-systems, and is composed of various exquisite jewels.
Interspersed and magnificently adorned, even as many lotuses as there are atoms in thirteen thousand great thousandfold world systems serve as its retinue.
At that time, the bodhisattva sits upon this lotus throne; the proportions of his physical form are perfectly symmetrical and harmonious—how much more so, then, for the Tathāgata?
This implies that if even those of the tenth bhūmi, who are inferior to the Perfectly Enlightened One, possess such qualities, how much more so must it be for the Tathāgata.

Is the victorious lotus fixed at one thousand petals? This clearly explains the definitive meaning of the initial stage. Regarding the first point, the capacity of the practitioner for whom this is intended:

because the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) is fulfilled in the second stage, the Buddha of the initial stage is able to establish the lower limit. This is explained according to its underlying principle.

If the sutras did not state that the first stage has one hundred petals and the second stage has one thousand petals, but merely said "one obtains one hundred and three," [the meaning would remain unclear].

One attains the vision of a hundred Buddhas and comes to know the bodies of a hundred Buddhas; one can shake a hundred Buddha-worlds, traverse a hundred Buddha-worlds, and illuminate a hundred Buddha-worlds;

one can teach and transform sentient beings in a hundred worlds, abide for a lifespan of a hundred kalpas, know the events of a hundred kalpas each in the past and the future, and enter a hundred gates of illumination of the Dharma to manifest them.
In each and every one of his hundred bodies, he can manifest a hundred bodhisattvas as his retinue. (As it is thus for the first bhūmi, so it is for the second through the tenth bhūmis;

only the number doubles, and all possess this aforementioned quality. One may now infer from these examples that on the first bhūmi one sees flowers with a hundred petals, while on the second bhūmi one sees flowers with a thousand petals, and so forth.
However, there are several characters in the cited text of the *Chao* that contain transcription errors.

As for the third stage, it should be said that [the number of petals] is one hundred thousand; (the *Chao* says "ten thousand"). For the eighth stage, it should be said that [the number of petals] is equal to the atoms in one million three-thousandfold world systems;

(the *Chao* says "hundreds of thousands of millions"). For the ninth stage, it should be said that [the number of petals] is one million *asaṃkhyeya*; (the *Chao* says "hundreds of thousands of millions of billions").
To say these are still merely abbreviated explanations means that, when considering the fruit of retribution attained at the tenth stage, it is truly ineffable.

The *Dengye* (Equal Leaves) states that even the passage cited above regarding the reception of office is still a brief explanation; this makes it clear that the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* subsumes both stages (*bhūmi*).
The *Chao* (Excerpts) states:
"If one explains directly below, there are three general models of correlation and interpretation herein; first, the three great [categories] are directly correlated with the three."
Next, regarding the body, based on the two greats—the essence and the marks of the Worthy Leader (Bhadramukha)—the Dharma-body is established through its function as the great;

this opens into the reward and transformation bodies. However, the reward body is exclusively the "other-reward" [body]. Regarding the mark-greatness, which is also the self-reward body, there are two meanings within its function:

first, it is established as the other-reward body; second, even when refuted, it remains only the transformation body. The general meaning is thus; one may understand it clearly by examining the details. (Within the initial and final meanings of "purity and coolness,")
This is the meaning of "Worthy Leader" (Bhadramukha). Regarding the statement that [the bodies] follow superior karma in terms of their own essence, great function, and so forth:

this means that the two bodies—retribution and transformation—manifest coarse and subtle functions according to the superior karma of sentient beings' conditions. Following the conditions of those on the stages (*bhūmi*), they manifest subtle functions, which is the retribution body (*saṃbhogakāya*);

following the conditions of those prior to the stages, they manifest coarse functions, which is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). There is a version of the text that reads: "following defiled karma, it is illusory."

That commentary states: "In accordance with the sentient beings to be transformed, [the Buddha] performs the karma of benefiting others through defiled dependent origination, illusorily manifesting the objects of the six sense organs.

It further says that both the essence (tǐ) and the characteristics (xiàng) of the Great [Vehicle] are called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), because in this school, there is no wisdom apart from suchness;

thus, the self-recompense is not established as separate, and there is only the single Dharma-body. However, Qingliang [Weoncheug], speaking in terms of the True Recompense (*zhen bao*), refers to the characteristic of the Great [Vehicle].
This refers to the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Regarding the commentary’s distinction against confusion: it distinguishes between establishing the Real outside of the Provisional and establishing the Real by incorporating the Provisional.

To speak generally of the three bodies, they are "provisional" in terms of the faculties of beings and the provisional nature of the teachings; yet their essence is the ten bodies—how then could they be fixed as merely provisional? To speak generally of the ten [bodies]...
If the *svābhāvika-kāya* (body) is defined by contrast against the other two as being "real," what obstacle is there? How could the three bodies be fixed as merely real?
Alternatively, from the perspective of total exclusion, the three bodies are provisional (*upāya*); from the perspective of total inclusion, the three bodies are themselves real.

If one were to unilaterally exclude the provisional to establish the real, one would lose the principle of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*). All of the above has been interpreted according to their respective meanings; as for the Buddha’s own essence, which [of these] is it?
It is inconceivable.
Regarding the statement in the *Shu-yao-chao* (Commentary on the Essentials) that "this samādhi is the essence of the Dharma" and so forth, the *Shizhu-chao* (Commentary on the Ten Stages) says:

First, as for the essence of the Dharma realized, if one wishes to expound this Dharma, the mind must first merge with this essence; second, it distinguishes [the practitioner] from those who have not yet realized it. Furthermore...

If one permits that the inferential mind (*anumāna-citta*) accords with the Dharma, then it is subject to arising and ceasing; this is precisely what the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* (and its commentary) states:

"The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is profound, mysterious, and wondrously transcendent beyond ordinary realms; it is not something known by a mind possessed of thought, nor can it be expressed by those who rely on eloquence. How could one wish to explain it using the mental activities of arising and ceasing?

To speak only after threefold transcendence of thought is also consistent with the principle that one must first sever the mind before being able to accord with the meaning of the essence of the realized Dharma (*adhigata-dharmatā*) mentioned above.

Regarding the statement that the former [verse] explains the reality through direct manifestation while this one explains it by way of negating errors, there are two differing interpretations by the masters.
If one follows Jizhao, he says: "The former is the first [case], which directly manifests the virtues of what is realized;

these latter two meanings both concern the negation of errors, as they equally contain the character 'non-'" (非). If one follows Zhixu, he says: "This merely serves to distinguish between 'two' and 'three'."
Because there would be the fault of redundancy and lack of distinction if the term "non-" (*a-*) were present in all three cases, I have specifically distinguished them here.

In the previous [section], the second [case] was used to manifest these three by means of negation and affirmation; therefore, it was not redundant. The first meaning is easy to understand and need not be analyzed, as it lacks the word "non-.
The latter explanation is correct because it states that the aforementioned three meanings are subsequently realized through the cessation of discursive thought (*niścintya*).

Realization accords with the essence of the Dharma; thus it is said that each subsequent [explanation] clarifies the preceding one. Furthermore, the aforementioned three meanings correspond to the intent of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Regarding the fourth point, "observing the faculties and examining the Dharma," the *Shizhu-jiaochao* states: "Observing the faculties means recognizing what is appropriate for the specific ailment;
examining the Dharma means knowing the efficacy of the medicine. One should not preach the Dharma without observing the faculties of the person."

If one explains the principles of phenomena with careful scrutiny, they may sometimes deviate from what is appropriate; yet, when the medicine is administered in accordance with the ailment, it can be ingested and practiced.

Because the five distracted states of mind cannot withstand the empowerment of the Buddhas, it is said that "the harmony of causes and conditions" refers to the harmony of causes and conditions for entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Only through this harmony can one enter concentration, and only upon arising from concentration can one speak [of the teaching]; thus, it is said that these six constitute the ritual protocol.
The *Shizhu chao* (Commentary on the Ten Stages) states: "A Bodhisattva is constantly in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) solely to serve as a model for sentient beings;
if even a Bodhisattva must enter concentration before preaching, how much more so must an ordinary person?

This commentary now contains the full meaning of the *Sūtra-śāstra*. The preceding section has already provided a preliminary explanation of the intent of the *Śāstra*, while this section below analyzes the actual wording of the *Śāstra*; thus, it is said to "contain" [the meaning].

The first four [points] concern the "intention" (the heading). "Quiescence" (*jing*) means being free from discursive thought (the third); "clarity" (*jian*) means realization (the second meaning, i.e., the capacity to realize);

"the essence of phenomena" (*futi*) is the primary [meaning]. Quiescence and clarity refer to the preceding principle; "observing the faculties and examining the Dharma" refers to the fourth. Above, according to the *Zhi-xuan*, if one says "quiescent-clarity" (*jing-jian*), it refers to the preceding principle.
This single phrase contains three meanings, including the preceding "demonstrating the method" and the subsequent "disciples. This constitutes the sequence.

The sixth meaning comprises four aspects: "quiescence" (jing) refers to being free from discursive thought (the third meaning); "mirror-like clarity" (jian) refers to realizing the essence of the Dharma (the first meaning;

by citing the capacity for realization, it reveals that which is realized); "quiescent clarity" (jing-jian) refers to contemplating the principle before one and examining the faculties while scrutinizing the Dharma (the fourth meaning).

Because the character "before" (qian) encompasses both the principle and the faculties, if one were to speak only of "before," it would refer solely to observing the faculties; since the character "before" contains these two meanings, it is so stated.
The "combined faculties" (jiāngēn) refers to the fact that both are combined; thus, it corresponds to the fourth sense.
Regarding its second sense, between the two explanations provided in the subsequent text, "quiescent illumination" (jìzhào) is the correct one, as the *Chāo* text clearly demarcates them.

However, if one follows the intent of the *Zhǐxuán*, separating the text of the *Chāo* would seem like forced interpretation. Nevertheless, the *Zhǐxuán* refutes this by stating: "Quiescent illumination [is found] in the first four... and so forth.

Sixth, regarding the difficulty of using the preceding character: here, "before" refers to the section preceding the main body of the *Chao* (Excerpts), not the "before" within the six [sections] themselves.
Furthermore, it is argued: "How can the single phrase 'the principle before Jingjian'—which is separately cited in the *Chao*—contain the meaning of the sixth [section]?
This is because the sixth [section] resides in the phrase concerning "Wugu. Now, upon careful examination, although this is a single separately cited phrase, [it does indeed contain the sense].
The first intention regarding the demonstration of the ritual has already been explained; therefore, including the preceding section, there are four intentions. Let the wise examine this.
Regarding the statement in the *Chao* (Excerpts) that "the Buddha’s empowerment can be known," this refers to the fifth intention, which is easy to understand and thus not explained here.

Regarding the statement in the *Chao* that "one does not speak unless there is proof," this refers to the second intention, "Quiescence and Illumination" (*jìzhào*); it is a concluding summary of the second intention, pointing back to its profound meaning.
This correctly corresponds to the second [point]. Now, examining the preceding two main texts, they do not state "it is not a proof" (*apramāṇa*).

Since our present *Chao* (Excerpts) also says "it is not a proof, it is not stated," how could there be the meaning of a "contrary conclusion"? If one takes the presence of the word "also" (*yi*) in the *Chao* as indicating that this is not a correct correspondence, that is not so;
for while the previous text has already provided the correspondence, this text provides it again, using "also" to correspond with what follows below.

It says "also" (*yì*) because it reveals that a single meaning is shared; it says "also" because the two lines of the commentary contain two meanings and thus are transcribed as two separate explanations.
Furthermore, since *Zhǐxuán* applies two interpretations, they do not constitute a direct correspondence.
As for the previous instance where the two characters "jìngjiàn" (靜鑑) were used twice, consider why they are not a direct correspondence. Reflect upon this.
The first volume of the *Commentary* (鈔) states in detail: "Entering the Samādhi of the Body-Treasury of All Buddhas, Vairocana Tathāgata.
It says that Samantabhadra "enters" because he expounds the Universal Dharma;

since it is only Samantabhadra who manifests the universal virtues of the Buddha, and his mind is in profound accord with the object, this is termed "entering. "Vairocana" is translated here as "Vast and Great" (廣大).
Because its arising and ceasing are boundless in compassion, its wisdom is vast and unsurpassed, and its marks of birth have been utterly exhausted, it is called "Nirvāṇa of Arising and Ceasing.
Because it is free from existence and eternally abiding, it is named "Tathāgata.

Encompassing all myriad virtues, this is called the "Treasury Body" (*garbha-kāya*), which is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) that has emerged from its entanglements. *Samādhi* is here translated as "equipoise" (*samāhita*); it is the state far removed from sinking.

Because it equalizes restlessness and holds the mind so that it moves toward a single object; and because it is said that "rightly experiencing" (*samyak-samādhi*) means not receiving any [disturbing] sensations, thus it is called "right experience";

and because it is said that "right reflection" (*samyak-manasikāra*)—as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi*—refers to the one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*) through careful and correct observation of the focal object.
Thus, there is no such thing as "right" or "wrong" reflection; rather, what is termed "reflection" merely serves to induce wrong mindfulness (*mithyā-smṛti*).

Unlike empty space, which is devoid of thought yet is forcibly designated as "right thought," if one understands this through the metaphor of pervasive illumination, Vairocana is the Tathāgata-body of Great Wisdom who is capable of contemplation, while the Tathāgatagarbha is the profound principle that is the object of contemplation.
Although this principle exists even in ordinary beings, it is only through Buddha-wisdom that it is illuminated. Furthermore, Vairocana also encompasses the primordially existent reality.

Because it truly realizes and knows the meaning of the universally illuminating dharma-realm, this is precisely the original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*). When deluded, one does not know it and cannot attain its function;
only when a Buddha awakens to this can there be nothing that is not accomplished. Therefore, it says "all Buddhas," which distinguishes them from ordinary beings and those on the causal stages.
It reveals that the environment and its inhabitants (*āśraya-vastu*) are inseparable from the *tathāgatagarbha*, as they have no separate self-nature apart from it; thus, one enters into this.

(First Assembly: This is because it explains the objects of faith—the environment and its inhabitants. ▲ In the third assembly, below [the section on] Dharmamati entering [the stage], since he is the leader of the assembly, it is revealed that Dharmamati is capable of preaching the Dharma of the Ten Abodes.
Because the profound principle of the Abode of Wisdom is explained by means of the Perfect Teaching, the ten mental states are presented as reaching the Cloud of Dharma.
To distinguish this from the fixed state of fruition, it says: "The Bodhisattva, by his natural capacity, possesses knowledge and skillful insight."
Therefore, it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*). Because each of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) encompasses many gates of skillful means (*kauśalya*), they are termed "immeasurable minds.
In the fourth assembly of the *Yanmi* (Commentary), it is stated that the various virtues of the ten practices (*daśapratipatti*) are established;

because the cause is distinguished from the fruit, they are called "Bodhisattvas" (the following two [terms] should be understood accordingly). Skillfully conforming to both principle and phenomena, their discernment is unimpeded; accomplishing deeds without a [discursive] mind is called "skillful reflection" (*sukha-cintā*).
Consider: because the *Vajradhvaja-śāstra* (Jin-gang-chuang-biao) explains that the "highly exalted" and so forth toward which one turns back are precisely wisdom, this wisdom is the essence.
That is to say, the light of fundamental wisdom has three meanings: first, the light of wisdom as a precursor, such as the "attainment of clarity" (*ālokalabdha-samādhi*) and so forth;

this refers to the stage of being situated within the final level of the Stage of Worthies (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*). Second, the light itself is the function of fundamental wisdom, serving as an antidote to ignorance (*avidyā*).

The "three lights" refer to the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), which comprehends its objects; because these two wisdoms are unimpeded and radiantly illuminate the *dharmadhātu*, this is explained in terms of the essential nature of the Vajradhvaja.

In the sixth fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā-ṭīkā*, it states that the roots of goodness of the wisdom of the stages (*bhūmi*) manifested by Vajragarbha are firm and solid, capable of destroying all afflictions that are otherwise difficult to destroy; thus, they possess the qualities of being both firm and sharp, like a *vajra*.

Therefore, it is called a "Treasury" (*garbha*) because it encompasses all virtues and gives birth to cause and effect; it is called "Wisdom" (*jñāna*) as its essence, and "Light" (*prabhā*) as its function of illumination.

It is termed "Insight" (*prajñā*) when it illuminates the two kinds of selflessness and realizes suchness, and it is termed "Knowledge" (*jñāna*) when it illuminates phenomena. These two are unimpeded;

on the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), they can destroy the delusions of views, and continuing through the ten stages (*bhūmi*), they sever ignorance (*avidyā*). For these reasons, it is called "Great Light," which carries two meanings.
First, it is called "Great" because it distinguishes itself from ordinary beings, the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas prior to the stages.

Second, it is called "Great" because it can sever great delusions, realize the Great Principle, and achieve the Great Fruit (whereas the previous [explanation] was "Great" in relation to others, this is "Great" by its own essential nature). Wisdom merges with the Principle; this is called "entering.
The *Bencaoshu* briefly omits the character "Great. (As in the *Caoshu*, fascicle 7, under the section beginning "The Tathāgata abides in... This refers to the present assembly, etc.
Because awakening to the supreme is identical to the Buddha-stage and is the same as the assembly of wondrous enlightenment, the Buddha himself enters and abides;
this is the meaning of "entry. As the Sutra says, he "enters the samādhi of all Buddhas at the limit of a kṣaṇa. This refers to reaching the ultimate source of reality.

That which is called a *kṣaṇa* denotes the most extreme brevity of time. When the temporal characteristics of that *kṣaṇa* are entirely stilled, the limitless limit is termed the "limit of the *kṣaṇa*" (*kṣaṇānta*).

This explains the reason for entering the Buddha-stage; herein, it is specifically termed the "limit of the moment" (*kṣaṇāntya*) because it is intended to reveal that the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is about to be explained.
When the Bodhisattva stages are exhausted, although the fruit is attained, there remains the birth-phase of the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*), which has not yet been stilled;

thus it is still called the "storehouse consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*). As long as there is even a single moment, if one awakens to the initial arising of the mind with uninterrupted wisdom, [one enters the stage of Buddhahood].
Because the mind has no initial characteristic and is far removed from subtle thoughts, there is no such thing as a *kṣaṇa*;

this is called the limit of the *kṣaṇa*. This refers to the state of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). As for "all Buddhas," if one enters this limit, one perceives that the nature of the mind is eternally abiding;

this is called Ultimate Enlightenment (*atyanta-bodhi*). Therefore, it is said that "all Buddhas are in samādhi. This assembly also speaks of Wondrous Enlightenment (*prakarṣa-bodhi*). (From *Fozu Sanzhong Huizang Chao*, Fascicle 8, Section on Pǔ).
Because the "Worthy One" (*bhadra*) who enters is the presiding host of this assembly, it is called "Universal Practice.

Because the *Buddhāvataṃsaka* is the blossoming and arraying of the ten thousand practices that adorn the Dharma-body, its essence is the ocean of the mind as the gateway of practice within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

As for "samādhi," it is the non-duality of principle and wisdom, mutually penetrating and fused until both subject and object, as well as self and other, are utterly transcended; thus the Sūtra speaks of two thousand [aspects].
Because practice possesses both cause and fruit. [The *Chao* (Commentary), Vol. 9, states: "Below, regarding the Tathāgata, it is shown that the Dharma-realm is exhausted only by the Buddha.
Thus, taking the fixed karmic function as a metaphor for its name, the four bodies (*catur-kāya*) are fully unfolded in a state of pervasive flow;

this is the essence of function. When the essence is quiescent and reaches its ultimate limit, the myriad distinctions are none other than the Dharma-realm. This is the function of the essence. It is not... [the text continues].

Because it acts universally and pervasively, the small and the great intermingle; because it arises through dependent origination without end, it is said that the meaning of spontaneous mastery is revealed all at once (as previously cited in full).
In the commentary [it is stated]: "Regarding those who have not yet entered the stages," because the nature of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) is not yet fixed, they are like light feathers;
among the five stages such as the stage of provisioning (*sambhāra-mārga*), they have not yet entered into correct faith, and thus they speak of the world.
Regarding the "intermediate dharma" (antara-dharma), there are two masters' interpretations. One supports the correct view by citing other teachings:

if even the causes and effects of humans and devas must involve entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*), how much more so for the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) in this sutra? As for "quiescent illumination" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), it refers specifically to this sutra, yet it has two meanings.

First, regarding the sequential progression (*caryā-pratipatti*), the impure contemplations of the three stages of worthiness (*tri-kṣānti*) belong to the external ordinary beings (*bāhya-pṛthagjana*); they are called "worldly" (*laukika*), as seen in the verse from the *Yāmāvatī-parivarta*.
The *Zanchao* states: "Those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) are called 'worldly,' while ascending the stages is 'transcendent' (*lokottara*);

this serves as an analogy for the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) in the Perfectly Interfused [Teaching], which are transcendent faiths that encompass the ocean of fruition. The subsequent *Chao* states: "In terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they are called worldly;

in terms of nature (*dharmatā*), they are transcendent. Second, it says: "In the first assembly, the 'Accomplishment of the World' and so forth explain that [the world] is produced by the karmic power of sentient beings."

Considering that even the impure worlds of outflows—the peripheral lands where defiled sentient beings dwell within the Flower Treasury World—require the entry into meditative concentration, how much more so must this be the case for the profound Dharma gates such as receiving empowerment and ascending to the rank [of Bodhisattva] during the ten stages of faith?
The three interpretations may be taken at will; they merely reveal omissions in the text.

Regarding those [categories] that do not enter [the fixed sequence], they shall be distinguished in the text. In the *Commentary* on the "Chapter on Names and Titles," it asks: "Why do they not enter meditative concentration? It answers:

"Because they have not yet entered the stage [of certainty] and their nature is not yet fixed. If this were so, would the final ten concentrations and so forth not be mundane, non-concentrated virtues?

However, the ritual of preaching the Dharma generally comprises four permutations: first, preaching after entering concentration, as in various assemblies; second, entering concentration after preaching.
As stated in the *Anantārthika-sūtra*, after entering the *Anantārthika-vyūha-samādhi*, it is taught within the three concentrations that, as in the ninth assembly, there is no utterance of words;

this signifies that only realized wisdom (*jñāna*) can expound [the truth]. Because one attainment is eternally constant and does not obstruct the arising of its function, the fourth [assembly] does not enter into such discourse.
This is evident in various passages throughout the seventh assembly, as well as in the *Śraddhā-bhūmi*, which are not few in number. The seventh [assembly] serves as...

Because the [first] manifestation is always in a state of meditative concentration, and because one enters [the second] to receive empowerment—which is not required for the former—it is said that the latter enters.

This is because it is said to exist within practice and is about to initiate practice. Therefore, movement and stillness are merely phenomena; for the Sage, there is no fixed rule. (The commentary points toward the meaning that [this] applies only to those heading toward the ten stages of faith and does not include those who have not yet entered.)

Regarding the phrase "the subsequent scripture says," this refers to what has already been explained in the *Guanming juepin* (Chapter on the Awareness of Radiance) within the section on the non-obstruction between the True and the Responsive;
however, the essential meaning here—that formlessness does not obstruct form—differs from the previous [explanation], as the scripture contains many layers of meaning.

▲The *Commentary on the Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "The lower part of the sub-commentary says: 'The first half-verse of the verse [on] realizing the ultimate nature and characteristics (*dharmatā-dharma*) realizes that the essence (*svabhāva*) is without marks (*animitta*);

the subsequent half-verse is the arising of the mark of functional activity (*vṛtti*). This combines with the two preceding [points of] non-obstruction between the absence of marks and the presence of marks.

The next half-verse shows that function does not depart from essence, such that essence is identical to the absence of marks. The final half-verse shows the cessation of both essence and function, because they are without marks.'"

The meaning of this is also not in accord with reality; if one perceives that no marks can be obtained, this too is still a mark, for one cannot eliminate the state of having mental objects and the mind is still being led by them—how could this be true non-markedness?
How could true non-markedness ever tolerate the simulation of mental objects?
The Commentary states that regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other such texts, that sūtra says: "He entered the Samādhi of the Place of Immeasurable Meanings;
his body and mind were unmoving. At that time, the heavens rained down *māndārava* flowers, scattering them over the Buddha (this is the 'raining of flowers').
The entire buddha-world shook in six ways (this is the 'trembling of the earth'). Then, the Buddha emitted light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows."

The eighteen thousand Buddha-lands of the eastern direction [are illuminated] (this refers to the emission of light). The *Yao* states that when he was about to preach the *Nirvāṇa*, his voice and light immediately proclaimed [the message] everywhere.
The Sūtra says: "At the time of entering *nirvāṇa*, he emitted a great sound;
that sound filled the world as far as the Summit of Existence (*bhavāgra*), universally proclaiming to all sentient beings: 'Today the Tathāgata is about to enter *nirvāṇa*. All sentient beings...'"

If there are those who harbor doubts, you may now ask all that you wish; this is your final question. Furthermore, from his mouth he emitted various rays of light that illuminated the entire trichiliocosm;
those who encountered them were cleansed of their defilements and gathered at the twin trees. The commentary on that passage states:

"The emission of light from the face-gate is mostly for the purpose of bestowing predictions of enlightenment," as it is further said below that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and shall all become Buddhas.
The Buddha then bestowed universal predictions of enlightenment. As stated in the *Commentary* regarding the section on the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:

"He extended his broad and long tongue and emitted immeasurable rays of light of various colors. Within each ray of light appeared precious lotus flowers, golden in hue, with a thousand petals, magnificent and fragrant.
Upon each flower pedestal was a transformation Buddha preaching the *Prajñāpāramitā* throughout the ten directions, across worlds as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers."

Regarding the "elements" (*dhātu*) and so forth: the *Chao* (Commentary) states that the six kinds of earthquakes consist of: shaking (*calana*), pervasive shaking (*pracaḷana*), universal shaking (*saṃpracalana*);

rising (*udvega*), leaping (*kṣubha*), and roaring (*raṇa*). Each of these, as described above, possesses three phases. The *Shu* (Sub-commentary) explains: "To sway unsteadily is called 'shaking' (*calana*');

to rise gradually from below is called 'rising' (*udvega*'); to suddenly soar upward is called 'leaping' (*kṣubha*'); to produce a deep, rumbling sound is called 'roaring' (*raṇa*'); and for a powerful sound to be suppressed [and then released] is called 'thundering' (*stanita*')."

The sounds "hūṃ," "pang," and "ke" that arise are called *kṣobha* (shaking); when movement occurs in only one direction, it is simply called *calana* (movement); when movement occurs in all four directions, it is called *saṃcalana* (universal shaking);
and when movement occurs in all eight directions, it is called *saṃpracalana* (universal universal shaking). The other [terms] such as *udvega* (trembling) should be understood by analogy.

Among these six, the first three refer to form and the latter three refer to sound; since only the first of each category is mentioned, they are termed "shaking. This is stated in the *Suvikrāntavikrāmī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* and the *Brahmaparipṛcchā-sūtra*.
There are seven purposes: first, to cause all māras to be terrified; second, because when the Dharma is being taught, the minds of the great assembly may become distracted;
third, to cause those who are heedless to give rise to awareness; fourth, to cause the assembly to know the characteristics of the Dharma;
fifth, to cause sentient beings to contemplate the place where the Dharma is taught; sixth, to cause those who are matured to attain liberation; and seventh, to cause...

Because one accords with hearing the meaning of the True Dharma, if one refers to the stages of the mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*), the noble stages (*āryabhūmi*), and the Dharma-nature stage (*dharmatābhūmi*), there is likewise the sense of "trembling" and so forth, which may be sought through emptiness.
Regarding the passage in the *Commentary* on the *Huayan* [Sutra] concerning "clouds of flowers, clouds of incense," etc., the sub-commentary states:
"Now, as for why all these implements of offering are called 'clouds,' there are many meanings; it is because their forms and appearances are manifest, and wisdom grasps them."
Being devoid of intrinsic nature, it arises from the emptiness of the dharma-nature as the unarisen dharma; that which manifests and that which is manifested are utterly without dependence.
It comes through application yet has no point of origin from which it comes; it departs when its function ceases yet has no destination to which it goes.
Yet, it can contain compassionate moisture and pour down the rain of Dharma, benefiting all things in manifold, layered, and unimpeded ways—thus it possesses the likeness of clouds.
The commentary on the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" lists five signs: first, the sign of light from the face-gate summoning the assemblies of the ten directions;

second, the sign of light from between the eyebrows indicating the master who preaches the Dharma; third, the shaking of the network of lands to awaken the various capacities of sentient beings; fourth, the manifestation of flowers before the Buddhas to signify that the explained environment (the *niṣyanda-bhājanaloka*) is being taught;
and fifth, the emergence of a multitude from the *ūrṇā-kośa* to signify that the teaching flows forth from the Buddha. [End of] Commentary. Addition.
"Sublime Virtue" (Miaode) refers to the Bodhisattva Wondrous Virtue Arising from the Nature of the Tathāgata (*Tathāgatagotra-samudgata-maudeśvara*).

The sub-commentary below states: "The reason this bodhisattva is added is because he is manifested according to his name. 'Nature' (xing) has two meanings: first, the meaning of 'lineage-nature' (*gotra*), for it is that which is produced by causes;
second, the meaning of 'dharma-nature' (*dharmatā*), for both the true [body] and the response [body] are produced from this. There is also an interpretation which says: "This..."
It is said that "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode) is Mañjuśrī; when he expounds this Dharma-gate, it is called the "Manifestation of Nature" (xingqi).

This interpretation does not contradict the Great Principle, for Mañjuśrī’s great wisdom acts as the manifestor (*nirbhāsaka*), while the Dharmadhātu of Samantabhadra is that which is manifested (*nirbhāsya*).

Together they constitute the appearance of Vairocana. Furthermore, because his practice and realization are perfected, this is the "appearance of the Buddha through the fulfillment of conduct. — *Chao* (Excerpts)
Regarding the radiance of the white tuft (*ūrṇā-kośa*): white is the foundation of all colors; "tuft" refers to the hair.
According to the *Buddha-dhyāna-samādhi-sūtra*, when the Prince was first born, it extended five feet; when he was under the Bodhi tree, it extended one zhang, four chi, and five cun;
after attaining Buddhahood, it was one zhang and five chi in length, with a color as pure and brilliant as white jade or snow.
Because it is clearly evident. Regarding the phrase "the face-gate" (*mianmen*) and so forth in the *Chao* (Commentary), the *Shu* (Sub-commentary) states: "The 'face-gate' is the mouth;

because it refers to the multitude of teeth, it symbolizes that the Way of Teaching extends afar, which is the light of the wisdom of teaching. As for the statement 'born from the Buddha’s mouth,' the *Lotus Sūtra* says:

'Born from the Buddha’s mouth, born from transformation by the Dharma, they obtain a portion of the Buddha-dharma. (The former symbolizes the pervasiveness of the teaching; this symbolizes the excellence of the faculty. Thus it is said.
"Total locus" (*saṃgraha-sthāna*) refers to the mouth as the locus for expounding the Dharma, because all dharma-gates are manifested from this [mouth].

Furthermore, it indicates that while the lower [part] is explained in terms of the teeth, the upper [part] is explained in terms of the mouth. The phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the fact that there are forty questions concerning the teeth. The *Chao* (Commentary) states that this generally indicates the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Regarding the phrase "the first assembly is the general [locus]," it means that since the first assembly is the general [locus], it applies to all nine assemblies; thus, it is called "general. It does not calculate the two extremes of existence and non-existence regarding the essence (*tattva*).
Regarding meaning, one does not cling to the extremes of various dharmic characteristics such as permanence or impermanence;

regarding practice, one does not cultivate the two extremes of suffering and pleasure (the view of annihilationism clings to the practice of pleasure, while the view of eternalism clings to the practice of suffering);

regarding the path, one does not abide in the two extremes of the heterodox and the orthodox, for since there is no heterodoxy or orthodoxy established apart from the true cause, one does not grasp at persons because cause and effect are mutually penetrating; and regarding teaching, one does not speak of the mundane.

Because the two extremes regarding transcendence are established in mutual dependence; because one does not perceive the two extremes of the true and the conventional within the Truths, as the Two Truths are neither identical nor different;
and because the provisional and the real are mutually identical within the indeterminate transformations [of the Buddha]—therefore, the Buddha emits light from between his eyebrows.
Regarding the statement in the *Yao* (Excerpts) that "it serves as the foundation for practice," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "As for the body attaining stability..."
All of this is due to the fact that the words are sufficient to encompass the ocean of fruits; as for the "lower wheel," it is because it is perfectly complete and without deficiency.

[Commentary]: Regarding "the toes rest firmly," the toes push against the ground to gain stability with power, thereby establishing a position from which there is no regression, and proceeding with constancy.
[Commentary]: Regarding "relying on the movement," the upper part of the foot refers to the instep; since movement necessarily involves motion, the instep relies upon the wheel.

Because it indicates that which is functional; because it represents the practice of faith and understanding so as to bring about utility. Regarding the phrase "the kneecap circle" (*jñānacakra*) and so forth: because the stages gradually ascend;
furthermore, because it represents the turning away from causes toward the fruit, possessing the characteristics of bending and extending, advancing and retreating;

furthermore, because compassion and wisdom guide one another, bending and extending without abiding; and because great wisdom illuminates the ultimate, causing all things to accord with the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Although "extension" (prasarana) broadly transforms sentient beings, wisdom remains within; although "contraction" (saṃkoca) keeps wisdom within, compassion is made to have no fixed object.
Although extension employs compassion externally, it ensures that wisdom does not remain in silent stillness; contraction likewise ensures that compassion and wisdom guide one another.
Whether extending or contracting, neither departs from the person, as both are directed toward the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi); therefore, there is no [duality].

The character "Zhu" (Abiding) appears in the lower section of the *Chao* (Commentary). It signifies that the Path of Manifestation transcends the two extremes of existence and non-existence; the Path of Non-abiding transcends the two extremes of the True and the Responsive.
The white curl between the brows (*ūrṇā-kośa*) symbolizes that the nature which manifests is immaculate; it is the source from which all teachings are manifested and explained.
It enters into the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Wondrous Virtue Arising from the Tathāgata’s Nature, so as to cause him to request the Dharma. — *Chao*.

Furthermore, light is emitted from the mouth to signify that the teaching and the path have been transmitted; it enters the mouth of Samantabhadra so that the teaching may be passed on, for it is as the Buddha has taught.
[From] the eighth assembly of the *Jingtu shuchao*, the lower section:

because the two thousand practices arise from the method of cultivating causes and acceding to the fruit according to the preceding six assemblies, the light of wisdom and understanding is produced only when these practices are perfected; therefore, there is no need to emit light [at this stage].

Alternatively, it may be absent because the scriptural text is incomplete. Regarding the phrase "the *Chao* [commentary] cites the proof," etc., this means that one should seek out the Light of Wisdom (*jñānāloka*) as the means of realization;
for it is the untainted, correct wisdom (*anāsrava-samyag-jñāna*) within the Middle Way of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) that is capable of realizing it.
The statement "it is explained extensively below in the *Shu*" refers precisely to what is cited here.

The Commentary (*Chao*) distinguishes between what is identical and what is different: if considered in terms of initiating what follows, they are identical and thus serve as conditions for the teaching;

the lamp serves as a metaphor for the causes of conditions and understanding (*pratyaya-hetu* and *jñāna-hetu*). In the latter half of the verse, the dharma is applied [to the person], yet no person is found.

Because of this deficiency in the causal condition of virtuous friends, even if there is a subtle and inferior wisdom-eye produced through cultivation, it does not achieve realization.
Because one does not see the true nature (this refers to being blind within the metaphor).
[The Commentary] asks: Now, regarding this speaker who "pervades the three worlds," how is he distinguished from the previous speaker who "fuses the three worlds"?

As stated in the *Xiangfan dengchao* (Excerpts on Fragrant Food and the Like): "The three worlds together with time constitute four;

Regarding the phrase "the sentient beings" (*sattva*) below: although the Buddhas lack affection and the like, they are called "sentient beings" because their consciousness of affection is purely untainted (*anāsrava*).
Regarding the phrase "the seven above" and the question below concerning the explanation of the Buddhas of the three periods:
if one asks how there can be ten when there are only the seven mentioned above, it is because, in addition to those seven, one specifically takes the Buddhas of the three periods.

Furthermore, when the seven aforementioned categories are combined with the ten meanings of "opening," they constitute the doctrine of the "repeated teaching throughout the three periods of time. How so? The answer is:
if one does not speak of the three periods of time, the seven categories could only be taught within a single moment.
Now, by taking those seven categories throughout the entirety of the three periods of time and teaching them perpetually, the seven become distinct and the three become the totality.
Regarding the phrase "taking the Dharma within time," this refers to the difference in meaning.

As for "the three are fused," the *Shu* (Commentary) states: "Person and phenomena are one in their common dependent origination; according to their meanings, they are differentiated yet fused and subsumed without duality.

If neither can be apprehended, what meaning is there in speaking? The answer is that it is called "speaking" because it causes the faculties of those to be addressed to understand the meaning of their mutual sublation.

because they are unobstructed regarding the identity or difference of those persons and dharmas, and because they are unhindered in their existence or non-existence, they are freely and perfectly interfused. (From the *Jiaochao*, the first section, "The Ten," etc.)
1. The *dharmadhātu* of phenomena refers to the tenfold abodes and so forth; 2. The *dharmadhātu* of principle refers to the single flavor and profound stillness and so forth;

5. The *dharmadhātu* of essence refers to quiescence and non-arising and so forth; 6. The *dharmadhātu* of function refers to the supreme supernormal powers and self-mastery and so forth.

The seven favorable factors of the dharma-realm refer to the six perfections, right practice, and so forth; the eight adverse factors of the dharma-realm refer to the five heats, lack of weariness, and so forth;

the nine factors of the teaching-dharma-realm refer to the spoken words one hears and so forth; and the ten factors of the meaning-dharma-realm refer to the intended significance that is elucidated and so forth.
These ten dharma-gates share a single dependent origination; they are unimpeded and fused together, each containing and being contained within the others.

All. Regarding the phrase "the person and the dharma-realm" in the *Commentary* (*Chao*), the *Sub-commentary* (*Shu*) states: "These ten are all the objective divisions (*nimitta-bhāga*) of dependent origination;

Regarding the places where Sudhana visited, he asked, "Why is it said that this Friend of the Dharma (Dharmamitra) is in the entire city? The answer, as stated in the sub-commentary (*śū*), provides two meanings:
first, since a friend must necessarily rely upon a city, there is one city and one friend; second, within a single city, one may encounter many friends.
Alternatively, one might seek a single friend while traveling through many cities, yet the requirement remains to reach exactly one hundred and ten [visits].

Because they accord with the manifestation of the Dharma (the manifestation of the Dharma is as previously stated), there are differing explanations regarding these one hundred and ten spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
One view holds that they should logically be complete, but the text is merely missing;

another holds that the fifty-four friends mentioned by the Venerable Xianshou (Bandhuprabha) in his earlier and later works, when combined with the addition of Guṇākara and Guṇavatsu as two, total fifty-five individuals, each of whom possesses both their own stage (*svabhūmi*) and the higher stages (*viśeṣa-bhūmi*).
Regarding the progression, the *Kandingpo* (Decisive Refutation) states: "The scripture says 'one hundred and ten,' after which one arrives at Maitreya;
it is clear that Maitreya and the other two are not included within the count of one hundred and ten. The *Kandingjie* (Decisive Explanation) states:
"This is merely a rounded number; in reality, there are only one hundred and eight persons, because the aforementioned [count] excludes Vyāghrabodhi."
The fifty-one individuals each have their own primary and secondary companions, totaling one hundred and two;
although Vyāsa was not a primary friend but rather a secondary companion, he is included to bring the total to one hundred and three.
Furthermore, there are King Anala staying in the sky, Gopā staying with the deity Viśoka-śrī, and Māyā staying with the host of deities Padma-dharma-guṇa-kāya.
The deity Subhāprabhā (Wondrous Radiance) who guards the Dharma Hall and the Rākṣasa Sukha-netra (Good Eye), together with the aforementioned, total one hundred and eight.
Because they engage in dialogue through the signs of the empty sky and so forth, they are included among the number of "friends" (*mitra*);

however, because they are not designated by name as primary leaders or friends, they are not "primary friends" (*mukhya-mitra*) but are merely called "associates" (*sahāya*). How remarkable is this teaching! It is said that the instruction flows from the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*). Regarding how these insentient things can thus "speak," the *Zhenyuan Shu* states there are briefly four meanings:
first, it is through the karmic power of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; second, it is because the nature of their qualities (*guṇalakṣaṇa*) is such that they are naturally capable of doing so;

By virtue of this power, there is not one thing that is not complete; therefore, one teaching is all teachings. When following characteristics from the nature, there is teaching and non-teaching;

Regarding the "briefly ten categories" mentioned in the *Shu* (Commentary), the *Miaoyan-pin Shu* (Commentary on the Chapter on Wondrous Adornments) explains them as follows: 1. **The Retinue of Influences**:

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas act as the primary figures and their companions, like a shadow following a form or an echo responding to a sound. 2. **The Constant Retinue**: Such as Samantabhadra and others, who act as assistants.
1. The assembly of protectors, such as the Vajrapāṇi deities and others, who constantly and diligently guard the abodes of all Buddhas;
2. The assembly of those who adorn the congregation, such as the Maṇḍala-devas and others, who constantly purify the Buddha’s palaces; 3.

The assembly of those who offer worship, such as those who offer praise in verse, Dharma-offerings, flowers, banners, and material wealth; 4. The assembly of those who initiate [the discourse], such as Vimukticandra and others.

Regarding the seven types of assemblies that pose challenges: first, the assembly of those with faculties (*indriya*) present at the gathering at that very moment; second, the assembly of those whose faculties are manifested through spiritual resonance in the present, future, or past;
third, the assembly of those who manifest the Dharma through outward signs (*vijñapti*), such as the ten leaders representing faith and the ten forests representing practice;

fourth, the assembly of Bodhisattvas emerging from their seats, who manifest their forms to uphold [the teachings] and thereby universally represent the fulfillment of all myriad practices (*sāhasra-caryā*); fifth, the assembly of those who have realized the Dharma (*adhigama-dharma*). As for the "realization": [it refers to the realization of the Truth].

Because the Dharma-Buddha, Bodhisattvas, and others testify that their teachings are not false, the tenth [member] reveals the assembly of the Dharma; this is like the revelation of the Dharma by the Śrāvakas as its unique feature.

In the eighth assembly, because cause and effect have reached full maturity, questions must be asked; these concern the six stages of unimpeded cultivation.

The request expressed through external words is subsumed under the "condition" (*pratyaya*), as the nature of these two meanings is somewhat distinct. Regarding the Tathāgata’s request, the *Shū* (Commentary) states: "He does not seek or request by means of ordinary speech."

Furthermore, speaking from the Cloud Terrace rather than from his ordinary body, and using radiant light and deeds (*karmaprabhāsa*) instead of physical prostration, is because he does not lightly regard his exalted status;

and requesting [the teaching] again is because he values the Dharma. This request made by means of radiant light and verses is called a "request through empowerment" (*adhiṣṭhāna-ādhyeṣaṇā*), as it is also a distinct meaning regarding the Teacher’s superiority.
As for its inclusion within the category of those who request, it is defined by the power bestowed upon the speaker.

Regarding this "additional empowerment" (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the *Commentary on the Ten Stages* (*Daśabhūmivyākhyā*) states that in the preceding section on empowerment, Vairocana provided only mental empowerment;

now, because he provides it fully through body and speech as well, there is a further empowerment. Alternatively, the empowerment follows from the request, since it is subsumed within those who request; thus, that commentary says:
"Because the empowerment prompts the teaching, it is termed 'request. Since the empowerment itself is the request, it is called 'empowerment-request' (*adhiṣṭhāna-yācanā*)."

Regarding the passage "The common people have no constant abiding," the commentary states: "That to which the people turn for refuge is not constant; rather, it is benevolent governance that is constant.
The spirits and deities do not protect a single individual; only one who is capable of sincerity and faithfulness will enjoy their sacrifices.

Therefore, in the subsequent text, the *Shuzhu pin* (Chapter on the Ten Abidings) sub-commentary says: "This refers to the unconditioned samādhi (*anabhisaṃskāra-samādhi*), which manifests the wisdom of self-awakening, tranquil and..."
Because they have lost their illumination yet remain in accord with the Buddha-mind, the three karmas manifest as an empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

[Commentary: However, regarding the phrase "if the Buddha were equal," since all the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) in the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* are spoken by the Buddha himself and do not depend on empowerment—as in the seventh assembly, where, excluding the first two chapters, the remaining chapters are spoken by Samantabhadra and others—it still requires the Buddha’s empowerment.
