because the speaker empowers with the same intention as the recipient's wisdom, it is said that their speech is identical. ▲

Taking realized wisdom as the fruit-division and skillful means—such as the provisional reliance on dharmas—as the cause-division, this further has two meanings:

first, when contrasting cultivation and realization, skillful means and creative practice constitute the cause-division, while the cessation of practice and conformity with reality constitute the fruit-division;

second, when contrasting expression and manifestation, the maintenance of the Dharma and the revelation of the distinctions between stages constitute the cause-division, while the true [nature] constitutes the fruit-division.

The realization-wisdom as the fruition-division has two parts. Regarding the ultimate Buddha-fruition, when explained in relation to the cause of Samantabhadra, its meaning pervades the entire section:

that is, this very realization-wisdom is in profound identity with the ocean of the ultimate fruition, serving as the fruition-division; just as the space within a footprint is no different from the great void, the causal ground-aspect is identical to the cause of Samantabhadra. To explain it extensively, there are [the following]: *Note: The text provided appears to be a fragment of a commentary on the *Guhyagarbha Tantra* (Gyud sde rgyal po gsang ba snying po).

The passage discusses the relationship between the realization-wisdom (*adhigama-jñāna*) and the ultimate fruition, specifically how it functions as the "fruition-division" (*phala-bhāga*) through its identity with the result, while simultaneously being the "ground-aspect" (*bhūmi-lakṣaṇa*) that corresponds to the causal state of Samantabhadra.*
Because immeasurable varieties of phenomena further exceed this through the power of supreme vows, this is thus the emptiness of the locus of traces;

Commentary: "If that were so, then regarding the *Saṃghāṭa* and other [sūtras]... If all Buddhas collectively bestow their empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), they would likewise speak together;

Thus, the two chapters on the *lakṣaṇas* and *anuvyañjanas* in the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* are both spoken by the Buddha himself; they should therefore not be considered the universal dharma common to all Buddhas, nor should they be excluded from it.

this above is a counter-argument based on the inversion of the preceding sequence.

Regarding the *Śāstra*’s response to the previous "identical teaching" and so forth, it answers the first two difficulties with the initial intention, following the *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya] which is subtle and conforms [to reality].
Because they are difficult to know, the Buddha himself said that they are "incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*);

alternatively, because they are difficult for those in lower stages to know, they are "subtle dharmas" (*sūkṣmadharma*) that follow [the marks], and because they are profound, beneficial, and supreme. Alternatively, both categories may apply simultaneously; the commentaries merely cite one corner of each case.

Regarding the phrase "the number of *asaṃkhyeyas* is layered upon layered," the sub-commentary (*shu*) states: "This is what is clarified in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*); it is profound and vast beyond measure."
The ultimate limit can only be fathomed by the Buddha; it is not something known by ordinary or small-vehicle practitioners.

It is like the calculation method of the Yellow Emperor, which contains only twenty-three numerical units, beginning from one and two and ending at the *zhengzai* (meaning: one through ten constitute the first order; then there are thirteen further units:

ten tens make a hundred, ten hundreds make a thousand, ten thousands make ten thousand, then *yi*, *zhao*, *jing*, *zi*, *gai*, *rang*, *jian*, and finally *zhengzai*). This has already been explained as being beyond the capacity of the world and incompatible with the Small Vehicle.

The tenth [stage] has already reached the "incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*); because it undergoes a doubling and redoubling of one hundred twenty-four times, it cannot be measured by anything else, and thus the end of the number is ultimately expressed as "unspeakable" (*anabhilāpya*).
How much more so for the beginning of the verse, which further accumulates the "unspeakable" across all atoms and lands to manifest its inexhaustibility.
The reason the Buddha himself provides the answer is precisely to indicate that it is inconceivable (this shares the same intent as the opening of the present section).

Furthermore, it is clarified that this chapter is taught by the Buddha because it comprehensively describes the ultimate virtues of the causal stage (this refers to the stage of perfect enlightenment, hence "ultimate virtues"; the separate mention is for the sake of emphasis).

Regarding the "light of the secondary marks," the sub-commentary below states that there are two reasons why the Buddha himself spoke of them: first, the causal stage of the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* concludes with this chapter, and the resultant stage concludes here;
second, since this chapter teaches the result and the secondary marks are the very last [topic], both are spoken by the Buddha. Second, [the reason for] the secondary marks.

Regarding the inferior characteristic (the single ray of light from beneath the feet), its application is inconceivable (the three layers being simultaneously perfected). Fearing that sentient beings might not believe it, the Buddha himself explained it:

the initial intention was distinct as one manifestation, while the subsequent intention is precisely this initial intention. In the *Chao* (Commentary), under the section "Transcending Cause and Effect," the subsequent intention answers the final difficulty:

if one were to exclusively add the Bodhisattva’s explanation, then the two characteristics of "speaking" and "not speaking" would remain fixed; however, here they are treated in relation to one another (*xiāngdài*).

The *Yi* (Commentary) answers: Regarding the phrase "like bird tracks," the *Dìjīng* (Sūtra on the Grounds) states: "Like bird tracks in the sky, they are difficult to describe and difficult to demonstrate.

The *Chāo* (Excerpts) notes that there is a slight difference in their manifestation; this is because the principles of the Dharma are subtle and hidden, and thus one must rely on concrete phenomena (*shì*) to manifest them—this should be understood.
The general meaning must be consistent; how could one encounter obstacles at every turn?

Regarding the phrase "there are two kinds of empowerment" (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the sub-commentary asks: "Between empowerment and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which comes first and which comes later?
If concentration were first and empowerment later, then one should not say, 'You are able to enter this samādhi because this is the collective empowerment of all Buddhas.'"

If you claim that empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) occurs first and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) follows, then it would be illogical for there to be a state of distracted mind after the stage of the "factors of samādhi" (*samādhy-aṅga*).

Regarding this, the ancients explained it as a simultaneous occurrence of empowerment and concentration, arguing that it is difficult to claim that one serves as the cause for the other, as this would differ from the meaning of a "simultaneous cause" (*sahabhū-hetu*).

Since empowerment and concentration can indeed be distinguished, the correct principle is shown: there are two kinds of empowerment, namely the hidden (*gūḍha*) and the manifest (*vyakta*); the hidden empowerment...

Regarding the statement "the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) before entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*) brings about the attainment of absorption," this indicates that the preparatory effort exists prior to absorption; for only after one has attained absorption is one capable of receiving the preparatory effort.

As for the passage in the *Chao* (Commentary) stating "the intention (*manas*) and the wisdom (*jñāna*), etc.," the first fascicle of the *Guangchao* (Extended Commentary) explains: "Because of the bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*), the intention also becomes manifest as preparatory effort (*prayoga*).

Regarding the statement "the hidden (*guhya*) is only with wisdom," this means that when there is no bodily or vocal manifestation, the mental preparatory effort (*manas-prayoga*) constitutes the hidden [preparatory effort].
This reveals that the three types of activity differ.

Regarding the two assemblies in fascicle 27 of the *Yanmi* (Commentary): the two assemblies are as previously described; in the seventh assembly, while the Buddha enters meditative absorption, Samantabhadra and others act as the primary speakers without entering absorption themselves.
Since they preach the "Ten Samādhis" chapter and other sections by receiving the Buddha’s majestic power (*prabhāva*), they do so solely through silent inspiration.
Addendum. [Question: In the eighth assembly, the previous commentary explained that entering meditative absorption was for the purpose of receiving the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Now, in this eighth assembly, since Samantabhadra has already entered absorption, why is there no empowerment from the Buddha? [Answer: This is answered by way of concession.
Because one portion of the sūtra text concerning the Buddha’s empowerment is missing, there is only the following portion of text regarding the arising of the functional activity. The sūtra says:
When entering this samādhi, all worlds in the ten directions shake in six ways and eighteen manners, emitting great sounds that everyone hears.
The commentary states: "The earth shakes to alert the various faculties; the sounds are emitted so that they may hear the Dharma.
Whereas the previous assemblies represented that liberation could be obtained from others—hence there was the empowerment by others—this assembly represents that practice arises from oneself.

Because it is established, it is initiated by its own power; furthermore, since the manifest action (*vijñapti*) arises based on understanding (*adhimukti*) and there is no separate dharma [that constitutes it], there is no manifestation [of the vow] through an additional [act].

Question: Since there is no additional act, why is it necessary to enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*)? Answer: To integrate the understanding and complete the action, one must also enter meditative concentration.

Therefore, the intentions of the Sage are manifold and cannot be reduced to a single standard. [End of] the *Chao* (Commentary), Section on the Dharmadhātu Chapter, Part II, explaining the Dharmadhātu Chapter. No [further text].
The manifestation of presence and the presence of the hidden have two meanings. First, the manifestation of absence: this is because the Tathāgata himself spoke it;

it is not merely that there is no manifestation, but also that there is no hidden empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Second, from "Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī" onwards, the manifestation of the presence of hidden empowerment:
this refers to the Tathāgata entering the *siṃhaviṣpandita* (lion’s yawn) samādhi, followed by Samantabhadra’s unfolding [of the teaching] and Mañjuśrī’s description of his virtues.
There is also a version of the text that reads "Seventh is Samantabhadra, Second is Mañjuśrī," which is an error.

This arose because later generations did not understand the intent of the *Chao* (Commentary) and erroneously made these changes. Furthermore, it has already been stated previously (referring to the passage on how the two [Bodhisattvas] do not enter meditative concentration, etc.).

Why, then, would it be said again here? Moreover, this explanation states that within the Dharma-realm there is no manifestation and only the hidden; since the Tathāgata himself has already entered samādhi, [how could there be further entry]?
How could there be a hidden empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) such that it would constitute an exegesis of the *Śāstra*?

Therefore, one should know that this demonstration below—wherein the development of virtues is described—is based on the fact that throughout the sūtra it is stated that [the Buddha] "receives power. Thus, within the "Dharmadhātu" chapter, there is the sense that while nothing is manifest, there is a hidden meaning.

The *Commentary* states: "Because the Tathāgata possesses power, he is able to bestow [empowerment]; because he possesses compassion, he is able to be universal; and because he is eternally present, there is hidden empowerment. This is precisely it.

The general meaning (*sāmānyārtha*) is that when one has not yet entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the conditions for manifestation are lacking; thus, "added" (*pratyupasthita*) refers specifically to the distinct meaning (*viśeṣārtha*).

The previous explanation of "latent" (*anugata*) does not necessarily imply that there is manifestation. In the *Commentary* (*Vyākhyā*), it is explained that at the time of "manifest addition," the aforementioned "manifestation" must necessarily involve the "latent.
The time of manifest addition is the distinct meaning, while the constant non-abandonment [of the latent] is the general meaning; this constitutes "constant addition" (*nitya-pratyupasthita*).

Furthermore, the *Commentary* (Chao) contains many thematic sections (*yìmén*); as these are explained in accordance with the *Sub-commentary on the Sūtra* (Jīngshù), it is said that they are fully revealed according to the text itself.

When the *Commentary* distinguishes [the various works] by their different titles, it refers to Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, Asvabhāva’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-ṭīkā*, and the Liang dynasty *Saṃgraha*.

Treatise. Regarding the ten superior characteristics (*daśa-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-bhāṣya*: 1. The superior characteristic of the basis of what is to be known (*jñeya-āśraya-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*); its essence is the characteristic of the ālayavijñāna. 2.

The superior characteristic of the characteristic of what is to be known (*jñeya-lakṣaṇa-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*); its essence consists of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*: the dependent, the perfected, and the imagined). 3. The superior characteristic of the entry into what is to be known (*jñeya-praveśa-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*); its essence is the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*). 4.

The superior characteristic of the cause and fruit of that entry into what is to be known (*tad-praveśa-hetu-phala-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*); its essence is the six pāramitās. 5. The superior characteristic of the distinctions in the cultivation of that [entry] (*tad-bhāvanā-prabheda-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
1. The superior characteristic of the essence (the ten stages); 2. The superior characteristic of the training in higher ethics to be known (the bodhisattva vows);
3. The superior characteristic of the training in higher mind to be known (samādhi); 4. The superior characteristic of the training in higher wisdom to be known (non-conceptual gnosis);
5. The superior characteristic of the abandonment of results to be known (non-abiding nirvāṇa); 6. The superior characteristic of the gnosis of results to be known.

Regarding the "characteristics" (the essence being the three bodies of all Buddhas), the *Chao* states that the phrase "all ten characteristics should be known" means that all phenomena, such as principle and phenomena (*li-shi*), should be known.
The phrase "all are supreme characteristics" is used because both the teaching master and the taught Dharma are sublime, or because both the signifier and the signified are superior.
However, these ten supreme characteristics are precisely what are indicated within the main body of the treatise.
This refers to the meaning of "inclusion" (*saṃgraha*), and does not encompass the meanings of the two or three Piṭakas.

The commentators of the *Śāstra* (the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*) further explain that the term "Piṭaka" (*piṭaka*) is designated because it "contains" (*saṃgraha*), as the sense of "inclusion" implies the act of containing.
Thus, they provide a further commentary on the meaning of inclusion.

Regarding the statement that "the *shū* (commentary) correctly translates [it] as 'thread' (*sūtra*) and so forth," the *Tànxuán jì* (Profound Exploration Record), fascicle 1, states: "The correct translation is 'thread. Why is it called a 'sūtra'?
It is because a thread can string together flowers, while a sūtra can hold together the warp; their functional applications are similar.

However, because this region values the name 'sūtra' and does not prize the term 'thread,' the translators followed what was valued here: they discarded 'thread' and retained 'sūtra. This is from the *Weishi* (Vijñaptimātratā).
The *Shu* (Commentary) also states, "The profound meaning of the 'threaded flowers' (*xianhua*)," from which we know that many virtuous predecessors of antiquity shared this same translation;
therefore, the subsequent *Chao* (Excerpts) says, "In this context, the virtuous predecessors of antiquity are cited in their entirety, not merely the single master Xianshou."
The term "Five Indus" (*Wǔ Yīndù*) is a transliteration from the Sanskrit language.

The *Yiqiejing yinyi* (Phonetics and Meanings of All Scriptures) states that "Tianzhu" (India) is a traditional pronunciation; according to the Sanskrit sound, it should properly be transcribed as *Dù*.

Anciently it was called *Shēndù*, or *Xián-dòu*; the current term "Indu" is a corrupted transmission. The correct name is *Yìntèjiāluó*, which translates to "Moon. In that region, there are a thousand moons.

This name is thus designated because, just as in this land there are names such as "the moon's shadow on the toad" or "the cassia tree," so it is recorded in the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions):
"It is truly because the Sun of the Buddha has already set in that land, and sages and worthies have emerged in succession to provide guidance, like the moon shining down;
therefore, that country received this name."
The Commentary has three errors: first, the phrase "the following sūtra" is an adversative statement, yet it is not adversative; thus, this is the second error.
Second, the character *qiè* (契) signifies a meaning and is not a name, yet it is treated as a name; thus, this is the third error.

Third, each of the Three Piṭakas and Twelve Divisions of the Teaching possesses two layers—general and specific—but [the author] divides them into only one layer; consequently, he takes *sūtra* as the specific name rather than the general name.

Therefore, it is an error. [The *Chao*] states that since the two characters "yù-dǐ" (欲底) do not exist in the Sanskrit original, it simply says "sūtra" (修多羅), making it clear that the character "qì" (契) was originally absent from the name.

[The *Chao*] states that regarding "jì-qǐ" (集起), it refers to the eighth consciousness gathering all seeds and giving rise to active manifestations (*pravṛtti*). As for "jù" (詎), it means "how could it be? [The *Chao*].
The text of the *Kanding ji* (Record of Determination) still seems somewhat difficult to perceive;

because it appears that the text is difficult to understand due to the merging of the *Pitaka* and the *Śāstra* for exposition, Qingliang [Xuanzang] provided an explanation by distinguishing between the *Pitaka* and the *Śāstra*, dividing each into two layers of meaning, whereby it becomes easy to perceive.
▲ Although the *śāstra* (commentary) uses a general designation, it may also receive a specific name;
for example, when the "First Piṭaka of Sūtras" is spoken of in contrast to the three piṭakas, it is simply "one piṭaka.

Yet, when contrasted specifically with the other two piṭakas, it also receives its general name, "Sūtra," because it penetrates the meanings that ought to be explained and sustains those beings to be converted, thereby functioning as a "thread" (*sūtra*).
Because the two characters [“comprehensive” (攝)] explain the name *sūtra*, one should understand the general and specific meanings of *sūtra* among the twelve divisions of the scriptures accordingly.
In the *Chao* (Commentary), the phrase “if one does not understand” marks the conclusion of the objection.

To say that it “accords with principle and accords with capacity” explains the character “pervading” (貫) from before by means of “accordance with principle,” and explains the character “comprehensive” (攝) from before by means of “accordance with capacity”; it does not mean that the character “accordance” (契) itself constitutes the name of *sūtra*.
The *Shuchao* (Commentary) now states that the following is Qingliang’s own explanation; it likewise refutes the meaning of the *Kanding* (Determination of Editions).

However, while within the Tripiṭaka there is only one layer of general and specific [classification], within the twelve divisions (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) there are two layers of general and specific, both of which are refuted.
In the subsequent section on the "repeated" and "comprehensive" versus "specific," each contains one error.

First, regarding the twelvefold division of scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), the error in treating the subsequent "repeated" category as restrictive rather than comprehensive is as follows: among the twelve divisions, the *sūtra* (discourses) fundamentally pervades all eleven other divisions as well as the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*).
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The Buddha taught the twelvefold scriptures; they emerge from the *sūtra*... [and so forth].
Because [the *Tara* and other texts] exist, we know that among the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), the *sūtra* division is the foundation.

However, since that [foundation] is restricted only to eleven divisions and does not encompass the three piṭakas, this fault arises. Consequently, the establishment of "general" and "specific" categories as determined by the *Kanding* (Catalogue) cannot be achieved.
Why? Because if it were general, it would not include the three piṭakas, and thus the general category would fail to be established; if it were specific, then the foundation...

Regarding the claim that it "penetrates" (*tōng*) the other three Piṭakas while being distinct from them, such a distinction is not established because you do not penetrate their specific differences.
Furthermore, to subsequently apply the term "penetration" (*tōng*)—which was previously restricted within the three Piṭakas—to those very Piṭakas is a logical error.

This is because, within the three Piṭakas, the Sūtra-piṭaka only penetrates the twelve divisions of its own Piṭaka and does not penetrate the other two; thus, having been definitively established as restricted, it cannot then be said to penetrate the other two Piṭakas.
Therefore, this error exists, and its general and specific categories are likewise not established.

This is because the twelve divisions of the scriptures are divided into the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka) based on their respective sections; thus, within each of the Three Baskets, there are twelve divisions.

The entire teaching of the Buddha throughout his lifetime is collectively divided into twelve parts, just as twelve varieties of fragrant incense are divided into three types of incense-cakes. It is like dividing the fragrance into three pills.
Within each of the Three Piṭakas there are twelve divisions, just as within three medicinal pills there are twelve flavors.
Now, the Sūtra Piṭaka applies only to the twelve divisions within its own collection, just as the first pill applies only to the twelve flavors within that same pill.
Because the volumes and sections are distinct, it does not apply to the other two Piṭakas, just like the first pill.
Because it does not apply to the other two piṭakas, there is no second level of general and specific questioning within the Tripiṭaka.

Regarding whether there is a sense of correspondence with the other two piṭakas: although there are questions belonging to the general category among the twelve divisions of the scriptures (dvādaśāṅga-pravacana) that apply to the Sūtra division, the Sūtra Piṭaka is distinguished from the general twelve divisions and applies specifically to its own piṭaka.

If the remaining two *piṭakas* are also divided from the general twelvefold division (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), why do they not also encompass the twelvefold division within their own respective *piṭakas*?
Answer: Because it is stated within the classification of names that "the *sūtra-piṭaka* [is so called]," the other two *piṭakas* are not analogous to this case.
Question: If all *sūtras* universally encompass the twelvefold division within their own respective *piṭakas*, should this not further constitute a single layer of categorization?

Regarding the general and specific answers: if one intends to provide a general and specific explanation within the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), it would not be logically established because the *Sūtra-piṭaka* pervades them all.
Furthermore, if one intends to provide a general and specific explanation within the three baskets (*tri-piṭaka*), this would also not apply to the other two baskets.
Therefore, there is no need for another layer of general and specific questions. Within each of the three baskets, the *Sūtra* division is pervasive.
Question: Within the Tripitaka itself, there are eleven other divisions; what further obstacle would there be to treating them as a second layer of general and specific categories? Answer:
Previously, it was established that among the twelve divisions in total, the Sūtra division alone suffices to encompass the ultimate meaning of the remaining eleven divisions within those twelve.
Since this has already been fully resolved, why is it necessary to speak further? Question: The three baskets do not exceed the ten divisions in total.
Since the two divisions have already been shown to encompass the eleven divisions, why is it necessary to further show that they encompass the Three Piṭakas?
The answer is: the temporal teachings of a single lifetime are broadly divided into two categories. First, the twelve divisions are distinguished by their differences in meaning;

second, the three piṭakas are distinguished by their differences in volume and collection. Therefore, both are encompassed. [The *Yichao* refutes Master Yuan’s view regarding the "three sūtras" which follows next.]

The citation below is appropriate. Regarding the initial "complete concession" (*quan zong*) in the *Chao*: if one considers the opponent according to the names [of the categories], then all four propositions are opponents;

yet, since the ancient masters regarded the "line" (*xian*) as the opponent and the "sutra" (*jing*) as not being the opponent, the meaning of those ancient masters is exactly what has been refuted here.
Regarding the phrase "half-defeat" (*ardha-nigraha*) in the *Śāstra*: if one were to interpret it according to its meaning as "one [sūtra] opposing three," this would not be correct.

The definitive explanation states that while it is said that the sūtras oppose [the śāstras], it is not stated that the opposition is to the "Holy Teaching" (*āgama*). Therefore, it is termed a "half-defeat. As for the intent of the current citation in the *Śāstra*:

the following section refers to the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, which uses the name "Sūtra" as a provisional designation. This is intended to distinguish it from all spurious interpretations of the *Śāstra* (bhāṣya), and thus it says: "The Holy Teaching."
It is clearly understood that this is a translation of the *Sūtra* into the sacred teachings.

Regarding the phrase "the Confucians, namely Confucianism, etc.," the *Commentary on the Zhuangzi* states: "In the past, there was a man from Zheng named Sui who studied in the land of Qiu for three years;
his skills were perfected, yet he transformed into a Confucian. A Confucian takes Yao and Shun as his ancestral model and the constitutional laws as his standard."

One who establishes the patterns of civil and martial conduct and practices the way of benevolence and righteousness, and distinguishes the positions of honor and subordination, is therefore called a Ru (Confucian).
Now, Sui Di’s name was Zhi; he transformed his younger brother and together they perfected the Mo (Mohist) way. The Mo way is the path of Yu:

it esteems the worthy, honors ritual, and values frugality through universal love; from the crown of the head to the soles of the feet, one exerts oneself to rescue all living beings—this is what is called Mo.
Regarding the "Nine Classics" and "Five Classics": the Five Classics consist of (1) the *I Ching*, (2) the *Shangshu*, (3) the *Mao Shi*, (4) the *Liji*, and (5) the *Chunqiu*.
To these Five Classics, the *Zhouli* is added to form the Six Classics; furthermore, by adding the *Lunyu*, the *Mengzi*, and the *Xiaojing*, they become the Nine Classics.

▲ Regarding the commentary’s inclusion of two meanings: first, since this land [of China] designates only the words and teachings of sages as "sūtras," the translated Buddhist scriptures each preserve the meaning of being the teachings of a sage;

second, among the four realities, a sūtra can hold the warp and the woof, and these present scriptures likewise can hold the Dharma and the faculties. Therefore, they are called "sūtras" (jīng), which encompasses both of these meanings.
It is also said that "conforming to both directions" means conforming to the North, which carries the meaning of conforming to the West;
or it may mean conforming to the two meanings of this direction: "constant" (常) and "canonical" (典), which likewise correspond to the two realities of the Western seat and the sacred teachings.
Regarding the phrase in the *Chao* [Commentary], "Since the ancients... and so forth, this refers back to what was previously stated, taking "meaning" (義) as the basis for the preceding discussion.

This is a loss of the name. Since the ancients already established the term "line" (*sūtra*) as a standalone term for the "opponent," it is clear that the character "seal" (*qì*) was not originally present.
We know that the addition of the character "seal" to the ancients' *jīng* (scripture) is merely a partial adoption of its meaning. Question:

According to the previous explanation, if one were to translate this directly as "Holy Teaching" (*āgama*), all errors would be avoided; why then take such great pains to provide this convoluted interpretation? It seems to involve...

Regarding the *Miaoyan Chao*, it states that if a passage is merely a minor textual discrepancy, one should interpret it according to one's own insight provided the core meaning is not violated and the underlying principle can be logically sustained;
this ensures that future generations do not treat the sacred teachings with contempt.
However, if the principle cannot be logically sustained, one must rectify it by consulting the Sanskrit original, clearly distinguishing between what is erroneous and what is correct.
Since there is now a logical principle by which this can be resolved, I shall set forth my interpretation to explain it.

Regarding the similarity between the meanings of "pervasive inclusion" (*guànsè*) and "containing" (*hánjù*): while these terms generally imply the sense of having a comprehensive and encompassing significance, here we adopt the meaning of pervasive inclusion from the sacred teachings to signify that [the *ālayavijñāna*] contains and possesses the three realities mentioned above.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that the meaning is like a well-rope and so forth: the flavor of the meaning within the sutra is inexhaustible and passes on infinitely, for its primary purpose is to draw forth sentient beings and cause them to penetrate the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
As for the phrase "to distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox": if one does not rely on the sacred word to resolve what is heterodox and what is orthodox, by what means could it be determined?
The statement "able to hold the warp" refers to the sense of grasping and maintaining both principle and meaning, as well as gathering [them together].

Because it maintains the faculties and the mind, it is said that "the thread can string together flowers"; this refers to both penetrating the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and penetrating the practice of the faculties.

Together with the preceding point—that inexhaustible and abundant [teachings] draw in sentient beings—this represents the intention of the sacred teachings to encompass and manifest principles in order to deliver living beings.
Thus, as stated above, the meaning and intent are similar; while the sacred teachings have a single name, they contain manifold meanings.

Regarding the phrase "the *Chao* (Commentary) relies on ancient sub-commentaries (*shu*) and so forth," this refers to the *Tongxuan ji*. As for the expression "taking what is convenient in meaning" (*qu yibian*), it means that [the text] first surges upward and subsequently emerges.
However, this was done by the ancients who relied upon the treatise (*lunwen*) to assist the intended meaning, arranging the sequence according to the sense to facilitate easy understanding;
it is not that the later authors possessed reasoning superior to that of the Master of the Treatise. [The commentary] states: "One is general (*tong*), two are specific (*ju*)."

As the treatise states: "Because it can penetrate (*anugata*) and encompass (*saṃgraha*) the meanings to be explained and the sentient beings to be converted" (the former phrase generally cites that which penetrates and encompasses;
the latter simultaneously cites that which is penetrated and encompassed). Since both the agent and the object are cited together, this initial explanation is given in a general sense.

However, most commentaries and sub-commentaries by various schools explain this only in a restricted sense: namely, "penetrating" refers to the meanings to be explained, while "encompassing" refers to the sentient beings to be converted.

Therefore, the *Tanyuan* (Probing the Profundity) speaks only of "penetrating" (*guanchuan*) the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (characteristics of phenomena) and "sustaining" (*shechi*) those to be converted; the *Ruyue Shuchao* (Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra) likewise restricts its meaning to this.

Thus, when the treatise cited below explains "penetration," it refers exclusively to the penetration of the *dharmalakṣaṇa*. Regarding the "causes and conditions of the sutra" mentioned in the *Shao* (Commentary):
the sentient beings to be reached are the "object" (*ji*), the Buddhas of the ten directions are the "bestower of empowerment" (*jia*), and Vimukticandra is the [interlocutor].
The requester states that these two serve as conditions; this refers exclusively to the causes and conditions within the human realm.

Therefore, it cites the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) translated during the Liang dynasty, which says: "This person [arises] by depending on the place, depending on the person, and depending on the purpose.
Furthermore, the *Chao* (Commentary) explains the intent of the sutra: [it asks] regarding the text of the "Chapter on Generating the Mind," following the previous second commentary.

Question: Since the term "explanation" (*ākhyāna*) is subsumed within the category of "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*), why is this passage not called "causes and conditions" but rather "the intention of the teaching" (*ākhyāyitavya-abhiprāya*)?
Answer: While the general explanation of causes and conditions does not exceed these three meanings, here we establish a further point:

first, the setting of the discourse (*nidāna*) and the two faculties (*indriya*) serve as the cause; second, the request [to teach] serves as the condition (*pratyaya*); and third, the dharma to be taught is the desire [of the listener].

Because the inexhaustible wisdom of benefit illuminates all dharmas so that they may practice sublime conduct, it opens up both the original and newly acquired Buddha-nature, causing them to reach the fruit of Buddhahood as the ultimate reality.
Since these [qualities] are all the dharmas strung together by the sūtra compiler, they differ from the preceding ones;
however, within the first ten phrases, there are two phrases: "by the spiritual power of the Buddha" and "by the power of the World-Honored One’s original vow."

Because it belongs to the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the preceding Buddha, the present passage merely cites [this] as a desire to lead into the subsequent phrases. The word "etc. (*ādi*) includes the remaining five phrases.

As for the statement that "it is used," this refers to the practice of benefiting sentient beings; because it reveals and manifests the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), it constitutes the supreme function of this sutra.

Regarding the *Commentary* (*Chao*) stating "as for the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)" up to "furthermore, there are no other characteristics": the question is, since the sutra explains the meanings of the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*) and so forth, how is this so?

Furthermore, there is no other characteristic; the answer regarding the Middle Way Truth (*madhyamā-satya*) also relies upon the two truths (*dvi-satya*), yet because their meanings are distinct, it does not depart from the three truths (*tri-satya*).

Moreover, the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is opened up based on the Real (*tattva*); alternatively, the two truths are both the basis for the essence (*svabhāva*), and since the essence does not depart from its meaning, [the Middle Way] is established.

The commentary states that each and every [phenomenon] penetrates both truths because, when the eight truths are viewed in relation to one another across four successive layers, all dharmas penetrate both truths.
Regarding the statement that "aggregates" refers to the five aggregates, the *Guangming juechao* says:
"The five names—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—are called 'aggregates' (*skandha*) in the sense of accumulation. Whether past or future..."
Whether present, internal, or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior;

near or far—all such things, when briefly gathered into a single collection, are called an aggregate (*skandha*). Within a single aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), visible and resistant form is coarse, while invisible and non-resistant form is subtle;
furthermore, invisible and resistant form is subtle in comparison to the former.
That which is invisible and non-resistant is coarse; invisible and non-resistant matter is exclusively subtle. That which is defiled is called inferior;
that which is non-defiled is called superior. That which is present is called near; that which is past or future is called distant. The same applies to the remaining aggregates (*skandha*).

There is, however, a distinction in terms of the single category of coarse and subtle: the four aggregates associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are subtle, while those associated with the five sensory consciousnesses are coarse.

The four aggregates are "coarse" because they depend upon the five sense faculties; alternatively, in terms of the nine stages, those of the lower stages are coarse while those of the higher stages are subtle.
To speak extensively, there are eight aggregates: the four elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—and the four mental aggregates—feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.

Among these, the aggregate of consciousness is explained in detail, while the other aggregates are summarized as two: namely, matter and mind. As for the eighteen *dhātus*, they refer to the six sense faculties...
The six objects and the six consciousnesses constitute the *dhātus*. "Dhātu" (element/realm) carries two meanings: first, the sense of a single genus;

second, the sense of a source of birth, because the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of these various classes differ from one another. The twelve bases (*āyatanas*) refer to the six faculties and the six objects.
"Āyatana" (base/sphere) carries the meaning of a gate of arising; that is, the six faculties and six objects are the places where the mind grows. They are also called the twelve entrances (*dvāras*).
The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) states that the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) and the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) are the bases where consciousness enters;

thus, the first three categories [the aggregates] are taught for those who are deluded regarding the mind as "self," the bases (*āyatana*) for those deluded regarding form, and the elements (*dhātu*) for those deluded regarding both mind and form.

Furthermore, those of superior faculties attain awakening upon hearing a brief exposition of the aggregates; those of middling faculties attain awakening upon hearing the intermediate exposition of the bases; and those of inferior faculties only attain awakening upon hearing the extensive exposition.
Because they are fully understood, the eighteen *dhātus* are taught; furthermore, because some prefer brevity while others prefer detail, three different presentations are taught.

As for what are called the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*): first, ignorance (*avidyā*), which has as its essence the single dharma of internal delusion, namely the root affliction of *moha*;

second, formations (*saṃskāra*), which have the meaning of volitional activity, taking as their essence the volition (*cetanā*) of the three types of karma—of body, speech, and mind; third, consciousness (*vijñāna*).

The term "vijñapti" (discernment) carries the meaning of "differentiation. However, it refers to seeds only insofar as they are in the state of being about to produce actual manifestations (*pravṛtti*).

The meanings of the following four members [of dependent origination] should be understood by analogy with this: that is, taking the seeds of the direct causal conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*) of the eighth consciousness as their essence.
Regarding the fourfold "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*): the seeds of the four aggregates consisting of mind and mental factors are "name," while the seeds of the aggregate of form are "form."
The "five or six bases" refers to the six internal faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), as they are the loci where the six consciousnesses arise and cease.

Regarding the "six contacts" (*ṣaṭ-sparśa*), because they are able to contact and confront their respective objects, they take as their essence the contact associated with the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and a portion of the seeds of non-verbalized contact belonging to the maturation (*vipāka*) of the first six consciousnesses.
The "seven feelings" (*sapta-vedanā*) refer to that which exists at the time of perceiving an object.

The meaning of "appropriation" (*upādāna*) also takes as its essence the seeds of the eighth [consciousness] associated with feeling, as well as a portion of the first six [consciousnesses], specifically those feelings that are maturation-born and indeterminate;
this refers to the seeds of both the producer and the produced. Regarding the ninth, "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*): it is called craving because it is a state of attachment and defilement toward an object;

it takes only the single dharma of greed (*lobha*) as its essence, and this includes both the active manifestation and the seeds from which it arises. The tenth, "clinging" (*upādāna*), is characterized by grasping and adherence.

"Following" (*anu*) signifies the meaning of "pursuing," which takes the afflictions of the entire realm as its essence. "Existence" (*bhava*) refers to the ten [factors] that are the actualized resultant phenomena, such as consciousness and so forth;

because they exist within the three realms, they are called "existence. "Birth" (*jāti*) signifies the meaning of "arising," for it is the arising of the seeds of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) into manifest activity.
"Old age and death" (*jarāmaraṇa*) signifies the meaning of "deterioration and destruction," referring to the state immediately preceding death.

Because there is death, it is called "old age and death. Regarding the Four Noble Truths: *duḥkha* (suffering) has the meaning of oppression; *samudaya* (origination) has the function of increasing birth and death;
*mārga* (the path) has the merit of eliminating afflictions; and *nirodha* (cessation) is named for the exhaustion of burdens.

Because all four are true, they are called "truths" (*satya*). Regarding "nutriments," these are the four nutriments, as explained at the beginning of the tenth chapter of Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*.

The treatise states that there are four kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*): First, the nutriment for dwelling in an impure basis, namely the four nutriments such as edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*)—the term "etc.
refers to the three nutriments of contact (*sparśa*), volition (*manasikāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—which cause sentient beings bound by desire to dwell in an impure basis.
Second, the nutriment for dwelling in a basis that is both pure and impure, namely the three nutriments such as contact—[the term "etc. refers to volition and consciousness.
It causes sentient beings bound by the afflictions of the form and formless realms to abide by means of a basis that is both pure and impure.

Because they have already abandoned the afflictions of the lower stages through this basis, it is called "pure"; because they have not yet abandoned the afflictions of the higher stages, it is called "impure.
Therefore, it is called a basis that is both pure and impure. Such a basis, by virtue of...
The food of contact (*sparśāhāra*) and the food of mental volition (*manaḥsañcetanāhāra*) are the three types of "pure sustenance for abiding.
This refers to the four foods, such as edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), which cause the Śrāvakas and others to abide by means of a pure basis.

The fourth is the "sustenance for abiding manifested for demonstration," meaning that the Buddhas manifest the acceptance of these very four foods and thereby abide; therefore, it is said that the Buddhas eat this [fourth].

Fourth, regarding the manifestation of dwelling in eating: in order to cause the accumulation of merit through the purification of conduct for those sentient beings who are able to give, the Tathāgata manifests the act of eating while not actually performing the function of eating.
When the Tathāgata eats, the devas receive [the food] and offer it to the Buddha with the intention that other sentient beings may, by this cause, swiftly realize awakening.
[The above is all from the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya*. If the *Lokadhātu-sūtra* asks: "What kinds of sentient beings consume solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*)?

It is like the people of Jambudvīpa who eat beans, parched flour, and so forth; those in the other three continents also eat subtle solid food. The same applies to the gods of the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one takes the joy of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-prīti*) as food. Second, the food of contact (*sparśa-āhāra*) refers to all those born from eggs who have obtained a body. Third, the food of volition (*manasikāra-āhāra*)... [text continues].

The food of fish, snakes, and the like is that which moistens the body through mental volition (*manasikāra*). The four types of consciousness-food (*vijñānāhāra*) pertain to the hells and the Heaven of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). The commentary states:
The four types of food, beginning with edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), as explained in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, apply universally to both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).

However, in the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*), edible food does not arise. The *Lokadhātusūtra* (Sūtra on the World System) explains each of these foods according to specific meanings; thus, it speaks from the perspective of their predominant characteristics.
It is not that [the distinction between] ordinary beings and noble ones is not understood; rather, regarding the four dhyānas: first, the dhyāna with vitarka and vicāra;

second, the dhyāna without vitarka and vicāra; third, the dhyāna free from joy; and fourth, the dhyāna free from bliss. As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "In the first [dhyāna], there are vitarka, vicāra, joy, and bliss;
in the subsequent [stages], one gradually abandons the preceding factors. Regarding the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*), they are as follows:

Because loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity arise toward immeasurable sentient beings, giving rise to immeasurable modes of practice and understanding, and thereby inducing immeasurable fruits, they are called "immeasurables" (*apramāṇa*).
Regarding the four formless states (*ārūpya*), these are the four spheres of emptiness: first, the sphere of infinite space;
second, the sphere of infinite consciousness; third, the sphere of nothingness; and fourth, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Regarding the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*):

First, the liberation of one who has the perception of internal forms and perceives external forms (meaning: having the perception of internal forms, in order to eliminate craving for them, one contemplates external impure forms such as bluish discoloration and so forth, causing craving not to arise;
thus it is called liberation). Second, the liberation of one who has no perception of internal forms and perceives external forms (meaning:

having abandoned craving for the perception of forms within one's own body, in order to make that abandonment firm, one contemplates external impure forms such as bluish discoloration and so forth, causing craving not to arise; this is called liberation). Third, the pure liberation of the body.

The dwelling in the perfection of realization (meaning that by contemplating pure form so that desire does not arise, it is called liberation; "contemplating pure form" indicates that the contemplation becomes increasingly superior;

attaining this pure liberation within one's own body, realizing it fully and perfectly, and abiding therein is called "dwelling in the perfection"). 4. The liberation of the sphere of infinite space; 5.

The liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness; 6. The liberation of the sphere of nothingness; 7. The liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. (The four formless attainments.)
Because each of these four successive liberations is able to abandon and turn away from the craving of the lower stages, they are called "liberations" (*vimokṣa*).

The eighth is the liberation of the attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti-vimokṣa*), wherein one realizes it through bodily witness and dwells in its full perfection; abandoning and turning away from sensation and perception is what constitutes this liberation. These eight are also called the "eight abandonments" (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*):

when one has not yet given rise to true untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) to sever the various karmas of the three realms, it is termed "abandonment"; once they have been severed, it is termed "liberation."

Regarding the "eight bases of mastery" (*aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni*), the *Huayan Kongmu* states: "They are called 'bases of mastery' because they master both objective spheres and afflictions. The *Zhidu lun* says:
"For example, it is like a person riding a horse who can both break the enemy lines before him and also control the horse itself;

therefore, they are called 'bases of mastery. They are also called the 'eight bases of removal' (*aṣṭau kṛtsnāyatanāni*), which refers to the subsequent entry into these contemplations following the first eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*). First: Internally...

1. Having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are few, whether beautiful or ugly (meaning one uses the aforementioned contemplation but does not contemplate extensively;

for if one were to take many as the object, it would become protracted and unable to transform, thus one would not attain mastery over the mind. If one takes few as the object, one can contemplate impurity and the mind attains mastery, such that hatred and attachment do not arise). 2.

Having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are many, whether beautiful or ugly (since the mind is already disciplined and compliant, there is no hindrance to contemplating many; one attains mastery and penetrates the realm of impurity). 3. Having no perception of internal forms...

1. Perceiving external forms as few, whether beautiful or ugly (the meaning and intent are as before). 2. Having no perception of internal form, perceiving external forms as many, whether beautiful or ugly.

3. Having no perception of internal form, perceiving external forms as blue—perceiving them as blue, perceiving their blue light (perceiving the transformation of the blue color with mastery, such that the little can become much and the much can become little;

the radiance of the light and color surpasses what is seen in the *vimokṣas*, and one does not give rise to craving for phenomena). 4. Yellow. 5. Red. 6. White. 7. Blue. 8. [The same applies to] yellow, red, and white.
The white [perception] is explained according to the above (the first two are like the first liberation, the next two are like the second liberation, and the final four are like the third liberation;

that is to say, the first two liberations each divide into more or fewer categories to become four, while the final four—namely blue, yellow, red, and white—are superior to the preceding ones because they overcome the mental objects). Regarding the "ten universal bases" (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*):

this refers to the contemplation of the ten phenomena—blue, yellow, red, white, earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—throughout the ten directions as being non-dual and immeasurable; thus, they are called "universal."

Regarding the mention of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), these are the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path, as already clarified above.

As for the four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), namely those of phenomena, meaning, language, and eloquence, they have likewise been explained previously. The samādhi of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*) is the samādhi of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*); since it is utterly detached from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
How could there be any dispute?

As for the phrase "as it is said, 'all things, etc.'"—because they are not explicitly revealed, they are called "secret. The three natures (trisvabhāva) that are taught therein are indeed explicit teachings.
Regarding the "four intentions" (catvāra āśayāḥ), the *Puxian sanmei chao* (Commentary on the Samādhi of Samantabhadra) cites the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* as being the teaching of Asaṅga.

First, the intention of equality (*samatābhiprāya*) refers to such statements as, "In the past, at that time, I was named Vipaśyin (translated here as 'Victorious Vision') the Perfectly Awakened One," and so forth.

As explained in the *Anuttarāśraya-śāstra* (Wu-xing shi), this means that because all Buddhas are mutually similar in terms of their accumulations, faculties, and other qualities, it is said that he [the Buddha] was myself;
it does not mean that the Vipaśyin of the past is identical to the Śākyamuni of the present. This is discussed in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
The fourfold interpretation of meaning consists of: first, the equality of intention; second, the equality of speech; third, the equality of body; and fourth, the equality of dharma.

It is called "real" because it is taught as being identical to that [reality], yet in truth it is not that [reality]; these two are intended for different occasions. This means, for example, as it is said:
"If one merely recites the name of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, one shall already attain certainty regarding unsurpassed enlightenment," and furthermore, "merely by generating..."
"May I immediately attain rebirth in the world of Ultimate Bliss. The *Wuxing shi* (Commentary by Wuxing) states:

"This means that because one observes that laziness prevents one from being diligent in the study of the Dharma, these words are spoken. The intent is to nurture the roots of goodness from previous times;
it is as the worldly saying goes: 'One obtains a thousand coins solely by means of a single coin,' which explains that one attains that [result] at a later, distinct time."
Taking one coin as a thousand coins; taking mindfulness of the Buddha as the cause for Bodhi;
and taking the making of vows as the cause for peace and happiness—these are the three distinct intended meanings (*abhiprāya*). Regarding this, it is said:

"If one has served as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, only then can one understand the meaning of the Mahāyāna Dharma. As the *Anabhāvavāda* commentary explains: "The intent refers to the aspect of realization (*pratyakṣa-lakṣaṇa*)."

This statement is made because the Mahāyāna does not restrict its teachings to specific doctrinal characteristics. Regarding the "intentional purpose concerning the inclinations of individuals" (*pudgala-āśaya-abhiprāya*):
for example, if the Tathāgata first praises generosity to one person and later censures it, this is because he acts in accordance with what kind of mind that individual has achieved.
If a person possesses a mind of stinginess regarding material wealth, [the Tathāgata censors generosity] in order to eliminate it.
The mind first offers praise to generosity; if one delights in practicing giving, that giving is a "lower goodness. This is intended to cause one to yearn for other superior practices.

Those who do not understand claim that these [praises and criticisms] contradict one another, but this applies to all other practices as well; such instances are all merely the Buddha’s underlying intention (*abhiprāya*).
Regarding the "four conformities" (*anuvartana*), they originate from the *Dhyāna-sūtra*. The *Wenming shu* (Commentary on the Inquiry of Wisdom) states: "First, conformity to pleasure..."

1. Protecting their minds by conforming to what they find pleasing; 2. Adapting to circumstances by attaching to their prior habitual tendencies so that practice is easily undertaken, because once practiced, it becomes their nature;
3. Adapting to treatment by observing the severity of the illness to prescribe medicine in appropriate measure; 4.

Adapting to the meaning and the time when the faculties have matured, such that one attains realization upon hearing [the teaching]. The word "etc. includes the four *siddhāntas* (the fourfold standards of truth) as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

One explanation states that there are four *siddhāntas* (translated here as "doctrinal principles"), which comprehensively encompass all twelve divisions of the scriptures and the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma;
all of these are entirely real and without contradiction. First is the *loka-siddhānta*:

there are phenomena that exist because they arise from the combination of causes and conditions, yet they have no separate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); persons are likewise so, for they are merely a combination of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

There are two types of *puruṣa-pudgala* (distinct individuals), each of whom is a *puruṣa-siddhānta* (human-centric standpoint); observing the mental activities of people, one preaches the Dharma accordingly.

Within a single teaching, some may accept it while others do not—for example, preaching "mixed karma" and "mixed rebirths" for those with nihilistic views (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), or preaching that "no person attains contact or sensation" for those with eternalist views (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*). Third is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (standpoint of therapeutic remedy).

In terms of treatment, there is a specific efficacy; in terms of intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*), there is none. For example, substances such as sour or salty flavors are medicines for wind disorders (*vāta-vikāra*) but are not medicines for other disorders;

likewise, impurity and so forth are [remedies] for greed and so forth (that which treats greed is a medicine, while that which treats anger is not). Fourth, the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint):
all phenomena and all distinctions of verbal discourse are entirely equal and of a single flavor. Furthermore, the *Guangchao* states:

The meaning of Tiantai’s interpretation is as follows: to distinguish [teachings] so that they accord with the faculties [of beings] and bring them joy is the Worldly (loka-saṃvṛti) [truth]; to cause the arising of wholesome states of mind is the Benefit for Persons (pudgala-artha);
to cause the elimination of evil is the Counteractive (pratipakṣa); and to cause entry into the Noble Path is the Ultimate (paramārtha).

Furthermore, it is said: to speak of both emptiness and existence together is the Worldly; to speak of existence alone is for the Benefit for Persons; and to speak of emptiness alone is the Counteractive. It is not [the case that]... [the Ultimate].

Emptiness and existence are the meaning of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), which is without spatial direction. Regarding the term "meaning of what is produced" (*kṛtya-artha*) in the *Commentary* (*Chao*):
since it states that it is called "meaning" because it is "what is produced," this clearly indicates that it is not the "name and meaning" (*nāma-artha*) that is the object of expression (*vācya*).
The *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) states: "In that place" refers to the aforementioned location; "for those sentient beings" refers to the aforementioned "by means of this";
"the various distinctions of formations performed based on that" refers to the aforementioned "for this purpose.

The three preceding [points] are identical to the basis (*āśraya*) in the *Saṃgrahaṇī*; therefore, he expounds immeasurable discourses associated with the aggregates (*skandha*), and so forth, at length.
The "Expositor" (*vyākhyā*) refers to the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the phenomena (*dharma*). Why?

Because it was previously stated that each of the various phenomena, such as the aggregates (*skandha*), penetrates both truths; thus, they are "characteristics," and the aggregates themselves are "phenomena. (Regarding their manifestation...
Or, as stated immediately following, "that which can lead to benefit and profit" refers to the former meaning; because it is the former meaning, it is the subsequent benefit and profit.
The former interpretation is correct.
Regarding the title *Dharmapada*, the Sūtra states that "Dharma-wheel" refers to the *Dharmapada*;

likewise, it applies to the *Geṇḍīya* (Verses), the *Vyākaraṇa* (Prophecies), the *Geya* (Repetitive Verses), the *Udāna* (Inspired Utterances), and so forth, up to the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), all of which are called "as-it-is" (*yathā*).

Since it is stated at the beginning of the twelve divisions of the canon that the *sūtra* is "conformable" (*yiqi*), yet here it says "Dharma-source" (*faben*), it is clearly understood that *sūtra* was translated as "Dharma-source.
In his commentary on the *Daśacakra-vyūha-sūtra*, Master Yuanyong explains this through five meanings:
first, the teaching is the basis of principle; second, the sūtra is the basis of the treatise; third, the general is the basis of the specific; fourth, the beginning is the basis of the end.

The five abbreviated [sections] serve as the basis for the extensive versions; the latter three are precisely the three *sūtras*. As for the term "direct exposition" (*pratyakṣa-vyākhyāna*), speaking in terms of general characteristics, it is called "direct exposition";
however, when each individual expression is analyzed according to its many meanings, it is called "non-direct exposition.
The meaning of the holy teachings and the sūtras is as previously explained. Furthermore, in the *Chao* [commentary], Master Huiyuan states that the "general characteristic" refers to *nirvāṇa*.
Section Fifteen: From the beginning with "Thus have I heard" until the end with "joyfully practiced," all are termed *sūtra*.
This constitutes the general [classification] as distinct from the specific. Second, regarding the specific characteristics:

when one distinguishes eleven [categories] from the aforementioned general characteristics, those not included within these eleven are subsumed back into the *sūtra*; this is termed the specific characteristic of function.
When these specific characteristics are viewed in relation to the *geya* and other categories, they serve as their basis; therefore, the first is called the "basis for the latter.
Regarding the three summaries (*saṃkṣepa*), within those twelve specific divisions (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), the initial general enumeration is named *sūtra*.

What follows as the detailed explanation corresponds to the specific names, just as when one speaks of "form" (*rūpa*), that is the fundamental summary characteristic, and it is further specified as "blue" or "yellow."

The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the extensive characteristics; therefore, it is said that the abbreviated [text] is established as an extensive version. Regarding the critique in the *Kuan-ting-chi* (Record of Determination) concerning the latter two points:

that work states that the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) lack scriptural authority and also contradict correct reasoning. As for the contradiction with the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, the *Samuccaya* states:
"Sūtra refers to prose compositions that briefly state the meanings that ought to be stated. This is the commentary of the *Kuan-ting*.

Regarding what is called the "brief exposition of the meaning that ought to be explained": this refers to the prose (gadya) composition which, from the outset, lacks a preliminary summary followed by a detailed explanation.
One should know that "brief" is a synonym for "general" (meaning that one portion of the *sūtra* is general), while the remaining eleven divisions are "particular.
Now, the *sūtra*, within the context of the Piṭakas and Śāstras, is established based on its general characteristics and functional activity.
Its name is the Mūlasarvāstivāda, meaning the School Based on the Root Canon (*mūla-piṭaka*). Why is this?

Because the function of the *sūtra* is able to penetrate and encompass [all other teachings]. Since that which is expounded by the other canons and other schools, as well as the beings to be converted, are only established when penetrated and encompassed by this [root canon], the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* (XV) states:
"From 'Thus have I heard' at the beginning, up to the final joy."
Since all that has been practiced is based on the *sūtras*, the critique states: "This is precisely the established intent for determining what is to be affirmed or refuted;
it accepts the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the *sūtras*, as there are no [such] latter two types of *sūtras*.

By this, one should know that regarding the two layers of general and specific [categories] previously established, the latter layer’s general and specific categories also adopt the meaning of Master Yuan’s 'general characteristics,' rather than being newly established by oneself. Thus it is said.

Regarding the phrase "and those rescued within the ten *kośa* (treasuries)," the sub-commentary states: "Furthermore, the latter two do not contradict the prose sections of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, such as the 'compilation' (*tse-chi*).
As for what is not included among the [other] eleven [treasuries], it is as stated in the *Bhadramukha-parivarta*:
'At that time, Mañjuśrī, having expounded the great merit of pure conduct free from turbidity and confusion,' and so forth."

The term "prose composition" (*gadya-bandha*) refers to the compilation; since this is a compilation rather than the Buddha’s direct teaching, it is said that it is not included among the eleven [categories].

If prose composition were identical to the *sūtra* of general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), then since it would already be the general category, why specify "prose" alone to exclude the verse (*gāthā*)?
(This establishes the specific characteristic. As for the "brief exposition of what ought to be expounded":

"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to a brief summary that serves as the basis for an extensive version, such as the "Chapter on the Wise and Virtuous" (*Bhadramukha-parivarta*), which is intended to reveal the merits of the bodhicitta;
it is of this same category. It is a brief characteristic and a concise indication of what is explained below.

Furthermore, according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, it is called "direct speech. This applies to all twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), and thus there is no contradiction with the *Saṃyuktāgama*.

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (also known as the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*) establishes the abbreviated characteristics. Among the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), the Sūtras encompass all three types [of characteristics].

Within the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*), the Sūtras are restricted solely to the general characteristics; however, by opening up the specific meanings within the *Saṃyukta*, they establish the latter two [types of characteristics].

For those who do not understand this, it is a vain criticism of the former sages and others to ask: "Where there is a place for general characteristics, must there necessarily be specific and abbreviated ones?"

Regarding the two characteristics, why does the Sūtra within the Tripiṭaka provide answers that are restricted solely to general characteristics? This is appropriate according to the underlying meaning, and this principle is already fully established.

Now, wishing to demonstrate that the Sūtra among the twelve divisions of the teachings possesses all three characteristics—extending beyond its own category to include the other eleven divisions as well as the entire Tripiṭaka—it is said that it "possesses the three characteristics. This is because the Piṭaka of Sūtras is established based on general characteristics, thereby distinguishing it [from the others].

Because the names of the two [other] Piṭakas are restricted in scope, they do not extend to both; even if there were specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) and summarized characteristics (*saṃgraha-lakṣaṇa*) within them, they would be limited to their own respective Piṭakas and could not encompass the specific and summarized characteristics found in the other two Piṭakas.

Furthermore, regarding the *sūtra* as a general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) among these three Piṭakas, when compared to the twelvefold division (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) as a whole, this *sūtra* is likewise merely a small portion.
Question: If that is so, do the other two Piṭakas not contain portions of the *sūtra* category among the twelve divisions?
Answer: Although there are indeed some minor portions [of *sūtra*] therein, they are designated by the names *vinaya* and *abhidharma*, and are not called *sūtra*.
Thus, the *Shizang chao* states: "In the other two Piṭakas, those passages that accord with [the *sūtras*] are precisely the *sūtra* division among the twelve divisions."
*Tara* (多羅) refers here to the meaning of "comprehensive" (*samgraha*). Why must two further layers of "general" and "specific" be established?
It is because, within the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*), the *sūtra* basket is exclusively of a general character; therefore, it does not extend to the other two baskets.

Thus, one should know that although the *sūtra* within the Three Baskets is said to be of a general character, it remains narrow—just like the general character found among the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*). This is precisely [the point].
The words express the general meaning while the intent distinguishes the particulars.
The commentary explains that "stopping" (*zhi*) and "acting" (*zuo*) apply universally; regarding the three karmas, not performing evil is called "stopping," while performing evil is called "acting.

This refers to "stopping" as the observance of precepts and "acting" as the transgression of them. Furthermore, performing good through the three karmas is called "acting," while not performing [evil] is... [the remainder of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
It is said: "This refers to 'stopping' (*zhi*) in terms of goodness, meaning the observance of precepts (*zuochi*) and the cessation of transgressions (*zhichi*). Therefore, Nanshan said:

'As for the term "stopping-observance" (*zhichi*), it means using skillful means and right mindfulness to protect the prohibitions originally received, guarding body and speech so as not to commit various evils;

this is termed "stopping. To stop and not violate [the precepts] such that the essence of the precepts (*jieti*) is radiant and pure, conforming to what was originally received—this is termed "observance" (*chi*). As for "active-observance" (*zuochi*):'"
Once evil has been abandoned, one must necessarily cultivate what is wholesome; this requires diligent exertion in training the three karmas through the practice of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
When a wholesome state arises and is protected, it is termed "active observance" (*kṛta-samvara*), the meaning of which is as previously explained. Regarding "active transgression" (*kṛtāpatti*):

when those within the fivefold monastic community possess the three poisons and harbor perversity in their hearts, they agitate their bodies and speech to create circumstances that contradict the principle; this is termed "active transgression."

To act in contradiction to or defile what one has originally accepted is called "transgression" (*āpatti*). To speak of "ceasing transgression" refers to the state where, due to a mind of delusion, indolence, or negligence, one acts in contradiction to one's original acceptance;

because one feels aversion toward various superior practices and fails to cultivate them, this is termed "cessation. Yet, within that cessation, there is still the violation of those accepted vows, and for this reason it is called "transgression.
Now, the intent of the present commentary encompasses the aforementioned meanings, though the text specifically addresses the cessation of evil and the performance of good.

Therefore, it is said that [the term] "penetrates" applies to words such as "cessation" and "action. Regarding those scriptural explanations found within the Sūtra Piṭaka, one should say that the capacity to express the Dharma—which accords with reality and suits the faculties of sentient beings—resides upon the Piṭaka itself; this is thus a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound.
The *Chao* (Commentary), based on the *Kandingji* (Record of Determining the Text), distinguishes between the meanings of the translations:

it states that the term "vinaya" (*lü*) is used as a proof-text because the *Hongjue zhi* says, "We do not take 'lü' in the sense of the musical pitch-standards (*lülü*), but rather in accordance with worldly legal codes (*lìng*). It was created by Yao and Yu, and later established as the Nine Chapters by Xiao He;
thus, the gradations of light and heavy offenses were gradually differentiated and made exhaustive. The *Erya* explains it as "law" (*fǎ*) or "legal code" (*fǎlǜ*).
The purpose of weighing the gravity of offenses, whether they constitute transgressions or not, and so forth, is to raise these points so that people may know how to avoid transgression;
this specifically relies upon Master Sù (Sōng). Regarding Master Sù: his name was Huáisù.

According to the *Kāiyuán Shìjiào Lù* (Record of Buddhist Teachings of the Kaiyuan Era), his secular surname was Fàn, he was a native of Jīngzhào, and his family had inherited the status of high officials for generations. In the ninth year of Zhēnguān...

Upon leaving the household life, he prostrated himself before Shi Sancang to become his disciple. By nature intelligent and quick-witted, he devoted himself exclusively to the investigation of the sūtras and śāstras.
After receiving full ordination, he focused his aspirations specifically on the Vinaya, studying under Master Chengdao to learn the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
Before long, he had become a preeminent leader; first residing at Hongji and later at Taiyuan, his disciples gathered like clouds, and his teachings flourished.

I have transmitted this without interruption; however, as for the collections compiled by former virtuous masters, many do not rely on the original texts but instead follow their own private views, recklessly adding or subtracting material.
Therefore, I have examined the Vinaya-piṭaka to produce this *Jie-xin-jiemo* (The Ritual of the Monastic Mind), which may be freely adopted as a formal text.

It is free from arbitrary fabrication and can truly be called a successor to Mahākāśyapa and a follower in the footsteps of Upāli. Furthermore, I have integrated the *Sifen-lü shu-yao-jizhu* (Essentials and Commentary on the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya) along with various sūtras and śāstras.

The commentaries and records (*shuji*) totaling over fifty fascicles are currently extant in the world; what follows is from the first fascicle of the *Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya* (*Sifen lü shu*).

first, it can produce various kinds of benefits, meaning it induces mundane and supramundane virtues; second, it can produce purity and rectitude in the two types of karma—body and speech;
third, it can extinguish karmic obstacles (this corresponds to the following commentary); fourth, it can lead toward the ultimate truth, guiding those who are householders... [text truncated].
It causes them to go forth from home, and even leads them to the Brahma-abodes, the noble Saṅgha, and the nirvāṇa without remainder.

These are the deeds performed by the five types of superior persons: namely, the Most Superior Person, who is the Buddha; next, the Solitary Realizers (Pratyekabuddhas) and the Śrāvakas, who are the Superior Persons;

and those who practice as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), who are also capable of practicing [these deeds] because they are themselves superior persons. Therefore, it is said that these are "transmitted."
Regarding those that are erroneous or abbreviated: the three [cases] below are erroneous and the one above is abbreviated; none of them retain the correct name.
The *Chao* (Commentary) states, "Furthermore, it says [this] at Dongta," because Master Sū (Sō) resided at Dongta Temple and because this was also his first commentary;
thus it says "furthermore. The *Chao* explains: "Below" refers to the critique of the meaning by Qingliang. Now, since it is *Viniścaya*...
The statement here that "already tamed" (*vinīta*) has the meaning of "extinguished" (*nirvṛti*) follows the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*.
