For seven days he did not rise from his seat, but remained observing the Bodhi tree, transforming seventy-one *koṭis* of beings so that they would give rise to the aspiration for the Way.
He contemplated in profound stillness as the earth shook in six ways.

At that time, there was a Brahmā named Śikhin who saw that the Buddha had newly attained the fruit of the Way and had sat joyfully for seven days without anyone having offered him food. Then there appeared a *pāri* tree.
Because of their habituated diligence, five hundred merchants were unable to proceed and stumbled; the Deva spoke in verse:
"The Tathāgata has attained the Way of Buddhahood and his vows are already fulfilled. Because you have offered this food, he shall now turn the Wheel of Dharma.

At that time, the five hundred merchants presented the Buddha with parched flour and honey, and the Four Heavenly Kings offered him an alms bowl. After the Tathāgata had finished his blessing, [he accepted them].
Immediately after eating, he was granted a prediction [of enlightenment], saying:

"Having attained this foundation, in a future age you shall become a Buddha among the various merchants, named Guhyasiddha Tathāgata, fully endowed with the ten titles" (the present text reads *Qicheng*, which should likely be *Miche*).
Regarding the Caityagiri Stūpa, the eighth fascicle of the *Tanyuan ji* states that Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha cited the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
The *Dvayanidāna-sūtra* states that eight types of persons should have stupas erected for them: first, for a Tathāgata, the *āmalaka* canopy should be eight stories or more;
second, for a Bodhisattva, seven stories; third, for a Pratyekabuddha, six stories; fourth, for an Arhat, five stories; fifth, for an Anāgāmin, four stories;
sixth, for a Sakṛdāgāmin, three stories; seventh, for a Srotāpanna, two stories; and eighth, for a Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*), one story. This is seen in the *Cakravartin-sūtra*.
One must not fail to pay homage to the King’s stūpa; it is not because he was a sage [alone].

Now that Tiwei has already attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which corresponds to the first stage (*bhūmi*) and so forth, he ought to have a stūpa with seven tiers of *āmalaka* disks constructed for him. Therefore, the *Chao* (the Sub-commentary) singles out this case;
otherwise, why would it suddenly mention his stūpa? Regarding the statement in the *Chao* that "this sūtra is the *Mahāratnakūṭa* and so forth," this refers to the sūtra as a whole.

Regarding the forty-nine assemblies in one hundred and twenty fascicles, the specific scripture cited here in this commentary is found within the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*, specifically in the "Assembly of the Secret-Keeper Vajrapāṇi," which constitutes the third assembly among the forty-nine.
As for the statement that it corresponds to the eighth fascicle: since the third assembly begins from the eighth fascicle, what is cited here is precisely [that portion].
This is the concluding portion of the eleventh fascicle and the beginning of the twelfth fascicle of the sutra. As the text is somewhat extensive, I have not cited it in full;
those seeking the essential points should consult it there. It was translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin dynasty.
Regarding the phrase "the *Chao* excludes the indeterminate and so forth," both the *Jizhao Huijie* and the *Guangchao* cite it as follows:

"To have emptiness first and existence later, or the Great first and the Small later, is the indeterminate. Now, by excluding this, the judgment that the Small comes first and the Great later, and that existence comes first and emptiness later, remains without error;
it does not mean that one is referring back to the previously mentioned indeterminate teaching (referring to the *Zhi xuan*, etc., which precisely refers to the aforementioned indeterminate).
This refers to the definitive teaching (*niyata-śāsana*). Because it is not fixed within the categories of gradual or sudden, the previous commentary states:

"Since the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* is neither the first, the Sudden Teaching, nor the very last of the second, the Gradual Teachings, its elucidation of the eternal abiding (*nitya-sthiti*) demonstrates that it is indeterminate;
thus, it is indeterminate within both the sudden and the gradual. This means it is indeterminate among the five periods of the Gradual Teaching alone. Therefore...
Regarding the statement that "if one excludes the indeterminate, there will be no error of failing to definitively establish [the teaching]," the critique says:
"Now, examining the intent of the *Chao* (Excerpts), it appears that the meaning of the *Xuan* (Profound) is superior.

Since the previous *Chao* states that 'it is neither the second nor the final [period] yet clarifies eternal abiding,' does this not also clarify the indeterminate teaching by way of the five periods of the gradual teaching? Moreover, the present *Chao* states that it does not contradict [this]."

Regarding the *Guhyakādhipati-sūtra* and other scriptures, the above refutes the teachings of the five periods through two types of objections: first, the objection based on the established timeframes;
second, the objection based on the established names and meanings. First, regarding the objection based on time:

as in the refutation of the second period, it is stated that the extensive precepts were only formulated twelve years after [the Buddha's enlightenment], and it is further stated that they began from the attainment of the Way up until Nirvāṇa.

In the fifth section of the *Páncháng Shuō Bānruò Nán* (Discourse on the Difficulties of Prajñā by Páncháng), there are those who raise difficulties based on the views of the Hīnayāna regarding the teachings for humans and devas.
This immediately cites the *Mìjì Jīng Chāo* (Extracts from the Guhyakapada Sūtra) to present the intent of the four preceding difficult points, stating:

"These four difficulties are all excluded because they are subsumed under the aforementioned 'indeterminate' (*aniyata*) teachings" (this does not mean that the preceding indeterminate teachings are excluded and thus discarded). Therefore, it says:

Because those that are indeterminate have been excluded, the *Jíxuán* (Collection of Profundities) states: "Revealing the indeterminate teachings accords with principle. Second, regarding the critique of the established names and meanings:
for instance, as in the first critique, one might object to the teaching of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) by claiming it speaks of emptiness and so forth;

or, as in the critique of the *Dàodì jīng* (Sūtra of the Path and its Grounds), one might claim it refers to all three vehicles. However, since these are spoken from the perspective of the majority of cases, they do not constitute a fault. Therefore...
The *Chao* states that this does not contradict the names and meanings established by himself.
Regarding "the Vinaya Master Guangtong of the Later Wei and others" in the *Shu*, the biography says: Huiguang’s secular surname was Yang; he was a native of Lu in Dingzhou.
At the age of thirteen, he followed his father to Luoyang. On the eighth day of the fourth month, he went to the abode of Dharma Master Fotuo and received from him the Three Refuges.
Guṇabhadra marveled that the boy’s gaze was directed outward like a flame; reflecting deeply, he realized the boy must possess extraordinary character and retained him to study the scriptures.
He became so widely learned that people called him the "Holy Śrāmaṇera. Guṇabhadra said, "This śrāmaṇera is no ordinary man.

If he is to receive the full precepts, he should first be instructed in the Vinaya. The Vinaya is the foundation of wisdom; if he relies first upon the Sūtras and Śāstras, he will surely hold the disciplinary rules lightly, which would be a hindrance to his progress on the Path."
After receiving instruction from the Vinaya Master, he studied the Sūtras and Śāstras under Bian Gong, spreading his fame throughout Zhaojun.

When Buddhayesha served as the head of Shaolin Monastery, Ratnamati first translated the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, and Guang was present at his seat. From that time on, the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) was transmitted;
he composed chapters to explain it, and also drafted commentaries on one section of the *Sifenlü* (Four-Part Vinaya), as well as for the *Avataṃsaka*, *Nirvāṇa*, and *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* sūtras.

He annotated the profound essentials of the *Dìchí jīng* (Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra) and other texts. Initially serving as the National Preceptor (*Guóshēngjiào*) in the capitals of Cháng'ān and Luòyáng, he later became the National Overseer (*Guótǒng*), hence his title "Guāngtǒng.

Regarding the phrase "Emperor Xiaowen held him in high esteem," the biography states that Emperor Xiaowen’s reverence was profound and his sincerity supreme; he established a separate Chan grove for him.

He carved stone to create niches (as detailed in his biography). Later, following the Emperor’s southern migration and the establishment of the capital at Yi and Luo, a *jingyuan* (meditation hall) was again established by imperial decree for him to reside in;
however, as he cherished seclusion among forests and valleys, he retired to Mount Song.
There, by imperial command, a temple was built for him on Mount Shaoshi—the present-day Shaolin Temple.
Later, when he realized this was what Heaven had chosen for him, he pointed toward the mountains and waters, flowing westward through the valleys; following the water, he went west.
At that time, he entered Luoyang, intending to save those with whom he shared a karmic affinity.

At the age of twelve, Huiguang was on the railing of a well in the main street, kicking a *di-pao* (a game of throwing bricks) with his feet in succession five hundred times, while the crowd watched in excited competition.
Upon observing him, the Buddha saw this and remarked with wonder, "This child has been skilled in worldly play; his affinity for the Way must surely not be obscured.
Desiring to lead him across, the Buddha used a staff to strike his head; the sound was clear and resonant.

Recognizing that he was well-versed in the science of sound and was a fit vessel for the Dharma, the Buddha asked, "Are you able to leave the household life? Guang replied, "It is indeed my original aspiration."

He then ordained him (the *Qianzhuan* states that he went to Shaolin on the eighth day of the fourth month; this should correspond to the present account, as he was only permitted to leave home [become a monk] thirteen years later).

He further ordered his disciple Daofang to ordain the śramaṇa Sengchou. Regarding these two worthies who propagated this transformation in the Eastern Land and attained the record of the Way, it is truly clear that they were deeply modeled after [the Buddhas].
As for the transmission concerning how Meditation Master Chou attained the Way, it says: Sengchou’s surname was Sun, and he originally came from...
In his later years, Changli resided in Yingtao, Julu. Having studied the classical canons from childhood, he was thoroughly versed in the Classics and Histories.

Summoned as a Doctor of the Imperial University, he lectured upon the foundational texts (*fensuo*), and his reputation spread throughout the court. He was destined to serve as a dignitary at the imperial temple, yet the subtle workings of the Way had already resonated within him;
suddenly weary of worldly turmoil, he perused the Buddhist scriptures and attained a sudden, profound spiritual understanding. At that time—
At the age of twenty-eight, he entered the monastic order under the Dharma Master Sengshi at Jingming Temple in Julu.
Initially, he received the practice of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* from Chan Master Daofang, who was a disciple of Buddhatrāta.

Having received the methods of meditation, he traveled north to Jiayushan in Dingzhou; after concentrating his thoughts for a long time, he attained meditative concentration and constantly relied upon the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Having practiced the Dharma of the four foundations of mindfulness for five summer retreats, he went to Master Daoming of Mount Zhanghong in Zhaozhou to receive the sublime Dharma of the six periods of practice.
Through diligent study and emulation over many years, he disciplined his mind through fasting; during the ninety-day period, he consumed only four *sheng* of rice.
Spreading his mat alone upon a stone, he was unaware of the passing of morning and evening. When coarse cloth fibers entered his flesh, he pulled them out, yet they would not come away. Or...

While cooking food that was not yet finished, he entered meditative absorption and was devoured by birds and beasts. Furthermore, while constantly cultivating the visualization of death, he encountered bandits;
they had no fear of him and instead explained their various karmic deeds to him. Having all their bows and arrows shattered, they received the precepts and departed.

Again, while once sitting in quiet meditation at Mount Que, a spirit came to harass him, embracing his shoulders and striking his waist, while its breath was exhaled upon the crown of his head. The Master...

Determined to die for the sake of his resolve, he entered a profound meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and remained there for ninety days. Upon emerging from concentration, his mind was serene and clear;
perceiving that the world was entirely devoid of true happiness, he went to Shaolin to present what he had realized.

The Buddha said, "From east of the Pamir Mountains to this land, you are the foremost among those who study Chan. You are indeed that person. (This is why he is now called "one who has attained the Way. Thereupon, [the Buddha] further bestowed upon him the most profound essentials.
After residing at Songyue Temple and other locations, he traveled to Mount Wangwu west of Huai Prefecture to practice the aforementioned method.

There he heard two tigers fighting beneath a mountain torrent, their roars shaking the cliffs for days without ceasing. He then took up his monk’s staff to separate them, and the tigers each retreated to their respective sides, as described in detail in that account.

The *shu* (commentary) states: "Reaching upward from below" refers to one who, through supreme and wondrous wisdom, thoroughly understands and ascends step by step according to their capacity toward the realm of the Buddha.

"Liberation" (*vimukti*) refers either to liberation through functional activity or, alternatively, to the ultimate fruit-virtue that transcends all hindrances; this distinguishes it from causal virtues. "Perfectly consummate" (*yuanji*) distinguishes it from the partial.
"Secret" (*mi*) means that those of provisional or limited capacities cannot fathom it; thus, names such as the "six aspects" (*liuxiang*) and the "ten mysteries" (*shixuan*) are employed.
This is the Dharma-gate of Sovereignty (*vaśitā*).
Regarding the statement in the *Chao* (Commentary) that it differs from Master Yan’s [classification of] "Great" and "Small," etc.:

The commentary states that Dharma Master Guangzhai of the Liang dynasty resided at what was formerly the "Dragon’s Lair" (Qianlong) of Emperor Wu of Liang in Jiangning County, Runzhou.

Wang Wan, Xu Xiaosi, and others—men of great renown and noble status of that era—were all his close and harmonious friends. Xu Xiaosi often remarked, "Whenever I see Master Yun, his brilliance and resolve inspire me, making my own shortcomings all the more apparent.
Initially, when Fayun was still in the stage of a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*), he possessed a refined appreciation for the classics and the arts.

Question: Since these Bodhisattvas have not yet reached the fruit, why is it said here that they have attained the ultimate (*niṣṭhā*)? Answer: This refers to the Small Vehicle having already [reached its limit].

Question: It is understandable that those of the Two Vehicles, knowing their own small fruits are not ultimate, seek a prediction; however, why do Bodhisattvas, who already know they shall attain the great fruit, also seek a prediction? Answer: The Bodhisattvas being transformed by the profound and secret *Prajñāpāramitā* are at the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). At this stage, although they have realized the emptiness of all phenomena, they have not yet fully perfected the cultivation of the various practices. Because they fear falling back into the stages of the Two Vehicles due to the power of residual habits (*vāsanā*), they seek a prediction from the Buddha. Furthermore, because they have not yet attained mastery over the transformations of birth and death, they seek a prediction so that they may manifest birth and death according to their will and thereby benefit sentient beings. Finally, because they have not yet attained the unimpeded wisdom regarding the distinctions between phenomena and meanings, they seek a prediction so that they may attain such unimpeded wisdom and preach the Dharma for the sake of others. Therefore, it is not contradictory for them to seek a prediction. Furthermore, there are two kinds of predictions: first, the prediction of the fruit; second, the prediction of the time. The predictions conferred upon the Two Vehicles are predictions of the fruit, whereas the predictions conferred upon Bodhisattvas are both predictions of the fruit and predictions of the time. This is because Bodhisattvas must wait until the end of the three great incalculable eons before they can manifest the fruit of Buddhahood. Thus, they seek a prediction of the time. For these reasons, it is not contradictory for Bodhisattvas to seek a prediction. The predictions conferred upon the Two Vehicles are predictions of the fruit, while the predictions conferred upon Bodhisattvas are predictions of the stage. Since the provisional and the real differ between the "present" One and the "past" Three, there is no contradiction with the scriptural teachings or the underlying principles.
As for the *Commentary*, it suppresses those Mahāyāna sūtras of definitive meaning from the past, such as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Awakening of Faith*.

If the vehicles are all provisional, then why suppress the meaning—that all sentient beings shall attain Buddhahood and so forth—which is also taught [in those scriptures], as being provisional? [The *Chao* says:
"If that were so," etc. This means:

if the Great Illumination of the past had already clarified the provisional and the real, then [the present passage] should have transcended [the previous discussion] (this is a difficulty raised by taking up the previous answer to the question).

If one were to interpret the texts by merging the three [vehicles] into one, then the past would have no reality; yet if there is no reality in the past, one cannot suppress the holy teachings of that time.
If one were to merge the two [vehicles] into one, then the past would have no provisional [teachings]; and if there is no provisionality, the doctrine of the four vehicles cannot be established.
How can you allow for the meaning of the four vehicles? This is the objection raised by Guangzhai against what Qingliang has elucidated.

Since both [interpretations]—following [the literal sense] or contradicting it—are illogical (as indicated by the phrase "surpassing the following"), the following explanation is offered to resolve this:

the response from *Qīngliáng* states that "harmonizing the provisional with the real" means harmonizing the three vehicles into one. Because there was a provisional Mahāyāna teaching in the past, your doctrine of four vehicles is permitted as being in accord with reason.
If one were to refute the Small Vehicle to manifest the Great Vehicle, this would constitute harmonizing the two [vehicles] into one, clarifying what existed in the past.
There exists the Mahāyāna of the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*), yet you suppress the ancient teachings of the sages; therefore, your position is contrary to reason.
The two meanings of the provisional and the definitive (*neyārtha* and *nītārtha*) from the past also exist; why do you not distinguish between the former great provisional and definitive?

The essence of quiescent illumination is the Dharma-body: clarity is *prajñā*, purity is *vimukti*, and the perfect essence is the Dharma-body.
While their functions differ, their essence is not separate; therefore, these three dharmas are not sequential.

If one were to say that the Dharma-body exists originally, followed by the cultivation of *prajñā* and subsequently the attainment of *vimukti*, this would be called "sequential," and they are also called the "three [dharmas]."
To distinguish between dharmas that possess distinct essences existing simultaneously, they are termed "horizontal" (*ping*), while those aligned vertically are termed "parallel" (*bing*).

Because they are parallel in contrast to verticality and distinct in contrast to unity, the Sūtra states: "If they were parallel, vertical, or distinct, they would not constitute the letter *i*; since each possesses a distinct essence, they are 'distinct.
Now, these three are simply inconceivable; how could they be vertical, horizontal, parallel, or distinct? For they are three while being one."
It is three yet one; it is neither three nor one, for it simultaneously illuminates both the one and the three.

One may contemplate them as one or as three, but if one treats them as having a single essence with distinct functions, one still cannot avoid the fault of dualistic differentiation. [From] the *Commentary*: "In the past, the three were already distinct...

means that although the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sutras clarify such real dharmas as the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), they did not incorporate the provisional teachings.
The faculties of those of the Two Vehicles are likewise fully endowed with the realization of this true Dharma; they all attain Buddhahood, which is called "not including the provisional.
This is like the letter *i*, which consists of only a single dot: the Śrāvaka is like one dot, the Pratyekabuddha is like another dot—these dots are distinct and not yet the *i*;
only when the present One Vehicle fully incorporates the former three, such that all shall become Buddhas, is it like the *i*.

"Endowed with the three dots, combining the three into one; lacking the three, they are distinct—thus the three are discarded as empty. (The preceding metaphor and the meaning within the "Combining" section apply generally to the fruits of the Teaching.

Regarding the phrase "there is a difference between now and formerly" in the Commentary (*Sū*), the character "difference" (*yi*) carries three meanings: first, it means that the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) of the *Lotus Sūtra* possesses a distinct teaching that is entirely different from the former Three Vehicles;
it does not mean "combining the three into one," but rather serves to distinguish [the present] from the previous section’s reconciliation of the past.
This establishes the meaning of the present teaching as being "fourfold. Thus, the *Chao* (Commentary) states:

"The previous [teaching] merely combined the three into one, etc. Second, this demonstrates how the present differs from the past: the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) of the present *Lotus Sūtra* differs from the One Vehicle of the past;
the present One Vehicle comprehensively subsumes the three provisional means (*upāya*), establishing the One in contrast to the three, whereas the One Vehicle of the past did not.

It is not that the One Vehicle is established in contrast to the Three Vehicles by being a non-synthetic convergence; rather, because the One is established in contrast to the Three, the principle of the Four Vehicles—three as provisional and one as real—is established.

If, however, the One were established without being in contrast to the Three, then it would mean that the One Vehicle was taught for a specific class of beings possessing the capacity for the One Vehicle, apart from those who previously followed the provisional teachings.
Consequently, the "real" [teachings] of the past would not have been hindered by the expedient methods.
Huayan does not interpret it as such; rather, its intent is to clarify that the meaning of the four vehicles is established as being in accord [with the One Vehicle].

To hold that, apart from the three provisional [vehicles], there exists a separate single reality is to contradict this. This constitutes the meaning of the commentary; it is not that the former [teaching] was real and thus also requires interpretation.
▲ "Prior to this citation, 'merely combining the three into one' serves to distinguish [this] from what preceded; that is, the first point mentioned above.
The character 'former' (*xi*) refers to the three vehicles. 'That which was not previously taught' refers to the text of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

As for the word 'so-called' (*yì*, 謂) in the phrase 'although there were [teachings] in the past,' at first glance the character 'so-called' seems to be a re-explanation of the preceding meaning, yet upon examining its explanation, it..."
The previous meaning was distinct in that it merely distinguished the One Vehicle as being separate from the three vehicles;
this current explanation distinguishes the One Vehicle from the One Vehicle of the past. This is the second point in the aforementioned commentary.

Students should examine this closely and not conflate these two meanings, lest they raise the objection that the Mahāyāna of the Real Teaching (shíjiào) of the past also expounds the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
The principle of the true permanence of the *nirvāṇa*-dharmakāya is identical to that of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
why then do you say that it is only in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* that what was previously unspoken is now being taught? Therefore, this second point provides the answer. Its meaning is as follows:

although there is a distinction between explicit and implicit teaching regarding the present and the past, when it says "never explicitly taught," it clarifies that while the past [teachings] were indeed real, they were not [explicitly] revealed.

Regarding the actualization of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the statement that there is "one vehicle" (ekayāna) while also acknowledging the "three vehicles" (triyāna) serves to synthesize the two preceding points below;

thus, both meanings together constitute the doctrine of the four vehicles (*caturyāna*), as clarified above. Regarding Master Ruyi (Sengrui), tradition states he was a native of Changle in Wei Commandery.
Yao Song, the Minister of State, held him in profound esteem and honor. When Yao Xing asked Yao Song about Master Ruyi: [text fragment ends].
As Sengsong replied to Shi Yao regarding the pines and cypresses of Mount Wei: "These are the preeminent leaders of the four seas; why should they be unique to this place alone?

When Master Kumārajīva was translating the sutras, Sengrui participated in the corrections. In the "Chapter on Receiving Predictions" (*Vyākaraṇa-parivarta*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, when Kumārajīva reached the passage where it says, "The devas see humans, and humans see devas," he remarked:
"This phrasing is identical in meaning to that of the Western Regions, yet it remains [in its original form]."
Daorong remarked, "Is this not the meeting of humans and devas, such that both are able to see one another? Kumārajīva replied with joy, "It is indeed so.
He then produced the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Chengshi lun) and had Daorong lecture upon it.

Kumārajīva said, "In this treatise on debate, there are seven passages where the text refutes the Abhidharma, yet these points are somewhat obscure. If you can understand them without asking, you may truly be called a man of exceptional talent."
Huiyi was able to illuminate the profound and subtle; indeed, he attained realization independently without consulting Kumārajīva.
Kumārajīva sighed and said, "In my transmission and translation of sutras and śāstras, it would have been no regret for me to have encountered you. Huiyi constantly cultivated the Western Pure Land;
at the time of his death, he bathed, turned toward the west with palms joined, and passed away. On that day, everyone in the same monastery saw five-colored fragrant smoke issuing from Huiyi’s room.
I am now sixty-seven years old. What I have cited here serves merely to verify my past realization;

though that awakening to the nature of things was vast, it was never explicitly taught. To claim that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision were inferior to the explicit teachings of the *Lotus Sūtra* is incorrect.
Furthermore, how could it be that profound sūtras such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* were entirely provisional? This is untenable.

Although there are words regarding "skillful means" (upāya) within [the text], these do not refer to it as provisional teaching (*neyārtha*); rather, they distinguish between the provisional and the real based on essence (*tattva*) and function (*vṛtti*).
How could the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) allow his own words to contradict one another? To speak of "those who practice the Way" refers to those who study the Way;
to speak of "vehicles" (*yāna*) refers to the persons who ride them. As for saying that the "substantial reality" is insufficient, it is because of the past...
Because it has never been explicitly taught that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, the actual substance [of the teaching] was insufficient;
that which now belongs to the *Lotus Sūtra* is precisely this current explicit teaching of the single reality (*eka-artha*) being fully endowed.

The passage beginning with "those whose faculties are ruined" is from the "Buddha-way" chapter of the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, referring to how the five faculties, such as the eye and so forth, function according to their presence.
Those who are ruined are unable to perceive, understand, or utilize the objects of the five sensory desires—such as forms—to benefit their own bodies and minds;

they are likened to *śrāvakas* who, having already severed the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), cannot remain within saṃsāra by retaining their afflictions to nourish rebirth for the sake of extensively benefiting all beings, and thus cannot attain the fruit of Buddhahood. Therefore, that sutra continues: "Even if..."

If one asks: "Since Śrāvakas, even throughout their entire lives, can never give rise to the aspiration for the Unsurpassed Way despite hearing of the Buddha's powers and fearlessnesses—and since they cannot even resolve their minds toward it—how could they ever attain the fruit of Buddhahood?
Does this statement not fail to incorporate the provisional teachings?
It is because the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states that the two vehicles do not attain Buddhahood, thereby revealing that the former [teachings] were indeed the definitive (real) teaching.

Is this not to say that while the [past] reality does not simultaneously encompass the provisional (the "real" being subtle yet not simultaneously encompassing the "provisional" of the past—this does not mean the past reality inherently encompasses the provisional), the present *Lotus Sūtra* simultaneously encompasses both the provisional and the real; therefore, there is a difference between the present and the past.

That the past is inferior and the present is superior is the fundamental intent [of this teaching]. Furthermore, the *Commentary* states: "Below, also from the 'Inconceivable' chapter of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*..."
The commentary (as previously cited) states that because one lacks the capacity for the Mahāyāna, it is like a rotten seed that cannot produce a sprout;

this clarifies that the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) have already been severed, yet one does not remain in delusion to moisten birth, but instead enters *saṃsāra* to transform sentient beings.
Thus, the "Buddha Path" chapter of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* further says: "One should know that all afflictions are..."
The *Zhao Gong Commentary* on the "Tathāgata-gotra" states: "Ordinary beings are submerged in the five destinies, obscured by afflictions;
they lack the joy of the unconditioned when advancing and possess the fear of birth-and-death when retreating. Furthermore, their own minds are haughty, and they admire only superiority.

Thus, they are able to set out from the toil of worldly dust while directing their minds toward the Unsurpassed [Buddhahood]; taking birth-and-death as the root of the tree, they spread forth Perfect Enlightenment."
Regarding the *Huā* (Flower) and other such [commentaries],
the term "having a basis in the text" means that the established doctrine has a textual basis in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Furthermore,
it is "thoroughly established" because the principle must necessarily be so, and thus it is mutually accepted by both [parties].
The Commentary states: Tiantai Zhiyi succeeded the Great Master of Nanyue; Nanyue’s name was Huisi, his secular surname was Li, and he was a native of Wujin.

He once dreamed of a foreign monk who exhorted him to leave the household life. At that time, Chan Master Huiwen was gathering several hundred disciples, so [Huisi] followed him to receive the True Dharma.
After practicing meditation for several summers, he had not yet attained any realization. Distressed by his own dullness and torpor, he leaned back and relaxed his body.
Before he had even reached the back wall, he experienced a sudden and vast awakening to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, the Mahāyāna gateway to the Dharma.

In a single thought-moment, he attained clear penetration of the sixteen special stages of liberation (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa-vimokṣa*). This realization flowed forth spontaneously from within him; it was not through the awakening of another that he attained it.

Consequently, his disciples increased daily, gathering both those from his own and other groups, both refined and coarse. From this, disputes arose like sharp peaks, and resentment and jealousy became as virulent as poison.

Poisons could not harm him, and when heretics raised schemes, they were unable to cause him injury. He then looked at his disciples and said, "Even when the Great Sage was in the world, he could not avoid malicious rumors;
how much more so for me, who possess no virtue—how can I escape this karmic debt? This debt is the result of past actions; when it comes, it must be endured.
However, the Buddha-dharma will not long remain; where should I go to avoid this calamity? At that time, the void became dark and silent.
A voice said, "If you wish to cultivate meditative concentration, you may go to Mount Wudang or the Southern Peak (Nanyue); these are mountains for entering the Way.

At the beginning of the Wuping era of the Qi dynasty, he left Mount Songyang and led his disciples southward. Upon reaching Guangzhou, he encountered the collapse of Emperor Xiaowen of the Liang dynasty and stayed temporarily at Dasu for several years.

His followers returned to him in numbers like a market; he subsequently commissioned the casting of golden characters for the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and later traveled to Jiangling.
When Zhiyi was acting as the lecturer for the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, he encountered a point of doubt regarding the passage on "one mind containing all dharmas. He thought to himself:
"The doubt you previously held concerns only the sequential meaning of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*; it is not yet the perfect and sudden principle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

In the past, during the summer retreat, I suddenly gave rise to all wholesome dharmas through single-mindedness; since I have personally realized this, there is no need to harbor doubts. Later, because of this...
Amidst the alarms of the beacon fires, he fled in haste toward Mount Nanyue and addressed the assembly, saying: "I have stayed here for ten years; once this period passes, I must surely depart.
He further remarked, "In my previous life, I walked these grounds; this is therefore the site of an ancient monastery.

Upon excavating the old foundations, he established a temple and practiced the Way, receiving manifold divine responses. He passed away on the twelfth day of the sixth month in the first year of the Dajian era of the Chen dynasty.
He dwelt on this mountain for ten years, just as he had said at the beginning. At sixty-four years of age, someone consulted him regarding his spiritual rank;
he replied, "It is not so. I am merely at the stage of the Ten Faiths, the position of the Iron Wheel-turning King."
As for the one called Zhi, his name was Zhìyǐ and his courtesy name was Dè'ān; he was surnamed Chén and a native of Yǐngchuān.

During the Jin dynasty’s relocation of the capital, his family resided in Huáróng in Jīngzhōu. He was the second son of Chén Qǐ, a Grand Master for Horseless Carriages (Sànqí) and Duke of Yìyáng during the Liáng dynasty.
His mother, Lady Xú, dreamed that fragrant smoke of five colors coiled and swirled within her breast; she wished to brush it away, but then heard the voice of someone speaking.
He said, "Because of karmic conditions from past lives, she has been entrusted to the Way; her merit will arrive of its own accord, so why would you abandon her?

On the night of her birth, the interior of the room was brilliantly illuminated, and this continued until the following morning. Those inside and outside congratulated one another, and they prepared a grand array of sacrificial vessels and offerings. However, the fires went out and the water grew cold, as if their undertaking had failed.
Suddenly, two monks knocked on the door and said, "Excellent! Excellent! This child is the result of the accumulated virtue of past lives."
"He will certainly leave the household life. Having finished speaking, he vanished. His guests marveled at this. A neighbor, remembering a previous auspicious omen, called him Wang Dao;
furthermore, because his light was so radiant, they also gave him the name Guangdao. Thus, two names were established for him, and he was commonly referred to as Wang.

His eyes had double pupils (*re-tong*). His parents concealed this fact, yet people of the time already knew of it. When he lay down, he would fold his hands in *añjali*; when sitting, he always faced west. This continued for one year.
Since his youth, he had never spoken falsely nor tasted anything improper; upon seeing images, he would prostrate, and whenever he encountered monks, he would surely show them respect.

At the age of seven, he delighted in visiting monasteries, later seeking out an enlightened master in the hope of following him into the homeless life. At eighteen, he entered Faguoyuan Monastery in Xiangzhou under the guidance of Master Faxu.
Subsequently, he went to Mount Dasu in Guangzhou to receive instruction from Master Sengsi, practicing mental contemplation (*citta-bhāvanā*). Master Si commanded him— [text continues].

Whenever [Hui]si lectured on behalf of others, he would personally attend to listen, saying to his disciples: "These are my own sons in righteousness; I only regret that their power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is slight.
When Si was about to depart from his teacher, [Hui]yi said: "You have a karmic affinity with the state of Chen; if you go there, you will surely bring benefit.
Si traveled to Mount Nanyue, while Yi went to Jinling. Over the course of eight years, Si lectured on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other texts, subsequently expounding the Chan gate for use.
After Qingxin, he went to Tiantai. When someone asked him about his spiritual rank, he replied:

"You all are too lazy to plant roots of goodness and instead ask about the merits of others—like a blind man asking about milk, or a person with a limp obstructing the path. I shall not lead a community; I will first purify my own six sense-faculties before benefiting others.
My own self-sacrifice is merely that of one within the stage of the Five Ranks. He was sixty-seven years old when he passed away in the tenth year of the Kaihuang era.
On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month of the seventh year, he passed away while seated before the Great Stone Buddha at Mount Tiantai.

His teachings spread east and west as a model for ten thousand *li*; he established thirty-five great monasteries, ordained over forty monks with his own hands, transcribed fifteen Tripitakas of all the Buddhist scriptures, and produced approximately one hundred thousand images made of gold, sandalwood, and painting.
In more than fifty provinces, the number of monastics and laypeople who received the Bodhisattva precepts is beyond reckoning.
There are thirty-two scholars who have transmitted his legacy, and the number of scholars practicing meditation who have dispersed throughout the Yangtze and Han rivers is limitless;
these are the disciples to whom the śramaṇa Guanding has been entrusted.
The commentary states that the single emperor of the Chen dynasty was none other than the Later Emperor (Chen Shubao). At that time, Master Yi was already practicing the Way at Tiantai.
The Later Emperor of Chen desired to pay him homage in person and consult with him; he questioned his ministers as to which śramaṇa was the most eminent. Chen Xuan memorialized, saying:

"The Chan Master of Waguan possesses virtue that surpasses wind and frost, and a meditative mirror as deep as the ocean. Formerly, when he was in the capital, he was among the assembly of many worthies..."
The one whom we now revere has taken high strides upon Mount Tiantai, where the Dharma-clouds gather in the east.

We pray that Your Majesty will issue an imperial decree for him to return to the capital, so that both monastics and laypeople may alike receive his grace. Consequently, the Emperor sent sealed letters seven times in succession; only when each was personally inscribed by the Emperor’s own hand did he consent to leave the mountains.
He was welcomed into the eastern hall of the Dajidian, where the Emperor personally performed rites of greeting and invited him to lecture on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The disciples at Lingyao Temple gathered like clouds, yet the temple was cramped and narrow;
seeking a more secluded and tranquil place, he suddenly dreamed of a man with a solemn and dignified retinue who introduced himself as Guanda. He requested that [Hui]yi reside at Sanqiao.
Huiyi said, "Guanda is the Dharma-name of Emperor Wu of Liang; is Sanqiao not Guangzhai? Thereupon, he moved his residence there. In the fourth month of that year—
In the month [of...], the Ruler visited the temple to practice great acts of giving and also preached the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra).

The Emperor rose from the assembly to pay his respects with profound earnestness; from the Crown Prince downward, all venerated his model of the precepts. There is a text regarding the reception of the Dharma, the end of which states:
"I now respectfully request you to serve as my Bodhisattva Precept Master. Then, placing incense upon his hand, he lowered his face and shed tears. This, too, was his virtue.

The gravity with which the sovereign treats such matters is evident here: when the Prince of Jin requested [the Master] to serve as his Preceptor for the Bodhisattva Precepts, the *Biographies* record that the Sui Emperor personally composed the text of the request.
Furthermore, at the time of the ordination, the Preceptor addressed the Great Being (Bodhisattva), saying:
"To deliver others and bring them across to salvation is our primary principle; thus name and reality correspond, and the meaning is not a trivial engagement. You may now act as the Dharani-holder."

This employs the principle of encompassing and integrating various aspects. The King received his instructions upon the crown of his head and said, "Great Chan Master, your Chan wisdom is internally fused;

you guide others with the moisture of the Dharma. I shall therefore honor you by the name 'Zhi-zhe' (The Wise One)," as indicated later in the text where it says, "The Emperor established this title for him," and so forth.

The *Chao* states that regarding the name of Mount Tiantai and so forth, it is traditionally said that when he first arrived in Jinling, he dreamed of cliffs and crags ten thousand feet high, with clouds and sun hanging half-way down their sides; the vast ocean lay boundless and limpid below.
He also saw a monk stretching out his arms from afar to pull him up the mountain. Upon waking, he told his disciples, "This is none other than Kuaiji’s Mount Tiantai."
Mount Shan was a place where, in the past, eminent monks such as Sengguang, Daoyou, and Falan—all men of outstanding talent during the Jin and Song dynasties—had resided.
Consequently, [Huiyi] accompanied more than twenty people, including Huidian, and traveled south to seek the Way, intending to hide away on this mountain.

Previously, there had been a monk from Qingzhou named Dingguang who had lived on this mountain for forty years; he was truly a divine being. Before Huiyi arrived, [Dingguang] had already been there for two... [years].
He informed the mountain villagers in advance, saying, "A great *kalyāṇamitra* is about to arrive;
you should plant beans, prepare fermented soy sauce, weave mats of *phoṭa* grass, and build houses to await him.

Later, when he went to Mount Tiantai and met with Guǎng, Guǎng asked, "Do you remember our meeting on the mountain years ago from afar, when we touched hands? Only then did Yǐ realize the full details of the dream.
He then settled there to live, and so forth. [The passage] "Next, he entered the Dharma-hall" and below refers to the biography composed by the Minister Wei Xuzhou.
It says that when Zhiyi first arrived at Dasu Mountain, he met Huisi;
Huisi immediately remarked, "We heard the same teaching on Vulture Peak," and then showed Zhiyi the Samantabhadra Dharma-hall and preached the Four Practices of Peaceful Bliss to him. Zhiyi...
He then practiced the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* on this mountain; after only three nights had passed, he reached the "Chapter on the Medicine King" (*Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta*).

As his mind focused on the passage concerning ascetic practices—specifically the phrase "this is true diligence"—he attained realization. He immediately perceived that he was together with his Master on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the pure land of the seven jewels, listening to the Buddha preach the Dharma.
He thought: "It is not you who do not realize it; it is not [the case that]... (The Master said: "It is not you who do not realize it; it is not...")
I do not know how it was that once again, at White Sand Mountain (Baisha Shan) in Xizhou, I entered meditative contemplation as before;
whenever I had doubts regarding the scriptures, thoughts would suddenly arise, and he would secretly provide explanations for them, as described in detail in that account.

The *Chao* (Commentary) explains at length that the *Sūtra* says: "Regarding the Four Noble Truths (*catur-ārya-satya*), 'Noble' (*ārya*) means correct, because the untainted (*anāsrava*) correct Dharma has been attained within the mind.
'Truth' (*satya*) has two meanings: first, it means reality (*tattva*).

This is distinguished in terms of the object (*viṣaya*), meaning that the characteristics as they have been described are not abandoned; they are real, and they are determinate. This refers to both the mundane and the supramundane."

The two types of causes and effects are necessarily not false and cannot be mistaken; these two are examined with precision. This refers to the clarity of wisdom, for noble wisdom observes them and finds them to be non-false.
Although ordinary beings possess suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*), they lack precise realization;

thus, these do not accord with the truths or are not inverted. Because noble wisdom examines them as they truly are, they are called the Noble Truths (*āryasatya*). As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "By means of two..."

They are called "truths" (*satya*) because they are conditioned; [this refers to] one, which is the *dharmatā* (the intrinsic nature of all phenomena). Second, because of superior resolve (*adhimukti*):

while fools possess the former but not the latter, the noble ones (*ārya*) possess both; therefore, they are specifically called "Noble Truths. The *Satyavyākhyāna-śāstra* states: "Truth has two meanings:

'noble' (*ārya*) applies exclusively to the sense of 'thorough investigation' (*parīkṣā*), while *dharmatā* in the *Yogācāra* system has the meaning of 'reality' (*tattva*), and superior resolve has the meaning of 'thorough investigation. Now, both..."

Regarding the so-called Four Noble Truths, they are the meaning of reality (*tattva*). These four sets of four truths will each be explained and interpreted according to the four subsequent teachings.
The sub-commentary defines "suffering" (*duḥkha*) as having the sense of oppression; this is the explanation of its name and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), which pertains specifically to the Hīnayāna.
The "Vehicle" (*yāna*) also encompasses the Mahāyāna; for the Mahāyāna merely infers that these characteristics are non-arising, immeasurable, and unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

Thus, the sub-commentary below states: "What are the nature and characteristics of the Four Truths? How are they oppressed as 'Suffering'? (This explains the names and distinguishes the characteristics).

"That which consists of contaminated form and mind" (this indicates the essential substance). "Increasing [therefrom] is 'Origination'" (this explains the name and characteristic). "That is karma and afflictions" (this indicates the substance; subsequent instances follow this pattern). "Quiescence..."

"Quiescence" (*śānti*) is named "cessation" (*nirodha*), which refers to *nirvāṇa*; "emergence" (*niḥsaraṇa*) is named the "path" (*mārga*), referring to *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, as well as the eightfold noble path.

This is explained according to their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the Hīnayāna, the three [truths] possess characteristics while cessation is without characteristics;

in the Mahāyāna, all four truths are without characteristics. (This is a distinction made solely according to the meaning of the Shared Teaching [*tongjiao*]; if one considers the Immeasurable and Unconditioned [teachings], it refers to the latter two meanings. [This concludes the] correspondence.

The present *Chao* states: "While the explanations of the names for Cessation (*nirodha*) and the Path (*mārga*) differ, 'transcendence' (*nairyāṇika*) and 'elimination of affliction' (*ādīnava-prahāṇa*) are identical in meaning despite differing in name;

furthermore, 'exhaustion of burdens' (*kṣīṇa-saṃyojana*) and 'quiescence' (*śānti*) differ in their scope. 'Exhaustion of burdens' applies exclusively to the cessation of delusions, as the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* explains with the analogy:
'Just as when a lamp is extinguished, both the oil and the light are exhausted. If one speaks of 'quiescence,' it does not refer solely to the cessation of delusions."

In truth, the Dharma-body is eternally abiding and quiescent; it is "extinguished" because it is extinguished from the very beginning. Thus, the *Commentary* states that what is called "extinguished" does not mean that something previously existing has now ceased to be;
rather, it is called "extinguished" because, while one has not yet cultivated the path and has not yet realized the principle, it is currently non-existent.
To say that the "True Path arises" means it manifests and is realized, and is therefore called "arising. For these reasons, it is named "Real."
"Lower" refers to that which is real; "truth" (*satya*) means reality (*tattva*), and thus "truth" signifies reality.

Because the objects and the wisdom [perceiving them] are distinct, the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) thoroughly know these as suffering and so forth. The *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), fascicle 2, states:

"The four kinds of the Four Noble Truths appear in the 'Chapter on Holy Practice' of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; they are distinguished into four types based on the differentiation between the partial and the perfect, and between phenomena and principle."

That which is called "arising and ceasing" refers to being deeply deluded regarding the Truth; thus, it receives its name from the perspective of phenomena (*dharma*) and is narrower than the "immeasurable" (namely:
1. a partial phenomenon, 2. a partial principle, 3. a perfect phenomenon, and 4. a perfect principle).

Question: Regarding the statement that the teachings of the Three Vehicles are equally received [by all], how does this differ from the Three Vehicles of the Tripiṭaka Teaching? Answer: They differ in their skillfulness or clumsiness and their sharpness or dullness.
This is because the Tripiṭaka Teaching analyzes form to clarify emptiness, which is clumsy; whereas the Shared Teaching takes form as its essence to clarify emptiness, which is skillful.

Thus, they are distinguished by sharpness and dullness. Question: If that is so, why do the Two Vehicles equally receive these teachings? Answer: It is to lead those of the Lesser Vehicle [to the Great].
Because one enters the ultimate reality by way of gradual stages.

Regarding the statement in the *Chao* that "dharmas arising from conditions have no intrinsic nature and are thus empty," a question is raised: since the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is non-existent, why is it called "arising from conditions"?
The answer is: because it is manifested through the cessation of delusions, it is likewise "arising from conditions."

Regarding the "Copy" (Chao) on the Four Noble Truths of Non-arising, the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) states: "Because delusion regarding the Truth is slight, it derives its name from principle (*li*) but does not possess [all] attributes;

thus it is termed 'partial' (*pian*). Because it contemplates the absence of intrinsic nature (*wuxing*), it is called 'emptiness' (*kong*); this is designated as 'non-existence' (*wu*), yet it is not a nihilistic non-existence.
The "Copy" further states that the interpretation of "understanding suffering as being without suffering" and so forth cites the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The Sūtra says: "All ordinary persons..."

There is suffering, but no Truth (because it is falsely conceived as pleasure through a lack of discernment). Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have suffering and the Truth of Suffering, yet they lack the ultimate reality (because they lack the realization of non-arising).
The Bodhisattvas understand that suffering is without suffering; therefore, there is no [conventional] suffering, but there is the True Truth (the Truth of Non-arising).
Ordinary persons have the Accumulation [of suffering] but no Truth; Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have both the Accumulation and the Truth.
Yet, for the truly realized Bodhisattvas, there is neither accumulation nor non-accumulation; therefore, although there is no accumulation, they possess the True Truth (*satya*).

Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have cessation, but it is not the true [cessation]; Bodhisattvas have cessation and possess the True Truth. Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have the Path, but it is not the true [Path];
Bodhisattvas have the Path and possess the True Truth, and so forth. (The reason the four [truths] of the Bodhisattvas are all called "True Truth" is that they are the four [truths] of non-arising.)

(Principle) However, regarding the statements that "suffering is understood as being without suffering," etc., the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) says: "Suffering has no characteristic of oppression; origination has no characteristic of conjunction;
the path has no characteristic of non-duality; cessation has no characteristic of arising. These various expressions differ from those of the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*).

The phrase "this is Mahāyāna" indicates its superiority in contrast to what precedes it; the phrase "it has not yet manifested the subtle within existence" indicates its inferiority in contrast to what follows.

The Way (the third teaching) is inferior to the third [teaching] because its wondrous existence has not yet been manifested; it is inferior to the fourth because its middle way has not yet been manifested.
Alternatively, although the latter two teachings differ in whether they are "identical" or "not identical," both clarify the middle way.
This [third teaching], while also clarifying the middle way, conforms to and enters into emptiness; thus, the previous *Chao* states: "The middle is also identical to emptiness, etc."

The purpose of expelling and purifying the mind that clings to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is to teach that the three vehicles (triyāna) equally receive this instruction, thereby enabling each of the three vehicles to individually realize the two kinds of emptiness (dvividha-śūnyatā).

Nevertheless, because they still maintain their own individual views, it is said that these teachings are "provisional" (pāratantrya), intended to gradually lead them toward comprehensive understanding and ease.
Regarding the text of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it has already been cited as before.
The sub-commentary (*chao*) states: "This [passage] doubly verifies both the name and the intended audience (*jī*). First, it presents the intent of the verification:

since the three vehicles are mentioned below as verifying the name, and the two vehicles are mentioned below as verifying the audience, how is this so? This is the exegesis of the *shu* text that follows the interrogation.

Regarding the phrase "the śrāvakas study non-arising," etc., it means that because the two vehicles analytically understand the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmas*) yet do not take realization as their goal, [they are thus distinguished]. Below...
It is said that by inferring from this principle, the practitioners of the Two Vehicles study the two kinds of emptiness.

Those who merely desire to proceed toward quiescence are the śrāvakas described in the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, who delight in extinction and sink into emptiness. Therefore, it is said: "If one hears of non-arising," which refers to the pratyekabuddhas;
those who know that arising proceeds from conditions immediately realize that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. It is said: "Immediately... [the realization follows].
Arising and ceasing, yet being without arising and ceasing: because that which arises through conditions has no intrinsic nature, it is not obstructed by arising and ceasing;
because that which lacks intrinsic nature arises through conditions. Regarding those Arhats who have attained this, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"In truth, there is no dharma named 'Arhat. World-Honored One, if an Arhat were to think, 'I have attained the path of an Arhat'..."

This refers to clinging to the notions of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span (these four categories are collectively the characteristic of "self," which carries the sense of being a sovereign;

however, they are designated by four names due to their successive applications and meanings). Because one is deluded regarding the objects of consciousness, one takes one's own substance as the characteristic of a self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*); calculating that the self will successively proceed to other realms in the future is the characteristic of a person (*pudgala-lakṣaṇa*); calculating that the self has undergone various births and deaths from beginningless time in the past is the characteristic of a sentient being (*sattva-lakṣaṇa*);

and calculating that the self’s present life-force remains uninterrupted for a single lifetime is the characteristic of a life-span (*āyus-lakṣaṇa*). By analogy with the Pratyekabuddhas mentioned above, one should know that these are what the Bodhisattvas understand.
Below, the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra* states: "Because there is nothing to be apprehended, the Bodhisattva, relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, has no mental hindrance;
thus he is without fear, far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, and attains ultimate *nirvāṇa*," and so forth.

The *Chao* (Commentary) explains that "Universal" (*tong*) means it is universal with respect to both what precedes and what follows: it is universal with respect to the preceding *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Jiao* (Teaching), and universal with respect to the subsequent *Bie* (Distinct) and *Yuan* (Perfect) teachings;
therefore, it is called the Universal Teaching. Furthermore, it is named according to its own specific teaching:

because practitioners of the Three Vehicles equally use words to explain that the substance of the path—form—is itself entry into emptiness, it is called the Universal Teaching. Based on this, the formal explanation as well as the cited evidence are established.
Because this teaching is so named, the *Śū* (Commentary) states: "Universal" (*tong*) means "common" (*tong*).

Here, resolving the objection regarding this "universal" refers to the universality of the name across both preceding and succeeding [teachings]. The reason for this is that within the bodhisattvas of this teaching there are two types of faculties:
the sharp and the dull. The dull merely perceive partial emptiness and do not perceive non-emptiness; they achieve only the fruit of this specific teaching.

The title reveals that although the causes of the Buddha’s practice differ, the fruit is equal to that of the *pitaka* teachings; thus, it is said here that "below" this [level] it is common to the two vehicles.
If a bodhisattva of sharp faculties not only perceives emptiness but also perceives non-emptiness, this refers to the Middle Way being divided into two kinds:

namely, the "mere middle" (*butian zhong*) and the "not-mere middle" (*feibutian zhong*). If one perceives the mere middle, they are met by the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*); if one perceives the not-mere middle...
Because the Middle [Teaching] is received by the Perfect Teaching, it is now said that the "Superior" encompasses the Shared and Distinct;

it is precisely for this reason that the name "Shared" (*tong*) is established rather than "Common" (*gong*). Question: Since it is shared with the other three [teachings], would there not be confusion? Answer: The Subcommentary below states:
"If one examines its definitive reality, the others do not establish themselves; it establishes only the meaning within its own teaching."

The *Chao* (Commentary) further states, "All are pervasive," which is a restatement of the *Shu* (Sub-commentary) to provide an explanation. Furthermore, it separately clarifies one specific meaning to explain this pervasiveness (whereas the previous section dealt solely with the capacity of the practitioner, this section now primarily deals with the Dharma).

There are two interpretations: first, it is said that among the eight dharmas such as teaching and principle, the "pervasive" refers to the *Zang* and *Jiao* vehicles, while the "distinctive" refers to the *Yuan* and *Bian*.
This is because the remaining three vehicles also all possess these eight dharmas; therefore, this [category] is merely named "pervasive."

Regarding the meaning of "common" (*tong*), it applies to both [the teaching and the principle]. It is called the "Common Teaching" (*tongjiao*) because these eight dharmas are studied, cultivated, and realized equally by the three vehicles.
As for the first sense, "the teaching is common," this is explained according to the latter meaning; it refers specifically to the commonality of the shallow meaning.

What is called the "principle of partial truth" (*pianzhen zhi li*) is precisely the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 82) states regarding the principle of the Śrāvakas: "The principle of the Śrāvakas is the emptiness of persons... [The text continues with the citation from *Guifeng’s* commentary on the realization of the emptiness of persons as the principle of partial truth.]

"Emptiness" refers to the partial truth (*ekāṃśika-satya*). Alternatively, it refers to cases where only emptiness is clarified while the virtue of non-emptiness remains unmanifest; this is also called "partial truth" (as in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which says that śrāvakas see only emptiness and do not see non-emptiness).

Regarding the phrase "skillfully delivering all-knowing ones," among the three knowledges in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, this refers to "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*). The *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states:

"Entering from the conventional into emptiness, when associated with the wisdom of emptiness, one is able to destroy the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhava-kleśa*), thereby accomplishing all-knowledge and attaining [liberation]."

Because the true essence provides a skillful deliverance (*kauśalya-yāna*) in contrast to the clumsy deliverance (*bāla-yāna*) of the ignorant and the two vehicles of the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*, it is called "skillful deliverance" (the clumsy being broken and the essence made skillful).

Regarding the phrase "afflictions within the realm" (*dhātu-antar-vighna*) in the *Shu-chao*: because the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) trigger the karma that moistens rebirth and prevent one from escaping the triple world (*tridhātu*), they are said to be "within the realm.

Both teachings agree that these two types of delusion—view-delusion (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and thought-delusion (*saṃjñā-kleśa*)—are severed during the stages of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). The only difference between the two teachings lies in their being "skillful" or "clumsy."

Therefore: ▲ Regarding "the five practices (*pañca-karma-patha*) are common," although the discernment (*satya*), conditions (*pratyaya*), and degrees (*mārga*) differ, they are all untainted (*anāsrava*) practices throughout the stages of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-bhūmi*).
▲ Regarding "the six stages are common," the sub-commentary cites the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* and the intent of Tiantai, stating:
"First, the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*); the initial mind of the three vehicles is collectively termed 'dry wisdom,' and in the Mahāyāna, it is..."

These three stages of worthiness, according to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), are explained as the five *sthānacitta* contemplations (*pañca-sthānacitta-vipaśyanā*). As the *Fahua xuanyi* (Third Fascicle) states: "Because there is concentration (*samādhi*), it is called 'stopping' (*sthāna*);

because there is wisdom (*prajñā*), it is called 'contemplation' (*vipaśyanā*). Contemplation can overturn delusion, while concentration can restrain distraction. 1. Counting the breath (*ānāpāna*) treats distraction. 2. Impurity (*aśubha*) treats greed (*rāga*). 3. Loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*) treat anger (*dveṣa*). 4. Dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) treats ignorance (*moha*). 5.

Mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) treats obstacles to the Path. The *Guangchao* (Fascicle 11) states: "Regarding the treatment through the analysis of realms (*dhātu-vibhāga*), I do not say that mindfulness of the Buddha treats obstacles to the Path; rather, one should teach that [the other methods] are different, yet they are not mutually contradictory. 2. The contemplation of the specific characteristics of the foundations of mindfulness (*svalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*).

(1) The specific contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) by assigning them individually: the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) as impure, the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*) as suffering, consciousness (*vijñāna*) as impermanent, and the two aggregates of perception and mental formations (*saṃjñā-skandha* and *saṃskāra-skandha*) as non-self.

(2) The general contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness: observing the five aggregates collectively as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. The above three types of general observation are called "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-vijñāna*), because they do not yet accord with the principle of the Four Noble Truths regarding non-arising;

this is because one has not yet attained the water of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Thus, it corresponds to the stage of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*). (3) The Stage of Nature (*gotrabhūmi*): from below this point... [text ends].

Because it is a lineage (*gotra*), its nature is acquired through cultivation rather than being innate; thus, the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) states that one attains a "water-like" nature of semblance-outflow-free (*anāsrava*) qualities.

If one employs the mindfulness of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*) to accomplish the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment: by taking impermanence as the gateway, one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*);

diligently cultivating the four contemplations is called the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*); cultivating within the mind of concentration is called the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*); because the five faculties (*indriya*) arise, they are called the five faculties; because they obstruct all unwholesome dharmas, they are called the five powers (*bala*); and the harmonious balancing of concentration and wisdom is called the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). Peace...

Practicing within the hidden path is called the Eightfold Noble Path; examples such as suffering (*duḥkha*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) can be understood from what precedes. Initially, when one first gives rise to tainted wholesome states and enters the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), these are all termed the Stage of Nature (*gotrabhūmi*), wherein one attains the rank of an Inner Worldling (*pṛthagjana*).
Second is the Stage of the Eight Persons (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*): this refers to those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).

Substantially, they perceive the conventional to give rise to the real, thereby severing the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) during the Path of Non-interruption (*ānantarya-mārga*). (Master Yuan [Huiyuan] said: "The ancients...")

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains that the candidate for the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna-pratipannaka*) is considered the eighth because, relative to the seven preceding stages of preparation (*prayoga*), he is the eighth; furthermore, when counting from the stage of Arhat back to the beginning, he is also the eighth. The *Xinjing chao* states that the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) constitute the path of non-interruption (*ānantarya-mārga*), while the [eight] knowledges (*jñāna*) constitute the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Because the power of the patiences is predominant, only the eight patiences are called the "Eight Persons" (*aṣṭau puruṣapudgalāḥ*). Since the knowledges follow the patiences and do not constitute a separate category, the eighth patience itself is designated as the "ground of the Eight Persons.

This is based on the explanation in the fiftieth fascicle of the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*. Regarding the fourth, the Ground of Seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*): this refers to the principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) which the three vehicles (*triyāna*) equally perceive, and the eight [afflictions] which they equally sever.

The eighteen *anuśayas* are exhausted. Regarding the fruits [of the path]: the *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states: "Under *duḥkha-satya*, all are present; under *samudaya* and *nirodha*, three views are excluded; on the path, two views are excluded; in the higher realms, anger does not function. The commentary explains: Under the *duḥkha-satya* of the desire realm, ten afflictions (*kleśa*) are present:

(1) greed, (2) hatred, (3) pride, (4) ignorance, (5) doubt, (6) the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), (7) the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), (8) false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), (9) the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and (10) the esteeming of precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Under the *samudaya* and *nirodha* truths, the view of a self-identity, the view of extremes, and the esteeming of precepts and rituals are each excluded, leaving seven to be abandoned in each case; thus, fourteen are abandoned in total. Under the *mārga-satya*, eight are abandoned, excluding the view of extremes and the view of a self-identity. All of these are abandoned collectively under the four truths of the desire realm.

Regarding the thirty-two [afflictions] of the upper two realms (*dhyāna*) and four truths of the lower realm (*kāmadhātu*), one removes anger from each of the former thirty-two, leaving twenty-eight in each; thus, there are fifty-six. When added to the original thirty-two, they total eighty-eight, all of which are abandoned through the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), as explained in the nineteenth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.

Question: For what reason do the lower three truths lack the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)? Answer: The view of a self-identity and the view of extremes exist only where there is the fruit of suffering (*duḥkha*).

To grasp the body as a self is called the view of a self-identity; to grasp the body as being subject to annihilation or permanence is called the view of extremes. Since the other three truths are not the body itself, these two views do not exist there. Question: Why does one who clings to precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) become deluded regarding both the truths of suffering and the path? Answer: The essence of the precepts is suffering, yet such a person grasps them as being pure.

Therefore, because one is deluded regarding the Truth of Suffering by taking wrong precepts and non-paths as the path, one is likewise deluded regarding the Truth of the Path. Question: Why is there no mention of the "clinging to precepts" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) among the Truths of Origination and Cessation? Answer: There are two types of clinging to precepts: first, calculating what is not a cause to be a cause, which arises from being deluded regarding the fruit of suffering; second, calculating what is not the path to be the path, which arises from being deluded regarding the Truth of the Path.

Thus, these two truths—Origination and Cessation—are not established [as objects] for this clinging to precepts. As explained in the *Hongjue*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā-śāstra*, and the *Xinjing-chao*: the ninth volume of the *Guangchao* states that the cessation of the three views consists of the view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the clinging to precepts and prohibitions (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Since the body is the root of suffering, when one contemplates the Truth of Suffering, the view of extremes is already severed; because it relies upon the body, it is also severed accordingly. Regarding the Truth of Origination, one does not calculate what is not the path to be the path; furthermore, regarding the Truth of Cessation, it is not something to be cultivated through such practices.

Because they occupy this stage, there is no "clinging to precepts" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) to be abandoned; that which constitutes clinging to precepts is the reckoning of what is not the path as the path. Furthermore, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "To reckon only precepts as the cause for attaining the Path, while failing to realize that the attainment of the fruit depends on penetrating the principle and cultivating meditative practice—this is clinging to precepts.

It is not the case that only dog or ox precepts constitute clinging to precepts. Fifth, the "thin stage" (*tanubhūmi*): six grades of the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) arise to sever the six grades of innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) of the desire realm.
The sixth grade of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) is realized, whereby the afflictions of the desire realm are rendered thin.

Regarding the second fruit, there are six stages of freedom from desire, meaning the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*) and the separation from the afflictions of the desire realm.

Regarding the third fruit: [the five lower fetters are] (1) the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), (2) attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), (3) doubt (*vicikitsā*), (4) sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), and (5) ill-will (*vyāpāda*).

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Chapter 21) states: "For what reason are these five called 'conducive to the lower part'? Because they favor the desire realm. Due to sensual desire and ill-will, one does not arise in the desire realm; even if one were able to arise, because of the view of a self-identity, attachment to precepts and rituals, and doubt, one returns to the lower [realms]. The verse says: "By two, one does not arise; by three, one returns again."

Because they lead downward, they are called "factors conducive to the lower realm" (*avarabhāgīya*). Having attained the stage of "one who has already accomplished" (*kṛtāvibhūmi*), one gives rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*) to sever the five factors conducive to the upper realm (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*):

(1) craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*), (2) craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*), (3) restlessness of the two upper realms (*auddhatya*), (4) pride of the two realms (*māna*), and (5) ignorance of the two realms (*avidyā*). Because the faults of these two realms are particularly heavy, they are explained separately; because the remaining three [cravings] are light, they are combined. When these five fetters are present, one does not arise in the upper realms, hence they are called "factors conducive to the upper realm.

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (21) states: "These five are beneficial to the upper realm, therefore they are called 'upper parts' (*ūrdhvabhāga*). Together with the eighty-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation, these are all exhausted.

Because the affairs of the three realms have been brought to completion, it is said that [the stage] is "already accomplished" (*kṛtāvin*); yet because residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*) cannot yet be eradicated, one should practice for the four fruits and the eight stages of the *pratyekabuddha*.
The power of the merit of the *pratyekabuddha* is the greatest among these, as it can eradicate and remove residual habit-energies—just as burning charcoal into ash.
From the ninth *bodhisattva* stage onward, one enters the provisional from emptiness; the path and contemplation flow together in tandem, and one deeply contemplates the two [truths].

Because one eliminates the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) through the truths, and because one attains mastery over form, mind, and so forth; because of ignorance regarding the dharmadhātu beyond the realms, the knowledge of the modes of the path (*mārgajñatā*),
