Regarding Tripiṭaka Master Prajñāvarman: according to his biography, his name was Prajñāvarman, which in the language of Tang means "He Who Acts as a Lamp of Knowledge," though he is also called Prajñā, meaning "Light of Wisdom.
He was a native of Central India and was originally of the Kṣatriya royal caste.
At the age of ten, he left home to follow his teacher, where he practiced and studied until he could recite one *lakṣa*—approximately one hundred thousand stanzas—of Mahāyāna sūtras.
After receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), he studied the Vinaya Piṭaka and became extensively proficient in the net of precepts.

His heart delighted in meditative contemplation, and he further cultivated the practices of concentration under a virtuous master. Continuing in this way without ceasing for twelve years, he subsequently traveled south to Magadha.
While at Nālandā Monastery in the kingdom, he encountered the Master of Śāstras Śīlabhadra, who was extensively propagating the *Saptadaśabhūmi-śāstra*.
Consequently, he further studied it under him; as this treatise also elucidates the Hīnayāna teachings, he recited one hundred thousand stanzas (*lakṣa*).

He was highly esteemed by his fellow disciples who transmitted the lamp of the Hīnayāna treatises and received their instructions, such as his disciple Prajñendrabhadra, whose scholarly achievements were firmly established.
Xue Ji had a profound mastery of the net of doctrine; now leading his followers to convert the king and his ministers in his own country, he was held in high esteem by them.

Together with ten monastics and laypeople from Bābā, they traveled northward in succession and reached the headquarters of the Western Khan, Yehe. He was then trusted and submitted to by the King of Rong.
At that time, in the ninth year of Wude, Prince Gaoping was dispatched on a mission to the barbarians; he met [Xue Ji] there and intended to take him eastward as part of the entourage.

Upon his return, the Uyghur Khan and his ministers were so deeply attached that they would not permit him to leave; the King immediately memorialized the throne, and an imperial edict was issued summoning him to court.

He then arrived together with Gao-ping Wang to pay homage to the Emperor. He reached the capital in the twelfth month of that year and was ordered to reside at Xingshan Monastery to engage in translation work and other duties.
However, the preface to the *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra* cited here states that the first year of the Zhenguan era corresponds to the Wude era.
The ninth year was changed to the first year of the Zhenguan era.
The *Jiaochao* states that it was on the twentieth day of the eleventh month, while the *Zhuan* (Biographies) states the twelfth month;

these are merely general references. The *Jiaochao* notes that the Sanskrit manuscript was carried upon the head to the capital, while the *Zhuan* records that its entry was requested by Prince Gaoping.
It is merely a slight variation. ▲ The term *pāpamitra* is also an abbreviation of a Sanskrit word;

for instance, the aforementioned "friend" (*mitra*) in the Chinese translation is explained in the commentary as "one who clarifies knowledge," where "knowledge" (*jñāna*) carries the meaning of "friend.

▲ Regarding the account of [the Bodhisattva] leaning against a wooden peg (*yaka*, pronounced *yi*, meaning a wedge) and raising smoke with his body to summon his companions, this is based on the transmission from Dharmodgata, who stated that [this occurred] while passing through Kucha.

Traveling through various kingdoms to the west, they ascended the Pamir Mountains and crossed the Snowy Mountains, passing through thousands of layers of obstructing vapors and ten thousand *li* of layered ice.
Below lay a great river with currents as swift as arrows; across it, they constructed a rope bridge by fastening cables to the flanks of the eastern and western mountains.
Ten men passed over at a time, and once they had reached the opposite shore, they raised smoke as a signal. Those remaining saw the smoke and knew that the preceding party had already crossed.
Only then can they proceed further; if smoke is not seen for a long time, they know that a violent wind has blown them into the river, and thus it is said here:
"Raising smoke to summon companions. After traveling for three days, they again cross the Great Snow Mountains (*Himavat*), where precipitous cliffs stand sheer with no place to set foot.
On the stone walls, there are old wooden peg holes facing one another everywhere; each person takes hold of four pegs first.
They pulled down the lower pegs and climbed up by grasping the upper ones, passing them on to one another in succession until they had traversed the distance over three days and reached level ground.
They arrived at the kingdom of Kaśmīra (which is the "Passing the Body by Attaching to Pegs" section). According to the records above, Dharmodgata went to the Western Regions;

as this account describes how the Tripitaka Master himself came from there, it first details his crossing of the Snow Mountains by attaching his body to pegs, followed by his passage across the suspension bridge.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "braving ice and frost to cross the Pamir Mountains," the *Faxian zhuan* (Record of Faxian) states that the Pamirs have perpetual snow throughout both winter and summer;
there are malevolent dragons that spit forth poisonous winds and rain down sand and gravel, making the mountain paths perilous and steep, rising vertically for thousands of fathoms.
The Tripitaka Master Xuanzang further stated that the Pamirs lie at the center of Jambudvīpa, bordering the Snowy Mountains to the south and [the region of] ... to the north.
This Hot Sea lies to the east of the Black Mountains (Uśīra) and extends westward as far as Persia; its length and breadth encompass several thousand *li* of various kingdoms.

Snow accumulates there throughout both winter and summer, and since more than half of the terrain consists of narrow and perilous cliffs and precipices where mountain onions (*palāṇḍu*) grow in abundance, it is named accordingly.
As people of old said, "The snow-still mountains are the Snow Mountains (*Himavat*). Now, having personally witnessed this with my own eyes, I know it to be so.
It is not the Snow Mountains, but rather south of the Pamir Range. Regarding the phrase "offending wind and heat while crossing the River of Sand," the *Faxian zhuan* states:
"From Chang'an, one travels west across the shifting sands; above there are no flying birds, and below there are no running beasts.
Looking out in all directions, it is vast and boundless, and one cannot discern where one is going; one can only rely on the sun as a standard for east and west. Human bones [are seen]...
This marks the path of travel; there are frequent hot winds and malevolent spirits, and anyone who encounters them will surely die.
Now, the Tripitaka Master has come from that region; he first crossed the Pamir Mountains and subsequently traversed the shifting sands. Regarding the term *zúi-zǐ* (上子于切，下音咨):

the *Erya* states, "The mouth of *zúi-zǐ* refers to the constellations Yingshì (營室) and Dōngbì (東壁). The commentary notes: "Yingshì and Dōngbì... [The text continues with the description of the constellations.]

The *Shi* (室) lunar mansion coincides with the *Bi* (壁) mansion; because it lies to the east of *Shi*, it is called "the Eastern Wall (*Dongbi*) of the *Yingshi*. The asterism is square and resembles a mouth, hence its name.
The year in which the *Bi* mansion governs the year corresponds to the current Year of the Pig (*Hai*). Regarding the statement that "Qin summoned Chongshou and others," the biography says:
*Jiumoluqipo* (鳩摩羅耆婆), which is translated as "Childhood Longevity" (*Tongshou*), because even during his childhood he already possessed the [wisdom] of the aged.
As for "Ji" (智), some say it is a contraction of the Sanskrit name Kumārajīva; because he was skilled at interpreting texts (*wen-shi*), he is called Jīva.
Thus, the term "Kumārajīva" combines both Chinese and Sanskrit.

Regarding the statement that he "used barbarian troops," this refers to the time of Fu Jian of the Former Qin, when an auspicious star appeared in the outer celestial division corresponding to his domain, and he dispatched Lü Guang to conquer Kucha (pronounced *qiu*). Zhi (pronounced *ci*).
Master Shi has already cited this previously. Regarding the phrase "the Han Emperor's invitation" and so forth: Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty dreamed of a golden man flying through the air.
The following morning, he summoned the learned official Fan Ye and asked him, saying, "I have heard that there is a divine being in the Western Regions whose name is Buddha;
the one you saw in your dream must surely be him. The Emperor was delighted and immediately dispatched the Court Gentleman Cai Yin.
The Dr. Qin Jing and others traveled to India to seek out the Buddha-dharma;

while on their journey, they indeed encountered Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna returning with scriptures and images upon white horses. They subsequently arrived together in Luoyang, where the teaching of the Dharma first flourished.
How could this be compared to the inferior [traditions] of the Xia dynasty? (In the original text, "xiàn" is a homophone for "jiàn," meaning "to see.")
Regarding the citation of Dharma Master Qishi, the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) states: "Dharma Master Lin of Qishi Temple established five categories:
first, the *Abhidharma*; second, the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*; third, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*—these constitute the Three Treatises; fourth, the *Lotus Sutra*, which says:
'After a long time, O World-Honored One, you must preach the ultimate truth'; and fifth, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and others, representing the doctrine of eternal abiding."
The Buddha-nature is fundamentally serene; this is the meaning of the sixth "Equivalence" (Ji), wherein defilement and purity are both fused and the Dharma-realm is universally perfect.
Regarding the statement that the first four [equivalences] are the Four Doctrines of Master Yan: these were established by the Great Master Yan of the Sui dynasty.
However, because the latter two doctrines differ [from the former], it is here stated simply that the first four are those of Master Yan. This is so.
Master Lin merely regards the teaching of "dharmas are like illusions" as the non-true school (*abuddha-yāna*), while taking the principle of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as the true school;
both [of these] are, according to Master Yuan, the non-true schools. Therefore, the subsequent refutation states: "The third and fourth [positions] differ only in terms of dharma and metaphor.
Master Yuan’s true school clarifies the teaching of the true principle of *dharmatā* and the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*); this is precisely what Master Lin refers to as the Dharma.

The Master’s "Constant" (Chang) refers to the initial stage of establishing a thesis (*zong*); it signifies the beginning of the distinction between the universal and the particular regarding the ultimate goal (*zongqu*).

This is what is to be refuted there. Furthermore, the *Xuan Yi* (Profound Meaning) under the section on the "True Thesis" also states: "If the True were not Constant-True, it would be subject to arising and ceasing;
if the Constant were not True-Constant, it would be false and deceptive. Regarding the statement "only the distinction between the Dharma and the metaphor," there are three [points].
The Non-True Vehicle (Abhūtaparikalpa-yāna) merely uses metaphors such as illusions and transformations to reveal ultimate truth;

this differs from the fourth, the True Vehicle (Tattva-yāna), only in its use of metaphors. Why, then, distinguish between two vehicles? Because of such objections, the sub-commentary does not cite them at all.

Regarding the second section of the Commentary, "Clarifying the Western Regions," the *Tanchuanji* states: "The original texts from the Western Regions established two schools, Xing (Nature) and Xiang (Characteristics).
The Xing and Xiang schools currently transmitted today are dependent upon those [originals], with many differences and few similarities."

Regarding the phrase "As for Paramārtha and others," the questioner asks: since Paramārtha and others were also Dharma masters from the Western Regions (India), why are they included here among those of this land (China)?
The answer is that because the *Tanxuan ji* (Record of Investigating the Profundities) categorizes them as belonging to the Western Regions, the word "然" (thus/indeed) is used to acknowledge this;

however, because [Hui]yuan personally arrived in this land and classified the teachings, he is included here among the great virtuous ones of this land. As for the two other great virtuous ones, they are likewise included here.
Because he only propagated the teachings in the western regions and did not come to this land, they were separately designated as the "Western Regions" (Xiyu).
As for Dharmagupta, the full name is Dharmagupta, which means "Dharma-secrecy" (Fami) in Chinese. He arrived at the capital during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
Although this master was not previously mentioned, he is cited here because he is discussed within the section on establishing the school. — *Chao* (Excerpts)

"Nālandā" translates here as "One Who Gives Without Weariness. According to the *Biography of the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty*, among all the monasteries in Jambudvīpa, none is superior to this one.
It was so named because five kings established it and provided for it with exceptional magnificence.
The monastery consists of five courtyards—or, according to some accounts, nine—sharing a single main gate and surrounded on all four sides.
The eighteen-storied pavilion is approximately eight *zhang* high and is constructed entirely of brick. Its uppermost wall is still six *chi* thick.
It has three tiers of encircling walls, also built of brick, standing about five *zhang* high. Between each tier, there is a very deep moat filled with water.

It is fully equipped with flowers and livestock, being magnificent and beautiful to behold. Since its establishment, it has been guarded with such purity and strictness that no women are permitted within.

Without discrimination and without ever withholding anything, he provided for more than four thousand members of the permanent monastic community, as well as visiting monks and laypeople, both orthodox and heterodox, totaling tens of thousands;
he supplied them all with food and clothing until their needs were exhausted. For this reason, the monastery was further named "The Unwearied in Giving" (Shi Wuyan).
[Previously it was said that within the Āmra Park there was a pond, and in the pond lived a dragon named Nālandā; because the monastery was near the dragon’s pond, it was named after him.]

It is further said that in the past, when a king built his capital here, the Buddha constantly practiced giving; because the people remembered his kindness, it was named accordingly. Within [the city] is a Buddhist monastery containing various sacred traces.
The vihāra is over twenty zhang in height. In the past, the Buddha preached the Dharma there for four months.

It is the constant custom of that country that whenever a master of the Abhidharma possesses clear and far-reaching wisdom, the king grants him an estate, ranging even up to ten cities, with the size gradually decreasing according to the degree of merit.

Rewards for merit were not less than those for three cities; there were currently over three hundred virtuous men (*bhadanta*) who had received official seals, all of whom had mastered the scriptures and above all did not perform manual labor for the monastic community.
From Uḍḍiyāna westward, throughout the realm, most of those who have left the household life are devoted to the study of meaning (*artha*).
Because the various masters of the kingdom encounter no obstacles, the students are widely learned and possess comprehensive knowledge. ▲
According to the *Biography of the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang*, it appears that Jñānaprabha was a disciple of Śīlabhadra;

thus, it is traditionally said that when the South Indian Prajñācandra composed the *Saptaśatikā-mahāyāna-nirākaraṇa-śāstra* (The Seven Hundred Verses on Refuting the Mahāyāna) based on the Saṃmitīya school,
King Śīlāditya went to the kingdom of Oḍra to suppress him, and the various Hīnayāna masters there held this treatise in high esteem and relied upon it.

When the King above invited [Śīlabhadra] to compete with the Master of the Mahāyāna, he composed a letter to Śīlabhadra stating that four monks—proficient in both the Great and Small Vehicles and in internal and external doctrines—should be dispatched to the royal residence to engage in debate.
At that time, Śīlabhadra dispatched his disciples Sāgaramegha, Jñānaprabha, Siṃhaprabha, and Xuanzang to respond to this summons. The evaluation states: "This wisdom..."

Kuiji was a disciple of Śīlabhadra. Furthermore, according to tradition, the great virtuous masters of Nālandā Monastery, such as Haribhadra and others, established the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Śata-śāstra* to refute the doctrines of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other works. Xuanzang said, "When sages compose treatises, they ultimately do not contradict one another;

it is only that students have their own inclinations and aversions. Consequently, he composed the *Huizong lun* (Treatise on Reconciling the Schools) in three thousand stanzas and presented it [to Śīlabhadra].

Since the masters Śīlabhadra and others praised [the teachings] as being well-aligned with this, it follows that at the time of Master Xuanzang, Siṃhaprabha and others had already established the school of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Śata-śāstra*.
Since it mentions Siṃhaprabha and others, Jñānaprabha must certainly have been among them.

Although Master Xuanzang sought to harmonize [the views], it was likely because Jñānaprabha’s version of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* was widely prevalent at a later time that he [Xuanzang] [aligned his views] with Śīlabhadra.
At the same time, at Nālandā Monastery, the two pillars of the *Hongzong* (Propagation of the School) and the *Ruojin* (If Now) commentaries have not yet been definitively resolved.

Regarding the phrase "The commentary records that Master Xingchan wrote... and so forth, this serves as direct proof that there were two schools in the Western [Land], while simultaneously proving their respective superiority and inferiority.
As for the phrase "the dark whirlwind has just arisen," it refers to Nāgārjuna holding the banner aloft throughout the Five Indias and establishing his treatises.
The phrase "there is no victor" (無有勝者) mentioned here as "dark whirlwind" (*xuánbiāo*) likely refers to this same category.
As for the statement that "Wuzhuo was led like a sheep," the intended meaning is that the tenets of Wuzhuo’s school fell into error. This [passage] uses the *Zuozhuan*; therein it says:

"In the spring of the twelfth year of Duke Xuan, the King of Chu besieged Zheng. After seventy days, the people of Zheng divined whether they should seek a peace treaty and the result was not auspicious; they divined whether they should surrender [lín (qùshēng)]..."
[The sound] "Hu" [was heard]. At the Grand Palace, they drove the chariots out through the lanes. The people of Ji cried out in great lamentation; those guarding the city walls all wept.

Duke Chu withdrew his army, but the people of Zheng repaired their walls and then advanced to surround him again. After three months, he conquered them. He entered by the Huang Gate and proceeded along the main thoroughfare.
The Lord of Zheng bared his shoulder and led a sheep forward to meet him, saying: "I, your orphan, have been ungracious to Heaven and was unable..."
That my lord has harbored such anger toward our state is the fault of this orphaned ruler; I dare not fail to obey whatever command you may give.

Whether you take its captives south of the Yangtze to populate the coastal regions, or whether you cut it down and bestow it upon the feudal lords to be treated as your handmaidens—this too we shall obey.
If you would kindly look back upon our former friendship and seek blessings from Kings Li, Xuan, Huan, and Wu, [we shall surely comply].
"To not abolish his state and allow him to change his allegiance to serve you as one of your nine commanderies is a favor from Your Majesty and a wish of mine;

it is not something I dared to hope for, yet I venture to lay my heart before you—may Your Majesty truly deliberate upon this. His attendants said, "It must not be granted; if one captures a state, there shall be no pardon.
The King said, "If that ruler can humble himself toward others, he will surely be able to win the trust and loyalty of his people."

How could this be considered sufficient? [The King] retreated thirty *li* and granted him peace. Pan Kuang entered to form an alliance, while Ziliang, the younger brother of the Duke of Zheng, went out as a hostage.
Furthermore, when King Wu had conquered Yin, Wei Zi Qi—the elder brother of Zhou—carried the sacrificial vessels to the army gates;
he bared his arms, prostrated himself face-down, and led a sheep by its left horn with his left hand while holding a knife in his right.
"Maow crawled forward on his knees, and King Wu then organized him into groups of ten" (the note says: "This refers to baring one's arms and leading a sheep, showing oneself as a servant").
Regarding the phrase "feathers momentarily soaring," "feathers" refers here to the feather-fan; this alludes to Zhuge Wuhou holding a white-feather fan to direct the three armies.
The application of this to the debate on doctrine by Nāgārjuna is likewise so. As for the phrase "Chenna [Dignāga] following a chaotic track," it is also...

In the *Zuozhuan*, the spring of the tenth year of Duke Zhuang of Lu, the army of Qi attacked our state. The Duke was about to go forth to battle (this being Duke Zhuang himself). Cao Jue requested an audience with him.
A fellow villager said to him, "Those who eat meat deliberate on such matters; why should you involve yourself? Cao Jue replied, "Those who eat meat are vulgar and cannot plan for the long term.
He then entered to see the Duke and asked, "With what means shall we fight? The Duke said, "That which provides security in food and clothing..."
“I dare not appropriate it for myself; I must share it with others. [Zilu] replied, “Such small favors do not reach everyone, and thus the people will not follow you.

The Duke said, “As for the sacrificial animals, jade, and silk, I dare not increase their number; I must be sincere in my offerings. [Zilu] replied, “Small acts of sincerity do not inspire deep trust, and thus the spirits will not grant you blessings.
The Duke said, “In cases of litigation, whether small or great, even if I cannot investigate every detail, I shall always seek the truth. [Zilu] replied, “This is loyalty.”
These [men] are capable of fighting a single battle; if we fight, I request to follow Your Majesty. He granted him a chariot and they fought at Changshao (pronounced *biao*).

Your Majesty was about to beat the drum [to signal an advance], but Gue said, "It is not yet possible. When the Qi troops had beaten the drum three times, Gue said, "Now it is possible," and the army of Qi was defeated.
Your Majesty was about to gallop after them, but Gue said, "It is not yet possible," and he looked down at their tracks (the ruts of the chariots), then climbed onto the crossbar (*she*) and...
Duke Mu looked at it and said, "It is sufficient," and he then pursued the Qi army. Having defeated them, the Duke asked him the reason for their success.
He replied, "Warfare depends on spirit. A single drumbeat arouses the spirit; a second drumbeat causes it to decline; by the third, it is exhausted. Their spirits were exhausted while ours were full;
therefore we were victorious. Moreover, a great state is difficult to fathom; one must fear hidden ambushes. I observed that their tracks were in disorder and I saw their banners fluttering."
There was no reason to pursue it. In the *Tongji chao*, [the author] personally inquired about this, citing the *Tanxuan ji*, which records that Xianshou himself asked Tripitaka Master Rizi:
"Do the various masters of the Western Regions distinguish between the provisional and the ultimate within the holy teachings of the One Vehicle?
Rizi replied: "In recent times at Nālandā Monastery in India, there were two great [masters] living simultaneously..."

The two masters—one named Śīlabhadra and the other known as Jñānaprabha—were both of such transcendent spiritual insight that they surpassed their contemporaries, and their reputations were equal throughout the five regions of India.
Multitudes of heterodox sects bowed their heads in submission, while those of different schools returned to sincerity; students of the Mahāyāna looked up to them as they would to the sun and moon.
They were each the sole peerless figures in India, yet because the lineages they inherited differed, the teachings they established were not the same.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that Śīlabhadra distantly inherited [the lineage] from Maitreya and others: previously, King Siṃhaghoṣa exercised his power throughout the land with cruel and unrighteous tyranny.
He decimated the Śākya clan and uprooted the Bodhi tree, cutting off its roots and sprouts. He selected more than three hundred men of renowned virtue and buried them alive;
all the remaining subjects were reduced to slavery. At that time, as Śīlabhadra was about to be cast into the pit, he was lifted up by a thief.
After emerging from his seclusion among the grasses and thickets, he once again caused the Buddha-dharma to flourish greatly at Nālandā Monastery.

(The King Śiśuka was subsequently destroyed by King Śīlāditya. When King Śīlāditya arrived at the Bodhi Pit, he made a vow: "If I possess the merit to rule over the realm within the seas and am worthy to behold the Buddha-dharma, may the Bodhi tree sprout from the ground. Having spoken these words, he looked and saw that the Bodhi tree had already begun to bud within the pit;
it sprang up, and he then executed King Śiśuka. At the time when Master Xuanzang beheld him, he was already one hundred and six years old, as witnessed by all.
The King Śīlāditya, who revered him as a treasury of the True Dharma, granted him ten cities and increased his tax revenue;
Śīlabhadra utilized these gains to establish monasteries. As for those who say that Xuanzang inherited the lineage from Maitreya and Asaṅga:

when Asaṅga first attained the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the Hīnayāna, he felt it was not yet settled. Thereupon, he traveled by means of his supernormal powers to Tuṣita Heaven to consult Maitreya.
The Bodhisattva preached the Mahāyāna contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) and returned to Jambudvīpa; as soon as he contemplated it according to the teaching, he attained realization.
At that time, the earth shook in six ways. Having attained the contemplation of emptiness, he was thus named Asaṅga, which means "Non-attachment.

Thereafter, he traveled repeatedly to Tuṣita Heaven to inquire about the meaning of the Mahāyāna sūtras, and upon returning to the human realm, he preached them for others, yet most people did not believe him.
Out of faith, he made a vow to invite Maitreya to descend to Jambudvīpa to explain the Mahāyāna.

Accordingly with his vow, Maitreya descended to the human realm at night, emitting great radiance and gathering all those with karmic affinity in the Hall of Dharma Exposition. There, he recited the *Saptadaśabhūmi-sūtra*, explaining it as he recited it;

though the recitation and explanation lasted for four months, continuing through the nights, they were only then completed. Although they were in the same hall listening together, [the others did not perceive him].
As for the Dharma, only Asaṅga attained it in its proximity to the Bodhisattvas; other people merely heard its sound from afar.

It was at night that Asaṅga heard [the teachings], and by day he provided the exposition. The commentary states: "Śīlabhadra extensively propagated the *Saptadaśabhūmi-śāstra* (which is the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*).

Because Maitreya recited it forth and Asaṅga further provided the exposition, it is said that [the lineage] is 'distantly inherited. To say that [the lineage] is 'proximately followed' refers to Dharmapāla, who was difficult to surpass."

Regarding the term "Dha," according to the commentaries of the two masters on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other texts, the proponents of Vijñaptimātra in the Western Regions were the master Jayasena of Śālavana Mountain, whom Master Xuanzang himself venerated.
The statement that Śīlabhadra was his immediate successor refers to the fact that both the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and Vijñaptimātra belong to the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school;
specifically, Vijñaptimātra is one branch of the ten sections of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* in which the banner of the Dharma was firmly established.
I have therefore composed this preface. Furthermore, Dharmapāla and Nanda did not merely propagate the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) school.
Regarding the scriptural evidence that Dharmapāla and Nanda had attained the state of a sage (*ārya*), the *Vijñaptimātra-kōyō* states:
"On the day of Dharmapāla Bodhisattva’s passing, celestial music welcomed him from the void, and his mournful cries shook the realm; the resonance echoed through the sky."
The Brahmin said: "This is one of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa. If that is so, he is a bodhisattva acting through expedient means;
yet, speaking of his manifest traces, he was also a preeminent talent of that time. 'Ying' refers to an outstanding hero, and 'yan' refers to a brilliant scholar.
This speaks of those who follow in the footsteps of others; 'footsteps' refers to later generations treading upon the tracks left by their predecessors."
The details of the equipment are as extensively described in the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) and the *Sanzangzhuan* (Biographies of the Tripitaka Master).

According to the tradition, when Xuanzang had traveled through various countries for a long time and was about to arrive at that monastery, the community dispatched forty virtuous monks (*bhadanta*) to welcome him. They escorted him to a guest house for the night;
this was the original village of Maudgalyāyana. The next day, after the midday meal, there were more than two hundred monks and over a thousand laypeople.
Carrying palanquins, banners, and canopies, they welcomed him into the capital city. After exchanging greetings with the multitude, he proclaimed that he would reside at the monastery.
Furthermore, twenty men were dispatched to escort him to the Abhidharma-piṭaka master, namely the Śāstrin Śīlabhadra, who was one hundred and six years old and held in high esteem by all;
because of his vast learning and powerful memory, he was titled the "Abhidharma-piṭaka Master," being a great authority in both Buddhist and non-Buddhist teachings.

There was no minor scripture among the entire Buddhist canon that he did not master. After Xuanzang had finished his prostrations and praises, [the Master] ordered him to sit and asked from where he had come.
He replied, "I have come from the country of Cīna, wishing to study the *Yogācāra* treatises and other works.

Upon hearing this, [the Master] wept and summoned his disciple Juexian to recount the old events. Juexian said, "Three years ago, the Upādhyāya suffered from an ailment as agonizing as being pierced by knives."
Desiring not to eat and thus die, he dreamed of a golden man who said: "Do not loathe this body. Go and become a king;

though you will take many lives, you shall repent and reproach yourself. How can you simply end your own life? A monk from Zhina (China) has come here to study the Dharma and has already been on his way for three years.
You ought to bestow the Dharma upon him, and as he circulates it further, your transgressions will naturally be purified."
"Because I have destroyed this Mañjuśrī, he has come to exhort me; my Upādhyāya is now on the verge of passing away.

When the keeper of the True Dharma asked how long it had been since he had departed on his journey, Xuanzang replied, "It has been three years. Since this coincided exactly with the dream, he was overcome with a mixture of grief and joy.

After he had finished paying his respects and offering thanks, he learned that the temple had traditionally maintained ten positions for those versed in the Tripiṭaka, such as Dharmatara and Fali, yet these positions had long remained vacant.

I heard from Xuanzang that upon assuming his position, he was provided daily with twenty plates of superior delicacies and one *dou* of "great man" rice (i.e., non-glutinous rice, as large as black beans, whose fragrance could be smelled for a hundred paces;
only those of this country who were kings or learned in the Dharma were permitted to partake). There were also areca nuts, cardamom, *nāgakesara*, milk curds, honey, and other items.
Four *śūdra* attendants and four *brāhmaṇas* formed one procession, while thirty men rode in an elephant carriage.
From then on, for twenty days, those who had mastered one entire scripture were provided with five dishes of food;

after these five days had passed, they were again admitted according to their monastic seniority. Xuanzang requested Śīlabhadra to lecture on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, and several thousand listeners attended.
It took fifteen months to complete one full cycle, and he lectured it once more, finishing only after nine months. All other works that accorded with reason were likewise treated.
He received instruction in the *Abhidharmasamudaya-śāstra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, and others; however, he devoted himself particularly to the study of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

For five years, he pursued his studies morning and night without ceasing. Fearing that his extensive knowledge would remain incomplete, he was initially reluctant to return east. His preceptor admonished him, saying: "I am old now.
I saw you devote your life to seeking the Dharma, traveling for ten years before finally reaching your own country. Now, do not decline my old age."
I, Xiu, have exerted my strength to clarify that the Dharma is precious and must be circulated; how could I expect to achieve solitary perfection?

Furthermore, I fear that by consulting other sections [of the canon], I might lose the opportune conditions for this work, as wisdom is boundless. Only the Buddha can exhaustively fathom human life, which is like dew—neither lasting from morning until evening, nor enduring from today to tomorrow.

It may soon be gone. Thus, I prepared my travel gear for Xuanzang, saw him off with gifts, and entrusted him with the scriptures and treatises. Consequently, Xuanzang proceeded toward Western Bamiyan.
He stayed in the country of Vatsa for two years, where he studied the *Vinaya-saṃgraha-śāstra* (the Root Treatise of the Saṃmitīya School), the *Dharmasaṃgraha-śāstra*, and other texts.
He then returned east to Nālandā, where he visited Śīlabhadra;

subsequently, he went to the householder Jayasena on Mount Yaṣṭivana to study the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-viniścaya-śāstra*, the *Arthaviniścaya-śāstra*, the *Abhayapaddhati-śāstra*, and others from beginning to end.

The years have gradually rotated eastward from this region; according to this, the teachings studied by Master Xuanzang were not from a single master, yet upon returning to his native land, he took Śīlabhadra as his primary school, and thus it is said that this is precisely the tradition of the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang.

The commentary addresses the doubt regarding the second period, stating: "In the second period, it is taught based on the *parikalpita* (imagined nature) that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is entirely empty;

yet, in reality, the *paratantra* (dependent) and *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) natures do exist. Why, then, is only emptiness taught, and not the existence of the *paratantra* and *pariniṣpanna*? The intent of the explanation is as follows:

Although in the second period [the teaching] is based on the *paratantra*—even granting this point—it is [ultimately] sublated by the [teaching of] the *pariniṣpanna*. Alternatively, [it may be understood that] although it is based on the *paratantra*, it is [thereby] refuted.
It can be understood that the former clarifies the superior [nature] and the latter clarifies the inferior.

As for the statement "to be explained below," this refers to the discussion within the section on the meaning of the emptiness and existence, and their identity and difference, regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Regarding the statement "this has two layers": first, it is taught that because of causes and conditions all phenomena arise, clarifying that they exist as the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); next, it is taught...

"All phenomena are empty" refers specifically to the *parikalpita* (imagined nature); thus, they are all empty [as the Commentary on the Śāstra states: "It is said that all phenomena are empty based on what is grasped by the *parikalpita*"].
Third, it explains all three natures: because the *parikalpita* has no essence or function at all, it is empty;

the *paratantra* (dependent nature) is free from grasping, yet as a provisional designation for expression, it is said to have two types of wisdom as its objects—namely, the conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) for the *paratantra* and the ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) for the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature). This is the third [point].
At that time, the phrase "the three natures" (*trisvabhāva*) in the commentary explains the meaning of the preceding two periods.
Second, the second section below takes the two phrases from the commentary—"the three natures and the three absences of nature," etc.—as a pair to reflect upon the previous two periods:
that in the second period the three absences of nature are all empty, while in the first period the three natures all exist; this constitutes the third period.
Because it possesses both the three natures and the three absences of nature, it is neither empty nor existent. At the initial stage, all three natures are present:
that which is grasped as a real self is the *parikalpita* (imagined); the dharmas such as form and mind are the *paratantra* (dependent);

and the principle of emptiness is the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected). The other two teachings can be understood accordingly. (The above explains the two major points. Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says:
The following explains the meaning of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Master Qingliang’s commentary states:

"It is said that based on the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), one speaks of the 'naturelessness of characteristics' (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*), because its essence and characteristics are ultimately non-existent, like a flower in the sky or a snake upon a rope.

Based on the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), one establishes the 'naturelessness of arising' (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*), as this is like a magical illusion that relies upon various conditions."

Because that which arises is naturally devoid of false attachment, the nature of ultimate non-substantiality (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*) is established based on the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

This means that the ultimate itself is so designated because it is far removed from the previously mentioned nature of the self and phenomena as they are imagined by the conceptualizing nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Since these three natures are established based upon [the absence of] the three natures, it was not stated that the three natures exist, but rather that there are only the three absences of nature (*tri-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Because it is empty, it is said that the Buddha spoke with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*). ▲ This means that if one were to speak in an explicit manner, it would establish a third teaching.
In contrast to the previous intentional meaning, it is called "explicit" (*nītārtha*); in contrast to the previous lack of completeness, it is called "dual clarification.

This means that because one does not obstruct dependent origination, one speaks of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*); because one does not obstruct the absence of nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), one speaks of the three absences of nature. Only when both are present is it [the ultimate truth].
This is precisely non-separation, which constitutes the Middle Way.

The statement in the *Chao* (Commentary) regarding the "ten layers" refers to the initial section of the *Biehui Erzong Shu* (Exegesis on the Separate Convergence of the Two Schools), which specifically establishes these ten layers.

As for the remark, "For now, based on the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, there are briefly four meanings," this means that the ten layers are still discussed in terms of the general principle (*zongtong*) of the school, while the four [meanings] are presented as a brief summary.

The meaning lies specifically in the profound and esoteric teachings as contrasted with the first two periods of teaching. "One" refers to the second layer within the previous *Chao* (Excerpts), and "two" refers to the first layer.
Since both the preceding and subsequent *Chao* state that the "three natures are empty," why does this text speak of the "emptiness and existence of mind and objects"?
Answer: There are two interpretations. First, it is said that the three natures and mind-objects are mentioned here by way of abbreviation.

However, Ming states that the three periods established by the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* based on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and the three periods established by the "wondrous wisdom" (*prajñā*) based on the mind and its objects are mutually inclusive, as each possesses two meanings.
Second, he says that in that school (the Yogācāra), the three natures are also established in terms of the mind and its objects;

the dependent and perfected natures constitute the "mind," because all five categories and one hundred dharmas are solely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), and thus they are collectively termed [the mind].

Because of the self-nature of mind-consciousness (the eight consciousnesses as the sovereign mind-kings), because of association with consciousness (the fifty-one categories of mental factors), because of being transformations of consciousness (the eleven kinds of form-dharmas),

because of being states of consciousness (the twenty-four kinds of non-associated formations), and because of the true nature of consciousness (the six kinds of unconditioned phenomena)— within these five categories,

the first four are the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the last one is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); [all] are devoid of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of self and dharmas.
All these are called "objects" because they are external objects to the mind; therefore, both are empty. Based on this, when establishing the Middle Way correctly here, one should say:
in the first two periods of the teaching, Consciousness-Only was not taught, and thus [objects] were either existent or empty. Now, in the third period, both are explained as Consciousness-Only;
thus, the emptiness of objects and the existence of the mind constitute the Middle Way.

The *Chao* (Commentary) states: "In this context, for the time being, we shall briefly explain—based on the lower [level]—the 'comprehensibility' and 'incomprehensibility' discussed in the *Shu* (Sub-commentary) regarding the emptiness of the *parikalpita* (imagined) nature and the existence of the *paratantra* (dependent) and *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) natures during the two periods.
The term 'for the time being' (*qie*) signifies that the matter is not yet exhaustive.

Although four points are set forth in this formal establishment, we now proceed by means of the first two points; thus, based on the second point, we shall clarify the first [point] as established in the formal exposition above."
Regarding the statement "there are two meanings because there is one meaning," the *Benchao* (Original Commentary) states that this belongs to the third period;
however, it is also appropriate to interpret this according to the doctrine of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and the three absences of nature (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*).

This is because the third period contains two layers of meaning, and thus it correctly belongs to this [latter] sense. As for the phrase "the remaining two gates," this specifically reconciles the two schools of Nature (*Xing*) and Characteristics (*Xiang*).
The distinction between the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles is clarified through the manifestation or concealment of the one nature and the five natures;

that is to say, when the nature is manifest, the characteristics are concealed, and when the characteristics are manifest, the nature is concealed. However, according to the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, among these four gates, those that fully possess both the three natures and the three non-natures are considered "fully understood" (*nītārtha*), whereas those that speak only of the three natures and so forth are considered "not fully understood" (*neyārtha*), as they take emptiness as the object and hold that consciousness exists.
To realize that both mind and objects are empty is "understanding"; to fail to understand the One Vehicle is "non-understanding"; to fail to understand the Three Vehicles is "non-understanding";

to understand that all possess the single nature and will attain Buddhahood is "understanding"; to fail to understand that there are five natures among whom some do not attain Buddhahood is "non-understanding.
If, regarding the latter, the subtle wisdom reverses these four points of meaning, it is likewise treated as "understanding" or "non-understanding."
The Commentary states that according to the judgment of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, it refers to what is said in its second fascicle:

"O Bhagavat, at one time in the past, while you were in the Deer Park, you turned the wheel of the sublime Dharma for those setting out on the Śrāvaka-yāna alone by means of the characteristics of the Four Truths;

although this was most wonderful, it was surpassed by something higher and left room for further interpretation, and thus it is of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). Later, O Bhagavat, in a second period..."

In the middle [period], for the sake of those who have set out to practice the Mahāyāna, the Bhagavān turned the wheel of the sublime Dharma by means of the hidden mode of teaching—that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature, unarisen, unceasing, primordially quiescent, and by nature in a state of nirvāṇa.
Although this was even more marvelous, it was still "surpassable" (*sottara*) and "admissible" (*saparyāya*), and thus remained of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). Now, at this third period...
In the middle period, for the sake of those setting out upon all vehicles, he turned the wheel of the Dharma by means of the characteristic of thorough illumination—
based on the fact that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, are without arising or ceasing, are primordially quiescent, are by nature in nirvāṇa,
and are the nature of the absence of intrinsic nature. This is the first, most marvelous, and unsurpassed wheel of the Dharma of definitive meaning.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that Master Jñānaprabha “remotely inherited [the teachings] from Mañjuśrī and others”:

because Mañjuśrī extensively revealed the purport of Prajñāpāramitā in various sūtras, and because Nāgārjuna composed the *Jñānasārasamuccaya* and the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* precisely to expound the purport of Prajñāpāramitā, it is said that he “remotely inherited” them.
Regarding the statement that he “recently received [them] from Candrakīrti”: Xianshou’s original text reads “recently received from Dì...”.
Because the name "Bāqīngbiàn" (婆青辨) is incorrect, it is also called Nāgārjuna and Āryadeva.

The reason for correcting this now is that, among the twenty-eight patriarchs, Nāgārjuna is the thirteenth and Āryadeva is the fourteenth; one must distinguish between the distant and the proximate, and thus Āryadeva cannot be taken as the proximate recipient [of the lineage].
Furthermore, while Āryadeva composed the *Śataśāstra*, we now take Qingmu (Pingala) and Qingbian (Āryadeva) to correspond with Dharmapāla.
Since Nanda and others were all commentators, I have now revised this accordingly. The Preface to the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* states:
"Among the various kingdoms of India, there are no scholars who do not study and savor this treatise as their essential core (*kaṇṭhagraha*).

Those who have taken up the brush to provide commentaries and explanations are likewise very numerous. That which has now been produced is by a Brahmin from India named Vimalākṣa (translated into Chinese as [Bingluojia]).
It is said that this was the commentary of Candrakīrti. Although this man had faith and understanding in the profound Dharma, his phrasing was not elegant or refined;
where it was discordant, eccentric, or redundant, the Dharma Master (namely, Kumārajīva) edited and supplemented it. The *Xiyuji* states:
"The master of treatises, Bhāviveka, outwardly assumed the garb of a Sāṃkhya while inwardly propagating the learning of Nāgārjuna. Upon hearing of Dharmapāla Bodhisattva..."
When the Bodhisattva was at the Bodhi tree proclaiming the Dharma teachings, he commanded his disciples to go and inquire after his well-being, saying:
"We have long looked up to your virtue with a humble mind; however, because our past vows have not yet been fulfilled, we have failed to pay our respects.

One who has come to the Bodhi tree must not see it in vain; upon seeing it, there shall be realization. You are called a Teacher of Gods and Men, a Bodhisattva who protects the Dharma. The messenger said to him: "O Man..."
"The world is like an illusion and life is as fleeting as a bubble; I have had no leisure for discussion and have ultimately failed to meet the Master of Treatises.
Therefore, I shall return to my native land. Thereupon, he reflected in stillness, saying, "If not until Maitreya becomes a Buddha, who will resolve my doubts?

He then recited the *Sui-xin tuoluoni jing* (Svāhā-hṛdaya-dhāraṇī Sūtra) before an image of Avalokiteśvara. After three years had passed, the Bodhisattva manifested his form and asked him, "What is it that you seek?"
Zhi replied, "I wish to remain in this body to await the appearance of Maitreya Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva said, "Human life is difficult to preserve;
you should cultivate supreme merit to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven, where you shall then behold Maitreya. The Master of Śāstras said, "One's resolve must not be swayed.
The Bodhisattva said, "If that is so, you should go to Mount Nan in the city of Dhānakaṭaka and practice as a Vajrapāṇi."
"The deity said, 'If you recite and uphold the Vajra Dhāraṇī with utmost sincerity, this vow shall be fulfilled. Thereupon, he went there and recited it.
After three years, the deity appeared and asked, 'What is your wish? The Master of Treatises replied, 'I wish to remain in this body until I may behold Maitreya.
The deity said, 'Within these rocks lies a palace of the asuras; if you act according to the Dharma, I shall request that the rocks be opened.'"
"The wall shall open; as soon as it opens, you must enter within. When Maitreya appears in the world, I shall inform you.

Thereupon, he again recited and maintained [the mantra] for three years, then used incantations to strike the stone wall with mustard seeds, whereupon the wall opened. The Master of Treatises then entered the stone wall with six others;
once they had entered, the wall closed back up.
Regarding the phrase "the *Śāstra* [referring to the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*] and others, including the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, etc.":
if both mind and objects arise from conditions, they are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature, equal and of a single flavor, and do not obstruct the two truths.

This reveals reliance on the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, as well as the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the *Dvādaśadvāra-śāstra*, the *Śata-śāstra*, the *Jñāna-prasthāna-śāstra*, and so forth, while also incorporating the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, and others. As for the two types of those who now incline toward tranquility (*śama-yāna*)...

The phrase "those who ride [the vehicles] and so forth universally attain Buddhahood" indicates that one relies not only on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, but also concurrently on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other treatises.
Regarding the passage "mind and object both exist," the *Guangchao* (Extensive Commentary) states: "Mind is the subjective perceiver, namely the sixth consciousness; mind and object..."

Because one takes the objects of cognition—namely, the principles of the Four Noble Truths and so forth—and each clings to them as being existent. Regarding the phrase "the object is empty while the mind exists":

this refers to the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), which negates external, false objects; it means that names, meanings, intrinsic natures, and distinctions exist solely as mind.

Because it negates only the existence of the object, the object is empty (meaning that the imagined self and dharmas existing externally to the mind are all empty); because it distinguishes consciousness from the emptiness of the mind, consciousness exists. Thus it is said.

Regarding the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only): as for the statement that "both mind and objects are empty," it means that since the objects of perception—such as names and meanings—are empty, the perceiving consciousness cannot be established.
As the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states: "Because objects do not exist, the fundamental consciousness does not arise."

The commentary’s preceding discussion on the emptiness and existence of mind and objects, as well as its mention of "covering" and "shadow," is merely an abbreviated reference based on this principle;
thus, one should know that the two schools each establish two meanings regarding mind, objects, and the three natures, which is why they are mentioned in alternation and abbreviated.

When it says, "Now, regarding the emptiness and existence of the three natures," the first teaching holds that what arises through conditions is definitively existent, which is precisely the *parikalpita* (imagined nature), as it is expressed in general terms.

Because [beings] cling to characteristics as being definitely existent, in order to refute the attachment to a substantial self, it is taught that dependently arisen phenomena are definitely existent.

Next, it is taught that the dependent nature is like an appearance; finally, it is taught that what is dependently arisen is itself emptiness, which is the equality of a single flavor—this is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Because this proceeds from the shallow to the deep, the former [teaching] concerns their conjunction and thus is merely termed "mental object" (*viṣaya*); now, we proceed according to their differentiation.

The meaning is divided into the three natures; as in the two preceding schools, the former was based on the relationship between mind and objects, while this [school] is based on the three natures, hence it is called "abbreviated by reflection" (*yǐnglüè*).

Alternatively, within its own school, the former was also based on the three natures, while the present [treatment] is based on mind and objects, hence it is called "abbreviated by reflection. *Chao*: It is like the emptiness of a vast marsh.

That which has water below it is called a marsh (*zhe*). Here, the "emptiness" heard in the context of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) refers to an emptiness like that of a vast wilderness, devoid of both water and grass.
As for the phrase "the sutra says," this refers to the *sūtra* cited in the *Śata-śāstra-vṛtti* (Extensive Hundred Treatise).
Master Hongjue identifies this as being from the fourth chapter, "On Impermanence," of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*. The *Jing yinyi* (Sutra Phonetics and Meanings) states:

"寧" (nìng) is a term expressing a wish. The two phrases beginning with "But remove its illness" (*dàn chú qí bìng*) are from the "Inquiry into Illness" chapter (*wénjí pǐn*) of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
The Tiantai commentary states: "Fire is a phenomenon that burns; if one touches it and suffers pain, one must be careful not to touch it.
This is 'removing the illness. However, one cannot remove the fire itself; to remove it would mean losing its ability to warm the body and illuminate the darkness."

The analogy of food and so forth is used to illustrate that while the attachment to the real existence of dependent origination (paratantra) as held by the Hīnayāna is eliminated, the phenomena of dependent origination themselves are not discarded.

The *Chao* does not maintain the existence of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which differs from the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school that maintains the dependent nature while asserting only the emptiness of the imagined nature (*parikalpita*).
This is because it reveals that the dependent nature is also empty. Regarding the phrase "equal and of one flavor" below, this...

This contains two meanings: first, because in the Dharma-nature school (*dharmatā-yāna*) that which arises through conditions is without intrinsic nature, emptiness is itself the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and there is no separate essence.

Thus, upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) does not exist; therefore, the dependent nature is itself emptiness, for it is the principle that emptiness is the state of being without intrinsic nature.
As the *Ghanavyūha Sūtra* states: "That which is called the characteristic of the imagined nature is that which arises dependently."
When both name and appearance are discarded, this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), which is true emptiness.

Since the other-dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) share the same essence, why is it that the characteristics of phenomena must be retained for the former, while the other-dependent is said to be empty of the imagined? In the school of the two emptinesses, the three natures are like flowers in the sky:

they exist in dependence upon the diseased eye [of ignorance], the second moon [appearing due to a double vision], and the pressing of the eye [upon the original moon]. Thus, they arise based on these conditions.
Therefore, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is so named; that which is conceptually constructed by deluded minds as being truly existent is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Although these two meanings are distinct, the phenomena they refer to are not different. Since all such things are non-existent, they are termed the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

However, because even this [perfected nature] lacks an intrinsic essence when spoken of in terms of the principle of the emptiness of both the dependent and the imagined natures, it is said that all three natures are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); thus, they are not identical.

The Dharma-lakṣaṇa school relies on the intentional terminology (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) regarding the three natures to explain the three absences of nature (*tri-niḥsvabhāvatā*), as already explained at length in the *Guangchao*.
The above also interprets the teachings of the first two periods according to the intent of the third period’s teaching.
The colophon to the title states: "Bodhisattva Vibhūticandra. This title refers to the person who composed the treatise.

Regarding the difference in the names of the translators: it means that the individuals who translated it differ; that is, "Vibhūticandra" is the name used in the translation by Baopō, while "Jñānaprabha" is the name used in the translation by Rìzhào.
Alternatively, this may simply mean that the names of the persons who composed the treatise were translated differently. Thus, they are reconciled.
The meaning is identical to the explanation of the words. As for the title *Prajñāpradīpa* (Lamp of Wisdom), the question is:
since it is an explanation of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, why is it called the *Prajñāpradīpa*? This is the answer.

The intent is to show that because this root treatise explains *prajñā* (wisdom), wherever the principles of *prajñā* within the present treatise are profound, hidden, and difficult to manifest, they are illuminated like a lamp; thus it is the "Lamp of Wisdom."
The commentary (*Śāstra*) derives its name from the root treatise (*Mūla-śāstra*) by means of a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.

As for the statement that "the essence is *prajñā*," the *prajñā* elucidated in the treatise refers to the essence of wisdom (*jñāna-svabhāva*). Its function of illuminating and comprehending all phenomena is like that of a lamp;
thus, *prajñā* is like a lamp, forming a *karmadhāraya* (appositional determinative) compound. Therefore, the introduction to that treatise states: "To borrow 'lamp' as a name would be incomplete."
Separate wisdom possesses the merit of both quiescence and illumination. However, the *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra* is simply another name for the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*.
Its preface states: "The *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra*, also known as the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, consists of five hundred verses and was composed by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna.
According to this, the title of the commentary (*Prajñāpradīpa*) is applied to the entire work being explained (the *Mūlamadhyamaka*).
Because there is now a fifteen-fascicle version composed by the Bodhisattva Vibhajyavibhāsa, it is distinct from the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* [in its original form].
Regarding the statement in the *Yichao* (Excerpts) that "it merely follows Xianshou’s citation," the *Tanchuanji* (Record of Exploring the Profundities) states:
"The sequence of these three is as fully cited in Master Jñānaprabha’s commentary on the *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra*, which quotes the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* to explain this."
It is said that the *Mahāyāna-sūkṣmajñāna-sūtra* was something never heard of before;
however, since this is not mentioned in the treatises translated by Prajñāvarman, it is likely merely an elaboration introduced by Ñi-ma’i ’od-zer (Sūryaprabha).

As for the statement that it might be the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtras* and so forth: according to the treatise, whenever various sections of the *Prajñāpāramitā* are cited, they are each identified by name one by one.
How could this sutra alone have been renamed the *Mahāyāna-suvimala-prajñā*? Therefore, the author of the *Chao* (Commentary) expressed doubt, stating "it is said that...
He then asked: "The treatise designates him as Bodhisattva Vibhūticandra; yet, when reconciling this by way of meaning, it is Jñānaprabha.

I wonder if this Jñānaprabha is the same as the disciple of Śīlabhadra? The answer is: "According to the fact that Vajrabodhi personally relied upon Śīlabhadra [as his teacher], [this Jñānaprabha is indeed he]."
When I was studying the *Seventeen Grounds Treatise* at the beginning of the Zhenguan era, it was precisely during this period that Master Xuanzang was traveling to India.
At that time, Siṃhaprabha and others had already composed treatises to refute the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
It is likely that Jñānaprabha had already produced a commentary explaining the verses of the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, which Prajñāvarman subsequently brought back from there and translated.
Therefore, it was not at all precluded that Jñānaprabha, as a disciple of Śīlabhadra, simultaneously propagated the school at Nālandā. [Note:
