Regarding the phrase "protecting the realm of sentient beings" and so forth, the *Guangchao* (Broad Commentary), fascicle 2, states: "Three-quarters of sentient beings will certainly not attain Buddhahood;
this is called 'non-decrease' from beginning to end. Yet, those said to possess Buddha-nature shall all attain it within the interval of long or short time."
One who attains Buddhahood is called the Buddha-realm; those persons who lack the nature [for awakening] ultimately do not emerge from birth-and-death, and are thus called the birth-realm.
Because those of the lineage destined for quiescence enter into nirvana regardless of whether their duration is long or short, they are neither the birth-realm nor the Buddha-realm.
Therefore, the birth-realm and the Buddha-realm neither increase nor decrease.

Regarding the "four kinds of ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*) and so forth, according to the *Fayuan* (Garden of Dharma), there are two parts: first, the explanation of the names; second, the determination of their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Within the explanation of the names, there are again two sections: first, the explanation of the general name; second, the explanation of the specific names.

As for the explanation of the general name, Dharmapāla explains that "ultimate" (*parama*) means "supreme" (*viśiṣṭa*). There are two types of meaning for this term: first, the meaning as an object (*ālambana*); second, the meaning as a principle (*nyāya*).
Regarding the third [topic], the meaning of "ultimate" (*paramārtha*): most treatises state that it is the ultimate itself, or that all four types of ultimates share the meaning of being "supreme.

Treatises explain that the two natures—the dependent (*paratantra*) and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*)—are, as appropriate, the objects of the two types of wisdom: fundamental (*mūla*) and subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*).
Therefore, wherever untainted true wisdom (*anāsrava-bhūta-jñāna*) resides within any of the truths, it takes "supremacy" as its defining characteristic.
Because True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the object, it is explained by the *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) compound.

Regarding the fourth ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), since it primarily relies on the principle of reasoning, it discards the conventional expression to discuss the intended meaning; thus, it is not an [ordinary] objective sphere.

As for the first three ultimate truths being termed "truths of objects" (*artha-satya*), they consist of actual entities as they truly are, actual facts as they truly are, and principles as they truly are. Because these phenomena and their principles are without error, they are called "truths" (*satya*).
Regarding the two explanations of "the ultimate as truth" (*paramārtha-satya*) and "truth of the ultimate" (*paramārthasya satyam*): first, concerning the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).

"World" (*loka*) refers to that which obscures the principle of emptiness, wherein things appear with characteristics, such as when a cloth is tied into the form of a rabbit; here, the original cloth is obscured while the appearance of the rabbit-form manifests. This is likewise.
Following the ancient terminology, this is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Furthermore, its nature follows arising and ceasing.

That which is called the "world" (*loka*) is designated as "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*) because its essential characteristics are coarse and manifest; thus, "world" is synonymous with "conventional," and it is termed "conventional truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Alternatively, the meaning is that it is the "convention of the world," hence "conventional truth. Furthermore, "truth" (*satya*) has the sense of "reality":
that which exists as it truly is, and that which does not exist as it truly is, is non-false; thus it is called "truth. Therefore, there are two: conventional [truth] and conventional-truth.

The explanation is as before. Next, regarding the explanation of the specific names: first, "the ultimate truth of the world" (*loka-paramārtha*) refers to phenomena whose characteristics are coarse and manifest, which can still be destroyed;
thus they are called "the world. Furthermore, because it is known by the noble ones (*ārya*) and transcends the first [level of] conventional reality, it is called "ultimate" (*paramārtha*).

Second, "the ultimate truth of principle" (*yukti-paramārtha*) refers to the distinctions among the causes and effects of wisdom, abandonment, realization, and cultivation; these are termed "principle."
The object of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) transcends the second conventional [truth] and is thus called the ultimate (*paramārtha*). Third, regarding the "attainment of the ultimate":

because noble wisdom relies on the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as its expression to reveal the principle, it is termed "attainment. This is beyond the comprehension of ordinary fools and transcends the third conventional [truth], and is thus called the ultimate.
Fourth, regarding the "ultimate of the ultimate": its essence is subtle and difficult to express, utterly transcending all phenomena; therefore, it is so named.
The ultimate truth realized internally by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) transcends the fourth conventional level and is thus further named "ultimate.

In this context, the phrases "the mundane is itself the ultimate truth" (*loka eva paramārthasatya*) up to "the ultimate is itself the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha eva paramārthasatya*) are all *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compounds.

Alternatively, there is no fault in taking it as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound meaning "the truth of the ultimate" (*paramārthasya satyam*). Among the four types of conventional truth, the first—the mundane conventional (*lokasaṃvṛti*)—conceals the reality.

It is logical that worldly sentiment falls into the midst of falsehood; this is called the "worldly stream of ordinary people," all of whom claim there is a basis for their sentiments and establish names based upon it—these are termed the two types of conventional reasoning (*saṃvṛti-yukti*).
Regarding conventional reasoning: establishing phenomena such as the aggregates (*skandha*) according to their respective meanings is called "reasoning";
because the distinctions in the manifestation of the true nature (*dharmatā*) are easily known, it is called "conventional."

Third, regarding the conventional [truth] of realization: it is called "conventional" because it establishes the distinctions between the causes and effects of affliction and purification for the sake of leading beings to enter [the path], and because it is characterized by signs and is knowable. Fourth, regarding the ultimate conventional:

that which is excellently transcendent among all phenomena and known by the noble ones is called "ultimate"; however, as it is a provisional establishment of characteristics, its essence is beyond verbal expression.
Regarding "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*), here "the world" (*loka*) is itself the conventional; thus, even the ultimate (*paramārtha*) is termed conventional.
This is an *appositional compound* (*karmadhāraya*). Next, concerning the essential nature (*svabhāva*):

first, as for the nature of the ultimate, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that the entities of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), as well as nirvāṇa, are called "existent by name but lacking reality. These aggregates, bases, and elements are also [termed] the ultimate.
Regarding the second ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "It refers to the substantial entities of cause and effect, such as the Four Noble Truths;
nirvāṇa is also called the 'Ultimate Truth' (*paramārthasatya*).

Regarding the third ultimate reality, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains that it is the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the two-fold emptiness revealed through the gateway of linguistic expression (*prajñapti-mukha*); nirvāṇa is also called "non-existence" (*abhāva*).
The eight characteristics of suffering are called the "ultimate" (*paramārtha*) because, when observing all phenomena as a whole, they are seen as the two kinds of selflessness;
thus, the absence of suffering and the other [seven] are termed "supreme truth.

Regarding the essence of this fourth ultimate truth, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that it is the non-conceptually-established single true *dharmadhātu*, also referred to as *nirvāṇa*, the "real truth," the Tathāgata, space, and the Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, it is said that the absence of burning, cutting, and so forth is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), because the true nature is revealed by not relying on a self (*anātman*).

This is because the first three types of ultimate truth possess characteristics (*sanimitta*) and are thus established (*vyavasthāpita*), whereas the fourth ultimate truth lacks characteristics (*animitta*) and is therefore non-established (*avyavasthāpita*).

Regarding the essence of the first conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states that it refers to things such as jars, armies, forests, and so forth (the "and so forth" including clothing, food, drink, etc.).

[This refers to] all things such as food, vehicles, ornaments, cities, houses, and so forth. My sentient beings and the like may lack substantial reality, or their substance may truly be non-existent;
they exist only as provisional names and possess no intrinsic nature at all. Nevertheless, they encompass two types of phenomena: those with utility and those without.

Vases and the like have utility, whereas [the self] and so forth lack utility. As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (13): "There are names but no reality," such as "self" and "sentient beings," and so on.
The wheel of a whirling firebrand, names, phrases, and so forth—these five kinds of worldly phenomena are called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Regarding the fact that sentient beings and the like have no essence such as a fire-wheel, and that there is no second conventional essence, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) which are established [as such] are conventional;
the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also says that the various aggregates, elements, and bases are named "conventional," meaning they are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Regarding the distinct entities and functions of all phenomena that differ from the first conventional [truth], the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* explains that the third conventional truth consists of the established fruits such as the stage of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), as well as their bases—namely, the principles of the Noble Truths and so forth—and even Nirvāṇa is said to possess the characteristics of the eight sufferings;
this is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Fourth is the worldly... [text fragment].
Regarding the conventional nature (*saṃvṛti-svabhāva*), the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that it is the very nature of the established ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) which is called "nirvāṇa.
It is said that if something can be burned, cut, killed, or destroyed, it is termed "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*).

Because such things as being burnable or cuttable lack the characteristics of permanence, unity, selfhood, and so forth—namely, the two kinds of selflessness (*dvividha-nairātmya*)—this is called the "conventional truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya*). This is the primary sense of the conventional.
The essence of the latter three [truths] is established as conventional (*saṃvṛti*) through provisional designation; their essence exists as an established characteristic.

Furthermore, regarding the four levels [of truth], the *Fayuan* states: "The first conventional truth is the non-existent external object, which is established by the mind based on its own perceptions, taking pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) as its essence.
The second conventional truth consists of the objects transformed by the mind. The latter two are conventional truths."
The principle of the transformation of mind and the establishment of its distinctions—that is, the first three truths—have the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as their essence.

The fourth truth, however, is realized solely by internal wisdom; it does not have the transformation of mind as its essence, but rather has the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) as its essence.

Regarding the phrase "The meaning of the *Chao* says," etc.: it means that if the preceding thought-moment, which acts as the inducer, were not to cease while serving as the cause for the subsequent thought-moment, which is the induced...
If one perceives the characteristic of the fruit, the preceding thought-moment would be permanent; however, because it now ceases due to its cause, it is not permanent.

If the fruit induced by the subsequent thought-moment were not to continue, then the preceding cause would have produced nothing and would thus be annihilated; however, because the fruit now arises, it is not annihilated.
Since it is neither annihilated nor permanent, it is called the Middle Way. For a detailed explanation, as found in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, see the treatise itself.
Question: Is the ālayavijñāna annihilated or eternal? Answer: It is neither annihilated nor eternal, because it is characterized by "constant revolution.
"Constant" means that from beginningless time this consciousness has continued as a single stream, eternally uninterrupted;

for it is the basis for the designation of realms, destinies, and births, and its nature is to firmly maintain the seeds so they are not lost. "Revolution" means that this consciousness, from beginningless...
Arising and ceasing moment by moment as they occur, with the preceding transforming into the succeeding, the cause perishes while the fruit arises;

because it is neither eternal nor unitary, it can serve as the basis for the perfuming of seeds by the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). The word "constant" (*nitya*) excludes interruption and expresses non-eternality, just like a violent torrent:
the law of cause and effect is such that, like the flow of a violent stream, there is a long-term continuity that is neither interrupted nor eternal, yet carries things along.

The drowning in this consciousness is likewise: from beginningless time, its arising and ceasing have continued in succession, being neither permanent nor annihilated, causing sentient beings to drift and drown so that they cannot escape.

Furthermore, just as a violent torrent continues its flow without interruption despite being struck by winds and other factors that raise various waves, this consciousness is likewise constant in its succession, even when encountering various conditions that give rise to visual consciousness and the others.
Furthermore, just as in a torrential stream, water flows up and down carrying along fish, grass, and other objects without ever abandoning them, so too is this consciousness:
it evolves in constant succession together with internal habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and external factors such as contact (*sparśa*).

Through these analogies and their intended meaning, it is shown that the nature of this consciousness has been, from time without beginning, a causal relationship that is neither interrupted nor eternal; that is to say, the essence of this consciousness has existed since the beginningless past.
At that very moment, as the cause perishes and the fruit arises, it is not a state of annihilation because the cause has perished, nor is it a state of permanence because the fruit has arisen;
since this principle of dependent origination is neither annihilated nor permanent, it is said that this consciousness perpetually revolves like a flowing stream.

The Commentary states: "The four simultaneous characteristics mark the absence [of the dharma] after its cessation. The first phrase contrasts with the Final Teaching (Niṣṭhā-yāna), while the second phrase reveals how it differs from that.
Alternatively, both phrases may represent the tenets of that school itself. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Weishi shu) says: "Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to marks or signs;

they are called "characteristics" because they serve as indicators. By means of these, one knows that a phenomenon is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). These four characteristics are all established upon currently functioning phenomena (*pravṛtti-dharma*)."
Therefore, it is said that among the four characteristics arising simultaneously, the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha*) only becomes manifest when a given dharma returns to the past.

If this is so, why say that cessation indicates that "this dharma is subsequently non-existent"? In response: the term "subsequent" refers to the present dharma relative to the other characteristics such as arising;

because the dharma does not exist at a time subsequent to its present state, it is termed "cessation. This is a conventional designation for the past; however, the substance of the past is non-existent and is not truly that [past] world.
Regarding the section of the treatise beginning with "The *Cheng weishi lun*," according to the intent of the present commentary and that sub-commentary (*shu*), it is divided into three parts:
first, the statement establishing the purpose of the characteristics (*xiang*). (From the *Cheng weishi lun*)...
II. Explaining and Establishing the Four Characteristics (4):
A. First, the individual explanation of the four characteristics (the original non-existence);
B. Second, distinguishing [them] from the Lesser Vehicle by means of the time periods (the first three).
1. Threefold explanation resolving external objections; 2.
Description of the characteristics signified [by the term "growth"];
3. Conclusion establishing that [the self] is a conceptual construct.
Regarding the phrase "the stage of arising is temporarily suspended," the *Śāstra* states: "Having arisen, the continuous succession of similar [moments] is called 'abiding' (*sthiti*);

this very succession’s transformation is called 'alteration' (*anyathātva*). The commentary on that passage states: "The dharma’s temporary suspension is called 'abiding'; its difference from the dharmas of preceding and succeeding moments is called 'alteration.
Thus, arising and ceasing can be known. Here, the text of the commentary is treated as the text of the *Śāstra*. (Note: This clarifies the distinction.)
Regarding the phrase "differing from the Hinayana and others" (the sub-commentary merely classifies this as "discerning according to time"), the *Bǎifǎ Chāo* states:

"The Hinayana explains that within the future, that which is characterized [as arising] undergoes a transition and flows into the present; this is called 'arising' (*jāti*), and so forth. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:

"That which was originally non-existent now comes into being is 'arising'; the continuous succession is 'duration'; the difference between the preceding and succeeding states is 'alteration'; and the cessation of the continuity is 'cessation' (*nirodha*)."

(These verses state that the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are the same as in the Mahāyāna, differing only with respect to time. The long prose states: "Although it is admitted that the four characteristics all have functional utility, their times of operation differ.
That is to say, the activity of 'arising' (*jāti*) occurs in the future; once [a dharma] has already arisen, it does not arise again.

Only when dharmas have arisen and are currently in the present do the activities of the other three characteristics—'abiding' (*sthiti*), and so forth—begin to function. These do not exist at the time of the activity of arising."
The other three [characteristics] function [simultaneously], and thus although they coexist, they do not contradict one another. (The above is from the *Śāstra*). The commentary states:
Based on this treatise, prior to citing the passage from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, one first refutes the Sarvāstivāda school, saying:

"If the intrinsic natures of the characteristics such as 'arising' were to coexist, their functions should all arise simultaneously at all times; however, because they are mutually exclusive, their functions do not [occur together]."
If their natures are mutually contradictory, how can they coexist? Furthermore, the functions of abiding, change, and cessation should not occur simultaneously;
yet if the natures of the agent (the cause) and the object (the characterized) exist together from the outset, their functions should likewise do so, as there is no distinct nature [between them].

If you claim that those functions depend further upon causes and conditions, then those required causes and conditions themselves would not be inherently present. Moreover, it would follow that birth and the other [characteristics] are non-existent.

If that which is characterized were to exist eternally, then its association with arising and so forth would be impossible, as even unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) would then possess arising and the like.

Furthermore, because cause and effect could not be established between them, the past and future would not be present; being non-eternal, they would resemble flowers in the sky and lack a real nature.
If "arising" is defined as existence, how could it reside in the future? If "ceasing" is defined as non-existence, it should not apply to the present.
If cessation were non-existent, it would follow that it could not exist; furthermore, since cessation contradicts abiding, how can you insist that they are simultaneous?

Since abiding does not contradict arising, how could they belong to different time periods? Therefore, what they maintain is irrational from every perspective. (The following section continues with "Furthermore, conditioned phenomena [arise] by the power of causes and conditions," which this commentary cites from the sub-commentary, categorized as the second major section:
"Stating one's own position. [Regarding the question in the *Commentary*: "How can a non-existent dharma... and so forth, that refers to the aforementioned sub-commentary.
It is said that an outsider asks: "If cessation (*nirodha*) is non-existent, how can it serve as a counter-correlate (*pratidvandva*) to a dharma that possesses a real entity in the present?

Regarding this, the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "The Master of this treatise answers: It does not indicate that the dharma currently exists, but rather indicates that the dharma is subsequently non-existent.
Since those who specialize in *hetuvidyā* (logic) maintain that 'non-existence' can function as a cause for [the cognition of] non-existence, there is no fault. If that were so..."

If one were to propose that "tortoise hair" and the like should be established as characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the answer is that this is not the same as those [actual characteristics], because they do not exist subsequently and because they did not exist originally;
thus, they are not characteristics. *Commentary*: Regarding the separate explanation of "expressing meaning," that sub-commentary states: "The meaning of this passage is clear:

it precisely describes the reasons for explaining the characteristics and the significance expressed by those characteristics. *Commentary*: Based on this, [the term] "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*).
Regarding the establishment of the four characteristics, the subsequent treatise states: "The various stages of a single lifetime may also be conventionally established as follows:

the initial existence is called 'arising' (jāti), the final non-existence is called 'cessation' (nirodha), the continuity of similar moments after arising is called 'abiding' (sthiti), and the transformation of this very continuity is called 'alteration' (anyathātva).

Therefore, all four characteristics are merely conventional designations. (This conventionalism refutes the Sarvāstivāda school’s position that the four are distinct and substantially real; however, the Sarvāstivādins also establish these based upon a single moment.)

[This] merely means that their actualities are different. Question: How can there be such distinctions in name and meaning for the four characteristics within a single *kṣaṇa*, when the duration is so extremely brief that it is difficult even for reason to comprehend?
Answer: There is an ancient analogy of a needle piercing paper. Suppose one uses a sharp needle to pierce a hundred sheets of paper;
the piercing occurs simultaneously, yet all hundred sheets are penetrated. Although the piercing appears simultaneous, the needle must necessarily pass through them in succession.

Furthermore, there must be hundreds of instances of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing occurring simultaneously; one must necessarily see that within a single *kṣaṇa* there are four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) existing before and after one another, for this is logically required.
Thus, the *Ratnaketuparivarta* (Renwang jing) states that within a single *kṣaṇa* there are nine hundred instances of arising and ceasing.
Question: Since "ceasing" (*nirodha*) signifies the absence of what follows, it should belong to the future; why then is it called "past"?
The answer is: Because the state of cessation is non-existent, it is called "past"; because the present has already fallen away, it is likewise [considered past].
However, if one looks toward the next moment, characteristics such as arising are still in the future; at the very time of arising, they still belong to the present.
One should contemplate this differently from the perspective of the Hinayana.

In the *Chao* (Commentary), following the section on "Establishing Proof through the Investigation of Causality" (*yinming duanzheng*), the subsequent section titled "Explaining the Objects of Cognition" (*yuanjing*) is divided into two parts:
first, a general presentation of the three meanings (the characteristics of the cause);
second, a detailed explanation of these three meanings (three).
First, the distinction of the objects of focus (2):
First, a general clarification of distinct illumination (the root text);
second, a detailed explanation based on the commentary (2).
First, the simultaneous contemplation (explained in terms of its meaning);
later, the distinct illumination (because the two sever delusions separately).
First, the correct explanation of the meaning of "abandonment" (1).
First, the abandonment of afflictions according to our own school (2).
First, the correct explanation of the specific types of abandonment (2).
First, there is the interpretation that [the first] has abandonment (*prahāṇa*) and [the latter] does not;
second, there is the interpretation that both have abandonment.
First, establishing that the subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) has abandonment (according to Dharmapāla).
Subsequently, the treatise is cited to provide full proof (2):
first, the citation of the treatise;
second, the explanation of its meaning. (From the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, as traditionally transmitted.)
Finally, the conclusion reveals the non-interruption [of delusion];
next, the distinction from other schools [is made] to show their differences;
finally, the brevity of the commentary's text [in the North and Central regions] is clarified.
III. The Distinction of the Principles Verified (2).
A. First, the specific elucidation of that which verifies (2).
1. The actual analysis (the phrase "by means of").
Part Two: Subsequent Differentiation (Earth Clarification);
Part Three: Dual Explanation of Subject and Object.
First: Differentiation from the preceding [conditioned] objects.

Regarding the subsequent formal explanation in the *Nengzheng Chao* (The Commentary on the Proof), which states that "the realization of the conventional arises from the realization of the ultimate," this implicitly employs the intent of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.

It corresponds precisely to the passage concerning the objective sphere of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*mahādarśana-jñāna*) among the four wisdoms that take objects as their domain. I shall now cite it; let us compare the texts directly.

The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Views) states: Regarding the mental complex associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), there is one interpretation that it takes only suchness (*tathatā*) as its object;
this is because it is non-conceptual and its mode of activity and object are unknowable, being distinct from subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

There is another interpretation that this mental complex takes all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) as its objects, for the *Sūtrālaṃkāra* states that the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is not deluded regarding any object.
Because it is deluded, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states that the objects of the Tathāgata’s wisdom appear as the various images of sense-bases, objects, and consciousnesses;

furthermore, because this [wisdom] definitely takes as its object the uncontaminated seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) and the various images of the body and the environment, and because its objective conditions are subtle, it is said to be "unknowable.
Like the *ālaya-vijñāna*, it also takes the conventional as its object, yet because it takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, it is without parts (*nirbhāga*).
Because it takes other objects as its conditions, it is subsumed under subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); its essence is one, yet it is divided into two according to its functions.
It realizes the conventional because it has realized the ultimate; thus it is called "subsequently attained" (as stated in the treatise). Now, employing this very intent:

since subsequently attained wisdom realizes the conventional by virtue of having realized the ultimate, it is evident that subsequently attained wisdom possesses the sense of dual observation, owing to the fundamental [wisdom].

Only when wisdom realizes the ultimate truth can it comprehend the conventional; this reveals that fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) possesses the meaning of dual observation, and thus both types of wisdom involve dual observation.

Regarding the statement in the *Commentary* (鈔) that "fundamental wisdom cuts off the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) regarding the delusion of principle," the *Ten Stages Sutra Commentary* (十地疏) states:

"Because they lie dormant within the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), following and entangling it, and because they cause delusion regarding the objects of both phenomena and principle, two names and two essences are established."

These are the seeds of the two obstacles; although their active manifestations (*samudācāra*) are also severed, this refers to the time of actual severance because the active manifestations have already been suppressed, and it is the seeds that are being severed.

This passage from the *Śāstra* (the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-bhāṣya*) follows entirely the tenth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, specifically the section explaining the "path of severance" (*prahāṇamārga*), which contains the interpretations of two masters.
I shall now quote the relevant passages from the treatise in full, section by section. First, there is the [severance]...

Regarding "that which is not to be abandoned," the *Śāstra* states: "There is a sense in which fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*mūla-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) directly realizes the truth manifested by the two kinds of emptiness;

because it is devoid of objective characteristics, it can abandon the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is not so, and therefore it is not that which is abandoned. (In this current commentary, it should state:

"Only fundamental wisdom abandons the latent tendencies regarding the delusion of principle, while subsequently attained wisdom does not abandon them. That it does not do so here is likely due to later additions made according to personal preference, or perhaps based on other sources. For now, I shall follow the classification of the *Śāstra*.)

The *Śāstra* (the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*) states that according to Dharmapāla, both [types of] wisdom possess the capacity for abandonment. The *Treatise* says: "There is one interpretation" (which is the correct position of Dharmapāla):

although subsequently attained wisdom with conceptual differentiation does not directly realize the truth of the two emptinesses and thus lacks the power to abandon the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that obscure that truth, it nonetheless clearly manifests the characteristics of the established and non-established [truths] and realizes them without error.

It is also able to permanently sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that delude one regarding phenomena (establishing that subsequent attainment possesses the capacity for such severance). The meaning is this:
if subsequent wisdom did not sever them, it would be unable to sever the latent tendencies that delude one regarding the principle, because it does not directly realize the principle.

Since its realization of the principle established by the Four Noble Truths is non-erroneous, and its essence is dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it only severs the latent tendencies that delude one regarding phenomena.
The Commentary states: "The latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) regarding the delusion of principle have a profound mode of activity; they can only be severed once that principle is realized.

The latent tendencies regarding the delusion of phenomena have a shallow and proximate mode of activity; even through the contemplation of their actual characteristics, they can be severed. This is based on the *Śata-dharmaka-śāstra*."
The *Chao* (Commentary) asks: "Regarding the statement that subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) can sever delusions, I do not yet understand which delusions it is able to sever.

Answer: There are two interpretations by Ci'en (Yijing). The first says: "This refers only to the subsequently attained wisdom of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), which can sever the innate (*sahaja*) latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) regarding the confusion of phenomena;
it does not refer to Bodhisattvas. This clearly shows that afflictions (*kleśa*) are severed by both the fundamental (*mūla*) and subsequently attained wisdoms. If... [text fragment].

Regarding the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is asserted that only fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) can sever it. Second, some claim that a Bodhisattva’s subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) can also sever the cognitive obscuration.

Within the cognitive obscuration, there are those that delude regarding principles (*tattva*) and those that delude regarding phenomena (*vastu*). Because the delusion regarding principles involves clinging, it is difficult to sever and can only be severed by fundamental wisdom.
If it is a delusion regarding phenomena and not clinging, it is easy to sever, and subsequently attained wisdom can also sever it.
The phrase "Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says... refers to Dharmapāla citing the treatise as proof. It states in full:

"Therefore, the *Yogācāra* says that within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there exists the supramundane path of abandonment (*lokottara-prahāṇamārga*) and the mundane-supramundane path of abandonment (*laukika-lokottara-prahāṇamārga*). There is no purely mundane path that can permanently destroy the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Regarding the latent tendencies abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*) and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) that delude one regarding the principle [of reality], only [the supramundane path can eliminate them]."

Because fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*mūla-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) directly realizes the principle (*tattva*), it is able to correctly sever the root of those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) regarding phenomena that are abandoned through cultivation;
subsequently, the post-attainment wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is also able to correctly sever them. (The above is from the treatise. The commentary states:

This Dharmapāla cites the *Yogācārabhūmi*’s account of the supramundane path of abandonment as proof that fundamental wisdom severs the latent tendencies regarding the principle. (Fundamental wisdom is termed "supramundane" because...)

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle nine, states: "This is supramundane non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). Because it abandons the mundane, it is called 'supramundane. The latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two-grasps (*dvaya-grāha*) are the root of the mundane;

only this [wisdom] can abandon them, and thus it alone receives this name. Alternatively, the term 'supramundane' is established based on two meanings: its essence is untainted (*anāsrava*), and it realizes suchness (*tathatā*). Since this wisdom possesses these two meanings, it alone is termed 'supramundane'; that is, the non-conceptual wisdom within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Now, because this wisdom abandons delusion regarding the principle (*li*), it is called the supramundane path of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*). This passage cites both the mundane and supramundane paths of abandonment to jointly prove that both the fundamental and subsequent wisdoms abandon delusion regarding phenomena.

Regarding the phrase "mundane and supramundane" (*laukika-lokottara*) used for the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), it is stated as "supramundane of the world" to distinguish them from purely mundane states;
thus, they are called "supramundane of the world. This refers to the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Here, the delusions regarding phenomena (*vastu-moha*) are termed "mundane," while those that distinguish them from the purely mundane are termed "supramundane. Since this path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*) encompasses both types of knowledge, [this passage] is cited as proof.
Alternatively, it may be understood that this delusion regarding phenomena is severed by the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), which is called "worldly" (*laukika*);
yet, because it is also a path that severs [delusions] through fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), it is further described as "supramundane" (*lokottara*).

The *Chao* (Commentary) transmits the following explanation: "The 'proper essence' below refers to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*)," and the explanation for the preceding [term] can be understood accordingly. — *Chao*.

Regarding the phrase "when severing delusion regarding principles," etc., although this clarifies the manner of taking an object as a condition, it is intended to reveal that the severance of afflictions is not immediate.
Since this clarifies that the object of focus is not immediate, the subsequent statement clarifying that the severer is not immediate also reveals that the object severed is not immediate.
The Commentary states that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is such that when one is severed, all are severed.
This refers to the nature of phenomena as taught in the Final Teaching (*paryantayāna*), wherein principle and phenomenon are mutually identical and the two wisdoms are fused.

If the fundamental wisdom is already identical [to the nature of phenomena], then at the time of correctly severing delusions regarding principle, one is simultaneously able to sever all delusions regarding phenomena; this is precisely what is meant by "when one is severed, all are severed. If, however, it is the subsequent wisdom...

The attainment of wisdom is itself the fundamental [realization], and it is also capable of realizing suchness; when delusions regarding phenomena (*dharma*) are correctly severed, all delusions regarding principle (*tattva*) are also severed—this is "severing one and severing all.

This is stated in terms of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wuai*), and not in terms of the Perfect Teaching’s (*yuanzong*) non-obstruction of phenomenon with phenomenon (*shi-shi wuai*);
thus, while the general intent is the same, the specific meaning differs. Furthermore, according to the doctrinal meaning, this refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Final Teaching (*zhongjiao*).

Within the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), there is no distinction between the innate (*sahaja*) and the intellectually acquired (*vikalpita*); rather, there are only the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*, here referred to as *zhengshi*, meaning "directly manifesting" or "primary drivers"), because these are what are directly abandoned [through the stages].

As the *Commentary on the Ten Stages Sutra* (citing the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya*) states: "In accordance with the sense of 'following and binding,' it is like a government official who follows a person and, finding an opportunity, binds them. Furthermore, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says: "It is like the outbreak of rat-poison. The *Lun-hui-xiang-cha* (Commentary on the Direction of the Laṅkā) states: "In the West, there is a rat that bites people;

its poison remains within the body, and although the wound has healed, if one suddenly encounters the sound of thunder, the wound breaks out again. The active afflictions are likewise: if one suddenly encounters the 'thunder' of sensory objects, they are activated once more. And...
The latencies (*vāsanā*) are suppressed prior to the stages [of the path of seeing], while their active manifestations are suppressed at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).

Their seeds are severed at the first stage and above, and the latencies are eliminated until they are ultimately purified at the Buddha-stage. (The above provides a general explanation; the following is a detailed exposition:

However, since one does not fall into the level of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) from the very beginning within the stage of the three types of worthies (*trividha-ārya*), the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are voluntarily suppressed rather than severed, in order to preserve them for the sake of future elimination.

Because of obstacles such as those of ignorance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the *Liang Translation of the Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that from the "Ten Understandings" (i.e., from the stage of the Ten Abodes onward) one attains supramundane pure mind.
It further states that those above the Ten Understandings are called "sages" and do not fall into the stages of the Two Vehicles.

The *Ratnaketu-Parākrama Sūtra* says that those prior to the [first] bhūmi realize the emptiness of persons but do not take realization [of the ultimate]. Furthermore, the *Awakening of Faith* states that they attain a partial vision of the Dharmakāya.

The formulation of the eight similes and so forth all share this meaning. (Regarding this principle of retaining afflictions, compared to the Dharma-characteristics school [Faxiang zong], it adds one *kalpa* of light.

Because these Bodhisattvas fear only the obstruction of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), they cultivate contemplations such as Consciousness-Only and True Suchness (*tathatā*) to suppress and sever that obstruction;

however, regarding the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), they not only do not fear it nor cultivate remedies against it, but rather intentionally retain it to assist in their accomplishment.

Because these are supreme practices, the two obstacles are not divided into those abandoned through seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). [In the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* system,] conceptual afflictions are abandoned through the path of seeing, while innate afflictions are abandoned through the path of cultivation.

However, upon reaching the first stage (*bhūmi*), both types of afflictions are completely exhausted; this is called "the abandonment of all at once. As stated in the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra-śāstra*:
"Within the paths of seeing and cultivation, all afflictions that can obstruct the bodhisattva’s practice for the benefit of sentient beings are eliminated. Thus, it is said:

In the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), all [afflictions] are abandoned simultaneously; within each stage (*bhūmi*), only the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are removed until the stage of Buddhahood, where the habitual tendencies are completely exhausted.

Based on this principle, other explanations regarding the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth—which state that afflictions are abandoned differently according to the stages—all serve to indicate the relative superiority or inferiority of the stages by means of the coarseness or subtlety of the delusions they address.
[The *Chao*] states that it speaks only in terms of abandoning the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*).

It is able to realize that the essence consists solely of words, thereby distinguishing it from the subsequently attained [cognition], because the subsequently attained does not realize the principle.

[The *Chao*] clarifies above and distinguishes below. Question: Since the fundamental severance of delusions has already been explained above, why is it treated again here? Answer: This is for the purpose of such a distinction.

Regarding the phrase "the section on the four wisdoms of the mind" (*catur-jñāna-citta-varga*), the intended meaning is that the four wisdoms are categories associated with consciousness and the mind;

therefore, the treatise states: "This transformation of the categories associated with the eight, seven, six, and five impure (*sāsrava*) consciousnesses results in the attainment of wisdom respectively.

Although wisdom is not itself consciousness, it arises in dependence upon consciousness; since consciousness is primary, it is said that one "attains [wisdom] by transforming consciousness. Furthermore, within the state of impurity, wisdom is inferior.
In the state where consciousness is predominant, wisdom is strong while consciousness is weak; this is taught in order to encourage sentient beings to rely on wisdom and abandon consciousness.
Thus, it is said that by transforming the eight consciousnesses, one attains these four wisdoms.

At the moment of the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), because one first attains Buddhahood, this wisdom first arises and continues uninterruptedly until the end of the future, maintaining the uncontaminated seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*).

In order that [the seeds] may not be lost, the mental state associated with the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) first manifests at the stage of the Bodhisattva’s path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because it opposes the two types of grasping;

only then does it first arise. Because grasping has not yet been severed throughout the subsequent ten stages (*bhūmi*), this [wisdom] may be interrupted during states such as those involving outflows (*sāsrava*).
However, after the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), it continues in succession with the pure eighth consciousness until the end of the future.

The mental states associated with the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) that constitute the category of the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) first arise even during the stage of vision (*darśana-mārga*) of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).

Thereafter, they proceed successively until the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), or until the end of the bodhisattva’s stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), or up to the higher stages.

However, they cannot manifest when there is an outflowing state (*sāsrava*) regarding the emptiness of persons, or during moments of non-consciousness (*acittaka*) following the fruit of wisdom. As for the category of the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), it may manifest at all times.
The Bodhisattva first attains this [wisdom] at the stage of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); thereafter, it continues successively up to the higher stages.
However, it can only manifest when it is not a contaminated dharma, when it is the fruit of the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*), or during states of non-conceptualization (*acittaka*).

The mental complex associated with the wisdom of accomplishing what was to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) first arises upon becoming a Buddha, yet it arises through repeated interrupted acts of attention (*manasikāra*). Thus, although these four types of nature are all...

Although these are inherently present, they must be activated by perfuming (*vāsanā*) before they can manifest. During the stage of a cause (*hetu-bhūmi*), they gradually increase; at the stage of Buddhahood (*buddha-phala*), they are perfected.
They neither increase nor decrease throughout the limits of the future, arising solely from seeds and not being newly formed as seeds through perfuming.

The commentary states that "the distinctions between the essence and characteristics of True Suchness" means that the three virtues and four virtues upon the essence of *nirvāṇa* are all distinct aspects of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) merits within the essence of True Suchness.

Regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) merits subsumed under the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*), there are two senses in which all four are included: first, as the functional activity (*kāritra*) of the wisdoms; [and second, as their inherent nature].

Because they are powerful and because they are manifested by way of the name "wisdom," all aspects of the mind are explained here in terms of two meanings—the actual [nature] and its coarse characteristics—as being subsumed within the four wisdoms.
Regarding the phrase "and their associated categories," this refers to the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth, as these are the categories belonging to those minds and mental factors.
As for the phrase "that which is transformed and attained" in the *Chao* (Commentary), it should be understood accordingly.

Within the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*) of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), there are two parts: first, the cause, which consists of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); second, the fruit, which is the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). The subsequent text is divided into four sections:

first, the path that effects the transformation; second, the basis that is transformed; third, that which is abandoned through the transformation; and fourth, that which is attained through the transformation. Herein, we are currently at the fourth section, within the category of "that which is attained through the transformation. This is further divided into two: first, the path capable of subduing [defilements] at the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrvamgama*);
second, the path capable of abandoning [defilements], which is precisely what was cited in the preceding section. [The latter is as follows:]... (text continues).
This refers to the meaning of "innate" (*upapatti-lābhika*). Regarding the phrase "up to and including," it signifies that one transcends the other [three] and is fully endowed with them;
thus it should be explained as follows. What are the mental states associated with the four wisdoms? First, the mental state associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*):
this mental state is free from all conceptualization; its objects and modes of activity are subtle and difficult to perceive; it is neither forgetful nor deluded regarding any objective phenomena.
The nature and characteristics of this [wisdom] are pure, free from all defilements, and serve as the support for the seeds and manifestations of the perfectly pure, circular virtues.

It can manifest and produce the reflections of bodies, lands, and wisdoms, continuing without interval or interruption until the end of the future, like a great round mirror manifesting various forms and images.
The mental state associated with the second, the Wisdom of Equality, refers to this mental state which contemplates all phenomena.
The third is the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (the wisdom of profound discernment), which is the uncommon basis for the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*, established upon non-abiding *nirvāṇa*.

It is characterized by a single-flavored continuity that extends to the end of the future, being eternally in accord with all sentient beings—both oneself and others—as they are entirely equal, manifesting various distinctions of the images of the bodies and lands according to the inclinations of those beings. This is the third *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*.
The category of associated mental states refers to this category of mind which proceeds unimpededly while skillfully discerning the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena;
it encompasses the meditative concentrations and doors of dhāraṇī that observe immeasurable phenomena, as well as the precious jewels of merit produced by the awakened mind;
it is able to manifest infinite varieties of functional activity within great assemblies, attaining mastery over them all, and raining down the Great Dharma.

The fourth is the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), which corresponds to the mental state that brings all sentient beings benefit and happiness by severing all doubts.

For the sake of benefiting and gladdening sentient beings, this mental state manifests various transformations throughout the ten directions through the three types of action (*trikarma*), thereby fulfilling the deeds required by its original vows and powers. Thus are the four [wisdoms].
Although each of these mental states associated with wisdom (*jñāna*) necessarily comprises twenty-two dharmas— consisting of the five universal (*sarvatraga*),

the five object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*), the eleven wholesome (*kuśala*), and the four types of wisdom (*jñāna*) corresponding to each respective mind-king— because the function of wisdom is predominant, they are designated by the name "wisdom. Consequently,
these four categories collectively encompass all conditioned merits (*saṃskṛta-guṇa*) of the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*) without exception.

▲ The sub-commentary states: "How could that which gives rise to consciousness [be unconditioned]? This refers to the fact that the essence of the eighth *anāsrava* (untainted) consciousness is the basis for arising and ceasing.

Since consciousness gives rise to wisdom (which serves as the dominant condition), why would it not be conditioned? Because it carries untainted seeds as its direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) capable of producing wisdom, wisdom is therefore conditioned.
▲ The sub-commentary states: Regarding the inclusion of the four wisdoms within the three bodies, the treatise says: "This..."
Although the four categories of mind are all capable of universally taking all phenomena as objects, their functions differ:
the category of mirror-like wisdom manifests the marks of the self-enjoyment body and the pure land, while maintaining untainted seeds;

the category of equality wisdom manifests the marks of the other-enjoyment body and the pure land; and the category of wondrous observation wisdom is able to manifest the transformation body and its lands.

The *Commentary on the Hundred Dharmas* states: "The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) subsumes the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*), because it contains and maintains the seeds and directly transforms the sense organs and the body as the universal basis for all forms and minds;
thus, the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) subsumes [the enjoyment body for others]."
The Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya) is designated by name based on its causes: because it manifests the ten aspects of equality by observing the equality of self and others;

because the wisdom of profound observation (pratyavekṣaṇājñāna) can observe the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena; and because it is most excellent in preaching the Dharma and severing doubts in both pure and impure lands.
It encompasses both [the Enjoyment and Emanation] bodies; if categorized by way of the wisdoms, it is subsumed under the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna).
The transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) refers to this very wisdom, which is uniquely capable of fulfilling the vows made in the past for the benefit of others;
because its manifestation as the three types of transformation bodies is preeminent, this commentary mentions only the "self-recompense" [body] and not the other two.
Alternatively, the other two are not the true recompense body, or it mentions the superior to include the inferior.

The Commentary states: Regarding this category of meaning, a question is raised below concerning the previous section on the "Establishment of the Teachings," where it was explained that the Initial Teaching (Śakyadeśanā) contains two aspects:

the negation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the establishment of characteristics. Now, in distinguishing their differences based on what is expressed (*abhidheya*), why is only the establishment of characteristics manifested, while the negation of characteristics is not mentioned?

Answer: This is because the distinction is clarified here based on the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (characteristics of phenomena) taught; since the negation of characteristics does not clarify such distinctions regarding the characteristics of phenomena, it is not mentioned.
Question: In the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*), dharmalakṣaṇa (phenomenal characteristics) are not taught at all; it only elucidates true nature (*tathatā*).
Why, then, does the preceding commentary state, "If one refers to the dharmalakṣaṇa that is taught"? Answer: Because the Sudden Teaching does not teach dharmalakṣaṇa, it differs from other teachings.

Furthermore, the distinction between the teachings is clarified precisely by means of the presence or absence of dharmalakṣaṇa and so forth. Question: Since the Sudden Teaching does not teach dharmalakṣaṇa, why is it still described as being extensive?

If it is asked: "The meaning of not speaking [of the ultimate] is explained as solely distinguishing the true nature and refuting characteristics; why is this not the case for the Initial Teaching? The answer is: It is understood by inference here.

Specifically, in the Sudden Teaching, one distinguishes the true nature; whereas in the refutation of characteristics, one reveals only emptiness. This is extensively detailed in ten gates in the *Commentary on the Essentials of the Complete Enlightenment Sutra* (*Yuánjué shūchāo*).

Regarding the statement that "the *Shu* (Commentary) expounds the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*) sparingly," the *Tanxuan ji* states: "It does not discuss the numerical categories of the hundred dharmas, nor is it like the Hīnayāna;
furthermore, because it lacks many gates of analytical discrimination, it is said to 'expound the characteristics of phenomena sparingly.

Since all dharmas are established through the True Suchness (*tathatā*) following conditions, it is said to 'expound the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) extensively. The characteristics of phenomena as taught here have no separate intrinsic nature."
All of these manifest the intent of the Dharma-nature (dharmatā) school because they reveal the nature; thus it is called the "Nature School. The *Guangshu Chao* states:

"However, regarding the doctrinal meanings expounded by the Dharma-characteristics (dharmalakṣaṇa) teachings of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, the derivative is extensive while the fundamental is concise.

For instance, works such as the *Abhidharmakośa* explain the phenomena of karma arising and retribution, and the characteristics of the three realms, the six destinies, and the primary and secondary elements, in great detail. In contrast, works such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* [expound] the two types of grasping within the six consciousnesses."
The hindrances are also extensive, whereas the fundamental basis of the eight consciousnesses and the three subtleties is concise;
thus, the meanings of the two types of awakening (original and initial), the three greatnesses, the gate of suchness, and even the source of the single true mind are not analyzed at all.

If one were to follow works such as the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, these would be established as separate chapters to extensively debate the meanings of the six coarse hindrances and attachments, while all else would be explained only briefly.
In the establishment of the teachings and the reception of their fruits, only the names are listed; from this, four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be established:

first, the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-naya*), which is fundamental and extensive while being derivative and concise; second, the Small Teaching (*hīna-naya*) and the Teaching of Establishing Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vyavasthāpana-ādikā-naya*), which are derivative and extensive while being fundamental and concise;

third, the Sudden Teaching (*tadaṅga-naya*), which is neither fundamental nor derivative; and fourth, the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-naya*), which is both entirely fundamental and entirely derivative.
Regarding the statement "such as the five aggregates," this has already been extensively refuted in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras*, such as the *Heart Sūtra*; how much more so in the larger versions?
The phrase "etcetera" in the subsequent section of the *Commentary* refers to the text from the "Chapter on the Praise of Verses by Yama.
Its sub-commentary states: "The aggregates are the world of dependent origination; their cessation is the supramundane. These two are spoken of as one essence."
Therefore, it is said that in the "Chapter on the Non-duality of Conventional and Ultimate Names," the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa states:
"The mundane and the supramundane constitute two worlds. That their nature is empty is itself the supramundane.

Within this, there is no entering and no exiting, no overflowing and no dispersing; this is what is called 'entering the gate of non-dual dharmas. Furthermore, the *Commentary* states: "There is contention..."
The text for the "Verse Praise" chapter at the end of the *Xuǎnmí* (Selection from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*) is as previously explained in the section on the "Interpenetration of Reality and Falsehood.

Here, the meaning is that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are entirely dependent on conditions; they are both termed "dharmalakṣaṇa" (phenomenal characteristics) and are both ungraspable, because they are identical to the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature).
The *Chāo* (Excerpts) states: "As for the mention of 'mind' and so forth, this refers to what is taught in the *Ratnagotravibhāga* (*Jìnxīnlùn*), which relies upon the *tathāgatagarbha*."
Therefore, regarding the statement that the mind has arising and ceasing, the *Treatise* says: "The essence of the mind is free from thought.

As for the characteristic of being free from thought, it is equal to the realm of empty space and is omnipresent; the single characteristic of the Dharma-realm is precisely the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body.
The commentary on this states: "To manifest that it is identical to the nature, it is free from deluded thoughts; to manifest that there is nothing [it does not encompass]..."
To realize that the dharma-realm has a single characteristic means that whether it is within the bonds of affliction or beyond them, it is eternally non-dual.

The *Chao* (Commentary) states that the passage beginning with "the Flower Treasury World" refers to the text of the "Flower Treasury" chapter; its sub-commentary says: "The first phrase indicates the name, while the subsequent phrases show that the dimensions are not destroyed, being identical to true nature.
However, all the passages from this very sutra cited above belong to the Perfect Teaching within the Middle [Teaching], which is identical to the Real Teaching.

The meaning of "one part" refers to the fact that the other texts cited therein precisely belong to the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao), because the identity between the subject and the object of comparison is not fixed;
for this reason, both sets of texts are cited. Furthermore, the *Guiyang Yuanjue Chao* states:
"Therefore, in the *Wuzheng lun*, as well as in the three treatises—the *Qixin lun*, the *Zhidu lun*, and the *Baoping lun*—there are no conflicting disputes among various masters."

This is the general principle for citing texts under the Dharma-nature school (Faxing zong). Regarding the "meaning within the same teaching" (*tongjiao*), it refers to the fact that the scriptures of this teaching are identical to those of the Sudden and Real teachings;

thus, because this concerns the meaning of being identical to the Real, citations from the original text will appear below in the section on the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*lishi wuai*).
In contrast, the citations from other texts appearing here within the Final Teaching (*zhongjiao*) serve as explanations based on external sources. — *The Commentary* (*Chao*) states: "Therefore..."

The first chapter of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states that what follows is as explained in the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda śāstra*: ignorance acts as the cause to produce the three subtle states (*tri-sūkṣma-vastu*), while objective conditions act as the缘 (*pratyaya*) to develop the six coarse states (*ṣaḍ-audārika*).
In this scripture, the latter meaning corresponds to the former verse, which uses a metaphor to clarify it, and the subsequent verse, which provides the doctrinal application (*dharma-yoga*).

A vast ocean is used as a metaphor for the ocean of the eternally abiding consciousness (*sthita-vijñāna-samudra*), and a violent wind is used as a metaphor for objective conditions (*viṣaya-pratyaya*), while the waves represent the [evolving] consciousnesses.
The preceding seven evolving consciousnesses serve as an analogy; here, the "mind" (*manas*) is cited to indicate that the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is itself eternally abiding.
This serves as a manifest proof that the eighth consciousness pervades the Tathāgata-garbha, for it is not merely subject to arising and ceasing, given the mention of its eternal abiding.
Regarding the phrase "the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna and other texts," the *Ben-shu* (Original Commentary) states: "That which is neither born nor extinguished is the pure Tathāgata-garbha."
The mind moves due to the wind of ignorance; because the three subtle states and the eighth consciousness arise and perish inseparably, they are said to be "in union.
This does not mean that there is a separate arising and perishing that comes to unite with True Suchness (tathatā).

Rather, it means that the mind of arising and perishing and the arising and perishing of the mind are non-dual in aspect; thus, True Suchness in its entirety moves. Therefore, the mind and arising and perishing are not [separate].
Because its true nature is eternally unchanging despite these differences, it is not identical to that which arises and perishes;
thus, within the eighth consciousness, movement and stillness are already contained (the three subtleties are the three divisions within the eighth consciousness).

Furthermore, according to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the defiled dharmas of the seven consciousnesses constitute arising and perishing, while the pure dharma of the Tathāgatagarbha constitutes non-arising and non-perishing; the union of these two constitutes the ālayavijñāna.

"Consciousness, because it is a composite, is neither one nor different," and so forth. As for the extensive discussion in the *Yao* (Commentary) that analyzes this according to the "Chapter on the Elucidation of Questions," these points are scattered throughout the preceding and following passages of this chapter.
The phrase "the commentary explains at length as previously stated" refers to the ten preceding sections where various sutras and treatises were cited.
However, according to the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, because one eliminates the five defects and gives rise to the five virtues, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
First, because those of inferior mind do not give rise to the bodhicitta, one knows that by possessing Buddha-nature, one is able to initiate right diligence.
First, because of the mind of pride: one thinks, "I possess the Buddha-nature while others do not.

By knowing that all possess the Buddha-nature, one can give rise to a heart of reverence and admiration. Second, because of the false arising of the two attachments: one is deluded regarding the two emptinesses.

By knowing that there is Buddha-nature, one can give rise to true *prajñā*. Third, because of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), one falsely perceives the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). By knowing that there is Buddha-nature, [one realizes it].
Because the conventional wisdom produced by this capacity reveals the wisdom that perceives reality;

fifth, because sentient beings harbor false views of self and perceive "self" and "other," one knows that the Buddha-nature exists, which gives rise to great compassion, and so forth, until it is said that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature;
therefore, one transforms them solely through the Single Buddha Vehicle.
Regarding the citation from the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, it refers to the fourth fascicle. The full text states:
"O Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome; it is capable of universally producing all realms of existence and births," and so on, up to:
"When it is perfumed by beginningless evil habits, it is called the Ālayavijñāna. The commentary on the "Chapter on Questions" explains that the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is beginningless.
The eighth *ālayavijñāna* is formed by the perfuming of the fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) and false, evil habitual tendencies. The *Yao* (Commentary) further states:
"Regarding the *tathāgatagarbha*, the fourth sutra [in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*] says in full: 'O Mahāmati, the seven consciousnesses do not undergo transmigration;

they do not experience suffering or pleasure, nor are they the cause of *nirvāṇa*. O Mahāmati, the *tathāgatagarbha* experiences suffering and pleasure, and is accompanied by their causes; if it were to arise...'"

The *Excerpts from the Chapter on the Ten Endurances* states: "The seven consciousnesses arise and perish moment by moment; they are impermanent, vanishing as soon as they arise, like the turning of a river.
Since their own substance is not established, they do not experience suffering or pleasure.
Being neither the basis for defilement nor the basis for untainted nirvana, the Tathāgatagarbha—which is truly eternal and all-pervading—resides within the delusion of the six realms."

This [Tathāgatagarbha], which is able to conform to conditions to produce phenomena and experience the fruits of suffering and pleasure, is called "concomitant with causes" because it arises together with the seven consciousnesses and does not maintain its own intrinsic nature.
Thus, the seven consciousnesses depend upon this [Tathāgatagarbha] to undergo arising and ceasing;

whether they arise or cease, this clarifies that the Tathāgatagarbha is itself True Suchness (tathatā) conforming to conditions to experience suffering, pleasure, and so forth. — *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* (Qixinlun chao).
It is also said [in the *Subcommentary*]: "The True [Suchness] follows along with the delusion. This means that the pure mind cannot move by itself;
it must be moved by the wind of ignorance. The *Commentary* states:

"However, the intent of the *Subcommentary* clarifies that sentient beings are merely the True Suchness established through following conditions. Therefore, all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature," thus completing the argument.
Regarding the meaning of "one nature" (ekasvabhāva): The *Chao* [commentary] addresses this by refuting false interpretations of the preceding "Initial Teaching" (shijiao).

This is because within the Dharma-character (Faxiang) school and the Dharma-nature (Faxing) school, there is only the principle of "conforming to conditions" (suoyuan) and no principle of "unchanging" (bubian); therefore, this [section] serves as a refutation. The question regarding the teaching and its meaning asks:
"If True Suchness (tathatā) is called a permanent dharma (nityadharma), how can it be said to arise and cease in accordance with perfuming (xun)? How, furthermore, can it be so described?"

Regarding the statement that True Suchness (tathatā) is "quiescent and constant," since it is said to be "constant" as True Suchness, this constancy is certainly not the kind of constancy that corresponds to ordinary linguistic expression.

Why is this? When the Sage describes True Suchness as "quiescent and constant," it is because when it functions in accordance with conditions to produce all phenomena, it does not lose its own essence;
therefore, it is called "constant. This is the constancy of non-differentiation, termed the "inconceivable constancy," and does not mean that it does not act.
The "suchness" (tathatā) of all phenomena is what is called "immutable"; it is because it is free from all emotional attachments that the Sūtra says it is "difficult to comprehend.

In the *Commentary* (*Chao*), the section beginning with "By virtue of non-change... provides a brief explanation, while the section beginning with "For what reason... provides an extensive explanation.

This means that even up to the point of True Suchness (bhūtatathatā) following conditions, it is precisely because of its non-change that it is able to follow conditions. If [it were not so]... up to the point of... what?
The explanation of "accomplishing the unchanging" is that it is precisely by following conditions that one is able to remain unchanging. This is because the following section provides a summary;
thus, the citation from the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* below can be understood as providing scriptural proof. Question: When the True [Nature] follows conditions, is it moving or unmoving?

If it were moving, it would have to be a substantial entity and would consequently possess a location; yet the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states that permanent dharmas do not abide in any place. Furthermore, the *Awakening of Faith*...
The Sūtra says, "The shore is truly not moving," and so forth. If [the nature] is unmoving yet does not contradict other conditions, it is therefore called "following conditions" (*anuparivartin*).

If this were the case, it would be like empty space, which is inert and solid, unable to transform in accordance with conditions. How then could metaphors such as seawater or the nature of gold be similar?
Answer: "Moving" and "unmoving" are like two ends of the same coin. Even if one posits both meanings simultaneously, one cannot avoid their mutual contradiction.
If one contradicts [the teaching], or if both sides are neither [correct], how can one escape conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*)? Question: Ultimately, how is this so? Answer:

Because the truth of *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature) is not an object for ordinary minds, the ultimate profundity transcends the reach of names and words. Furthermore, if one perceives differences [within it], one falls into an infinite regress.
Thus, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "The deluded and floating mind abounds in various clever views; it cannot bring about the realization of perfect enlightenment."

Regarding the *Fangbian* (Expedient Means) commentary on the emptiness and existence of the three natures: both the dependent (*paratantra*) and the imagined (*parikalpita*) are empty; it is not merely that the imagined is empty.

Regarding the statement that "emptiness" refers specifically to the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*), one asks: in the Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) school, True Suchness (*tathatā*) is free from both existence and non-existence.

Question: What is this emptiness that is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*)? Answer: This dependent nature (*paratantra*), being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), is itself the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Since the phenomenon (*vastu*) is identical to the principle (*tattva*), it constitutes an unimpeded principle; there is no second essence.

Therefore, as they are mutually integrated, they do not differ from the emptiness of that which arises dependently (*pratītyasamutpanna*); it is not a nihilistic emptiness (*uccheda-śūnyatā*). [From the *Yiji*: Herein, "absence of nature" refers to the absence of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).*]

In the *Bie shi* (Separate Commentary), the two characters "wu xing" (absence of nature) are explained as follows: that which is "able to be non-existent" (*neng wu*) refers to the meaning of emptiness in the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*);

that which is "non-existent" (*suo wu*) refers to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Because the imagined nature exists upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the dependent nature is not empty;

however, since the imagined nature is absent from the dependent nature here, the dependent nature itself is empty. This is not the same as the Dharma-characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) school, which holds that only the imagined nature is empty.
"Emptiness also depends on the other-dependent nature. Regarding the phrase "in the Faxing school" in the *Chao*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"In the Abhidharma-sūtra, the Blessed One taught that there are three aspects of phenomena: first, the defiled aspect; second, the pure aspect; and third, the both-defiled-and-pure aspect.
Based on what meaning are these three aspects taught? They are distinguished within the other-dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)."
The *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) constitutes the defiled portion; the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) constitutes the pure portion;
and the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) constitutes both the defiled and pure portions. Based on this meaning, the *Tri-svabhāva-nirdeśa-śāstra* states:
"In the *Abhidharma-sūtra*, it is taught that the *parikalpita-svabhāva* has afflictions as its nature, while the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* has the pure portion as its nature."
Because the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) possesses two aspects and takes the two natures (*svabhāva*) as its essence, it is taught that there are three types of phenomena:
first, the aspect of affliction; second, the aspect of purification; and third, the aspect of both phenomena. It is based on this meaning that this statement was made.
Master Xianshou’s commentary states: "The preceding text of the treatise clarifies that the truth encompasses the delusions of the branches, leaving nothing unaccounted for."

When truth and falsehood thoroughly penetrate the true source, the essence is entirely quiescent; when truth and falsehood mutually interpenetrate, the two divisions are fused as one. (From the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-vyākhyā*, citing the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra*):

"Both name and appearance are discarded" serves as proof that both the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
