*Commentary:* Now, beginning with "Because wisdom is itself luminous emptiness," the text addresses the objection and re-explains the aforementioned Buddha-nature.
The name "emptiness of the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) refers to the wisdom that realizes emptiness;

this explains that what was previously termed the "emptiness of the ultimate truth" is in fact wisdom, which is the eternally constant nature of gnosis. Below, it explains that the Buddha-nature is eternally constant and undergoes no change.

Regarding the two passages concerning "emptiness" and so forth in the *Chao* (Commentary): these refer to the earlier citation by the ancient masters stating, "How is the Buddha-nature empty? and so on. This is the first [point].
In the passage below it says, "All dharmas are equal in one place.

Now, upon examination, this actually serves as proof for the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha* as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), because the Sūtra states, "according to the place of their cessation," and so forth; thus it is called the "emptiness-store" (*śūnyatā-garbha*).
As for the question, "How is it not non-empty?"—this follows immediately from what was cited previously: "How is it not non-empty? Because it is eternal. How...
Because that which is neither empty nor non-empty can serve as the seed for wholesome dharmas, it is precisely this realization that is designated as wisdom;

this refers to the meaning of the "Non-Empty Treasury. It is said that when the wisdom of emptiness and [the wisdom of existence] are both possessed together below, they constitute the true meaning of Buddha-nature.
Thus, one knows that what follows clarifies how these two meanings are mutually requisite.

The Commentary further states that regarding "emptiness of the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), the preceding and following sections explain this through the two truths of emptiness and existence, establishing that the two *piṭakas* are not mutually exclusive and that emptiness and wisdom are mutually constitutive. Here, it is explained again by means of the three truths;

since the preceding discourse on the ultimate truth addressed both emptiness and existence, the former clarified that the ultimate truth is itself emptiness, whereas this [section] clarifies the [nature of] the ultimate truth...
Since emptiness is the ultimate truth that penetrates both emptiness and existence, the wisdom of emptiness and its characteristic are fused into non-duality.
The statement "the initial word is precisely the emptiness of the ultimate truth" serves as a scriptural citation;
specifically, it refers to the two passages from the *Jianfu* [Sutra] cited previously, wherein the first passage states: "All phenomena are merely provisional and follow their own cessation."
"Since it is stated that 'the locus is the emptiness of the ultimate meaning' (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), this reveals that the ultimate meaning is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
That which is provisionally false and quiescent is emptiness; thus, it establishes the emptiness discussed above within the context of the ultimate truth.
Furthermore, the *Commentary* (*Chao*) states: "To see all as empty, yet not to see [anything] non-existent..."
Regarding the passage from "emptiness" up to "is called the Buddha-nature," the commentary on this section of the sutra by Jianfu explains:
"Because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas contemplate both the ultimate and conventional truths simultaneously, illuminating both existence and non-existence equally, it is called the Middle Way.

For this reason, Qingliang cites the sutra to challenge Jianfu’s interpretation. The phrase "above, he cites the sutra" refers to the passage "if that were so, they would see both [truths] together," while the following portion constitutes the formal refutation.
Because the middle [section] presents a challenge, we know that the following section extends the present correct principle, as can be understood from above.

Much of what has been clarified thus far is explained by way of common meaning (*sāmānyārtha*), for the purpose of reconciling those [points]. If one links it with the preceding section, because there is but a single nature (*ekasvabhāva*), the establishment of one brings about the establishment of all;
this is precisely the reconciliation whereby the universal enters into the particular.
Regarding the phrase "The Commentary further states 'appears,' etc.," the Commentary says: "First, it clarifies that there is not a single sentient being who does not possess [this nature];
thus one knows that those without nature are not counted among sentient beings, such as grasses and trees. This surpasses the view of the five natures. This is precisely what is gathered:

that the two types of sentient beings possess the cause of being enmeshed in bondage and already possess the fruit of being free from bondage; therefore, it is said that they "possess the Tathāgata’s wisdom. It is not [that they do not possess it].

It is also illogical that there is only the nature [of Buddhahood] which must later be realized. If wisdom comes first and subsequent knowledge follows, then since Nirvana is contrasted with former expedient means, it is already said that there is "nature" and later one studies;
yet even this is still called "speaking of existence while concealing non-existence. How much more so when hearing of the "wisdom of the fruit"—who would believe it?
This refers to the specific meaning within the general category. Third, the wisdom of the fruit within those causes is precisely the [wisdom] of other Buddhas.

Regarding the statement that "the fruit-wisdom [is established] because, according to the school of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), the causes and effects of self and others are non-dual in essence," this principle does not exist outside of the Huayan [school];

the phrase "there is nothing that does not exist" below is the wording of the commentary (*shu*), which explains that because of the single nature (*ekadhātu*), the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is established.
The commentary states, "By means of various dependent originations," etc., because since all phenomena arise only by depending on conditions, it is clarified that they all lack intrinsic nature;

thus, the fact that what arises from conditions lacks intrinsic nature establishes the subsequent point that what lacks intrinsic nature arises from conditions. As for the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* and other texts, they merely serve as proof for the principle that what lacks intrinsic nature arises from conditions, which is precisely the meaning being employed here.
Furthermore, following the section on the "True Mind," the text proceeds separately to discuss the "True Nature."
"Solid, real, numinous, and luminous" refers to the mind (*citta*), used here to urge the deluded mind toward awakening.

The *Commentary* states that "the non-arising and non-ceasing [nature] and the arising and ceasing [nature] are in union," which is already explained in the section on the establishment of the teaching and the opening of the school within the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*, specifically under the exposition of the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*). The phrase "that is, possessing both parts" is the wording of the *Commentary* explaining this point in full.
This is a compound ideograph (*huiyi*). The *Yichao* states: "The following section enumerates divergent interpretations to distinguish the term 'partially complete' (*jufen*).

Here, the union of truth and falsehood is taken as 'partially complete,' which differs from the Abhidharma definition where the union of the substance and its reflection constitutes 'partially complete.
Regarding this Abhidharma meaning of substance and reflection, if one consults the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, it is said that within the Hīnayāna schools, the Saṃmitīya..."
The other nineteen schools maintain that because the self-characteristics are like reflections in a mirror, they are designated as "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*);

however, since the objective essence (*bimba*) exists outside of consciousness and is not designated as consciousness-only—because it is not fully grasped—they refer to this as the "Half-Portion Mahāyāna.

If both the reflection and the essence are transformations of the mind and are thus collectively termed "consciousness-only," then it is called the "Full-Portion. This is as stated in the *Ji xuán* (Compendium of Mysteries) and elsewhere.

The *Zuǎn xuán* states: "Shadow" refers to the objective images (*xiàng-fēn*) manifested by the preceding seven consciousnesses; because they are like shadows appearing upon a clear mirror, they are empty and unreal, and are thus called "shadows.
"Substance" refers to the eighth consciousness’s objective image (*xiàng-fēn*) and subjective aspect (*jiàn-fēn*);

that is to say, the first six consciousnesses rely upon the objective image manifested by the eighth consciousness as their "substance," while subsequently transforming their own distinct objective images.

The seventh consciousness likewise relies upon the perceived aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) transformed by the eighth consciousness as its substantial basis (*ālambana-svabhāva*), and it also separately transforms its own objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*);
this is a reflection. Thus, the objective aspects transformed by the seven consciousnesses each arise from what is transformed by their respective consciousnesses;
they are called "consciousness-only" because the substance [of the aspect] does not exist outside the transformation of the seven [consciousnesses], but is half [within them].

The term "not-only-consciousness" (na-vijñapti-mātra) is called "half-headed vijñapti-mātra. When the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) transformed by the eighth consciousness is viewed in relation to the first seven consciousnesses, it serves as their "original substance" (*bimba*).
However, when viewed in relation to the eighth consciousness itself at the moment it is simultaneously perceived and transformed, it is also called an "image" (*pratibimba*).
Because both this substance and its image are transformations of the same eighth consciousness, they are both designated as "images"; thus, it is said that "substance and image are together."
Because the objective essence (*bhāva*) is not external to the reflection, it is said that [consciousness] possesses both the quiescent and the illuminating aspects.

Furthermore, it is said that the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) transformed by the eighth consciousness, when compared to its own *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-verifying aspect), is also called a "reflection. Therefore, both the objective essence and the reflection are termed "reflections" because they constitute the complete [system of] Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Thus far, this has been entirely according to the "complete aspect" (*sakalāṃśa*) of the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school; hence, it is not [the case here].
It is the same in this case as well.

Regarding the "Verses on the Forest of Enlightenment" (*Jue lin ji*), the *Commentary* (*Shu*) states: "The illumination of the mind from its beginning to its end is called the 'Forest of Enlightenment'.

As for the statement that there was first a metaphor, this refers to the verse cited in the *Commentary* which is the very first verse providing this general metaphor. That *Commentary* says: "First..."

The first phrase is a general metaphor for the one mind; the next phrase is a metaphor for the transformation through the influence of conditions (*pratyaya*) to become the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);

the following phrase is that because one does not understand the dependent nature, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is established; and the final phrase is a metaphor for the exhaustion of the characteristics of the dependent nature, wherein its essence is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Regarding the statement that the first phrase corresponds to the analogy "just as a skilled painter," the commentary on that text states: "The first phrase refers to the mind in its general aspect."
"Containing both the true and the delusive, with subject and object—these worldly realms are precisely these various colors. This phrase serves as a general heading;

the following passage enumerates the various characteristics, which are the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas). Therefore, it says, "there is no phenomenon that is not created.

Next, the citation of scriptural evidence also states, "one should likewise distribute the various colors. The commentary on that passage says: "It is like how, in the world, the five aggregates arise from the mind."
The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) created by the Buddhas are likewise; as they are, so too are those of all other sentient beings. All are created from the mind.
Since the mind is the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), its awakening is called Buddhahood, forming pure dependent origination (*viśuddha-pratītyasamutpāda*);

its delusion produces sentient beings, forming defiled dependent origination (*kliṣṭa-pratītyasamutpāda*). Although dependent origination possesses both the defiled and the pure, the arising of the mind is no different. Yet, regarding the fruit of Buddhahood...
The mind accords with reality because it is coextensive with the True; since deluded phenomena have limits, they are not mentioned.

If the Jin translation says, "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction," one should rather say, "The essence-nature of mind, Buddha, and sentient beings is all inexhaustible.
Because the substance of delusion is fundamentally True, it is likewise inexhaustible; therefore, the Tathāgata does not sever the nature.

Evil is likewise like the icchantika’s failure to sever their inherent goodness. If we speak of the mind from the perspective of a single person, it is the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*):

the Buddha is original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*), while sentient beings are non-enlightenment (*anavabodha*). Thus, original enlightenment follows conditions to give rise to these two states; this is the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*).

One should know that the Buddha and the mind are equal, and that the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of these two is inexhaustible; this is the gate of true suchness (*tathatā-mukha*) following conditions.
Because they do not lose their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this correctly accords with the preceding passage concerning the lack of differentiation among the great elements (*mahābhūta*).

If one were to claim that there is any difference between the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings, this would constitute a false grasping at the differentiation of forms (*rūpa*). Based on this, it corresponds to the second half [of the verse].

Now, the *Jiaochao* states that "it also corresponds to the distribution of various colors," which still completes the preceding term "various" (*zhū*); therefore, it corresponds to the "distribution."
The various colors are laid out, and furthermore, the exegesis on the meaning is presented; thus, the statements are all as explained below.
In the commentary on the passage "The nature of mind is one," that commentary asks: "Since the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*) is one, how can there be [distinctions]?"
Because the various faculties (*indriya*) of the five destinies differ in their collective and individual retributions, they are said to be "various and not the same.

The phrase "the difficulty regarding the contradiction between conditions and nature" is a gloss from the *Śāstra* (commentary). Regarding Bodhiruci’s response, the aforementioned *Śāstra-ṭīkā* states:

"The first phrase refers to the preceding point that the nature of the mind is one, which is the meaning of being unchanging; the second phrase answers the preceding question: 'How is it that there are various differences seen?'"
This refers to the meaning of "following conditions," which is the manifestation through the transformation of mind alone.

It fully embraces true nature (*dharmatā*), for apart from the *tathāgatagarbha*, there is no substantial entity that could serve as the subject or object of perfuming to produce what is not truly produced; thus it is called a "manifestation. Since it embraces true nature to give rise to birth, the characteristic of birth is itself empty;
therefore, it is called "manifesting birth. To say that this is the True Suchness following conditions is also an explanation of the term provided by the Commentary (*ṭīkā*). Furthermore:
The sub-commentary on that passage states: "As for the phrase 'all phenomena' (*dharmas*), it generally encompasses all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

The fruit arises from the cause, yet the fruit has no self-nature (*svabhāva*); the cause is established by means of the fruit, yet the cause has no substantial essence. Since the cause lacks substantial essence, how can it have the function of producing a fruit?
Since the fruit lacks substantial essence, how could it have the capacity to repay the cause? Furthermore, because they depend upon one another, they lack independent power."

Furthermore, because it takes the other as itself, it lacks intrinsic substance. The statement "it clarifies that following conditions does not lose [its nature]" is also a commentary on Master Kumārajīva’s words.
The *Chao* (Commentary) states: "Conditions arising from the True [Suchness]" means that the conditions capable of producing all phenomena all arise from the True [Suchness]; therefore, everything...
"All phenomena are established based on principle. Regarding this term "based upon," it is like waves being based upon water; this is explained below in relation to the *tathāgatagarbha*.
The following section, the "Chapter on the Clarification of Questions" (*Prasannapadā*), further elaborates on the meaning briefly clarified above.

The commentary clarifies that it is not only because there is no *parikalpita* (imagined nature) [that this is so], which serves to distinguish it from the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school (Faxiang). This distinction has two meanings:

first, that school holds the *parikalpita* to be empty while the *paratantra* (dependent nature) is not empty; second, that in their school, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are not mutually identical.

Regarding the verse by Bodhisattva Balavan-vana (鈔力林菩薩), that commentary states: "Because wisdom realizes the nature and characteristics of the three kinds of worlds and is unmoved by any extremes, it is called 'Power Forest' (Balavan-vana).
Regarding the continuous sequence of the three verses, that commentary states: "The first two lines inquire into the name and essence of the aggregates (*skandha*);
since the world has the aggregates as its essence, what is the essence of the aggregates? The next two lines provide the answer to the above."

The substance of the answer in the first line is "unborn" (*anutpāda*); the name in the subsequent line should be called "the five aggregates of the unborn. The following verse explains that because they are empty, they do not perish; nor is there any entity that does not perish.

That which does not perish is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) of the defiled portion; its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is precisely the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Thus, one knows that it is fundamentally unborn from the beginning—this is the meaning of "unborn. The subsequent verse illustrates this by way of analogy with the supramundane, manifesting correct wisdom.

One realizes that the world (*loka*) likewise lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) through conditions; the pure aspect of the *nirmāṇakāya* (the dependent nature) is itself the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*).
Now, there are two senses of "world": first, in terms of phenomena, that which precedes the stages (*bhūmi*) is the world, while entering the stages is the supramundane (*lokottara*);

second, in terms of characteristics and names, it is called the world, whereas in terms of essence, it is called supramundane. Here, the latter sense is intended. Furthermore, this is realized as being without [intrinsic nature].
Because the principle of nature (*dhātu*) constitutes its own essence, the True Body (*dharmakāya*) is without nature. (This explains "lack of nature" with reference to the True Body.

Regarding the phrase "it is like the endurance of an echo," that commentary states: according to the Jin translation and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, the analogy of the single valley represents the Tathāgatagarbha as the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*);
the two sounds represent ignorance and habitual tendencies—these two are the conditions.
The analogy of an echo relies upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); that which arises from it—namely, all phenomena (*dharma*)—exists in four ways but is not real.

This demonstrates the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). Since the dependent nature is itself the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), it is said that it does not contradict the *dharmatā*.

The five types of delusion of the small [vehicle] claim that there is a thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); yet, since this too does not contradict the *dharmatā*, the thoroughly imagined...
"Calculation" (*kalpanā*) is also precisely the "perfectly accomplished nature" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Regarding the phrase "that is, supreme wisdom," the aforementioned commentary states:

"Because one understands the Buddha’s supreme wisdom and follows the purity of the empty mind, it is so named. Now, having understood the "causal condition for realization" (*upalabdhi-hetu*), one overturns external grasping;
that is, to realize that all phenomena are the very nature of the mind, and that this nature is itself no-nature. This explains the two phrases within the commentary. One has understood them.

All phenomena are the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). That which is the very nature of the mind itself, being devoid of any [intrinsic] existence, is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Regarding the second half [of the verse], the sub-commentary states: "When deluded attachment is destroyed and principle manifests, one sees Śāntamukha (the Buddha of Peace);

this accords with the Dharma-nature, wherein there is neither internal nor external. Furthermore, once deluded attachment—the parikalpita (imagined) nature—is destroyed, true reality manifests, thereby causing that which is grasped through conceptualization to be [realized as non-existent].
The term "pariniṣpanna" (perfected nature) refers to the true dharmakāya of Vairocana. Prior to this, there is a verse, the commentary on which states:
"Because one grasps the characteristics of the internal aggregates and does not understand the nature of the aggregates, one does not see the Buddha.

If one takes them as an object of cognition, that is the paratantra; if one clings to them, that is the parikalpita. Not understanding the nature of the aggregates means not understanding the pariniṣpanna; thus, these are the three natures."
The fault of not immediately [realizing this] is likewise due to being a deluded follower of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), and is thus called "ignorance.
Its profound intent is briefly explained below as above.

Regarding the passage in the *Chao* (Commentary) beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, even if... the aforementioned *Shu* (Sub-commentary) states: "This clarifies that marks have neither increase nor decrease; first, it raises a metaphorical question."
The answer uses the metaphor of manifesting transformations without form to establish that there is no difference between the "no" and the "not";

it uses the metaphor of many minds transforming to illustrate the cultivation of numerous causes, and the metaphor of many Buddhas being manifested through transformation to illustrate the realization of numerous fruits. Finally, Samantabhadra’s subsequent praise of the "good" serves as the conclusion.
The Sub-commentary (*Chao*) states: "Although there are slight differences in wording, the meaning of the text is largely the same. That sutra says: "Śāriputra, what is called a great peril is this:
grasping at the increase of sentient beings with stubborn attachment and false clinging; grasping at the decrease of sentient beings with stubborn attachment and false clinging;
and all foolish ordinary people who do not know the single dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu*) as it truly is, thereby falling into the various evil destinies in future lives."

Therefore, because one cannot truly perceive the single dharma-realm (ekadharmadhātu), one gives rise to a mind of false views, asserting that the realm of sentient beings increases or the realm of sentient beings decreases.
Regarding the phrase "in the midst of following conditions" in the *Chao*: previously, establishing phenomena based on principle was precisely the meaning of "following conditions"; now...

When phenomena (the particular) are contrasted with principle (the universal), they are able to obscure the true principle; yet because phenomena also possess the quality of following conditions (*pratyaya*), they are termed "distinct" in meaning.
Because phenomena are established by following conditions, this refers back to the previous statement that these phenomena pervade the true principle. The *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* states:
"Thus, when these phenomena conflict with principle, they cause the phenomena to manifest while the principle remains unmanifest. The *Xuanjing* says: "Since..."
Because it contradicts principle, it is "hidden" (*yin*). An earlier version reads, "Since it encompasses principle," yet it omits the character for "contradiction" (*wei*).
Here, the characters "pervasive" (*bian*) and "encompassing" (*zha*) are synonymous; because this refers to a mutual opposition, it is termed "contradiction.
Thus, while the phenomenon is manifest, it is hidden within true reality (*zhentili*).
The *Shu* (Commentary) states that according to the *Dharmakāya-anutpādānirodha-sūtra*, the Dharmakāya follows conditions and is called "sentient beings.
Although the Dharmakāya and sentient beings share the same meaning, they differ in name; from the very beginning, it has never moved or been still, nor has it been hidden or manifest.

Because the names differ, there is a mutual appearance of hiding and manifesting. Regarding the *Wenming-pin* (Chapter on Questioning and Clarifying), the sub-commentary (*Shuchao*) says: "Based on..."
Discourse causes one to investigate names and so forth, leading to entry into contemplation as it truly is;

that is, to realize that names and their referents are merely mental verbal discrimination (*manojalpa-vikalpa*) and that there are no separate names and so forth. For what reason? Because "mental" refers to the discrimination of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which is precisely what is meant by "verbal expression.
Since verbal expression is merely the discrimination of the mind, the referent of the name likewise has no separate essence. Therefore, it is called "discourse."
Since the simultaneous application of names and meanings follows conceptual discrimination, the mind flows toward false imaginings of external objects;

these are all merely worldly discourse (*lokavāda*) and have not yet realized that the mind alone abides in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). (Having previously explained this in accordance with the Sūtra, it is now shown by way of contrast:
If one can thus awaken to oneself and penetrate through to the point of no longer accepting external objects, this is not worldly discourse; it is the skillful means for entering Vijñaptimātratā.
That is to say, when this very mind has no characteristics to be grasped and delusive thoughts do not arise, one immediately enters the *dharmatā*.

From a higher perspective, although the mind deviates from its essence, it is not that they are not identical; yet, "not entering" occurs because the essence of delusive thought is empty and there is nothing into which to enter. The commentary states:

"Now, based on the fact that phenomena can obscure principle, this precisely refers to the meaning of the mind deviating [from its essence]. The *Chao* (the *Yuanjuejing dashu yanyi chao*) says: "The phrase 'the essence is empty' also simultaneously reveals [this point]."
This is because it has a distinct meaning.
The commentary states, "Because this is the principle of dharma-nairātmya (the selflessness of phenomena)," thereby providing the reason.

If it were merely emptiness existing outside of phenomena, it would not be identical to those phenomena; yet, how could there be any principle that exists apart from phenomena, since it is precisely these phenomena themselves that constitute the principle of selflessness?
Therefore, the principle is empty and non-substantial; it takes the fact that all phenomena are fundamentally empty and quiescent as the true principle.

Thus, principle is entirely identical to phenomena, for they are but one. Since emptiness is form, the text of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that principle is beneath phenomena, for their substance is not distinct.
The commentary states that "because phenomena must rely on principle" refers back to the third gate, and "because principle is empty and lacks substance" refers back to the sixth gate;
therefore, the following section establishes this present gate.

Regarding the phrase "the Commentary says 'and so forth,'" that sub-commentary states: "The first correspondence concerns the substance of the characterized phenomenon (*lakṣya-dharma*) and discusses how its nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are not in conflict;
the latter correspondence concerns the four characteristics as the characterizers (*lakṣaṇa*) and distinguishes their lack of conflict. This is merely a brief mention of one instance.
That the nature does not conflict with the characteristics means that ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is identical to phenomena (*dharma*)."

The *śāstra* states that when one contemplates dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and so forth as being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), this reveals that the expression which elucidates the principle is identical with the principle it elucidates;
therefore, it is said that "the entire substance is itself the truth. Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says: "If a phenomenon arises from conditions, it has no intrinsic nature;

if it has no intrinsic nature, how can such a phenomenon exist? That which lacks intrinsic nature is precisely the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Therefore, phenomena are themselves [the truth].
Regarding the principle:

the *Chao* (Commentary) states that "the Forest of Diligence" refers to what is said in that *Shu* (Sub-commentary): because one diligently contemplates the non-differentiation between principle and phenomena (*li-shi*), and is free from the marks of body and mind, it is called "Diligence.
As for the phrase "all phenomena are without differentiation," the following section establishes both the knower and the known in terms of the dharmas.
The first phrase indicates that the five categories of phenomena—consciousness, mental factors, and so forth—are all without distinction.

The remaining three phrases clarify this with respect to persons; the second phrase distinguishes these from other objects, while the latter half [of the verse] shows that only the Buddha has fully exhausted them.

The analogy of gold and the color of gold explains that for the "objects of knowledge," the essence and the form are not distinct: the first half provides the analogy, and the second half applies it to the dharma.

Regarding the phrase "one wholesome dharma" (*eka-kuśala-dharma*): first, if one discusses different dharmas horizontally from this point downward, then each phenomenon (*dharma*) is without distinction; although this accords with the general term "all dharmas" used in the preceding heading, it is not what is intended here. Second, if one discusses them vertically from this point downward according to the mutual penetration of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) and principle (*dharmatā*), then the *dharmatā* serves as the norm for generating understanding of phenomena; however, because the principle is severed from practice and cognition, it is termed "non-dharma" (*adharma*). Thus it is said: "As for the 'one wholesome dharma,' if one speaks of it horizontally, all phenomena are without difference; if one speaks of it vertically, the nature of phenomena is non-dharma. This is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the one wholesome dharma": if one speaks of it horizontally, it refers to the fact that among all phenomena, there is not even a single dharma that is not wholesome; if one speaks of it vertically, it refers to the fact that within the nature of phenomena, there is not even a single dharma that is not wholesome. This is why it is called "one wholesome dharma. Regarding the phrase "the one wholesome dharma": if one speaks of it horizontally, it refers to the fact that among all phenomena, there is not even a single dharma that is not wholesome; if one speaks of it vertically, it refers to the fact that within the nature of phenomena, there is not even a single dharma that is not wholesome. According to the *Shurangama Sutra Commentary*, the first half of the verse in the lower section of the *Ghanavyūha Sūtra* provides the doctrinal explanation (*dharmadeśanā*), while the second half provides the illustrative explanation through metaphor (*dṛṣṭānta*). The reference to a "finger-ring" pertains specifically to its form.
The nature of form (*rūpa*) and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is without differentiation because of the union of the true and the false.
The commentary on the *Sumeru-gāthā* states that the first two lines below correctly establish the meaning of the four characteristics arising simultaneously;

the remaining lines are all cited incidentally. It says that for ordinary practitioners, the process of fluxing and flowing is called "formations" (*saṃskāra*); there are no subtle four characteristics that are not grasped.

The phrase "swiftly returning to extinction" (*kṣipraṃ kṣayaṃ gacchati*) reveals that the four characteristics [of conditioned phenomena] occur simultaneously. According to the interpretation in the lower commentary (*śū*), the first verse directly reveals "extinction":
because all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and arise and perish swiftly, the nature of the conditioned is as tranquil as empty space;

this is precisely the eternally pervasive essence of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The second verse "sweeps away traces to enter the profound. The first two lines sweep away the preceding notion of non-existence.

The question is raised: "Since it is like empty space, how can there be the characteristics of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? The latter two lines refute the preceding notion of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
This means that since it is discussed in terms of its own nature as being inexhaustible, it does not undergo destruction even within exhaustion; therefore, it is called "inconceivable exhaustion.

Thus, the subsequent commentary in the sub-commentary establishes this by showing that it does not depend on a subsequent non-existence, thereby distinguishing it from the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (characteristics of phenomena).

The *Chao* states that because phenomena are empty and lack intrinsic substance, they are empty and without substance precisely at the moment of their arising; therefore, cessation occurs simultaneously [with arising].
Regarding "the Bodhisattva Śubhamati," the *Shu* says: "To have perfected the wisdom of prajñā such that one’s discernment is immovable—this may indeed be called 'good' (*śubha*)."

The commentary also states that it "leads to ultimate [realization]" (*niṣṭhā*) and so forth; it is called "ultimate" because it exhausts the principle. However, citing the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* as proof establishes the departure from subject and object of the cutting-off (*prahāṇa*).

As was already clarified in the section on the teachings established and the schools opened, within the scope of the Final Teaching (*paryantayāna*), it is explicitly stated that there is no cutting-off during the two periods, because the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is identical to the nature (*dharmatā*), and only when one is able to cut-off can the nature be identical to the characteristic.

Therefore, it is said that the final phrase refers to the characteristic of *prajñā* because the first phrase involves the severance of delusions through both types of wisdom, whereas this phrase involves the realization of principle through exclusively non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Since this wisdom is precisely the wisdom that realizes principle while also incidentally severing delusions, it is stated that "it is also capable of severing.
This is the intended meaning of the sub-commentary (*vyākhyā*) regarding "non-conceptual wisdom."
The statement that it is "not the same as the Śrāvakas" serves to distinguish the inferior from the superior.

This means that while Śrāvakas give rise to true wisdom by relying on the teachings of sound (*śabda*), here true wisdom arises from within; therefore, they are not the same. The first fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states:

"There are three gateways for entering the Buddha-dharma: first, the teaching (*śāsana*); second, the meaning (*artha*); and third, the practice (*pratipatti*). The teaching is shallow, while the meaning is deep."

Regarding the practice of the most excellent Śrāvakas: those of inferior faculties who attain realization through instruction are called "Sound-Hearers" (Śrāvaka) because they hear the instruction and awaken to understanding through that sound.

Next, the Pratyekabuddhas are superior; their title is established according to their meaning (*artha*). They are called "Condition-Enlightened" (Pratyekabuddha) because they awaken to understanding through the meaning of conditions.
Finally, the Bodhisattvas are superior; their name is manifested according to their conduct, for they are able to accomplish the two benefits [of self and others].
Because they follow the Way, they are called Bodhisattvas. Thus, the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: "From hearing, reflection, and cultivation, the names of the Three Vehicles are established.

This serves as a concluding summary for the lower section, returning to the capacity for severing [delusions]. Furthermore, regarding the statement in the *Commentary* on the "Dedication Chapter" (Huixiang pin) that it also proves the severing of delusions and so forth:
however, observing the intent of the sub-commentary (*shu*), it appears to cite the "Ten Stages Chapter" (*Daśabhūmika*) to prove that the subject and object of severing delusions are non-dual.

The citation from the "Chapter on Dedication" (*Pariṇāmanā-parivarta*) serves as proof that the realized principle (*pramiti-tattva*) and its object are non-dual. The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) here is that it does not merely prove the realization of the principle;

it also proves the severance of delusions (*kleśa-prahāṇa*). This is because when both the subject and object of realization are unimpeded, this constitutes the non-obstruction of phenomenon and principle (*sāṃvṛti-paramārtha-avyatibheda*);

likewise, when both the subject and object of severance are unimpeded, this too constitutes the non-obstruction of phenomenon and principle. Alternatively, this may be the intended meaning of the *Jiyao* (Essential Extract) manuscript.
It is simply that both cited passages prove that the realization and the severance are non-dual; hence it is said, "it is also thus.
As for the statement "the meaning is as previously explained," this has already been clarified within the exposition of the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhāyāna*).

"In this section, the Dharmakāya—which is non-existent yet follows conditions—is constantly manifested without differing from phenomena; in the subsequent section, sentient beings—which are non-nonexistent yet quiescent—are constantly [manifested] without differing [from the Dharmakāya]."

Thus, the application of this analogy below can be understood accordingly.

The statement "the *Chao* relies entirely on Xianshou" refers to the *Tanyuan* (Exploring the Profundities); it may also be suspected that the *Xinxiu lüeshu* (Newly Revised Brief Commentary) was entirely based on the *Chao*.

Regarding the second section of the *Chao*, the "Gate of the Sovereignty of Extent and Narrowness," which corresponds to the *Fajieguan* (Contemplation of the Dharma Realm), this corresponds to the sixth meaning within that contemplation: the principle of universal inclusion and non-obstruction.

However, although the fifth section of the *Contemplation Sutra* is titled "The Gate of the Unimpeded Interpenetration of the Vast and the Narrow," it primarily clarifies that while not destroying a single atom, one can extensively contain the entire Dharma-realm;

this refers only to the meaning of extensive containment. Now, taking the non-destruction of a single atom while extensively containing the Dharma-realm as "the narrowness within the vast," and taking this single atom pervading the entire Dharma-realm as "the vastness within the narrow," [the two are shown to be identical]. Thus:
Yunzai says: "This refers merely to the identity of meaning; thus it is said [the meaning is the same] while the names differ slightly" (this is the interpretation from the *Shanghui*).

If [one asks], "Is 'quiescent illumination' (*jizhao*) the same as the 'contemplation of the Dharma-realm' (*fajie guan*)?"—it is so, insofar as it represents one portion of the general meaning of "vast capacity and universal pervasion. One might object:

First, "encompassing" means there is nothing outside; not a single dharma exists that is even as minute as a speck of dust.
To explain the meaning of "narrow" below, it says: "The flowers and leaves do not leave their original positions. How could this be the same as [the previous sense]? Answer:

Since the ten gates exist by virtue of the two meanings of "vast inclusion" and "universal pervasion," these constitute the general meaning. Now, the narrow meaning merely takes what is within the vast inclusion, excluding the universal pervasion.
The meaning of "destroying the fundamental position" does not involve the inclusion of other meanings, but only partial agreement;

likewise, the meaning of "universal pervasion" also involves only partial agreement, because within the meaning of universal pervasion there are many distinct senses. The critique states: "Quiescence and illumination share partial agreement.
As for the comprehensive interpretation of the general meaning, they differ; thus, in the sixth section, each has its own justification, and one may adopt either of the two explanations accordingly.

The Commentary states that this section on the "Non-obstruction of the Broad and the Narrow" was newly established by Xianshou. When asked why it is called "newly established" given that the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* already establishes a fifth gate, the answer is as follows:

Because the *Zhìxiàng* (Ultimate Characteristics) school did not establish the broad and the narrow, but only established purity and impurity, [Xianshou] revised the categories of purity and impurity to separately establish the broad and the narrow;
therefore, it is called "newly established. Furthermore, this current treatment of the broad and the narrow is consistent with the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*.

The interpretations differ; within the *Guan* [the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*], the distinction between the broad and the narrow is established solely from the perspective of extensive inclusion (*guǎng róng*) while maintaining the aspect of non-confusion (*bù huài xiàng*).
Here, however, both meanings—extensive inclusion and non-confusion—are fully present, and this is also a new formulation. The intent is as follows:

below, Xianshou (Fazang) replaces "pure" (*chún*) and "mixed" (*zá*) with "broad" (*guǎng*) and "narrow" (*xiá*), respectively. This is not because they are actually interchangeable, but rather out of concern that they might be confused; thus, he revised them according to the meaning of the teachings.

This is explained within the section on the Traces (*ji*). In the "Chapter on Primary and Secondary Teachings" (*zhāo*), it clarifies that while Fazang (Xian-shou) established the "Distinct Establishment of the Ultimate Reality" (*zhixiang weili*) gate, Fazhao did not;
rather, he established the "Gate of the Perfect Accomplishment of the Mind’s Revolving" (*weixin huizhuan shancheng men*).

Consequently, this gate remains preserved within the doctrinal system (*jiaoyi*). As the lower fascicle states: "The ninth is the Gate of the Perfect Accomplishment of the Mind’s Revolving. All the meanings mentioned above are merely the transformations of the single Tathāgata-garbha, the intrinsically pure mind. The three vehicles are but one mind, which is also fully endowed with ten kinds of virtues; even all the aforementioned categories of meaning are the sovereign functions of this mind, and as there is nothing else besides it, it is called "the revolving of the mind-only" (cittamātra-parāvṛtti), and so forth—this is the reason for the "Mysterious Gate" (xuánmén) as established in the *Tàn xuán jì* (Probing the Profundity Commentary).

"It is because they are merged that it is said thus. [End of] Fascicle Four. Regarding the phrase "thereby containing the other," etc., this fourth section follows upon and establishes the third:

Regarding "encompassing others" and "visible to others": this does not mean being seen by the physical eye; rather, it is called "visible" because its manifestation is not obscured.

Alternatively, it is termed "seen" in the sense of being perceived by wisdom (*jñāna*). Otherwise, while such might apply to functional activity (*karman*), how could a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) such as a quality (*guṇa*) be designated as "manifest" only upon being seen?

The *Chao* [commentary] states that the characteristics of virtue (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*) also have a lower [level of] inquiry. Regarding the previously explained four gates, there is a reason why those [characteristics] possess virtue and function while [others] lack them;

how is this to be reconciled? This is answered as follows: because entering into activity is not restricted solely to functional utility (*karma-vyāpāra*), and based on this, even if one generally encompasses the lower [levels], they are sublated by the fact that essence and phenomenon are non-different, and virtue and function are mutually integrated. If this virtue were lacking, the cause of True Suchness would be obscured; since it is already present, it reveals the cause of True Suchness."
If these qualities are not lacking, then the fruit of the marks of virtue (*lakṣaṇa*) also involves active engagement. There should not be three characters [here].
Although the text is located at the beginning, its meaning extends through the subsequent statement. The word "universally" (*pǔ*) comprehensively includes what follows.
In the section on the dedication of the marks of *tathatā*, the Sūtra says: "Tathatā universally encompasses all dharmas. This is the forty-third quality among the hundred gates of virtue.

Since True Suchness (*tathatā*) inherently possesses the virtue of universally encompassing all phenomena, whenever any single phenomenon accords with its nature, it likewise universally encompasses all phenomena;
this is precisely what is meant by "incorporating the other into oneself. Regarding the phrase following the character "and" (*ji*), the Sūtra states:

The word "also" (*api*) should be understood as applying downward to the following three qualities. Regarding "that which is able to establish":
the Sūtra says that True Suchness (*tathatā*) has the capacity for maintenance, which is the ninth quality; the Sūtra says that True Suchness sustains all worlds, which is the fifty-fifth [quality].
The *Dejing* (Scripture on Virtue) states: "True Suchness accomplishes all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

This refers to the ninety-ninth virtue, which is another name for the "establishment of accomplishment through action" (*an-lì chéng-chù zuò*). To "sustain" (*chí*) means that once the action has been performed, the phenomena do not lose their reality;

it accords with principle and also carries the sense of being inherently present as an act. This serves as proof that the aspect of virtue possesses the meaning of acting with characteristics (*xiàng zuò yì*). Therefore, the phrase "constantly entering into action" at the end is the conclusion.
Alternatively, the first phrase concludes the authority of the sacred word (*āptavacana-pramāṇa*), while the second phrase concludes the authority of right reasoning (*yukti-pramāṇa*).
As in the *Yichao* (Commentary), following a verse, there is a further citation of the sacred teachings to prove that the marks of virtue are eternally present;

furthermore, the phrase "the true dharma" generally refers to this sutra as well as other sutras to substantiate the meaning previously established. In the *Yichao*, the section beginning with "its being of the same substance constitutes... [continues].

Regarding those [categories] within the marks of virtue (*guṇalakṣaṇa*), the sixth and seventh are identical to this [present case] in their reliance on phenomena (*vastu-pratītya*), such as the "net of Indra" (*indrājāla*) and so forth.

Since these instances of relying on phenomena apply universally to both virtues and functions (*guṇa-kriyā*), why would they be restricted solely to the marks of virtue? Furthermore, if they were restricted only to the marks of virtue and did not accord with the sense faculties (*indriya*), how could one know them now?

Since they are indeed known now, how could it be that they do not accord with the sense faculties? Moreover, that which follows clarifies that [the former interpretation] does not rely on the Honored One Xianxiu (Xianshou).

This is because time is established merely through the differentiated states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). Thus, it enters the gateway of the profound.
This should also be understood by correlating it with the "Original Gate" (*mūla-mukha*) below.
