Non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) likewise falls within the category of Buddhas; it is like one who has newly entered the monastic order and thus falls within the category of the Saṅgha, yet because they have not fully received the precepts, they are not called a "Great Bhikṣu.
Similarly, as long as one has not fully realized Buddha-wisdom, one is still called a Bodhisattva.

The *Yao* (Commentary) further cites the passage from the "Appearance of Signs" chapter (*Lakṣaṇaparivarta*) concerning the Buddha’s emission of light from between his eyebrows, as found in the "Manifestation" chapter (*Nirmāṇaparivarta*). Furthermore, there is the *Dharmadhātu-sūtra*.

This is the text for the "Chapter on Vairocana" (Vairocanābhisambodhi), and thus it concludes accordingly with the following section. *Commentary*: If one distinguishes this based on the lower [section], this is done by way of the fascicles of the collection.

As for other sutras that contain expositions of the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), they are not excluded, as they likewise possess the principle of the primary and its associates (*pramukha-parivāra*).
Thus, the *Jiaoyi* (Exegesis of the Teachings) explains the *Lotus Sutra* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra): "I possess such seven treasures..."
The great vehicles are immeasurable in number; this constitutes the "gate of principal and attendant. Here, however, they function solely as retinues because they flow from this [source].

Since they are restricted by following their respective faculties (*indriya*), they cannot serve as the principal; thus, they belong to the category of attendants. This may be understood by reference to other sutras.

Now, it is said that below these, they mutually serve as principal and attendant. Furthermore, regarding the term "retinue" (*parivāra*): those who are close to one another are called "retinue" (*jūan*), and those who accord with one another are called "attendants" (*shùn*).

It is said that "belonging" refers to those who are human; since their dharmas resemble those of humans, they too receive this name. According to the *Ji* (Collection) and *Xuanying* (Xuanying’s Commentary), four permutations should be established: 1.

There are cases where there are only the principal and its associates (*bān*), but these are not [in the technical sense of] retinue (*juànshǔ*). This is as in the case of the *Ten Abodes Dharma-gate*, where this region serves as the principal and other regions serve as the associates.
Because they do not follow along by attaching to the original [principal], they are not called "retinue. 2. There are cases where there is [the category of] retinue... [text fragmentary].
"Belonging to but not being the principal and its retinue" refers to cases such as other sutras which serve merely as superior skillful means for the *Avataṃsaka*, and are thus called "retinues";
they do not arise simultaneously with the *Avataṃsaka* in a state of mutual interpenetration and perfect fusion, and are therefore not termed "principal and retinue.
Third, "both principal and retinue" refers to when the *Dharmadhātu-sūtra* arises, it encompasses the *kṣetra-rajas-pramāṇa* scriptures.

Those that arise simultaneously with the *Dharmadhātu-sūtra* and act as its support are called "retinue" (*parivāra*); furthermore, when they arise as both principal and attendant, they are called "principal and retinue" (*nāyaka-parivāra*).
Those that are neither retinue nor principal and retinue refer to other sūtras in relation to one another, or external treatises and the like.

Regarding the "Commentary" (*Chao*) which provides an analogical explanation for the three layers: in the previous direct explanation, only the primary and secondary [elements] were clarified, while the visible and invisible were not discussed;

therefore, this section provides an analogical explanation. That is to say, regarding this "Method-Wisdom" (*dharmapravicaya-prajñā*), when this Method-Wisdom serves as the primary, the Method-Wisdoms of the ten directions necessarily serve as its companions. Consequently, this particular direction cannot function as a companion to itself.

"Who can be the companion for the subject? This explains that when it is said "companion does not see companion," at the time when the ten-directional Dharma-wisdom acts as the companion, this very ten-directional Dharma-wisdom must necessarily be the subject.
Therefore, within the ten-directional Dharma-wisdom, the aspect of being the subject cannot see this ten-directional Dharma-wisdom; this explains the subject.
Because the primary [factors] do not see one another, the following section below explains this:
the primary factors here do not see the primary factors there; the primary factors there do not see the primary factors here.
By implication, the secondary [factors] here cannot see the secondary factors there, and the secondary factors there cannot see the secondary factors here.
However, for every principal there must be an attendant, and it is permissible for there to be many; as for the rest, it is as explained in the *Jiaozhi* (Traces of the Teaching).

Regarding the various dharmas cited above, each has its own principal and attendant; thus, it is clear that the *Jiaozhi* explains the "principal and attendant" relationship primarily in terms of the ritual protocols for the preaching of the Dharma by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

The *Chao* (Commentary) states that regarding "the extensive explanation above" and so forth: when speaking in a general manner, one follows any single gate and explains non-obstruction based collectively upon the ten pairs of essence and phenomena.

Now, when discussing them individually, it is restricted solely to the gate of phenomena (*vastu*), taking the flower as the comprehensive gate while including the remaining essences and phenomena as being simultaneous, continuing thus up to the gate of principal and attendant.
Furthermore, within these phenomena, there are both teaching (*dharma*) and meaning (*artha*).
There are other gates, such as the gate of simultaneous possession of all other entities and phenomena, up to the gate of the primary and its attendants, and so on, totaling up to one hundred gates;
all of these take "entities" (vastu) as their primary subject. Since it has already been stated that all entities are simultaneously and fully possessed, one might ask:
how can the principle (li), and other such phenomena, be included within this? How is it that there is the complete perfection of the ten pairs? The answer is: they are manifested.

The *Pǐnchāo* states: "Whenever a single matter is raised, it must necessarily encompass the Ten Mysterious Gates; whenever a single Mysterious Gate is presented, it must necessarily include the ten pairs.
Generally speaking, when a single dharma is elucidated, each and every aspect is perfectly subsumed.

According to this principle, a single matter or dharma perfectly subsumes all teachings and meanings, and even response and resonance are perfectly subsumed within all things. Nevertheless, because the gates are distinct, they do not overlap."
Regarding the phrase "the second fascicle [discusses] the basis of phenomena, etc.": In the ten pairs mentioned above, only one matter was explained without its underlying principle;
the remaining nine pairs were explained in combination because their meanings were obscured when presented solely through the gateway of principle, and thus they were omitted for brevity.

In the *Shu* (Commentary), it is exemplified that when the "mysterious gates" (*xuánmén*) are based upon [the preceding], they also constitute one thousand mysterious gates. Question: Previously, when the "substantial phenomena" (*tǐshì*) were taken as the primary basis, there were one thousand mysterious gates.
Now, since the "mysterious gates" themselves are taken as the primary basis, there should likewise be one thousand [gates] corresponding to the substantial phenomena.

Why, then, does this also result in one thousand mysterious gates? Answer: When each of the preceding substantial phenomena is individually taken as the primary basis, there are one thousand mysterious gates. It is for this reason that they also constitute one thousand mysterious gates.

Now, if one considers each distinct gateway to the profound (*xuanmen*) in relation to the ten [categories] as they correspond to the substance and phenomena, they constitute a thousand gateways to the profound.

Furthermore, because one wishes to expand these gateways to the profound until they are inexhaustible, it is said that they "possess the simultaneous teaching and meaning" (*jiaoyi tongshi*). This is because the gateways to the profound are primary;
thus, it differs from the previous [classification]. Some versions of the text read "teaching and meaning are simultaneous" (*jiaoyi tongshi*), but this is merely a scribal error. Alternatively—

The term "conformity" (*shun*) also establishes the meaning of the "thousand gates"; it refers to the preceding section’s general and specific distinctions, as well as the differences between the prior and subsequent parts.
The former was based on the sequential arrangement of ten gates, whereas the present is based on the circular interpenetration of the ten gates' conditions;
each constitutes a distinct principle.
The *Chao* states that "taking [them] layer upon layer" has two meanings.
First, regarding "taking [them] layer upon layer," as in the initial section below, it refers to taking them layer upon layer according to the Mysterious Gate (*xuánmén*).

To say that the initial section contains ten means that within the Simultaneous Gate (*tóngshí mén*), there are ten instances of simultaneity (from the doctrinal meaning up to response and transformation). From among these ten, one takes the single instance of simultaneity.
The doctrine must also possess ten aspects; since each of these ten aspects possesses ten further elements, they constitute one hundred gates.

Just as the doctrine of the "Simultaneous" [teaching] possesses one hundred gates, so too do the other nine simultaneous teachings each possess one hundred gates, thereby constituting one thousand gates.
Because the phenomena of dependent origination are mutually inseparable, it is said that just as it is with the one, so it is with each of the ten within the thousand gates.
However, where "thousand" (千) appears above and "ten" (十) appears below, it is an error in transcription; it should be "ten" above and "thousand" below.

This means that each of the ten gates contains one thousand [items], and since this is so for one gate, it is likewise so for each of the ten gates—this can be understood by analogy with what precedes.
Regarding the phrase "within the ten thousands," it extends down to the end.
"Principle" (*li*) is a general term. For example, "one thousand coins" serves as the primary metaphor for the general meaning.

Having finished explaining the first meaning above, the phrase "furthermore, layer upon layer" below refers to the second intention, which takes up the matter of the body and phenomena (*tǐ-shì*) in successive layers.

Within the "ten pairs," just as there are many phenomena, each one is individually explained through the ten mysteries (*shí xuán*), extending even to the various types of "response and resonance" (*gǎnyìng*).
Each and every one of these speaks of ten mysteries, which further interpenetrate one another to form the inexhaustible.

Regarding the phrase "these thousand gates" and so forth in the Commentary: to understand them thoroughly from beginning to end is called "perfect" (*yuan*); to exhaustively penetrate the subtle and fathom the profound is called "evident" (*ming*).

While the term "evident" (*ming*) primarily explains the meaning of "clear," the term "ultimate" (*liu-jing*)—or "thoroughly understood" (*liao*)—also explains the meaning of "perfect. Thus, it is encountered at every turn.
The object is the realm of the Dharma-dhātu, a state of infinite, layered profundity.
The *Commentary* states that "these and so forth" means that each individual [aspect] possesses inexhaustible virtues; this is still merely a gateway for entering the Dharma.
Only the *Subcommentary* on the *Vairocana Chapter* of the *Puyan* (Universal Eye) says: "A single eye already possesses the ten [eyes]."

The eye is fused and without obstruction; when there is no dharma outside the eye, only then is it the true universal eye (*samantacakṣus*). Since all conditions give rise to seeing, each condition acts as an eye;
when the cause has subsided within the fruit, all conditions are designated as "eye. Thus, taking form entirely as the eye, one constantly sees form yet remains without conditions;
taking the eye entirely as form, one constantly calls it "seeing" yet it is not the self. This non-self is free from emotional attachment.
When thought is without object, craving and seeking are severed; the myriad forms are gathered before one's eyes, and the ten directions are encompassed within the range of vision.

Thus, the principle of conditions is inexhaustible, and as one perceives, perception is never-ending. The nature of things is inconceivable, and as phenomena accord with the Dharma, they are difficult to standardize.
When the Dharma is universal, the eye is universal; when the meaning is pervasive, vision is pervasive—the very essence of the body is inherently hidden yet shines forth in silent illumination.
[The opponent] then repeatedly says: "If those of superior intelligence can enter [the Dharma-realm], then those of middling and inferior capacities have no share.

[The respondent] answers: Since Sudhana, upon seeing Mañjuśrī, was instructed to recollect his roots of goodness from past lives, we know that he had already cultivated them previously before achieving superior intelligence.
How could he have deceived himself by constantly remaining at the level of middling or inferior capacity? He persevered in superior progress without ceasing.
...up to the ultimate stage.
*Huayan Xuantan Hui Xuan Ji*, Scroll 30,
Phonetic Glossary.
*Di* (pronounced *di*, meaning "to pass on" or "exchange"). *Cū* (pronounced *cū*, meaning "coarse," not fine).
*Avataṃsaka Xuántán Huìxuán Jì*, Scroll 31, Compiled by the Bhikṣu Pǔruì of Zàiguāng Temple on Mount Cāng.

The second section of the Commentary clarifies that which is the cause of the "virtuous function" (*guṇavṛtti*). All the principles of the ten mysteries (*daśa-guhya*) that are established are permeated by virtuous function;

now, the reason for establishing them is revealed through their names based on those established principles. Regarding the name "cause of virtuous function," it is designated according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.

Within the ten causes themselves, there is inherently virtuous function; thus, it is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound, meaning "virtuous function itself is the cause. It is established as such.

Regarding the phrase "The commentary [states] that because it is difficult to elaborate further," the *Tanyuan* (Probing the Profundities) also says: "Furthermore, those [ten points] are listed there as follows:

first, because of the mutual dependence of causal conditions (*pratyaya*); second, because of the interpenetration of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); third, because each is a manifestation of the mind; and fourth, because they are unreal, like illusions."
Fifth, because the large and small have no fixed measure; sixth, because they arise from infinite causes; seventh, because the merit of the fruit is perfectly consummate;
eighth, because of supreme supernormal powers and mastery; ninth, because of the great function of samādhi; tenth, because of inconceivable liberation. The *Zhigui* (The Return to the Ultimate) says:

first, because there is no fixed characteristic; second, because it is a manifestation of mind-only; third, because it is like an illusory phenomenon; fourth, because it appears like a dream; fifth...

1. By the power of supreme supernormal faculties; 2. By the function of the six profound meditative concentrations; 3. By the power of liberation; 4. Because causes are infinite; 5. Because of the characteristics of dependent origination;
6. Because the nature of phenomena is interpenetrating. The critique states: The ultimate aim converges upon the virtues of the fruit within the infinity of causes.

Within this infinity of causes, the manifestation [of the fruit] like a dream is opened up, thus forming ten meanings. When the *Tanyuan* (Exploring the Profundity) opens up cause and effect, it forms six or seven items, with certain elements being removed.
Like a dream, it exists only as such; like an illusion, it is unreal—these also suffice for the ten meanings.

Now, this commentary combines the essential points of the third and fourth [sections] to form the fifth, and combines the eighty [verses] of the *Tanyuan* to form the tenth; therefore, they are named "Supernormal Powers and Liberation.

This is because supreme penetration is itself supernormal power (*abhijñā*), mastery is itself liberation (*vimukti*), and that which is inconceivable arises precisely from the mastery of supernormal powers and liberation.
Therefore, it is difficult to conceive; thus, they are combined as the tenth [topic], while the sixth is separately opened up. Using the analogy of a reflection serves to complete the ten meanings.
As for the reason why the ultimate goal (*tātparya*) is treated like a dream, the intention is that this refers solely to the analogy of illusion, which serves as an example for the other analogies.
This is why the two categories are not listed separately. However, the meaning of cause and effect is separately opened up, as will be reconciled below in the current commentary (*ṭīkā*).

Approximately three metaphors are divided into two sections; since the meanings of the "dream" and "illusion" are somewhat similar, they are combined into one, whereas the metaphor of the "reflected image" is slightly different and thus treated as a separate section (as can be seen for oneself in the commentary of the *Śāstra*). Question: Since there are seven metaphors in total in the "Chapter on the Ten Patiences," why are only three taken here? Answer: There are two reasons. First, as the commentary states, because it is difficult to present them in full detail, they are briefly summarized. Second, [the remaining four] are included within these three. As for the first point, the commentary says: "Because it is difficult to describe extensively, they are briefly extracted. This means that although there are seven metaphors, they are condensed into three. Regarding the second point, the commentary says: "The remaining four are included within these three. This means that the four metaphors not included in the three—namely, the metaphors of the echo, the city of the Gandharvas, the reflection, and the transformation—are all contained within the three already mentioned. For instance, the metaphor of the echo is included within the metaphor of the illusion, the metaphor of the city of the Gandharvas is included within the metaphor of the dream, and the metaphors of the reflection and the transformation are both included within the metaphor of the reflected image. Thus, by taking these three, the seven are fully encompassed. Furthermore, the commentary says: "These three are the most essential. This means that among the seven, these three are the most fundamental. Why? Because the first three metaphors correspond to the three types of delusion regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*): the first corresponds to the delusion regarding the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the second corresponds to the delusion regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the third corresponds to the delusion regarding the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Therefore, these three are the most essential. Furthermore, the commentary says: "They are easy to understand. This means that these three are easy to comprehend. Why? Because they are things commonly experienced in the world. For example, dreams and illusions are things everyone has experienced; reflections are things commonly seen in water or mirrors; and transformations are things commonly seen in the realms of the gods and so forth. Because they are familiar to the world, they are easy to understand. Furthermore, the commentary says: "They are easy to refute. This means that these three are easy to refute. Why? Because they are things that ordinary people do not believe in. For example, when one explains that phenomena are like dreams or illusions, ordinary people do not believe it; when one explains that phenomena are like reflections or transformations, ordinary people do not believe it. Because they are things ordinary people do not believe in, they are easy to refute. Therefore, these three are the most essential, easy to understand, and easy to refute. Consequently, they are taken as the primary metaphors. Furthermore, the commentary says: "They are the most excellent. This means that these three are the most excellent. Why? Because they are the most profound. For example, the metaphor of the dream is more profound than the metaphor of the illusion; the metaphor of the reflection is more profound than the metaphor of the echo; and the metaphor of the transformation is more profound than the metaphor of the city of the Gandharvas. Because they are the most profound, they are the most excellent. Therefore, they are taken as the primary metaphors. Furthermore, the commentary says: "They are the most pervasive. This means that these three are the most pervasive. Why? Because they pervade the three times. For example, the metaphor of the dream pervades the past; the metaphor of the illusion pervades the future; and the metaphor of the reflection pervades the present. Because they pervade the three times, they are the most pervasive. Therefore, they are taken as the primary metaphors. Furthermore, the commentary says: "They are the most subtle. This means that these three are the most subtle. Why? Because they are difficult to perceive. For example, the metaphor of the dream is difficult to perceive because it is a state of mind; the metaphor of the illusion is difficult to perceive because it is a manifestation of external objects; and the metaphor of the reflection is difficult to perceive because it is a combination of internal and external factors. Because they are difficult to perceive, they are the most subtle. Therefore, they are taken as the primary metaphors. Furthermore, the commentary says: "They are the most supreme. This means that these three are the most supreme. Why? Because they are the most noble. For example, the metaphor of the dream is noble because it is a state of meditative concentration; the metaphor of the illusion is noble because it is a manifestation of supernatural power; and the metaphor of the reflection is noble because it is a manifestation of wisdom. Because they are the most noble, they are the most supreme. Therefore, they are taken as the primary metaphors. Furthermore, the commentary says: "They are the most beneficial. This means that these three are the most beneficial. Why? Because they lead to liberation. For example, the metaphor of the dream leads to liberation from the delusion of self; the metaphor of the illusion leads to liberation from the delusion of phenomena; and the metaphor of the reflection leads to liberation from the delusion of subject and object. Because they lead to liberation, they are the most beneficial. Therefore, they are taken as the primary metaphors. Furthermore, the commentary says: "They are the most complete. This means that these three are the most complete. Why? Because they encompass all dharmas. For example, the metaphor of the dream encompasses all internal dharmas; the metaphor of the illusion encompasses all external dharmas; and the metaphor of the reflection encompasses all dharmas of the internal and external union. Because they encompass all dharmas, they are the most complete. Therefore, they are taken as the primary metaphors. Furthermore, the commentary says: "They are the most harmonious. This means that these three are the most harmonious. Why? Because they accord with reality. For example, the metaphor of the dream accords with the fact that all dharmas are empty; the metaphor of the illusion accords with the fact that all dharmas are without characteristics; and the metaphor of the reflection accords with the fact that all dharmas are without activity. Because they accord with reality, they are the most harmonious. Therefore, they are taken as the primary metaphors. Furthermore, the commentary says: "They are the most appropriate. This means that these three are the most appropriate. Why? Because they suit the capacity of the listener. For example, for those of dull faculties, the metaphor of the dream is appropriate; for those of medium faculties, the metaphor of the illusion is appropriate; and for those of sharp faculties, the metaphor of the reflection is appropriate. Because they suit the capacity of the listener, they are the most appropriate. Therefore, they are taken as the primary metaphors. Furthermore, the commentary says: "They are the most effective. This means that these three are the most effective. Why? Because they remove delusion. For example, the metaphor of the dream removes the delusion of attachment to self; the metaphor of the illusion removes the delusion of attachment to phenomena; and the metaphor of the reflection removes the delusion of attachment to subject and object. Because they remove delusion, they are the most effective. Therefore, they are taken as the primary metaphors. Furthermore, the commentary says: "They are the most enduring. This means that these three are the most enduring. Why? Because they are not subject to change. For example, the metaphor of the dream is not subject to change because it is a state of mind; the metaphor of the illusion is not subject to change because it is a manifestation of external objects; and the metaphor of the reflection is not subject to change because it is a combination of internal and external factors. Because they are not subject to change, they are the most enduring. Therefore, they are taken as the primary metaphors. Furthermore, the commentary says: "They are the most stable. This means that these three are the most stable. Why? Because they are not subject to destruction. For example, the metaphor of the dream is not subject to destruction because it is a state of mind; the metaphor of the illusion is not subject to destruction because it is a manifestation of external objects; and the metaphor of the reflection is not subject to destruction because it is a combination of internal and external factors. Because they are not subject to destruction, they are the most stable. Therefore, they are taken as the primary metaphors. Furthermore, the commentary says: "They are the most constant. This means that these three are the most constant. Why? Because they are not subject to interruption. For example, the metaphor of the dream is not subject to interruption because it is a state of mind; the metaphor of the illusion is not subject to interruption because it is a manifestation of external objects; and the metaphor of the reflection is not subject to interruption because it is a combination of internal and external factors. Because they are not subject to interruption, they are the most constant. Therefore, they are taken as the primary metaphors. Furthermore, the commentary says: "They are the most unchanging. This means that these three are the most unchanging. Why? Because they are not subject to transformation. For example, the metaphor of the dream is not subject to transformation because it is a state of mind; the metaphor of the illusion is not subject to transformation because it

Because there are ten categories, only three are selected to fulfill the ten meanings. These two [categories] also derive from these three, as they serve as the basis for the ten mysteries (*daśa-guhya*).

Since many metaphors—such as a flame, an echo, a transformation, and space—illustrate that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are unreal, and because this does not accord with the principle of the non-obstruction of phenomena (*dharmadharmāpratighāta*), only three are briefly explained and the others are not taken up.

Regarding the phrase "the first six among the ten" in the Commentary: if one were to speak according to the principle of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), then the qualities and functions would indeed interpenetrate one another.

However, here we are speaking according to the sequential arrangement (*xingbu*) to clarify their characteristics, and thus there are differences in terms of universality and limitation. When it says "universality refers to the dharma-nature," this means that the fourth [stage] is the dharma-nature;
the first, "mind-only," is the meaning of awakened illumination upon the dharma-nature; and the second, "dharmas have no fixed nature," is because...

Because they are constituted by the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they lack a fixed nature. As for the third [cause], dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), how could it exist apart from the nature of phenomena?

The fifth and sixth [causes] both serve as metaphors for the fact that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is unreal; they are unreal precisely because they are constituted by the nature of phenomena.

Therefore, while the first six [causes] apply universally to the nature of phenomena, the latter three are restricted to specific virtuous characteristics (*guṇalakṣaṇa*). Question: Should not the first six causes be identical?

Regarding the "causes" (*hetu*), if summarized, they do not transcend the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena). However, from a specific perspective, what prevents there being distinctions among the six causes?

This is because their specific functions and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are established only in dependence upon the faculties (*indriya*). Thus, the latter two [the efficient cause and the homogeneous cause] are restricted to their functional application.

As for the statement that "seven are based on the arousal of cultivation," if one refers to the arousal of training, these constitute the causes of functional application; if one refers to the essential nature of each individual causal practice, they are the fundamental nature itself.

Because it is endowed [with these qualities], it is the cause for the marks of virtue (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*), and thus one attains supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Eighth, because the fundamental dharma (*mūla-dharma*) follows after the person of fruition (*phala-pudgala*), it is restricted to the marks of virtue.
The *Chao* (the *Zongjing lu chao*) states that regarding "the function upon the Buddha-body," the *Zuanxuan ji* says: "Now, this function of virtue has a dharma..."

There are those who initially explain it according to the *dharma*: that suchness (*tathatā*) possessing all virtues is called the "characteristic of virtue" (*guṇalakṣaṇa*), while the functions such as supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are called "functional activity" (*karmakriyā*).
If, however, one explains it according to the person (*pudgala*), then with respect to the Buddha, it is called the "characteristic of virtue," because virtue is the characteristic [of the Buddha];

with respect to the faculties (*indriya*), it is called "functional activity," because it causes those who see [the Buddha] to immediately enter [the path]. Now, the intent of this passage is to bring forth the *dharma* by means of the person; that is to say, it refers to the Buddha.

Thus, when the entirety of the marks functions as activity—as in the case of the Buddha’s vocal tones, eloquence, and other such functions, which are the very marks that constitute his inherent virtues—then, from the perspective of the faculties, the entirety of the marks constitutes the function.
This is because it causes sentient beings to newly recognize the Buddha’s inherently present marks;
therefore, the marks are called "function."

The Commentary now clarifies that although the Buddha’s virtuous marks are such that both defiled and pure aspects are exhausted, the manifestation of defiled functions is likewise like the "Arising from Nature" (xingqi), which is purely pure;

whereas "Dependent Arising" (yuanqi) permeates both the defiled and the pure. Thus, the teaching in the *Xingqi pin* regarding the mutual penetration of Buddhas and sentient beings and the harmonious integration of the defiled and the pure is precisely identical to this.
Question: If he is already able to manifest the defiled, how can the defiled aspects be said to be exhausted? Answer: [As explained below...]

Because its manifestation through function is identical to its essence and yet eternally empty, it is called the Lion Throne. The following citation from the "Lower Section" (Zhongxia) is likely a scribal error;
according to the *Gandavyūha* chapter (*Miaoyan pin*), this refers to the manifestation of all sentient beings' dwellings and houses within the Buddha’s palace.
The commentary states: "Sentient beings are the primary [occupants], while the house is their support. Being devoid of self-nature through delusion, they in turn rely upon the True."
Because they appear. As the *Commentary* states, according to the full text of the *Ten Stages Sūtra*, Chapter on the Ten Concentrations:

"O Son of the Buddha, it is like the rising sun that circles Mount Sumeru, illuminating the seven-jeweled mountains and the spaces between those jewel mountains (the spaces between which are the fragrant-water seas).

In all these places, there are distinct shadows and reflections clearly manifest; the solar reflections upon all the seven-jeweled mountains are without exception clearly visible within the mountain intervals."
Within those reflections, the solar images present in the intervals between the seven mountains are likewise all reflected upon the mountain peaks;

in this manner, they are successively and reciprocally reflected. Some say that the solar images emerge from the seven jewel-mountains; some say that the solar images emerge from the intervals between the seven mountains;
some say that the solar images enter the seven jewel-mountains; and some say that the solar images enter the seven mountains.
In the intervals between these [mountains], the shadows of the sun mutually reflect one another without limit; their essential nature is neither existent nor non-existent.
They do not abide in the mountains yet are not separate from the mountains; they do not abide in the waters yet are not separate from the waters. The Commentary states:
"Between the seven-jeweled mountains there are seas of fragrant water; the seas manifest the shadows of the sun, and the mountains, being of pure gold, are likewise able [to reflect them]."

Regarding the manifestation of reflections: when the original reflection on the mountain appears as a reflection in the water, this manifested reflection emerges from the mountain and enters the space between the mountains;

conversely, when the original reflection on the mountain appears as a reflection in the water, this manifested reflection emerges from the space between the mountains and enters the seven-jeweled mountain.
Therefore, at the very moment it enters, it is called "emerging. This is the analogy.
It should be understood that this very shadow, beneath which light reappears infinitely, serves as a metaphor for the Bodhisattva’s body and lands in the Indra-net array (*indrajāla*).

(The *Chao* states: "The ancients established the doctrine of the Indra-net; although the Sūtra contains the name 'Indra-net,' there was no place where it was explained in detail, because previously this chapter of the scripture did not exist. Thus, this passage can serve as authentic proof.")
The Commentary states that "because all phenomena are nothing other than mind" means that every encountered thing is mind.

The phrase "revolving in accordance with the mind" refers to the ancient "Gate of Skillfully Accomplishing Revolutions According to the Mind," which serves as the reason for what follows; its meaning is as previously indicated.

The sub-commentary (*Chao*) states that the capacity of the deluded mind to transform objects serves as an illustration for the true mind by means of the principle of the deluded mind manifesting objects according to the *Faxiang* school.
According to the *Baichao*, it is said: "Just as when a single person’s mind transforms and manifests wood and stone, they mutually obstruct one another;
so too do all sentient beings of the desire realm collectively transform mountains, rivers, the great earth, wood, stone, and so forth."
The characteristics of these transformations vary according to the individual mind; yet they interpenetrate one another like the light of many lamps, which do not obstruct each other.

This means that although they arise from the common seeds of all sentient beings, because their karmic forces are similar and their locations are no different, they mutually encompass and enter into one another.
Thus, the treatise says: "Although the transformations of all sentient beings are distinct, their characteristics..."

It is as if there were no difference in their locations, like the lights of many lamps, each pervading everywhere yet appearing as one. (Regarding the phrase "similar characteristics," this means that through the power of shared karma, the resulting characteristics are similar.

Question: If the transformations produced by many people do not obstruct one another, why is it that the wood and stones transformed by the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) of a single person are indeed obstructive?
Answer: It is because of the presence of both commonality and difference in the seeds perfumed by past karma that such is the case. As it is said:
When the sixth consciousness perceives mountains, rivers, and the great earth, it does not form discriminations of "this" or "that," but merely perfumes their seeds;
therefore, when the subsequent fruits arise, they mutually encompass one another.

As for things such as wood and stone that obstruct one another, this is because when the sixth consciousness perceives them, it invariably forms distinct conceptualizations of "wood," "stone," and so forth, thereby perfuming seeds from which [the subsequent obstruction] arises.
At the time of fruition, each also has its own distinctions; however, we now take only those that do not obstruct one another.

Since even the delusive objects manifested by the delusive mind above can be non-obstructive, how much more so the true dharmas endowed with all virtues manifested by the true mind? This involves two layers:
first, the true mind of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is able to manifest the myriad objects, which are the true dharmas—namely, the ten pairs of essence and phenomena mentioned previously.

Secondly, because one can immediately enter [the state below], and since it is known that the self-nature of these dharmas is solely mind, the ten mysteries are established as interpenetrating and unimpeded (the former section distinguished the causes of dharmas;
this section distinguishes the causes of meanings).
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The two dharmas lack a fixed nature,” etc.: for example, form has resistance as its nature;

since these [two dharmas] now lack such a fixed nature, they are said to be “without a fixed nature. As for the phrase “since it is a manifestation of mind alone,” this follows upon the preceding to introduce what follows.

Regarding the phrase “both nature and characteristics are transcended,” the *Jíxuánjì* states: “Dependent phenomena arise from conditions and are provisional; they have no real substantial nature (*svabhāva*).”
Since they fundamentally lack form, measure, and characteristics, and are likewise unattainable, it is said that they are "separated from both nature and characteristics" and "empty of both.
Therefore, their size is not fixed. The *Xuanjing ji* states: "There is no real, fixed nature;

that is to say, heat is not necessarily heat, moisture is not necessarily moisture, motion is not necessarily motion, and solidity is not necessarily solidity. Furthermore, there are no fixed characteristics; that is to say, length is not necessarily long."

Since short is not fixed as short, large is not fixed as large, and small is not fixed as small, and so forth—because these are phenomena produced through conditions, their nature and characteristics lack fixity;
thus, they interpenetrate one another without any obstruction.

Regarding the phrase "the periphery and the center within one side": the periphery is itself the center, and the center is itself the periphery; this principle applies equally to breadth and narrowness, which are explained as being non-obstructive with respect to a single dharma.
As for the phrase "the extreme limit of the Cakravāḍa mountains," this refers to the Great Iron Ring Mountains surrounding a single trichiliocosm, which are named Cakravāḍa.
Regarding the statement that "the two modes of practice are different," some say these refer to the two modes of practice: the ultimate (paramārtha) and the conventional (saṃvṛti).

Because particular phenomena and particular principles differ from one another, the extremes are not identical to the Middle Way; yet, in terms of their mutual interpenetration, even phenomena and phenomena are unimpeded.
If the True is not identical to the Conventional, this is termed "differentiation"; because they are established through mutual dependence, it is called the "Middle Way of Phenomena.

Because it transcends all marks, it is called the "Middle Way of Principle. That the extremes and the Middle are mutually identical also applies to the unimpededness of phenomena and principle. Now, taking [this perspective]:
The former interpretation states that if the two modes of exiting and entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*) were distinct, they would constitute extremes;
since these two are not fixed as extremes, their middle way is likewise not fixed. Therefore, it is said that phenomena are unimpeded in each particular thing (*shishi wuai*).

Alternatively, if taking accord with principle as the "middle" and non-attachment to the two modes of concentration and distraction as the "extremes," this constitutes the unimpededness of principle and phenomena (*lishi wuai*). These two explanations follow [the respective contexts].

Regarding the phrase "the mutual dependence of the characteristics of conditions" (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa-anyonya-āśraya*) in the Commentary: if the fruit is named after the cause, it is the arising of the condition;
if the cause is named after the fruit, it is the condition for that arising. This is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Dependent origination is precisely this mutual dependence.
Possessing these ten [conditions], the underlying principle is sufficient for it to be so;

this is because the ten are used to manifest perfection. As for the phrase "like external earth, water, and so forth" in the *Chao*: this refers to that which is not the eighth consciousness’s appropriation (*upādāna*).

That is to say, all non-sentient things are termed "external earth, water, and so forth"; taking these as conditions, sprouts and the like arise. (The word "and so forth" includes such conditions as yeast, warmth, and human effort, by which curd arises; or clay serving as a wheel.)
When a potter and other conditions cause a vessel to arise, this is the single external dependent origination (*bāhya-ekārtha-pratītyasamutpāda*).

When consciousness arises with sentient beings possessing cognition as its condition—namely, with ignorance (*avidyā*), volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and so forth as conditions for consciousness and the rest—this is the single internal dependent origination (*ādhyātmika-ekārtha-pratītyasamutpāda*).

Furthermore, all of the above constitute defiled dependent origination (*kliṣṭa-pratītyasamutpāda*); the causes of the Three Vehicles serve as the conditions, while the fruits of the Three Vehicles constitute the arising.
Regarding the name "Pure Dependent Origination" (*viśuddha-pratītyasamutpāda*): the following section first distinguishes from what precedes it and then reveals that which is distinguished.
Therein, the current explanation clarifies the means of distinction, which possesses two meanings: First, the general inclusion. This explains by way of the phenomena of dependent origination;

since the ten preceding pairs encompass all phenomena without exception, they are called "Great. Furthermore, when these are viewed in mutual relation, they are equally dependent origination. This establishes the causes of phenomena.

To distinguish [the two], it is either that many dharmas share a single object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), or—as explained below according to the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)—it is that a single dharma possesses multiple conditions. Because it thus embodies the ten mysteries (*daśa-guhya-dvāra*), it is called "Great" (*mahā*). These mutually serve as conditions for one another, fully possessing the ten gates of mystery; this is based on the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) used for the purpose of distinction. Alternatively, it may mean that a single dharma possesses multiple conditions. This further clarifies that because there are two types of "discriminating capacity," there are likewise two types of "objects discriminated. The former section used the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) to discriminate between internal and external phenomena;
this section uses the meaning of dependent origination to discriminate the three vehicles’ doctrine of the insubstantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*) of dependently arisen things.

If it is insubstantial, it is provisionally "discriminated as conventional" according to the meaning of the teaching on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-dharma*); if it is insubstantial, it is "discriminated as emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) according to the initial [teaching].
If the doctrine were without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it would be like the meaning of "selecting the ultimate" (*zhōngyì*).
This is why the *Chao* (the Sub-commentary) mentions "identical and different natures" and so forth; the *Shidi pin* (Chapter on the Ten Stages) states:

"It encompasses all *pāramitās*, purifies the stages, and [discerns] their general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), identical characteristics (*samalakṣaṇa*), different characteristics (*vilakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of formation (*saṃbhavalakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of destruction (*vibhavalakṣaṇa*). The *Shu* (the Commentary) and *Chao* cite this passage from the *Daśabhūmika*.
The *Dilun* and the *Xianshou* teachings explain that "universal" (*zong*) means one contains many virtues; "particular" (*bie*) means many virtues are not identical;
"identical" (*tong*) means many meanings do not contradict one another; "different" (*yi*) means many meanings are not similar;
"formation" (*cheng*) means dependent origination is established through these various meanings; and "destruction" (*huai*) means the various conditions each abide in their own nature.

Because there is no movement, the distinctness [of the conditions] is destroyed; this refers to the principle of non-dependence within this context. Because the various conditions are each distinct, the collective identity is established;

this refers to the principle of mutual dependence between these two aspects within this context. Regarding the statement that "within the cause, one does not depend on conditions," the *Jiaozhang* (Chapter on Teaching) says:
"The primary cause depending on conditions has only three meanings: first, the cause possesses power... [text continues].

1. Because it arises as its entire substance in dependence upon conditions, it does not depart from the power of conditions; thus, the two causes possess power, for they mutually assist one another in their arising in dependence upon conditions.
2. Because the three causes lack power, they do not produce anything at all in dependence upon conditions; the causes revert to the conditions.

Now, by analogy, if within the causes they were to arise as their entire substance without depending on conditions and were not to depart from the power of conditions, this would mean that they themselves possess inherent virtue—this is the second characteristic.

Because, according to the principle of meaning within the causes, they mutually assist one another by depending on conditions, it is said that "the former is the gate of identical substance" (*tongti men*) and "the latter is the gate of different substance" (*yiti men*).
There are editions that state, "The former is the gate of different substance; the latter is the gate of identical substance.

The meaning of these two is essentially the same and need not be further questioned or explained. According to the present [text], since there is a question and explanation, it should be that "the former is the gate of identical substance."

The phrase "later, it is precisely the distinct entity" (後即異體為正也) is likely a later erroneous emendation. If that were so, the following section constitutes a challenge (*paryanuyoga*). The intent of the challenge is as follows:
If the first case [of identity] means they are of the same substance (*ekadravya*), why does the Commentary (*ṭīkā*) state that "the various conditions are each distinct and do not intermingle"?

If the second case [of difference] means they are of different substances (*nānādravya*), why does the Commentary state that "they must mutually pervade one another for dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) to be established"? This is the meaning of the challenge.

The commentary states: "The contradiction between the *Shu* and the *Chao* is an obstacle. The explanation says: "The following is the response. Its meaning is as follows: It is only by virtue of the various conditions being distinct that they can mutually depend upon one another; therefore, although they are of different entities (*bhinna-svabhāva*), they are also called of the same entity (*eka-svabhāva*). Thus it is said that the first [section] is the gate of the same entity. Furthermore, it is only by virtue of their mutual pervasive correspondence that they are each endowed with their own attributes; therefore, although they are of the same entity, they are also called of different entities. Thus, the second [section] is the gate of the different entity. This is the meaning. Therefore, the two gates of the same and different entities are not contradictory; rather, they are mutually inclusive. This is because the principle of the same entity is established based on the principle of the different entity, and the principle of the different entity is established based on the principle of the same entity. Consequently, the two gates are neither identical nor separate; they are both identical and separate. This is the meaning of the phrase "the two gates are neither identical nor separate. The phrase "subsequently" refers to the gate of distinct entities (or alternatively, this dependent origination possesses two meanings: first, mutual dependence; second, non-mutual dependence). This constitutes their difference. Second, they mutually act as the provider and the recipient.

In the *Sūtra* (*Shu*), from the perspective of the recipient, the various conditions are each distinct entities, yet they mutually pervade and support one another as being of the same entity. In the *Commentary* (*Chao*), from the perspective of the provider, non-mutual dependence is instead treated as the gate of the same entity, while mutual dependence is treated as the gate of distinct entities.

When these two meanings are explained together, the principle is complete. The *Zuanxu Ji* states: "The *Sūtra* explains based on the cause, while the *Commentary* explains based on the result. That the various conditions are each distinct is the 'gate of distinct causes. Because the causes are each distinct, they are able to depend upon one another; thus it is called the 'gate of the same entity. They mutually pervade..."

The "identical substance" (samatā-svabhāva) cause refers to causes that are mutually pervasive; because they do not depend on one another, they are termed "different substance" (bhinnasvabhāva), as they are mutually contradictory.

Thus, among the various conditions, each being distinct, three things arise: first, those that are mutually powerless are called "dependent," because they rely upon others; those that possess power are called "supporting," because they sustain others.

Second, those that are mutually capable of accomplishment are called "having substance" (*savastuka*), because they stand in opposition to that which is accomplished. Third, [they are] mutually... [text fragmentary].

This immediately reveals that the following section takes the "many" and "one" of the "capable of corresponding" (the subject) as its basis. The remaining cases of three, four, and so forth should be understood by analogy with this example.

Regarding the phrase "The *Chao* [states] 'Because this is the totality,' etc.": it is simply because the ten gates of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) establish the preceding ten pairs of essence and phenomenon;
however, it is only when they are subsequently perfected through mutual penetration and interpenetration that they truly constitute dependent origination.

The "Commentary" (Chao) below, under the nine gates, provides examples of interpretation. For instance, the phrase "because by abiding in one, there is universal application" first explains the meaning;
the subsequent statement, "the gate of the freedom between the broad and the narrow," concludes by assigning it to its specific category. All other cases follow this same pattern. Question:

Previously, it was stated that the ten pairs of the broad and the narrow are all [cases of] breadth and narrowness. Now, you speak only of "abiding in one and having universal application. How can there be ten?

In response: Abiding in one [reality], there is nothing that is not subsumed, because it is no different from what was previously stated regarding the identical substance (*samatā-svabhāva*) and its corresponding counterparts.
Regarding the *Chao* (Commentary) stating "separately taking the former, etc.":

since the former universally takes both the gates of mutual inclusion of identical and distinct substances as the gate of mutual inclusion, the present passage takes only one specific gate as the gate of subtlety (*sūkṣma-dvāra*). As for the statement "entry is universal":...
Regarding "subject and object" and so forth: within the gate of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mukha*), that which can contain is the subject (*neng*) and that which is contained is the object (*suo*).

Thus, there are two meanings: the subject that enters and the subject that contains. Now, in the gate of subtlety (*sūkṣma-mukha*), from among these two meanings of containing and entering, only the meaning of containing is taken;
since one subject can contain many objects, it is called "only one half. Question:
[Question: One enters immediately into both the identical and distinct bodies; how is it that the subtle [nature] is exclusively of the distinct body?

Furthermore, if it is said next that the distinct body’s mutual identity possesses concealment and manifestation (*saṃvṛti-vivṛti*), does this not then negate the meaning of concealment and manifestation within the identical body? [Answer:

It should be understood that the phrase "possessing" (*ju*) here refers to the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*). As for the statement in the *Commentary* (*Chao*) that "the principle of identity is like space," it means that space is without characteristics (*animitta*).

That which is manifest is thus called hidden. To say that the two meanings are not destroyed means that because the preceding section discusses merging into existence, one might fear it implies a one-sided view;
therefore, here it is said that while merging, the two meanings remain undestroyed. Thus, at the very moment of merging, there is no "entering" [into non-existence].
They exist simultaneously and together, such that merging and existence are unimpeded and inconceivable. (The *Chao* [Commentary] states: "The same substance mutually enters.")
That "one already contains many" means that the original one already contains many ones.
To say "further entering into different entities" means that the original one further enters into two different entities;

these two different entities already encompass the remaining different entities, and each of those remaining different entities is further associated with many ones of the same entity. Thus, there is the principle of "layer upon layer."
This can be understood through reflection.
This passage from the *Commentary* (*Śāstra*) on the Bodhisattva’s skillful contemplation of dependent origination, within the section on "patience like an illusion" (*māyopama-kṣānti*), states:

"This reveals that the characteristics of illusion have, briefly, two interpretations. First, the interpretation by way of analogy: if one understands that one [phenomenon] lacks reality, then one knows that all are likewise."

However, because both arise from conditions, there are three further meanings regarding the interpretation of their perfect interpenetration (*yuanrong*): First, following the principle according to the phenomenon, one speaks of mutual identity (*xiangji*).
For example, the cloth on the horse’s head is not different from the cloth on its feet; thus, one speaks of the head being identical to the feet. This is "one being identical to many.

Second, through the principle that integrates phenomena, one speaks of the mutual identity of the one and the many. For example, the horse’s head has no separate existence apart from the cloth itself. It is precisely by means of the cloth that [the identity is established].
Because the head and the body are perfectly interfused (*yuanrong*), the head is made identical to the feet; thus it is said that "within one, many are understood.

Thirdly, by the power of the mutual dependence of conditions (*yuanqi xiangyou*), the entire *dharmadhātu* is a single illusory net; therefore, the one and the many are mutually identical. This is like a magician’s illusory arts, which cause the many to be identical to the one, and so forth.

(The Commentary states: "The first [pair] is the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena; the second is the fusion of principle within phenomena. The following two gates concern the meaning of the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena.")

This is the "Gate of the Interfusion of Dharmatā" (the third being the "Gate of the Mutual Dependence of the Characteristics of Dependent Origination"). Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, it says," the verse immediately preceding the sutra text states:
"If one sees the Buddha and one's own body as equal and abides therein, without abiding and without entering anywhere, one shall become one who is difficult to encounter. The commentary explains:
"The final verse reveals that by knowing the Dharma, one accomplishes the preceding Dharma-assembly’s pervasive nature. The first half-line indicates the gate..."
This is the "Gate of the Mutual Interpenetration of the One and the Many" among the Ten Mysterious Gates.

The next phrase explains the reason for this, which corresponds to the "Gate of the Mutual Dependence of Conditions and Arisings" among the ten types of reasons. As explained in the *Yi-fen-zi* (Analysis of the Scope of Meaning), the principle of the Dharmadhātu of Dependent Origination is eternally thus;

if one perceives it in accordance with this, what is there to fear? (In this passage, there is a refutation of the doctrine of the extinction of phenomena, as discussed previously in the ten points of the *Zao-shu*).

1. Regarding "the entire substance," etc.: taking up any single phenomenon, it is entirely of a different substance; the characteristics of mutual inclusion and mutual identity are both fused in terms of substance and function.
2. Regarding "the entire substance is entirely of the same substance": the characteristics of mutual inclusion and mutual identity are both fused in terms of substance and function.
3. Combining the above two phrases: within any single phenomenon, the two meanings of same-substance and different-substance are both manifested simultaneously.
Because the essence of the Dharma is non-dual. [The phrase] "Therefore, by means of wisdom, the principle is revealed" is the concluding summary and explanation.
Since the various principles revealed when wisdom exhaustively investigates the beginning and end of all phenomena differ from one another, ten distinct gates are taught.

When wisdom is discarded and illumination ceases, the raft for revealing the principle becomes such that nothing can be said; yet, whether there is speaking or no speaking, this unimpeded and inconceivable state remains nonetheless a cause.
The phrase "merging into the sea of identical fruition" (men mo tong guo hai) means that speech and thought find no resting place; it can only be established beneath the realm where words cease.

Thus, externally one discards the images of words, and internally one cuts off the seeking of thoughts. This brings one close to the realization described in the *Appended Statements* (*Xici*) of the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyi*), which cites:
"The son of the Yan family was perhaps close to perfection. When he had something unwholesome, he never failed to know of it; and once he knew of it, he never again practiced it."
The commentary states: "Dai" (dài) means perilous; "shujì" (shùjǐ) conveys the sense of "nearby," meaning to be close to the Way.
Now, I urge future students to transcend words and relinquish illumination, so that they may approximate the subtle significance of dependent origination, as did the sages and worthies.
In the fourth section of the Commentary, the "Gate of the Interpenetration of Dharma-nature," the two meanings of dharma-nature are briefly explained: first, "dharma" refers to all phenomena;

second, that which maintains the tracks [of these phenomena] is called "dharma-nature," meaning true nature. These two explanations correspond respectively to the *ādhāra* (locative) and *karmadhāraya* (possessive) interpretations.
The *Chao* (Commentary) states that, as explained below, one relies upon True Suchness (*tathatā*) and its possession of attributes as the cause to explain the name "Gate" (*mukha*).
In the passage beginning with "In the text," there is a separate topical analysis and explanation; the section beginning with "It is known" concludes by refuting alternative interpretations.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "a single phenomenon that is not distinct from principle," the *Chapter on the Merits of Arousing the Mind* says:
"If one wishes to know the differentiated nature of all worlds within a single hair-tip, and the unitary nature of a single hair-tip within all worlds.

The commentary explains: "This is explained by means of the gate of the interpenetration of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), clarifying the reason for the preceding scripture’s statement 'immediately entering,' namely, all worlds..."
Because the differentiation of realms (*dhātu*) and the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of a single hair-tip are non-dual, phenomena (*dharma*) accord with this nature and merge;

thus, this and that are mutually identical. When phenomena embrace this nature, they arise, and this and that are mutually inclusive. Each of these—whether of the same substance (*ekadravya*) or of different substances (*nānādravya*)—should be contemplated according to the above principles.

(Why are they of different substances? Because each individual world-system (*kṣetra*) and so forth has its own distinct body. Why are they of the same substance? Because the bodies of the differentiated realms share one and the same essence. Based on this, we now maintain that it does not contradict reason.

When a single phenomenon fully encompasses the principle of nature, it constitutes the meaning of "identity of substance" (tongti). This causes the many phenomena—which do not differ from that principle—to manifest within the one, according to the principle upon which they depend;
this is the manifestation of "difference of substance" (yiti) in accordance with "identity of substance."

The Commentary states: "Because a single phenomenon now completely encompasses the principle"—here, the single phenomenon is the encompassing agent (*grāhaka*) and the principle is the encompassed (*grāhya*.

To say that "all phenomena are brought into a single phenomenon" means that the principle is the bringing agent (*nāyaka*) and the entry agent (*praveśaka*), while all phenomena are the brought object (*neya*) and the entered object (*praveśya*).
The single phenomenon, conversely, becomes the object of entry.

The *Chao* (Commentary) now states, "The true principle is profound and still," and so forth, to follow and clarify the statement. If one were to negate this fault, it would be negating the fault of this true principle being divisible;

thus, it is said that "the fault is even more profound. This means that although previously the true principle was divided [into phenomena], it did not fall into the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism;

yet now, if one posits a principle apart from phenomena, then phenomena would fall into the extreme of eternalism and the principle would fall into the extreme of annihilationism—therefore, it is a fault.
Nothing is greater than this.
Regarding the division of the meaning of the ten gates into [sections] below, the first is the "preface to the text" (*pūrvamukha*).

It is said that the eighth dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) and so forth refers to the *Śāstra* (Commentary), which states: "True" (*bhūta*) means reality, indicating it is not false; "as" (*tathā*) means as-it-is, signifying...

This Dharma-character school (lakṣaṇa-vāda) maintains that there is no change; whereas the Dharma-nature school (dharmatā-vāda) speaks of "non-changing as the True" and "following conditions as the Such.

Because it does not change, it has the sense of being non-identical with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); because it follows conditions, it has the sense of being non-different from conditioned phenomena.
Regarding the arising of faith: "Non-dispelling is called 'True' (*tathatā*); non-establishing is called 'Such' (*tathā*). Only this.
By means of apophatic negation (*paryudāsa*), the ultimate truth is revealed instantaneously. Furthermore, Guifeng said: "True" (*zhen*) means reality;
"as it is" (*ru*) means resemblance. Within form, there is a resemblance to reality; within sensation, there is such true similarity. Other dharmas cannot truly resemble this.
Thus, this scripture’s hundred gates harmonize principle and phenomena, making them infinitely layered and inexhaustible. The phrase "one analogy" serves as a metaphor for this.
As the *Zhēnrú* (The True Suchness) sub-commentary states: "While manifestations differ according to their meanings, their substance is fundamentally and eternally integrated.

Merely by realizing the One Suchness (*ekayāna*), one naturally encompasses all virtues; it is not through deliberate effort that one accords with the differentiated aspects. Since the capacity for dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is itself integrated and unobstructed, it is called 'arising from Suchness.
The very substance of this arising practice is Suchness itself. Yet, even those who believe in the virtues of Suchness still remain deluded regarding dedication."
Therefore, because the virtue of suchness (*tathatā*) is used as a metaphor for the virtue of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), it is said:
"For example, just as suchness is equal to all phenomena"—this refers to the thirty-eighth virtue—and "inseparable"—this refers to the forty-fifth virtue.
To state it fully: "For example, just as suchness is inseparable from all phenomena; since suchness is [inseparable] from all..."

Regarding "correspondence with phenomena" (*dharmasamprayoga*): as previously stated, since a single lotus petal possesses the sense of being non-different from principle, it likewise corresponds equally with all phenomena, such that all phenomena are fully present.
Thus, each of the nine gates below and the ten pairs of dharmas contained within those gates possesses the meaning of correspondence; this is what is meant by "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*).
They are "simultaneous" because they do not abandon one another, being fully conjoined and lacking any sequence of before or after;

this serves as the gateway through which one enters by means of skillful methods (*upāya*). (In this commentary, two virtues are used in secret to form a single gate; the following sections are to be understood accordingly). Second, the analogy:
as stated in full below, "For example, in True Suchness (*tathatā*), the nature of all phenomena is eternally equal. This corresponds to the thirtieth [verse].
The forty-third virtue, "the nine virtues universally encompassing all phenomena," is "broad" because it is pure and equal like the petals of a lotus flower;
it is "narrow" because it is specific, as all phenomena are universally encompassed within these flower petals without their distinct characteristics being destroyed.
It is called the "Gate of Unobstructed Freedom between Broad and Narrow" because it possesses both breadth and narrowness simultaneously; thus, it is said to be "inherent."
In this context, it is said that there is no obstruction regarding depth, breadth, narrowness, purity, or mixture. ▲ Third, "nowhere not present" (wusuobuzai):
the full text below states, "For example, True Suchness (Tathatā) is nowhere not present," which refers to the sixty-first virtue. The Commentary (*Shu*) states:
"Following each and every phenomenon, [the essence] is entirely present within them; even the fused lotus leaf is nowhere not present, entering into and abiding within non-existence."
Because they are distinct. ▲ Fourth, "not separate from all dharmas" (below, fully stated as: "For example, True Suchness is not separate from all dharmas") refers to the fortieth virtue;
"sharing its essential nature with all dharmas" refers to the forty-fourth virtue.
"Fusing the lotus leaf so it is not separate from all dharmas" means that the one is identical to the many, sharing the same essential nature as all dharmas.
Because all phenomena are detached from [inherent existence], they accord with suchness; thus, what is pervasive across a single leaf is identical to that which is manifold.
Regarding the fifth point, "having no limitations," the commentary cites a sutra: "For example, True Suchness (tathatā) pervades all places without boundary or limit.
This refers to the first virtue. Here, the sub-commentary (*shu-wen*) employs only this single virtue to establish the Gate of Manifestation and Concealment (*yin-xian men*).

It is said that because luminosity (*prakāśa*) manifests within conditions, there is nothing that does not pervade; and because clarity and concealment manifest as "being here" and "being there," it constantly maintains its fundamental nature.
This refers to the third quality. The Commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "Luminosity following conditions means it is not pervasive. It says "maintaining the fundamental nature":

because clarity manifests while remaining within conditions, the lotus flower is manifested; because concealment remains within conditions, the lotus leaf is concealed. Thus, all phenomena [manifest or conceal accordingly].

"For example, like true suchness (*tathatā*), it is ultimately inexhaustible among all dharmas. This refers to the forty-first virtue. The commentary (*śāstra*) states:
"It is precisely within the dharmas that it is taken as inexhaustible, like the space within a mustard seed. Therefore, even the lotus leaf is fused [with it].

The first month is the sixty-fourth virtue. Regarding the term "years," the Sūtra says: "For example, True Suchness pervades years and ages";
