The continuous flow and scattering [of defilements] without interruption is termed "outflow" (*āsrava*). Just as a leaking vessel or a leaking house is deeply loathsome, so too these [defilements] are damaging, polluting, extensive, and blameworthy;

thus they are established under the name of "outflows. There are three: first, the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*); second, the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*); and third, the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
These take as their essence the primary afflictions and secondary afflictions (*anuvyañjana-kleśa*) of the three realms. Although the afflictions of the three realms should [collectively] be named...

They are called "outflows" (*āsrava*) because they leak out into the three realms of existence. Since the afflictions of the lower realms mostly take the desire realm as their object, they are designated by their predominant characteristic as "desire-outflows" (*kāmāsrava*).
In the upper realms, they are simply called "existence-outflows" (*bhavāsrava*), and are not characterized by other dharmas;

thus, they are termed "ignorance-outflows" (*avidyāsrava*). These are the explanations of the names according to the Ci'en (Kuiji) school. If one were to establish their essential nature (*svabhāva*) according to the Nature School (Xingzong), then it is the faculties... [text ends].

Fundamentally, because one does not realize [the nature of mind], the three subtle and six coarse [evolutions] are not distinguished, nor are the differences between the seeds and manifestations of the three realms.

Through delusion, all is defiled; through awakening, all is pure. Because there is no inherent substance or nature, in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), when deluded, everything within the entire dharma-realm—whether sentient or insentient—is entirely outflowing (sāsrava);
when awakened, as mentioned above, it is entirely non-outflowing (anāsrava). Thus it is the conditionality of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.

The "Chapter on Arising in Equality" states: "In terms of the gate of sentient beings, both Buddhas and ordinary beings are all realms of arising and ceasing, existence and non-existence, good and evil.
This is because their emotional conceptualizations have not been shattered; thus, the Buddhas they perceive are likewise identical to those conceptualizations.

One has never seen a single Buddha who is pure. Therefore, when consciousness is inverted, the Buddha is also inverted; when the mind is deluded, the Buddha is also deluded. This is discussed in relation to the Buddha."
Sentient beings and Buddhas are both fundamentally empty and quiescent; this is because all emotional conceptualizations have been exhausted and names and marks have already been forgotten.

Since that which is perceived as empty and quiescent is identical to that of all Buddhas, one has never seen any sentient being transmigrating. Because the Buddha-mind is pure, sentient beings are also pure;
it is only the mind that revolves. Critique: According to this, one should not say "this."
"These are with outflows; these are without outflows.
Regarding the various masters of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* mentioned in the *Chao*, they are the aforementioned masters such as Nanda, Guṇamati, Sthiramati, Prajñākaragupta, and Viśeṣamitra.
As for the statement "the author of this treatise," it refers to [one of] these ten masters; there was not one among them who did not teach the Dharma.
There is nothing that does not explain this Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "the gathering and manifestation," the *Shuchao* states there are two interpretations: first, it means that when hearing the Dharma, the five consciousnesses arise in succession;
because many syllables arise together, this is called "gathering. Because one understands clearly and distinctly, this is called "manifestation."
Second, it is said that the seeds perfumed by hearing are stored within the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and are termed "accumulation" (*caya*).

When subsequent syllables are heard, they bring along the mental images (*nimitta*) of the previously heard syllables, which gather and reside in the present; this is termed "manifestation" (*vyañjana*), because it causes the sixth consciousness to produce a mind of correct understanding by making the signified meaning appear upon the consciousness.

Regarding the "explanation of continuity" (*liàn-dài-jie*) concerning "arising" (*shēng*), the *Shè-chāo* states: "The preceding mind can induce the succeeding mind, and the succeeding mind continues from the preceding mind;

this is called 'continuity' (*lián*). The succeeding mind can recollect the preceding mind and brings forth the marks of the preceding [state]; this is called 'bringing along' (*dài*). Clearly awakening to the principle is called 'arising through understanding' (*jiě-shēng*).
This very mind of understanding, grasping what has been heard, is called 'equal permeation by marks' (*děng-xiāng-xūn*), which forms seeds as the essence of the teaching."

Furthermore, it is explained that when one hears the various preceding characters, seeds have already been perfumed; now, upon hearing the character *xing* (行), the manifestations arise carrying the images of the preceding characters.
These combine with the image of the subsequent character within a single moment, simultaneously grasping the images of both characters to again perfume seeds.

This continues until one hears the character *chang* (常), where the manifestations arise carrying the images of the three preceding characters, which then combine with the subsequent character *chang*.
Because the mutual influence causes the sixth consciousness to produce correct understanding, it is called "arising through association" (*sānubandha-udaya*).

This means that when the subsequent syllable is heard, it brings along the preceding mental images (*nimitta*) and gives rise to the active manifestation (*pravṛtti-vijñapti*), which then combines with the images of the subsequent syllables to produce an understanding of the specific characteristics of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*).
This is termed "arising through association. It perfumes seeds to serve as the essence of the teaching (*deśanā-svabhāva*).
Regarding the three masters in the *Commentary* (*Chao*), the first master holds that if one takes the sudden auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) as the first,
the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as the second, the seeking [consciousness] as the third, and the determining [consciousness] as the fourth,
then each of these four stages would possess four minds, resulting in sixteen. Now, when it says there are twelve, it should be understood that the sudden auditory consciousness is treated as one.

At that time, the auditory consciousness and the mental consciousness combine to form a single mind, because the simultaneous auditory consciousness and the sudden (rate-er) mental consciousness are collectively termed "mind" (*citta*).
[Having already grasped the general meaning, we shall now explain it point by point. Regarding the phrase "when pronouncing various syllables," etc.:

the sudden auditory consciousness and the simultaneous sudden mental consciousness are both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and since they take only sound as their object, they combine to form a single mind.
Question: Since the consciousness that seeks (*paryeṣaka-manovijñāna*) is an inference (*anumāna*), why does it not take the name (*nāman*) as its object?

The answer provided below explains this from the perspective of the second moment of consciousness. The meaning is as follows: although the second-moment consciousness investigates this sound over many moments, because it does not yet know what various syllables (*akṣara*) refer to, it does not take the name of the syllables as its object.
Regarding these two types of mind, they are the *ābhoga* (sudden/impulsive) and the *paryeṣaka* (seeking) [minds].
Regarding the inquiry into the two minds, there is a source that states "three minds," which is an erroneous transcription.
If there were three such minds, and each were determined to be fourfold, with four characters for each, there would necessarily be sixteen; yet now there are only twelve minds in the sūtra.

Therefore, we know that the *sūr-er* (initial sudden) consciousness and the simultaneous mental consciousness (*yǔshí yìshì*) are combined into one mind. This [reading of] "two characters" is correct. This is also...
To resolve an external objection, it is asked: "Since these two minds have already transformed the sounds into phonemes (*akṣara*), why do they not take them as their objects?
To this, the answer is given: "It is like the characteristics of arising and so forth. This is stated by providing an example to establish the point:

when visual consciousness and other such cognitions perceive form and other sense-objects, although the characteristics of arising, abiding, and change (*sthiti-anyathātva*) exist upon those forms and so forth...

The four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are extinguished and no longer serve as objects; now it is the same here: although the transformed sound possesses phonemes and names, these are not taken as objects, but rather only the sound itself is taken as the object.

*Shu-chao* (Commentary), Vol. 1, states: "The ear-consciousness of sudden encounter (*sūry-er*) and the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)"—this refers to the intention of the second master, who distinguishes the ear-consciousness of sudden encounter and the simultaneous mental consciousness as two separate entities.
Because the mind of certainty (*niścaya-citta*) must be excluded, there are also twelve moments of mind (*citta*), making fourteen phases (*lakṣaṇa*).

It is only when there is no distraction regarding these that the mind of certainty arises. As for the statement "seeking" (*paryeṣaka*) and so forth, it also refers to the reason why syllables and names are the objects of cognition;

this is because it is an inference (*anumāna*). Regarding the statement that "the four phases appear at the third, sixth, and ninth [moments]," it means that when one hears various syllables, there is sound.
When one hears the word "name" (*nāman*), there are three aspects; together with the previous [three], this makes six. When one hears the word "non-word" (*an-akṣara*), there are also three aspects;
together with the previous, this becomes nine. When one hears the word "permanent" (*nitya*), there are likewise three aspects;

combined with the previous, this totals twelve. Together with the single phrase and its meaning, there are fourteen aspects. The subsequent cases should all be understood accordingly. — *Commentary* (Chao)
One interpretation states that the sudden ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) merely takes sound as its object; this is the view of the third master.

Within this, there are two sub-explanations. The first explanation also includes the "seeking" mind (*paryeṣaka-citta*) in the count, resulting in twelve types of consciousness, which differs from the latter explanation.

However, the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) also takes the syllables and names as its objects, which differs from the second master mentioned previously. Question: Since... [text ends]

At the same time, one might ask: why is it necessary for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) to engage in four types of investigation when it takes the name associated with the syllable as its object?

The answer is given below: although the mental consciousness takes the name associated with the syllable as its object, it cannot yet form a continuous connection because it is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

It is only upon reaching the stage of investigative thought—that is, through inference (*anumāna*)—that it can finally establish a continuous connection and attain completeness. This second interpretation is not accepted.
Because they are sought as a specific number, there are only eight consciousnesses.

Since it is admitted that the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) can function through inference (*anumāna*) to take past phenomena as its object, and since it takes past phenomena as its object, would one not admit that it possesses the quality of continuity (*sambandha*)?

Therefore, there are only eight consciousnesses. The section beginning with "Simultaneous" provides a question and answer based on the first interpretation. The intent of the question is as follows: [the mental consciousness...]

Question: Since this is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and its occurrence is extremely rapid, how can it take as its object a word (*nāman*) or a name (*saṃjñā*)? Answer: The intended meaning can be understood;
this should be reconciled with the *Nyāyamukha* (Introduction to Logic) regarding the resolution of contradictions.

As for the statement, "because one does not take as an object the mutual connection between the name and the referent (*artha*)," this means that one does not take as an object the name or the like insofar as they are connected to a referent, but rather takes as an object the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the name itself; therefore, it is said [that there is no contradiction].
Regarding "being bound" (*pratisaṃyukta*): for instance, all names are bound to their referents (*artha*).

Because they cannot be cognized due to the rapidity of time, they are not [perceived] as being bound to their referents, such as names and so forth. However, the four explanations—general and specific—outlined above proceed from the dull toward the sharp;

this sequence of shame (*hrī*) is logical, and it accords with the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-ṭīkā-pradīpa* (The Lamp Commentary on the Treatise on Consciousness-Only), which recounts the exegesis of the Western masters.
Although these are the same, not all are taken as the primary [reading].

As for the *Chao* (Commentary), it possesses one hundred and five characteristics; however, the text of the *Chao* is now obscure and abbreviated, so we shall provide a complete explanation according to the *Fayuan*.

Regarding the statement that there are two characteristics when pronouncing the character "zhū" (諸): the *Fayuan* says that when pronouncing the character "zhū," other [consonants] such as "è" (惡) and so forth...
The characters are all in the future; there is only a single character and the name formed based on that single character which appears before the mind.
This is the meaning of a single character forming a name. There are also cases where a single character does not form a name, but these are not what is being clarified here.

(Regarding these characters, there are two aspects: one refers to the individual characters, and the other refers to the individual names. *Qiyuanji* says: "This is explained provisionally according to the ritual procedure; every character is a name, and this is the first [point]. )

Regarding the statement that "the letters have not yet gathered because the subsequent letters to be spoken are unknown," or alternatively, that they are spoken as a gathering because a single letter consists of multiple moments: when the letter *a* (惡) is subsequently uttered, there are seven characteristics.
The *Fayuan* states: "When the word 'evil' (*akuśala*) is spoken, the other letters are all in the future;

although the preceding letters have entered the past, they currently lack a substantial essence. Nevertheless, by the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*) and the power of the transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*), [they still appear]."

When this mindfulness pronounces the syllable *pā* (evil), it appears upon the mind (the following should be understood accordingly): there are two instances of the single syllable (one is the syllable *pa*, the other is the syllable *pā*);

one instance of the body of a syllable (one is the body of the syllable *pa*, [and one is the body of the syllable *pā*]; since a "body of a syllable" is constituted only from the second syllable onward, all subsequent cases should be understood accordingly);

and two instances of the name formed by the single syllable (one is the name *pa*, the other is the name *pā*); one instance of the body of a name formed by the single syllable (combining with the preceding [syllables] *pa* and *pā*...).

The second is called the "name-body" (*nāmakāya*). The *Xiàchão* (Lower Excerpts) states: "From the second [character] onwards, they are termed 'name-bodies. 'Body' (*kāya*) has the meaning of an aggregate. All subsequent instances should be understood accordingly. A single name-body is formed by two characters;
(this combines with the preceding single name-body formed by the two characters "zhū-è"). Next, regarding the character "yán" (言), there are sixteen aspects. The *Fǎyuàn* (Dharma Garden) states:
"Furthermore, at the time of the character 'yán,' there are three instances of the single character 'yī' (the characters 'zhū', 'è', and 'yán'), two instances of the 'name-body' (one being...)"

Regarding "all evils" (*sarvapāpa*), the term "two" refers to the combination of two [syllables]. The subsequent cases should be understood accordingly, as they cannot be formed by skipping over intervening elements.
There is no such thing as a "single syllable" combined with the "body of names" (*nāmakāya*). (The above constitutes five aspects.

A single "three-syllable body" or "multi-syllable body" (*bahuvyañjanakāya*)—that is, the three syllables of *sarva-pā-pa* combined to form a multi-syllable body, since it is only from one syllable onward that there is a "multi-syllable" entity. (This constitutes six aspects. Three instances of a "single-syllable formation" (the various syllables...).

The "name" (nāman), the "named" (nāmika), and the "name of the named" (nāman-nāmika)—these three constitute the third category [of the nine aspects]. Two single syllables (*akṣara*) form what is called a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*);

as with the aforementioned "syllable-body" (*vyañjanakāya*), these two are explained in pairs. (The two names for "evil," the one name-body for "evil," and the one name-body for the "name of the named"—together with the preceding, these constitute eleven aspects.

One single syllable forms what is called a "multiple-name-body" (*bahunāmakāya*). (Including the preceding "various syllables," the "name of evil," the "name of the named," and the "name of the name of the named" as one multiple-name-body, they total twelve aspects.)

Although there are two theories in the treatise, we now adopt the view that three syllables constitute a "name" (*nāman*) and multiple [names] constitute a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*), rather than four syllables;

the subsequent cases should be understood accordingly. (The *Qiyuan ji* states: "In the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are two masters' explanations: one says that from three names upward is a 'multitude of names' (*bahunāman*); the other says that from four names upward is a 'multitude of names.

As for those consisting of three names, they are subsumed under 'name-body' alone; here we rely on the former interpretation. Furthermore, the names formed by two pairs of two syllables are also explained as being combined in twos (that is, all...).

The two characters "evil" (*akuśala*) constitute one name; the two characters "one who is evil" (*akuśalin*) constitute another name. Together they form fourteen *lakṣaṇas* (phases). Question: How does this differ from the "body" (*kāya*)? Answer: This refers only to the explanation of a single intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The "body," however, discusses the union of both the nature and its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Question: What is the difference between a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*) and a "phrase" (*pada*)? Answer: A "phrase" discusses only a single differentiation, whereas the intrinsic nature of a "name-body" still consists of two elements. One element is that which is formed by two characters, called a "name-body.
(Combined with the previous two—namely, the two names "all evils" and "one who is evil"—they form one "body," making fifteen. One element is that which is formed by three characters.

The name [“all evils” (*sarvapāpāni*)] consists of three syllables and thus forms one name, making sixteen [syllables in total]. Next, when the syllable *ma* is uttered, there are thirty characteristics. The *Fayuan* states:

“Furthermore, when saying *ma*, there are four instances of the single syllable [i.e., the syllable *sa*, the syllable *pa*, the syllable *a*, and the syllable *ma*, which constitute four characteristics].

Regarding the three word-bodies (*padakāya*), they are also explained in pairs; this should be understood according to the previous principle (namely, that the word-body of ‘all,’ the word-body of ‘evils,’ and the word-body of ‘ma’ form seven characteristics).”

Two three-syllable multi-syllabic bodies (the *nāma-kāya* "those who do evil" and the multi-syllabic body "do not [be] evil," combined as three sets of three, mutually excluding the first and last syllables;
these constitute nine aspects). One four-syllable multi-syllabic body (the four syllables "those who do evil, do not" form one multi-syllabic body, constituting ten aspects).
Four single-syllable designations (the designations "those who do evil," "evil," "name," and "non-name," constituting fourteen aspects).

The term "name-body" (*nāmakāya*) refers to that which is formed by three single-syllable units; it is explained as a combination of two pairs (referring to the various "evil name-bodies," where "evil" refers to the name-body and "name-body" refers to the non-name-body, totaling seventeen aspects).
The term "phrase-body" (*padakāya*) refers to that which is formed by two single-syllable units;

it is explained as a combination of three triplets, with the first and last syllables mutually excluded (referring to the various "evil phrase-bodies," where "evil" refers to the phrase-body and "phrase-body" refers to the non-phrase-body, totaling three names). Including the aforementioned [name-body], it constitutes...
(19) One name consisting of one syllable is called a *pada* or a *nāmakāya*. (This refers to the four names: "mā," "pāpa," "kārī," and "mā. This constitutes the twentieth characteristic.

Three names consisting of two syllables each are called [a group of names] formed by combining pairs; that is, the two syllables "mā pā" form the name "pāpa," the two syllables "pā kār" form the name "kārī," and the two syllables "rī mā" form the name "mā.
(This constitutes the twenty-third characteristic. Two names consisting of two syllables each are called a *nāmakāya*; that is, the combination of "mā pā" and "pā kār" [forms a single name].

Two [syllables] form one *nāmakāya*: combining the preceding two syllables "evil" (*akuśala*) and "one who is evil" (*akuśalī*), along with the two syllables "and" (*ca*) and "do not" (*mā*), forms one single three-syllable *nāmakāya*, resulting in twenty-five characteristics.

Three syllables formed by two [units]: when names consisting of three syllables mutually exclude the first and last syllables (i.e., from the name consisting of the three syllables "all evils and one who is evil," the term "evil" [is removed]).

The name formed by the three characters "zhě mò" (者莫), combined with the preceding [elements], constitutes twenty-eight characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). A single name formed by three characters is called a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*);

together with the two names formed by the previous three characters, this constitutes one name-body, forming twenty-nine characteristics. A single name formed by four characters—referring to the name formed by the four characters "zuò è zhě mò" (作惡者莫)—constitutes thirty characteristics in total.
Regarding the fifty characteristics that occur when the character "zuò" (作) is subsequently chanted, the *Fayuan* states: "Furthermore, it says..."
When forming the characters, there are five instances of the single character (the characters *zhū* [諸], *è* [惡], *zì* [字], *mò* [莫], and *zuò* [作] constitute these five aspects).

There are four instances of "character-bodies" (*zìshēn*), meaning two pairs spoken together (namely, the character-bodies of *zhū*, *è*, *zì*, and *mò*; together with the preceding, these constitute nine aspects).

There are three instances of "three-character bodies," namely *duō* [多] (the three-character body of *zhū*, *è*, *zì*; the three-character body of *è*, *mò*, *zì*; and the three-character body of *mò*, *zuò*, *zì*; these complete twelve aspects).

Two instances of four-syllable polysyllabic bodies (referring to the four-syllable polysyllabic body "Do not do evil" [mā pāpaṃ kārṣīḥ] and the four-syllable polysyllabic body "One who does evil" [yaḥ pāpaṃ karoti], making fourteen aspects);

one instance of a five-syllable polysyllabic body (referring to the five syllables "Do not do evil" [mā pāpaṃ kārṣīḥ] as a single polysyllabic body; including the aforementioned syllables, syllabic bodies, and polysyllabic bodies, there are fifteen aspects);

five instances of names formed by single syllables (referring to the name of the syllable "all," the name of the syllable "evil," the name of the syllable "one who," the name of the syllable "do not," and the name of the syllable "do," making twenty aspects).
Four instances of a single syllable form what is called a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*); this refers to two pairs being spoken together (i.e., "Do not commit various evil name-bodies";

"evil" is the name-body, and "do not" is the name-body; thus, the name-body is formed as twenty-four aspects). Three instances of a single syllable form what is called a "name-group" (*nāmagrāma*) or "name-body";

this refers to three sets of three being spoken together (i.e., "Do not commit various evil name-groups"; "evil" is the name-group, and "do not" is the name-group; "name-group" is the name-body; thus, it is formed as twenty-seven aspects).
Two instances of single-syllable names forming four instances of multiple-syllable names;

mutually excluding the first and last single syllables (i.e., the four instances of *mā pāpam* forming a multiple-syllable name and the four instances of *mā kārṣīḥ pāpam* forming another multiple-syllable name, constituting twenty-nine aspects).

One instance of a single-syllable name forming five instances of multiple-syllable names (i.e., the five instances of *mā pāpam* forming a single multiple-syllable name, constituting thirty aspects). Four instances of two-syllable names.

The term "derived name" (*nāmakṛta*) refers to the combined utterance of two pairs [of syllables] (e.g., as in the phrase "all evils," "evil-doer," "do not do evil," which constitutes thirty-four phonemes).
Three instances of two-syllable units form what is called a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*): 1. Combining the two-syllable unit "all evils" with the two-syllable unit "evil-doer" forms one name-body;

2. Combining the two-syllable unit "evil-doer" with the two-syllable unit "do not" forms one name-body; 3. Combining the two-syllable unit "do not" with the two-syllable unit "do not do" forms one name-body. Thus, there are thirty-seven phonemes. Two [instances of this].

Two characters forming a name constitute three or more names, termed a "body" (kāya). (1) Combining the two-character name "all evils" (zhū è), the two-character name "evil ones" (è zhě), and the two-character name "do not" (biàn mò), they form one body of three or more names.

(2) Combining the two-character name "evil ones" (è zhě), the two-character name "do not" (biàn mò), and the two-character name "do not do" (mò zuò), they form one body of three or more names. This results in thirty-nine aspects.

One instance of two characters forming a name constitutes four or more names, termed a "body" (i.e., combining the preceding two-character name "all evils" [zhū è] and the two-character name "evil ones" [è zhě]...).

Regarding the names of the syllables: the two syllables *mo* and *ma* are treated as a single name; thus, there are four names for the multiple syllables, which together constitute forty phonetic characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

The names formed by three triplets of syllables—namely, the name formed by the three syllables *sarva-pāpam*, the name formed by the three syllables *na kuryāt*, and the name formed by the three syllables *ma kārṣīt*—constitute forty-three phonetic characteristics.

The names formed by two triplets of syllables constitute a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*): namely, the name formed by the three syllables *sarva-pāpam* taken together, and the name formed by the three syllables *na kuryāt*.

The resulting name is called a *nāmakāya* (name-group). 1. "Mò zhě mò" (莫者莫) consists of three characters; the resulting name is called a *pada* (phrase). 2. "Jí zhě mò zuò" (及者莫作) consists of three characters; the resulting name is called a *nāmakāya*. 3.

Calculating these four and five characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there is one instance of a three-character resulting name being a *bahuvrīhi-nāmakāya* (many-name-group)—that is, combining the previously mentioned three-character resulting name "zhě è zhě" (者惡者), the three-character resulting name "jí zhě mò" (及者莫), and the three-character resulting name "biàn zhě mò zuò" (便者莫作)—which constitutes one three-character *bahuvrīhi-nāmakāya* with forty-six characteristics. 4. There are two instances of four-character resulting names. Furthermore...

Mutually omitting one character from the beginning and one from the end (that is, taking the four characters "all evils do not" [sarvapāpāni na kuryāt] as one unit and the four characters "do not commit evil" [pāpaṃ na kuryāt] as another unit constitutes forty-eight aspects).

Taking one set of four characters as a single unit constitutes a *nāmakāya* (that is, combining the previously mentioned four characters "all evils do not" with the four characters "do not commit evil" to form a single *nāmakāya*, which constitutes forty-nine aspects).
Taking one set of five characters as a single unit (that is, the five characters "all evils do not commit" [sarvapāpāni na kuryāt] as one).

Regarding the names: the aforementioned names (*nāman*), name-bodies (*nāmakāya*), and multiple name-bodies (*bahunāmakāya*) total thirty-five; when combined with the fifteen phonemes (*vyañjana*) and so forth, there are fifty characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in total. When added to the preceding [categories], they collectively constitute one hundred and five characteristics.
Question: According to the *Fayuan*, this is explained based on the completion of a single sentence (*pada*).

Since the phonemes, names, phrases, and sounds together constitute a total aggregate of fifty-one, how can there be one hundred and five characteristics? Answer: This is because... [the text continues from here].
When the five syllables of "Śrī" (Real) are fully heard, one sentence is excluded, leaving fifty characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Here, the method is established based on doubling and further doubling; since this also includes the "repeated" [syllables], there are one hundred and five characteristics.

However, the two full verses mentioned above—"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent" (*sarvasaṃskārā anityāḥ*) and "One should not commit any evil" (*sarvapāpasyākaraṇam*)—are as they appear in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
The *Madhyama Āgama* states: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they possess the nature of arising and ceasing. Since what is born must perish, their tranquility is bliss.
The subsequent verse says: "Commit no evil; practice all that is good; thoroughly subdue your own mind—this is the holy teaching of all Buddhas."
The Commentary states that these five minds distinguish their respective differences. According to the *Fayuan*, they are as follows:

first, the impulsive mind (*ābhoga-citta*), which arises when encountering an unfamiliar object and is not accompanied by desire; second, the seeking mind (*paryeṣaka-citta*), which operates in conjunction with desire because it seeks after an object;

third, the determining mind (*niścaya-citta*), which confirms and understands the object because it is accompanied by resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*); fourth, the defiled or pure mind (*kliṣṭa-śubha-citta*).

Those associated with faith and so forth are called "wholesome" (kuśala) and "pure" (viśuddha); those associated with hatred and so forth are called "unwholesome" (akuśala) and "defiled" (kliṣṭa). Because the intermediate state of neutrality is neither defiled nor pure, it is not included here.

Regarding the five types of mind-streams, the term "initial" refers to the first moment and "subsequent" refers to the later moments, because they flow equally from the preceding state as a similar outflow (niṣyanda).

The phrase "initial and subsequent" distinguishes between the various consciousnesses based on whether they are "sudden" (ābhoga) or "outflowing" (niṣyanda); the "sudden" mind is termed "initial," while the "outflowing" mind is termed "subsequent."
The six consciousnesses all possess [the five mental factors of] seeking (*paryeṣaka*), determination (*niścita*), and defiled or pure states; these are termed the "three intermediate minds.

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, these exist only in the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*). In reality, however, all six consciousnesses possess these five minds.

The seventh and eighth consciousnesses possess only four, as they lack the mind of seeking because it is not associated with desire (*chanda*). This is stated in reference to both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states.
Furthermore, regarding the previous three [categories] and the subsequent three natures (*trisvabhāva*), this selection is made solely based on the state of being with outflows (*sāsrava*);

in the state without outflows (*anāsrava*), everything is designated as wholesome. Moreover, regarding the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*) that arise suddenly (*ābhoga*), they are selected as being indeterminate;

furthermore, regarding the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the two types of sudden arising are distinguished and both can be known. For the remaining meanings, they are explained extensively in other chapters.
This has been explained extensively through twelve gates in the "Chapter on the Five Minds" in the first fascicle of the *Dharmāyana*.

I shall not cite it here at length. Question: Why is it necessary to distinguish these five minds? Answer: It is to cause one to understand the stages of the mind so as to enter into the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and the characteristics of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Only shadows, without a basis,” the *Awakening of Faith* says: “The Buddhas and Tathāgatas are solely the body of the Dharma-body and the aspect of wisdom;
they are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and possess no realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). They are free from purposeful activity.

The sub-commentary on this states: “If one sets aside the response of the faculties [of sentient beings], then the Tathāgata is merely the wondrous principle of fundamental wisdom, with no further manifested or transformed bodies in the world.”

The *Satyadvayavibhaṅga* (Discourse on the Characteristics of Arising and Ceasing, etc. further states: "It is merely according to the seeing and hearing of sentient beings that they obtain benefit," and so forth.
The verse from the *Yāmaka* (Night-Moving) says: [Omitted]. The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "This verse explains a doubt. The doubt asks:

Is it because there is a dharma that cannot be heard, or is it because there is no dharma that can be spoken? The first half [of the verse] answers by following the latter part of the doubt. Next, the doubt asks: "If..."
"Why do you claim to have personally heard the teaching? The second half of the explanation states: "It is merely a transformation of one's own mind; it is not something realized by a Buddha.
Furthermore, the *Mahādharmolkā-dhāraṇī-sūtra* says: "Because sentient beings harbor the notion that dharmas exist, the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma for them;
yet in reality, the Tathāgata has nothing at all to preach. [Commentary: Regarding Nāgamitra and Sthiramati—Nāgamitra... (text incomplete)
To explain further, the Sanskrit name for Jianhui (堅慧) is *Varamati*, which translates as "Firm Wisdom.

According to tradition in the Western Regions, he was the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha appearing in the world seven hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, born into the great Kṣatriya caste in Central India.

He subsequently composed such works as the *Ratnagotravibhāga-mahāyānottaratantra-śāstra* (The Treatise on the Ultimate One Vehicle Nature of Jewels) and the *Dharmadhātunirviśeṣa-śāstra* (The Treatise on the Non-differentiation of the Dharmadhātu).
The commentary states, "It is not merely that outside the mind... and so forth; this is an explanation according to the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao). "Merely" (*zhí*) means "only.
It is not only that there is no Buddha-form outside the minds of sentient beings; as explained previously in the Final Teaching, there is simply no external substance.

Therefore, it was said before that there are only images within the self-mind of sentient beings. Now, the phrase "they are also empty" explains that their nature is fundamentally detached [from such images].

To establish the aforementioned meaning, it is correctly stated that at the time of teaching and listening, because the nature of the original and the reflection is fundamentally detached, one forcibly says they are "neither original nor reflection.
In reality, however, as there is no basis for speech or thought, it is said that "there is no teaching. Because this is a teaching that transcends all dependencies, it is called "the teaching.

Thus, in the *Sumeru-gāthā*, the first half of the verse is cited as proof for the absence of a reflected image, while the second half is proof for the absence of an original substance; alternatively, it may be interpreted as follows.
There is no realization through grasping, no realization through external observation, and no realization through internal [observation]; the nature of phenomena is fundamentally empty and quiescent.
Realizing that this nature is inherently detached and ungraspable, it transcends thought and deliberation. This purity is easy to know when named.

The commentary [states] that "etc. includes the sudden teaching (*tongo*) of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. This refers to the meaning of the sudden teaching contained within the commentaries on the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtras*, such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*;
it means that these works clarify the meaning of the sudden teaching therein. Regarding the statement, "This only clarifies the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*)," a question is raised:

"If one takes only the single principle of emptiness, this should correspond to the Initial Teaching (*shikyō*); why then is it called the Sudden Teaching? The answer is: Because these three contemplations (*sankan*) are fused.
To take the single meaning of emptiness within the "middle" is precisely the emptiness of the middle; because it is not merely empty, it is the Sudden Teaching (Dunjiao).
However, the term "superior" (shang) above also encompasses the emptiness of the Initial Teaching (Shijiao); otherwise, the scope of inclusion would not be exhaustive.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "the first four explanations, etc.": if one considers them from the perspective of the *yuanrong* (perfect fusion) within the *xingbu* (gradual unfolding), they are all combined into one;
if one considers them from the perspective of the *xingbu* within the *yuanrong*, they proceed from the shallow to the deep.

Regarding the sub-commentary’s statement, "Fusing them into a single flavor accords with the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*)," this fully incorporates the preceding four [explanations]. The *Tantanxuanji* states: "These four do not obstruct one another, for each follows its own [principle]."

Because this gate is common to the other three, the *Yamāntaka-gāthā-stotra-ṭīkā-śāstra* states: "If one follows this school, all four propositions are employed because one knows that all phenomena are the self-nature of mind;
thus, even substantiality is one's own mind. This merely integrates the preceding four [propositions] and constitutes the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

The previous commentary’s two [sections] are both established as the four propositions based on the various teachings; if one refers to the lower [teachings], they do not obstruct [this]. As it says: "Like... (as in the original).

The preceding section differentiated the four gates from the shallow to the deep in order to explain how they gather and transform sentient beings, so that each may enter the Perfect [Teaching] according to their respective gate.

Regarding the commentary’s first point on establishing the four propositions based on the "teaching of commonality" (*tongjiao*): the former was based on the various vehicles (*yāna*), whereas this refers exclusively to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
"Identical" (*tóng*) means the same. Furthermore, while above [the text] used a broad sense of "identical" to include the various preceding vehicles, here it uses a profound sense:

because [this vehicle] is identical to the Sudden and the Real in terms of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena, it is called "identical. Regarding the statement "only teaching, no listening," one asks: "In the previous Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-deśanā*), there was only the reflection and no original;
now, there is only teaching and no listening—is this not contradictory? The answer is: "This is for the sake of establishing the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*)."

The *Yi* (the *Commentary*) explains each side separately in the preceding and succeeding sections; however, in terms of the ultimate reality, it is only when the final teaching (*zhongjiao*) asserts that there is neither form nor sound and yet they are unimpeded that one fully exhausts the principle.

As for why the *Chao* (the *Sub-commentary*) establishes three or four propositions and so forth, it is because the *Tanxuan ji* (Record of Investigating the Profundities) only constructs a single layer of four propositions.
There are two meanings here, as they correspond to the two sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) in the present commentary.

First, it is raised as a question: "How does the true mind integrate these two? Second, it is explained: because the true mind follows pure conditions, its characteristics are exhausted and its nature is manifested, whereby it is called the Buddha;

thus it is named the "principle" (*li*). Because the true mind follows defiled conditions, it becomes sentient beings; thus it is named the "phenomenon" (*shi*). Since these do not depart from the one mind, birth and Buddhahood are attained.
The speaker and the listener are fully encompassed within it, or rather, both the sentient beings and the Buddhas share the same single true mind;
because there is this principle, it appears as the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena, and thus they must be distinguished.
In the Commentary, if the preceding section is taken as the "Gate of Mutual Identity," then the true mind is used as the cause manifested by the "mind-only" (cittamātra);

thus, even the Buddha is designated according to the meaning of the identity of characteristics. In this case, the first four lines contain both the meanings of "identity" and "difference," while the latter four lines pertain solely to the meaning of the Separate Teaching (pratyekabuddha-yāna).
The Commentary states: "Because the Buddha-fruit accords with the nature" refers to the cause, which is the interpenetration of the dharma-nature;
"clarifying that it is not different from the nature" means that the Buddha is the entirety of the nature.

Since it is revealed that the Buddha is not composed of parts but is the whole of the true nature, and since the Buddha formed by this entire true nature can truly encompass all phenomena without omission, the Buddha who is thus formed likewise encompasses all phenomena without omission.

Furthermore, the *Vyākhyā* quotes the "Appearance" chapter (*Avataraṇa-parivarta*), which poses the following questions: "If one universally perceives all sentient beings as having already attained Buddhahood as Tathāgatas, for what reason does the Tathāgata preach the Dharma?

Since sentient beings have already become Buddhas, how can they be said to be 'subsumed within the fruit,' and furthermore, how can they be said to be 'listeners'? The answer to this is as follows: This perception...
The original nature of sentient beings causes them to hear this Dharma; because they have not yet truly realized it, it is called the "cause.

Precisely because they do not understand it in this way, the Buddha speaks of this as the general realization of the Buddha-mind, which encompasses all phenomena, while specifically taking up the meaning of receiving and hearing [the teaching].
The statement "all sentient beings are entirely within the wisdom of the Tathāgata" is the formal explanation; "by means of suchness-wisdom" and so forth brings forth what is to be produced.
Regarding the question "Why? which cites the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, the answer is that this is not necessarily restricted to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*). There are two meanings here:

first, if what is referred to as "suchness" (*tathatā*) is taken as the reason why sentient beings do not transcend it, this also applies to the principle of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*lishi wuai*).

Now, because this suchness is so designated, the Tathāgata is the subject who gathers sentient beings and sentient beings are the objects gathered; this refers to the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*).

The meaning of "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) is found only in other sutras and treatises; when there is a distinct teaching (*bhinna-śāsana*), it immediately enters the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*). Therefore, the *Jiaozhang* states:

"Furthermore, regarding the severance of delusions through the various gates of the three vehicles and so forth, if one obstruction is all obstructions and one severance is all severances, then one enters this teaching;
if [the severance] follows the sequence of individual gates, it constitutes the three vehicles. Thus, I now cite another treatise to establish this distinction.
This is the teaching.

The *Chao* (Commentary) states that because it is not inverted, it is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*). The *Zhen-sbu*, fascicle four, says: "There are two meanings of 'as' (*ru*): first, because it is non-inverted.
It is called 'inverted' due to deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*); Suchness, as both object and wisdom, is far removed from such delusion."

Because it is conceptualized, it is termed "appearing as two" (*dvaya-pratibhāsa*); yet, in its true sense, it abides eternally. Although its nature is obscured by afflictions (*kleśa*), its essence—adorned with meritorious qualities—is without change;
therefore, it is termed "as it is" (*tathā*). This brief excerpt from the *Yao* (Commentary) summarizes only the first of these meanings.

The *Yao* states, "As for 'Tathāgata' (*rulai*)," which serves to cite and explain the two characters "Tathāgata. Regarding the term, it refers to that which comes from self-nature (*svabhāva*) until the attainment of the fruit.
The term "etc. refers to *mūla-awakening* (original awakening), while "as" refers to *ādi-awakening* (initial awakening). A question is raised:

since the nature (*dhātu*) is fundamentally one, how can there be a distinction between original and initial awakening, as well as the Tathāgata? The phrase "though the nature is... provides the answer;

its meaning is that original awakening, while existing in the causal stage, is termed "that which should be attained," whereas initial awakening, upon reaching the fruit, is termed "that which has been attained. Therefore, the name "Tathāgata" is distinguished [from these two]. This is stated merely because...
"Clear and turbid are different," and the aforementioned treatise continues: "The designations are not the same. "When in the causal stage" is the specific explanation of the two names.
"For example" uses a metaphor to illustrate; "it should be understood" is the application of the principle (*dharmas*).

Regarding the term "storehouse" (*garbha*), the subsequent citation and explanation are identical to the *Śāstra*. *Chao*: Furthermore, there are three kinds of storehouses. [End of section. "Furthermore" [introduces the next point].
The Tathāgata’s capacity for inclusion is of three kinds; here the wording is abbreviated, and it should be stated:
"Furthermore, the Tathāgatagarbha has three kinds. To say that "by means of this fruit, all sentient beings are included" means that the Tathāgata-garbha takes sentient beings as its essence.
The phrase "now, below in the commentary" indicates that the commentary briefly cites the underlying intent. The intent is as follows: [the commentary].

In the *Zhong* (Commentary), only the intermediate passage is cited, while the preceding passage concerning the "name-store" (*nāmakāya*) and so forth, as well as the subsequent passage beginning with "Furthermore, there are three kinds of storehouses," are omitted; thus, the beginning and end are left out.

Alternatively, it may be that the *Shu* (Commentary) cites only the intermediate passage, whereas the present *Chao* (Excerpts) has abbreviated by citing only the initial and final passages. These two interpretations follow [the respective texts].
This concludes the general explanation above regarding the meaning of the "one treasury that is subsumed" (*eka-saṃgraha-kośa*).
Next, the *Chao* (Excerpts) briefly cites the texts of the latter two treasuries from the aforementioned *Chao*. 2. Regarding "the treasury as concealment" (*saṃvṛti-kośa*):

herein, both "that which is to be attained" (*prāpya*) and "that which has been attained" (*prāpta*) are equally termed *Tathāgata* (unlike the preceding section, where "to be attained" is termed *tathā* and "attained" is termed *āgata*). That treatise states: "It comes from abiding in its own nature."
Because he has attained the ultimate reality whose essence is immutable, he is called the Tathāgata (this explains "Tathāgata").

Because sentient beings do not perceive him prior to the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) as he is obscured by their afflictions (*kleśa*), he is called the *tathāgatagarbha* (this explains the character "garbha").
This *tathāgatagarbha* takes the afflictions as its substance; furthermore, that which is obscured—the Tathāgata—is itself the *garbha*. As that treatise states: "The Tathāgata is himself hidden."

Because it is not manifest, it is called a "treasury" (*garbha*). Regarding how it functions as a treasury by way of inclusion, that treatise states: "All merits attained upon reaching the stage of fruition are called the 'nature to be attained' (*prāpya-dhātu*) by the Tathāgata; this is termed the 'Tathāgata-garbha,' taking the nature to be attained within the causal state as its essence. Question: Since the "nature to be attained" resides in the causal state, how can it include the fruition? Answer: [It does so because] it is the very cause of that fruition. Just as a sprout is the cause for the attainment of a fruit, so too is the nature to be attained the cause for the attainment of all the qualities of a Buddha. Therefore, although the fruition has not yet arisen, it is included within the causal nature. Furthermore, because the fruition is already contained within the causal nature, it is said to be "included" even though it has not yet manifested. This is like saying that a sprout contains the fruit, or that a person contains their own future son. Thus, the fruition is included within the causal nature. For this reason, it is taught that the Tathāgata-garbha is the "womb" (*garbha*) of all Buddhas. It is also called the "storehouse" (*kośa*) because it stores immeasurable virtues, just as a storehouse stores various goods. It is also called the "matrix" (*dhātu*) because it is the source from which all the qualities of a Buddha arise, just as gold ore is the source from which gold is produced. It is also called the "essence" (*sāra*) because it is the ultimate reality, free from all adventitious defilements, just as the core of a tree is the most essential part. It is also called the "seed" (*bīja*) because it possesses the capacity to produce all the qualities of a Buddha, just as a seed possesses the capacity to produce a great tree. It is also called the "foundation" (*āśraya*) because it serves as the basis for all mundane and supramundane phenomena, just as the earth serves as the foundation for all things. It is also called the "support" (*ālambana*) because it is the object of the wisdom of the Tathāgatas, just as a visual object is the support for the eye-consciousness. It is also called the "refuge" (*śaraṇa*) because it provides protection from all suffering, just as a fortress provides protection from enemies. It is also called the "ultimate goal" (*parāyana*) because it is the final destination of all noble beings, just as the ocean is the final destination of all rivers. It is also called the "unexcelled" (*anuttara*) because there is nothing superior to it, just as space is unsurpassed. It is also called the "inexhaustible" (*akṣaya*) because its nature is eternal and indestructible, just as the nature of space is never exhausted. It is also called the "unchanging" (*avikāra*) because it is free from the three types of change, just as the nature of space is unchanging. It is also called the "pure" (*viśuddha*) because it is free from all afflictions and secondary afflictions, just as pure water is free from turbidity. It is also called the "blissful" (*sukha*) because it is free from all suffering and is the supreme bliss, just as Nirvāṇa is the supreme bliss. It is also called the "peaceful" (*śānta*) because it is free from all disturbances and is the ultimate peace, just as the cessation of fire is the ultimate peace. It is also called the "noble" (*ārya*) because it is the domain of the noble ones and is free from all faults, just as a noble person is free from all defects. It is also called the "excellent" (*praṇīta*) because it is the most sublime among all phenomena, just as the Dharma is the most excellent of all teachings. It is also called the "liberated" (*mukta*) because it is free from all bonds and is the ultimate liberation, just as a released prisoner is free from all shackles. It is also called the "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) because it is not produced by causes and conditions, just as space is not produced by causes and conditions. It is also called the "eternal" (*nitya*) because its nature is constant and unchanging throughout the three times, just as the nature of space is eternal. It is also called the "steadfast" (*dhruva*) because it is firm and immovable, just as Mount Sumeru is steadfast. It is also called the "cool" (*śiva*) because it extinguishes the heat of all afflictions, just as cool water extinguishes the heat of fever. It is also called the "auspicious" (*śubha*) because it is the source of all auspiciousness and is free from all inauspiciousness, just as a virtuous person brings auspiciousness to others. It is also called the "beneficial" (*kalyāṇa*) because it brings benefit to all sentient beings and is the supreme benefit, just as a compassionate father brings benefit to his children. It is also called the "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-satya*) because it is the truth of the ultimate nature, free from all conventional designations, just as the nature of space is the ultimate truth. It is also called the "reality-limit" (*bhūtakoṭi*) because it is the limit of reality, free from all extremes of existence and non-existence, just as the horizon is the limit of the sky. It is also called the "suchness" (*tathatā*) because it is the suchness of all phenomena, free from all distortion, just as the nature of space is suchness. It is also called the "dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*) because it is the source of all dharmas and is the ultimate realm of the Dharma, just as the ocean is the source of all rivers. It is also called the "body of the Dharma" (*dharmakāya*) because it is the body of all Buddhas and is the ultimate body of the Dharma, just as the sun is the body of light. It is also called the "great vehicle" (*mahāyāna*) because it carries all sentient beings to the other shore and is the supreme vehicle, just as a great ship carries many people across the sea. It is also called the "path" (*mārga*) because it leads to the city of Nirvāṇa and is the supreme path, just as a royal road leads to the capital. It is also called the "wisdom" (*jñāna*) because it clearly perceives the nature of all phenomena and is free from ignorance, just as the sun clearly illuminates all forms. It is also called the "liberation" (*vimukti*) because it is free from all fetters and is the ultimate liberation, just as a liberated soul is free from all bonds. It is also called the "nirvāṇa" because it is the extinction of all suffering and is the ultimate peace, just as the cessation of fire is the ultimate peace. It is also called the "unborn" (*ajāta*) because its nature is originally unborn and unarisen, just as space is originally unborn. It is also called the "unproduced" (*anutpanna*) because it is not produced by causes and conditions, just as a lotus born in the sky is unproduced. It is also called the "unceasing" (*anirodha*) because its nature is eternally quiescent and does not cease, just as the nature of space does not cease. It is also called the "quiescent" (*śānta*) because it is free from all disturbances and is the ultimate quiescence, just as the cessation of all movement is ultimate quiescence. It is also called the "blissful" (*santa*) because it is free from all suffering and is the supreme bliss, just as the bliss of Nirvāṇa is supreme bliss. It is also called the "non-self" (*anātman*) because it is free from the self and what belongs to the self, just as space is free from a self. It is also called the "empty" (*śūnya*) because it is free from all conceptual proliferations and is the ultimate emptiness, just as an empty house is free from inhabitants. It is also called the "signless" (*animitta*) because it is free from all signs and characteristics, just as the sky is free from all signs. It is also called the "wishless" (*apraṇihita*) because it is free from all desires and aspirations, just as a person who has renounced the world is free from worldly desires. It is also called the "ungraspable" (*agrāhya*) because it cannot be grasped by the mind or mental factors, just as the wind cannot be grasped by the hand. It is also called the "unmanifest" (*anidarśana*) because it cannot be seen by the eyes, just as the wind cannot be seen by the eyes. It is also called the "unob
That treatise states: "If it were only at the time of attaining the fruit that one speaks of obtaining this nature, then this nature would be impermanent.

Why? Because it would not be something newly acquired. Therefore, we know it exists fundamentally; thus it is called 'permanent. To say that it now takes up the fruit also captures the underlying intent of the sub-commentary."
The *Chao jing* (Excerpts from the Sūtra) states: "As for 'the Tathāgata,' the *Xianchu pin shu* (Commentary on the Chapter on Manifestation) says:

First, regarding the samādhi upon which he relies, it is called 'Excellent Awakening' (*Sujñāna*) because his awakening does not stagnate in quiescence; he employs this to encompass both movement and stillness, and because he awakens to their single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*), he uses it as a skillful means (*upāya*).
Second, from 'having entered' onwards, it reveals the function of the single body. Since he takes the single characteristic as his skillful means, all things..."
Because they are of one characteristic (*eka-lakṣaṇa*), they manifest as many; just as when one attains perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*), the subsequent categories reveal the remaining bodies.

When a Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, clouds of *rūpa*-bodies pervade the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); each and every one of these is a vast body, yet all appear simultaneously as if they were a single body.
The meaning of the word "even" (*api*) here is that even kalpas, lands (*kṣetra*), and so forth are [contained within] a single body.
If one suddenly manifests [the body], does this not mean that for a certain class of listeners of the Dharma, it is not a single person who suddenly manifests?

There is a version of the text that reads "one who manifests the Dharma" (一顯法人), but the character "manifest" (顯) is an error. The *Chao* (Commentary) correctly takes the passage from "Great Wisdom" (*Mahāprajñā*) onwards:

since the Buddha-wisdom is identical to emptiness, what is there that it does not encompass? How much more so would the "total body" (*saṃbhogakāya*) not encompass all phenomena? The *Chao* states: "Sentient beings are... [and so forth].

Regarding "the cause and so forth": because the cause is called the principle-dharmadhātu (li-fajie), it is not different from the dharma-nature (faxing); sentient beings are likewise subsumed within it without omission.

This is the passage stating that the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment without departing from this very mind. The phrase "If it were so... and following serves as an inquiry. Its meaning is as follows:

This provides a general outline followed by a detailed explanation. Within the detailed explanation, there are two parts: first, the Common Teaching (tongjiao), and second, the Distinct Teaching (biejiao).

Within the Distinct Teaching, there are three sections: first, a general outline; second, a detailed explanation; and third, the integration [of these teachings], which accords with the meaning of the main text of the *Shu* and *Chao*.
Regarding the phrase "citing one line, etc. from the *Śāstra* (鈔): among the four lines, citing any single line necessarily entails all four, as they are inseparable;

yet they remain distinct categories so that they do not overlap with one another. Consequently, throughout all the holy teachings, any single passage cited according to its context must necessarily possess these four lines.
As for the statement "whether Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna," this is because [the teaching] encompasses all without exception.
Since this is the measure of the vehicle, it is based on the principle of "comprehending the whole by means of one. Which teaching does not clarify this?

The proximate conclusion necessarily possesses these four phrases, which universally encompass the aforementioned four phrases of the "same teaching" (tongjiao) as well as the four phrases of "original and reflection" (benying).
Only when one is raised such that the whole is comprehended can it be considered the ultimate, profound principle of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra).
The first [section] of the Commentary, "Subsuming the derivative within the fundamental," means subsuming the internal within the external. It brings together the preceding six gates:

the Hīnayāna’s teaching on the destruction of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-bhaṅga*) and the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-śāsana*) on the establishment of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-sthāpana*), all of which clarify what is shallow and near—these are all termed "derivative.

Their common entry into the single reality (*eka-tattva*) is the fundamental essence, which is precisely the immovable *tathatā*. The second [section], "Bringing characteristics together to reveal nature," means bringing the external together with the internal. It brings together the external so that it is identical to the internal.

The shallow and proximate teachings elucidated throughout the first six gates from beginning to end all enter the absolute, single reality (the first meaning applies to both the provisional and the real, while the latter meaning applies only to the real;

however, although the "thusness" entered via the first meaning is not itself provisional, it is said to apply to the provisional because the teachings subsumed therein have not yet explicitly taught that thusness). This above is an explanation based on the provisional teaching (*tongjiao*);

if one relies instead on the meaning of the perfect and distinct (*yuanbie*) teachings, then within the first six gates, even the term "perfectly interfused and endowed with all virtues" [is included].
Since all phrases, sentences, and so forth are subsumed within the unobstructed true nature, and since the ten gates of mutual integration are explained below,
one knows that the emergence and dissolution of the preceding and following passages— from their beginning to their ultimate conclusion— constitute a perfect exposition.

Regarding the phrase "The Commentary on that Sub-commentary says, etc.," this refers to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-vyākhyā* (Commentary on the Treatise on Consciousness-Only). That explanation contains two meanings.

The first explains it by way of the "outflowing teaching" (*pravacana*). The statement "by means of this stage" refers to the third stage, the Stage of Radiance (*Prabhākarī-bhūmi*). As the treatise states:
"Because one achieves superior meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and the great dhāraṇīs, and is able to emit the light of boundless, wondrous wisdom, it is called the third [stage]."
"Wisdom illuminates the Mahāyāna Dharma" means that when one contemplates this fundamental basis of the teaching, it is called "the truly flowing Suchness.
This refers to contemplating the fundamental basis of the teaching by means of the three types of wisdom; it is a retrogressive inference back to the source.
The phrase "or realizes this" is explained below in two ways according to the Dharma being taught, as the Bodhisattvas of this stage realize this.
The *tathatā* (suchness) that attains the excellence of the teaching is so called because the source is excellent, and thus the derivative is also excellent.

Regarding this "excellent derivative *tathatā*," both interpretations are *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compounds: the first clarifies the name by referring to the derivative teachings, while the latter clarifies the name by referring to the excellent Dharma that is taught.
The commentary states that although that school does not establish [the principle of] "following conditions" (*anuparivartana*), the subsequent passage contains both concession and refutation.

If one speaks according to that school’s tenet, it refutes them by asserting that if they do not establish "following conditions," then there is no meaning of "flowing from the True" (*zhenliu*). However, if one speaks according to the underlying meaning, one concedes it by subsuming the derivative under the fundamental, which is also called "flowing like suchness.

Thus, the reason for distinguishing [and rejecting] based on the tenet while including based on the meaning is that the Master of the Commentary acknowledges that the treatise possesses [both aspects].

Regarding the meaning of "following conditions" (*anuparivartana*), those who adhere solely to the doctrine of the unchanging nature of *tathatā* (true thusness) hold that it does not change. Therefore, the sub-commentary below states:

"The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other texts also state that *tathatā* is the true nature of consciousness; however, later commentators insist that it is 'unchanging,' thereby falling into the error of neglecting its quality of 'following conditions.
This fault belongs to the later generations. As that treatise says: "This ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena is also precisely *tathatā*, which is eternal..."

Because it is according to their nature, it is the true nature of all dharmas; since True Suchness (tathatā) is the true nature of consciousness, it is clear that Vasubandhu also took the *tathāgatagarbha* to constitute the substance of consciousness.
However, because later commentators of the commentary selected only the unchanging aspect, they stated that the error lies with these later generations.
Thus, one knows that this "existence" has the meaning of being both pervasive and real, rather than being exclusively provisional; were it not so, [the critique would not hold].
Consider this: how can this section be said to "converge the provisional to enter the real"?

Therefore, the *Chao* (the Sub-commentary) explains it as follows: "The fundamental wisdom, relying upon True Suchness, successively induces the subsequently attained wisdom, and so on up to the twelvefold teachings;
this meaning is called 'flow. This refers to the sequence of arising."

Regarding the statement "this great compassion" and below: the previous section spoke of four dharmas, while this speaks of five. The answer is that the former combined compassion and wisdom, thus there were four;

here, compassion and wisdom are distinguished as two, thus there are five. This is because they are derived by distinguishing [compassion] from within the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
The commentary below cites the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (*Renwang jing*) and other texts to corroborate the first of the two meanings presented in the preceding sub-commentary:

that the teachings arise from conditions and lack intrinsic nature, which is precisely the meaning of True Suchness (*tathatā*). "The Dharma-text" (*faben*) refers to the prose sections (*gadya*) of the sūtras.
"Not reciting the verses" refers to the *gāthās*, or isolated stanzas. The rest is as explained previously. It says: "O Great King, it is as follows... and so forth.
All words and letters are themselves the nature of suchness (*tathatā*). By studying and practicing in accordance with suchness, one can give rise to the Buddha-wisdom;
therefore, these words and letters of suchness are called the "Mother of the Wisdom of all Buddhas.

When it is said that this refers to one meaning within the *Nidāna* (Causes and Conditions) section of the sūtras, it is because each of the twelve divisions of the teachings possesses two meanings, and this *nidāna* likewise has two meanings: first, the cause (*hetu*).
It is requested that the explanation be given for two reasons: first, because the Dharma is a matter of great importance; and second, because one must understand both the origin and the details.
Now, when it is said that the precepts were established "due to a specific incident," this refers to the second of the two meanings of "causal conditions" (*nidāna*).

Furthermore, regarding the term "boundary" (*sīmā*) as having the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*), the *Jātaka* Sūtras state that there was one occasion when the Tathāgata received a body during his causal phase, and another occasion when he received a body while still within the causal state.
Because the disciple receives a body within the causal stage (*hetu*), it is called the "meaning of the cause.
Regarding the "essence of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena" in the eighth section of the Commentary:

although the previous section on the reconciliation of teachings already established the sense that they are "identical yet not different" and "not separate," it is only when one fully possesses the nuances of being "neither identical nor separate" and "neither one nor different" that the meaning is complete; therefore, this is now clarified.

Furthermore, following the previous examples of the sixth and seventh gates, this [gate] should clarify the non-obstruction between phenomena (事) and principle (理) by incorporating the contents of the preceding seven gates.
That is to say: although the entirety of all teachings below are identical to phenomena, they do not obstruct principle;

yet the twelvefold division of the scriptures and so forth remain distinct, such that principle does not obstruct phenomena. Although the entirety of principle constitutes all teachings, principle does not obstruct phenomena.
Furthermore, ultimate truth is profoundly serene, and phenomena do not obstruct principle. Since ultimate truth is both nature and appearance (*dharmatā* and *dharma*), it is without obstruction;

likewise, the Buddha’s teachings and doctrines are harmoniously integrated in accordance with this nature, because the taught dharmas all correspond to the "thusness-wisdom" (*tathatā-jñāna*) that is their source.
Possessing such non-obstruction, as explained extensively below, one should establish the pervasiveness of phenomena.

The ten gates, such as the gate of principle (*nyāya*), have already been clarified according to their respective delimitations of meaning; however, those [gates] take the signified (*vācya*) as their gateway, whereas this [gate] takes the signifier (*vācaka*) as its gateway, so they do not overlap.

Question: Since the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle (*dharmadharmatā-avighāta*) was already explained within the previous discussion on sound, name, phrase, and syllable (*śabdānāmapadavyañjana*), how does it differ from this?
Answer: That [non-obstruction] was explained with respect to the four factors—sound, name, phrase, and syllable—upon which the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle is based.

This passage clarifies that the preceding seven gates all bring about the non-obstruction between phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*). Question: In the previous analysis, this [eighth gate] was categorized as belonging to the "teaching of commonality" (*tóngjiào*);

how can it cause the meanings of the "non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena" (*shìshì wú'ài*) within the first seven gates to all converge upon the "non-obstruction of phenomena and principle" (*lǐshì wú'ài*)?

Answer: Since it is named the "teaching of commonality," how could there be the meaning of the "non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena"? It is clear that this is merely the "one aspect" (*yīxiàng*).

Regarding these words, if we now clarify the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle (*dharmas* and *tattva*) according to the "Gate of Endowed Virtue," there is nothing that is not encompassed.

As for the *Chao* (the *Jianyi quwen*) stating that it selects the meaning and adopts the text, the *Huigie* says: "Because the *Shu* states that both text and meaning are perfect (*yuan*), this selects the previous [interpretation of] 'meaning' as explained before;
whereas 'listening fully encompasses,' etc., refers to the perfection of 'meaning. Now, both text and meaning are simultaneously designated as perfect."
Therefore, the previous [classification] was selected for its perfect meaning (*artha*); now, in explaining this sūtra, both the text and the meaning are perfect.

If the expressed meaning were perfect as in the *Tattvārthapatala*, one would select for perfect meaning; however, since we are currently taking the expressive text (*vyañjana*) as the gateway, we select for perfect text while setting aside perfect meaning.

Regarding the phrase "the commentary is the perfect sound (*pariṣphuṭa-svara*) and so forth": because it takes the expressive sounds, names, phrases, and syllables as its gateway, there is no phenomenon that is not subsumed within it;
thus it says, "the rain of Dharma fills and pervades all. Since the words and meanings differ from one another, within a single phenomenon one understands many [aspects] and so forth.
One universally enters into all aspects of words and meanings, and by discerning the ineffable nature of all phenomena, one immediately touches upon reality in every encounter.
Because the Dharma is expounded instantaneously in a single thought-moment, it is said that "all are perfect. Regarding the statement that these are the "retinue teachings" and so forth:
other teachings adapted to various capacities are the retinue of this primary teaching.

Therefore, although they differ from this [primary teaching], even when the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) and so forth are taught as the primary subject in one direction while being taught as the accompanying retinue in the ten directions, they nonetheless function as the primary subject; these retinue teachings are likewise [perfect].
The category of "accompanying teachings" (*bànjiào*) is included within the "accompanying" (*bàn*) because it is intended to demonstrate that no phenomena are omitted from the inclusion.
Regarding the second point, since the term "and so forth" (*děng*) is used, this has already been clarified in the previous section on the two masters who combined the teachings.

As for the statement that "if 'one' (*yī*) refers to a single sound (*zhíshēng*), the ancient interpretation is not correct," the *Chūxianpǐn Sùchāo* states: "The perfect sound (*yuán yīn*) is also called the 'one sound' (*yī yīn*)."

it is formless and soundless, yet manifests immeasurable forms and sounds directly according to the capacities of sentient beings, just as an empty valley has no inherent sound but echoes whenever called. Thus, with respect to the Buddha—
That speech has no sound is one way of describing it according to the capacity of the listener;

that speech consists of manifold sounds yet is not manifold but is a single sound—the "perfect sound" (maṇḍala-svara)—is truly because, at a single time and in a single assembly, beings of different species understand equally, each receiving a single sound according to their own faculties and nature, without hearing any other sound, and without confusion or overlap.
Because this manifests such wonder, it is called the "single sound," and this sound pervades all.
Because it is heard by all according to their faculties and wherever they are matured throughout the ten directions, it is called the "perfect sound" (*paripūrṇa-svara*).

This does not mean that it pervades everywhere like space without distinct melodies; rather, as the Sūtra says: "According to the sounds of their respective kinds, he universally addresses all sentient beings"—this is what is meant.
Second, speaking from the perspective of the Buddha himself, he truly possesses form and sound; his voice pervades everywhere, reaching all places without exception. However...

Because it lacks the distinctions of the five notes and four tones, and because there are no differing melodies, it is called the "Single Sound" (*ekasvara*). Because it is not non-pervasive, it is called the "Perfect Sound" (*paripūrṇa-svara*).
It is simply this Perfect Sound that acts as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), manifesting a multitude of sounds according to the differences among the faculties (*indriya*).
It is like the full moon, which has but a single perfect form, yet manifests many reflections according to the differences among the vessels; it is also like...

A long wind follows the sounds of its various apertures, resulting in many kinds of voices. The Sūtras state that when the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind.
