Thirdly, it is said that within a single vocal action, the Tathāgata expounds all the verbal expressions of all sentient beings;
therefore, he causes those sentient beings each to hear their own language. It is not otherwise.

When [the Tathāgata] comes, he utters but a single word; yet because his verbal karma is identical [to all], it is called "one sound" (*ekasvara*), and because that which is uttered is manifold, it is called the "perfect sound" (*saṃbhinnasvara*).
If even the voice of Śāriputra emits many sounds simultaneously, how much more so the Tathāgata?

Regarding the contradiction with the second [scriptural] authority, taking any one of the three previous interpretations exclusively results in error. First, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is formless and soundless.
Because it is not the meaning of the sound itself, but merely follows the sounds of others rather than its own sound;

secondly, because it is only a single utterance and lacks multiple sounds—since the one is not identical to the many, how can it be the "perfect sound"? If [the one] exists, then the many should also exist;
if [the one] does not exist, then the one must also not exist. How can it be that the one exists while the many do not? Thirdly, although it consists only of the many...

Because there is no "one," if vocal karma were identical to that of all sentient beings, would it not then be a single sound? Therefore, it is neither [identical nor different]. Regarding the third point, the comprehensive reconciliation:
the above merely criticized partiality; it does not mean a total failure. Only by combining the three preceding meanings does one arrive at the meaning of the "Perfect Sound" (yuan-yin).
This means that the many are identical to the one; if the many were not identical to the one, it would not be a single sound. Furthermore, the one...
If many were identical to one, they would not be many; this is not the Perfect Sound (1).

If two were identical to emptiness, and emptiness were identical to two, then if two were not identical to emptiness, it would be something grasped as an object and would not lack intrinsic nature; thus it would not be perfect, nor would it be one.

If one were not identical to two, it would not be empty, nor would it be perfect. Therefore, their seamless fusion without obstruction is the Perfect Sound. Among these ten [meanings], three meanings constitute the Perfect [Sound]. (2) *Jiyuan* (即圓).

(Regarding the three meanings among the ten meanings of sound: The first refers to the meaning of being without arising or ceasing; the next one refers to the meaning of being without deviance or crookedness; and the last one refers to the meaning of universal reach.
This implies that if one understands the correct meaning, then all related aspects will be inclusively gathered without omission;

however, if one fails to grasp the correct intent, all interpretations will deviate from the principle. The commentary states: "What is now criticized in this *Chao* (Excerpts) is precisely the interpretation of the second master. [The *Chao* below cites various...]
The term "sūtra" (*jing*) refers to the various scriptural passages found throughout this specific section.

In the *Chao* (Commentary), it is stated that under the heading "Three Rains of Dharma," because each individual sound expounds the inexhaustible Dharma pervasively, and because each individual dharma-gate accords with the nature (*dharmatā*), they all fill the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
This is distinct from the meaning of "pervasive filling. Therefore, it is said below: "The three sections already contain four meanings," referring to the first...
The third section contains the meanings of the preceding two; thus, "one" refers to the unfolding [of the one], while "universal pervasion" specifically clarifies the four phrases below.

There is a version of the text that reads "three unfoldings, one universal pervasion," but the three characters [for "unfoldings"] are erroneous scribal errors; the meaning of the following three phrases can be understood accordingly.

The *Chao* (Commentary) provides an analogy, as the *Shu* (Sub-commentary) states: "Pervasively entering the non-abiding" is a metaphor; within both the words and the metaphor, there is also a self-reflection.
In the abbreviated [version], within the metaphors, one should also state "universally entering all places," and so on, up to "within all retributions";
and regarding the phenomena (*dharma*), one should also say "universally entering all matters," and so on, up to "the supramundane sphere.

Therefore, in the passage beginning with "the various languages of all sentient beings," which describes drawing others in by encompassing them within oneself, one should also include the "signified" (*vācya*); these are all omitted for brevity in the text.
How can this be taken as a proof for the cause of the mutual interpenetration of the *dharmatā*? It is like writing characters: there is no phenomenon that is not recorded (the *Shiming* states:

"Writing" [shū] means "to encompass" [sho]; because it encompasses all things, it is also called "to record" [chaku]; because it records the myriad things, it is so named). Thus, there is nothing into which it does not enter; when one seeks it, how could it have a fixed abode?
Although the metaphors interpenetrate one another, they lack any fixed dwelling—this may be called profound (*xuan*). [The *Chao*] follows the meaning to assign different names; "below" refers to...
"Containing" (yōnyū) refers to the inclusion [of meanings]; while the names established as "containing" differ, their essence is identical, meaning they are one in substance. *Commentary*:
For example, from the passage "such as the Lord of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven," this refers to the celestial maidens (*cāmarī*) of the Lord of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. *Commentary*:
Regarding those that have already been repeated several times, one simply takes a single dharma from each of the aforementioned Buddha-dharmas and brings forth its wondrous sound.
The sound cannot be described as being "this," which constitutes the first layer; the turning of the wheel of Dharma is the second layer;
further expounding the sūtras is the third layer of sūtra; again, analyzing the dharma-gates is the fourth layer of dharma-gate;
and further explaining all dharmas is the fifth layer. Therefore, it is said that although there are already several layers, one speaks of only a single dharma.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "if one classifies this as applying universally to all dharmas," the ten mysteries previously explained were based solely on the four factors of sound, name, phrase, and sentence as their gateway to elucidate them.
If one uses all dharmas to manifest the meaning, the principle is the same as with sound and the others;

thus, what dharma is not a signifier (*vācaka*) that possesses the significance of the ten mysteries? Taking these signifiers themselves as the gateway, they follow immediately upon this [previous discussion].

That which is expressed also possesses the ten mysteries (daśa-guhya), as explained in the *Yìfēnzhì* (The Limits of Meaning); all of these constitute the substance of the teaching (*deśanā-dharmakāya*).

Regarding the phrase "the ocean-seal clearly manifests" in the tenth section of the Commentary: while the preceding nine sections explain them individually, this one section explains them collectively.

Thus, the three vehicles, the one vehicle, and so forth, all clearly manifest within meditative concentration (*samādhi*). To say that this refers to the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*) is because the Sūtra states:

For example, just as the great ocean universally reflects the forms, appearances, and physical characteristics of all sentient beings throughout the four continents—and for this reason it is collectively called the "great ocean"—so too is the bodhi of the Buddhas:
it universally manifests the mental activities, faculties, dispositions, and inclinations of all sentient beings, yet nothing is manifested. Therefore, it is called the bodhi of the Buddhas.

This refers to the Buddha’s Sea-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*). As for the statement "if one considers the stage of the cause," it means that from the stage of perfected faith up to the first abode (*prathamabhūmi*), one also attains the manifestation of the seal;
alternatively, even within the stage of faith in the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), one may attain the manifestation of the seal.
For details regarding the "Chapter on Worthy Leaders" (*Bhadramukha-parivarta*), refer to the analysis provided previously.

Regarding the phrase "what is esteemed in the words of the commentary," Guifeng says: speaking in terms of the discourse between guest and host, "what is esteemed in the words" is called the *zongqu* (essential purport).
This means the underlying intention or the direction toward which one moves; that is, the place where the mind and intentions ultimately converge.
This is because whatever is esteemed as the primary principle (*zong*) must necessarily have a point of intentional convergence.
Regarding the phrase "the author of the commentary and others," this is because they take as primary the doctrines of their own respective schools, while other matters are treated only incidentally;
furthermore, they clearly elucidate the tenets they uphold, whereas other points are mentioned only briefly.
Regarding the two manuscript versions, namely the Sthavira and Mahāsāṃghika schools, the *Nanshan Jieshu* (Commentary on the Vinaya Precepts) states:
"The two root schools, as found in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, refer to the time of the first council when five hundred people were selected;
these were the Sthaviras within the cave, led by Kāśyapa. Those not included in this number were called the Mahāsāṃghikas, who were outside the cave."
This refers to the initial schism during the first council convened by the Elder Mahākāśyapa and the Great Assembly;

thus, the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states that the "two fundamental divisions" are precisely these. More than one hundred years later, King Aśoka, who ruled over Jambudvīpa, governed with such harmony that his influence extended to both humans and deities.
At that time, there was a man named Mahādeva who, prior to his ordination, had committed [an offense].
Regarding the three heinous crimes—namely, killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, and killing an Arhat—he felt deep remorse after committing them and sought to extinguish his transgressions.
He then encountered a community of monks from the Mahāsāṃghika school outside a cave; as they were unaware of his commission of a heinous crime, they granted him ordination and the full precepts.

Because of his intelligence, he was held in high esteem by King Aśoka, who honored him. Later, together with [the aforementioned... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragment, likely from a commentary on the *Vinaya* or a hagiographical account. The final phrase "later with the above" suggests a connection to a preceding narrative.)

Regarding the schism within the Sthavira school (as expressed in the five verses on the five matters attributed to Mahādeva: "The outflowing of the Aśaikṣa [is caused by] demonic affliction, ignorance, doubt, and being led astray by others; the Path does not arise;

calling one who merely utters sounds 'Tathāgata'—this is called the True and Pure Teaching"), at that time Mahādeva said: "If a dispute is to be settled according to the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, it should rely upon the majority vote.
At that time, although the venerable elders of the Sthavira school were few in number, they were highly esteemed, whereas among the faction of the Mahāsāṃghika school, the venerable elders were many.
Although the number [of followers] was small, they were extremely numerous; because the King considered Mahādeva to be such a person, the two schools proceeded in opposition.
As the *Yogācārabhūmi-ṭīkā* (Lüe zuǎn) of Cien states:

"In the hundredth year after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, due to that Mahādeva’s dispute over the five points—where Mahādeva was noble in name and possessed the realization of great fruits, while the King was lowly in age yet esteemed for his prestige—the two sides opposed one another."
The monastic community looked up to the Way, yet because [the Master] stood out so preeminently without peer, he was consequently envied by the common world.
They slandered him for committing the three transgressions and added to this the five excesses; competing for fame and contending for profit is a phenomenon common to all ages.
This hollow scaffolding of empty rhetoric is shared by all ordinary people, and it is due to such turmoil that the various Hīnayāna schools arose from the differentiation of sects.

The division of the Buddha’s relics into several segments of white cotton cloth began from this point (according to this, the fundamental division into two schools occurred only after one hundred years).
Furthermore, the *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra-śāstra* states that eight schools branched out from the Mahāsāṃghika and ten schools branched out from the Sthavira;
including the two original schools, there are twenty schools in total. Therefore, it says [in that text]: "In the second century..."
In the second century after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, three schools emerged from within the Mahāsāṃghika: first, the Lokottaravāda; second, the Gokulika;
and third, the Prajñaptivāda. Subsequently, in the second century, another school named the Bahuśrutīya emerged from the Mahāsāṃghika.
Following this, in the next second century, yet another school named the Prajñaptivāda emerged from within the Mahāsāṃghika. Thus, in succession...
When two hundred years had passed, there was a renunciant of non-Buddhist origins who abandoned heterodoxy to return to the True Dharma;

he was named Mahādeva (not the same Mahādeva who previously committed the offense of immediate retribution). He went forth and received full ordination within the Mahāsāṃghika school, became learned and diligent, and resided on Mount Caitya.
Together with the monks of that school, he re-examined the five points. The verse concerning these five points states: "Being led by others, ignorance, and doubt."
Because he caused [monks] to enter the Path through sound, the arising of a lack of compassion led to a schism within the True Buddhist Teaching, which subsequently divided into three schools:
first, the Caitīya School; second, the Aparaśaila School; and third, the Uttaraśaila School. Including the original and its branches, these constitute nine schools.
Second, the Sthavira School [arose] at the beginning of the third century [after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa]. (The Mahāsāṃghika elders were approximately two hundred fewer.)

After [that] year, the Sthavira school was divided; it is said that more than three hundred years later, they were further divided. Kātyāyanīputra entered the monastic order within the Sthavira school and extensively propagated the *Ekottarika-śāstra* (Treatise on the Single Flavor).
Because he spoke little of the Sūtras and Vinaya, which deviated from the tenets of the school, it was subsequently divided into two sects.
One was the Sarvāstivāda, also called the Hetuvāda (School of Causation), because this school established its doctrines by extensively producing logical reasons (*hetu*).
For this reason, the two Sthavira schools were renamed the Haimavata (Snowy Mountain) Sthaviras. The disciples of the Sthaviras originally propagated the Sūtra-piṭaka;
the Hetuvādins arose and extensively propagated the Abhidharma. Because they were well-versed in its principles and meanings, they eclipsed the Sthaviras.
Later, when the Sthaviras grew weak, they moved to the Snowy Mountains to avoid them; thus, the school was named after their place of residence. Next, [the section on] the three hundred [years].
In the first three hundred years, a school named the Vātsīputrīya emerged from the Sarvāstivāda.
Then, in the second three hundred years, four schools branched out from the Vātsīputrīya: first, the Dharmottarīya; second, the Bhadrayānīya; third, the Saṃmitīya;
and fourth, the Mahīśāsaka. Furthermore, in the third three hundred years, another school named the [Mahīśāsaka] emerged from the Sarvāstivāda.
Three hundred years after the Mahīśāsaka school, a branch named Dharmaguptaka emerged from the Mahīśāsaka.
At the end of the next three hundred years, a school named Kāśyapīya emerged from the Sarvāstivāda.
Four hundred years later, another school named Sautrāntika emerged once again from the Sarvāstivāda.

The sub-sects are also called the *Śāthavāda* (Saytuan) school; including their branches and origins, they constitute eleven schools, which together with the aforementioned Mahāsāṃghika make twenty schools in total.
Since all are based upon these two primary schools, they are referred to as "the two originals. Regarding the passage in the *Jiaochao* (Commentary) stating "neither right nor wrong," etc.:
previously, the prose section of the sutra stated that [this teaching] can cause the Dharma to abide, enabling all to attain the four fruits of arhatship through the equality of the Tripitaka.
Just as the ocean has no diverse flavors, so it is with the twenty sons of a man. Regarding what the Tathāgata truly taught: the former [section] was spoken concerning the Buddha;

because they follow their own emotional attachments, there are no such Four Noble Truths and the like for them, nor is there any other teaching. Thus, there is nothing that is "not-is" (non-erroneous).

Or rather, if each merely claims their own position to be correct, how can this be called being "truly is"? Therefore, it is said there is "no-is. Since each mutually negates the other, how could this possibly be the case?
Names and realities are not fixed, which is why it is said there is neither "is" nor "is not. Furthermore, since all [teachings] emerge from the Mahāyāna, how could there be "is" or "is not"?
Or rather, because one can rely upon them to practice and thereby invariably obtain benefit, it is said that there is neither "is" nor "is not.

As for the phrase "arising in the future," this refers to the period after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, specifically after one hundred years have passed since the time the sutra was preached; thus, it is called "the future."

The details of its initial emergence are as described above. Regarding the passage in the *Jiaochao* (Commentary) stating "grouping them by their doctrinal characteristics," this refers to the fact that the various sectarian calculations of the Hīnayāna consist of eighteen schools; these were previously combined into two.

Now, taking twenty schools and further grouping them according to their doctrinal characteristics, they are consolidated into six sects. Because the Mahāyāna is also included, there are ten sects in total.
The Commentary states that those who wish to engage with the Mahāyāna early on may seem to be engaging with it through the meaning of "provisional names" which lack fixed reality;
yet, because they take the Sūtras as their definitive authority while not relying upon the Vinaya or the Śāstras, they are called the Sautrāntikas.

The phrase "merely excluding [the lower]" refers to the sense of "mere emptiness" (but-śūnyatā). As for the phrase "wondrously existent true nature," it means that what follows is non-empty and serves as the basis.
The wondrous existence of true nature is not an existence that is identical to emptiness which constitutes "wondrous existence.
The Commentary now summarizes the teachings of all periods into ten schools;
furthermore, among the first four schools, Master Zizuo added a fifth, the Dharma-realm School (*dharmadhātu-nikāya*), which is the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The Dharma Master Lin of Qishu Monastery further categorized the six schools as described in his previous commentary; however, none of these are currently in use.

The present ten schools are fully subsumed within the eight schools of Dharma Master Dashi: the sixth school therein is incorporated here as the seventh, the *Paramārtha-ubhaya-śūnyatā* (Ultimate Emptiness of Both) school;
the seventh is now designated as the eighth, the *Zhēnkōng-juéxiàng* (True Emptiness Beyond Characteristics) school; and the eighth is [retained] as the *Yìnglǐ* (Conformity to Principle) school.
The Yuan-shi (Perfectly Real) school is the seventh; the schools of the Three Natures as Empty and as Existing are the ninth and twelfth.
Since the Master of the Commentary added these two new schools beyond those of Dharma Master Dashi, there are ten schools to encompass the temporal teachings of a single era.
*Huayan Xuantan Huijuan Ji*, Scroll 34, Phonetic Explanations:
Xié (hújié qiè): to harbor and maintain; to store and protect. Luò (lǚjué qiè): outstanding and eminent. Kè (gǔbó qiè): the yoke of a large carriage. Zhòu (zhíyòu qiè): descendants or lineage.
*Huayan Xuantan Huixuan Ji*, Fascicle 35, compiled by the Bhikṣu Pueri of Zai Guangsi on Mount Cang. Commentary, Part One.

Regarding the "School that Maintains Both Self and Dharmas" (*wǒ fǎ jù yǒu zōng*) and so forth, the *Tàn xuán jì* states: "This refers to the stages of humans and devas, as well as the Small [Vehicle]..."
Among the vehicles, the Vātsīputrīyas and others do not mention humans and devas here because the text is abbreviated;

furthermore, they do not mention them because humans and devas do not establish the existence of a self (*ātman*) as their fundamental tenet. As for the mention of the "three aggregates" (*triskandha*) and so forth: "aggregate" (*skandha*) has the meaning of accumulation, while "repository" (*kośa*) has the meaning of containment.

Within the five [categories], the aggregate of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-skandha*) is divided into the three time periods to form the third [category]; the fourth name is identical [to the original].

The fifth is that which is neither of the two aggregates; that is, it is neither the aggregate of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor the aggregate of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), meaning it cannot be described as either conditioned or unconditioned.
Since it is neither a conditioned nor an unconditioned dharma, it is the Self (*ātman*). Furthermore, the commentary on the dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) at the end of this section states:
"Those of both internal and external paths, relying on their own cleverness, read the Buddha’s scriptures and give rise to [a certain view]..."
Because they arose in association with the Buddha-dharma, they received this name of "Vātsīputrīya. When reading the *Śāriputra-abhidharma*, they separately established the statement:

"I exist outside the four categories" (the three times and unconditioned phenomena constitute the four categories). Within the fifth, the "Ineffable Treasury," the Buddha said that such a person is no different from the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
All treatises infer that because he does not accept [any of these categories], he is called a non-Buddhist.
Regarding the phrase "The Vātsīputrīya school, etc.," the *Commentary on the Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra* states: "This is the name of the founder of the Vinaya school.
Long ago, there was a rishi dwelling in a secluded mountain retreat who, when desire arose within him, did not know what to do.

Later, because he fathered a son by a cow, all those of his lineage thereafter called themselves 'Vatsa' (Calf); this is a Brahmin clan name. [This occurred] while the Buddha was still in the world..."
In the world, there was once a non-Buddhist follower of the Vātsīputrīya school who went forth as a monk under the Buddha, as described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Subsequently, his disciples transmitted this lineage without interruption until it reached the present division; because it originated from that distant ancestor, it has come to be known by the name "Vātsīputrīya.
As for Dharmottara, this is the name of the founder of the Vinaya school. He is called Dharmottara because he is superior (*uttara*) in the Dharma, or perhaps because the Dharma has emerged from him.

Regarding the phrase "above all assemblies," Shi Chao states: "This school extensively upholds the Vinaya-piṭaka, and they themselves claim that the Dharma they propagate stands above those of all other schools.
Regarding the term "descendants of the Three Sages" (*sanzhen zhou*), the *Zuanyuan* and the *Zonglun shu* state: "'Sage' (*xian*) is the name for a patriarch of a school;
'descendant' (*zhou*) has the meaning of lineage. They are thus the descendants of the Arhats who were sages. Thus it is said.

They are named after the patriarchs from whom they were originally derived. Regarding the four Saṃmitīyas: "Saṃmitīya" means that which weighs, measures, and definitively establishes [the truth], thus it is called "measure" (*pramāṇa*);
because this measure is free from error, it is called "correct" (*saṃmita*). The profound meanings established by this school are definitively determined and free from deviation;
they call themselves "Correct Measure," deriving their name from the doctrine they establish. Fifth is the Ghoṣaka school (or the Mountain of Dense Forest).
The mountain forest where the head of the school resided was lush and dense; it was named after that residence.
Regarding the statement that the *Sarvāstivāda* and others are "those who say all exists" (*sarvam asti*), this means they maintain that nothing exists apart from form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).

This refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)—one aggregate of form and four aggregates of mind—which encompass all phenomena (*dharma*). It is said that they may also establish three [categories].
Regarding the statement that there are no unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena in the world, this is because the aforementioned "unspeakable self" (*avaktavya-ātman*) has been excluded.
As for the statement that they may be divided into five categories, this refers to the seventy-five dharmas of the five categories of the preceding Hīnayāna system:

namely, one mental dharma (*citta*), forty-six mental concomitants (*caitasika*), eleven material dharmas (*rūpa*), fourteen non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and three unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta*); hence, they are called the five categories.
In this context, because there is no self (*ātman*) alone while all phenomena (*dharma*) exist, they are called the Sarvāstivāda (School of All-Existence).
Regarding the "Haimavata school" and others mentioned in the *Yao* (Commentary), the meaning is as explained above;

since the Sarvāstivāda originally branched out from among them, they are said to be largely identical, differing only slightly in their propagation of the *Abhidharma*, as well as the *Sūtras* and *Vinaya*. Third, the Bahuśrutīya.
Regarding the Śrāvaka schools: because the founder of this school was learned in the Tripiṭaka and deeply realized the Buddha’s intent, it is called the "School of Much Learning" (Mahīśāsaka).

Regarding the Mahīśāsaka school: the founder was formerly a king who transformed and governed the people upon the earth; later, he renounced his throne to leave the household life and practice the Way.
He was named after this original deed, hence it is called the Mahīśāsaka school. As for the statement that there is also an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), this...
There are two interpretations. The first states that "intermediate existence" (*antarābhava*) refers to the *antarā-bhava* situated between the two existences of birth and death.
However, according to the teachings of the Mahīśāsaka school cited in the *Fayuan*, intermediate existence definitely does not exist; thus, this must be a later fabrication.

It is called a "later fabrication" because its tenet differs [from the orthodox view], which is why it says, "there is also intermediate existence. Therefore, a separate question-and-answer section has been composed outside of the main commentary (*chao*).

Question: Does the intermediate state (antarābhava) exist as a substantial reality or not? Answer: The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that there is an intermediate state and that there is no intermediate state;
such debates and recitations belong to the domain of the Buddhas and are not something known through the conceptual discrimination of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
If a person gives rise to such doubts, they are still able to destroy immeasurable afflictions (*kleśa*) like Mount Sumeru. If, regarding...
This "certainty" refers to what is called "clinging to the two. Regarding the phrase "within existence," it means that within the past and future, there is also the present dharma.
However, according to the text of the *Benchao*, the character "also" (*yu*) is added; it reads:
"Also within existence, there is all dharmas. This implies that it is not necessarily the case that the present dharma exists within the temporal state of existence.
This constitutes a different interpretation.
Regarding the establishment of "correct causes and conditions" (*samyag-hetu-pratyaya*) in the Commentary, it asks: what is meant by "correct causes and conditions"?

It is that from the causes and conditions of the three poisons arise the three types of karma—meritorious and so forth—and from the causes and conditions of these three karmas arise the phenomena of the three realms. From these causes and conditions, all phenomena come to exist.
Regarding the commentary’s initial statement that "the ninety-five types [of heterodox views] are like those in the sixth dedication," the *Śāstra* (Sūtra Commentary) says:
"In many places it is said that there are ninety-five distinct types of heterodox doctrines.

According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, each of the six teachers of the non-Buddhists possesses sixteen kinds of teachings: one teaching for their own study, and fifteen each taught to individual disciples."
The *Zi shi tu he lun* (Combined Treatise by Disciples and Masters) states that there are ninety-six heterodox doctrines;

the *Zhenyuan shu* (Zhenyuan Commentary) says there are separately ninety-five kinds of heterodox and erroneous treatises, while the scriptures constitute the one among these ninety-six that is the Buddha-way. However, because it is most subtle and profound, it is called the "Way" (*mārga*) as it accords with correct principle (*nyāya*).

Although the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) has not yet thoroughly penetrated the source, it perceives a small portion of it, and thus one transcends birth within the realm of segmented existence (*bhavāgra*).
If death were not thus, how could such power and function exist? From this point onward, all are termed "non-Buddhists" (tīrthika).

Regarding the four virtues of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) and so forth: as for the first principle (*dharma*), the *Sāṃkhyakārikā* (Seventy Verses on Sāṃkhya) asks, "What are the characteristics of *dharma*? [The answer is: *nyama-niyama*. There are five aspects to *nyama*: first, freedom from anger;

second, reverence for teachers and elders; third, internal and external purity; fourth, moderation in food and drink; fifth, non-negligence. *Niyama* also has five aspects: first, non-killing; second, non-stealing; third, truthful speech; fourth... [fifth, non-attachment].

The Brahma-faring consists of five [qualities], the first of which is freedom from deceit and crookedness. Second is wisdom (*prajñā*). That treatise asks: "What is called wisdom? Wisdom is of two kinds: first, external wisdom; second, internal wisdom. External wisdom refers to the six Vedāṅgas:

(1) Śikṣā-śāstra, (2) Vyākaraṇa-śāstra, (3) Kalpa-śāstra, (4) Chandas-śāstra, (5) Nirukta-śāstra, and (6) Jyotiṣa-śāstra. These six branches of knowledge are called external wisdom. Internal wisdom refers to the three *guṇas* and the Self (*ātman*).

Between these two lies intermediate wisdom. Through external wisdom one attains worldly success; through internal wisdom one attains liberation. Third is the renunciation of desire (*vairāgya*), which is also of two kinds: external and internal. Regarding the internal, it is the perception of suffering within all material possessions throughout the three periods of time.

*Upāyāsa* (distress) refers to the three stages of seeking, guarding, and losing [objects], as well as the two faults of attachment to signs and the infliction of harm. Because one perceives these [faults], one leaves the household life out of desire for renunciation (*vairāgya*).

Although one has thus left desire, one has not yet attained liberation. This external cause of renunciation leads to the accomplishment of internal renunciation; having recognized that the person is distinct from the three *guṇas*, one seeks renunciation. First, one attains internal knowledge (*jñāna*), and subsequently, one attains renunciation. Due to this renunciation, one attains liberation.

External renunciation merely leads through the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), whereas internal renunciation is able to attain liberation. The four masteries (*vaśitā*) are of eight kinds: first, subtlety, reaching the limit of the atom (*paramāṇu*); second, movement, reaching the limit of the mind; third, pervasiveness, reaching the limit of space; fourth, attainment.

"Obtaining as one intends the five [senses], being the sovereign of the world, and being superior to others in all respects—this is the first; being able to employ the objects of desire at will and simultaneously—this is the second; not being subject to others and being able to direct the beings of the three worlds according to one's own will—this is the third;

dwelling according to one’s intent, meaning dwelling according to time, place, and mind—these four dharmas are the characteristics of a *sattva*. If the *sattva* increases and is able to subdue both *rajas* and *tamas*, then because of my great joy and pleasure, I obtain the four virtues such as equanimity (*samatā*).
These are called the characteristics of a *sattva*. Regarding the phrase "Having obtained this wisdom, based on great compassion, he speaks," etc., the treatise states in full:
When Kāpilavastu beheld this world submerged in blinding darkness, he gave rise to a heart of compassion, exclaiming: "Alas! Birth and death exist within the midst of darkness!
Surveying the world, he saw a brahmin of the Aśvalāyana lineage (some versions read Aśvaka;
the character *he* is likely an error). This man had performed the Great Hidden-body Sacrifice for a thousand years. [The Buddha] went to him and spoke these words: "Aśvalāyana, you..."
Having finished speaking these words as a joke regarding the life of a householder, he immediately departed. After a full thousand years had passed, he returned once more and spoke the same words.
The brahmin then replied to the seer, "World-Honored One, I was indeed joking when I spoke of the pleasures of the householder's life.
When the seer heard this, he departed again; yet later, he came once more and spoke the same words.
The Brahmin answered him in the same manner. The Rishi asked, "Are you able to dwell in the pure practice of the holy life (brahmacarya)?
The Brahmin replied, "I am indeed able to dwell so. He then abandoned the ways of the household and practiced the life of a renunciant as a disciple of Kāpya.
This was the initial summary of the teaching by Kāpya for Āśvalāyana.
Only from darkness does this darkness arise; within this darkness there is the field of wisdom (*jñānakṣetra*), and the field of wisdom is precisely the person (*pudgala*).
Because people do not yet possess wisdom, it is called a "field. Next, through successive transformation and change, this first turning arises, up until liberation.
For the *Aśvalāyana-ṛṣi*, it is briefly explained as *Paṃsukūla*; for the *Paṃsukūla*, it is explained in detail. It is also like this. This is the detailed explanation of the *Paṃsukūla*.
This knowledge consists of sixty thousand verses. It was transmitted from Khagākhaga to Ulūka;
Ulūka transmitted it to Vāgbali (the *Chao* notes that the character "he" is also an error); and Vāgbali transmitted it to a Brahmin of the Kauśika clan named Īśvarakṛṣṇa.
Having obtained this knowledge, he saw that the *Mahā-śāstra* was difficult to uphold, and therefore he abridged it.
The *Chao* (Excerpts) cites seventy verses and so forth.
Regarding the passage "The *Chao* [discusses] the world being subject to contention," this refers to a debate with a monk from Eastern India.

That monk asserted that the world is eternal; the [Chinese] monk challenged him, saying: "It must currently be undergoing destruction, because at the time of the world's dissolution, the world necessarily perishes."
It is now proven that while this [monk] perished, the other certainly did not; he was like the mountains of today.

The Saṃgha could no longer say that the king’s partisan, a non-Buddhist (tīrthika), had caused the monks to suffer humiliation by making them ride donkeys. Because the king held the non-Buddhist in high esteem, he bestowed seventy *jin* of gold upon him as a gift (*yì*, pronounced with a departing tone).

He said, "Let it be renowned" (*lìng yù*, with the character *lìng* pronounced with a departing tone, meaning "to beautify"). (According to the *Weishi shu*, in a later age, Vasubandhu appeared in the world.)

He then composed the *Tattvārtha-śāstra*, also known as the *Paramārtha-saptati*, to counter the Sāṃkhya school and refute the arguments of those non-Buddhists. He stated that their critique was flawed because they failed to recognize the defects in their own thesis, reason, and example; furthermore, he argued that neither he nor his fellow monks existed at all.

He further addressed their reason (*hetu*)—that "because there is no destruction now, there will be no destruction later"—pointing out that it suffers from the fallacy of being unestablished for one party (*anyatarāsiddha*). He explained: "My fellow monks merely state that phenomena such as the great earth must undergo transformation prior to destruction, and that this [transformation] exists after [destruction], just like the flame of a lamp.

He concluded that it was not his fellow monks who were ignorant of logic, but rather the opponents themselves. At that time, the King took Vasubandhu’s treatise and circulated it throughout all regions, proclaiming its dissemination. As no one could withstand its challenge, he subsequently summoned the former King and the Sāṃkhya non-Buddhist proponents to serve as witnesses to the truth.
[Regarding] these [people], they may bind straw into human figures to represent the assembly of that time and subject them to flogging, as described in the *Vasubandhu-ācārya-carita*.
As for the "eighteen schools," the commentary states in full: "The Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika each have eighteen different sects.

Regarding the statement "because they say [the world] arises during the rainy season," the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) explains that in that land, one year is established [in this manner].
There are three seasons: from the sixteenth day of the first month (in that land, each month is divided into fifteen days of the "white" and fifteen days of the "black";
the former half-month is white and the latter half-month is black, as the black is taken as the beginning) until the fifteenth day of the fifth month is the hot season;

from the sixteenth day of the fifth month until the fifteenth day of the ninth month is the rainy season; and from the sixteenth day of the ninth month until the tenth day of the first month is the cold season.
Five days constitute a period of cold; this refers to when these non-Buddhists (bāhyaka) are born during the rainy season.

Regarding the statement that their Sanskrit pronunciations differ, the *Weishi lüeshu* (Commentary on the Summary of the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi) states that Vāliśa and the Bāṣpa of the *Sāṃkhyakārikā* are one and the same person.
This is the reading of the number (qùshēng). The tone for "du" (度) is rùshēng.
The commentary states that the original source was composed by Kapila; this refers to the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*, which identifies the author as "composed by the sage Kapila" based on its original source.
In reality, it was actually Īśvarakṛṣṇa who composed it.

As for the statement that the prose commentary (*vṛtti*) was an explanation by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, this means that he first composed the prose commentary with the intent to refute that school’s tenets.

Having thoroughly mastered the doctrines of other schools, Vasubandhu composed the *Saptati-śāstra* (The Seventy Verses) as a polemical treatise to refute them. Thus, the *Vasubandhu-biography* states that he composed the *Tattva-saptati-śāstra* to destroy the Sāṃkhya school;
from beginning to end, their system was utterly dismantled, such that not a single sentence could stand.
Consequently, the non-Buddhists were filled with grief and distress, as if their own lives had been destroyed.
Regarding the phrase "The Ātman is the sovereign," the *Śata-śāstra*, in the chapter "Refuting the Ātman" (*Brahma-parivarta*), states in full:

"The Ātman is the sovereign; it is eternal, conscious, and characterized by pervasiveness; it abides eternally without decaying or dispersing, and it encompasses all dharmas. (The *Chao* [Commentary] notes that the character "root" [*gen*] is an error.
It continues: "One who knows these twenty-five principles attains liberation; one who does not know them does not escape birth and death. This is what is stated externally.
[Objection: It is truly existent that there is an initial [consciousness], as stated in the Sāṃkhya-sūtra (i.e., the *Sāṃkhya-kārikā*):
"The characteristic of consciousness (*buddhi*) is the self (*ātman*). [Question: Is the self and consciousness one, or are they different? [Response: They are one. [Objection:
If consciousness were the characteristic of the self, then since consciousness is impermanent, the self would have to be impermanent—just as, for example, heat [is impermanent].
This characteristic of fire is heat and impermanence; fire itself is also impermanent. Now one realizes it is truly impermanent. Why is this?

Because its characteristics are distinct; because it is dependent on causes and conditions; because it was originally non-existent and now exists; and because having existed, it returns to non-existence.

The opponent says: It is eternal because it is not produced. That which has the characteristic of being produced is impermanent, but the self (*ātman*) does not have the characteristic of being produced; therefore, it is eternal. The proponent says: If...
If you claim that consciousness (*buddhi*) is not a characteristic of the self (*ātman*), then this [self] is impermanent. You assert that the self is permanent;

therefore, it must be distinct from consciousness. If the self and consciousness were not distinct, then because consciousness is impermanent, the self would also have to be impermanent. This is explained at length through the refutation [found in the *Śata-śāstra*].
To say that the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*) are also capable of producing [consciousness] follows this same reasoning as set forth in the *Śata-śāstra*.

The five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*) differ from those in the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*; in the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*, the five great elements are not considered productive causes, while all other points are identical.

One should know this by following the examples below. In the *Yichao* (Commentary), it states that "Primal Nature (*prakṛti*) is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*)," followed by three alternative names.

Before the section explaining Primal Nature, it says "if one explains it as arising"; after that, it explains it as "Supreme Nature" (*pradhāna*), and in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, it is explained as follows.

Regarding the statement, "To be in darkness and not knowing is called the *tattva* of darkness (*mṛtyu-tattva*), etc.," this is as previously explained by the Kāpila [Sāṃkhya] to Āśvalāyana, briefly stating that in the beginning, only darkness (*tamas*) arose, and so forth (as detailed above).
As for the phrase "I know" (*ahaṃ vedmi*), the *Bai-fa-ming-chao* (Exposition of the One Hundred Dharmas) states:
"'I know' refers to the *puruṣa* (the spiritual self). Because the *puruṣa* possesses cognition and the capacity for deliberation, it is called 'I know.'"

[The commentary] states: Regarding "the five tanmātras arise from *ahaṃkāra*," that treatise says: "Because *ahaṃkāra* arises from the *mahat*, it is a transformation capable of producing the five *tanmātras*;

therefore, they are called 'fundamental. Because the five *tanmātras* arise from *ahaṃkāra*, they are transformations capable of producing the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the five sense organs;
thus, they are called 'fundamental. [The commentary] states: "Like hot vapor dispersing into space, etc. The treatise properly says: "The *prakṛti* is real."
Because it is subtle, it is not seen; for example, smoke and the like, when dispersed in the air, cannot be seen because they are fine, and its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is likewise.
It is not like a second head or a third hand, which, being absolutely non-existent, cannot be seen (and so forth).

Regarding the passage beginning with "Sattva-rajas-tamas," this is based on the *Vijñaptimātratā* (Consciousness-Only) school. As for "Sattva-rajas-tamas" in the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*, the Sanskrit term is *sattva-rajas-tamas*.
As for the terms "Old" and "New": the *Yìjǐng Chāo* states that they are named differently according to whether they were translated during the ancient or modern periods of this land (China);
hence they are called "Old" and "New. Alternatively, they may be distinguished based on their numerical order in the Western [Indian] tradition.
There is no harm in the various schools of thought asserting that ancient and modern views differ;

this is also the case regarding the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*. As for the statement "its color, quality, and so forth," the *Sāṃkhyasaptati* states: "That which is light, luminous, and subtly radiant is called 'joy' (*prīti*).
If joy increases, all the faculties become light and free from weakness, and they are then able to grasp their respective objects. At that time...
One should know that when joy and pleasure increase, the mind becomes haughty and disregards others like a rutting elephant wishing to fight;

therefore, this is true growth. If sorrow increases, such a person constantly desires to fight, their mind is perpetually restless and unable to settle in one place, and their obscured virtues cause the entire body to feel heavy as the sense faculties are shrouded.
It cannot grasp the various objects (*viṣaya*). The *Bai fa chao* (Notes on the Hundred Dharmas) states:

"Due to the three qualities (*guṇa*) conforming to the Self (*ātman*), they undergo transformation (*pariṇāma*) to give rise to the remaining twenty-three principles (*tattva*), thereby forming the various worlds and sentient beings.

The first transformation, up to the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), forms the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*); thus this subtle body consists only of the five subtle elements. This subtle body is produced."
Upon entering the womb, the union of the red and white elements increases the subtle body (*sūkṣma-kāya*) to form the coarse body (*audārika-kāya*).

With the subtle body as the interior and the coarse body as the exterior, because the merit of joy (*prīti-guṇa*) increases through correspondence with the movement of phenomena (*dharma-caryā*), one is born among the gods.
Because the merit of joy increases, other qualities remain hidden and do not manifest; this is because those who possess joy have a light appearance that is subtle. Thus it is for the gods.
If one possesses middling lightness, mastery over light, much pleasure, and much desire, or if the quality of *sattva* (purity) increases, one is born among humans;

yet, due to an increase in sorrow, one experiences much grief, much suffering, and much anger. If one acts in accordance with what is contrary to the Dharma (*adharma*), the quality of *tamas* (darkness) increases, thereby suppressing the other two qualities;

one is then born among beasts. Because *tamas* has the characteristic of heavy obscuration, beasts are characterized by much delusion and darkness. This applies whether one practices according to the Dharma or contrary to the Dharma.
There is a distinction among these three qualities (*guṇa*), such that they increase in pairs of two, or one is born among the gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, or even among non-mobile sentient beings.
When, at a later time, the previously [accumulated] dharma and non-dharma have been extinguished, one abandons this body;
the earth element within the body returns to correspond with the external earth element, and so on, up to the internal space element.

Furthermore, the external space returns to the five great elements, the five faculties of cognition return to the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and so on until the mind-faculty also returns to the five subtle elements.
These five subtle elements, together with the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*), then proceed to another place; such an uninterrupted succession is called "revolving" (*saṃsāra*).
The commentary’s verse replies: The first two lines [of the verse] concern the *dharma* (the subject); the third line is the metaphor; and the fourth line is the application (*yoga*).
The prose version states in full: "I who seek to see the three virtues" means that I possess such an intention: "I shall now see the self-nature of the three virtues.
Therefore, I unite with the self-nature to become that which exists in isolation. (The inclusion of the entire verse in this commentary may be an error. I.

This afflicted person—(in the verse, "person" carries the meaning of "self," which is why it is frequently referred to as "person" or "self" in the treatise)—is one who is capable of seeing and knowing;
I shall now act for his sake so that he may attain solitary existence. For this reason, the self-nature is conjoined with the self, just as a king is conjoined with his subjects.
I should cause this person to also be conjoined with the king, and the king should bestow [favor] upon me.
Because they live together, these kings are in harmony; by this principle, the meaning of the union of intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) is established.
Furthermore, just as I exist for the sake of perception, while intrinsic nature exists as something distinct and independent, it is like the union of the lame man and the blind man.
Regarding this, there is an analogy: in the past, there was a caravan that went to Ujjayinī and was plundered by bandits, so that they were each separated.
As they were running about in a scattered fashion, there was one who had been blind from birth and another who had been lame from birth.
The crowd abandoned the blind man and ran off in mockery, while the lame man sat watching. The lame man asked, "Who are you? The blind man replied, "I am one who has been blind from birth;
because I do not know the way, I ran along in mockery. And who are you? The lame man replied, "I have been lame from birth."
"A person can only see the path but cannot travel it; therefore, you should now place me upon your shoulder.
I shall lead the way while you carry me. Thus, through their mutual cooperation, the two reached their destination.
This harmony is like the union of self-nature with the "I" that gives rise to the world; having reached the destination, the two [parted].
"Each is mutually distinct; when one perceives the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of the self, one immediately attains liberation—this is the truth of self-nature (*svabhāva-satya*).
It also causes me alone to exist," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "Self-nature first gives rise to Mahat," the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-ṭīkā* states: "Because the self contemplates its objects, it proceeds from self-nature..."
The specific meaning of *mahā-vidyā* (Great Knowledge) is as explained in the *Śāstra*. That treatise asks: "What is the characteristic of 'great' (*mahat*)?
The verse answers: "Decisive wisdom is called 'great'; the Dharma is wisdom; it is free from desire and possesses mastery; *sattva* is the opposite of this.
This refers to the long vowel *tā* in *tamah*. [The commentary] states: "Decisive wisdom is called 'great' means that the name of this thing is 'obstruction' (*āvaraṇa*)."
The term "entity" (*vastu*) refers to such consciousness and perception; this is called "decisive knowledge" (*niścaya-jñāna*). It is called "Great" (*mahat*); this "Great" has eight parts:
four parts are joy (*prīti*) and four parts are darkness-delusion (*tamas-moha*). Regarding the four parts of joy: first, dharma; second, wisdom (*prajñā*);

third, detachment from desire (*vairāgya*); fourth, mastery (*vaśitva*). (These are all explained as before. These four dharmas are the characteristics of *sattva*; their opposites are the characteristics of *tamas*.
The four characteristics that subvert the Dharma are: first, non-Dharma; second, non-wisdom; third, craving; and fourth, lack of self-mastery. These four are the characteristics of *tamas*.

Regarding the subsequent arising of the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), the treatise asks: "What are the characteristics of the conceit of 'I' (*asmimāna*)? It is the notion of 'I' regarding sound and the notion of 'I' regarding touch."

"I am form," "I am taste," "I am fragrance," "I am merit," and "I am lovely"—such attachments as these are called *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am"), which is also termed the "five greats" (*pañcamahābhūta*).
Regarding the first [of these] and its transformation, the verse says: "The eleven types of *sattva* undergo transformation;

from *ahaṃkāra* (ego-consciousness), the Great Elements (*mahat*) arise. From the Great, darkness (*tamas*) arises, which is intensely blazing. Two kinds [arise]; the first two lines refer to the first."
That is to say, when joy increases within the *sattva* element (which is the increase of *sattva*), the conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*) arises; this is able to suppress both sorrow and delusion.
This conceit of "I" is of the nature of joy (that is, of the *sattva* nature); the Noble Ones call it "transformation.
This conceit of transformation is able to give rise to eleven faculties, because it possesses pleasure, goodness, lightness, clarity, and purity, and because it is able to grasp its own objects.

Regarding the third phrase, which describes the eleven as being of the *sattva* lineage: if the *tamas* increases within the Great One (*mahat*), then the *ahaṃkāra* (ego-sense) arises, which is capable of suppressing both joy and sorrow.
Because this *ahaṃkāra* is of the nature of delusion (*moha*), the Sages call it the "Great" (*mahān*), meaning the first of the five Great Elements (*mahābhūta*).
This *ahaṃkāra* gives rise to the five *tanmātras* (subtle elements); therefore, both the five *tanmātras* and the five Great Elements are entirely of the nature of darkness and delusion.

Regarding the fourth phrase: if suffering increases within the great elements (*mahābhūta*), then the conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*) arises; this is able to suppress the pervasive joy and obscure [the path].
Because this conceit of "I" is a seed of sorrow (*daurmanasya*), the Noble Ones establish its name as "blazing" (*jvalita*). This conceit of "I" gives rise to two types [of results]:

it can produce the eleven faculties (*indriya*) and also produce the five "solely" [associated] factors, such as the faculty of change (*vipariṇāmamāna*). When the various faculties arise from the conceit of change, they grasp [their objects].

Because the *atigṛddha-ahaṃkāra* (the excessively greedy ego) acts as its companion, when the *mahā-ahaṃkāra* (great ego) produces the five *tanmātras* (subtle elements) and the five *mahābhūtas* (gross elements), it likewise takes the *atigṛddha-ahaṃkāra* as its companion;
thus, the *atigṛddha-ahaṃkāra* gives rise to two kinds. The commentary states:
"By this principle, the *Chao* (Excerpts) says that this [passage] generally clarifies that all [products] arise from *ahaṃkāra*. If explained specifically, [it concerns] transformation (*vikāra*)."
From the *ahaṃkāra* (ego-sense), eleven faculties arise; if it is the *mahat-tattva* (the Great Principle), the *ahaṃkāra* first gives rise to the five *tanmātras* (subtle elements).
The "five great [elements]" (*pañca-mahābhūta*) generally give rise to two kinds. This is based on their distinct functions. If one takes the sequential order, as stated in the *Śāstra*:

"One should first produce the five *tanmātras*, and from the five *tanmātras*, the sixteen [categories] arise. This intention accords with the relationship between the general and the specific in the *Sāṃkhyakārikā* and the *Śataśāstra*.
Although the sequence differs, the principle is the same; thus, the *Sāṃkhyakārikā* (Seventy Verses on Sāṃkhya) states:

"Within the sixteen [evolutes], five arise from these [five tanmātras] to produce the five great elements. This means that within the sixteen, there are five [tanmātras] which alone are capable of producing the five great elements.

Regarding the passage beginning with "The five *tanmātras* are without distinction because they are subtle and tranquil," the verse of the treatise states: "The five *tanmātras* are without distinction;
from these arise the five great elements, which possess distinctions. This refers to tranquility (*śānta*), fear (*bhīta*), delusion (*mūḍha*), and activity (*pravṛtta*).
As for "the five *tanmātras* are without distinction": the five *tanmātras* arising from the *ahaṃkāra* (ego-sense) are subtle and tranquil. Because...
Joy and bliss are its characteristics; this is because there is no distinction among the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) of the various devas, as they are free from sorrow and delusion.

From this arise the five great elements (*mahābhūta*), which do possess distinctions. Regarding the distinctions among these five great elements: from sound, only space (*ākāśa*) arises; and so on, up to from fragrance, only earth arises.
These are the distinctions among the five great elements. What are the characteristics of these distinctions? First, tranquility (*śānti*).

Second, it causes fear (the syllable *bhī* in the verse); third, it is darkness and delusion. These five great elements are the characteristics of the human realm: earth, water, fire, wind, and space. How so?
It is like a wealthy man who enters a private inner chamber and enjoys the pleasures of the five senses, or who ascends a high tower to gaze afar upon the great expanse of space.
Because he experiences pleasure through space, space is tranquil; or, while in the air, he is buffeted by cold winds.
When one touches emptiness, suffering arises. Furthermore, there may be a person traveling through a vast wilderness who sees only empty space and perceives no village or place to rest;
such a person gives rise to darkness and delusion. The other great elements (*mahābhūta*) are likewise.

Thus, because the five *tanmātras* (subtle potentials) serve as objects for the devas and are entirely tranquil, there is no differentiation among them; whereas human beings perceive the five great elements.

"Because the Great Element (mahat) possesses three qualities, there is a distinction. The commentary explains: "In contrast to the *Śāstra*, the *Vyākhyā* should state that the five *tanmātras* have no distinction;

they are the celestial *tanmātras*. Since the celestial realm is free from sorrow and delusion, it consists only of joy and bliss. Therefore, what is here called 'the Great' (*mahat*) is a scribal error for 'celestial' (*divya*).
Question: Previously it was stated that each [element] is composed of the three qualities; why then are the celestial *tanmātras* said to be five?
"Is it only that there is no sorrow or delusion? Answer: Although other virtues exist, they are hidden and do not manifest; therefore, it is said that they are "non-existent.
The meaning is as previously explained.

Regarding the statement in the *Chao* (Commentary) that "it depends on the presence or absence of sensory objects (*viṣaya*) and so forth," this refers to what the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* quotes from the *Saṃgha-sūtra* (that [is] volume...).

The seventy-eighth [section] states: "That is to say, from sound and subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) arises the great element of space (*ākāśa-mahābhūta*); from sound and tangibility arises the great element of wind; from color, sound, and tangibility arises the great element of fire; from color, sound, tangibility, and taste arises the great element of water;

from color, sound, tangibility, taste, and odor arises the great element of earth. From space arises the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*); from wind arises the body-faculty (*kāya-indriya*); from fire arises the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*); from water arises the tongue-faculty (*jihvā-indriya*); from earth arises the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇa-indriya*). In this manner, they gradually proceed from the subtle to the coarse, as explained at length in the *Saṃgha-sūtra*.
However, regarding the statement that there are "five great elements" (*pañca-mahābhūtāni*), the treatise says: "Because their essence and function are great, they pervade the three worlds."
This means that because the earth, space, and the three classes of sentient beings—namely animals, humans, and devas—are all universally present, they are called "great" (*mahābhūta*).

Regarding the statement in the *Shō* (Commentary) that "sound arises only from the great element of space, and space constitutes the ear," this refers to the explanation found in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, the *Śata-śāstra*, and others, which also treat the five great elements as being capable of producing [sensory objects]. However, the *Saptati-śāstra* merely states:

Regarding the term "etcetera" (*ādi*), it means that the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) do not act as the productive cause; however, the treatise (*śāstra*) correctly states: "The ear-faculty arises solely from sound.

Although the word "solely" (*mātra*) is present here, the text reads "but" (*tu*) instead. This use of "but" is explained in two ways: first, in contrast to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and other texts which include the five elements;

second, in contrast to the subsequent principle of "universal production" (*sarvatra-nirmāṇa*). Therefore, it says "but" (*tu*). Furthermore, each of these points is explained within the treatise itself.
The five *tanmātras* (subtle elements) arise individually from the five sense organs (*jñānendriya*), and so forth;
it is said that the nose organ arises from fragrance alone, which is of the same category as earth, and for this reason, it perceives only fragrance and so on.
Regarding the *Ulmūka* ṛṣi, he is none other than the owl-ṛṣi. As for *na-kau*: [text continues].
The *Jixuan* (集玄) states: Some say this [term] means "merit" (*guṇa*), yet the *Śata-śāstra* frequently uses the term *guṇa* without translating it;
this refers to the functional capacity (*kāritra*) of form (*rūpa*). If one follows the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-vyākhyā* and its *Yinyi* (音義), it says this [term] means "reliance" (*āśraya*).
This is because fire relies upon form as its primary basis in order to be established; thus, its functional application is predominant, and it is therefore called "eye" (*cakṣus*).
"Only seeing form. In the *Chao* (Excerpts), where it says "generally composed of the five great elements," the character for "only" (*wei*) should likely be the character for "only" (*yu*) here;
for according to the *Saptati-śāstra*, the five great elements are not the producers [of the faculties]. The treatise states: "The five function as faculties and have five functions.

This refers to the tongue faculty (i.e., the organ of speech), which is associated with the faculty of cognition and is able to articulate names, phrases, and meanings, and so on, up to the great excretory faculty.
"Knowledge-faculty-associated [faculties] are able to discard filth and impurity. The commentary states: "The tongue, hands, feet, and so forth are each associated with the five knowledge-faculties.

Although these five knowledge-faculties perform distinct actions, because all the action-faculties are associated with the knowledge-faculties, it is said that they collectively function through the five [knowledge-faculties] alone to achieve [their tasks].
The term "that" refers to the body-faculty as the skin-faculty (*tvak-indriya*).
Regarding this, the verse of that treatise states: "The ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose—these five are called the faculties of cognition (*jñānendriya*).

[The prose commentary continues: Each perceives its own respective object; thus there are five cognitions. The eye and ear perceive from a distance; the nose and tongue perceive through contact; the skin pervades both the internal and external, being able to perceive tangible objects such as touch and so forth. "The tongue, hands, feet, and the human faculty (which is the organ of urination, also called the male and female faculties)—the great ones are only five that function as faculties.

The tongue is able to speak names and phrases; the hands are able to grasp and seize; the feet are able to walk; the male is able to engage in pleasure; and the great [organ] is able to discharge and eliminate. Therefore, they are called faculties (*indriya*)."

Regarding the statement that "discrimination (*vikalpa*) constitutes its essence," the *Śāstra* says: "The faculty of discrimination is called the root of mind (*manas-indriya*); it is taught that there are two kinds of discrimination, which constitute its essence.
If this root of mind is associated with the faculty of cognition (*jñāna-indriya*), it is named the faculty of cognition;

if it is associated with the faculty of action (*kṛti-indriya*), it is named the faculty of action. This root of mind is capable of discriminating the objects of the faculty of cognition and [the faculty of] differentiation."
To perform a distinct function of a faculty (*indriya*) is, for example, like a single person who is either called a craftsman or a skilled debater.

To distinguish [them] as mental characteristics (*citta-nimitta*)—that there are such characteristics—is the "matter" (*vastu*). These two sentences are the passage from the prose commentary (*bhāṣya*) of the treatise explaining the three intrinsic characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) as "matter.
Next, one should fully cite my own view to see its meaning; the words are also complete.

Regarding the two phrases "the five *tanmātras* constitute the universal because they take all objects as their conditions," these are the master’s interpretation according to the commentary (*śāstra*). Furthermore, the treatise states:
"The object of the great *ahaṃkāra* is the mental sphere" (this phrase is the heading of the prose; the full text reads: "Next, the object and sphere of the great *ahaṃkāra* shall be explained").

"The third has its own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object"—this one phrase is the verse itself; the full text reads: "Third, having its own specific characteristics as its object. (13)
Regarding the first phrase of the long prose commentary on the five winds, such as *pāna* and so forth, which have non-common objects yet share common functions, it states:
"The great matter of conceiving [the aggregates] as a self is the characteristic of pride (*māna*). This characteristic is the objective basis (*vastu*) of pride;

its differentiation is the characteristic of the mind (*citta*), and this characteristic is the objective basis of the mind. (The remaining three phrases are not utilized here, as explained in the treatise. It is said that the mind is able to universally grasp both differentiated and undifferentiated objects.
This is also the doctrinal explanation of our patriarch.
Regarding the phrase "The *Chao* [commentary] on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Hetuvidyā* both state... and so forth: this single sentence is entirely from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
Its commentary states: "The *puruṣa* (spiritual self) takes volition as its essence; therefore, the *Hetuvidyā* says that the grasping of a self is volition. If it refers to the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*:

Regarding the Sāṃkhya claim that "the self (ātman) is the thinker," the commentary states: The Sāṃkhya school establishes the essence of the principle of the divine self (puruṣa-tattva) as the experiencer;

because the self performs the function of thinking regarding the five sensory objects, the primal nature (prakṛti) undergoes transformation into the twenty-three principles. Therefore, the self is the thinker.
The *Chao* states: "Just as a person relies upon a body, the 'self' (*ātman*) is like the person who relies [upon it];
the twenty-four truths (*tattva*) are like the body which is relied upon. Now, taking the name of the one who relies [upon them], we call it 'reliance.

Regarding the phrase "because the five are individually distinct," the *Lun* (Treatise) says: "As for 'because the five are individually distinct,' if there were only the body, that which the Noble Ones have taught..."
Since the means for liberation would then be entirely useless, we know that there exists a self distinct from the body.

If there were no separate self and only the body existed, then when the bodies of parents, teachers, or elders are left behind after death—whether burned, submerged, or otherwise treated as offerings—one would incur sin rather than merit. For this reason, we know that there is a separate self.
The commentary states: This explains that because there is a self existing separately and independently apart from the body, it is called "independently separate.

Regarding the phrase "not similar" and so forth in the *Vyākhyā* (鈔): here, the *Vyākhyā* explains this in terms of the difference between intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and transformation (*anyathātva*). However, that treatise explains it in terms of the difference between transformation and intrinsic nature, as the verse says:
"There are nine kinds of non-similarity," which generally indicates that [things] have causes: (1) impermanence, (2) multiplicity... [and so on].

(3) Non-pervasive, (4) having an object, (5) disappearance, (6) possessing parts, (7) dependence, (8) belonging to another, and (9) transformation—these are the differences in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This is the summary. Now, following this commentary, [the first point] regarding "having no cause" means that all twenty-three principles (*tattva*) possess causes;
for example, *prakṛti* is the cause of the Great One (*mahat*), and the Great One is the cause of the I-principle (*ahaṃkāra*), and so forth. *Prakṛti*...
1. Regarding "that which is not produced by causes is eternal": since [the elements] such as *mahat* arise from *prakṛti*, they are impermanent;
because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not like that [of *prakṛti*], it is eternal. 2. Regarding "that which is common to many is one": this refers to [the elements] such as *mahat*;
they are "common to many" because many people are distinct from one another, whereas the intrinsic nature is only one, being shared by many people. 3. Regarding "that which pervades all": its own...
The nature (*prakṛti*) and the self (*ātman*) pervade all places—namely earth, space, water, fire, and so forth—whereas the five non-entities (*avastu*) do not pervade;

these refer to the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and other such things. When birth and death are about to arise, they depend upon these thirteen [principles] which together enable the subtle body (*sūkṣma-deha*) to revolve through saṃsāra, expanding and contracting, going and returning.
Their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), however, is not like this; it does not expand or contract.

Therefore, regarding the six that do not disappear: when objects such as the "Great" (mahat) and so forth transform from their derivative states back to their fundamental source, they become invisible; this is called "disappearance.

For example, when the five great elements (pañca-mahābhūta) and so forth transform and disappear into the five subtle potentials (pañca-tanmātra), the five great elements and so forth can no longer be seen.

Even when the Great disappears into the primal nature (prakṛti), the Great and the others likewise cannot be seen within the primal nature. The primal nature, however, does not undergo transformation in this manner. Thus, it does not disappear.

8. Because it does not perish, the seven [elements] are without parts; for while the Great Elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth all possess parts—since their constituent parts are distinct—their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not like this, as it is eternally without parts.

9. Because it does not depend on another: this means that while the Great Elements depend on the primal nature (*prakṛti*), and the ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*) depends on the Great Elements, the primal nature does not arise in dependence on anything else. 10. Because it does not belong to another: the Great Elements [arise] from...
Because the derivative (mūla-ja) lacks autonomy, it is like a child who cannot be independent while his parents are still alive;

intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not like this, for that which has no root is dependent upon another. [The *Śāstra*] states: "Since every person possesses a self (*ātman*), what is the characteristic of the self?
Is there one self common to many bodies, or is there a distinct self for each body? Answer: There are many selves, corresponding to [the number of bodies].

Regarding the verse stating that each body has its own self (*ātman*): because the roots of birth and death are distinct, because the performance of actions is not shared, and because the three qualities (*guṇas*) are different, the doctrine of individual selves is established. First, "because the roots of birth and death are distinct":
if the self were one, then when a single person is born, everyone would be born; yet since they are not born simultaneously, we know there are many selves. Furthermore, if the self...
First, because when one person dies, all would die, we know that there is not a single self;
furthermore, because the various sense faculties are distinct, if the self were one, then when one person is deaf or blind, everyone should likewise be deaf or blind.
Since this is not the case, we know there are many selves. The remaining three propositions are explained as in the treatise.
Regarding the statement that "the nature of the *pradhāna* (the Unmanifest) possesses six characteristics similar to transformation and so forth," the verse says:
"The three *guṇas* (1) are inseparable; (2) they are objects; (3) they are in equilibrium; (4) they are insentient; (5) they are the source of both the primordial and the derivative;

and (6) they resemble the *ātman*. There are six types of similarity—both similar and dissimilar. First, the commonality of possessing the three *guṇas*: for example, black cloth is produced from black threads. Great...

Since the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) inherently possesses the three qualities (*guṇas*), these two are inseparable; likewise, transformation (*pariṇāma*) cannot be separated from the three qualities, and the three qualities cannot be separated from the primordial nature.
The three great elements (*mahābhūtas*) and so forth are the objects of my enjoyment, and the primordial nature is also an object of my enjoyment.
Regarding this, it is said that all selves (*ātman*) possess the four great elements and so forth.
That which is experienced is like a single maidservant; this is called "one.

Furthermore, because the self-nature (*svabhāva*) is also that which is experienced by all "mine," it cannot be distinguished from the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth regarding the three qualities (*guṇa*); the self-nature is likewise [indistinguishable].

Sixth, because both the root and the branches are capable of producing [effects], they are identical. Therefore, the *Vyākhyā* states in summary: "I" (the self) is translated as "resembling" or "not resembling. That treatise says:
Regarding transformation and intrinsic nature, there are six kinds of similarity; since the self lacks these similarities, it is the opposite of the similar.
Regarding transformation and intrinsic nature, there are nine kinds of dissimilarity; since the self is the opposite of eight of these, it is called "the opposite of the dissimilar.
Other meanings may be understood as follows: that is to say, in the preceding explanation, the self has eight qualities and two qualities, while the remainder...

The transformation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) also possesses qualities and variations; as these can be understood by analogy with what precedes, it is said that "the remaining meanings may be known.

The *Chao* (Commentary) states: "By means of the three qualities (*guṇa*), etc. This should be understood according to the intent of the *Jñāna-sūtra*. As for "bondage and liberation," this refers to the self (*puruṣa*).
Regarding the statement in the *Sāṃkhya-kārikā*, "bondage and liberation" refers to the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*). It is said that "the person (*puruṣa*) has no bondage."
"There is no liberation and no transmigration through birth and death"—these two lines constitute the verse itself.
"Because there are no three qualities," and so forth, are the three types of reasons; these are the explanations in the prose (*dīrghapaṅkti*).

If that is so, the following inquiry and response—"transmigration, bondage, and liberation belong only to *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature)"—these two lines constitute the verse, which is identical in its entirety to the preceding two lines.
The verse [itself] is as stated, while the remainder is the prose commentary explaining its meaning.

The *Chao* (the Sub-commentary) refutes this extensively, as in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (*Weishi lun*) and other treatises such as the *Śata-śāstra*. Regarding the *Śata-śāstra*, as cited above from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, it says:
"The Sāṃkhya school clings to the notion that the 'Self' (ātman) is the thinker and the enjoyer, and that it is composed of the great elements produced by sattva, rajas, and tamas."

The twenty-three factors, such as the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth, are composed of three things; thus, they are real and not merely conventional, being established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Their [the opponents'] position is irrational. Why? Because the various factors such as the great elements are produced from many constituent parts;

therefore, like an army or a forest, they should be conventional and not real. How then can it be said that they are apprehended by direct perception? Furthermore, if the great elements and so forth...
If these [three] were substantially existent, they would have to be like the primary causes (*prakṛti*);

since the three—sentient being (*sattva*) and so forth—are not composed of the three [qualities], they would have to be like the Great Elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth, which are also composed of the three. The case of transformation (*pariṇāma*) is likewise.
