Furthermore, since each of the three primary causes possesses multiple capacities, their essence (*ātman*) should also be multiple; yet, because the essence is one, the three essences would already be pervasive in a single location.
When there is transformation, the others should likewise be so, because their substance is not distinct. Yet you admit that these three things have distinct substances and characteristics;

how then can they combine to form a single characteristic? They cannot be combined when they are not in conjunction. If it is argued that they become a single characteristic at the time of conjunction, this is because their substance is not distinct from the time of conjunction.
If you claim that the three things have different substances but identical characteristics, this contradicts your own tenet regarding substance and characteristic.
These three characteristics are identical to the characteristic of suchness (*tathatā*), yet they are obscurely one while the substance of these three characteristics is manifest as three;

therefore, one should not say that the three combine to form one. Furthermore, since the "three" are the specific [elements] such as the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the "one" is their general [nature], and because the general and the specific are one, it follows that they cannot be both one and three.
When these three undergo transformation, if they do not harmoniously combine to form a single characteristic, one should know that [the state of being one] has not yet been attained.

How can it be perceived that these [factors] manifest as a single color and so forth? If the three harmoniously combine to form a single characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), they would lose their original individual characteristics (*svabhāva*);

furthermore, those individual characteristics would also necessarily be lost. It cannot be said that each of the three possesses two characteristics—one general and one particular—because if the general were identical to the particular, then the general would likewise be threefold. How then could it manifest as one? If you claim that each of the three entities possesses [its own characteristics]...
Because the three characteristics are mixed together and difficult to discern, one perceives them as one. Since there are already three characteristics, how can one perceive them as one?

Furthermore, how can one know that the three things are distinct? If each individual [entity] were to possess all three characteristics, then each single entity should be able to constitute form (*rūpa*) and so forth;
what need would there be for them to be deficient, or to depend upon the conjunction of the three? Moreover, the essence (*svabhāva*) of each should also be threefold, because of the essence itself.

Furthermore, because they are identical in their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and other phenomena are all composed of the three [qualities]. When viewed in relation to one another, there would be no distinction between them;
thus, cause and effect would be merely a single measure (*mātra*). Consequently, the distinctions between the great elements and the sense faculties (*indriya*) could not be established.

If that were the case, a single faculty should be able to perceive all objects, or else a single object should be perceived by all faculties—yet this is clearly contradicted by what is directly perceived in the world.

Sentient and insentient things, pure and impure objects, and so forth—whether apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*)—would all become indistinguishable; this would constitute a great error.

Therefore, the "real dharmas" they cling to are not established; they are merely the result of false conceptualization. Regarding the summary refutation provided in the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) under the phrase "they assert them to exist," [it states]:
All phenomena arise from the truth of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-satya*), yet they are merely empty fabrications following after conceptual attachment.
To falsely conceptualize and speculate is called a "false cause" (*mithyā-hetu*).

Regarding the statement that the *Ṣaṭpadārtha* system established by the [Vaiśeṣika] is the most excellent, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The treatise on the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) constructed by their own calculations is rarely equaled by other treatises;
therefore, it is called the 'Excellence of the Treatise' (*Vaiśeṣika*)."

Those who have practiced the Way for many years cultivate the contemplation of the six matters (disgust with the lower realms as suffering, coarse, and obstructive; and aspiration for the higher realms as pure, subtle, and detached).

By subduing the afflictions of the lower stages, they attain the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the form realm and above. Relying on these absorptions, they give rise to the five mundane supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), falsely claiming to have realized *bodhi*.
Regarding the commentary on those who defile their wives and children, the *Sūtra on the Origin of the World* (*Lokaprajñapti-sūtra*) states:

"When a newly born son of the gods in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven has not yet seen the celestial maidens, the karmic fruit of his previous life arises; as this karma matures, he clearly perceives his past lives and then forms this thought:
'May I, upon dying from this heaven, be reborn in the human realm to cultivate the three types of wholesome karma.'"

Returning to this [world] because one has seen the forms of celestial maidens, one violates and loses right mindfulness, becoming attached to the desires of the present life and crying out only, "O celestial jade maidens!
O celestial jade maidens! This is what is called the bond of craving and desire;

because this fault is subtle and difficult to eliminate, it is said that they are "difficult to transform and guide. (From the *Yao*, regarding the fact that virtuous deeds do not depend on a substantial self-nature.)

Regarding the phrase "because they are equal," this means that one does not rely on the general categories such as "existence" (*mahāsattā*) to express and know [the object], but rather relies solely on the "substance" (*dravya*).

As for the statement in the *Jian* (Commentary) that "there are nine kinds of real substances," the *Weishi shu* (Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*) says: "As for the nine substantial entities:

if there are color, taste, fragrance, and tangibility, it is called 'earth' (*pṛthivī*), because it attains the nature of earth; if there are color, taste, tangibility, and moisture, it is called 'water' (*ap-*)..."

Visible form and tangibility are called fire; if there is only tangibility, it is called wind; if there is only sound, it is called space (for it is by depending on this great element of space that sound arises, and thus this sound is said to be a quality of space).
There is a distinct great element of space, which is neither the unconditioned space nor the space-element.
If visible form is "this" or "that," whether they are conjoined or not, the causes for their designation as slow or fast, as well as the causes for the cognition thereof, are called time.

The past and future are designated as "that," while the present is designated as "this. When these two meet, it is called "simultaneous" (*sahabhū*); when they do not meet, it is called "not simultaneous. That which is obstructed is called "slow," and that which is unobstructed is called "swift.

Since the substance of time is real, the designating names and the cognizing mind serve as its causes; all other cases should be understood accordingly. If the causes for designating [directions] such as east, south, west, and north, as well as the causes for cognizing them, are named "direction" (*diś*).
If the nine qualities—cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, hatred, effort, formation, dharma, and non-dharma—are [the causes], they are named "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*).
The causal conditions of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) can give rise to the characteristic of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*), which is termed "self" (*ātman*).

My intention is that the phrase "conjunction with the self" acts as the causal condition; it is through this conjunction that the nine qualities, such as consciousness (*buddhi*), are conjoined with the self to give rise to the characteristic of cognition.
Therefore, by citing both the conjunction and the resulting cognition, the essence of the self is revealed. Thus, the *Hetuvidyā* states: "The Vaiśeṣika school maintains [the existence of] the self."

This is precisely the meaning of "the conditions of harmony and combination. If it were the case that the nine qualities—such as perception, pleasure, pain, and so forth—could give rise to the characteristics of cognition through conditions of non-harmony and non-combination, this would be called "mental" (*manas*).
However, the mind itself is actually incapable of acting like me to perform the causal function of harmoniously combining these nine qualities.
What is termed "arising from non-combination" refers to the production of cognition; it does not mean that the nine qualities are entirely absent.
The ability to give rise to cognition through conjunction is called "mind" (*manas*); lacking the causal conditions of conjunction, it is not the "self" (*ātman*).
The above has all manifested the essence by means of its qualities (*guṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "one color, etc.," the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-ṭīkā* states: "As for the essence of these various qualities, that which is apprehended by the eye is designated as 'one' based on its support (*āśraya*)."
That which is grasped by the nose among visible forms is called "a single basis" (*ekāśraya*), up to that which is grasped by the skin, which is called "tangible.

(This means that because they depend on [the primary elements of] form and so forth, the eye and other faculties arise; since form is the basis, it is called "a single basis. Alternatively, qualities (*guṇa*) are the dependent and the substantial entities (*dravya*) are the basis; here, because form and the others are the dependent and share the same number as the basis, it is called "a single basis.

A single real entity (*eka-dravya*) and non-single real entities are the causes for the conceptualization and expression of "number" (*saṃkhyā*). (That is to say, a single atom is called "a single real entity," while two, three, four, and so forth are called "non-single real entities. Or rather, it is simply...)

The term "extreme atom" (*paramāṇu*) refers to that which is a single real atom; those above this level are called non-single-real-atoms, possessing three numbers: first, the father; second, the mother; and third, the son. There are five kinds of dimensions:

(1) the nature of the minute, which exists only upon the fruit of two atoms—this fruit of two atoms is called the "two-atom fruit," which is the son-atom; (2) the nature of the large, which exists upon the fruit of three atoms; (3) the nature of shortness, which exists only upon the fruit of two atoms;
(4) the nature of length, which exists only upon the aforementioned two [in the horizontal] and the latter two [in the vertical]; and (5) the nature of the cube. Third.

On the subtle fruit (*sūkṣma-phala*), there are five: the nature of being round (*vṛttatva*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), time (*kāla*), direction (*diś*), and self (*ātman*). On the four substantial entities (*dravya*), there is one substantial entity;

these distinctions such as "not one substantial entity" and so forth are the causes for the conceptualization and designation of distinct natures (*pṛthaktva*). Second, when that which has not previously reached an object now reaches it, this is called conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
This conjunction is threefold: first, arising from the action of one [factor], such as when a hand strikes a drum—the hand possesses movement.
The conjunction produced by that which has already arisen is "action" (*karman*), because when both hands are joined and arise together, they both perform action.

The conjunction produced by the three [factors] is like the arising of a sprout and so forth; it is the conjunction produced at the time of actual contact with emptiness and the like, which is devoid of action.
Second, that which was previously present but is no longer present at the current moment is called "disjunction" (*vibhāga*); this also has three types.

The first two [categories] are combined as before and can be understood accordingly. Third, "separation" (*vibhāga*) refers to the prior production of a real fruit which, due to the arrival of external conditions, undergoes separation;
the fruit is then destroyed and becomes equal to space. Because it is separated from that which was produced, it is called "the nature of separation" (*vibhāgatva*).

It is called "remoteness" (*paratva*) because it depends on real entities such as numbers like one or two, time, and direction, as perceived by remote cognition; it is called "nearness" (*aparatva*) because it is perceived by proximate cognition.

That which is depended upon is called "this nature. Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) are called "cognition" (*buddhi*). When the five sense organs grasp their objects, it is called "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*); when one knows fire from smoke and so forth, it is called "inference" (*anumāna*). Pleasure is defined as gratification; suffering is defined as affliction.
The longing for forms and other objects is called "desire" (*rāga*); the harming of forms and other objects is called "hatred" (*dveṣa*).
When about to perform an action, that which first arises as an exertion is called "vigor" (*vīrya*). The falling [of rain] due to the conjunction of earth and water is [called] "gravity" (*gurutva*).

The cause for what is termed the "heavy earth element" is the flowing together of fire and water; the cause for what is termed the "liquid earth element" is the gathering together of earth, water, and so forth.

"Moistening" and "mindfulness" (smṛti) are designated as two causes—mindfulness being named from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), and "action" (*kriyā*) being named from drilling and casting.

The force produced by repeated practice is termed "formative activity" (*saṃskāra*). The cause for producing a desirable body is termed "Dharma" (referring to humans, devas, and supramundane states), while the cause for producing an undesirable body is [termed] non-Dharma.
It is merely designated as "non-dharma" (referring to false wisdom and so forth). That which is apprehended by the ear relies solely on sound.
Regarding the five kinds of *karma* (action), the *Weishi shu* (Commentary on the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi) states:

"If, in locations such as above, below, or in empty space, the cause for the prior conjunction and subsequent separation of atoms is called the karma of taking up (*ādāna*) and discarding (*nikṣepa*). The opposite of this (meaning prior separation followed by subsequent conjunction) is [the karma of] moving far..."

Regarding "separation from proximity" (*viyoga*) and "conjunction now" (*saṃyoga*): the causes for bending and extending are the reverse of this (meaning first conjunction and subsequently separation).

That which possesses resistance (*sapratigha*) and is real, serving as the cause for first conjoining and subsequently separating, is called "action" (*karma*). (For example, the feet of a person and so forth each possess resistance; because they first conjoin with the ground and subsequently separate from the ground, they are called "action.

In the *Shu* (Commentary), regarding the statement that "the Great Existence (*mahāsattā*) is unique," the *Weishi Shu* (Commentary on the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi) states: "The essential natures (*svabhāva*) of substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*) are not..."
The cause that is capable of denoting and capable of being the object of cognition is called "the nature of great existence" (*mahāsattā*), because all phenomena equally possess it.

Regarding the commentary on the phrase "the same and different are also one," the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Wei-shi shu) states: "That is to say, upon the three categories of substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*), there is the 'nature of generality' (*sāmānyatva*).

The specific natures of earth and so forth, and the natures of particularity (*viśeṣatva*) within them, do not mutually apply to one another; they are what is apprehended by all the sense faculties. The commentary on the phrase "and harmony" states:

Regarding the term "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Wei-shi shu) states: "It is that which causes [factors] such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth not to be separated from one another, but to be mutually connected;
this is the meaning of 'conjunction' (*saṃyoga*), referring to the causal basis for the designation.

The *Chao* (the sub-commentary) follows both the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Śāstra* as cited above—namely, the text of the *Śāstra* itself—and now further cites the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya* to refute that treatise.
It is said that the Vaiśeṣikas maintain that the category of substance (*dravya-padārtha*) is for the most part substantially existent and is apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

This position is irrational. Why? Among the categories, those which are permanent, if they were capable of producing effects, would necessarily be impermanent because they would possess functional activity (*kāritra*).
Furthermore, like the effects they produce, they would not have a substantially existent intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) apart from consciousness.

Regarding things such as rabbit horns that are impermanent: if they possess material obstruction, they must have spatial dimensions and be analyzable, like an army or a forest, and thus lack a real intrinsic nature.
If they lack material obstruction, like the mind and mental factors, they likewise cannot exist apart from these with a real intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, the earth, water, fire, and wind asserted by them should not be substantially existent entities possessing resistance.
Since it is subsumed under the category of meaning (*artha*) as that which is touched by the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), just like hardness, moisture, warmth, and motion;

therefore, those things they grasp—such as solidity, reality, and heat—should not be included within the category of the quality of non-obstruction (*apratighāta-guṇa*), because they are touched by the body-faculty.

Just as earth, water, and fire, when paired with blue and other colors, are all objects seen by the eye, one should likewise apply this critique. Thus, it is known that [the opponent's categories] do not exist.
In reality, earth, water, fire, and wind do not each possess a distinct intrinsic nature that is visible to the eye.

Furthermore, regarding those "real categories" (padārtha) they assert, those which are both resistant and permanent must be impermanent—just like gross earth and so forth—because all things that possess resistance are impermanent.
Among these categories, there are also phenomena perceived by the sensory faculties that lack material resistance.
They must all possess resistance, because you admit that they are apprehended by the material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*), just like earth, water, fire, and wind.

Furthermore, those things you claim to be real qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth should not have a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) apart from consciousness, because they are subsumed under "unreal," just like the son of a barren woman.
Things that are non-existent should also not have a distinct intrinsic nature apart from consciousness, because they are subsumed under "non-being," just like a flower in the sky.

That which they [the opponents] grasp as existing must have no distinct intrinsic nature (svabhāva) apart from substance (*dravya*) and so forth, because it is admitted not to be non-existent, just like substance, quality (*guṇa*), and so forth.

If it were separate from substance and so forth, it would not be of the nature of existence, because it is admitted to be different from substance and so forth, just like absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
Just as non-existence has no distinct intrinsic nature, how could substance and so forth have a distinct intrinsic nature? If they were separate...
If there were a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in an existent phenomenon, it would have to be distinct from the non-existence of that phenomenon;
since that is not the case, how could this be so? Therefore, their "existence" is merely a false conceptual construction.

Furthermore, the logical claim that the natures of substance, quality, and action are distinct from actual substances, qualities, and actions is certainly untenable. On this basis as well, the natures of substance and so forth are not distinct from actual substances and the like.

Therefore, just as qualities (*guṇa*), activities (*karman*), and so forth, should likewise not be subsumed under "real" (*sat*) and so on— because they differ from the nature of being real and so on—
one should understand that this applies by analogy to the mutual interrogation of the natures of quality, activity, reality, earth, and so forth, in relation to the substances of earth and so on.
Just as there is no distinct "reality-nature" apart from reality itself, there is likewise no distinct "activity-nature" of reality, nor is there any distinct "reality-nature" apart from activity.

If, apart from real entities and so forth, there were a "nature of reality" and so forth, then apart from unreal entities and so forth, there would likewise have to be a "nature of unreality" and so forth.
Since that is not the case, how could this be? Therefore, the categories of sameness and difference are merely conventional designations established by others.

Furthermore, the category of inherence (*samavāya*) which they maintain cannot possibly be a real entity, because it is not subsumed under any of the categories such as reality and so forth, just like a *piśāca*.

In the end, there is no such thing as "substance" (dravya) and so forth that is apprehended by direct perception (pratyakṣa), for even when subjected to logical analysis, it is not established as truly existent;
how much less could that which they themselves admit—the category of "inherence" (saṃyoga)—be truly existent since it is not apprehended by direct perception?

Even if one were to insist that inherence is an object of direct perception, according to the reasoning previously stated, it too is not truly existent. Furthermore, those [categories] such as substance do not arise from conditions apart [from their own parts].

It is accepted that consciousness has a real intrinsic nature because it is apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and is commonly known, unlike [non-existent things] such as a tortoise’s hair.

Furthermore, the wisdom that takes reality as its object is not a wisdom that takes an intrinsic nature apart from consciousness as its object; rather, it is subsumed under the wisdom of direct perception because it arises through a conventional synthesis, like the wisdom regarding virtue and so forth.
This is explained at length up to the point that wisdom taking a composite as its object does not take an intrinsic nature of a composite apart from consciousness as its object.

Because direct perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*) is comprised of that which arises from provisional conjunction and is thus equivalent to suchness-knowledge (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), the categories of substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*) posited by the Vaiśeṣikas are likewise merely false constructions based on worldly sentiment.
Regarding the heretics who smear themselves with ashes, the *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra* states: "In immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, there was a Buddha named..."
When the Dharma of Kausṇḍinya-Bhadra was on the verge of extinction, there was a forest-dwelling bhikṣu named Buddhajñāna.
A lay donor had given him a priceless robe, which he wore while thieves plundered his body, leaving him naked with his arms outstretched as they tied him to a tree and departed.
While he was gathering flowers, a brāhmaṇa saw him and gave rise to a false attachment, thinking: "This śramaṇa must surely know [the truth]."
The *kāṣāya* robe is not the cause of liberation; it was because of this that non-Buddhist ascetics (tīrthika) began the practice of plucking out their hair and going naked.
Later, when a certain bhikṣu attained liberation, he took tree bark and smeared himself with red ochre to cover his body, and tied grass to make a whisk to brush away mosquitoes and insects.
From seeing this, other non-Buddhist ascetics who had left the home life began [similar practices]. Furthermore, a bhikṣu would enter the water at dusk to bathe, while a cowherd [watched him].
A person discarded a worn-out garment to cover his body; for three days he bathed while wearing that worn-out garment.

An outsider saw this and, based on it, [misconstrued] the bhikṣu as one who covered his bodily sores with ashes because flies and other insects were feeding upon them. Because of seeing this, the outsider [mistook him for an ascetic].
Furthermore, a bhikṣu, finding the pain of his sores unbearable when cauterized with fire, threw himself from a cliff and died; it was because of this [that the outsider misunderstood].
The emergence of non-Buddhist practitioners such as those who worship fire or throw themselves from cliffs occurs in this manner.
All ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhists give rise to false conceptualizations based on the various physical forms of these bhikṣus. Thus, the first fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"There are those who cling to the idea that the essence of Maheśvara is truly real, eternal, and omnipresent, and is able to produce all dharmas. (This portion ends at "is able to produce all dharmas"; the subsequent text beginning with "For they... is not part of the original treatise.)
That commentary states: "First, they are of one essence; second, they are real; third, they pervade all things; fourth, they are eternally abiding;
and fifth, they can produce all dharmas. Such types of calculations are extremely prevalent in the West (India).
The *Chao* further calculates that those heavens have two dwelling places; this is what is taught in the scriptures of those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Regarding the statement that "the two are on Mount Malaya in the South Sea," the *Yijing Chao* says:
"The two are on Mount Malaya in the South Sea (which is Mount Potalaka, here translated as 'White Flower Mountain'). At the summit of the mountain is a palace where the devas reside, encircling it."
In the palace there was a great spring that flowed into the great ocean. At that time, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Bhasmaka who worshipped Maheśvara;
carrying medicinal herbs for fasting, he followed the water upstream until he reached the mountain peak.
There he saw a great city with the color of red copper, guarded by a great yakṣa deity. He then asked that deity, "I have heard that this place..."
"I wish to see personally the palace where the Lord Maheśvara resides; could you provide me passage?
The yakṣa replied, "This is not the palace where the Lord Maheśvara resides; it is the palace of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. He asked again, "Is the Bodhisattva in the palace?
The yakṣa replied, "I merely guard the gate and do not know whether he is there or not; however—"
Hearing the clear and resonant sounds of celestial music in the air, he thought, "I believe a Bodhisattva has arrived at my palace," yet he did not see anyone.
When that non-Buddhist (tīrthika) heard this account, he immediately returned to his kingdom, abandoned heterodoxy to embrace the Right Path, and entered the monastic order.
Regarding the phrase "The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Chapter Seven, etc.," the preceding passage in that treatise states:
"Alternatively, a certain śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, having observed that sentient beings in this world do not act according to their desires within the context of cause and effect, forms this view.
Why is this? It is because one observes that these sentient beings of the world, at the time of the cause, desire to cultivate purity..."
Karma does not fulfill its original intention and instead results in something even more evil;

at the time of its fruition, one wishes to be born in a happy realm within a blissful world, yet failing to fulfill that original intention, one falls into the evil destinies and so forth. This means that while experiencing pleasure, one fails to obtain what was desired and instead undergoes various sufferings.
Because of seeing this, they reflect as follows (the rest is the same as in the *Chao*). The *Chao* refutes this extensively, as in the treatise (*lun*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* refutes the preceding passage as follows: "Now we shall question them:

how is it that they maintain the *udāna* (summary verse) stating 'the capacity lacks intrinsic nature'—is this subsumed or not? There is a contradiction between having utility and lacking utility, which results in the fault of establishing [a thesis] based on a reason.
The long exposition states: 'The capacity for transformation by Īśvara and others constitutes the function, and this function is the activity (*karman*)."*

Is this [function] caused, or is it causeless? If it takes the application of karma as its cause, then only this function would take the application of karma as its cause and no other worldly things would; this is not reasonable.
If it were causeless, then only this function would exist without a cause and no worldly things would; this is also not reasonable. Furthermore, what do you [mean by this]?
Is this Maheśvara included within the worldly realm or not?
If one says he is included, then it is unreasonable that this Maheśvara, being identical to worldly phenomena, could universally produce the world.
If one says he is not included, then it is unreasonable to say that he who is liberated can produce the world. Furthermore...
What is your position: does the world arise through transformation for a purpose, or for no purpose?
If it is for a purpose, then there would be no sovereignty over that purpose while there is sovereignty over the world;
this is not logical. If it is for no purpose, then for it to arise when nothing is required is also not logical. Furthermore...
What is your position regarding this that has arisen? Is it caused solely by Maheśvara, or does it also take other things as its cause?
If it were caused solely by Maheśvara, then whenever Maheśvara exists, there would be arising;
and whenever there is arising, Maheśvara would exist. However...
To say that the production [of the world] has Maheśvara as its cause is not logical.
If one says that it also takes other things as its cause, this would mean taking only desire (*icchā*) as the cause;
for apart from desire, there is no other cause. If it takes only desire as the cause, then this desire must itself take Maheśvara as its cause.
Is it that other things are also taken as causes? If Maheśvara alone were taken as the cause, then whenever Maheśvara exists, there would be desire;
and whenever there is desire, there would be Maheśvara.
Consequently, there would be constant production from the beginningless past, which is also not logical. If one says [it is] also...
To take something else as the cause is unreasonable because such a cause cannot be found;
furthermore, it is unreasonable to claim that one has mastery over the world while having no mastery over one's own desires.
Thus, [the opponent's position] is untenable on account of its functional capacity, its inclusion or exclusion, its utility or lack thereof, and its nature as a cause.
This is logically consistent; therefore, this treatise is not a reasoned exposition. The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and other such works all refute [the opponent] in the same manner.
If one refutes [this] within the context of Vijñaptimātra, it says: "That position is irrational. Why? Because any phenomenon that is capable of producing [an effect] must be impermanent;
whatever is impermanent is necessarily non-pervasive; and whatever is non-pervasive is not ultimately real."
Since the essence is eternally present and possesses all functional capacities, it should produce all phenomena at all times and in all places simultaneously.

To claim that they can only be produced by depending on desire or conditions contradicts the theory of a single cause; otherwise, desire and conditions would also have to arise simultaneously, because the cause is eternally present.
The *Vyākhyā* states that "Veda" means "clarification" (*vidyā*), while ancient translations rendered it as "wisdom" (*jñāna*).

First, it clarifies the ritual of fire-offerings and repentance; second, it clarifies the methods for giving alms and performing sacrifices; third, it clarifies all methods of warfare; and fourth, it clarifies the methods of warfare against foreign nations.

The *Record of the Western Regions* (*Xiyuji*) states: first, it is called "Longevity," referring to the cultivation of life and the refinement of one's nature; second, it is called "Sacrifice," referring to the roasting [of offerings].
The third is called *Ping* (Equilibrium), referring to ritual propriety, divination, military tactics, and battle formations.

The fourth is called *Shu* (Art), referring to extraordinary abilities, technical calculations, incantations, and medical prescriptions. The *Hongjue zhi* states: "In the past, Brahmā composed the Vedas;
subsequently, the Rishi Śukra composed the four Vedas: first, recitation; second, sacrifice; third, chanting; and fourth, [the Atharva]."

There were forty thousand verses each for the rites of averting calamity, yet it was not known which was correct. Regarding Nārāyaṇa, the *Yiqiejing yinyi* (Phonetic Meanings of All Scriptures) states:
"Nara" means "human being," and "āyana" means "origin of birth"; thus, he is called the origin of birth for human beings, which is none other than Brahmādeva.
As for the phrase "giving rise to the great lotus flower," this refers to the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra).
It is said that at the beginning of the kalpa, a single being with twenty-four hands and a thousand heads was born by transformation within the waters;
in his navel there was a thousand-petaled lotus, and from within the flower there was light like ten thousand suns. Because of this flower, the Brahmā King descended to take birth.
Having been born, he thought to himself: "Why is it empty and devoid of sentient beings? While he was thinking this, from another world...
Among sentient beings who ought to be born here, there are eight celestial sons (*devaputra*) who are suddenly born through transformation;

these eight celestial sons are the parents of these sentient beings, and the Brahmā King is the parent of these eight celestial sons. Therefore, it is reckoned that he can give birth to all things, and thus he is called the "Birth-giver of the Brahmins.
Regarding this, the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: "Brahmin" means pure conduct; they maintain the Way and dwell [in it].

The *Śūdras* are those of pure conduct and white virtue who belong to the *Kṣatriya* royal lineage; for generations they have presided over the throne, and their resolve is rooted in benevolence and forbearance.
The *Vaiśyas* are merchants who trade goods to exchange what they have for what they lack, pursuing profit far and near.

The *Śūdras* are farmers who exert their strength upon the fields and toil with their bodies at the work of sowing and reaping. It is said that those born with two legs are lower than the *Śūdras*. That treatise continues: "All..."
The great earth is a field for cultivating merit; various flowers and fruits serve as implements for offering.

By manifesting birds, beasts, donkeys, horses, pigs, and sheep, they cause all people of the world to slaughter them at the proper times. Within the site of the precepts (*śīla-maṇḍala*), they offer these to Brahmā so that one may be born in his realm and clearly realize *nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, the Vedas state that the name "Brahmā" is eternal and is the cause of *nirvāṇa*.
The *Śāstra* states: "As for the Brahmins being of the pure white class: according to the Brahmin dharma, those over seven years of age leave home to study the four Vedas;
at fifteen and above, they receive the full Brahmin precepts and travel to various regions to pursue learning;
at thirty, fearing the extinction of their lineage, they marry; and at fifty, they enter the mountains to cultivate the Way. Within secular society, they may be called 'pure' (*śukla*)."
The refutation of their claims has been extensively set forth; as that treatise states: "During the age of strife (*kali-yuga*), certain Brahmins hold such a view.

For what reason do they hold this view? Because they see that in the world there are true Brahmins whose lineages possess the precepts (*śīla*), and out of greed for fame, profit, and honor, they form such a view. Now, one should question them: only...
Is it likewise for other types who are born from their parents as brahmins? It is clearly seen in the world that all brahmins are produced from mothers;
therefore, your denial of this manifest fact is unreasonable.
If that is so, your claim that "brahmins are of superior lineage while kṣatriyas and others are of inferior lineage" is incorrect. Thus it is constructed.
By performing unwholesome deeds or wholesome deeds, one performs sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind;
one then experiences pleasant or unpleasant fruits in the present life, and is subsequently born in the various evil realms or the good realms.
If these three conditions are present—this being that and this being this—one enters the mother’s womb and is born from it. Such is the case for those in the world.
Whether it be in a skillful occupation, a place of labor, or in what is wholesome or unwholesome;
whether one be a king or a minister, or even one who, having practiced the Brahma-life, has been born into the Brahma-world—or likewise those below it: furthermore, what do you intend?
Is this called "superior" because of birth from a superior lineage, or because of ethical discipline, learning, and so forth? If it were by virtue of birth from a superior lineage...

O Jāti, in your treatise you state that among sacrificial rites, if one is superior in terms of ethical discipline (*śīla*), learning (*śruta*), and so forth, they are taken as the standard of measurement;

such a statement is not reasonable. If it were by virtue of ethical discipline, learning, and so forth, then your claim that the Brahmins are the superior caste while other classes are inferior would be illogical. Therefore, this is a false conceptualization of superiority.
This is not a statement made according to reason. [In the] *Yao* (Commentary), regarding the section on the calculation of the primordial limit by the Āṇḍa-teacher, a question is raised:

"Why does the *Yao* not specifically point out the refutation of this? The answer is that because the previous calculation—that Brahmā is the creator—was already refuted, this case is treated as identical to the prior refutation and is therefore not pointed out separately.
Thus, in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, following the refutation of the theory that Maheśvara is the creator, it continues: "The others..."
The [notions] that there exists a single Great Brahmā, time, space, the primal limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), the Lord (*īśvara*), space (*ākāśa*), the self (*ātman*), or eternal,
real entities possessing various capacities that produce all phenomena— all are refuted in the same manner as this.
Regarding the phrase "When chaos was not yet divided," etc.: although this is a speculative calculation of our own region, it is also a tradition transmitted from the Western Heavens (India).

According to the *Calendar of the Five Emperors*, when heaven and earth were in a state of chaotic confusion, Pangu was born within them. Every day he underwent nine transformations; his spirit ascended to heaven and his sanctity descended to earth.
Each day heaven increased by one *zhang* in height, and each day earth increased by one *zhang* in thickness; Pangu also grew [by the same measure].
One *zhang* [of his body] corresponds to eighteen thousand years; only then were heaven and earth opened and established. Pangu had the body of a dragon and the head of a human:
his head reached to the extreme east and his feet to the extreme west; his left hand reached to the extreme south and his right hand to the extreme north.

When he opened his eyes, dawn was formed; when he closed his eyes, night was formed. His exhalation became summer and his inhalation became winter; his blowing breath formed wind and clouds, and his shouting voice became thunder.

When the primordial giant Dian Pangu died, his head became Jia, his throat became Yi, his shoulders became Bing, his heart became Ding, his gallbladder became Wu, his spleen became Ji, his ribs became Geng, his lungs became Xin, his kidneys became Ren, and his feet became Gui. His eyes became the sun and moon;
his beard became the stars; his eyebrows became the pivot of the Dipper; his nine orifices became the Nine Provinces; his breasts became Mount Kunlun; and his knees became...
The Southern Peak is his thighs; Mount Tai is his buttocks; fish and turtles are his hands; flying birds are his fingers; tortoises and dragons are his nails;
gold and silver are his bones; grasses and trees are his hair; wild ducks and geese are his body hairs; jade and stone are his teeth; sweat is rain and water;
the large intestine is the rivers and seas; the small intestine is the Zhun and Si rivers; the bladder is the hundred streams; and the facial orb is...
The *Dongting* (Record of Mount Dongting) by Wei Zhao states: "According to popular tradition, Pangu underwent seventy transformations in a single day;
he overturned to become heaven and lay prostrate to become earth, dying after eighty thousand years. However, the accounts of Pangu are in fact utterly fictitious;
since there are no historical records, they cannot be relied upon and are merely ancient legends of a deceptive and false nature.
The *Śataka-śāstra-ṭīkā* states: "This treatise was composed by the Bodhisattva Āryadeva, and Dharmapāla provided its commentary.
Regarding the statement 'extensively refuting as in that [work],' the subsequent passage cited in the *Ṭīkā* contains further establishing arguments which say:

'At the time [of production], the causes upon which it depends are entirely unobservable; because the cause is not seen, there is no arising. Because there is no arising, [there is no cessation, etc.]'"
One thus knows that there is neither cessation nor arising, because there is no cessation. Furthermore, the term "eternal" is used to refute that attachment. Therefore, a verse is spoken:

"If a substance truly exists, its functions of contraction and expansion would be obtainable; since this [substance] is definitely produced from another, it falls into the theory of producing an effect through grasping.
The treatise says: "The functions of time, such as contraction and expansion, are established only by depending on others; therefore, these functions of time follow conditions."
If the transformation of the essential nature were devoid of the distinctions of grasping and abandoning, the arising and ceasing of all functional activities would be impossible.

Furthermore, since temporal activity proceeds in dependence upon others—just as the color and other qualities of the earth are certainly impermanent—one must take this very fact as its homologous instance (*sapakṣa*).
How, then, could that which serves as the basis for such activity be permanent? Therefore, the Venerable Bhadantakṣaṇika spoke thus:
Drawn forth by the winds of karma, the various classes of celestial beings take their own kind as the cause, continuing in a succession that revolves and alternates, ending and beginning again.
As they differ according to conditions, the sensations of heat and cold vary; these distinctions in states are what are called "time.
Although time possesses causes and conditions for arising and ceasing, and continues in a similar succession, it is obscured and difficult to perceive—how could this be?
Because one does not know [it], one says it is "without cause," and so forth. The *Śata-śāstra* also states:
"Below, this refers to what was composed by the Bodhisattva Deva and explained by Vasubandhu. To say 'this' means that one knows the cause by seeing the effect. Next, the treatise says:
"Furthermore, because of such characteristics as being simultaneous or non-simultaneous, and distant or near, one can know that there is time, and not a timelessness. Therefore..."
If this [time] were eternal, it would mean that the past and future do not exist within the present; therefore, there would be no future.

Just as when a lump of clay is in the state of "earth," it is the past state of the jar, and when it is in the state of "clay," it is the future state of the jar; because these temporal characteristics are eternal, the past time does not become the future time.
Your own sūtra states that time is a single dharma; therefore, the past time can never become the future.
When [the future] comes, it does not become the present time; if that which is past were to become the future, there would be the fault of confusion.
Furthermore, the future time does not exist within the past. Therefore, the future does not exist. The present is also refuted in this same manner, and so on at length.
The *Vyākhyā* on the *Śata-śāstra* states: "The opponent says: 'Direction and permanence exist as real entities; that which is the locus where the sun first meets is direction and so forth.
(Note: The character 'yǒu' [有] in the original text is an error for 'yuē' [曰]. The treatise continues: "As stated in my sūtras:
whether past, future, or present, the place where the sun first meets is called the eastern direction; likewise, the other directions are named according to the sun."

The internal [proponent] says: It is not so. Because the east has no beginning, as the sun travels through the four continents and circumambulates Mount Sumeru, it is midday in Uttarakuru when it is sunrise in Pūrvavideha; the people of Pūrvavideha consider that to be the east.
When it is midday in Jambudvīpa, the sun rises in Jambudvīpa; the people of Jambudvīpa consider that to be the east. Jambudvīpa... [is thus relative].
At midday in Aparagoyānī, the sun rises for the people of Aparagoyānī, who consider that direction to be the east;
at midday in Uttarakuru, the sun rises for the people of Uttarakuru, who consider that direction to be the east. Thus, all these are indeed the east.
Furthermore, regarding the south, west, and north: the place where the sun does not join [with the horizon] is the center, which has no cardinal direction because it lacks [a fixed orientation].
Furthermore, because it is indeterminate—such that what is the east for one is the west for another—it is therefore not real;
this is extensively refuted [in the *Śāstra*].

As for the statement in the *Yiji* (Commentary) that "the child does not exceed the parents," it means that the subtle particles of the offspring do not exceed the subtle divisions of the generating parents.
Regarding the statement that "because of their measure, they are merely consciousness," it says: "Their measure is only as large as the primary parents upon which they depend;
a single atom (*paramāṇu*) is permitted to be as large as a primary parent, up to the great earth being permitted to be as large as its one primary parent.
As for the claim that "the atoms are eternal while the sons and so forth are impermanent," this has also been refuted at length in that same treatise, which states: [text follows].
This, too, is irrational. Why? If the asserted atom possesses spatial dimensions (*dig-bhāga*), its substance would—like the trail of ants—necessarily be non-substantial.
If it lacks spatial dimensions, it would—like mind and mental factors—not be able to aggregate to produce gross derivative matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
Since it is capable of producing an effect, how can it be said that the atom is permanent, given that it is like those things it produces? Furthermore, [it is irrational].
The produced effect cannot exceed the magnitude of its cause; it should be like an atom (*paramāṇu*) and not designated as "gross matter" (*audārika-rūpa*).
If that were so, this resultant matter would not be apprehended by the sense organs such as the eye, which would contradict your own tenets.

If you argue that the effect is not gross because it possesses the quality of magnitude (*parimāṇa*), then since the apprehended resultant matter is identical in magnitude to its cause, it should likewise be like an atom.

If it is argued that the subtle atom (*paramāṇu*) must also possess the conjunction of coarse qualities because there is no distinction [between them] regarding the location of the coarse resultant form, then how can it be called "coarse"?

For if the resultant form were to pervade its own causes, and since those causes are not one, the substance of this resultant form would necessarily not be unitary, as it would occupy each distinct causal location. This being the case, this resultant form...
Furthermore, it would not constitute a coarse object, for this reason it likewise could not be apprehended by the physical sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*).

If the effect is coarse because it is composed of many parts, then the collection of atoms as its causes should likewise not be subtle; if they suffice to constitute the objective field of the faculties, what purpose would the effect serve?
Since it is composed of many parts, it must be unreal. Thus, your own assertions are internally contradictory. Moreover, the effect and its cause would exist simultaneously.
That which possesses resistance must occupy different locations, like two atoms (*paramāṇu*).

If it is argued that cause and effect receive one another in their essential nature and characteristics—just as sand receives water or medicinal herbs enter molten copper—who would grant that the essence of the sand or the copper receives the water or the herbs?

Alternatively, they would have to be subject to disintegration and transformation, being neither unitary nor permanent. Furthermore, if the essence of a gross material effect were a single entity, then upon obtaining one part, one should obtain the whole.
Since all things are one with one another, that [entity] ought to be thus; yet, to deny this contradicts reason, while to accept it contradicts facts.
Thus, what they maintain fails to be established from either perspective; it is merely a baseless and false conceptualization following their own whims.
Regarding the passage from the *Vyākhyāyukti* (or *Xianyang lun*) cited as "The ninth fascicle of the *Chao* says... and so forth, that same treatise, in its tenth fascicle, refutes it as follows:
"Furthermore, regarding those who maintain the doctrine that atoms (*paramāṇu*) are eternal, I now ask you: answer according to your own understanding.

Do you maintain that atoms are eternal based on analytical investigation (*parīkṣā*), or do you maintain their eternity without such investigation? If it is without investigation, then they are devoid of wisdom (*prajñā*)."

It is unreasonable to determine that [atoms] are permanent through observation. Furthermore, if you claim they have already been observed, that contradicts the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is therefore unreasonable. Moreover, what is your position?

Is it because the nature of atoms is subtle that you consider them to be permanent, or is it because their characteristics differ from those of gross resultant objects that you consider them to be permanent? If [it is the former],...
It is unreasonable to claim that the subtle [atoms] are eternal when their nature is fragile, inferior, and subject to disintegration and diminution.

Furthermore, if it is argued that they are distinct by virtue of their characteristics, then since these atoms transcend the characteristics of earth, water, fire, and wind—possessing characteristics of a different kind—it is unreasonable to say that they can produce those effects. Moreover, as for those atoms...

Furthermore, because no distinct characteristic can be apprehended, it does not accord with reason; this is refuted at length, and the statement that "Yoga [śāstra] is the same as this" is identical in its entirety to what is found in the sixth fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (*Xianyang shengjiao lun*).
The *Vyākhyā* on the *Śataśāstra* also states: "Even up to [the point where it is said] 'because one believes that [space] exists,' etc.

The refutation there is as extensive as in that text. Regarding the word "etc.," it refers to other passages establishing the proof. It continues: "Worldly people believe that space exists in all places;
therefore, they universally believe that space exists at all times—past, present, and future—and for this reason, it is eternal. The internal [opponent] says:
Because parts are joined together with other parts, the parts are not distinct from one another. If there were space within a jar, would that space within be the whole or would it exist as a part?
If it were the whole, it would not be pervasive; if it were pervasive, the jar itself would also have to be pervasive.
If it exists as a part, then space would merely be a part and would not possess the status of being a "whole" (avayavin).
"Space is therefore neither omnipresent nor eternal. The opponent says: "Space certainly exists; it possesses the characteristic of omnipresence and is also eternal because it acts.
If space did not exist, there would be no lifting up, no lowering down, no coming, no going, and so forth.
Why? Because there would be no place for containment. Now, since there is indeed that which is acted upon, space must exist."
[Objection: It is also omnipresent and eternal. [Reply: This is not so. If space were to exist within space, then as a spatial phenomenon it would have to have a place of abiding.
If there is no place of abiding, then it is a non-entity. If the voidness of cavities were that in which space abides, then space would be abiding within space;
however, this is not the case because space possesses the capacity for containment. Therefore, space [does not abide].
It does not abide within a cavity, nor does it abide within the substance itself. Why? Because in substance there is no emptiness.
If that substance were not called empty, and if there were no emptiness, there would be no other place for it to abide, as there would be no space to contain it.
Furthermore, regarding your claim that the locus of activity is empty space: since there is no locus of activity within substance, there would then be no empty space. Therefore—
Space is neither all-pervading nor eternal. Furthermore, because it is without characteristics (*animitta*), space does not exist. All phenomena each possess their own characteristic;
because they have characteristics, we know that phenomena exist—such as the characteristic of solidity for earth, moisture for water, heat for fire, motion for wind, and cognition for consciousness.
Since space lacks such characteristics, it is non-existent. [The opponent] says: "Space exists externally."
Because you do not know its characteristics, you claim that there is no characteristic of formlessness, and thus this is the characteristic of space.
This is not so. "Formlessness" means the destruction of form; it is not a further existent dharma, just as when a tree is cut down, there is no further existent dharma remaining.
Therefore, there is no characteristic of space. Furthermore, space has no characteristic. Why? Because you say that formlessness is space.
Regarding the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*): if it were prior to the arising of form (*rūpa*), there would first be the characteristic of empty space.

Furthermore, form is an impermanent phenomenon (*anitya-dharma*), whereas empty space is a permanent phenomenon (*nitya-dharma*). If form did not yet exist, empty space as a phenomenon should already exist beforehand. If there were no form, there would be nothing for it to cease;
thus, empty space would lack a characteristic. If it lacks a characteristic, it is not a phenomenon. Therefore, it is not [the case that empty space exists prior to form].
Regarding the formless [realms], the characteristic of space is merely a name without reality; all such [notions] as "pervasive" and "eternal" are likewise refuted in general.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-vyākhyā* states: "For what reasons... up to establishing such a treatise? This refers to the subsequent section of that treatise.

Later it says: "Now one should question him: What do you assert? Is the suffering brought about by present methods caused by past karma, or is it caused by present methods, or is it caused by both past karma and present methods?

If you hold that it is caused by past karma, then as for what you previously stated—that through diligent effort one expels old karma—[the new karma of the present would likewise be produced by past causes]."
Because it is harmed by its own causal conditions, it is unreasonable to claim that such [defilements] will not exist again in the future,
and so forth, as explained at length. If you maintain that the skillful means of the present life serve as the cause, then your previous assertion—
that all that is experienced by any worldly person or individual (pudgala) is caused solely by past karma— would be untenable.

For this reason, this treatise does not represent a reasoned exposition. Question: Since that [treatise] asserts that suffering and pleasure result from past actions (*pūrvakṛta*), which is identical to our own internal teaching, why do you not accept it?

Answer: The *Guangchao* (Extensive Extracts) cites the text on repentance from the *Buddhanāma-sūtra*, which states that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) frequently give rise to doubts regarding karmic retribution.
It says there are three types of karma: namely, that which ripens in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), that which ripens in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), and... [the text continues].

Regarding the four permutations concerning birth that follows [karma] in subsequent lives: first, karma where the retribution is fixed but the timing is indefinite; second, karma where the timing is fixed but the retribution is indefinite;

third, karma where both timing and retribution are fixed; and fourth, karma where both timing and retribution are indefinite. These are not accepted because they maintain that there is only such a thing as "previously performed" (pūrvakṛta) karma, and do not allow for other types.
Thus, they do not accept them.
The *Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra* extensively refutes this view in thirty-five fascicles; this refers to the Southern version of the sutra.
If it were the Northern version, it would be found in the fortieth fascicle, where it says: "When Subhadra arrived at the Buddha's dwelling, he asked the Buddha:
'There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who speak thus: "All sentient beings who experience the retribution of suffering and pleasure all follow their past [karma]...'"*

Because of the causes and conditions of karma in Japan, if there are those who maintain the precepts and exert themselves, undergoing physical and mental suffering, they can destroy their original karma.
Once that original karma is exhausted, all sufferings are extinguished, and one immediately attains nirvana.
What is the meaning of this? The Buddha said: "If someone were to speak thus, I would ask them: 'Virtuous one, do you truly say this? If they..."
He replied: "It is indeed so. I see sentient beings who habitually practice various evils, yet possess abundant wealth and treasure and enjoy mastery over their bodies;
I also see those who cultivate goodness, yet are poor and destitute, lacking even basic necessities and failing to attain mastery.

Furthermore, I see some who possess a compassionate heart and refrain from killing, yet meet an untimely death; I see others who delight in killing, yet live out their full lifespan. Moreover, I see people whose bodies..."
Among those who cultivate the holy life, practice with diligence, and maintain the precepts, some attain liberation while others do not.
For this reason, I say that all sentient beings who experience the retribution of suffering and pleasure possess the causal conditions of their own past karma. The Buddha asked:
"Do you truly see past karma? If such karma exists, how much is it? Can present suffering and pleasure destroy it?"
"To what extent can one know whether this karma has been exhausted or not? Once this karma is exhausted, is everything exhausted?
He replied, "I truly do not know. I then drew an analogy: "Suppose there is a person whose body is struck by a poisoned arrow.
His family hires a physician to extract the arrow so that his body may find relief. After a thousand years have passed..."
People still remember clearly and distinctly how the physician extracted the arrow for me and restored my well-being;
yet, since one does not know one's past karma, how can one know that present ascetic practice will certainly destroy past karma?
If they were to say, "In the Sūtras of Gautama it is said: 'If one sees someone who is wealthy and noble...'"
"One should know that this person was fond of giving in previous lives; is this not called 'past karma'? The Buddha said:
"One who knows in this way is said to have inferential knowledge (*anumāna-jñāna*), not true knowledge (*bhūta-jñāna*).
In my Dharma, one may know the effect through the cause, or know the cause through the effect. In my Dharma, there is past karma and there is present karma."
In your doctrine, karma is not severed through skillful means; in my doctrine, it is not so, for karma is severed through skillful means.
Once your karma is exhausted, you claim that suffering is exhausted; I do not hold this view, for when the afflictions (*kleśa*) are exhausted, both karma and suffering are exhausted.
Therefore, I challenge you: if you know that present ascetic practice can destroy past karma, [then why do you not apply it now? Present...
Furthermore, by what means is asceticism destroyed? If it were not destroyed, suffering would be permanent; if suffering were permanent, how could one speak of attaining liberation from suffering?
If there were further practices that destroy asceticism, then since past [actions] have already been exhausted, how could there still be suffering?
One should know that all sentient beings possess past karma and present causes.
Although birth involves past life-span, it necessarily depends upon the present conditions of food and drink.
O Benevolent One, if you say that the suffering and happiness experienced by sentient beings are determined solely by the causal conditions of past karma, this is not so.
For example, suppose there is a person who, for a king, eliminates an enemy and thereby acquires great wealth; because of this wealth, he experiences happiness in the present life.

This person currently creates the causes for happiness and currently receives the retribution of happiness; it is like someone who kills the beloved son of a king, and by this cause and condition, loses their own body and life.
This person currently creates the causes for suffering and currently receives the retribution of suffering.
O Benevolent One, all sentient beings currently experience the suffering and happiness of the four great elements, the seasons, the land, and other people.
Therefore, I say that not all sentient beings necessarily experience suffering and pleasure solely as a result of their past fundamental karma.
Venerable sir, if one were to attain liberation merely through the power of severing the causes and conditions of karma, then no noble ones would ever attain liberation.
Why is this? Because the past fundamental karma of all sentient beings has neither beginning nor end.
Therefore, I say that when one cultivates the Noble Path, this Path is able to obstruct karma that has neither beginning nor end.
Venerable sir, if one were to attain the Path merely by undergoing ascetic practices, then all animals would likewise attain the Path.
For this reason, one should first subdue the mind rather than the body; thus, in my sutras, I have said: "Cut down this forest, but do not cut down [the trees]."
As for felling trees: why is it that fear arises from the forest and not from the individual tree? If one wishes to discipline the body, one must first discipline the mind;
the mind is likened to the forest, and the body to the tree. (The above points extract the essentials; they are explained in full detail within the sutra.)

In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 7, the passage "the lower part of the Great Vehicle Dharma Master’s Commentary" refers to the text of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun), which maintains that there is a cause for natural arising (*svabhāva*).
However, the subsequent section of that treatise refutes this, stating: "Now one should question them:
what do you assert? Do all things in the world, whether internal or external, arise in their various forms suddenly (*akasmāt*)?"
Is arising without a cause, or is it with a cause? If it were without a cause, then various arisings would occur suddenly;

that they sometimes do not arise would be unreasonable. If it were with a cause, then the self and the world would arise without a cause, which is unreasonable. ... [and so on] ... Therefore, this treatise is not a reasoned exposition.
The statement that "this has no cause and is spontaneous, rather than being a separate entity" is a refutation of the Dharma Master of the Mahāyāna.
As for the *Chao* (the Sub-commentary), if one were to provide a detailed analysis below—referring to the various treatises as previously cited and explained in each instance—one might ask:
"Why does the *Wen Chao* not cite them extensively? Guifeng replies: "Because this [view] is biased and circuitous."

The meaning [of this] is difficult to reconcile with the profound Dharma, and one would need to expend limitless mental effort. Since this region lacks [such works], there is no need for me to labor extensively to refute them.
If one were instead to direct that effort toward studying the profound Mahāyāna sūtras, one would naturally come to penetrate their subtle mysteries.

Therefore, I shall now refer [the reader] to other explanations; whether or not [the reader] understands them, it will not hinder the propagation and elucidation [of the teachings]. However, I fear that students may wish to know [more].
The foregoing is a brief citation from the beginning to the end [of the text].
*Huayan Xuantan Huijuan Ji*, Scroll Thirty-Five,
Phonetic Glossary.

Xí (pronounced sì rù; meaning "to enter" or "to join"). Wǒng (pronounced wū kǒng; meaning "dense and luxuriant"). Yù (pronounced yū wù; meaning "trees growing in thick clusters"). Hè (pronounced hé gé; meaning "a coarse garment").

Xiāo (pronounced xiū). Jiū (pronounced liú; xiū-liú are names for certain birds). Nú (pronounced nǎi dū; according to the *Shūchuán*, it means "children"). Zuàn (pronounced zǐ luàn and zǐ yóu; that by which one pierces). Jì (pronounced qī jí;

meaning "to govern" or "to interrogate regarding offenses"). Wě (pronounced wū mò; meaning "to swallow"). Lǒng (pronounced lì chǒng; meaning "mounds and graves"). Gǔ (pronounced gōng hù). Xū (pronounced xǔ wù; meaning "to rise suddenly").
In the *Huayan Xuantan Huiquan Ji*, Scroll 36, compiled by the Bhikṣu Puri of Zai Guang Temple on Mount Cang, it is stated:

"That which summarizes all reckonings and does not exceed the four views and so forth is precisely the meaning of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only). As that treatise says: [and so forth].
Although the various classes of non-Buddhists are numerous, the entities they grasp as existing do not exceed four types.
First, they grasp that the entity of an existent phenomenon and its nature of existence (sattā) are identical in essence, as in the Sāṃkhya school and others. Their position is irrational. Why?

Because it would follow that all phenomena are not distinct from the nature of existence, and thus all would be like the nature of existence itself, with no difference in their essential substance. Furthermore, if form and so forth were [identical to existence]...
If the nature of form and so forth were [identical to] form and so forth, then there would be no distinction between blue, yellow, and the like.

Furthermore, the two [positions] maintain that the entity (dharmin) and its existence-nature (sattā-svabhāva) are definitively different in essence, as in the Vaiśeṣika school and others; however, such a position is irrational. Why?

Because it would follow that all phenomena lack the nature of existence (asat-tva), just as a non-entity that has already ceased cannot be apprehended; this would contradict the fact that the self-essence of substance and so forth is not non-existent.

This contradicts what is perceived by the world, namely that things exist; furthermore, if the nature of form and so forth were not distinct from form and so forth themselves, then they would not be objects of the eye and other senses, just as sound and other such phenomena are not.

These three [positions] maintain that the entity (*dharmin*) and its existence (*sattā*) and other natures are both identical and different, like shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and so forth (this is *duḥśīla*, here translated as "asceticism" or "shamelessness," being the Sanskrit term). Their position is irrational. Why? Because the arguments regarding identity and difference are the same as those previously stated.
Because they are distinct entities, the two would be contradictory; because their natures as one or different would both be untenable;
lest all phenomena become a single identical nature; or else, oneness and difference would be merely conventional and not real, yet you insist they are real—this logic is certainly untenable.
(The Commentary states: If one asserts that the subject and its existence, etc., are neither one nor different, like false views...)

My son, this refers to the enumeration of the six teachers; specifically, it concerns Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, who is indeed a Nigaṇṭha. Therefore, he is singled out as one of "wrong views. Why is his adherence considered irrational?

Because his adherence to neither-identity-nor-difference is identical to the [faulty] positions of identity and difference. If the term "neither-identity-nor-difference" were purely affirmative (*vyavaccheda*), there should be no double negation.
If it were merely negative (*paryudāsa*), there would be no position held at all. If it were both negative and affirmative, they would contradict one another.
If difference were neither a negation nor an affirmation, it would result in mere frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).

Furthermore, it would contradict the common worldly knowledge that things exist as either identical or different, and it would also contradict one's own tenet that phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) are definitively and substantially real.
Therefore, those words are merely a deceptive evasion of faults; let no wise person mistakenly accept them.

As for the distinction: those who hold that the effect exists within the cause are the Sāṃkhyas, who calculate that within the principle of *prakṛti* (the ultimate reality) there are twenty-three principles;

this is "the effect existing within the cause. Those who hold that the effect does not exist within the cause are the Vaiśeṣikas, who calculate that apart from substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*), there is a separate entity called "existence" (*mahāsattā*);
this is "the effect not existing within the cause."

The Commentary states that these are all as extensive as the *Śata-śāstra*, because that treatise contains the chapters "Refuting the Effect Existing in the Cause" and "Refuting the Effect Non-existing in the Cause," in which these two positions are extensively set forth and refuted. To summarize:
if the effect already exists within the cause, or if it does not exist within the cause—neither case can have an arising. Why? If the effect does not exist within the cause...
Why is it that there is only a jar in the clay and cloth in the threads? If both were non-existent [in their causes], then the clay should be cloth and the threads should be the jar.
If the effect already exists within the cause, then the effect would be produced while already existing within the cause; this is not the case. Why?
Because the cause is itself the effect, for according to your doctrine, cause and effect are not distinct. Within the cause...
Whether the effect exists prior [to the cause] or does not exist prior [to the cause], in both cases it is not produced.

Furthermore, if the effect already existed within the cause, then curd and ghee would already exist within milk; if the cause already existed within the effect, then curd, milk, and so forth would already exist within ghee.
If curd, ghee, and so forth already existed within milk, then one cause would have multiple effects; if ghee possessed curd, milk, and so forth...
Thus, if there were multiple causes within a single effect, there would be the fault of cause and effect existing simultaneously in such a sequence;

likewise, if the effect were absent within the cause, there would be the same fault. Therefore, whether the effect exists within the cause or does not exist within the cause, in both cases there is no arising.
Furthermore, it is said: if the jar were not different from the lump of clay, then when the jar arises, the lump of clay should not perish.
The lump of clay should likewise not be the cause of the jar. If the lump of clay were different from the jar, the jar would not arise;
nor could the jar be the effect of the lump of clay. Therefore, whether the effect exists within the cause or does not exist within the cause, a thing cannot produce another thing.
(The above refutes their attachment by means of the argument that there is no arising. Furthermore, it says: The Outsider says: "If all phenomena are empty and signless..."

Ordinary people of the world do not all believe and accept this; internally, we say it is because of the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) that the people of the world believe and accept it.
Why is this? Because phenomena produced through causes and conditions are characterized by the absence of marks (*animitta*).

Do you claim that there is curd and ghee within milk, that a young girl has already conceived children, that excrement is already present within food, or that there is a house existing separately from its beams and rafters?

Apart from the threads, there is no separate cloth; whether one says that the effect exists within the cause, or that the effect does not exist within the cause, or that phenomena arise apart from causes and conditions—all such views are actually empty and should not be spoken of. Worldly affairs are clung to by people;
who would believe them? My Dharma is not like this, for it does not accord with worldly people, and thus all shall believe and accept it.
The Commentary states: "That which arises from empty space is causeless. Question: Among the eleven prior speculative views (*paryeṣaṇā*), there is already a view of causelessness;
why, then, is empty space specifically identified here as the cause? Answer: The former refers to the existence of causelessness within the objects of speculation themselves;

this [present case] refers to the relationship between the ten speculative views as they relate to one another, wherein empty space is presented in contrast to what is commonly perceived by all other sentient beings.
It is said that because there is no substance, empty space is pointed out as being "without cause.
In the *Chao* (Commentary), regarding the phrase "that which was non-existent suddenly comes into being," there are two parts: first, a brief explanation of the two types of causes;

second, a detailed exposition of the two causes in reverse order. First, it explains "false causes" (*mithyā-hetu*); subsequently, under the section "all dharmas," it explains "causelessness" (*ahetu*).
The "corresponding visible [passages]" refers to the summary explanations found outside the main body of the *Śāstra* (the *Sūtra*).

Regarding the passage in the *Chao* (the *Commentary*) that reads, "There is an entity that is formed in confusion, born before Heaven and Earth," Emperor Minghuang of the Tang dynasty annotated it as follows:

"Because one wishes to clarify the origin of naming the Dao, it says 'there is an entity. This means there is an entity formed in a state of chaotic integration, encompassing and gestating all things."
Investigating its transformation and generation, it exists prior to heaven and earth; it is silent and vast, the ultimate mother of the world.
The commentary states: "The substance of that which exists is silent and vast, empty and still;
its wondrous essence is profoundly serene and eternally tranquil, thus it stands alone without shifting or changing. Its application pervades all beings, thus it circulates everywhere without peril."
The myriad things rely upon it for their generation and growth, being covered by its flourishing and auspicious virtue; thus it can serve as the Mother of the world.

Because its name is unknown and it is most remote, it is called "Returning to the Origin. The commentary states: "I see that things have generation and growth, yet they remain hidden without name or surname;
therefore, to express its virtue through its universal production, I style it 'Dao' (the Way), and to designate it by its capacity for inclusion, I call it 'De' (Virtue)."

The substance of strength is called "Great"; its wondrous function is without fixed direction, and because it cannot be grasped by means of names, if one seeks it from the standpoint of the "Great," it will vanish and depart;
if one seeks it from the standpoint of "departing," one will go too far to reach it.
If one can attain awakening, it returns to the body and mind and is realized therein. (The *Chao* commentary states: "Because of that which is great," and so forth.)
This explains the passage concerning the Great King of Heaven and Earth, who is also Great.

"Within the realm" refers to the interior of the eight extremities; it means that people call the king by this title. Regarding the term "etcetera," the *Guangchao* (Broad Commentary), fascicle seven, states:
"Based on what was previously explained, humans are born from Heaven and Earth, and Heaven and Earth are born from the Dao; therefore, [the king] is considered a human."
"The King returns to the law of the Origin" means that the intent of the words lies in the Way and the Law of Nature (*ziran*).
