This refers to the fact that although the *Chao* (Commentary) cites the text in detail according to its phrasing and structure, the fundamental intent of the *Shu* (Sub-commentary) lies solely in the Way and the Law of Nature;

therefore, although the preceding section provides an extensive explanation, it takes Nature as the ultimate. In the *Chao*, following the passage on "the movement of the Way," it explains the generation of the One from the Way.
"Also, below the phrase 'producing beings,' one name is added to explain the preceding [passage]: 'one gives birth to two. This explains that the Yang energy cannot descend [to produce alone].
'Accumulating the Qi of the Abyss' and 'covering from below' explain the meaning of the preceding [passage] to accord with the text of the *Classic*.

As for the statement, 'The myriad things carry Yin on their backs and embrace Yang,' the sub-commentary below states: 'The myriad things obtain the harmonious Qi of Yin and Yang to be generated and completed.'"
For this reason, they embrace the Yin and Yang and contain the primal breath (*chong qi*) to become supple and harmonious.
The passage cited from the "Da Zong Shi" chapter is the third chapter; the commentary states:
"Though great as heaven and earth and rich in the myriad things, that which they take as their primary teacher is the mindless. As for the words "possessing feeling and possessing sincerity," etc.:
That commentary states: "Clear mirror" means it illuminates sentient beings; "responding like an echo" refers to its accordance with their capacities;
"tranquil, serene, and still" refers to non-action (*wuwei*); and "viewed but not seen" refers to its formlessness. The *Chao* (Excerpts) states:

"That which can be transmitted but cannot be received"—the commentary explains that "transmission" refers to the fact that words are used as a provisional means to explain the principle, while "cannot be received" means that the essence is beyond measure and number.
It can be attained through solitary awakening within one’s own mind; it is apart from form and color and thus cannot be seen.
The *Chao* states: "From antiquity it has existed as a constant. The sub-commentary (*Su*) says: "From" means following; "existence" means being present.
The ultimate Way is void and pervasive, without beginning or end. Since the very beginning, before heaven and earth existed and the five pneumas had not yet manifested, my Way has existed therein.

▲ Regarding the phrase "The God of Riches, the Lord of Ghosts and Spirits" (*caoshen guishendi*), the sub-commentary (*shu*) states: "It is said that the Great Way is able to manifest spiritual power among ghosts and spirits, and divine power among the celestial deities.
It illuminates the Three Luminaries (*sanjing*) and establishes the Two Polarities (*eryi*). This efficacy arises from the power of the Ultimate Non-being (*zhìwú*).

This is what is meant by being 'spiritual without being spiritual' (*bùshén ér shén*), 'generating without being generated' (*bùshēng ér shēng*), and 'being spiritual and generating without being spiritual or generating' (*fēishén fēishēng ér shén fēishēng ér shēng*)."
Therefore, the *Laozi* states: "Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; the spirit attains the One and becomes numinous.

The *Chao* [commentary] on the passage "prior to the Great Ultimate" (*taiji*) quotes that sub-commentary (*shu*) as saying: "The Great Ultimate refers to the five pneumas (*wugqi*); the six ultimates refer to the six directions (*liuhexiang*). Now, consider this:
being above the five pneumas does not make it high and remote; being below the six directions does not make it deep and profound."
Born before heaven and earth, it does not become long-lived; enduring through all eternity, it does not become ancient.
It is said that the Way is neither high nor deep, neither long nor old; therefore, the Way is nowhere not present, yet wherever it is, it is as if non-existent.
Regarding "Xiweishi": the sub-commentary states that Xiweishi was the title of an ancient sovereign prior to the era of written characters.

Because he attained the Way of spiritual penetration, he was able to drive and control the myriad beings and sustain the two polarities (Heaven and Earth). Furthermore, as for the character "qi" (契), it means "to harmonize";
it signifies one who can blend all things into unity and bring them into accord with the two polarities. I prostrate myself... [text ends].
Fuxi was able to subdue oxen and ride horses; because he subdued sacrificial animals, he is called Fuxi. "Xi" (襲) means to inherit and combine.
The "Mother of Qi" (氣母) is the Mother of Primordial Qi (*yuanqi*), which corresponds to the Dao.

Because he attained the Ultimate Dao, he was able to draw the Eight Trigrams (*bagua*), develop the Six Lines (*liuyao*), harmonize Yin and Yang, and unify the Six Qi. "Wei" refers to the Dipper, specifically the Northern Dipper, which serves as the leader for all.
The stars serve as the structural framework, which is why they are called "coordinates" (*wei*); the Dipper (*dou*) is that which measures deviations.
Since antiquity, those who have attained the Ultimate Way have traversed from beginning to end; thus, in maintaining Heaven and Earth, there must be no deviation or error.
The sun and moon provide testimony through a single path, and therefore they are able to shine from beginning to end without ever ceasing. Mount Kunlun is its name; it is located in the Northern Sea.
To the north is Mount Kunlun; "Kambe" is the name of its deity, meaning "to enter by succession. Kambei has a human face and a bestial body;
having attained the Way, he entered Mount Kunlun and became a deity. His surname is Feng and his given name is Yi; he was a native of Tishou Village in Tongxiang, Huayin, Hongrong.
By ingesting the divine elixir of eight minerals, he attained the rank of Water Immortal at the Great River, the Yellow River. He is a deity of the Heavenly Emperor.
[The text] records that [the Yellow Emperor] appointed Fengyi as the Lord of the River (Hebo), and thus he dwelt amidst the great mountains at Mengjin.

Jianwu is the name of a spirit (according to Sima Qian, he was a mountain god who did not die; he existed until the time of Confucius). Having attained the Way, he resided on the Eastern Peak as the deity of the great river.
Huangdi is Xuan-yun. He collected copper from Mount Shou and cast cauldrons at the foot of Mount Jing. When the cauldrons were completed...
There was a dragon that lowered its beard-like whiskers to welcome the Emperor;

the Emperor then took his ministers and seventy-two members of the inner palace and ascended to the celestial realm by day, riding upon clouds and drawn by dragons, where he transformed and departed as an immortal.

Furthermore, the *Chao* (Excerpts) states regarding the phrase "knowing what Heaven does," that the commentary (*Shu*) says: "Heaven" refers to spontaneity (*ziran*), and "the ultimate" (*zhi*) refers to creation (*zao*).

That which is called the "Ultimate" and attributed to Heaven refers to the alternation of light and darkness of the three luminaries, the generation and destruction of the four seasons, the spreading and rolling of wind and clouds, and the coldness and warmth of thunder and rain.
That which is attributed to humans refers to grasping with the hands, walking with the feet, seeing with the eyes, hearing with the ears, and knowing with the mind—whether skillful or clumsy.
All mental activities and actions are known to be entirely of this nature; they all arise spontaneously from within.
This is not a matter of deliberate fabrication, nor does it arise from the power of intellectual effort. Therefore, internally one releases the body and externally one merges with all things;

in this vast and expansive contemplation, one attains profound identity with the myriad mysteries. Having exhausted all principles and fully realized one's nature, it is for this reason called "the Ultimate."
The *Chao* (Commentary), which consists of the text of *Zhuangzi*, states in full: "The crane is not bathed daily and yet is white;
the crow is not blackened daily and yet is black" (this is the natural state of each). The sub-commentary (*Shu*) explains:
"That the crane is white and the crow is black is received from nature; how could it require bathing and dyeing day after day to become so? Thus it speaks of things."
The principle of their nature is such that even the words of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* state accordingly; specifically, the fortieth fascicle says:
"The Brahmin clad in rag-robes said: 'Just as thorns grow naturally sharp, birds have naturally distinct colors, and venomous snakes, once born, naturally consume earth;
likewise, fish see bait and naturally swallow it, and turtles, once born on land, naturally enter the water.'"
"A calf, once born, is able to drink milk on its own; who is there to teach it? The Buddha said, "Good son, this principle is not so.
If you say that entering water occurs without causes and conditions, why does it not enter fire?
If you say that drinking milk occurs without causes and conditions, why does it not suckle at horns and the like?"
Regarding the phrase "The Commentary (Chao) II cites the *Zhouyi*, etc.," the two characters "etc. (*deng*) are redundant. As for the term "binding" (*xi*), it means "to attach" or "to connect.
The aforementioned sub-commentary (*shu*) states that the term "Commentary on the Words" (*Xici*) has two meanings:

first, regarding the character "discourse" (*zi*), it takes the sense of "attachment," because the Sage attached these words beneath the hexagrams and lines; second, as for pronouncing it as "tethering" (*xi*), it takes [the sense of binding].
Regarding the meaning of "systematic connection" (*xi*), both the hexagrams and their constituent lines each have their own explanatory texts (*ci*) to elucidate their significance;

thus, the hexagrams and lines each possess a systematic connection, which is why it is termed "connection" (*xi*). The Master’s original work, the *Ten Wings* (*Shi Yi*), further explains the textual content of the two sections, the *Upper* and *Lower*, regarding the "Appended Statements" (*Xici*).
These are organized as distinct volumes to clarify the principles and meanings, collectively titled:
Regarding the addition of the two characters "is therefore" (shì gù) before this passage in the *Xi cí*, it is because the original text contains those two characters;
that text says, "Is therefore, the *Yī* has the Great Ultimate," and so forth. The note marked with a triangle (▲) refers to the commentary by Han Kangbo.
The mention of "Kong" refers to the sub-commentary (*shū*) by Kong Yingda. This refers to the section beginning with "the primordial chaos" (*hùnyuán*).
Question: In the passage "One gives birth to Two," Laozi previously stated that the One is the Qi of Emptiness (chōng qì) giving birth to the second, Yang-Qi.

Why is it now said that the Great Ultimate (tài jí) gives birth to the Two Forms (liǎng yí), which is the same as Laozi’s "One gives birth to Two"? Answer: The *Guǎngchāo* (Broad Commentary), fascicle seven, states:

"It is said that when the Dao moves, it produces the Qi of the Original Source (chōngyuán); this is 'the Dao gives birth to the One. However, in terms of the principle of things, this is not yet sufficient."
Furthermore, it gives rise to the two qi of yin and yang: from one comes two. Yin qi condenses below to become earth; yang qi ascends to become heaven;

and harmonious qi forms in the middle as humanity—this is "two producing three. Once the Three Powers are established, the eight trigrams arise and the myriad things are born—this is "three producing the myriad things.
Wenzi (Wen Tong) takes these two meanings and cites them as evidence; however, the interpretations adopted by various schools differ.
This is not contradictory. ▲ The *Jiaoyao* (Excerpts) comments on that passage, stating: "It refers to the fundamental nature (*zhìxìng*).

Furthermore, the interpretation identifying "Taiyi" (The Great Ease) with the "Taiji" (Great Ultimate) of the *Zhouyi* (Book of Changes) is the commentary by Zhang Zan of the Han dynasty. I have now recorded these annotations in full so that their origins and conclusions may be seen.
The *Liezi* states: "There is Taiyi, Taichu, Taishi, and Taisu. (The note says: "This clarifies the phases of transformation as things evolve from the subtle to the manifest.")

(Inheritance. "The Great Ease" (*tāiyì*) refers to that which has not yet possessed *qi* (vital energy). (*Yì* is a designation for the absence of stagnation; when one is stilled and silent within the realm of emptiness, what could possibly be seen?

It is like the "Supreme Ultimate" [*tàijí*] in the *Yì* Appendix and the "Mingled Perfection" [*hùncéng*] of Lǎozi.*) "The Great Commencement" (*tāichū*) is the beginning of *qi*. (When yin and yang have not yet been differentiated, it is what is called "the chaotic mass" [*húnlún*] below;

"chaotic mass" means that all things are blended together and have not yet separated from one another. "The Great Beginning" (*tāishǐ*) is the beginning of form. (Once yin and yang have been differentiated, the various categories of things flow forth in their forms. The Great...

"Sù" (the raw) is the beginning of substance (substance refers to nature; once something has become a thing, its squareness or roundness, hardness or softness, stillness or agitation, buoyancy or sinking each possesses its own nature).
[The *Jiǎocháo*] states that "the Great Beginning is not the Great Ease," etc., which accords with the intent of Kong’s Commentary (*Kōngshū*).

This means that since Zhang Zan already identified the Great Ease as the Great Ultimate (*Tàijí*), Kong’s claim that the Great Beginning is [the first stage] is incorrect. (Because the Great Beginning is the second name, if it were identical to the Great Ease, it would not be the first.)
[This is] the second name. However, the text of the *Chao* (Commentary) is slightly disordered; it should read: "This, then, is Taiyi" (meaning "it is Taiyi"), rather than "not Taichu.
Only then would the sequence of the principles be correct, as they constitute Taiji at the beginning. Let the wise examine this carefully.

Furthermore, if one follows the *Yi Zhuan* (Commentary on the Changes), specifically the "Gouming" section, Taiji actually appears later. Nevertheless, when the *Yi* refers to Taiji, it takes that which exists [as its basis].
The ultimate limit (*ji-chu*) is precisely non-existence (*wu*). The *Gouming jue* calls this the Great Ultimate (*taiji*);

this is explained as referring to the point where the form and substance are perfectly complete. One is the ultimate of the beginning of existence (therefore it is the same as the *Taiyi* above), and one is the ultimate of the end of existence (therefore it follows after the four movements).
Thus, while their names are the same, their meanings differ. Furthermore, the commentary on Guishan’s *Yuanren lun* states: "That..."
It begins with the Fivefold Rotation of Taiyi (Great Ease), culminating in Taiji (the fifth stage, Gouming). From Taiji, the Two Polarities (Liangyi) arise.

The commentary states: "Because the Pure and Cool (Qingliang) both exist, the *Jiaochao* says that although there are slight differences, they are all simply the Primordial Qi (Yuanyi) giving birth to Heaven and Earth.
Guishan directly equates the Taiji of the *Yi Jing* with the Taiji of the *Gouming jue*. It appears as such.

This does not accord with the current text; however, since the *Gouming jue* (Decisions on the Hooking of Life) posits that the single qi contains the five movements, it follows that the single qi is one and the same, which is not contrary to reason.
The *Jiyao chao* (Excerpts from the Essentials) states that "Zhèn is wood, Lí is fire," and so forth, referring to the four directions and the four seasons;
furthermore, Xuǎn is the same as the four intermediate corners (*sìwéi*). The *Shuogua* (Explanation of the Trigrams) says: "Qián is heaven, is round, is the sovereign, is the father..."
Jade is categorized as metal and thus shares the same trigram as metal, *Dui*; wood, wind, and the eldest daughter are all attributed to *Xun*, and thus share the same trigram as wood, *Zhen*.
Regarding the establishment of the Eight Trigrams (*Ba Gua*), they proceed from the northwest as the starting point: *Qian*, *Kan*, *Gen*, *Zhen*, *Xun*, *Li*, *Kun*, and *Dui*.
If one summarizes their symbolic forms, *Qian* has three long lines, *Kun* has six short lines, and *Li* has a central [line].
The hollow *kan* has its center full; *zhen* is like an upturned bowl; *gen* is like an overturned cup;

*dui* is deficient at the top; *xun* is short at the bottom. Furthermore, *qian* is heaven, *kun* is earth, *li* is fire, *kan* is water, *gen* is mountain, *dui* is marsh, *zhen* is thunder, and *xun* is wind—these are the Eight Trigrams (*bagua*).
As for the mutual inference of the lines (*yao*) and their images (*xiang*), this is the first [point].
The trigrams are eightfold, and from these eight come sixty-four hexagrams;
each hexagram has six lines, totaling three hundred and eighty-four lines. By inferring through these combinations, there arise good and ill fortune.
"‘The alternation of one yang and one yin is called the Way; the unfathomability of yin and yang is called the Spirit.
These two phrases are not consecutive in the original text; therefore, the *Chao* repeats the first phrase and cites the commentary to explain it.
Regarding ‘the unfathomability of yin and yang is called the Spirit,’ the commentary states: ‘Spirit is the ultimate point of transformation, which wondrously brings all things into being...’"
"Words cannot be refuted by means of forms; therefore it is said that Yin and Yang are unfathomable.
Regarding the passage "Furthermore, [to claim] there is no cause, or that an improper cause leads to great error," etc., the *Guishan Yuanyin Lun* states:
"The two teachings of Confucianism and Daoism assert that humans, animals, and so forth are all generated and nurtured by the Great Way of Non-being (*xuwu*). They claim that the Way itself..."
However, life arises from the primal qi (*yuanqi*); the primal qi gives birth to heaven and earth; heaven and earth give birth to the myriad things.

Therefore, whether one is foolish or wise, noble or lowly, poor or wealthy, suffering or happy—all are received from Heaven and depend upon the timing of one's destiny. Thus, after death, one returns to heaven and earth and reverts to emptiness and non-being (*xuwu*).
Now, to briefly cite this and examine it: you claim that the myriad things all proceed from the Great Way of emptiness and non-being.
As for that which is born, the Great Way is the very root of life and death, of the wise and the foolish, and the foundation of good fortune and misfortune, of calamity and blessing.
Since this fundamental basis exists eternally, then chaos, disorder, wickedness, and folly cannot be eliminated; nor can blessings, celebrations, virtue, and goodness be increased.
What use, then, is the teaching of Zhuangzi and Laozi? Furthermore, the Dao nourishes tigers and wolves, brings forth Jie and Zhou, and shortens the lives of Yan Hui and Ran Geng.

How can Bo Yi and Shu Qi be called honorable? Furthermore, if you claim that all things are produced through spontaneous transformation (*ziran*) rather than through causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), then everything that lacks causes and conditions should likewise be subject to such transformation.
This would mean that stones should produce grass, grass might produce humans, humans might produce livestock and so forth;
furthermore, [new beings] should arise without temporal sequence and without distinctions of early or late, and immortals should not depend upon elixirs.

If medicine brings about peace and stability without relying on the worthy and the virtuous, and benevolence and righteousness do not depend on instruction and practice, then what use would there be for the teachings of Zhuangzi, Laozi, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius to establish as standards?

Furthermore, if it is said that all things arise from the primal qi (*yuanqi*), then how could a spirit that suddenly comes into being—having never undergone training or reflection—be capable of love, hate, pride, or indulgence as soon as it becomes an infant? If you say that these qualities exist spontaneously and naturally...
If one can immediately recollect things such as likes and dislikes, then one would be able to understand the five virtues and six arts through mere recollection;

why wait for them to be accomplished through causes and conditions and study? Furthermore, if birth were merely the sudden presence of vital energy (*qi*) upon receiving it, and death were the sudden absence of that energy upon its dispersal, then who would be a ghost or spirit?
Moreover, there are those in the world who possess insight into past lives and can recall former events.
Thus we know that the continuity of existence before birth does not arise suddenly through the reception of vital breath (*qi*);

furthermore, verifying that the spiritual cognition of ghosts and spirits is uninterrupted, we know that after death one does not vanish suddenly as the breath disperses. Therefore, the classics contain texts regarding sacrifices and prayers for blessings.

Moreover, there are those who have returned from death to speak of matters in the dark pathways, or who, after death, move their wives and children to seek vengeance for enmity or requite kindness. Now...
Have these always existed since antiquity? Furthermore, the qi of Heaven and Earth is fundamentally without consciousness;
how can humans, who receive this insentient qi, suddenly arise with consciousness? Moreover, plants and trees also receive qi—why do they not possess it?

Again, you say that poverty and wealth, nobility and meanness, worthiness and folly, good and evil, fortune and misfortune, and calamity and blessing all derive from the mandate of Heaven; this is the allotment of Heaven.
As for destiny, why is it that the poor are many and the wealthy few, the lowly many and the noble few, and even calamities many and blessings few?

If this proportion of more and less resides in Heaven, how could Heaven be unjust? Furthermore, there are those who lack virtuous conduct yet are noble, while those who maintain such conduct are lowly;

those without virtue are wealthy, while those with virtue are poor; the benevolent meet with early death while the violent live long; and even those who possess the Way [meet with misfortune]. How can this be?
If the rise of those who lack the Way and the ruin of those who possess it are both caused by Heaven, then why does Heaven reward the promotion of the unrighteous while ruining the righteous?
Wherein lies the merit of rewarding virtue and humility, or the punishment of bringing calamity upon the licentious and harming the full?

Furthermore, if disorder, rebellion, and perversity all derive from the mandate of Heaven, then when sages establish their teachings, they would blame the person rather than Heaven, and punish the object rather than the mandate. This is not so.

It is indeed so. Thus, the *Shi* (Odes) satirize chaotic governance, the *Shu* (Documents) extol the Way of the King, the *Li* (Rites) praise the stabilization of superiors, and the *Yue* (Music) is said to transform customs;

how could these be considered serving the will of Heaven above or following the mind of the Creator? Therefore, we know that those who devote themselves solely to these teachings have not yet fathomed the origin of humanity.

The *Śāstra* (Commentary) asks: "If this [treatise] is exclusively for the Mahāyāna, then one might wonder: since it uses the causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) of the Hīnayāna to refute various [opponents], why would they be confused regarding the Hīnayāna causes and conditions?
Why, moreover, are they also confused regarding the Mahāyāna causes and conditions? Answer: If we consider their confusion itself, how could one distinguish between 'Great' and 'Small'?
However, when it comes to the time of refutation, using only the causes and conditions of the Hīnayāna is precisely what constitutes the refutation of them.
Regarding the statement that there is textual evidence for the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) in the *Mahāyāna*, the Sūtra says: "All that exists within the three realms is but the single mind;
the Tathāgata has here analyzed and expounded the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), all of which are established based upon this single mind.
The *Yichao* (Commentary) states that "the mental phenomena are momentary" means that the eighth consciousness, the mind, serves as the basis for all [other] consciousnesses.
Because each moment perishes and the next arises, with each succeeding state continuing in its own kind from moment to moment, there is no beginning.

As for the term "dhātu" (element/realm), it carries the meaning of "cause," which refers to the seed-consciousness (*bīja-vijñāna*). Transmitted through successive stages, it perishes previously and thus is not eternal;

yet it arises subsequently and thus is not annihilated. These mental phenomena exist in dependence upon causes and conditions through mutual correspondence; they do not arise from the reception of vital breath (*qi*).
Since it is established that this is solely the mind of consciousness acting as a condition and an object, how could it be the same as what follows, which clarifies its difference from that?
As for the character "至" (zhì), the syntactic flow is slightly extended, but the meaning is easy to understand. Regarding the *Shu* (Commentary): "This refers to the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.
The first phrase is entirely the text of the sūtra; the second phrase is an explanatory introduction. "From delusion there is craving": here, "delusion" (*moha*) is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*).
"Craving" refers to the craving for the three realms of existence (*tribhava*). These two [craving and ignorance] constitute the root, for because of them, birth and death are endless.

Regarding the statement that "ignorance initiates karma," this clarifies the single-layered cause-and-effect across two lifetimes in the Mahāyāna tradition; that is, the ten links from ignorance through craving, grasping, and becoming are the causes of the present life, while the two links of birth, old age, and death are the effects of the future life.
As for the statement that "ignorance initiates karma," it means that although the capacity to initiate karma extends to all three poisons, it is specifically ignorance [that is emphasized here].

To establish the correct [meaning], the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "In this context, ignorance (*avidyā*) takes as its essence only that which can initiate karma that truly evokes good or evil in future lives;
that is to say, it refers to both the entirety of the discriminative [ignorance] and a portion of the innate [ignorance].

Regarding the statement that "craving (*tṛṣṇā*) can moisten karma," although "moistening" encompasses all three poisons, the craving for the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*) increases predominantly. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: "Regarding moistening..."

In the stage of karma (*karmāvasthā*), the power of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) increases predominantly; craving is said to be like water because it can moisten and nourish. It is only through repeated irrigation that the sprout of existence (*bhava-aṅkura*) arises.

Regarding the phrase "the two past [factors] below" (if according to the Mahāyāna doctrine, there is a single layer of cause and effect across the three times; if according to the Hīnayāna doctrine, there are two layers of cause and effect across the three times):

according to the Mahāyāna doctrine, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "These twelve links consist of ten causes and two fruits, which are definitely not of the same time period. (The commentary on that [text]...)

It is said that because the maturation (*vipāka*) itself does not receive its fruit in the very same body that performed the karma, it is reckoned in terms of death and rebirth as being of the same time-period (*sahabhū*). Among the ten causes, the first seven—along with craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*)—may be either different or the same [time-period].

If it is karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya-karma*), then at the moment craving first arises, their time-period must be the same; from the second birth onwards, up until the karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya-karma*) and so forth, the time-periods are different.

Since craving and grasping arise only when one is about to receive the fruit in the second or third future life after having performed the karma in this present body, the critique states: "If they are of the same time-period, this refers to the meaning of the previous two lifetimes; if they are of different time-periods, this refers to the meaning of the present three lifetimes."

If the two [sets] of seven [links] are each fixed as belonging to the same lifetime—namely, the seven links beginning with ignorance (avidyā), which include the three [karmic factors] of craving (tṛṣṇā), grasping (upādāna), and existence (bhava), and the five [resultant factors] beginning with consciousness (vijñāna) since it is through delusion that karma is produced and the seeds for retribution are perfumed—then these first seven links must necessarily arise in the same lifetime.

Furthermore, craving and grasping moisten the preceding six seeds (consciousness and so forth), causing them to transform and be termed "existence" (bhava); this also does not occur at a different time.

It is not the case that the moistening agent and the moistened object belong to different lifetimes; rather, birth (jāti) and old age and death (jarāmaraṇa) are known to be of the same lifetime. It is said that "Ritual (*li*) is the thinning of loyalty and good faith, and the beginning of disorder" (the commentary notes: those who establish ritual do so because loyalty and good faith have declined, and they take ritual as the primary means to remedy disorder).
Furthermore, *Zhuangzi* says, "Ritual is the flower of the Way (*dao*) and the beginning of disorder. This implies that the principle (*li*) derives from the Way.
The *Dejing* (Chapter on Virtue) states: "Without stepping out the door, one knows the world; without looking through the window, one perceives the Way of Heaven" (the commentary notes:...).

With hands hanging loose and non-action, one issues no edicts beyond the threshold of the door. Thus we know that when the way of governing the world is understood through human affairs, the celestial signs accord with it; therefore, without the trouble of peering through the window, the Way of Heaven can be known.

"The further one goes out, the less wisdom one possesses" (if one cannot practice non-action, even if one's comings and goings extend ever further, the wisdom for the way of governing the world becomes increasingly deficient).

"Accomplishment without acting": this means that without employing formal teachings, the world is transformed and perfected. "He who acts brings about failure": because ordinary sentiments cannot rely on natural spontaneity, they laboriously strive beyond their proper limits; for one who acts thus seeking fulfillment, failure is the inevitable consequence.

"Defeating it" means that success lies in timing. The *Daodejing* says: "He who wishes to take possession of the world by acting for its sake—I see that he cannot succeed. (The world is the position of the Great Treasure.
One who possesses the Way must wait until the mandate of the calendar and destiny rests upon his person. If a violent and chaotic person attempts to take it as his lord through force, he will fail;

hence some say, "I see that he cannot have it. This means it does not lie in contention. As for the phrase "it does not lie in [contention]," there is a source text that reads: "It does not lie in... (The character "本," meaning source, indicates this).
This matter is indeed so; the dispute concerns which term is the correct expression for "desire" (*yù*).

Regarding the passage in the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) stating that "all sentient beings, from the beginningless past, because they possess various forms of affectionate attachment and greedy desire, undergo saṃsāra," since one can sever these, one transcends birth and death.
As for the statement that "the teachings are distinct," "teachings" (*fāng*) refers to the Dharma (*fǎ*). This refers to what is elucidated by these two types of teaching.
Since the Dharma is distinct, the principle that the two teachings are entirely different is easy to understand.

Regarding the phrases "returning to non-being" and "returning to difference," one manuscript reads "returning to difference" (歸異) and "returning to distinction" (歸別), while another reads "returning to distinction" (歸別) and "returning to difference" (歸異);

however, both cases distinguish the differences based on what is returned to. As for the expressions "can be plucked" (可搴) and "can be pulled out" (可拔), "搴" is pronounced qiān and also [carries the meaning of drawing up].
The characters for "sound" (*yin*) and "stammering" (*jian*) both signify "to take. The phrase "to control and restrain those below" refers to the beginning and end of faithful understanding;
from this point downward, all refer to practicing according to the principle. The phrase "soaring upward" (*hui deng*) refers to the actual realization of Bodhi;
its wondrous wisdom reaches everywhere, just as one gazes afar from a high tower. Thus, the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* (Renwang jing) says: "It is like ascending a high tower to universally observe all."
There is nothing whatsoever that is not clearly understood; this is called the Garden where the holy spirits of the virtuous Nirvāṇa gather.
It is profoundly serene below, covering all, where the wondrous fruit of the ultimate reliance exists and ceases without obstruction, towering (yì) with majesty.
"Life and death are destiny. (The *Zhuangzi* says: "Life, death, existence, and non-existence—whether one is worthy or unworthy—is destiny.
To resist it is to be able to abide in peace. (The *Zhuangzi* says: "This is to flee from Heaven, to go against one's nature, and to lose what has been bestowed [upon one].

The nature and what is received each have their own allotted portion; they cannot be escaped, nor can they be added to. Abiding in the times and dwelling in accordance with the natural order, one is beyond the reach of grief and joy.

"Entering. (Now, grief and joy arise from gain and loss. But for the man of profound penetration who adapts to change, there is no time he is not at peace, and no situation he does not dwell in with equanimity. Being darkly one with the process of creation (*zaohua*), he has no fixed abode and no sense of self.

What would he have to gain or lose? Who could say what is born? Therefore, he accepts whatever comes to him, and grief and joy find no place between. Regarding the words "gū shào": the first tone is *qiáo*, and the second tone is *shào*.
If it is pronounced as *qiáo*, it carries the meaning of "refined intention"; if it is pronounced as *shào*, it means "exertion. Thus...
Standing alone, one attains the refined essence within the phenomenal world (*huánzhōng*), and likewise exerts oneself within that world.
The words are serene; as Zhuangzi says: "Serene and infinite, all manner of beauty follows it.

When one is easygoing and tranquil, anxiety and calamity cannot enter, and depraved influences cannot assail them. (Thus, they merge indistinguishably with the True Principle. Therefore, there are no natural disasters. (Disasters arise from opposing the Way.)
"Free from the encumbrances of things" (for encumbrances arise from opposing things; the pronunciation of "po" is like "pa").

This means that since their ultimate destinations differ, the following summary concludes that because the destination reached is ultimately different, the departure of those who set out is likewise distinct. One person travels east and one person goes west;
they are separated by such a vast distance that even a thousand li cannot limit it.
The commentary states: "These ten differences above are intended to encourage scholars to reflect upon them with deep sincerity and careful deliberation.
However, there is a textual variant which reads: "Li Sishen’s deep sincerity," implying that his surname was Li and his given name was Sishen.

Thus, according to the *Hongjue*: "Since ancient times, former sages have long distinguished between the true and the false; yet even the renowned and virtuous of recent times [have remained divided]."

Because this is not like the Confucian secular tradition, which still distinguishes between clear and turbid water—as seen in Li Sishen’s *Ten Differences* and other texts—we know that his surname was Li and his given name was Sishen;
there is no need for a separate explanation. As for the term "zhong" (衷), it means "correct.

This refers to the extremely profound and central principle of this person; therefore, he spoke much [of it]. Regarding the phrase "by means of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) and so forth," this is the judgment of the author of the *Chao* (the sub-commentary).

This indicates that the Mahāyāna is used sparingly; therefore, those versions which claim it is "frequently used" are incorrect. Moreover, since the lower realm is itself Mahāyāna, the five teachings can be understood accordingly.

In the *Chao*, the section beginning with "no attainment" (*wude*) refutes errors, while the section beginning with "practicing the heterodox" (*xiexi*) clarifies the impairment of the Perfect [Teaching].
The *Jue* commentary states: "Having encountered heterodox schools in previous lives, these have already permeated his mind, accumulating into habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-bīja*)."
Therefore, regarding the difficulty of generating faith in the Noble Path, the transmission is entrusted to those who are diligent;

furthermore, the teaching is specifically cautioned against those who, being unable to properly discern between the false and the correct, preach for others, causing listeners to follow them in blind obedience like a guide leading the blind.
Thus, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "If sentient beings, though seeking a virtuous friend, encounter one with false views..."
Not having attained correct awakening is what is called the lineage of external paths; this is the fault and error of false teachers, not the blame of sentient beings.
*Huayan Xuantan Huiyan Ji*, Scroll 36.

Phonetic Explanations: Xi (pronounced *xǐ*, also *yìzhī*): wild boar. Qiè (*kǔjié*): to lift up; to carry. Tè (*tādé*): to deviate; to err; to change. Bēi (*bùhuí*): cup; goblet. Rán (*rǔmíng*): beard;

whiskers on the cheeks. Yǎo (*shēndiǎo*): deep; distant. Juàn (*gǔxiàn*): impetuous; urgent. Yóng (*niúxiōng*): to look up; to gaze upward. Yǐ (*niúqǐ*): serene; tranquil. Nán (*núdāo*): a type of bird.
*Huayan Xuantan Huixuan Ji*, Scroll Thirty-Seven.
Compiled by the Bhikṣu Puri of Zai Guang Temple on Mount Cang.
In the *Chao* (Commentary), regarding the school that maintains that the three dharmas have no coming or going, it is stated that there are eight full schools and one partial school.
First, the Mahāsāṃghika: this refers to the "Great Assembly" that held the council outside the cave;

alternatively, when the Mahādeva schism occurred, those monks who were numerous in number formed the Mahāsāṃghika. Regarding the Dṛṣṭāntika school, some texts state it is the Śvetāśvatara school, but this is incorrect.
The Sthaviras migrated to the Snowy Mountains, and from them the Saṃkrāntivādins emerged;
this school was previously subsumed under the doctrine of "the existence of dharmas and the non-existence of a self. It is now precisely this Saṃkrāntivāda that is being discussed.

This master asserts that there is only a single seed which, through its present continuity, transmigrates to future lives; therefore, they are called Saṃkrāntivādins. The original name of this school was Sautrāntika.

The Sautrāntika school relies solely on the sūtras as a source for inference (*anumāna*), rather than the vinaya or the abhidharma; because they take the sūtras as the basis for validating all meanings they interpret, they are called the Sautrāntikas.

They are also said to be the *Vibhajyavādins* (those who distinguish). (However, some versions of the *Chao* [commentary] state that there are seven schools in full and one in part, and do not mention this [Sautrāntika] school.

Since the fundamental Sautrāntika is already included within the first category [of Vibhajyavādins], the version omitting it is likely correct. Alternatively, if it is categorized under a different meaning, there is no contradiction in including this school here as well. Third, the Kasyapīya school.
In ancient times, there was a rishi who, being overcome by lust, fathered a son upon a hen. Because he was born from that species, he was named Kātyāyana;
he is thus the lineage of the rishis among the Brahmins, and the current head of the school belongs to this clan.
Therefore, it is so named. The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states that this is the surname of the master of the Vinaya. [This is] the Caturvīśatimātṛkā-vihāra school.
This *caitya* is translated here as "Numinous Temple" (*lingmiao*). This place is named after the many *caityas* located there. The *Zuanyuanji* states:

"In the first life [of a Buddha], there are numinous temples at four locations: the site of birth, the site of attaining enlightenment, the site of turning the wheel of Dharma, and the site of parinirvāṇa.
This is one such location. Because there are many *caityas* on the mountain and people dwell depending upon them, it is named after the mountain. That is to say...
This was the later residence of Mahādeva (the rest as described above). Regarding the two schools, the Pañcavastuka and the Ṣadvastuka:

to the west of Mount Caitya it was called the Western Mountain (Aparagiri); because they were in disagreement with Mahādeva, they resided separately on the Northern Mountain (Uttaragiri), which is likewise one of the mountains north of Mount Caitya.
These three schools above all derive their names from their respective residences. [These constitute] the nine Dharma-piṭakas.
The school is also called the Dharmaguptaka (Dharma-Secret School); "School Master" (*buphu-zhu*) refers to its founder, namely Maudgalyāyana’s disciple.
Because they practiced what their teacher had taught after Maudgalyāyana’s parinirvāṇa, it is so named. Furthermore, "Secret" (*mi*) and "Treasury" (*zang*) share essentially the same meaning.

Since this master [the founder] contained and preserved the True Dharma like the secrecy of a treasury, it is also called the Dharmaguptaka; "Gupta" (*hu*) means protection, specifically defensive protection, thus it is the "Secret Treasury."
Regarding the meaning: as for the Kāśyapīya school, in ancient times there was a rishi whose bodily radiance was so intense that it eclipsed all other light, rendering it invisible;
because the founder of this present school is his descendant, it is named after him.

Regarding the term "Mahīśāsaka," this has already been explained above. To say it means "narrating the turning of the snow" is incorrect; it should rather be said to mean "expounding the turning [of the wheel]. It says "four."
Regarding the meaning of the Dharmaguptaka school: in Sanskrit it is called Dharmagupta, which is translated here as "Dharma-treasury" (Fazang);
this is the name of the founder of the *Four-Part Vinaya*. Regarding the meaning of the Mahāsāṃghika school: its full name is Mahāsāṃghika, which is translated as "Great Assembly.
This school is comprehensive in its practice and understanding, free from narrow attachments, and in accord with the five schools.
Because it is what has been observed, some say "Mahāsaṃghika" (Great Assembly). This is not the same as the Mahāsāṃghika school;
rather, the "Saṃghika" (Assembly) here refers to the Great Assembly within the cave of the Sthaviras. Thus, it differs from the Great School outside the cave.
Now, examining this in detail, since it is called the *Saṃghika-vinaya* of the Mahāsāṃghika school, it is the Mahāsāṃghika that is identical with the Saṃgha.
The *Ji-lü* (Mahīśāsaka-vinaya) is the same as the aforementioned *Sifen-lü* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya), as both belong to the Dharmaguptaka school.

Regarding the statement in the *Shuochao* that it is the "Prājñaptika" school: this school teaches that all mundane and supramundane phenomena are both provisional designations (*prajñapti*) and real entities.
As for the claim that the *Chengshi lun* (Tattvasiddhi-śāstra) was originally a disciple of the Sāṃkhya school: this treatise was composed by Harivarman.
Regarding the statement that Guṇavarman composed this treatise while within the monastic community (*saṃgha-dharma*):

his school held that the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are the creators (*bhūta*) and the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*) are the created (*bhautika*). This was the reverse of our own school’s position regarding creator and created;
consequently, he later entered the Buddha-dharma. This treatise belongs to the Sautrāntika school. As for the phrase "The Tripiṭaka Master says" below:

To establish that the Sautrāntika masters are included within this school, it is said that while the subtle is real and the coarse is provisional. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Weishi shu) states:

"The ten bases of the Sautrāntikas (the twelve bases excluding the mind-base and dharma-base) are coarse and provisional, while the subtle is real. [This is because] the ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*) are real, whereas coarse forms and so forth are provisional aggregates;

since the subtle constitutes the coarse, the latter is provisional. In the Mahāyāna conventional [truth], the coarse is real and the subtle is provisional. This is because all forms and so forth arise from seeds, are transformations of consciousness, and are subsumed under the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*)."
The coarse and the real atoms (*paramāṇu*) exist only as analytical constructs of the mind’s contemplation; therefore, they are termed "subtle" in the sense of being conventional (*prajñapti*).

The Sarvāstivādins and others maintain that both the coarse and the subtle are real, because the atoms are subsumed under form (*rūpa*) and other aggregates, and the subtle is derived from the coarse through their aggregation. The Ekavyavahārikas and others maintain that both the coarse and the subtle are conventional. Now, we shall first adopt the former position, as it is somewhat similar to the doctrine of the Prajñaptivādins;
thus, these are combined into a single school. The phrase "this [school] asserts conventionality" below serves to distinguish it from the others.
The treatises followed by the latter two schools among the three distinct Nikāyas explain the conventional designation (*prajñapti*).

This is because, within the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), both the provisional and the real exist; thus, they differ from the Ekavyāvahārika school, which holds that all things are merely provisional and makes no distinction between the true and the conventional.

Furthermore, they differ from the Lokottaravāda school, which maintains that only the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is real while all conventional truths are merely provisional. This [text] serves to distinguish [the positions].
Regarding the statement that within the section on the aggregates (skandha), the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) includes both the provisional and the real:
when a phenomenon is subsumed within the category of the five aggregates, it is considered real;

however, when the five aggregates are divided into the twelve bases (āyatana) and eighteen elements (dhātu)—that is, by opening up form (rūpa) and combining mind (citta) to form the twelve bases, or by opening up both mind and form to form the eighteen elements—since the aggregates of form and mind have been thus opened up into elements and bases, they are [provisional].
"Provisional designation" (meaning that since the five aggregates have been analyzed as accumulations, the names "dhātu" and "āyatana" are provisional designations for those accumulations).
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The conventional is provisional," etc.: this school clarifies that mundane phenomena arise from inversion;
because their cognition is false, they are not substantially existent and are entirely provisional names. Supramundane phenomena do not arise from inversion and possess the path.
Because it is the fruit, the object of the two kinds of emptiness is real, and the single wisdom of emptiness is also real.
Since the real object can give rise to real wisdom, and real wisdom can penetrate the real object, it is called "real" and is named "supramundane.

This is designated by way of what is established; because this section accords with the Mahāyāna, the *Chao* (Commentary) says it "resembles the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* to a small degree," and the *Chao* further notes that it "resembles [it] slightly."
Regarding the phrase "the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and so forth," this refers to that which is slightly similar to the first half of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.

In the first half of the "Chapter on the Four Truths" (*Catuḥsatya-pariccheda*) of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, emptiness is used to refute the existence of the Four Truths; in the second half, emptiness is used to establish their existence. Now, taking the two kinds of emptiness as the ultimate reality, it resembles the meaning of the first half.

Alternatively, it may be understood that the conventional is false and thus slightly resembles the teaching of the "dependent origination of phenomena" (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*), while the supramundane is...
To say that it "slightly resembles" what I have taught as "emptiness" is because one has not grasped the full verse; thus, it is called the "first half.

However, this statement of "slightly resembling" implies a partial correspondence with the meaning of the Mahāyāna *Pratītyasamutpādahṛdaya-śāstra* (the "Destructive" or *Lakṣaṇa-bhanga* Initial Teaching).

Yet, even when compared to the first half of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, it is not entirely identical. Therefore, [the claim] that the mundane is false and the supramundane is real does not fully coincide with the former verse.

It is merely said that because the first two lines of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* state that dependently arisen phenomena (*pratītyasamutpanna*) are empty, all mundane and supramundane phenomena are entirely empty.
However, since the fifth school [of the Three Treatises] asserts that only the mundane is empty while the supramundane is not, the mundane is false and the supramundane is real;
thus, in the first half-verse of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, it only resembles their notion of emptiness.
Because it is but a portion of the world, it is said to be "slightly similar" and so forth. If it were entirely similar, how would it differ from the Mahāyāna?
Consider this. Regarding the Ekavyāvahārikas (One-Name School): their name is derived from their doctrine; they are called "One-Name" because they assert that only conventional designations are real.
Thus, while previously [in the previous school] that which transcends the world was held to be real, now [for this school] even that which transcends the world is merely conventional.
It is named thus.
Since the *Jiaochao* states "there being no worldly [teaching]," one should consult the *Lun* (the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*), which says: "Since there is no worldly [teaching]. The *Tanxuanti* records:
"This also applies to the beginning of the Initial Teaching; that is, the initial entry into the skillful means within the Initial Teaching of the Refutation of Characteristics."
Regarding the "Commentary on the School of the Rational, Perfect, and Real" (*Yingli yuanshi zong*), the *Jinguangming jing chao* states: "‘Rational’ (*ying*) means to accord with;
it accords with correct principle, being perfect and real, and is not a provisional teaching because it reveals the explicit meaning (*nītārtha*).
Therefore, it is called the ‘School of the Rational, Perfect, and Real. Now, although that [text] considers itself "perfect and real," its interpretation of the latter three schools is not complete.
Therefore, it is renamed the School of the Three Natures’ Emptiness and Existence (*trividha-svabhāva-śūnyatā-sattva-vāda*).

The *Śāstra* states that “the dual extinction of mind and object” encompasses both the intent of the *Pratītyasamutpāda-śūnyatā* (emptiness of dependent origination) in refuting characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the intent of the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*) in severing characteristics;

as for the phrase “directly manifesting the essence,” this refers exclusively to the meaning of the Sudden Teaching. Now, because we proceed from the profound to the shallow, they are arranged in this order.
If the *Tanyuan ji* (Record of Exploring the Profundities) does not establish a seventh school called the "School of All Being Empty" (*yiqie jie kong zong*)—

which refers to the initial teaching of the Mahāyāna— and instead names the eighth as the "School of True Virtue Not Being Empty" (*zhende bukong zong*) and the ninth as the "School of the Simultaneous Severance of Characteristics and Conceptions" (*xiangxiang jujue zong*),

then by merging the ninth with the seventh to form the eighth, "True Emptiness Severing Characteristics," and placing the seventh, "Three Natures: Emptiness and Existence" (*sanxing kongyou*), alongside it:
According to the teaching on the "characteristics as they truly are" (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*), one must transpose that eighth [category] to become the present ninth;

only then is the inclusion of the meaning complete. Regarding the commentary’s statement on the Mahāyāna tenet that "emptiness and existence are unimpeded": although within the Mahāyāna tenets the seventh [category, the *parikalpita-svabhāva*] is existent, it is said to be empty because it is empty of the conceptual grasping of sentient beings (*sattva-abhiniveśa*).
Nevertheless, because the *paratantra-svabhāva* appears as existent and the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* is truly existent, [the two are unimpeded].

Because existence exists, it was established below as the eighth thesis: that both truths (the two satyas) coexist. Now, the ninth [thesis] integrates emptiness and existence so that they are non-obstructive.
Regarding the phrase "because the characteristics are not destroyed" in the *Chao* (Commentary):
previously, through mutual integration, it was clarified that emptiness and existence are not different; next, both are simultaneously negated and swept away.

The characteristics of emptiness and existence are now simultaneously brushed away; yet, in doing so, one does not destroy the characteristics of emptiness and existence, which serves to preclude the view of annihilationism.

Regarding the phrase "True Suchness following conditions," the commentary uses the two characters for "True Suchness" (*tathatā*) to distinguish it from the perspective of the Emptiness School (*śūnyavāda*).

This means that since the preceding discussion of mutual fusion and dual transcendence—without obstructing their simultaneous preservation—is sufficient to manifest the intent of the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*).

Why must the school further speak of *tathatā* (suchness)? Therefore, it is said here: the previous discussion of the non-obstruction of emptiness and existence was stated directly on the basis of emptiness and existence alone.
If one did not further speak of *tathatā*, the elimination of confusion would not be exhaustive;

for since the non-obstruction of emptiness and existence can still be confused with mere emptiness, it is taught that *tathatā* is itself emptiness and emptiness is itself *tathatā*. [Question: Regarding these words...
Question: Since "True Suchness" (*tathatā*) has already distinguished it from the eighth school, why is it necessary to further mention the two characters "following conditions" (*suiyuan*)?

Answer: It is to distinguish it from the Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) school; thus, it is further said to "follow conditions. Question: If True Suchness merely follows conditions, how does it fulfill the meaning of "True Suchness," and furthermore, how does it differ from the seventh school which maintains that it is merely "unmoving" (*niǎngrán*)?
Answer: It is precisely by means of "following conditions" that it is distinguished from the seventh school, which holds that it is merely unmoving.

The School (Zong) is not without the two meanings of "invariability" (*abhinna-lakṣaṇa*) and "unchanging" (*avikāra*); only when both are fully present can it be said to possess unimpeded speech as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Below this, the text again distinguishes it from the School of Emptiness (*śūnyatā-vāda*). Thus, Guishan established ten distinct gates for the Nature of Emptiness (*śūnyatā-svabhāva*).

However, while the Western Regions (India) established the School of Nature (*svabhāva-vāda*), the present [tradition] categorizes the Sudden, Real, and Perfect [teachings]—all of which are termed the School of Nature—by distinguishing their relative depth according to their meaning.
There is a difference.
When the *Jiyao* (Excerpts) now shifts the seventh [chapter] to become the eighth and so forth, it is precisely to clarify its underlying intent:
since the positions established by Xianshou in the *Tanxuan ji* largely follow that [system], the seventh is named "All Are Empty" and the eighth is named "True Virtue."
The ninth [stage], Amogha (Not-empty), is characterized by the simultaneous cessation of both names and conceptualizations;

although there are differences between the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages—beginning with the seventh and ending with the eighth—the two systems of the seventh and eighth stages both rely on that sequence, differing only in nomenclature.

To explain the meaning of the eighth stage, it is said that according to Master Xuanzang’s teaching on the turning of the Dharma wheel, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and the principle of the non-emptiness of *tathatā* (suchness) constitute the final teaching (*paryantavyavasthāna*).

However, because this would overlap with the meaning of that "correct, perfect, and ultimate" [teaching], and because I now wish to overturn what they have established, I take their seventh as the eighth and their eighth as the seventh, adding a ninth to integrate those two.

This is done so as to accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Question: "Worthy Leader, since you follow those eight schools, how can there be anything profound and subtle? Answer: It is simply because...
The latter two schools surpass it; however, there are now three schools that are superior because the eighth school contains the doctrine of suddenness (*tun-yi*).
Regarding the phrase "as previously mentioned in the Western Regions," the previous commentary states that because it teaches provisional existence (*jia-you*), it constitutes the second period.

This seventh school, which reveals the principle to the point of emptiness (*kong*) and brings the convergence of conditions (*yuan-xiang*) to their exhaustion, constitutes the third period. This refers to the present [seventh] school.

Regarding the statement that "the eight schools and so forth accord with the Dharma-nature": as previously stated, the four unenlightened schools all revert to the Dharma-character (lakṣaṇa), while the four enlightened schools all revert to the Dharma-nature;
thus, those [distinctions] of the seventh and eighth [schools] are overturned.

Regarding the statement in the *Chao* (Commentary) that "the fifth and sixth schools are established within the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*)": the fifth school is established in the Lokottaravāda, and the sixth school is established in the Ekavyāvahārika.
The preceding *Chao* explains that both of these two schools cite the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* to demonstrate their compatibility with the Mahāyāna;
thus, the first fascicle of the *Tanxuan ji* and the *Jiaoyi* state: "This marks the beginning of the Initial Teaching (*Ādikarmika-yāna*)."

Question: If it is said that this position is established within the Hinayana while its meaning is common to both Mahayana and Hinayana, then the third school should also be common to the Mahayana, since the Mahayana also asserts that the past and future are non-existent while the present exists;
and the fourth school should also be common to the Mahayana, since [it holds that] present form, mind, and so forth are real, arising from their own seeds.

Because [the unconditioned] arises, it is not associated with [the mind]; since it is provisionally established as a state (*avasthā*) of matter and mind, why would this apply only to the two schools—the third and the fifth?

Answer: Because the third school holds that the present exists, and the fourth school holds that the reality of the present is all substantially existent apart from consciousness (*vijñapti*), these do not accord with the Mahāyāna. It is for this reason that they are not mentioned in the Commentary (*ṭīkā*).
Alternatively, it may be aligned with five or six meanings; the commentary cites one corner [of the principle] so that one may infer and understand the rest.
Regarding the "seven, namely the dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and so forth" in the commentary: according to the *Awakening of Faith* commentary, there are five schools.

First is the school of attachment to phenomena based on appearances (*suxiang faxi zong*), which refers to the various masters of the Hīnayāna who, relying on sūtras such as the *Āgamas*, established and composed the various treatises of the Hīnayāna. Second...

1. The School of True Emptiness and Signlessness (*śūnyatā-niḥsvabhāva-vāda*) was established by Nāgārjuna and Āryadeva based on the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras, and they composed treatises such as the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.

2. The School of Consciousness-Only and Dharmalakṣaṇa (*vijñaptimātra-dharmalakṣaṇa-vāda*) was established by Asaṅga and Vasubandhu based on the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and other sūtras, and they composed treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. 3.
The School of Tathāgatagarbha and Dependent Origination (*tathāgatagarbha-pratītyasamutpāda-vāda*) was established by Aśvaghoṣa, Sthiramati, and others based on the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
The five schools established in such scriptures as the *Awakening of Faith* and other treatises—the school of the Perfectly Interfused Endowment of Virtues—is precisely the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu’s *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya* establishes the meaning of the six aspects of perfect interfusion (*ṣaḍ-lakṣaṇa-saṃvartana*). Of these, the first [of the five] corresponds to the first six schools;

the second and third correspond to the eighth and seventh schools respectively; and the fourth and fifth correspond to the latter two schools. Nevertheless, the characteristics of the Dharma (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) still persist.

Because it relies on provisional names, it is definitively expedient; because there are two aspects of signlessness—namely, that if one takes dependent origination as emptiness, they are equal and of a single flavor—it is sudden and real.
However, because it clarifies only emptiness without manifesting non-emptiness, it is the expedient of "refuting characteristics" (*poxiang*).

The *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* places the sudden and real within the context of the expedient of refuting characteristics; therefore, it is situated before the Yogācāra school of the "characteristics" (*xiangzong*), which clarifies the "middle."
Because it is the Way, it is now cool; because it uses the provisional to break through appearances, it is subsumed within the sudden and real teaching.

Since the conditions for appearances are exhausted, it follows after the dharma-characteristics. Therefore, the subsequent section states that the eighth is the "Sudden Teaching," which does not explicitly mention the meaning of breaking through appearances as it remains implicit.
The *Chao* (Commentary) uses the five teachings to distinguish [the stages], which is done by correlating them according to the corresponding aspects of doctrine and practice;

it does not necessarily follow the sequential order of the teachings. Question: If that is so, then the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*) should be shallower than the Final Teaching (*zhong-jiao*), since it is said that "the earlier are shallow and the later are deep.
Answer: Although the "True Emptiness Beyond Characteristics" (*zhenkong juexiang*) belongs to the Sudden Teaching, it nevertheless...
The "Pervasive" (tong) refers to the Initial Teaching (shijiao), yet it is categorized as "Sudden" (dun) based on its predominant aspect and its implicit initial meaning.

Thus, Qingliang said: "Furthermore, as for the 'doctrinal essence' (zong), it is spoken of according to the predominant aspect; since the present case also follows the predominant aspect, assigning it to the Sudden is not contrary to the underlying principle—that the former is shallow and the latter is deep."
Regarding the *Vyākhyā* (the Commentary) composed by the Bodhisattva Bhāviveka, the *Xiyuji* states:

"The Master Bhāviveka outwardly donned the robes of the Sāṃkhya while inwardly propagating the school of Nāgārjuna. Desiring to debate with Dharmapāla, Bhāviveka vowed that he would not see the Bodhi tree in vain;
if he saw it, he would become a Buddha. However, Dharmapāla had no leisure to leave the Bodhi tree."
Unable to meet him for discussion, he remarked, "If Maitreya does not attain Buddhahood, who will resolve my doubts?
Before an image of Avalokiteśvara, he recited the *Svacittadhāraṇī* while abstaining from food and water for three years. The Bodhisattva appeared and asked, "What is your vow?
He replied, "I shall preserve this body to await the vision of Maitreya" (as previously described). His *Tattvasaṃgraha-śāstra* (*Zhangzhen lun*) consists of two fascicles.
Regarding the statement "only by explaining these two means of valid cognition," the *Cien Shu* (Compendium on the Hundred Dharmas) says:
"In that ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are empty. The first means of valid cognition states:

"All conditioned phenomena are empty because they are the true nature [of reality] and because they arise from conditions, like illusory things. (The *Ming Chao* [Commentary on the Meaning] states: "This is to prevent the fault of contradicting worldly conventions; for those who study, all conditioned phenomena...")

Since the world and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) all admit that conditioned phenomena exist, and since scholars and the world alike admit that unconditioned phenomena exist, if one does not make a distinction, this fault arises. Now, when we speak of "true nature" (*tathatā*), we do so in reliance upon ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and not in reliance upon worldly convention;

therefore, this fault does not apply. The initial formal argument (*prayoga*) should be stated as follows: The true nature of conditioned phenomena is empty—this is first established by exclusion; subsequently, the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) and the predicate (*sādhyadharma*) are distinguished from one another, and their inseparable nature is combined to form the thesis (*pratijñā*).

The reason (*hetu*) is: "because they are dependently originated, like illusions and the like. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: "like illusions and the like. Question: If true nature is the ultimate, what are the characteristics of the conventional ultimate (*saṃvṛti-paramārtha*)? Answer: In the sense of true nature and ultimate truth, everything is empty. Within conventional truth, however, there can be the cultivation and realization of form and mind.

Regarding the principle that "all marks whatsoever are empty and false," as stated in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, these are the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). That "marks are not marks" is the vision of the Tathāgata; this is the ultimate mark (*paramārtha-lakṣaṇa*). Question: This must entail the fallacy of contradicting one's own teachings (*svavacana-viruddha*), because it contradicts the meaning of non-emptiness found in various scriptures.

For instance, the *Bhadrakalpika Sūtra* and others state: "The conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are called 'existence' (*sat*); 'self' (*ātman*) and 'what belongs to self' (*ātmīya*) are called 'non-existence' (*asat*). Answer: I also have such teachings, as cited previously. Furthermore, there is the fallacy of contradicting one's own words (*svavacana-viruddha*):

our school asserts that "true nature" (*tathatā*) is expressed by relying on the ultimate (*paramārtha*). Yet, according to your school, all phenomena (*dharma*) are utterly non-existent in the ultimate sense, yet you further claim that the conditioned has the meaning of "existence. Although this may resemble a formal thesis (*pakṣa*) according to the rules of logic (*hetuvidyā*), [it is nonetheless contradictory].

Within this [position], there is no fault of self-contradiction regarding the *dharmin* (the subject); however, since it deviates from reason, it is nonetheless a fault. One should understand that the phrase "true nature" (*tathatā*) is employed to prevent such faults and thus encompasses both means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

It merely refers distantly to the first fault as a general indication; it is not intended to be the actual *dharmin* of the thesis. The intention is first to point out: "I establish 'conditioned phenomena' (*saṃskṛta*) as the *dharmin* based on true nature, and their emptiness is the thesis. Alternatively, because one wishes to demonstrate the principle of being free from fault, there is no contradiction.

Therefore, one should formulate the syllogism as follows: "Conditioned phenomena are the *dharmin*; they are empty based on true nature—this is the thesis. Thus, there is no fault. As the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Pal-zhen-lun) states: "For example, take the single category of the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*); with respect to the ultimate (*paramārtha*), its essence is empty, and so forth."

▲ Regarding the claim that the order of the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) here is inverted: in the three-membered syllogism, the sequence is first the thesis (*pakṣa*), second the reason, and third the example;

yet in this verse, the thesis comes first, followed by the example and then the reason. Therefore, it is said to be "inverted" (*qù*, which here means "subsequent"). Alternatively, it may be because the translator’s re-arrangement of the text was incomplete.
Thus, regarding the "inference (*anumāna*) of the two unconditioned phenomena," the *Bǎifǎ Shū* (Commentary on the Hundred Dharmas) states: "As for all unconditioned phenomena..."
Because it is the true nature (*tathatā*), it is not real; because it does not arise, it is like a flower in the sky. The *Mingchao* states that the refutation of errors is as above.

Furthermore, this subsequent inference is established based on ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and is therefore different from the previous inference. Alternatively, if one follows the reasoning of the previous inference, there is likewise no contradiction.
The reason (*hetu*) is stated as "because it does not arise," meaning that which is fundamentally non-arising—among all things that do not arise—is [the case].
It is certainly not the case that there is no real example, such as a flower in the sky. The *Pāṇy-āmalaka-vāda* (Treatise on the Jewel in the Palm) states:

"One does not say that by merely negating [the opponent's position], one fails to establish a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). (However, according to the *Mingchao*, both types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) incur the fault of contradicting one's own scriptures; yet, since we ourselves also possess scriptural authority, this is not considered a fault. Although that school regards the teachings of this school as non-definitive (*neyārtha*), this school likewise regards their teachings as non-definitive.

Thus, as in the previous case where the four non-definitive sūtras of the Western Regions are all subsumed under the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school, both types of valid cognition are true means of establishment (*sādhana*) and true means of refutation (*dūṣaṇa*). This is especially so since it is a passage from the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*).

Could this be considered a semblance of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Therefore, the seventh fascicle of the *Śataśāstra* (Hundred-Verse Treatise) composed by the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla also states: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) arise in accordance with conditions; thus, like magical illusions, they do not possess a real essence.

Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) likewise do not possess a real essence, because they are unarisen—like the hair of a tortoise. Clearly, the master who composed this treatise was free from bias or partiality.

The *Chao* (Excerpts) refers to a portion of the meaning within the *Prajñā* and the Three Treatises (*Tri-śāstra*). The mention of "Prajñā" here refers to the various *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras. "Three" refers to...
The *Madhyamaka-śata-śāstra* (Treatise in One Hundred Verses on the Middle Way) addresses the profound *Guhyasamāja-yoga* mentioned previously;
thus, the phrase "there are those who say" (*yǒu yán*) below is a statement of censure directed at others.

This refers to those within the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school (Faxiangzong) who have lost the true intent of the Nāgārjuna school (Nàngmǎng zōng)—whose formal name was Nàngmǎng, though formerly called Lóngshù—rather than refuting the Nāgārjuna school itself. Otherwise, why would the word "study" (*xué*) have been added?

Now, when Qingliang says that these words are "frightening," he is likewise prohibiting the study of the Dharma-character (Faxiang) school; he fears that adherents might cling to these words and thereby destroy the school of Nāgārjuna.
As for the phrase "the ultimate truth does not obstruct the conventional" in the *Chao*, it has already been explained in the section on the "distinction between nature and characteristics.

Furthermore, the phrase "it must be integrated with what precedes" means that, as in the case of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), it incorporates the four preceding teachings; therefore, this is the tenth [teaching].
The first school is precisely the tenth school, that of Perfect Integration and Endowment; it is not something contended over by the other schools.
Therefore, the Commentary does not mention it. Guifeng stated: "After the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, various schools propagated and elucidated the Buddha’s scriptures;
as their traditions of study and practice differed, they each became a distinct school."

Regarding the distinction between teachings (*śāsana*) and schools (*nikāya*): a single scripture may contain multiple teachings, whereas a single school may contain multiple teachings, and a single number [of teachings] may contain multiple schools.

Furthermore, "teachings" refer to the distinctions between the provisional and the real according to the Buddha’s intention, while "schools" refer to the differences based on what people’s minds prefer.
However, this analysis of these two meanings differs from the present [text]; the former is direct...

Regarding the difference between the breadth and narrowness of the teachings through the lens of doctrine versus practice, this commentary now explains the breadth and narrowness based on the scriptures according to doctrine and practice.
Next, concerning the difference between the Buddha’s intent and the human mind, the current section addresses what is esteemed according to the various stages.

As for the statement, "If one were to judge narrowly," this is precisely the meaning of our own school’s doctrinal classification (*panjiao*); because it is solely this principle that is superior to other masters, it is [the correct view]. Now there is...
Those who point to a single sūtra or a single section and claim, "This is the beginning" or "This is the end," have lost much.
When the *Chao* (the Sub-commentary) mentions "such as the *Vimalakīrti*," it clarifies that a single sūtra may universally contain all five teachings; thus, it is said to be "universal.
While there may be many instances within the *Shu* (the Commentary), it is not necessarily so; for instance, a single sūtra may contain four, three, or two teachings.
Regarding the statement that the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other [sūtras] also possess these five [characteristics], many scholars claim that *prajñā* is merely a teaching on emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

One should carefully examine this text and consult those sūtras in their entirety; only then will one know that it does not consist solely of the meaning of emptiness. Lest one incur the calamity of slandering the Dharma, we shall here briefly illustrate its essential tenets:
for instance, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* extensively elucidates the non-obstruction between principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), taking this as its core.
Because the primary principle is what is esteemed, it is simply termed the "Principle-Phenomena Unobstructed Doctrine" (*lǐshì wú'ài zōng*).
The phrase "manifesting the penetration of the doctrine" (*xiǎnmíng zōngtōng*) indicates that one doctrine penetrates many scriptures; thus, while it is "penetrating," it casts its shadow upon them.

As for being "restricted" (*jú*), this means that within a single scripture, all the meanings of the five teachings and so forth do not interpenetrate with one another, and are therefore restricted. Question: Other scriptures may be like this, but how about the *Avataṃsaka*?

Question: Since a single sūtra contains the meanings of all five teachings, they should be mutually interpenetrating; if they are interpenetrating, this text is contradicted, and if they are not interpenetrating, the previous commentary is contradicted.
[The commentary] states: "This means that there is what is interpenetrated, but there is no restriction.

Answer: This discussion concerns other schools which do not speak of the *Avataṃsaka*. If one speaks of the *Avataṃsaka* according to the method of negation (*paryudāsa*), then it is neither interpenetrating nor restricted.
In terms of positive expression (*paryudāsa*), because the universal and the particular are unimpeded, it is said that they are "perfectly integrated and endowed with all virtues.
What was previously called "having no limitation" was explained from the perspective of negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).
Regarding the "eight ranks" mentioned in the Commentary, these refer to the four fruits and the four stages of progress toward those fruits.
