seventh, no one can reach its bottom; eighth, it is vast and immeasurable; ninth, it is the dwelling place of beings with massive bodies; and tenth, its tides do not overstep their limits.
Just as a great rain falls everywhere without overflowing, so too is the practice of a Bodhisattva;
for ten reasons it is called the "unshakeable" practice of a Bodhisattva, namely: because in the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), great vows arise and gradually deepen;
because in the Stage of Purity (*vimalā-bhūmi*), one does not accept the corpses of all broken precepts; and because in the Stage of Radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*), one abandons the mundane...
Because it employs provisional designations, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī); because the qualities of a Buddha are of one single flavor, the Ground Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjayā);
because it gives rise to immeasurable skillful means, supernormal powers, and the various treasures produced in the world, the Ground of Presence (Abhimukhī);
and because of the thorough investigation by vast awakening wisdom, the Ground of Far-Going (Dūraṃgamā).
In the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), because one manifests vast and magnificent adornments, one attains profound liberation;
in the Good Wisdom Ground (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*), one acts within the world while knowing it as it truly is, without transgressing its limits;

and in the Cloud of Dharma Ground (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), one can receive the great rain of the Buddhas’ and Tathāgatas’ Dharma-light without ever being satiated. (The ocean metaphor represents the entirety of the essence of Buddha-wisdom; although the ten virtues differ, these virtues are not separate entities from wisdom, and thus they are called "wisdom.")

Furthermore, karma is mutually pervasive yet distinct, unlike a mountain; it is the differentiation of the undifferentiated, and the non-differentiation within differentiation. The four metaphors above all derive from the "Section on the Reflections of the Ground of Fruition" (*phala-bhūmi-pratibimba-vibhāga*).
First, the pond metaphor represents the merit of cultivation; second, the mountain metaphor represents superior merit;
third, the ocean metaphor represents the merit of the great fruit; and fourth, the jewel metaphor represents firm merit. Therefore, the sub-commentary below states: "Four."

The four metaphors illustrate the perfect fusion [of the gradual and the sudden]. The first metaphor, that of the jewel within the pearl, illustrates the gradual within the perfect; the metaphor of the sea illustrates the perfect within the perfect.
These four metaphors demonstrate their mutual fusion. (The *Chao* states: "This differs slightly from what was taught at Tiantai.

There, 'the gradual within the perfect' referred to the perfection within the gradual teachings; here, it refers to the ultimate limit of the formal arrangement within the Perfect Teaching. Furthermore, 'the perfect within the perfect' also differs from that [earlier] usage; it is called 'perfect-perfect' because the beginning and the end are mutually fused.")
This is not the "Perfect" (yuan) of the Perfect Teaching (yuánjiào); rather, it is called "Perfect-Perfect" (yuányuán).
Regarding the *Commentary* (Chǎo) on the "Ten Samādhis" chapter, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 50, states that this is named the "Samādhi of Unobstructed Wisdom.

It is subsumed within the Bodhisattva’s path of training (xuédào), specifically the Vajra-like Samādhi (jīngāngyù dìng). Its sub-commentary (*shū*) states: "This clarifies the Bodhisattva whose causal [practices] are fulfilled."
This is the final stage among the stages; this stage is also called Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Since this sutra wishes to manifest the unimpeded interpenetration of opening and closing [the stages], it preserves the meaning without explicitly revealing the name. The *Sūtra on the Tenth Dhyāna* states that this Bodhisattva is identical to the Buddhas of the three periods;
this refers to Equal Enlightenment, which cannot be counted by ordinary numbers. Starting from one hundred *lakṣas*, those who are able to count... [the numbers increase].
One *lakṣa* is one *koṭi*; this is the middle count. One *lakṣa* is ten thousand *koṭis*, which is one hundred million;
all numbers below this are the upper count. The numerical system doubles at each stage: from *koṭi* to *koṭi* [as a unit], then to one *ayuta*, and so on until the "unspeakable" (*anabhilāpya*).
This is the meaning of the prose section. Furthermore, by accumulating these "unspeakables," one reaches ten levels of calculation.
Regarding "equal in measure," this refers to the meaning of the verse: first, that which is accumulated is unspeakable even unto the unspeakable (the verse says "unspeakable and unspeakable");
second, it cannot be fully described within unspeakable eons (it fills all unspeakable and unspeakable eons, such that the unspeakable remains inexhaustible even when spoken);
third, each of the aforementioned unspeakable [units] is a single world-system (*kṣetra*), and each of these is shattered into atoms (unspeakable...).
1. All Buddha-fields are completely pulverized into minute atoms. 2. Within each and every atom, there are unspeakably many fields; as it is with one atom, so it is with all of them. 3.

The fields within all those aforementioned atoms are, in a single thought-moment, universally pulverized into dust; these unspeakably many Buddha-fields are pulverized into unspeakable dust in a single thought-moment.
4. In every thought-moment, the pulverization of dust continues for many more eons; even as each thought-moment pulverizes dust, it likewise exhausts [the process] over unspeakable eons.
7. To speak of eons as being thus constant; furthermore, the dust particles previously pulverized occupy many lands (the number of these lands is unspeakable).
8. These many lands are again pulverized into dust (it is even more difficult to describe these lands becoming dust). 9.

Using many calculations, one passes through many eons, counting the aforementioned dust particles (using the method of unspeakable calculation, for unspeakable eons, one counts in this manner). 10. Using the number of these dust particles to count each eon.

Each eon further consists of one hundred thousand unspeakable eons (calculated by taking these particles of dust as the number of eons, with one particle representing one hundred thousand unspeakable eons).
As for the comparison, the verses of the subsequent scripture state: "Even if one were to praise a single Samantabhadra for that many eons, one could not exhaust the measure of his merit.
Within the space of a single minute hair-tip, there are unspeakable numbers of Samantabhadras; this applies to all hair-tips without exception."
It is likewise thus, continuing even unto the entirety of the Dharma-realm. The Commentary states: "Briefly citing three levels:
first, the aforementioned eons are insufficient to exhaust the praise of Samantabhadra’s virtues; second, how much more so that within a single atom there are many Samantabhadras;

third, how much more so that throughout all atoms pervading the Dharma-realm, there are many. If one does not contemplate this with a mind that accords with the nature of reality (dharmatā), [one will not understand].
If even the perceptions of those who are insane or deranged are thus [inconceivable], how much more so the virtues of the Buddha?
Regarding the statement that *asaṃkhyeya* is the foremost of the great numbers: *asaṃkhyeya* means "incalculable" (*wúshù*). It is the first of the ten great numbers, namely:
incalculable, immeasurable, boundless, unequaled, uncountable, incomparable, unthinkable, and unfathomable.
That which can be spoken and that which cannot be spoken—this "inexpressible" refers to the perfect fusion of eons and thoughts;

the phrase "downward" corresponds to the methods enumerated in the *Saṃkhyā* (Numerical) chapter, while the first two phrases concern time and correspond to the subsequent *Āyuḥpramāṇa* (Life Span) chapter, and the latter two phrases concern place and correspond to the subsequent *Vihāra* (Abode) chapter.
Regarding the statement "taking eons as days," this means that within the sutra, [the lands] of the preceding realm...
Because a *kalpa* serves as a day for the subsequent lands, each successive one is double the duration of the preceding.
This statement regarding "the upper" refers to the ultimate reality, while "the lower" points to the aforementioned dust-like lands, which encompass all things.

The *Chao* (Excerpts) consists of ten sections on manifestation: first, a general clarification of the dharma of manifestation; second, the body-action (*kāyakarman*); third, the speech... [text continues].
1. Karma; 2. Mental karma; 3. Objects; 4. Conduct; 5. Practice; 6. Attaining Bodhi; 7. Turning the Wheel of Dharma; 8. Entering Parinirvāṇa; 9.
Seeing, Hearing, and Associating with [the Buddha]. The word "manifestation" (chūxiàn) precedes each of these ten gates.

Since all ten arise from the nature (xingqǐ), and taking one encompasses the whole, they are said to be "perfectly interfused" (yuánróng). [The] Commentary: Regarding the preceding text, looking back at it closely...

This is precisely the eighth assembly above, the section on entrusting the Dharma to advance in practice and perfect the conduct. Regarding the statement that it "distantly takes up the various assemblies":
"Faith" refers to the first assembly, the section on citing the fruit to encourage joy and give rise to faith;

"Understanding" refers to the second through the seventh assemblies, the section on cultivating causes to accord with the fruit and give rise to understanding; and "Practice" refers to the eighth assembly, the section on entrusting the Dharma to advance in practice.
Regarding the section on "Accomplishing Practice" (*siddhi-pratipatti*), it refers to the fourth part, "Entering Realization Based on Persons" (*pudgala-praveśa-siddha-guṇa*).
This serves as a general outline of the overall structure of the entire scripture, dividing it into four sections.

However, if one considers the practitioner according to their specific capacity and stage—whether they possess or lack faith, understanding, practice, and realization—it is inherently difficult to provide a detailed analysis for each individual according to their faculties. ▲ (End of Section)

Regarding the statement that the *Chao* (Commentary) encompasses both the sudden and the gradual: in terms of the text, the primary assembly is exclusively sudden, while the final assembly is gradual;
yet, as the faculties of the roots are perfected and realized, the sudden and gradual are interpenetrated and fused, such that they do not obstruct their distinct classification.

In the course of examining the text, one must not lose sight of the profound intent, so that through practice and realization within this very mind, the sudden and gradual become non-existent as separate entities. Thus, the *Fajiepin Su* (Commentary on the "Dharmadhātu Chapter") states: "Now, the Perfect..."
The ocean of the complete teaching encompasses all phenomena without exception; sudden and gradual approaches are interwoven, and the fundamental and the derivative mutually illuminate one another.
The integration of person and dharma lies in the value of wide propagation. Thus, without the sudden, the perfect cannot be revealed; without the gradual, there is no way to ascend;
without the fundamental, the derivative cannot be bestowed; without the derivative, the fundamental cannot be revealed; and without the person, the dharma cannot be realized. Without the dharma...
Because it concerns the perfected person, the former clarifies how the sudden is not different from the gradual; through many gates, the multitude simultaneously accords with it.
The latter clarifies how the gradual is not different from the sudden; through a single person traversing the stages, one practices in a perfect manner.

In the former case, the end is not different from the root; though it is rolled up, it is always extended. In the latter case, the root is not different from the end; though it is extended, it is always rolled up. This is the root.

The final unimpeded [assembly] likewise enters the Dharma-realm; furthermore, to summarize it briefly, it is said that the final assembly returns to the Bodhimaṇḍa, whereby the ten assemblies are complete and luminous.

As for the statement "the brief account concludes from here," it is because the original text was transmitted to the Eastern Land (China), and thus it is merely stated that the brief account concludes.
*Huayan Xuantan Huiquan Ji*, Scroll 37, Phonetic Explanations (the "yin" is pronounced with the *nan* entering tone).
Jīn (pronounced *jū yín*; a small sash for clothing; also *chā jù jīn*; a knot in clothing). Kuì (pronounced *qiú guǐ*; to measure). Jǐn (pronounced *qú zhèn*; remainder; barely).
(Inferior; few). *Zhé* (zhī shè qiè): to bend. *Chǔn* (cú yuǎn qiè):
to suck. *Huáyán Xuántán Huìxuán Jì*, Scroll 38, compiled by the Bhikṣu Pǔruì of Zàiguāng Temple on Mount Cāng.

The *Shoushu jing* (Sūtra on the Enumeration of Names), one fascicle, which is the "Chapter on Names and Titles," was translated in Luoyang during the Zhongping era of the Later Han by the Yuezhi śramaṇa Zhi Chen.

The *Pusa benye jing* (Sūtra on the Original Vows of Bodhisattvas), one fascicle, which is the "Chapter on Pure Conduct," is also known as the *Jingxing pin jing* (Sūtra on the Chapter of Pure Conduct);
it was translated by the Yuezhi upāsaka Zhi Qian during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty.
There is a one-fascicle *Shorter Daśabhūmika Sūtra* (小十住經) consisting of prose without verses; this is the "Ten Stages Chapter" (*Daśabhūmikavarga*).
However, upon a thorough examination of the catalogs of various collections as well as the *Huayan zhuanji* (Record of the Avataṃsaka), neither the terms "large" nor "small" appear.

It is only in the *Tanchuan xuanyi ji* (Profound Meaning Record of Exploring the Mysteries) that the distinction between "large" and "small" is made. Now, Qingliang [Zongmi] relies upon this; this is [the case].
Worthy One, because one wishes to distinguish the different stages of the *Daśabhūmika*, the terms "small" and "large" have been added;
they do not exist in the original titles of the translated scriptures. Why is this? For instance, regarding the various translations of the *Shorter Daśabhūmika Sūtra*:

first, there is the one fascicle titled *Bodhisattva-daśabhūmika-sūtra* translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa; furthermore, this same master translated another one fascicle titled *Mahāvaipulya*.

The *Bodhisattva-daśabhūmi-sūtra* (also known as the *Bodhisattva-daśabhūmi-sūtra*, i.e., the "Ten Dwellings" chapter), translated by the śramaṇa Jī Qiaye during the Yanxing era of the Northern Wei, in one fascicle;

titled *Mahāvaipulya-bodhisattva-daśabhūmi-sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra from North India during the reign of Emperor An of the Eastern Jin, in one fascicle; and titled *Bodhisattva-daśavihāra*.

[The above all rely on the *Dazhou kanding mulu* (Catalogue Compiled during the Dazhou Period). The *Huayan zhuanwen* (Account of the Avatamsaka) states that during the Eastern Jin dynasty, the Śramaṇa Jīmūta from the Western Regions translated one fascicle titled the *Bodhisattva-daśabhūmi-sūtra*.
None of the aforementioned translations mention it being a "small" [version]. The *Kaiyuan shijiao lu* (Kaiyuan Era Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings) collects only two translations:
the first is titled *Bodhisattva-daśabhūmi-caryā-prakaraṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle; the second is titled... [one fascicle].

The *Bodhisattva-daśabhūmika-sūtra* in one fascicle; its expanded version, the *Mahā-daśabhūmika-sūtra* in four fascicles, was translated by Kumārajīva of the Later Qin together with the Kapiśa Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas (whose name means "Awakened Clarity" in the language of Qin).

It is titled the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and does not include the word "Great. Regarding the *Anupūrvasamudgata-sarvajñatāguṇavyūha-sūtra* in four fascicles, all catalogs state that it consists of five fascicles. Now...

In the Tibetan canon, according to the *Kaiyuan lu*, this work is also in five fascicles; the *Zuānlíng jì* likewise states it is in five fascicles. This [present edition] follows the *Tànxuán*, and thus it is said to be in four fascicles.

It is the *Sūtra on the Samādhi Asked by the Bodhisattva Samantadarśin*, translated during the seventh year of the Yuankang era of the Western Jin dynasty by the śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa (translated as "Dharma Protector") from the country of Yuezhi. It was indeed translated by Dharmarakṣa.
*The Sūtra on Boundless Merit*, one fascicle; its full title is *The Sūtra Revealing the Merit of Boundless Buddha-lands*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty. *The Tathāgata-gotra-pravṛtti-guhyagarbha-sūtra*; some translations call it *The Mahāvaipulya Tathāgata-gotra-pravṛtti-sūtra*.
The title currently used also includes the characters "Mahāvaipulya" (*Dafangguang*), which are omitted here. It was translated during the Yuankang era of the Western Jin dynasty.
Both translations do not record the names of the translators. The *Dushi jing* (Sūtra on Crossing the World), six fascicles, was translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin.
The *Magajing* (Māgandiya Sūtra), three fascicles, was translated by the śramaṇa Jian of Xiqin (some say a śramaṇa of the Western Jin);

it is also said to have been translated by An Faxian of the Cao Wei, and again by Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang; [another version] is one fascicle, also translated by Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang.
The differences between this and the translation by Faxian regarding breadth and brevity all stem from the deficiency of the *Dharmadhātu-parivarta* [in the latter].

Nevertheless, the exegesis provided in this commentary follows the explanations in the *Tanxuan ji* (Profound Exploration) when correlating and interpreting the original sūtra. According to the *Dazhou lu*, there are thirty-six sūtras in total, all of which are branches;
however, the *Kaiyuan lu* collects only twenty-four of these branch texts. These branches are thus combined here.
Therefore, there are thirty-six and twenty-four [categories].
Regarding the term *zhī* (支) in "branches" (*zhīliú* 支流), the sub-commentary first explains the character *zhī* as "dividing flow" (*fēnliú* 分流).
Belonging to the category of branches means being a tributary; it is also called "dividing flow," and thus "branch-flow" (*liúzhi* 流支) is simply the name for the flow itself.

The term "flowing-class" (*liúlèi*) refers to the "flowing" (*liú*) and the "class" (*lèi*). Below, the character "class" (*lèi*) is explained: the character "flowing" (*liú*) belongs to the category of "class" (*lèi*), which carries the meaning of "resemblance.

Because it is both flowing and a class, it is called "flowing-class. Regarding the phrase "the small ten abodes": the "small" refers to the wisdom of comparative observation that dwells within profound principles;
the "great" refers to the realization of non-abiding. Therefore, it possesses meanings such as "basis," "arising," and so forth. Alternatively, [it may be interpreted differently].
It is also called "The Grounds" (*bhūmi*).

Regarding the phrase "within the images of the ancient grounds" (*purāṇabhūmi-pratibimba*) in the *Śāstra*, it refers to the ten sections of the "Ten Grounds Chapter": first, the introductory section; second, the section on the three samādhis;

third, the section on the increase [of merit]; fourth, the section on the emergence; fifth, the section on the fundamental [ground]; sixth, the section on the request; seventh, the section on the exposition; and eighth, the section on the ground itself. (Note: The remaining two sections are the section on the conclusion and the section on the summary.)
The section on images consists of nine stages, the section on benefits consists of ten, and the section on further elucidation is now the eighth stage, the section on images.
Within this, there are four metaphors; here, the commentary abbreviates the metaphor of the mountain, which may be understood as before.

Regarding the *Sūtra on the Cultivation of Loving-kindness* (*Cizong jing*) and others, all three editions contain the characters "Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka" (*Dafangguang Fo Huayan*), beneath which the character "Section" (*fen*) appears;
this is omitted here. All were translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Ti-yun Prajñā of Khotan. The *Tanxuan ji* states:

"Recently, at the Divine Capital (Luoyang), together with the Khotan Tripiṭaka Master, he translated one fascicle of the 'Section on the Cultivation of Loving-kindness' (*Huayan Xiuci fen*) from the *Avataṃsaka*. It is inconceivable.

The *Vastu-vibhāga* (Discourse on the Divisions of the Realm), one fascicle; and the *Vajramālā-vibhāga* (Discourse on the Vajra Garland), ten fascicles—these were left unfinished as the Tripiṭaka Master passed away.
(Currently, only the aforementioned two parts are preserved in the canon, as the *Vajramālā-vibhāga* was not fully translated; thus, it is not included in various catalogs or the *Zaoling ji*).

Now, while residing in the Divine Capital (Chang’an), he further obtained a copy of the fifty-thousand-verse *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* presented by the Kingdom of Khotan, and the Tripiṭaka Master has arrived in the Divine Capital to translate it.
(Regarding this [translation by] Śikṣānanda: The Sanskrit manuscript at Cien Monastery is identical to the old version without any difference;
however, the newly arrived Sanskrit manuscript differs slightly in its chapter divisions and phrasing. This is because there were several versions of this Great Sūtra.

These are all branches of the Great Sūtra, explained according to their respective chapters. (Based on this, since the ancient masters already referred to them as "branches of the Great Sūtra," one knows that the *Tanxuan ji* does not treat them as belonging to the same category.)

The commentary states that the remaining details are as recorded in the *Zuǎnlíngjì* (Records of the Manifestation of Spirits). The *Dàfāngguǎng huá yán rù rúlái bùsīyì jìngjiè jīng* (Avataṃsaka-sūtra:

Entering the Inconceivable Realm of the Tathāgata), one fascicle (sometimes lacking the characters "Dàfāngguǎng"; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of North India during the Sui dynasty; "Jñānagupta" means "Wisdom Virtue" in the Sui language);

the *Dù zhū fó jìngjiè zhìyán jīng* (Sūtra on the Wisdom Adornment of the Realms of All Buddhas), one fascicle (translated by the Śramaṇa Saṃghavarman of Pǔshā in Fúshā during the Liáng dynasty; "Saṃghavarman" means "Saṃgha Armor"); and the *Dù zhū fó jìngjiè zhìguāng* (Sūtra on the Wisdom Light of the Realms of All Buddhas).
*Śrī-sūtra*, one fascicle (translator lost); *Mahāvaipulya-tathāgatācintyaviṣayāvatāra-sūtra*, two fascicles (translated by Śikṣānanda during the Dazhou period).
The above four sūtras are different translations of the same text, all stating they were preached in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-dharmasabhā*).
*Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-buddhaviṣaya-vibhāga*, one fascicle (translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara from Khotan during the Zai-chu era of the Tang dynasty). *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka*.

*Gocara-sūtra*, one fascicle (translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the Great Zhou Dynasty). The above two sūtras are different translations of the same text, both spoken under a tree.
*Sudhana-avatamsaka-buddhakāya-adbhuta-lokadhātu-vastu-nirdeśa-sūtra*, one fascicle (spoken concerning the unspeakable world-systems within the Buddha’s body;

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of the Great Zhou Dynasty). *Buddhāvataṃsaka-mahāvaipulya-sūtra-karuṇāparivarta*, one fascicle (translated by Tiyun Bore during the Zai-chu era of the Tang Dynasty).
The above sections, such as the *Acintyavimokṣa*, although absent from the extant editions of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, are all fully present in the Sanskrit original.
It is certain that these were separate recensions of this sūtra; because the Sanskrit manuscript did not specify chapter titles, they were not included in the great compendium.
(The preceding is from the biographical records.)
The commentary states, "The ancient masters observed that which is absent from the current sutra," etc.; this expresses the intent of the ancients.

However, the ancient masters did not distinguish between the *zhiliu* (branch-streams) and the *zhilei* (branch-categories); as seen in the *Tanchuan Xuanyi* and the various biographies (*chuandeng lu*), these works treat them solely as the meaning of the branch-streams (*zhiliu*).

Therefore, this [commentary] may be based on the newly composed *Lüeshu* (Brief Commentary), which classifies them as branch-categories (*zhilei*), or it may rely on what was stated in the aforementioned biographies.
As for the fact that it is not titled as a "Brahma Chapter" (*brahmavarga*) and is not included in the main body of the collection, this too suggests it belongs to a similar category.
Regarding the statement at the end of this section, Master Qingliang’s intention was that the entirety of the sutra has not yet arrived here;

since the sections on the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-bhāvanā*) and so forth are incomplete, what else could these be but separate branches or individual recensions of this sutra that have not yet reached their full extent? Furthermore, why would they be so?

It can be definitively determined that this version possesses the complete original text of the *Liulèi* (類). How could it be reconciled with the judgment that it is a separate recension (*biéxíng*) possessing the complete original text?
Furthermore, how could it be established if [the original] were absent? Therefore, the commentary uses the word "perhaps" (*huò*).

Regarding the phrase "one who hears much but has doubts," the "Government" chapter of the *Lúnyǔ* says: "One who hears much but has doubts should be cautious regarding the rest of what they say. Thus...
Regarding "few errors," the aforementioned commentary states: "Though one may be extensively learned and well-informed, one should leave a matter deficient when in doubt;
thus, by being cautious regarding other matters that are not doubted, one incurs few errors.

Following the meaning of this first phrase, it implies that since this matter is not yet resolved, it should be left deficient and not spoken of. To say "not speaking" simply means there is no definitive judgment.

Commentary: Once Nāgārjuna obtained the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*—the full title of which, according to the transmission from the Western Regions, is the *Brahmaparipṛcchā*—he subsequently composed the *Mahā-acintya-śāstra* in one hundred thousand stanzas to explain this sūtra.
Since his profound faculties had not yet been awakened, [the disciples] could not fathom its ultimate purport. [This refers to the] *Daśabhūmika*.
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* in sixteen fascicles was composed by Nāgārjuna as an exposition on the meaning of the "Ten Stages" (*Daśabhūmika*) chapter.

During the Later Qin dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Yaśas orally recited its text, which was translated together with the Dharma Master Kumārajīva. Within the exposition of the "Ten Stages" chapter, the remainder of the text concerning the second stage was omitted because Yaśas did not recite it;
consequently, the commentary for that portion is missing. It is traditionally said that this treatise is a great work.

This is one part of the *Siyilun* (Treatise on Contemplation). Furthermore, there is the ten-fascicle *Shizhulun* (Treatise on the Ten Stages), also composed by Nāgārjuna; it was translated by Dharma Master Kumārajīva during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty.
In the *Huayan zhuan* (Biographies of the Avataṃsaka), under the section on Vasubandhu, it states: "Vasubandhu Bodhisattva is here called Tianqin (Heavenly Relative).
In the mountains, he expounded the 'Ten Stages' (*Daśabhūmika*) chapter; layering the text of the original sūtra, he sequentially analyzed and explained it.

When the Bodhisattva first completed his treatise—[the passage continues as follows, such as the earth shaking and light streaming]—during the Later Wei dynasty, there was the Tripiṭaka Master from North India, Bodhiruci, which in Wei means 'Lan'."
It is said that on the day this first translation was begun, Emperor Xuānwǔ personally transcribed it by pen.

On another day, it is further stated that the Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamati (translated as Bǎoyì in Wei) from Central India arrived here and, together with [Bodhiruci] Liúzhī, each translated a version—one to the north and one to the south of the Luò River.
Subsequently, the Monastic Head Huìguāng requested these two venerable masters to collate and verify their respective versions against one another.
The similarities and differences together form a single text. Furthermore, another tradition states that Vasubandhu composed a commentary on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*;
since the complete manuscript has not yet been obtained, this *Daśabhūmika* was perhaps translated as it was acquired.

It is also said that the Bodhisattva Asaṅga went to Tuṣita, where Maitreya Bodhisattva instructed him in the *Avataṃsaka* and other sūtras, and that it was through his power that these were subsequently propagated. I therefore ask: [what is the relationship between these accounts?]
The Tripitaka masters from the West, all Brahman monks, state that the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* composed by Vajrasena Bodhisattva consists of twelve thousand stanzas;
if translated, it would amount to over thirty fascicles. Furthermore, Sthiramati Bodhisattva also composed a brief commentary (*piṇḍārtha*), neither of which has been transmitted to this land.
However, a manuscript currently exists in the kingdom of Khotan. Śikṣānanda remarked that he would attach [a copy] to his correspondence.

Suo Ru-de also intended to translate [this work], and furthermore, within the "Chapter on Abiding" of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the text of the "Ten Stages" chapter of this sutra is extensively transcribed in its proper sequence and annotated.
This is because the classification of the stages of the three sages and ten saints in this sutra is the most extensive;

as it serves as a model for all other sections, there have been no fewer than several commentators who produced exegeses upon it (Tiantai took the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* to be an exposition [of this sutra]).
The *Huayan jing* [commentary] is likewise based on this.

The *Zuǎnlíngjì* (Records of the Spiritually Inspired) states that Liu Qianben was originally a eunuch, yet through seven days of sincere devotion, he received a spiritual response and composed six hundred fascicles of treatises.
The *Huayan zhuan* (Biographies of Huayan) cites this incident and judges it as belonging to Jingying Monastery.
In his later years, Dharma Master Huiyuan composed this commentary on the sutra up to the Chapter on Dedication (*pariṇāmanā-parivarta*).

Suddenly, he felt a pain in his heart; upon looking at it, he saw blood flowing from the pores of his chest. Furthermore, he dreamed that he was carrying a sickle and climbing a mountain, cutting the vegetation in succession until reaching the midpoint.
There, his strength failed and he could no longer rise. Upon waking, he said to his disciples, "I have had a dream."
He thought, "This commentary will certainly not be completed," and so he desisted. Furthermore, Master Xiu of Paizhou listened to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* more than fifty times;
yet as he investigated and recited its principles and phrasing, his understanding became increasingly obscure. He then admonished himself, saying:

"How can these words of the Supreme Sage be grasped through the mere conjectures of an inferior ordinary person? The erudition and vast wealth of these two worthies are such that they are rarely seen even in antiquity."

"Among those who have investigated this profound and outstanding [work], none have been able to exhaustively illuminate it; yet Xunyan examined it before even a few decades had passed, and now he has annotated this great treatise—how strange this is!
Indeed, that the Great Sage’s hidden transmission is thus should not be considered strange at all. [The *Jingde chuandeng lu*] Commentary does not mention Qingliang;
for the most part, this is because [the author] wished to glorify his own region by following the perspective of those from the Taiyuan area alone.

Residing there, he took Mount Xuēnwèng in Taiyuán as his base to clarify [the text]; furthermore, the places clearly documented in the *Chuan* (Biographies/Record) that he visited include several locations:

Qingliáng Temple, Mount Xuēnwèng, Gāoyán Temple, as well as the Dōngbǎi Hall and Huīyīn Hall in Luóyáng, and the Shìguǐ Hall on the upper story—over the course of five years from beginning to end, he finally completed the one hundred fascicles.

Commentary, Part Eight: On the Accounts of Miraculous Responses and Spiritual Resonance in Translation. First, there are those sentient beings who, lacking discernment, preemptively abandon the words of the Sages;
they follow their own deluded minds and further associate with evil friends, practicing in violation of the teachings through skillful hypocrisy and deception—these are called "evil persons.
Second, there are those who likewise turn their backs on the holy teachings, yet claim—with a straightforward mind—that [the teachings] are...
1. Those who undergo arduous ascetic practices in pursuit of liberation but ultimately gain no benefit; 2. These first two types both abandon the holy teaching and do not rely on its principles; 3.

Those who merely recite the sacred words without understanding their meaning, relying on the holy teaching only to seek fame and profit, thereby contradicting what they themselves recite and acting as evil persons;
4. Those who merely pursue the literal phrasing without knowing the underlying principles, yet possess only a sincere heart.

Although there is no artifice in their recitation, it provides no benefit; these two aforementioned types of persons both fail to relinquish the teachings and fail to grasp their underlying principles.

The first four [types] are all unreliable. Fifth, regarding the study and recitation of the holy teachings, one distinguishes between understanding and practice: those who read many words and phrases have little actual cultivation.
Sixth, one extensively seeks out the holy teachings to gain a pervasive knowledge of understanding and practice, then gradually simplifies the sacred words to grasp their essential meaning.
Seventh, by single-mindedly practicing and upholding [the teachings], one attains the meaning solely through cultivation and no longer seeks it in words;

eighth, by seeking the teaching, one attains the essential principle, knowing that all phenomena are without exception in accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), and thus does not even wait to abandon the teaching—this very verbal teaching accords with the nature, and one practices according to the teaching;
ninth, constantly upholding the words that accord with the nature, neither abandoning nor clinging to them, one perpetually contemplates the state beyond [conceptualization].
The principle of discourse is neither abandoned nor obstructed; yet these preceding five gates have not yet reached the ultimate.

Only when one attains the true teaching through tenfold investigation, such that the principle of the teaching is unimpeded, constantly contemplating the principle without hindrance while upholding the teaching, and constantly upholding the teaching without hindering the contemplation of emptiness—when teaching and principle are thus fused into a single contemplation—is it called the ultimate.
Furthermore, this is because one has attained the essential meaning and forgotten the expedient expressions.

One must not forget that the means of interpretation depend upon the teachings; therefore, one must not abandon them, but rather rely on the Dharma to practice and study. The responses and manifestations are truly manifold.
Regarding the statement in the *Chao* (Commentary) that Kāśyapa was a native of the country of Vimalavai, this refers to Central India.
Why, then, does the *Shu* (Sub-commentary) refer to Northern India? The answer is that according to the *Zuanlingji*, his ancestors were originally from the country of Kapilavastu.
His father was Dharmadeva (translated here as *Fǎtiān*), who resided in North India while traveling as a merchant. His father’s name was Dharmasūrya (translated here as *Fǎrì*).
Although the *Éngxián* states that he became an orphan at the age of three, the *Běncù shūsòng* says he currently resides there;
thus, there is no contradiction. As for the statement that he is a descendant of King Amṛtodana, this refers to the Buddha’s paternal uncle.
He was a descendant of his father; being fatherless from childhood, he was called a "gū" (an orphan). His maternal kin were those of his mother’s family.

His paternal uncles (*bóshǔ*) were those from whom he traced his ancestry. He was intelligent and quick-witted; there was no matter that required telling twice, and nothing, however obscure, that he did not penetrate.
A *śrāmaṇera*—here translated as "seeking tranquility"—refers to one who studies alongside others. The *Zuǎnlíng jì* states that at the age of seventeen, he was with several fellow students.
All took recitation and study as their vocation and labored for a month; however, Huanxian could match them in a single day.
His teacher sighed, saying, "Huanxian’s one day rivals thirty men. When it came to receiving full ordination, he quickly understood the profound subtleties;
his analysis was thorough, and his mastery of both the text and its meaning was so elegant and interwoven that he attained complete penetration. Thus, from his youth, he devoted himself to study.
The fame of his clarity in the Vinaya had already spread abroad.
It is recorded that he once stayed with his fellow student Saṃghadatta for many years while traveling together in the kingdom of Kaśmīra.

Although Saṃghadatta acknowledged his brilliance and quick-wittedness, he did not perceive the depth of his realization. Once, Saṃghadatta was sitting in meditation within a private room with its doors closed.

Suddenly seeing Bhadrika approaching, he asked in surprise where he was coming from. Bhadrika replied, "I have come for a moment to pay my respects to Maitreya in Tuṣita, and thus I have come to take my leave.
As soon as he had finished speaking, he vanished. Thereafter, Upatiṣya repeatedly witnessed his miraculous transformations and developed deep sincerity and reverence.

He questioned him about what he had realized and learned that he had already attained the fruit of equality. The *Tanyuan ji* (Record of Investigating the Profundities) states: "The three fruits of the Mahāyāna."

The Bodhisattva Dhyāna Master (the *Vyūha-śāstra* states: "The first stage is the Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), the eighth stage is the Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the tenth stage is the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), and the Buddha-stage is the Arhat; these are the four fruits of the Bodhisattva, which are rare.
Most Mahāyāna masters who claim to have attained the fruits have attained these very fruits. This refers to a meeting. Kasmīra is a Sanskrit term;

it is sometimes called the Land of Evil Names, sometimes the Land of Woolen Cloth, and sometimes Aśmaka (lit., "Who Enters"). Formerly, this country was a great dragon lake, and no one dared to approach it. Later, an Arhat requested from the dragon a space large enough to contain his knees.

At that time, the dragon granted permission, and the Arhat transformed his body, gradually increasing its size until his knees filled the dragon pool. Because the dragon’s word was trusted, he departed. Later, when the water dried up, he ordered the common people to establish a state there.

Everyone said, "This was not the power of a sage; who else could have entered here? For this reason, it was so named. As for the term *Jiaozhi*, the *Shanhai jing* (Classic of Mountains and Seas) states that the people of Jiaojing have legs that are crooked and twisted, crossing over one another;
thus it is called "Crossed Ankles" (*Jiaozhi*). Regarding the phrase "attaching to ships" (*fubó*), this refers to traveling by sea on large ocean-going vessels.
The biography relates that when the ship passed beneath a certain island, Xian pointed to the mountain with his finger and said, "We may stop here.

The captain replied, "A traveler must cherish the day; since a favorable wind is difficult to encounter, we cannot halt. After traveling more than two hundred li, the wind suddenly shifted and blew the vessel back toward the base of the island.
Only then did the people realize his divine power, and they all took him as their teacher, listening to his instructions.
While they were proceeding, they later encountered a favorable wind and his companions all set sail; Xian said, "We must not move," and the captain accordingly stopped.

Shortly thereafter, those who had set sail first were all simultaneously wrecked. Later, in the middle of a dark night, he suddenly ordered all the ships to set sail together, but none were willing to comply.
Xian rose of his own accord to gather the mooring ropes, and one ship alone set forth; in an instant—
When the bandits arrived, those who remained were all plundered and harmed. Shortly thereafter, while traveling through perilous regions, he reached Donglai Commandery in Qingzhou.
Hearing that Master Shi was in Chang’an, he went there to follow him; this was the fourth month of the tenth year of Hongshi in the Qin dynasty.

Master Shi was greatly delighted, and they discussed the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), which brought forth profound subtleties and provided much insight and benefit. Consequently, [the visitor] said to Shi:
"How is it that what you explain does not exceed the capacity of ordinary people's minds, yet you have attained such high renown? Kumārajīva replied, "It is simply because I am old;
why must one necessarily be able to produce elegant discourse? Whenever Kumārajīva encountered points of doubtful meaning, he invariably consulted with and resolved them together with Buddhabhadra.

When Prince Hong, the heir apparent of Qin, wished to hear the Venerable’s exposition of the Dharma, he summoned the assembly of monks to the Eastern Palace for a formal debate; there, Kumārajīva and Buddhabhadra were present.

After several rounds of exchange—(as the *Huayan zhuan* says, "the text is voluminous and not recorded here; I shall now cite it in full")—Kumārajīva asked: "In what sense is 'dharmas' empty? He replied:
"A multitude of atoms (*paramāṇu*) compose form (*rūpa*); because form has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), although it appears as form, it is eternally empty. He asked again:

"Since you have already refuted form as being empty by means of the ultimate atom, how do you further refute the atom itself? He replied: "Various masters may refute an atom by breaking it down into parts, but my intention is..."
"It is not so," he said. He was then asked, "Is the subtle atom (paramāṇu) permanent? He replied, "Because of the single atom, the collection of atoms is empty;

because of the collection of atoms, the single atom is empty. When Bao Yun translated these words, he did not understand their meaning, and both monastics and laypeople alike claimed that Xian’s reckoning was that the subtle dust (paramāṇu) is permanent.
On another day, monks from Chang’an requested him to provide a further explanation.
Xian said: "Now, phenomena do not arise of themselves; they arise through the convergence of conditions. From a single atom there comes a multitude of atoms.
Since a single atom lacks self-nature, it is empty. How can one say that because a single atom is not destroyed, it is not empty? This is the general purport of the dialogue.
The ruler of Qin, Yao Xing, devoted himself exclusively to seeking the Buddha, providing offerings for more than three thousand [monks].
The monks all frequented the imperial palaces and busied themselves extensively with worldly affairs; only Xuan maintained his stillness and did not conform to the crowd.
Later, he said to his disciples, "Yesterday I saw five ships set sail together from my native village.

When the disciples reported this to outsiders, the monks in Guanzhong all considered it a display of supernatural powers intended to delude the masses. Furthermore, while in Chang’an, Xuan widely propagated [the Dharma].
Those who delighted in tranquility from the four quarters heard of his reputation and came to him one after another.

However, as their engagement in the study of meditation varied in depth and their realization differed in intensity, there arose among them a band of corrupt and deceitful individuals who employed craftiness and guile. One such person, having observed a few practices during his youth, claimed to have attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
Before the Venerable could verify this through inquiry, rumors spread and he was subjected to widespread slander and defamation.
Fearing that an unforeseen calamity was imminent, the disciples all concealed their names and departed in secret;
some scaled walls and fled by night, so that within half a day the assembly had almost entirely dispersed. Xuán remained composed and took no heed of it.
At that time, the former monks Sēngqì and Dàohéng said to Xuán, "Even the Buddha did not permit [the disclosure of] what one has attained for oneself; first, he spoke of the five [precepts]."
The ship was about to depart; it was empty and without substance. Furthermore, among the disciples, who were they to be deluded? They rose up with conflicting views regarding right and wrong.
Since this would violate the Vinaya and contradict reason, it was appropriate to leave immediately rather than lingering.
Xian said, "My person is like a drifting duckweed; going or staying is very easy. It is only because my aspirations have not yet been fulfilled that I feel such regret. Thereupon, he...
The disciple Huiguan and over forty others simultaneously resolved their spirits to depart with composure, showing no sign of distress.
Those who recognized the truth all sighed in lamentation together; more than a thousand people, both monastics and laypeople, escorted them.
When Yao Xing heard of their departure, he was filled with regret and said to Daoheng, "The śramaṇa Buddhabhadra came here traveling along the Way wishing to proclaim the Bequeathed Teachings."
My words remain unspoken, and I feel profound regret; how can the fault of a single person cause ten thousand men to lose the Way?
He then issued an edict to pursue him. Xian replied to the messenger, saying: "I truly know the imperial grace, yet I have not received the command.

(From Hu Youzhen’s *Biographies*, it is recorded that the assembly of monks in the capital performed a *karmavācanā* ritual to expel the Tripiṭaka Master. Thereupon, he gathered his robes and bowl, ascended into the void, manifested various supernatural transformations, and soared through the air to the south, flying like a bird through the sky.)

The entire assembly was struck with remorse, realizing it was too late to rectify their error. They further recounted the previous debate, noting that when Yao Xing and the Tripiṭaka Master held a discussion at the Eastern Palace, there were over three thousand scholars in attendance.

Among them were Buddhists such as Shi Dao-sheng, Zhu Fashang, Seng-rong, and Huiguan, and Confucians such as Xie Lingyun and Fei Changfang; none dared to raise a question. Then, Master Kumārajīva raised his voice and asked: [as recorded in the text]. Regarding the claim that Fei Changfang and Xie Lingyun were contemporaries, this is incorrect.

Fei Changfang was originally from the Sui dynasty, separated by several generations—including the Song, Qi, Liang, and Chen dynasties—from the time in question; thus, they were not contemporaries. Furthermore, Xie Lingyun was a person of the Jin dynasty and did not live in the Qin state. Therefore, the account transmitted by Xian-shou is to be regarded as correct. (End of passage)

He led his companions on a journey through the night to the Southern Lu Mountain to visit the śramaṇa Huiyuan. Having long admired Yuan’s reputation, he was filled with joy upon hearing of his arrival, as if reuniting with an old friend.

Huiyuan remarked that Xian’s expulsion was due to the transgressions of his disciples, adding that the prophecy concerning the five ships mentioned in the *Upadeśa* (or *Sūtra*) agreed with this view;
furthermore, according to the Vinaya, there was no offense committed. Thereupon, Yuan’s disciple Tanyong sent a letter to the Yao ruler.

When the monastic community in Guanzhong resolved the matter of his formal suspension (*pravāsanīya-karman*), Huiyuan then requested that he emerge [from seclusion] to propagate the various sutras of the Chan and doctrinal traditions.
Xianzhi’s intent lay in traveling for the sake of conversion; finding no place where he could settle in peace, he stayed for about a year before departing again for westward toward Jiangling.

There, he encountered foreign ships arriving. Upon inquiry, it was confirmed that these were indeed the five ships from India that he had previously seen; the local people of the region were all moved with awe.
For the most part, he declined all offerings made during his visits for ritual services; he maintained his alms bowl and wandered for food, showing no distinction between the noble and the lowly.
Yuan Bao of Chenjun served as the Chief Secretary to the Grand Marshal of the Song Emperor Wu.

When Emperor Wu was campaigning southward against Liu Yi, the imperial headquarters arrived at Jiangling. The monk Huiquan, a disciple of Faxian, went to Yuan Bao to beg for food. Yuan Bao was naturally... [text ends]
He did not treat him with respect or faith, and when the meal was far from finished, he took his leave. Zhibao said, "It seems you have not yet had enough;
please stay a little longer. Xian replied, "The donor's intention in giving is limited, which is why what has been prepared is already exhausted.
Zhibao immediately called his attendants to bring more rice, but the food was indeed gone. Zhibao felt great shame and asked Huiguan, "What kind of person is this śramaṇa?"

Ren Quan remarked, "His virtue and capacity are so lofty and remote that they cannot be measured by ordinary men. Bao deeply sighed in admiration of this excellence and informed the Grand Marshal (Taishou), requesting an audience with him.
The Grand Marshal treated him with the utmost reverence and provided him with the most abundant provisions.

Shortly thereafter, when the Grand Marshal returned to the capital, he invited Bao to return with him and settled him at Daochang Temple. Previously, the śramaṇa Zhi Falin had [been active] in Khotan... (as noted in the previous excerpt).

Regarding the country of Yuezhi-juban (遮拘盤), it was a minor state of Khotan. [The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*] had already been obtained in its earlier portion consisting of thirty-six thousand verses, but it had not yet been translated.
In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era (398 CE) [details as in the *Shuchao*].

Now, since the *Shuchao* states that "Xiesikong Temple" is the Daochang Temple, named after its patron (*dānapati*), we can verify that the temple’s formal name is indeed Daochang Temple, according to the terminology used by the people of that time.
Regarding the fact that donors are all addressed as "Xie Sijing" (謝司空), this is stated in the *Sushun su* (疏順俗) because it is easy for people to understand according to worldly custom.

Furthermore, the *Tanxuan ji* (探玄記) states: "The Jin dynasty śramaṇa Zhi Falin obtained thirty-six thousand verses of sutras from the kingdom of Khotan, and he also invited a Mahayana monk from North India who was a third-stage Bodhisattva named Fo (佛)."
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan) by Tuo Bala and others also records this account.
According to the current *Chao* (Excerpts), the *Sengzhuan*, the *Huayan zhuan* by Xianshou, and other sources, Zhiyan requested Buddhayaśas;

however, it was previously Zhi Falin who had requested the scriptures and returned to the country. Thus, Falin first requested the scriptures from Khotan, and subsequently Zhiyan requested Buddhayaśas.

It was only after Buddhayaśas had crossed the frontier in Kaśmīra that [the translation] was finally rendered. One should take the present *Chao* (Excerpts) and the *Sengzhuan* (Biographies of Monks) as authoritative.

Although the *Tanyuan* (Exploring the Profundities) states that he also invited Buddhayaśas, this was likely because the author did not wish to provide a prolix account and mentioned it only incidentally.

Hu Youzhen’s version follows this, yet by explaining it as being "caused by" [the invitation], it results in a loss of the proper sequence; for the various monastic histories and Buddhist teachings...

The records are all identical to the present *Chao* (Excerpts), and thus may be known from this; as for the statement that "the rest is extensive as in the *Zhuan* (Biographies)," it is fully indicated above.
Regarding Zhiyan, the *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu* states: "Zhiyan was a native of Xiliangzhou. He entered the Western Regions and received the methods of dhyāna from Buddhayaśas.
He invited Buddhabhadra to return and reside in Chang’an, but was unjustly [interfered with] by monks of the Qin."

Huiyan parted from his fellow disciples from the West and exited the Pass; however, before Huiyan had entered the monastic order, he had once received the five precepts and had committed some violations.
Later, upon entering the Way and receiving full ordination, he constantly doubted whether he had attained the precepts and lived in perpetual fear.
Although he practiced meditative contemplation for many years, he could not resolve this on his own, and so he eventually traveled by sea back to India to seek further instruction.
The various enlightened ones encountered an Arhat bhikṣu and questioned him thoroughly regarding the matter; however, the Arhat did not dare to deliver a definitive judgment.
He then entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and went to Tuṣita Heaven to inquire of Maitreya, who replied: "One who has attained the precepts and possesses great joy shall walk back.
Upon returning to Jibin, he passed away without illness at the age of seventy-eight. In that country, both ordinary people and sages cremated their bodies in separate locations.
When they moved the corpse toward an ordinary cemetery, it was too heavy to lift; when they changed course toward the sacred tomb, it became light and floated away of its own accord.
Yan’s disciples Zhimeng and Zhiyuan had previously come from the Western Regions to report this omen, and both subsequently returned to their foreign lands.
Inferring from this, Yan was surely one who had attained the Way.

The details regarding Master Gong’s career are not fully known; however, because he first composed the *Zhigui* (Essential Return) and conceived the plan for the expansion of the Tripitaka, he is described here as well.

His style was elegant and orderly, meaning his literary grace and formal structure were both brilliant and well-proportioned. Regarding the statement that "in learning there is no constant teacher," the *Analects* says:
"In what did the Master not learn? And how could he have had a constant teacher? The term "officer" (*si*) refers to one who presides over or is in charge of something.
The South signifies the meaning of clarity and correctness; "yù" (鬱) means flourishing, "huáng" (遑) means to reach, and "yānzhì" (淹滯) means stagnation.
Because these works were in their initial stages, they did not immediately attain ultimate perfection; or, because many years have passed, their original essence is rarely seen.
The second part of the *Jiaochao* (Commentary) concerning the "Eight Talents": The Eight Talents were Daosheng, Sengzhao, Daorong, Huirui, Jingying, Huiyan, Huiguan, and Daoping.
Regarding their accounts being complete in the *Sengshi* (History of the Sangha), the *Sengshi* states: Huiyan’s secular surname was Fan; he was a native of Yuzhou.
At the age of twelve, he became a disciple of [Master] Sheng and was widely learned in the Odes and the Books. At sixteen, he left the household life. Furthermore—

He refined his mastery of Buddhist principles until his early twenties, by which time his learning had thoroughly penetrated the various scriptures and his reputation had spread far and wide, such that his influence reached distant lands.

Hearing that Master Kumārajīva was in Guanzhong, he went there again to study under him; investigating the correct pronunciation and meaning of the texts, he acquired much that was previously unknown.
Later, he returned to the capital and resided at Dong’an Temple. Emperor Gaozu of the Song dynasty had long known and esteemed him; when the Emperor campaigned against Chang’an, [he followed him].
He subsequently invited [Huiyuan] to travel together; later, he composed the *Treatise on Non-arising and Non-extinction* (*Wushengmie lun*) and a brief commentary on the *Laozi*.
He Chengtian of Donghai, who was renowned for his vast learning, once asked Yan Foguo which calendar he would employ. Yan replied:
"In India, on the day of the summer solstice, at the zenith, there is no shadow. Therefore, among the Five Elements, the color associated with the Central Region is yellow."
The number five was esteemed for the Yellow [Lords], and eight inches constituted one foot; ten *liang* corresponded to these twelve *liang*.

The month of Jichen (the seventh month) was established as the beginning of the year. In investigating the solstices and equinoxes, calculating eclipses, and observing the movements of light and shadow, their methods were extremely detailed.
The stellar positions and chronological records all possessed systematic regulations. Zuo Chengtian had no grounds for raising objections, and subsequently, the *Pobo*... [text ends].
A man from Ligu came and confirmed Guṇabhadra’s account; subsequently, he collaborated with Xie Lingyun and others to edit the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (the "Southern Text," as previously mentioned).
At the age of eighty-one, he passed away at Dong'an Temple in the twentieth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
The Emperor issued an edict stating: "Master Yan was of profound and far-reaching character and insight, a master craftsman of the Way. He has suddenly departed."
The Emperor ascended [the throne] and mourned him deeply in his heart, granting him fifty thousand coins and fifty rolls of silk. Thus was Huiquan esteemed by Emperor Wen. As for Huiquan:
his surname was Cui, and he was a native of Qinghe. At the age of ten, he already gained renown for his vast learning.
He left home at a young age to travel and study under various masters. Later, he went to Mount Lu, where he sought instruction from Huiyuan. It is heard that...
When Master Kumārajīva entered Guanzhong, he traveled from the south to the north to investigate and verify differences and similarities, and to provide detailed exegesis on the new and the old.
His spirit was elegant and his thoughts profound, penetrating the subtle and the profound; his contemporaries praised him, saying: "In comprehending the essence of the Dharma, Sengrong is foremost;
in refining difficult points through debate, Daosheng and Sengzhao are first. He composed the *Preface to the Essentials of the Lotus School* to summarize for Kumārajīva, who remarked: "Excellent!"
"The treatise composed by this man is truly excellent. You should withdraw for a while and travel between the Yangtze and Han rivers, making it your primary task to propagate [the Dharma] widely.
After Kumārajīva passed away, he traveled south to Jingzhou. Sima Xiuzhi, the regional governor there, held him in great esteem and respect.
He established Gaoli Temple for him, so that the people of Jing and Chu might turn from heterodoxy back to the Right Path.
When Shi Youban of the Song dynasty arrived at Jiangling, he met Sengguan. He received him with a sincere heart, treating him as if they were old friends from the past.
By imperial decree, he was then assigned to serve as an attendant to the Western General of the Middle Command—this was Emperor Wen. Shortly thereafter, Daorong also arrived at Daochang Temple.
Sengguan excelled in the profound principles of Buddhism, deeply investigated the teachings of Laozi and Zhuangzi, and was also extensively proficient in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
Because he gathered [teachings] from various schools, his days were never spent in vain as he sought the Dharma and inquired about the Way.

At the age of seventy-one, he composed the *Bianzong lun* (Discourse on Distinguishing the Tenets), which discusses the meaning of sudden and gradual cultivation along with ten parables, as well as prefaces and hymns for various sutras;

all of these have been transmitted to the world. As for the term "Tanchao" (Donor-Commentary), it is used to address him by his patrons; the *Bianzheng lun* states that "tan" (donation) is a Western [Central Asian] term...

As for the "sword of the seven stars," it refers to the sword of the Seven Stars. The *Xijing zaji* states: "The sword with which the High Ancestor [Liu Bang] slew the white serpent was adorned with nine-jade flowers and seven-starred pearls.

The light within still shines outward. Furthermore, Cui Bao’s *Gujin Zhu* states that "meteorite" is a name for a sword.

The *Dian Lun* by Emperor Wen of Wei says: "I selected this fine gold and commissioned the master craftsmen of the state to refine it with precision up to a hundred times, tempering it in the waters of the Qingzhang River until its luster resembled a falling star;
it was named 'Flying Scene' (*Feijing*). Now, only its [blade] is taken."
Regarding the statement that "the meaning of benefit is explained extensively as the source of illness," Vasubandhu’s separate biography states:
Because Vasubandhu adhered to the Hīnayāna, he did not believe in the Mahāyāna, asserting that the Mahāyāna was not the word of the Buddha.

Fearing that Vasubandhu might compose a treatise to refute the Mahāyāna, Asaṅga resided in the country of Puruṣapura and dispatched a messenger to the country of Ayodhyā (where Vasubandhu was at that time composing [his works]).

In the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* and other works, [Vasubandhu] informed his brother Asaṅga, saying: "I am now critically ill; you should come quickly. He immediately returned to his native land to inquire about the source of his brother's illness.
His brother said: "I now have a grave illness of the mind, and this illness arose because of you.
You did not believe in the Mahāyāna and constantly harbored slander; by this evil karma, you will surely sink forever into the evil realms. I am now suffering in grief, and my life—"
When Vasubandhu heard that [his brother] would not remain in the world, he was struck with alarm and fear, and immediately requested his elder brother to explain [the Dharma].

His brother then briefly expounded the essential meaning of the Mahāyāna. Vasubandhu, being of keen intelligence, immediately attained realization and understood that the principles of the Mahāyāna should surpass those of the Hīnayāna.
He then went to his brother to study the Mahāyāna doctrines in their entirety; having mastered everything according to his brother’s explanations, he finally realized that the Hīnayāna was...
"If one does not believe in the Mahāyāna, there will be no fruit of the three vehicles" (and so forth, including the account of the cutting out of the tongue).
His elder brother said, "If you wish to extinguish this sin, you must skillfully explain the Mahāyāna. After Vasubandhu died, Asaṅga subsequently composed various Mahāyāna treatises.
When the masters of other schools and non-Buddhist teachers heard the Dharma Master’s name, none failed to be struck with awe and submission. At [A]...
In the country of Yuezha, he passed away at the age of eighty; though he dwelt among ordinary people, the principle [of his attainment] is truly inconceivable.

(The above is from the *Biographies*). Regarding the statement that the earth shook when he spoke, the *Zuānlíngjì* continues: The king asked, "If one wishes to attain the holy fruit, can it be obtained?

He replied, "With the mind of a Bodhisattva, one vows to deliver all beings. I loathe the small fruits and do not take them. If you wish to obtain [the great fruit], [you must cultivate this resolve]."
It is like taking a clod of earth and throwing it into the void; before it has even fallen, one finds its owner.
When Vasubandhu, lacking faith, took up some soil intending to throw it into the air, various devas manifested their bodies in the sky, prostrated to the Bodhisattva, and sang in unison:
"The Bodhisattva has resolved his mind for the sake of saving all beings; how could he take [this soil] for the sake of a single person?"
"Little Fruit, we only pray that the Noble One will have compassion for us so that we do not regress from our great resolve.

Upon hearing this, the ruler prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, paid his respects, and withdrew. The *Chao* (Excerpts) states regarding eunuchs: "The term 'eunuch' (*huan*) means to 'cover' (*yan*).
To cover is to shut the gates. They are also called 'Yellow Gate' (*huangmen*). 'Yellow' refers to the center; the center signifies the Sage who dwells in Heaven."

Those of lower and middle rank who have access to the principles of governance are called *huángmén* (eunuchs); they are also called *huánghuán*, meaning they close their doors at dusk. Thus it is said they are "gatekeepers.
As for those who lament their own status as "remnants of punishment," there is a source stating that "physical impairment" (*xíngcán*) refers to being maimed or deficient.

Regarding the phrase "in the year of Daliang," the *Yiqiejing yinyi* (Phonetics and Meanings of All Scriptures) states that "Daliang" refers to the constellation Miao (pronounced *mao*), which according to the *Erya* is the name of a western asterism.
According to the calculation, when the planet Jupiter (Sui-xing) arrives at Miao, it is the year of Yiyou.

As for the statement that "the rest is as detailed in the biography," the biography says that in the second year, he moved his residence to Xuanwengshan Songyan Temple; at that time, Emperor Xiaoming...

Empress Dowager Hu, who held the Way in high esteem and revered the person [of the Master], personally requested that he attend at the palace gate; however, the Dharma Master declined on the grounds of illness and did not go.
At the beginning of summer, she again sent an edict with insistent requests; since he could not avoid her entreaties, he was invited into the Dongbai Hall.

He was subsequently transferred to the Shigui Hall and later resided in the Huiyin Hall, where he continued his compilation and discussion without ceasing. In the summer of the first year of the Shenguī era, an imperial decree was issued.
It was said: "The Great Dharma is vast and expansive; its exposition depends on those who cultivate it. The Dharma Master possesses spiritual eloquence and a profound, elegant character.
Having early established a great reputation, he may be invited to attend the Xuanhuang Palace to lecture on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

Thereupon, the fourfold assembly rejoiced and the ten directions awaited blessings. When the lecture concluded, an imperial edict was issued to the Attendant-in-Ordinary and Grand Tutor, Prince Yuanze of Qinghe."
He established the Master’s ritual hall upon the upper story of the temple, following the previous protocols for the summer retreat.

During the summer, he lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and during the winter, he lectured on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The Dharma Master and his disciple, Lingyuan, waited for the proper times to compile their work, forgetting both sleep and food.
In the ninth month of the autumn of the third year of the Shenguī era, their task was finally completed; comprising both concise sutras and extensive treatises, there were one hundred works in total.
The work was completed in ten fascicles over five years (thus the previous mention of "several locations" is correct). Later, due to the disturbances of the times, the sound of the Dharma ceased.
The Master suspended his lectures to cultivate the True and preserve the Way;
on the eighth day of the first month of the Zhengguang era, he passed away at Rongjue Temple at the age of thirty-six. Thereupon, Emperor Xiaoming issued an imperial decree:
It is said that this treatise was composed by a bodhisattva of this land and entrusted to the entire canon of scriptures, as recorded in the aforementioned catalog for widespread circulation.
The disciples Daoquan, Lingyuan, Tanying, and others, lamenting the premature passing of their former master and grieving that the profound scriptures were about to be obscured,
together with lay followers of pure faith, respectfully transcribed a clean copy and disseminated it throughout the world.
Although this treatise was widely circulated among the common people of Fen and Jin, its eminent masters in the capital of Luoyang and Chang’an always looked toward it with longing.

In the second year of the Yongchun era, the śramaṇa Daoxian of Zhixiang Monastery, along with the lay devotees Wang Xuanshuang, Fang Xuanling, and others, all devoted themselves to the study of this sūtra and applied their minds to its profound contemplation;
they subsequently formed a bond of shared purpose and traveled together to Qing...
While on his way to Bingzhou to pray to Mañjuśrī at Mount Liangshan, he saw the manuscript of this treatise at Tongzi Temple;
through his earnest entreaties, he was finally granted its transmission and subsequently disseminated it in the capitals of Chang’an and Luoyang.

Regarding the phrase "the Later Wei, Anfeng Commandery, etc. in the *Chao* (Commentary), the *Zuānlíngjì* (Record of the Compilation of Spiritual Manifestations) states that it refers to Yuán Yánmíng.

According to the supplementary notes by the monk Deyuan, as transmitted in other accounts, it is said that when the *zhǔ* tree reaches three years of growth, its fragrance becomes intensely pervasive. Gradually perfuming the incense and stripping the bark from the paper mulberry trees, they were soaked in aloeswood water; once the purification was complete and the paper finished, it was not until the end of the year that the work was done.

Within the hall, a square seat made of cypress wood was specially provided, surrounded by scattered incense and flowers, with precious ornaments suspended above.

On his birthday, he observed the fasts and precepts, bathing three times in fragrant water, wearing a flowered crown and pure robes, appearing like a celestial being.
Whenever he was about to enter the scripture chamber, incense was burned along both sides of the path, and chanted hymns led the way; Huìyuán’s appearance and attire were likewise solemn.
Having purified the incense burner and respectfully led the way with offerings of scattered flowers, one then proceeds to transcribe [the text].

Kneeling in the *paryaṅka* posture, one should cultivate visualization, fixing the gaze and inclining the heart. As soon as several lines have been written, each character emits light that illuminates the entire courtyard;

the entire assembly sees this together, and there is none who does not feel moved by deep inspiration. After a long while, the radiance finally subsides. Furthermore, a divine being appears holding a halberd to issue a warning.
Wei Yuan saw it together with a scholar, yet others did not perceive it.

Furthermore, a blue-robed *brahmacārin* boy arrived unexpectedly, holding celestial flowers in his hands, and suddenly extended them as an offering. Such miraculous manifestations followed one after another in rapid succession.
After two years had passed, the transcription was finally completed; it was placed in a fragrant casket and set within a precious canopy, where it was enshrined.
Whenever Jingtang prostrated himself in homage, he would later find that when the case containing the scripture was opened for recitation, it emitted a wondrous light;

its solemn purity and reverence were unsurpassed in antiquity or modern times. This scripture has been transmitted down to the present through five generations, and whenever there are those who recite it with pure devotion, spiritual responses manifest clearly.
The scripture is currently being guarded and venerated at the residence of Dharma Master Xianshou of Xi Dayuan.
Furthermore, there was the Meditation Master Xiude of Yang, who also planted paper mulberry trees and engaged in similar activities as described here; as the biography states:

"Xiude of Zhongshan in Dingzhou during the Tang dynasty, whose clan and surname are unknown, was by nature committed to austere discipline. He maintained the Way in the mountain forests, taking the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Awakening of Faith* as his means of settling the mind and completing his practice.
In the fourth year of the Yonghui era, he resolved to transcribe [the scriptures]."

To ensure the purity of the writing process, he established a separate clean courtyard and planted paper mulberry trees; after three years had passed, he further purified the paper by irrigating the trees with scented water.
He then constructed a separate clean platform upon which a hall was erected.

He summoned the calligrapher Wang Gong of Wei Prefecture, who, having fasted, bathed, and donned clean robes in the separate courtyard, burned incense, scattered flowers, and hung various banners before beginning his work.
Indeed, according to the ritual scriptures, one ascends the seat only after performing repentance; the brush is dipped while holding incense and raised while exhaling.
This was his daily constant practice. Nevertheless, the Dhyāna Master would daily enter a pure chamber to cultivate meditative visualization.

When the scripture was completed, Bi’er followed the invitation to perform a vegetarian feast (zhāi) to celebrate its accomplishment.

Once the great assembly had gathered, Sengde burned incense and scattered flowers before the multitude, making a great vow (*mahāpraṇidhāna*). No sooner had he opened the scripture repository than it emitted a great radiance that extended for more than seventy *li*, illuminating the city of Dingzhou.
The men and women within the city all witnessed this together during the Zhongshan vegetarian feast.

The assembly threw themselves down, rolling on the ground, sobbing with grief as they repented according to the two preceding traditions; one must know this. If one creates scriptures or images, the principle is that they should be pure and clean;
if one can be as refined and thorough as this, such spiritual responses will truly be numerous. When the Buddha was in his golden coffin, regarding the honoring and making of scriptures and images:
if the master says, "I am looking after the craftsmen," he is truly a celestial demon; even if he eats wine, meat, or the five pungent herbs...

To create scriptures and images as numerous as dust motes and grains of sand brings very little merit; the sin of failing to show reverence is such that one will not enter the Dragon Palace when the kalpa-fire burns, but will instead fall into the Hell of Death—better, therefore, not to create them at all.
Furthermore, according to the *Chao*, there was a man from Wannian County in Yongzhou named Kang Alu (Kang being his surname and Alu his given name).

Master Rong then entrusted Lu Shan with these words: "My younger brother’s fourth son, Xingzheng, possesses a modicum of benevolence;
you should speak to him and have him copy one volume of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. If he copies this sūtra, all seven hundred people will attain liberation.
Once Lu Shan had been released and returned, he went to the Eastern Market to sell medicine at He's house, [recalling] Master Rong’s words.
He related in detail how his practice and realization had moved the Great Compassionate One (Avalokiteśvara), who consequently appeared to him at Xiyuan Monastery before the Dharma Master Xianshou.

He requested a copy of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and commissioned others to transcribe it. On the evening of its initial transcription, the entire family dreamed that their father had come to them, and they rejoiced beyond measure.
In the eighth month of the first year of the Yonglong era, when the magnificent transcription was completed, he invited monks for a vegetarian feast to celebrate the occasion.
Then, the spirit master Zhongnai and seven hundred other spirits arrived together at the place of the fast;
they paid homage to the Triple Gem, knelt before the monks in circumambulation, repented, and received the precepts. Having completed these matters, they departed.

Having left home at a young age, he made it his practice to recite the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Upon encountering Chan Master Huichao, who was living in seclusion at Gaoshan in Langu Valley, he withdrew from worldly distractions and, with sincere devotion, requested instruction.
Subsequently, on the southern ridge of the monastery, he constructed a hall for the *Avataṃsaka*.

When asked whether he had attained supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), he replied that he had not. Immediately, the spirit lifted the monk up and soared into the air, arriving in an instant at his dwelling.
Suddenly, he beheld a magnificent palace with grand halls, vast and resplendent; the courtyard was laid out with precious delicacies sufficient to provide for a thousand people.
As the time for the meal drew near, he saw Dao’an seated upon a high throne. Dao’an asked, "Are there any other monks? The spirit replied, "There are many indeed. After a short while—
