in principle, you are worthy of honor and excellence. Suddenly, several hundred strange monks appeared, descending from the air with fly-whisks and alms bowls in hand.
Sengwu was startled and rose to prostrate himself, but the monks stopped him, saying, "Please do not."
Once the Master had accepted the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra, he became an object of veneration for us;

each of us ate in silence and then departed through the air, flying away so that no one could discern their destination. Awakening informed the deity, saying, "I would be grateful if you, O Dānapati, would show me the way.
Within the deity’s courtyard were more than ten small children, about three years old in appearance, who were naked.
A divine youth playing there said, "One of you should attend upon the Dharma Master. The other youths pushed one another and hesitated, failing to step forward.
The spirit called out in a stern voice, and one boy immediately obeyed the command. He said to Wù, "Please, Master, open your mouth.
Once he had looked into the master's mouth, he said, "The Master has a great illness. The boy then took the grime from the master's fingernails.
He cast it into the mouth of the monk; after a moment, [the monk] said again, "Open your mouth. Having seen it, he said, "The Master’s illness is now nearly gone.
He then leaped up and flew into the monk's mouth. The child was indeed the essence of the medicine. Having attained awakening, Wuzhuo subsequently acquired supernatural powers.

A deity said, "I have troubled the Master with your descent; there is no lavish offering to provide, so I offer this meager recompense. I hope you will not hold me accountable. Wuzhuo replied, "I am ashamed."
Feeling ashamed, he took his leave and soared into the clouds. After passing through three old sites, he sat cross-legged in mid-air and spoke from afar to his companions, saying:
"By the power of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, I have been graced with this elixir of immortality and attained the rank of a transcendent being (*ṛṣi*).

He ascended into the air and vanished into the distance; the manuscript he was reciting followed him along, and its whereabouts remained unknown.

The *Jiaochao* (Excerpts) states that it was as clear as looking into a mirror. According to the *Zhengzhuan* (Biographies of the Correct Lineage), he suddenly recited the text after being instructed by Samantabhadra in a dream, such that the beginning and end were as clear as a mirror.
Furthermore, there was a śramaṇa named Huīyǒng at Bǎofù Yán in Fénzhōu.

Jixuan states that those under fifteen are called "in their youth. As for the mention of "several hundred grains" before and after, tradition says these were *śarīra*.

traveling to no distant famous mountains or sacred sites. Later, while residing in the village of Chisha in Fangzhou,
there was a mountain three *li* north of the village containing a stone cave where the practitioner Juedao had dwelt for twenty-four years, reciting [the scriptures] by day.
Huayan spent his years in leisurely cultivation of meditative contemplation during the night, making this his constant practice.

Once, he was robbed by wicked men who pushed him down from a cliff; though he hung suspended over the precipice, [he remained unharmed].
It stood a hundred *ren* tall, appearing as if it had suffered no damage. In the first year of the Yongchun era, people saw a strange light within the niche;

They cremated the remains and erected a stupa; at that time, he was seventy-six years old. According to the *Yinyue Cao*, the term "inverse guest" (*nili*) refers to the act of welcoming (*yin*). It pertains to the Passes.
"To call out from the east is to oppose the barrier; to call out from the west is to welcome the traveler. This refers to the specific designation for a sojourning guest, namely a guest-house.

"zhǐ" (止) means to stop; "xiūluó" (修羅) refers to the asuras. "Lù" (屢) means frequency; "xù" (恤) means to suppress or crush; "qū" (屈) means to weary or bend; "qíng" (勍) means powerful or strong. This describes those who are sent back in a mere moment.
The transmission concludes with the completion of the Asura Array. All the devas said, “We shall grant you whatever your heart desires.
The śrāmaṇera replied, “I do not seek any other wish; I seek only unsurpassed bodhi. The devas thanked him, saying, “As for your great vow, it is truly beyond our power.
We wonder, Dharma Master, what else do you seek? He answered, “Nothing else.”
In accordance with his wishes, after a short time had passed, he was sent back; the robes were imbued with a celestial fragrance that did not cease for the rest of his life.
For several years, he lay on his right side and passed away without illness, stating himself that he had been reborn in a Pure Buddha-land.
On the fourth day of the second month of the first year of the Yongchang era, the Tripiṭaka Master Indrabodhi from Khotan was at Shen... [text ends].
In the Eastern Monastery of the Wei State capital, [Dao]xuan personally recounted this to Xianshou.

The *Chao* (Excerpts) states that "inquiring and seeking what is abandoned" refers to inquiring and seeking the mind that abandons meditative concentration—namely, mental states such as torpor (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*). "Before long" means not for a long time; it indicates a request.
"Those who realize this mind pray that the Buddhas may bear witness to this awakening of the mind.

from that time on, his realization and entry [into the path] grew ever deeper, and he followed the lofty example of the high mountains."
People from far and near flocked to him to seek instruction as if in a flowing stream; those who received his teachings and admonitions numbered over three hundred.
Subsequently, as the great assembly gathered and the weary awaited relief, he exhorted the fourfold community to observe the practice of eating only once a day.
Since their dwellings were cramped and narrow, many had to sit in the open air; consequently, water jars, alms bowls, and rope beds came to fill the valleys and mountains.
He was patient and gentle in his guidance, directing others according to their specific circumstances with the sole aim of resolving their obstructions; he followed no fixed standard.

Consequently, among those who entered his gate, there were none who did not penetrate the innermost depths of his teaching. Although he never stepped outside the monastery for fifty years, those who completed their studies and became accomplished practitioners of Chan numbered more than eight hundred.
Since then, those who have sought his legacy have been so numerous that the waves of his influence have once again surged beyond measure.
It is several times greater than that. Furthermore, to the west of Mount Heng and to the southeast of Qingliang, there is a mountain locally known as Dahei Shan (Great Black Mountain).

While eating, she suddenly heard a voice from the air saying, "Within the Buddha-Light Mountain on Mount Wutai, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva is currently teaching and transforming beings;

you should go there, and you will surely attain enlightenment. When the entire assembly heard this, they were all struck with awe and followed the voice from the sky, rushing toward Buddha-Light Mountain.
Along the way, the terrain was perilous for over two hundred li, yet the blind girl pressed forward.
When his hand first reached him, Huida had no one to guide him; startled by this sight, he immediately rose and was granted the profound teaching.

Based on these words, some may consider it merely the skillful means (*upāya*) of a Great Sage. When his end approached, Huida knew that his fellow practitioners were harboring doubts throughout the night.
That night, a large beast arrived at the spring where Huida always drank; he wept piteously for a long while before departing. The next day at noon, as expected...
Having shaved his head and finished prostrating before the assembly of monks, he returned to his original meditation cell and sat upright until his passing.

He was eighty-one years old; this was the sixteenth year of the Zhenguan era. Both monastics and laypeople mourned him as if they had lost their own lord. They immediately excavated a niche within the monastery for him to reside in;
the niche faced southwest toward a pair of doors only a few inches apart. Even today, when one observes it, he appears solemn and majestic.
He was like one who had been born anew.
According to the records of his life and conduct, which are extensive and widely transmitted by tradition, after practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* at Baitisi (Baotisi),
he resided at Shengguangsi in the capital and studied the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* under Dharma Master Tanyuan.
Huiqian especially appreciated his extraordinary nature; during the intervals between his lectures, he would often perform menial service for the monks.

He would present principles through specific affairs to harmonize his mind, frequently saying: "When I sit in meditation with my eyes closed, it is as if I have reached a certain realization; yet once I open my eyes, I return to ordinary consciousness.
Therefore, regarding worldly affairs and excursions, he employed his mind to ensure that neither existence nor non-existence would cause him obstruction. However, this was his constant practice...

While sitting in meditation, his eyes remained open like a thin slit for more than two nights without blinking once; later, when entering meditative absorption, he displayed increasingly extraordinary signs.

Once, while serving as the temple’s supervisor (*zhisui*), he quarreled with someone over a plot of land, whereupon a corpse suddenly appeared in the marketplace, its color changed and its body beginning to swell.

Upon returning to the temple, he took refuge in the Dharma and repented; the corpse then spoke and laughed as usual. Furthermore, he sat in meditation by a pond for six nights and lay amidst the snow.

For three nights, he spoke only of fire-roasting and dust-burying; truly, his state was difficult to fathom. One day, while lecturing on the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* (Qixin lun), upon reaching the section on the Gate of True Suchness (Zhenru men), he suddenly fell silent.
His disciples were alarmed and approached him to observe him closely; they found that his breath had ceased and his body was cold.

Knowing that he had entered the state of cessation of perception (*nirodha-samāpatti*), they left him as he was. After several nights had passed, he finally arose from his meditative absorption. Furthermore, during a severe drought (as detailed in the *Shuchao*, etc.)... and so forth.

As he was about to pass away, he requested to have his hair shaved, returned to his seat, and donned his great robe (*saṃghāṭī*). He addressed his disciples, saying, "Impermanence has arrived; do not deceive yourselves.
He then ordered that this sutra and the *Śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda-nirdeśa* (The Verses of the Worthy Head) be recited.

When his breath finally ceased, he commanded his attendants to chant the name of the Buddha, and his spirit departed suddenly. This was in the ninth month of the tenth year of the Zhenguan era. He was eighty years of age at the beginning of his life.
As he was about to pass away, tens of thousands of birds gathered and wailed mournfully around his chambers. Two youths dressed in green entered carrying flowers;

a purple light, like a radiant aura, issued from his body, its flames leaping several zhang high. When it grew bright, a mist coalesced for twenty li around, causing people and creatures to turn pale with fear;
it did not subside until three days later. When the fellow practitioners traveling for proselytization in Jinzhou heard of these portents, they rushed there immediately.
As if mourning for a close relative, he was further moved by the lowing of the ox that had carried him; its tears flowed incessantly, and for seven days it refused water and grass.
When they were about to inter the remains, as soon as a single spade struck the earth, the ground shook violently for fifteen *li* around, causing great terror among all.
Furthermore, two swarms of white ants formed two lines extending far toward the niche and the coffin, and two white birds [perched there].

The head soared and cried out, following him as far as the burial niche. This was because Xiangying’s Way opened up things for others, and his awakening and wisdom were understood by both humans and spirits;
thus, he attained auspicious signs that were rich and pervasive, with the living and the deceased gathered together. Truly, such a person did not fail his life or the world.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Cao Linggan et al.," the postscript states: In the third year of the Daye era, Dajian Temple was established;
by imperial decree, he was appointed as the presiding monk (shangzuo) of the meditation hall. His disciples flourished, and he rendered meritorious service in providing salvation.
On the twenty-ninth day of the first month in the eighth year, he passed away at the temple at the age of seventy-eight. He was subsequently buried at Zhongnan...

*Yin*. According to the *Jiaochao*, regarding Guṇabhadra’s “Five Sciences” (*pañcavidyāsthāna*): first, grammar (*śabdavidyā*); second, medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*); third, arts and crafts (*śilpakarmasthānavidyā*);

fourth, spells (*adhidharmavidyā*); and fifth, logic (*hetuvidyā*). Since these are exclusively mundane dharmas, they are placed at the end; only after this does the section on venerating the Buddha-dharma follow.
He studied the Buddha-dharma. Other matters are as related in the traditional accounts. The tradition further states that toward the end of the Yuanjia era, Prince Qiao repeatedly had ominous dreams.
Guṇabhadra replied, "There will soon be calamity and disorder in the capital. Less than a year later, the primary offender plotted a rebellion.
As for the Prime Minister’s secret schemes, [Guṇabhadra] presented the essentials of his three admonitions in advance, and Emperor Shizu gazed at him from afar with deep anticipation.

Knowing that the One is contained within it, he took up his staff amidst the Yangtze waters; a divine child suddenly arrived, and as incense was burned on the tower, mountain ghosts moved the seat of honor of their own accord.
Ascending the imperial throne, he sat in lofty equanimity; fishing at the Terrace of the Immortals, he reached the very essence of things.
While such magnificent virtues need not be detailed here, from his youth he has constantly held the incense burner, never letting his hand rest, and would always pause his meals [to offer incense].
He distributed alms to the birds, some of which became so tame that they would gather on his hand to eat from it.
In the first month of the fourth year of the Taishi era, he realized his body was not recovering and took leave of the Emperor, the high officials, and others.
On the day of his passing, as he gazed out with longing, he saw celestial flowers and sacred images filling the sky, and then he died at the age of seventy-five.
Emperor Taizong deeply mourned him and bestowed generous consolatory gifts; when the high officials assembled for the funeral, both honor and sorrow were fully displayed.
This excerpt states that those holding *hù* (official tablets) are also called *shǒubǎn* (hand-boards), which are carried by officials of various ranks.

According to the *Shìmíng* (Explanation of Names), the *hù* is so named because when there is business to record upon it, one may rely on it to prevent sudden forgetfulness (*hūwàng*). The term "Dujiang" (General Lecturer) is from the *Sēngshì* (History of the Sangha).
When a master proclaims the Dharma and strikes forth its essence, it does not originate from a bystander; the opening of the discourse arises uniquely within the assembly.
Formerly, when Zhi Dun lectured on the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra*, Xu Xun served as the assistant lecturer (*dujiang*). Once Xu Xun posed a question, the assembly said that Zhi Dun had no answer for it;
once Zhi Dun presented a principle, the assembly said that Xu Xun had nothing with which to challenge it. Such exchanges continued in an unending chain. This is it.
It is known that the Dutong (Head Lecturer) is truly difficult to find; the Dutong of today merely chants the scriptural texts and is thus a mere semblance of the ancient Dutong.
As for the term "burning incense," it corresponds to the office of the Shizhe (Attendant).
The Weina (Chant Master) should properly be called *Karmadāna*, which here means "one who assigns tasks," as he directs and instructs the various affairs of the assembly.
A person is also called a *zhishi* (one who knows the affairs) or a *yuezhong* (one who gladdens the assembly); this means one who understands the matters and brings joy to the assembly.
Regarding the term *fanzhai* (Brahma-chant): *Fan* (Brahma) is translated as "quiescence" (*jìngzhǐ*), and *zai* (chant) is fully written as *nizhai*;
its correct form is *boshi*, which is translated as "praise. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that the person named *Yier* (Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa) produced three types of rhythmic sounds.
In praising the Buddha, though there is sorrow, one does not grieve; though there is joy, one does not become licentious. Because it is harmonious, it constitutes the joy of the Dharma.

Regarding the many accounts of Master Dushun’s life, according to the *Chuanji* (Biographical Records), his surname was Du, and he was a native of Wannian County in Yongzhou (i.e., the Western Capital, Jingzhao Prefecture).

The two counties under the walls of the Western Capital were Wannian and Chang’an. Currently, the Master’s original residence was several *li* outside the Qixia Gate, in the village of Duguang, which belongs to [Wannian County].
(Du Guang Village within the borders of Wannian County is Du Ling. When the Venerable was only three days old, a wet nurse came of her own accord to suckle him.
After three months, the woman ascended into the air and departed. During his childhood, he frequently preached the Dharma for the multitude atop a tomb behind his residence;
all who heard him were awakened to the Mahāyāna. To this day, the "Preaching Dharma Tomb" remains visible.

Fifteen generations ago, when my elder brother was leading a military camp of one hundred thousand men, there were no provisions for firewood or water. He requested that I alone manage the firewood and water;
with one carrying-pole of water, the three armies were fully supplied, and with one carrying-pole of firewood, there was more than enough for all the laborers.
During one night, he secretly gathered the soiled and greasy garments of the hundred thousand men and washed them all thoroughly, ensuring that no one knew of it.

Without raising his blade, he alone brought the enemy army to surrender; the generals and soldiers retreated without injury, yet he took no pleasure in official honors and requested to return home to care for his parents.
When he reached the age of eighteen, he sought ordination from the Chan Master Wei (the Chan Master Mi of Yinsheng Temple, whose secular surname was Wei, hence he was called Chan Master Wei).
At that time, the earth shook as a sign of spiritual resonance; the Chan Master personally shaved his head, and suddenly the ground...
A deity held up a platter to receive [the food], whereupon the Zen Master sighed and said, "If Śākyamuni was like this, how could he not be a sage?
Later, while traveling to propagate the Dharma in Gyeongju, the Prefect privately invited him; he departed in an instant. Furthermore, five hundred poor people followed him to attend the assembly.
Fearing that the provisions would be insufficient, the Master said, "As long as the mind is impartial, there will be nothing lacking."
When the preparations for the vegetarian feast were completed, those five hundred poor people transformed into bodhisattvas and arhats and departed through the air.
There was a man named Zhang Hongchang who kept oxen and horses that were extremely vicious; everyone suffered from them, and no one would buy or rent them.
The Upādhyāya showed him the way of compassion and kindness. Having heard this, from that time forward, they no longer gored or bit anyone.

Once, while leading the assembly at Mount Li during the summer, the Master found that the area where they were dwelling in seclusion was infested with many insects and ants, making it impossible to plant vegetables.

Fearing that there might be harm caused to them, the Master pointed directly to the ground and ordered the insects to move elsewhere. Not long after he went to inspect the site, the area was exactly as he had indicated, and there were no insects at all.
At that time, the Master suffered from a swelling that burst open and oozed pus; everyone regarded him with even greater reverence.
Some who sucked [the pus] or wiped it with silk cloth were immediately healed;
the remaining pus emitted such a fragrant flow that its scent was incomparable, and even after the silk cloth had been removed, the fragrance did not cease.

A man from Sanyuan County named Sadāpa suffered from deafness since birth, and another named Zhang Su also suffered from congenital muteness; when the Master came and spoke with them, they subsequently returned to normal.
A man was permanently cured. At Wengong County, a monk was possessed by a venomous dragon; the community requested the Master to save him.
The Master immediately sat upright facing him, and the dragon then feigned illness. The monk said, "Since the Chan Master has arrived, it is improper for me to remain long;
I have greatly troubled you. Thereupon, he became instantly relieved. Thus, those near and far who were afflicted by miasmic fevers or depraved spirits were all freed from their suffering.
He would not employ spells nor apply other arts, but would simply sit facing them; there was none who did not recover.
Consequently, whenever he encountered divine trees or dragon temples, he would immediately burn them down; he personally cleared away whatever the shamans and sorcerers worshipped.

Once, while traveling through the southern wilds, he was about to cross the Huangqu River when its waters were surging and overflowing; yet as soon as he arrived, the current ceased, and he had barely stepped onto the bank when it flowed again.

He appeared exactly as he had been at the beginning. When he first went to attend a vegetarian feast, the host of the feast was holding a baby and wished to pray for its long life, saying, "Several children born previously have all failed to survive;
I am now specifically preparing this feast, and pray that the Venerable Master will empower it so that the child may attain longevity.

The Venerable Master looked at it intently and said, "This is your karmic enemy. After the feast is finished, I shall perform a repentance ritual for you. This occurred after the conclusion of the feast.
He ordered the couple to carry their child to the riverbank; the monk then threw the child into the water.
The husband and wife wept bitterly, yet the monk remained unperturbed. He said, "Your child shall not perish," and immediately pointed his finger.
The child was transformed into a man six feet tall who stood amidst the waves. The monk rebuked him, saying, "In a previous life, you killed me and took my [belongings]."
"Gold and silk were pushed toward me as I was drowning, yet it was not because the Upādhyāya had resolved our karmic enmity for me that I did not forgive you;
the Upādhyāya once placed a pair of shoes at a city gate for three days without them being lost. When people asked him the reason, the Upādhyāya said:
'Since immeasurable kalpas past, I have never stolen so much as a single coin from another; such is the retribution.'"

Thereupon, those who had committed theft all repented their transgressions and changed their hearts. At Mount Zhongnan, they gathered the meanings expounded in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and composed the "Contemplation of the Dharma Realm" (*Fajie guan*).
Once the text was completed, they piled firewood and set it ablaze; the flames conformed perfectly to the sacred intent, leaving not a single character damaged.
At that time, the Bodhisattvas of the ocean-like assembly manifested their forms to offer praise and collectively extended their offerings in harmony.

Possessing a nature of profound sincerity and a disposition of intimate compassion, he extended his kindness to both the clergy and the laity, as well as to those of noble and humble station, accepting invitations from all.
He never took to heart either censure or praise; thus, his spiritual resonance reached both the hidden and the manifest realms, moving the ears of both the monastic and secular worlds.

Emperor Taizong, awestruck by his divine and extraordinary qualities, invited the Master into the palace. The Emperor personally went out to meet him and addressed the Master, saying: "I, Your Majesty..."
The Emperor had long been afflicted by chills and fevers that did not subside. Hearing of the Master’s supernatural powers, he asked, "How may this be dispelled?

The Master replied, "When a sage's virtue governs the realm, how could such baleful influences prevail? Simply bring peace to the common people and issue a general amnesty; Your Majesty’s health will surely be restored.
The Emperor accepted the Master’s words, selected an auspicious day, ascended the imperial throne, and issued a great amnesty throughout the empire. Consequently, the Emperor’s illness was cured.
He was bestowed with the honorary title of Imperial Heart Chan Master (Dixin Chanshi). Members of the royal clan and eminent ministers turned their hearts toward him and requested the precepts.
In the fourteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away while sitting in meditation at Yishan Temple in the southern suburbs, at the age of eighty-four.
Furthermore, a stele inscription was erected again, stating that on the twenty-fifth day of the tenth month of that year, he entered [nirvana].
The Inner Record states that Emperor Taizong ascended the Taijie Hall and passed away upon his imperial bed.

His remains were kept within the inner palace for seven days of offerings, after which they were escorted to the northern plain of Fanchuan and interred in a pit dug there—this is the present-day Huisheng Monastery.
The people of the capital lamented together; the robes made for him covered the fields, yet his countenance remained unchanged, becoming even more radiant after a month as he sat peacefully.
His body remained intact for three cycles [of years], and the skeletal remains persist to this day; spiritual wonders are frequently heard of.
The Emperor turned his heart toward him, and the king and ministers venerated him with respect. Every year on the twenty-fifth day of the tenth month, an assembly is held at the site of the stupa;
this is the Huayan Stupa. Furthermore, the *Record of the Inexhaustible Lamp* states that before a certain master’s death, he informed one of his disciples:
The Master asked, "Where are you going? The monk replied, "I wish to go briefly to Wufeng to pay homage to Mañjuśrī.
The Master smiled and said, "If you truly intend to go, I have a verse that may assist you on your journey; you should take note of its meaning. The verse says:
"The traveler wanders aimlessly across the waves, To pay homage at the earthen slopes of Mount Tai. Mañjuśrī—where exactly is he?"
A monk was seeking Maitreya, but finding no one who could explain his purpose, he departed for Mount Tai. There he met an old man who asked, "Whence have you come?
The monk replied, "I have come to pay homage to Mañjuśrī. The man said, "Mañjuśrī is not currently on this mountain;
what benefit is there in your coming? The monk asked, "Where is Mañjuśrī now? The man replied, "He has gone to Chang’an to teach and transform sentient beings. The monk—
The monk asked, "I am a man from Chang'an; who currently serves as Mañjuśrī in Chang'an? The layman replied, "The Venerable Du Shun is Mañjuśrī himself.
Upon hearing this, the monk was struck with awe and cried out, "Du Shun is my teacher! Suddenly, the old layman vanished.
The monk realized that what had been told him was not false, and he returned home by way of the San River, arriving at the banks of the Shan River.
Suddenly, the river surged for three days, and only after it subsided did he reach the monastery; by then, the Master had already passed away.
It was only then that he realized this was a manifestation of Mañjuśrī.

Regarding the *Yōshū Fukan Zazengi*, the "Zatsu" (Miscellaneous) section refers to those under Master Tsūgen who were joyful and capable of exerting their full strength. As the *Lunyu* says regarding such service: [the text here appears to be truncated].
His parents exerted all their strength for him; from this point on, he "submissively accepted" [the teachings], which means he followed them from below.

Here, "submissive" (*fu*) refers to bowing, and "accepting" (*ying*) refers to the chest. The intended meaning is that from this time forward, he applied the etiquette of a disciple and deeply penetrated the profound, inexhaustible principles of the *Avataṃsaka*.
For further details, as found in other biographies—such as the biography of Cui Zhiyuan—they are very thorough.

I have not yet seen its original source; however, the *Zuǎnlíng jì* (Record of the Compilation of Spirits), which is currently cited three times in this compilation, states that when Huayan [Fazang] was about to pass away, while Xuanyan was still in lay attire, Xuanyan said to the various virtuous ones:

"This worthy one has attained self-awakening without a teacher. I pray that you lend him your remaining radiance so that together we may accomplish the work of the Buddha and greatly promote the Huayan [Avataṃsaka]."
Only this man, during the Xianheng era, was recommended by a collective memorial from various virtuous monks; consequently, he was ordained as a monk but did not yet receive full ordination.
By imperial decree, he lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Taiyuan Temple, his reputation for excellence rising daily until clergy and laity gathered like clouds.
He delivered the lectures more than thirty times in total. During the Shengli era, by imperial decree, he [lectured] at Foshouji Temple in the Eastern Capital.
While lecturing on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at a monastery, he experienced the Buddha hall suddenly shaking; the Emperor praised this and ordered it recorded in the national history.

The *Song Gaoseng Zhuan* states that the monk Faxiang’s courtesy name was Xuanshu (this matches the present *Chao*; the *Zuǎnlíng* says it was the title bestowed by Empress Wu, while the *Yuánjué Chāo* states it was a posthumous title conferred by the Emperor).
His demeanor was extraordinary and upright, and his sharp intelligence was peerless. He traveled briefly to the capital... [text fragment ends]... slightly.
Exposing his sharp wit, he belonged to the school of Master Xuanzang’s translation of the *Tripiṭaka* and was initially selected for the ranks of monks specializing in doctrinal studies (*yixue*).
Later, due to differences in perspective regarding the transcription of the correct meaning and the refinement of the text, he departed from the translation hall.

(According to the *Zuǎnlíng jì*, Master Yǎn was still a layman at the time of his death; it was only during the Xiánhéng era that he finally took the tonsure. Since Master Xuanzang’s translation activities took place during the Zhènguān era—more than twenty years prior to Xiánhéng—and since Xuánshòu became a monk after Xuanzang had already passed away, [the accounts appear inconsistent].)

It has been a long time since it was claimed that he was selected for the ranks of eminent monks and translated scriptures alongside Xuanzang; this clearly demonstrates the errors in the Song dynasty transmission. Furthermore, regarding the accounts of his life, many are not firsthand reports, and it is unknown from what source they were originally derived.
During the reign of Empress Wu, Śikṣānanda brought the Sanskrit manuscripts of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to the Tripitaka office; there, he once again held the same position as Yijing and Falin.
Subsequently, in Yijing’s translation bureau, he served alongside Shengzhuang and Dayi as a verifier of the meaning (*zhèngyì*). (The subsequent account of the transmission of the Dharma follows.)

Regarding the contemplation of the realms (*dhātu-vipaśyanā*), there is the *Tiān Shuō Jīn Shīzǐ Zhāng* (The Golden Lion Chapter Spoken by Tiān), along with the analogies of the mirror and the lamp, and accounts of the earth trembling during sutra lectures; other titles are not recorded here.

However, according to various commentaries and records, whenever the deeds of the Patriarchs are discussed, they mostly refer to them as being in separate fascicles, and those that provide detailed accounts are few.

As the years have grown distant, these biographical records appear and disappear inconsistently, and scholars have failed to compile them. I fear that the deeds of the Patriarchs will [be lost] to future generations...

Because there were omissions in what I had heard, I have compiled this from beginning to end; my only regret is that I was able to obtain only half of this biography from the extensive version by the Cui family.
I hope that those among the learned who possess insight will supplement it.
The *Chaozuan lingji* states: "A person from Jingzhao surnamed Wang named Minggan," and so forth. However, the *Huayan zhuan* merely says:
"In the first year of the Wenming era, a person from the capital surnamed Wang whose name is lost," and so on;
the facts are the same as in the present *chao*. Furthermore, the *Hu Youzhen zhuan* states: "In the fourth month of the second year of the Chuihong era, at Daxiangshan... [and so forth].
After finishing his lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Cien Monastery, Daochen dispersed the assembly and went to pay his respects to the Venerable Cheng and the Vinaya Master Daochen.
He reported to Xianshou, saying: "This summer, Guo Shenliang of Xian'an Ward died and was revived seven days later.
He entered the monastery to pay his respects to me and said that he had entered the underworld. There, a monk ordered him to recite a verse, which begins: 'If a person wishes to fully understand...'"
Xian-shou replied to Chen, saying: "This verse is from the fourth assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

At first, Chen did not recognize it as being from the *Avataṃsaka*, nor did he yet fully believe Xian-shou. Xian-shou then requested that Chen consult the 'Ten Practices' chapter (*Daśabhūmika*) to verify it;
indeed, it was the final verse within the section on the Ten Practices. Master Chen sighed and said: 'As soon as I heard this single verse...'"
If ten million people were simultaneously liberated from suffering, how much more so those who received the complete lectures and mastered the profound meaning!
The critique states: In Xianshou’s own account, he says his name was Wang Minggan; in Huayan Master’s *Lingji*, it says his name was Wang Minggan;

in Hu Youzhen’s compilation of Huiying’s records, it says his name was Guo Shenliang. Now, according to the *Huayan Zhuan* (Biography of Huayan): [The text continues with the specific details regarding the lineage and transmission of the Avatamsaka teachings.]
It is said that during the Yonglong era, Guo Shenliang, a native of Chang’an County in Yongzhou, whose pure conduct was immaculate, suddenly met with a violent death.
The devas led him to the Tuṣita Heaven palace, where he paid homage to Maitreya.
A certain bodhisattva asked Shenliang, "Why do you not uphold the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*? He replied, "Because there is no one to preach it. The bodhisattva said, "There is."
People currently discuss this, yet why was it said that [Gao] Liang had no such experience? Later, after he revived, Liang recounted the matter in detail to Dharma Master Bocen.
Based on this, one can clearly see that Xianshou’s propagation of the Wheel of Dharma was a secondary manifestation that participated in the traces of the Sages.
According to the textual evidence transmitted above, it was Dharma Master Cen who explained to Xianshou the account of Guo Shenliang entering the heavenly palace.
However, Hu Youzhen’s account of the events concerning entering the underworld is clearly unreliable;

this can be seen from the fact that Master Yuan must have inquired after Xianshou’s passing and obtained the name [of the person]. Therefore, the current narrative follows the *Zuānlíng* as authoritative, hence it states "Wang Minggan.
Regarding the mention of the long-eared Brahmin and others in the *Chao*, this is based on the *Huayan zhuan*.

It is stated that the Elder Brahmin Maitra of Siṃhala, a person who had attained the third fruit [of Arhatship]—translated here as "Nengyou" (Capable Friend)—arrived in China at the beginning of the Linde era.
He was held in the highest esteem by Emperor Gaozong and Empress Wu, who requested that he reside at the Penglai Palace;
both the *Changshou* and this work were transcribed there. However, it is an error to conflate this with the *Sengzhuan* (Biographies of Monks) and the *Huayan zhuan* (Biography of the Avataṃsaka).
Everyone says he is merely an old śramaṇa. The *Shūchō* (Sub-commentary), specifically the sub-commentary on the lower fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra*, states:
"Furthermore, there are two meanings of 'hearing': first, hearing in a general sense for the sake of distant benefit; second, not grasping at the characteristics of hearing. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
"If one hears the sūtra, one does not form the characteristic of hearing, does not form the characteristic of speaking, and does not form the characteristic of phrases."
To form the characters [of this scripture] is to embody all things; thus, to listen to the sutra is to act in accordance with its fundamental principle.
Because the beginning and the end are perfectly integrated, one hears it in truth. To say "equal to the Buddha" means that this sutra explains the Buddha’s wisdom and the objects of contemplation;

if one can now correctly hear it, it is identical to that true contemplation. Regarding the passage "How much more so... and below: the question asks, since hearing [this] makes one equal to the Buddha, why is there further comparison? The answer follows.

How much more so for those who are equal [to the Buddha]! Since they engage in recitation and so forth, are they not indeed equal to the Buddha? Alternatively, it may be that because they further engage in recitation, cultivation, and so forth, they surpass the Buddha;

thus, the non-obstruction of the one and the many constitutes the ultimate truth. [This concludes the explanation of the passage. [The following addresses an objection regarding the text: The Sūtra merely clarifies "hearing," yet why does the Commentary speak of "reciting, reciting, contemplating, and cultivating"? [Having finished the explanation: Regarding the phrase "how much more so for those who are equal": since they engage in activities such as reciting and chanting, how could they not be equal to the Buddha? Or perhaps it means that if they further engage in reciting, chanting, practicing, and so forth, they would exceed the Buddha;

therefore, the non-obstruction between the one and the many constitutes the true ultimate. This concludes the explanation of the preceding section. As for the subsequent clarification of potential objections: the Sūtra only manifests the aspect of "hearing," whereas in the Commentary, why is it stated as "reciting, reciting, contemplating, and cultivating"? [The explanation is now complete.]
This may be known.

In the *Shuyao* (Excerpts), regarding the various instances of spiritual resonance mentioned below, I shall now briefly cite one or two examples. There was a monk named Sengqiao, whose secular surname was Zhuang;

he left home at a young age and took the study of the Hīnayāna as his vocation. He gained renown throughout the regions of the Yangtze and Han rivers. At that time, there was the Venerable Xiangwang Zhe, who was lecturing at Longquan.
When the three masters of the *Sanlun* school could not bear this and spoke out, they declared, "The *Sanlun* clarifies emptiness!
As the lecturer finished speaking these words of attachment to emptiness, his tongue protruded three feet, and blood flowed from both his eyes and ears. He remained silent for seven days.
When Vinaya Master Fu heard of this, he said, "You are far too foolish! The sin of disparaging the sutras with a single word exceeds the five heinous crimes; you must believe in the Mahayana."

Once he was able to escape [the danger], he was then made to perform repentance; his tongue returned to its original state, and he was carried to the residence of Zhe. He listened exclusively to the Mahāyāna.
When Zhe passed away, a seven-site, eight-assembly Fangguang (Vaipulya) fast was established for him. When the hundred-day period was completed, [Hui] went to Xiangshan Shenzu Temple.
Without ever crossing the threshold, he constantly practiced the Mahāyāna, lecturing on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* during each of the four seasons.

In the *Yanjing* (Sutra of the Adornment), he set forth his repentance and confession. On the third day of the fourth month in the eleventh year of the Zhenguan era, while practicing seated meditation in a pine grove, he saw three men whose appearance and attire were most elegant.
Wearing red robes, they prostrated themselves and requested that he confer the Bodhisattva precepts upon them.

Once the conferral was complete, they said: "Master, you possess such sharp faculties; if you do not transform your mind, you will surely fail to believe in the Mahāyāna. Thereupon, [he] changed his heart. He who would have been among the thousands [who did not believe]...

When the Buddha appeared in the world, [the practitioner] was still in hell; hearing this grave exhortation, his tears flowed profusely as he wept aloud. He returned to the monastery to circumambulate the Buddha and repent.

Furthermore, he exhorted laypeople and monastics to produce one hundred copies each of the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Vimalakīrti*, the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*, the *Akṣayamatinirdeśa*, the *Buddhapiṭaka*, and the various *Mādhyamika-śāstras*. On the ninth day of the third month in the twelfth year, the Buddha...
Before performing his final rites of repentance, he sat in peaceful meditation until his passing at the age of eighty-some years.
Seven days after his death, the trees and forests turned white and a great spring became turbid; only after this did things return to normal.
Furthermore, Rizhao recounted that near the city of Campā in India, there was a monastery named Viśeṣa (the name of a person). Within it resided several *dhūta* monks, all of whom...
While the followers of the Hīnayāna were negligent, a Mahāyāna Dharma Master arrived at their location carrying a bundle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The monks showed no respect for that master and departed with the bundle of scriptures. As they did not believe in the Mahāyāna, they subsequently threw the bundle of scriptures into a well.
Later, they repeatedly saw a brilliant light surging upward from the top of the well, resembling a fierce conflagration.

The character *jie* (界) is the root; when assisted by *bi* (毗), it is translated as *fangguang* (方廣, Vaipulya);
when assisted by *tu* (陀), it is translated as *juezhe* (覺者, Buddha). Such are the conventions of these dialectal characters.
If the character *jie* is assisted by *ren* (人), it becomes the character *chu* (儲); if assisted merely by *qing* (靑), it becomes the character *qing* (請). This is why [the translations differ].

By abbreviating the function and preserving the essence, this accords with the preference of the people of Tang for brevity.
