Question: Why is *sūtra* not translated as "契經" (*qìjīng*) but simply as "經" (*jīng*)?

Answer: Here, the name is translated according to its essential correspondence; it is simply translated as "經. This is because the Sanskrit original lacks the word *yukti*, and therefore it is not translated as "契.
[Objection: If that is so, why is the term "契" also used in the commentaries regarding the classification within the *piṭakas*? Answer: That was for...
Fearing that using the term *jing* (sūtra) alone might lead to confusion with secular texts, the word *qi* (scripture/treatise) was added as an auxiliary to distinguish it;
however, since saying "Huayan jing" (Avataṃsaka Sūtra) here does not lead to such confusion, the word *qi* is not used. One might ask: why not translate it directly as "holy teaching" (*shengjiao*)?
The answer is that this also accords with the fact that in this land [of China], holy teachings are likewise referred to as *jing*.

Regarding the "first three alternative names" (*pūrvāṇi trīṇi paryāyāṇi*) and so forth in the *Śāstra*: the Liang commentary merely mentions their number, while the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and others generally refer to them as "wisdom" (*jñāna*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* speaks of them as the "totality of dharmas" (*sarva-dharma-samgraha*). "One" and "three" are colloquial references to alternative names;

"totality" refers to the second [category], and "incomplete" refers to "abbreviated" (*saṃkṣipta*), or perhaps all three names are "total" while being slightly abbreviated in their individual characteristics. There is no need to further divide these into two chapters or ten sections.
For the most part, names are established based on specific meanings and cannot comprehensively encompass all underlying principles.

Regarding the statement in the *Chao* (Commentary) that "it cannot comprehensively encompass [all]," there are three successive sections that unfold this point: first, it demonstrates that [the title] cannot serve as a general name for the entire scripture;
second, each of the ten chapters has its own name established according to a specific meaning; and third, each individual specific name... [is not comprehensive].
Because it encompasses the meaning and principles of the entire section as a whole, it cannot be established as the title of the sutra. One might ask:
"If all ten headings are applicable, may they not collectively serve as the title of the sutra? The second point answers: "No;

because it is impossible to cite them all in full, they likewise cannot constitute the title of the sutra. The intent is that one cannot take all ten distinct headings and present them together as a single title.

The first name is "Also Questioned. If one cannot cite them all in detail, they may be inferred from the commentary on the ten headings in the *Shu* (Commentary), which explains the manifestation of the ten headings as follows:
"The preceding nine are specific meanings, while the tenth comprehensively encompasses the preceding nine; all are the inconceivable, ultimate Dharma.
Furthermore, the commentary on the ten headings in the "Chapter on Leaving the World" states: "The first is the expressive [name], because it possesses the following nine."

Because each of the latter nine [chapters] conveys its own distinct specific meaning, if one were to cite the first chapter, "The Worldly," or the tenth chapter, "The Manifestation," one would already have grasped their general sense.
Why, then, must all ten titles be enumerated together to constitute a general summary?
Therefore, the third intention answers: although each individually provides a general sense, it remains restricted to its own respective chapter and does not extend to others.
The general title of one section appears as ten names, while the general and specific titles of another are restricted solely to the "Appearance" chapter;
and the general and specific titles of yet another are restricted solely to the "Transcending the World" chapter. How could these possibly serve as a concluding summary for what follows?

Regarding the phrase "therefore, the present translation, etc.": The original intent of establishing the title was to invoke the specific set of words and phrases that can express the meaning of this section.
Why, then, is it further called the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*? It is because the sūtra expresses that meaning;

thus, the six characters of the expressed meaning (*vācya*) serve as the name of the sūtra. First, "Dharma" refers to the *Mahāvaipulya*; second, "person" refers to the *Buddhāvataṃsaka*. These two constitute the Dharma.
"Great" (Dà) refers to the Great Vaipulya Buddha; "Vaipulya" (Fāngguǎng) refers to the three bodies of the *Avataṃsaka*; "Buddha" (Fó) refers to the complete perfection of function.

Thus, there are four aspects: first, the fruit, which is the Buddha; second, the cause, which is the *Avataṃsaka*. Furthermore, because each is both singular and all-pervasive, it is said that the principle is exhaustive and the meaning is perfect.
Moreover, the principle is exhaustive in four ways and the meaning is perfect in eight ways. Because these are presented individually, they are placed at the beginning of the sutra.
The commentary states that this possesses the four pairs [of categories] mentioned previously;

because it fully contains the meanings of the four pairs found in the various preceding sūtras, even when time, place, and so forth appear to be missing from the explicit text, they are understood to be implicitly included by way of their meaning.

That is to say, time has no separate substantial entity and is provisionally established based upon phenomena (*dharma*); thus, "time" is contained within the six characters. Regarding "place," there are four kinds of great [elements].

If the Dharma-nature land (*dharmatā-bhūmi*) is itself the Land of Self-Enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga-kṣetra*), and its vastness constitutes the Land of Other-Enjoyment (*parasambhoga*) and the Transformation Land (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*), then what would it not possess?
Question: The titles of other sutras are all established based on what is stated within those scriptures; yet, for this present title, there is no such basis mentioned in the sutra below.
Upon what is it established? Answer: It is because the present sutra lacks the specific textual passage required to establish its title.

Within the original [text], one should establish [the title] accordingly; or, as in the case of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and other sūtras, the compilers established the names, which cannot yet be definitively determined.
The above has merely been a general discussion on how [the name] was obtained.
Regarding the second section, "Distinguishing the Openings and Closings through Pairing," this refers to how this commentary uses seven pairs of terms to distinguish between openings and closings.
Among these five pairs, there are five layers of opening and closing, all of which involve first closing and subsequently opening. First, the single title is closed;

it is then opened into the "teaching" (the means of expression) and the "meaning" (that which is expressed). The teaching is established based upon the meaning, and thus the teaching and the meaning are mutually interrelated. (Below...)

(Regarding the formation of pairs, they all stand in a relationship of mutual reference; this should be understood accordingly. Question: If all seven characters are equally designators (*vācaka*), why is only the character "Sūtra" considered the teaching (*śāsana*)?

Conversely, if each were judged according to its designated object (*vācya*), they would all be meanings (*artha*); how then can they form a pair? Answer: The character "Sūtra" directly refers to the designator of the entire collection [of scriptures]; therefore, it is the teaching.
The six characters beginning with "Great" (*Mahā*) refer to the objects designated within that same collection; thus, they are the meaning.
Furthermore, although the six characters [of the title] are also capable of signifying meaning, they are the "signifiers" (vācaka) in contrast to the word "sūtra," which is the "signified" (vācya).

Thus, while the meaning of the sūtra generally encompasses both signifier and signified, here the meaning of the signifier is made explicit in relation to the aforementioned six characters; therefore, they constitute one pair.

When combined, they represent only the meaning; when separated, they are divided into the Dharma and the metaphor. Moreover, regarding the traces of the teaching, the *Chao* states that there are both general and specific aspects.
The pair "Yan" (嚴) constitutes the general [term], while the preceding five characters are all particulars. The *Gangyao* (綱要) states:

"Because the character 'Yan' encompasses both subject and object, as well as persons, dharmas, and so forth, when the three are combined, it refers only to the dharma that is the object of metaphor; when expanded, it distinguishes between the subject and object of realization.

It is also called the pair of "object and wisdom" (*viṣaya-jñāna*). Regarding this pair: Question—The Sanskrit term *buddha* is translated here as "the Awakened One" (*juezhe* 覺者), which refers to one who possesses awakening.

Question: It may be that the person who realizes [the truth] is so designated; why then is it also called "wisdom" (*jñāna*)? Answer: The previous [explanation] referred to the subject as the one who realizes [it] by way of conventional designation;

now, referring to the essential nature (*prakṛti*), only wisdom can realize it. Therefore, it is also called the "object-knowledge pair" (*ālambana-jñāna-yugala*). This is just as when a Bodhisattva realizes the first stage (*bhūmi*):
could it be that a mere conventional person realizes it? In reality, it is precisely wisdom that can realize it; thus, it may also be said [that the person realizes it].

The Bodhisattva realizes [this] or takes a distinct dharma among humans as the means of realization (the *pramāṇa*). When the four [aspects] are combined, they constitute only the dharma to be realized (*prameya*);
when expanded, they are divided into "discrimination" (*viniścaya*) and "retention" (*dhāraṇī*).

Because the term *vaipulya* (extensive) applies universally, the word "Great" (*mahā-*) is used for discrimination, signifying "the extensive that is Great. Regarding the single character "Great," the *Tanyuan ji* states: "As for the character 'Great'..."

This [term "Great"] serves to distinguish the Vaipulya (Extensive) as that which is distinguished; this is the meaning of "distinguishing. It should logically follow that the Vaipulya is the "holder" (*dhāraka*) and the "Great Meaning" (*mahārtha*) is that which is held (*dhārya*).

Regarding the statement that the term "Great" distinguishes the Great from the Small: this means that when one says "Vaipulya," among the categories of Great and Small, it is the Great and not the Small.
Thus, the word "Great" acts as the distinguisher (*vivecaka*), while the phrase "holding this Great Meaning" refers to what is held upon the Vaipulya.
"Selecting the real as distinct from the provisional" means that this term "Vaipulya" (Extensive) is real among the provisional and the real, and not provisional;
thus, the character "great" acts as the selector. To indicate that it is real, the Sūtras state that the dharma is vast and profound, which is not clarified by the provisional schools.

This contains six levels of the provisional and the real: first, the Vaipulya of the Initial Teaching of the Refutation of Characteristics is provisional, while the Initial Teaching of the Establishment of Characteristics is real.
1. Teaching the Vaipulya as the ultimate (real) because it clarifies emptiness alone, whereas this [teaching] explains the Middle Way; 2.

Or, establishing the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) as provisional and the negation of characteristics as ultimate, because that [teaching] holds only the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) to be empty, whereas this clarifies that even the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is empty;
3. The beginning is provisional and the end is ultimate; 4. The end is provisional and the sudden is ultimate; 5. The gradual is provisional and the sudden is ultimate; 6. [The sixth...]

"Partial" refers to the provisional (*upāya*), while "complete" refers to the real (*bhūta*). These two terms distinguish the various provisional teachings mentioned above; "extensive" (*vaipulya*) and "great" (*mahat*) distinguish the various real teachings mentioned above.

To say that these terms distinguish the result from the cause means that this term "extensive" refers to the result within the context of cause and effect, rather than the cause, because it is what has been realized by the Buddha.

Since the word "great" functions as the distinguishing agent, it indicates that which is realized as the great result, rather than the dharmas belonging to the stage of the cause; thus, it is distinguished from the others.

Question: Since the *Vaipulya* (Extensive) lacks this greatness, why is it not called a "result" (*phala*)? Question: The subsequent sutra extensively expounds the True Dharma; does it not thereby speak of the "cause" (*hetu*)? Answer:

Although it speaks of the cause, it belongs to the following character "Flower" (*puṣpa*). What is here termed "Vaipulya" is that which is realized as the result. Regarding the statement that it is also a pair of essence and function (*tattva-vṛtti*):
either it constitutes a pair of essence and function through the opening and closing [of categories] as previously described; however, according to the teaching...

The square shape represents the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), while the large character represents the nature (*dharmatā*); thus, nature and characteristic form a pair. When combined, they constitute that which is realized;

when opened, they are distinguished as the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). Therefore, when the five are combined, it refers only to the person (*pudgala*); when opened, they are divided into cause and effect.

This concludes the seven characters from bottom to top within the first title, consisting of the aforementioned four [characters] paired with one. Now, the fifth [character] is paired with the preceding sequence.
If one separately takes the third pair of persons from among the external [categories] as the fruit, it alone does not constitute a "pair.
Furthermore, by borrowing the character "flower" (*hua*) below to metaphorize its cause, it then becomes a single "pair" of cause and effect.

It is called "borrowed" because the character "flower" already belonged to the preceding metaphor, yet it is now taken again as a metaphor for the cause; therefore, the concluding explanation below uses the character "flower" alone.
The individual characters and their combination differ; here, we correlate them with the Buddha as the fruit, while the single character "flower" (*hua*) serves as the metaphor for the cause.
If the two characters "Flower" (*hua*) and "Adornment" (*yan*) are combined to form the body of the metaphor, they universally symbolize the mutual adornment of the preceding four characters:
that is, people adorn the Dharma and the Dharma adorns people; essence adorns function and function adorns essence; nature adorns appearance and appearance adorns nature.

All such [explanations] refer to the *Avataṃsaka* (Huayan). Furthermore, using the character "flower" (*hua*) alone or the character "adornment" (*yan*) alone also carries the sense of mutual adornment, and both can serve as metaphors for the aforementioned four characters.

As the *Gangyao* states: "By means of the flower-adornment of virtuous conduct, one accomplishes the fruit of Buddhahood in its ten bodies within the Dharma-realm of the Great Vaipulya," as explained extensively therein. Moreover, this may be verified according to the *Jiaozu ji cao*.
Furthermore, "also" (*yi*) and "flower" (*hua*) constitute the "capable of adorning" (*neng yan*), while the four characters "ability to adorn" (*suo yan*) constitute the "that which is adorned.

This constitutes one pair of "capable" and "adorned. Altogether, from the preceding section, there are ten pairs: (1) teaching and meaning; (2) dharma and metaphor; (3) person and dharma; (4) object and wisdom; (5) selection and maintenance; (6) essence and function; (7) cause and fruit. Based on the traces of the teaching, three pairs are selected:

(1) general and specific; (2) nature and characteristic; (3) capable and adorned. Thus, there are ten pairs in total. If explained according to their sequence, the first character "Sutra" (*jing*) refers to the teaching, and the six [characters] above...

This meaning corresponds to the "Teaching" (jiao) and "Meaning" (yi), which are the pair of the two characters "Adornment" (yan). This is the general; the preceding five are the particular—this is the pair of the general and the particular.

The three characters "Flower" (hua) act as the "adorners" (neng yan) for the preceding four "adorned" (suo yan) elements—this is the pair of the "adorners" and the "adorned. The four characters "Flower Adornment" (Huayan) are the "analogy" (yu) for the preceding four "dharmas" (fa)—this is the pair of the "dharma" and the "analogy.
The character "Flower" (hua) represents the "cause" (yin) and the character "Buddha" (fo) represents the "fruit" (guo)—this is the pair of "cause" and "fruit. Sixth.

1. "Buddha" refers to the person who realizes; the three aforementioned realized dharmas refer to the person and the dharma—this is the correspondence between person and dharma. 2. "Buddha" refers to the wisdom that realizes;

the three aforementioned realized objects refer to the object and the wisdom—this is the correspondence between object and wisdom. 3. "Extensive" (*vaipulya*) refers to function; the two aforementioned [realized dharmas] are the essence—this is the correspondence between essence and function.

4. "Great" (*mahā-*) serves as a selection; "extensive" (*vaipulya*) serves as a maintenance—this is the correspondence between selection and maintenance. 5. The single character "one" (*eka*) refers to the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

The "Great Characters" (Dazì) are the nature; thus, these ten pairs are relative to the nature. Therefore, while the preceding [terms] can possess the succeeding ones, the succeeding ones do not possess the preceding.

These have all been explained above in a general manner as "combinations" (hé), yet they are distinguished as "openings" (kāi) according to their specific meanings. When opened, the teachings and meanings differ;
when combined, they form a single pair of teaching and meaning, and so forth. The ten pairs presented above rely upon the perfect number (yuánshù) merely to indicate a general direction; however—

The principle can be understood through the application of what is appropriate; thus, the *Xuánjìng* states: "The 'Great Vaipulya' refers to the Dharma realized, while the 'Buddha Avataṃsaka' refers to the person who realizes it," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "superior virtue like a valley" in the *Chāo*, Emperor Ming’s commentary explains: "Superior virtue like a valley means it is empty and receptive..."

To accommodate all things, one appears as white as snow yet humble; to possess pure integrity while harboring impurities. To possess vast virtue while appearing insufficient, one achieves great perfection yet maintains humility.

To establish virtue while appearing as if acting with haste, one accomplishes merit without ostentation. To possess genuine substance while appearing as if it were changing, one remains pure and unified while blending with the light of the world.
To be of great capacity without corners, one does not set up petty sharp edges. A vessel of great magnitude is perfected late.
Furthermore, there is no immediate efficacy; "the great sound is rare and silent" means it does not adorn itself with petty words.
"The Great Image is formless" means it can respond to the myriad categories. "The Dao is hidden and nameless" means its functional utility is not manifest.
It is the "Nameless One. Truly, only the Dao is skilled at lending and completing; though it is hidden and nameless, it is in fact skillfully perfected through its profound harmony and subtlety.
This is the explanation provided by the author of the sub-commentary (*xiaochao*), intended to assist in lending [the meaning] to all things and to bring them to maturity;
the rest is merely cited for convenience. Since the primary purpose is to employ the single phrase "The Great Square has no corners," only this one phrase is explained.
The statement that "its words are borrowed for use" intends to show that its meaning is not being adopted; it refers to the fact that the essence of the Great Way is without fixed direction.
Because it is a corner [of the path], those who study the Way do not establish minor sharp edges; now, the "Great Square" below clarifies the present intent.
In the *Chao*, the phrase "using adornment to encompass both the subject and object" is a general heading, while "Huā (Flower) as the subject of adornment" is the specific explanation.

If one considers the mutual adornment of the three greatnesses (*trimahātmya*), Huā is likewise the subject of adornment; therefore, when it says "the Buddha is the fruit of perfected adornment," this is because...

Regarding the two meanings: first, looking upward at the three great dharmas—since the person who has perfected the fruit of Buddhahood is adorned by the three great dharmas, the Buddha is the object of adornment (*adheya*) and the three great dharmas are the agent of adornment (*ādhāra*).
This also corresponds to the case where the person adorns the dharma; here, the "shadow" is the object of adornment and the "flower" is the agent of adornment.

Within this, secondly, looking downward at the two [subsequent] sections: [The text continues: ...the *Mahāvaipulya* (Great Vaipulya) is the object of adornment, while the middle section is the agent of adornment. Second, looking downward at the two [subsequent] sections...
Furthermore, the phrase "adorned by causes with a view toward the fruit" refers to the Buddha as well; here, through a concise illustration, the fruit adorns the cause because they adorn one another.
Thus, the two characters "Huayan" (Flower Adornment) taken together also serve as a metaphor for the aforementioned four characters.
Regarding the explanation of "adornment," specifically within the section explaining the character "yan" (adornment), it refers solely to the meaning of mutual adornment.
The metaphors for the substance [of the text] will be fully explained below.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* (Sū) that "the ten meanings are explained in brief," one asks: since the categories of meaning are already fully manifested, why is it further said to be "brief"?

Answer: Although a single word of the Dharma-gate is such that even the oceans of ink could not exhaust its writing, and although each [meaning] is fully manifested, the ten [meanings] are still explained in brief.

Since the meanings are intended to express the inexhaustible, is it not appropriate to call this "concise"? Nevertheless, although each is explained through ten meanings, their structural forms are not uniform;
they are further divided into five sections. First, regarding the three characters *mahāvaipulya*: each is explained by classifying them according to their respective meanings and functions.
Thus, "great" (*mahā*) signifies that all ten meanings are eternal and pervasive; "direction" (*diś*) signifies that all ten meanings serve as a guide and support.
Broadly speaking, all ten [terms] are manifold; in meaning, they are the same as the two [preceding] Buddhas. Regarding the word "Buddha" (佛), it is identical in essence;

the commentary explains that while the seven characters are assigned to the ten meanings, their essence is entirely identical rather than merely identical in meaning. Third, regarding the word "Flower" (華), the dharma and the metaphor are similar; the commentary explains that the ten meanings of the Buddhas resemble the ten flowers.
Fourth, regarding the word "Adornment" (嚴), there is mutual adornment between subject and object; the commentary explains that these characters are identical in essence.

Therefore, while the characters of the Five Classics are restricted to their respective specific meanings, the sub-commentary below states that although the seven characters are explained interchangeably, the ten meanings of the character "sūtra" (經) are not so explained.
This is because their general purport differs, their essential form and function are not uniform, and the meanings they manifest are indeterminate.
Alternatively, it may be that although the character "sūtra" is not explained by the other six characters, the other characters are explained by means of the character "sūtra."
Because there are six characters, the Greatness (*mahat*) and so forth are also explained in relation to one another according to the teaching.
In the commentary, under "the Greatness of Essential Nature" (*svabhāva-mahattva*), it means that the principle of the unobstructed fusion of all phenomena constitutes the essence;

its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and functions (*vṛtti*) are all identical to the true nature (*tathatā*), and each possesses the meaning of being eternal and pervasive. The statement that this is the character "Great" (*ma*) intends to reveal that, although—
The "enumeration of characteristics, functions, and so forth" which are "constant and pervasive" refers exclusively to the large characters within the title [of the treatise].

Regarding the statement in the *Chao* (Commentary) that "the ancients also each had ten meanings," the *Tanxuan ji* (Record of Exploring the Profundities) states: first, greatness of object; second, greatness of mind;
third, greatness of practice; fourth, greatness of stages; fifth, greatness of cause; sixth, greatness of fruit; seventh, greatness of essence; eighth, greatness of function; ninth... [and so on].
Regarding the ten great meanings of the Teaching, I shall now clarify the intention of the Lower Qingliang [Zhiyi]:

that a single phrase of the Dharma endowed with all virtues contains everything, just as a single drop of the ocean possesses the flavor of all hundred rivers. Furthermore, this drop is not identical to those other drops;

for now, I shall clarify this through the title alone, as the principle can be understood by extension to the texts of the individual sections and so forth. This should be made manifest through its meaning.
Furthermore, relying on the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as it functions through mutual dependence, we shall now interpret the text according to a single gate:

the character "Da" (大) serves as the condition (*pratyaya*), while the remaining six characters serve as the arising (*samutpāda*). Since that which arises does not exist apart from the condition, and since that which arises is entirely contained within the condition, the character "Da" encompasses the other six characters;
all six characters are within the character "Da. Therefore, it is said that all seven characters are "Da," and they are not [separate].

This means that if one were to entirely lose [the meaning of] "Great" and instead take the remaining six characters—referring to "constant" (*chang*) and "pervasive" (*bian*)—as the conditions, then such meanings as "normative" (*gui*) and "sustaining" (*chi*) would all be constant and pervasive, yet they would not be mutually conflated.
Thus, the *Xuanjing* states: "Because it possesses the ten kinds of inexhaustibility, it is called 'Great'.

If, however, one takes "greatness of essence" (*ti-da*) as the condition, then what dharma would not be the essence? All subsequent cases should be understood accordingly. Therefore, the *Xingyuan Chao* says:
Within each of the seven characters, there is the meaning of all seven characters. The *Niepan jing chao* states:

"Regarding the phrase 'that which is called Great,' the following [passage] proves the two meanings above," etc. This addresses the question: "The title of the sutra generally mentions only the character 'Great' (Dà);
how do we know this refers to the 'Greatness of Essence' (Tǐdà)? The answer is that since the text of the current sutra is incomplete, one must take the text from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* as a supplement.
For example, in that sūtra, the Buddha himself explains the name of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Since his explanation of the word "Great" (*mahā*) states that it is "eternal and pervasive," it is clear that this "Greatness" is precisely the Greatness of Essence (*dharmatā-mahattva*).

This is because the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* explains the Greatness of Essence as having True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its essence. Thus, by employing the texts of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, one establishes the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

The meaning of this is the ultimate in subtlety. Regarding the statement that "first realizing the meaning of permanence is *nirvāṇa*," the third [section] and so forth, the aforementioned commentary states:
"The Buddha said" and below praises the excellence of the teaching. Following the text of the sūtra, it is divided into beginning, middle, and end as superior, middling, and inferior;
because it accords with the capacity of the faculties and can give rise to the mind of practice, it is called "excellent. In the second phrase, there is the flavor of the meaning.
"Profound" (*gambhīra*) refers to the meaning (*artha*); it is called "flavor" (*rasa*) because its meaning differs from that of names and words in other contexts.

It is able to nourish the mind and cause people to feel affection and joy, just like worldly delicacies; therefore, it is called "flavor. Regarding the third phrase, "its phrasing is excellent" (*suvyañjana*):

this means the diction and expression are skillful, being neither redundant nor deficient; thus it is said the phrasing is excellent. Regarding the fourth phrase, "purely endowed with *brahma*-... [the text continues].

The practice being perfected clarifies the perfection of conduct; the treasury of jewels being without deficiency clarifies the perfection of principle; and its being pure and complete also clarifies the perfection of cause.
Because the treasury of jewels is without deficiency, it clarifies the fulfillment of the fruit. Since this sutra possesses such excellence, it exhorts one to uphold it.

From here below is the second section, which distinguishes the merit of the sutra’s title so as to inspire joy in its upholding. First, there is the general command to listen and permission to proclaim it.
In the formal exposition below, there are eight successive sections. The first correctly sets forth the greatness of the sūtra’s merit, which is termed "constant" (*nitya*).
Based on this name, its great virtues are distinguished. This sūtra possesses six meanings; the explanation of "greatness" has already been analyzed above (referring to the first commentary).
Now, let us first clarify it through the meaning of "constancy," as in the passage beginning with "the eight great rivers" and following.

The Nirvāṇa Sūtra explains the virtues of Nirvāṇa by means of a preceding analogy (in its third fascicle, the "Chapter on Life," it says: "First is the Gaṅgā, second is the Yamunā, third is the Sarayū, fourth is the Aciravatī, fifth is the Mahī, sixth is the Sindhu, seventh is the Vakṣu, and eighth is the Sītā.

These eight great rivers, along with all the small streams, all enter the great ocean. Now, these eight great rivers are said to each flow from one side of Lake Anavatapta, forming four great rivers. After flowing forty *li* outwards, each branch further divides into four directions, forming twenty rivers. That only eight are mentioned here follows the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*. ) Nirvāṇa is named for its discernment of the virtues of Nirvāṇa. First, it uses the analogy [of the rivers]: (In the third fascicle, the "Chapter on Life," it says: "First is the Gaṅgā, second is the Yamunā, third is the Sarayū, fourth is the Aciravatī, fifth is the Mahī, sixth is the Sindhu, seventh is the Vakṣu, and eighth is the Sītā.

These eight great rivers and all the small streams all enter the great ocean. However, these eight great rivers are said to each emerge from one of the four sides of Lake Anavatapta, forming four great rivers. After the four rivers have flowed out forty *li*, each further branches into four directions, forming twenty rivers. That we speak of only eight here is based on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.)

Passing through the five rivers of the East, all people see them clearly; as for the other three great rivers, their names are widely renowned, while the twelve small rivers are neither seen nor heard of;

therefore, only the eight great rivers are mentioned. Subsequently, this sutra likewise [proceeds] to break down appearances and incline toward tranquility. Since what is elucidated in this sutra is the same as the aforementioned eight rivers, it says:
"In this way, subduing afflictions, one leaves behind the demon of afflictions and the nature of all demons, and extinguishes the remaining three demons. Thereafter, it continues below.
To realize the mark of relinquishment means to verify the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) so that delusion is eliminated and no delusion remains; this can be called "relinquishment.

Because the mark itself is difficult to relinquish—just as one’s own body and life are—it may instead be understood as being able to set aside one’s body and life, as in the sense of attaining accord with the Great Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, the following summarizes this point.
The phrase "Therefore, Master Sheng’s Preface says" serves as a scriptural citation.

It specifically refers to the concluding passage which states, "Since it is already called 'Great,' it is therefore termed 'Eternal' (Chang)," thereby proving that the aforementioned [text] fully possesses the meaning of eternity. Thus, the *Shuchao* states: "This correctly accords with the present intention.
If one were to explain that passage, it means that when the natural truth is realized through wisdom, it should likewise accord like the fitting together of two seals.
When the Truth realized has not yet been realized, it is already true without deviation; once realized, how could that realized Truth be subject to change?
Its unchanging essence is profound, quiescent, and ever-illuminating. Thus, whether the Truth is realized or unrealized, there is no difference;
it is only due to the deluded sentiments of the self that one becomes estranged from the Truth.

The principle is such that the realm of ultimate truth does not reside within the self; if one can truly enter into it through cultivation and inquiry, one will turn back from delusion and return to the ultimate principle.
Although one returns to the ultimate and recovers the fundamental reality, this has no beginning.
If there were truly a beginning, there would necessarily be an end; if there were truly a beginning and an end, the principle of true permanence would thereby become obscured.

If one seeks its underlying intent, it is that my original assembly did not possess the essence of quiescent illumination, whereas the present assembly possesses the essence of quiescent illumination, which emerged from antiquity;
thus, nothing is more primordial than the Great. Therefore, it is called "constant.
Since it is constant, it must extinguish the burdens of birth and death; hence it is said to be *parinirvāṇa*. *Parinirvāṇa*...
"Nirvāṇa" is simply "Nebhāna," a difference in the lightness or heaviness of the Sanskrit pronunciation.

In the twenty-fifth fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, it is explained that because it is profound, it is called "Great. Now, since the meaning of profundity establishes the preceding meaning of permanence, it is said:
"Because its essence transcends the realm of permanence. This means that although it is called "permanent," it emerges from beyond conceptual thought; how could it be otherwise?
Can it be taken as an ordinary object and thus perceived? Or can it transcend the realm of the ordinary to manifest its profound meaning through its general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*)?
To say "like the eldest among men" is to manifest its excellence, and is therefore called "Great. Now, by means of this supreme meaning, the preceding sense of "eternal" is established.
Regarding the phrase "there is not even a single dharma," the *Lüchao* (Brief Commentary), fascicle three, states:
This meaning refers to the sequence of significance rather than the sequence of time; it is called "Great" because it is foremost.
It is like a person who is called "elder" because they were born first; this does not refer to physical stature when speaking of "great" or "small.
Therefore, Laozi says [in the *Daodejing*]: "There was something undifferentiated and complete, born before heaven and earth," which serves as proof.
Its prior meaning is that it is strongly designated by the name "Great" (*mahān*); because there is a prior meaning beneath this "Great," the commentary states:
"Below that, they take emptiness and non-being as the Way, and thus call it 'Great. It was born before heaven and earth.
Therefore, we do not adopt that interpretation here; rather, we take its greatness and its verbal expression as proof of this truth for all.
The essence of the Dharma lies in the meaning of being "great" and "foremost," and for this reason it is cited here.
In the passage from the *Caturlakṣaṇa-parivarta* (Chapter on the Four Characteristics) of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Buddha tells Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
"One who possesses four virtues is able to preach the *Mahānirvāṇa Sūtra* for others: first, one's own practice is not deviant; second, one can correctly guide others."
Answering according to the questions posed, these four virtuous causes and conditions penetrate the nature of the faculties;

since this single fascicle of the sutra extensively investigates and explains these four dharmas, it is titled the "Chapter on the Four Characteristics. According to the *Niepan shu* (Commentary on the Nirvana Sutra) by Master Huiyuan, cited in the *Chao*, the second section states:
"First, explaining the great meaning. Regarding the initial term 'Great' (*da*), its nature is vast and extensive."
The extensive explanation of "great" (*mahat*) has two parts. First, explaining "great" by means of "constant": this is merely a metaphor for being constant;

it does not include a formal application (*upanaya*), yet its meaning is similar to what was stated above regarding that which is called "great" being termed "constant. Third, explaining "great" by means of "superiority": there are two kinds of superiority.

First, regarding the phrase "if this person abides in the True Dharma," they are called superior among humans because they abide in the True Dharma; thus, they are superior due to their abiding. Second...
It is superior because it is fully endowed with virtues. Regarding this, the *Niepan shu* (Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra), Volume One, Part One, states:
"There are six great meanings: first, it is called 'Great' because it is eternal; as the text below says, 'The Great is named the Eternal. Second, it is called 'Great' because it is supreme;
as in the world, those who are superior people are called 'Great Men'; as the text below says, 'If this person can bring peace...'"
Because those who abide in the True Dharma are the most excellent among humans, Great Nirvāṇa is likewise so called. It is "Great" for three reasons: first, because it is extensive;
as the subsequent text says, "Great" means vast and broad, its substance exhausting the entirety of the Dharma-realm, and its nature being expansive. Fourth, because it is manifold;
as the subsequent text says, "It is like a great treasury containing many rare treasures; Nirvāṇa is likewise manifold."
It is called "Great" (mahā) because it contains various wonderful dharmas and precious jewels; it is called "Great" because it is high, as the text below states:
"For example, because a great mountain cannot be ascended by ordinary people, it is called a 'great mountain. Nirvāṇa is likewise;

because ordinary beings, followers of the two vehicles, and even those in the tenth stage cannot reach it, it is called 'Great. It is called "Great" because it is profound. It is called "Great" for these six reasons.
Just as the ocean is called a "great sea" because its abyss is deep, the text below states: "Great" refers to that which is inconceivable;

being an abyss so deep it is difficult to fathom is what is called "inconceivable. [Commentary: Now, by means of "many," [the text] addresses the application of the term from below to resolve an objection.
One might ask: "Since that sūtra describes 'great' through six meanings, such as 'many' and so forth, why does it [only]..."

"Is it drawn forth as eternal and pervasive?"—this is the explanation. To say "many" refers to its function (*yòng*); this is subsumed within the three [aspects of] the Greatness of Function (*yòng-dà*).

This explains the Greatness of Essence (*tǐ-dà*), and therefore "many" is not mentioned. To say "high" refers to its fruit (*guǒ*); this is subsumed within the four [aspects of] the Greatness of Fruit (*guǒ-dà*).
This explains the Greatness of Essence, and therefore "high" is not mentioned. As for the remaining two meanings, "profound" and "supreme,"...
Since the meaning of "eternal" is already contained within [the term] "pervasive," only the two meanings of "pervasive" and "eternal" are used to explain the "greatness of essence.

Furthermore, the *Chao* (Excerpts) treats this as a separate passage because the *Shu* (Commentary) states: "Its nature is vast and expansive like empty space," which resembles a single textual unit from the Sūtra.
Thus, it distinguishes them: the first phrase, "its nature is vast and expansive," constitutes one textual unit, while the second phrase...
It is like the phrase "just as space is a distinct location," which uses the pervasiveness of space as a metaphor for the pervasiveness of the essence of reality (*dharmatā*).
This establishes its name "Great" (*mahā*) by virtue of its universal presence.

However, according to that sutra, the text should read "liberation is also thus," which seems to use the nature of space being free from oppression as a metaphor for the meaning of *nirvāṇa* being free from oppression; I shall now borrow this [metaphor].
The meaning of the text’s metaphor for "pervasion" can be understood through reflection.

Regarding the second point in the *Sūtra*, under the section on the "Greatness of Characteristics," the text merely explains the characteristics of the common and the distinct; that the Great [Nature] possesses constancy and pervasiveness should be understood according to the previous explanation.
The Commentary: Master Huiyuan’s [classification] below serves to distinguish the spurious from the authentic. One might ask:
"Master Huiyuan’s three kinds of *nirvāṇa* also consist of essence, characteristic, and function; how does this differ from the present [teaching]? To distinguish this, it says:

Master Huiyuan’s "three greatnesses" (*san da*) apply to both cause and fruit, because the *nirvāṇa* of intrinsic purity exists for both ordinary beings and sages. Here, however, we clarify that which the Buddha has realized.
Within the Dharma, there are three greats, which exist only as the fruit.

Regarding the phrase "the activity is universally pervasive" in the Commentary (*Shu*), the *Xingyuan Shu* (Commentary on the Vows) states: "Because the essence encompasses all-pervasiveness. Its sub-commentary (*Chao*) explains:
"This refers to the aforementioned characteristic of being boundless; because [each] pervades the essence, and each is identical to the essence, they constitute the great function, one by one."
It is able to encompass and pervade; one enters into all as pervasion, and all enter into one as encompassment.
They interpenetrate and intersect, mutually unimpeded, layered upon layer without end. Here, "zhou" (周) means pervasive, and "pu" (普) means universally encompassing.

In the *Commentary on the Sūtra*, in the lower section of the "Chapter on the Four Marks," it says: "Kāśyapa asked again... This is a restatement of what the Buddha had already said, presented as a question.
"If the Buddha has already delivered [Yashodharā]... This is a difficulty raised based on the traces [of his past actions].

"Yaśodharā" means "Holder of Renown. "By these causes and conditions... This is a doubt regarding the reality of the traces. "I only pray that... and so forth, is the request for the Buddha to provide a comprehensive explanation.
The Buddha first rebukes the difficult words of the objection below; then he explains how the meaning of the explanation is established.

How does he clarify that the matter of taking a consort and fathering a son is the manifestation of the functional power (*guṇa-vṛtti*) arising from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, rather than actual afflictions? How does he explain the characteristics?
He provides a general enumeration of the manifestations of the functional power arising from *nirvāṇa* as a category to explain it: the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* is capable of establishing [these qualities].
"Great Meaning" (*mahārtha*) refers to the general enumeration of categories in response; "meaning" (*artha*) here signifies function (*prayojana*). "Establishing" (*kṛta*) means to initiate.

The Great Parinirvāṇa is able to initiate great functions, and since these functional characteristics are not of a single kind, they are termed "establishing the Great Meaning. Below, this will be extensively analyzed. Within this section, there are first four distinct parts:

(1) commanding the audience to listen and exhorting them to speak while cautioning against harboring doubts; (2) [the subsequent] exposition for their sake; (3) [the next] exposition; and (4) [the final] exposition. First, [it] raises the Bodhi...

The Great Parinirvāṇa of the stage of Bodhisattva can establish the great purpose, which is analogous to that of the Tathāgata. [Regarding] "I have long dwelt in this Great Nirvāṇa," there are two parts:

first, it clarifies how the Bodhisattva realizes the truth and gives rise to transformations, up to the statement that "the Bodhisattva dwells in Nirvāṇa," which follows accordingly within the Great Nirvāṇa. At the beginning, there are two [sections]: first, it clarifies the Bodhisattva’s realization of the truth and the arising of transformations; second, it explains the meaning of dwelling in Nirvāṇa.

Regarding the initial section, it clarifies that from the time the Bodhisattva realizes the truth and gives rise to transformations, up to the words "the Bodhisattva dwells in Nirvāṇa," [this occurs] in accordance with the Great Nirvāṇa.
Because it is divided into sections and serves as a basis for realization, it is called a "dwelling. That which enters into the nature of nirvāṇa is a dharma that functions through conditions;
therefore, upon entering therein, there is mindless emanation, continuing even up to the second clarification concerning the Buddha’s ability to establish meaning.
Having first clarified how the Tathāgata dwells in great nirvāṇa and manifests various emanations, the subsequent text extensively explains these emanations.

The twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) and so forth (the fourth section, which is currently missing, is cited here). The *Chao* [commentary] states that the sutra first discusses this in terms of the function of the fruit, and subsequently distinguishes it by means of "this" and "that.
The present intention in clarifying that "it is the function of the essence itself" is to reveal that the three great aspects (*san-da*) of this sutra are mutually identical.
Because the character "broad" (*guang*) is used here to explain the character "great" (*da*), it is said below that the Buddha-fruit exists, thereby harmonizing [the two].
This is explained in two ways. First: since that sutra speaks of the function of the fruit (*phala*), how does it prove that this is the function of the essence itself?

The explanation says: because the marks and functions of the Buddha-fruit mentioned in the following text all arise from being inherently possessed from the beginning, the marks and functions of the Buddha are themselves the inherently possessed marks and functions;
therefore, the function of the fruit is used to prove the aforementioned [identity].

The essence and its function are two; one might ask: "Since the seven characters explain each other, and the subsequent explanation of the character 'Buddha' (佛) contains ten meanings where the Buddha-fruit (*buddhatva*) also possesses both aspect (*nimitta*) and function (*vṛtti*), how does this differ from that sutra? Answer:

Although the Buddha-fruit here possesses both aspect and function, they are all inherently present (*prakṛti-stha*); therefore, it differs from that [sutra]. Second, the explanation according to general application (*anuvṛtti*).

The commentary states that the "Greatness" of the four fruits refers to wisdom (*jñāna*), abandonment (*prahāṇa*), the support (*āśraya*), and the supported (*āśrita*). Wisdom is *bodhi*; abandonment is *nirvāṇa*; the support is the land; and the supported is the Buddha-body.
That they "pervade the entire dharma-realm" explains their greatness by means of their ubiquity.

Regarding the meaning of "constancy," the commentary holds that great wisdom is primary, while the remaining practices are subordinate. Just as the blind require sight, wisdom is like the eyes; because it functions through wisdom, [the other qualities] are able to proceed.
Because they reach the other shore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the first five perfections are like blind people, while the sixth, Prajñā,
is like one who has eyes. If one does not obtain the guidance of Prajñā, the first five will fall into evil realms and fail to achieve transcendence from the world.
Commentary on the Seven [Points]: Regarding the "Greatness of the Teaching," there are two intended meanings. First, the *Xingyuan Chao* states:
"Whenever a single assembly or a single section of meaning is expounded, it is always concluded by stating that it is likewise taught throughout the ten directions. Second, the *Jingwei Chao* states:

"This means that every single word and phrase within this sutra is a teaching that universally pervades all quarters; therefore, its extension throughout the ten directions is also a designation [of its universal nature]."

Because this discourse on nature (*dhātu*) permeates the three periods of time and pervades the ten directions—and because the ten directions likewise permeate the three periods of time—it is said to be "layer upon layer" (*chóngchóng*).
Regarding the eighth point, the *Yìdà shíxíngyuàn cāo* states: "Its inexhaustible layering is certainly beyond words;

yet within the gate of following appearances (*suíxiàng mén*), it is also explained in terms of both the shallow and the deep. Within the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmiḥ*), the ten evils and ten virtues are extensively clarified, which encompasses the realms of humans and devas."
The "Vehicle" section, the "Four Noble Truths" chapter, and the tenfold Four Noble Truths of the fifth stage encompass the Śrāvaka Vehicle;
the tenfold Twelve Links of Dependent Origination of the sixth stage encompass the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle;

and the eight divisions of the *Prajñāpāramitā* are fully expounded within the three-day verses and one or two sections of the "Appearance" chapter of the *Nirvāṇa* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras. Such categories of matters are not limited to these alone.
It may be fully explained.
Ninth, "greatness of the object" (*ālambana-mahattva*): this refers to taking the sentient beings to be converted as the great object. Tenth, "greatness of activity" (*karma-mahattva*):
this refers to the fact that the aforementioned activity of the converter—which takes the aforementioned object of conversion (sentient beings) as its domain—is constant and pervasive.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the Commentary (*śāstra*), the text below is divided into two main sections: first, an exposition of the "great nature" (*mahatva*) of the four treatises;
second, from "Now, the Great Nature of the Essence" (*tattva-mahatva*) in this commentary, the ten great natures of the commentary are correlated with those seven great natures.

Thus, by saying "and so forth," the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (Compendium of the Great Vehicle) is included. This root treatise was composed by Asaṅga, while its commentary was composed by Sthiramati; these two works were originally circulated separately.
Later, the Bodhisattva Sthiramati compiled and merged [the texts] into a single volume named the *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*.
As for the phrase "The *Śāstra* does not explain it extensively," this is a commentarial gloss (*śāstravṛtti*).
Regarding that [text], it provides a general explanation of the term "great" (*mahat*), stating that it refers to the seven kinds of greatness.
Because their natures are mutually associated, they are not explained separately and at length. Regarding the phrase "thoroughly understanding the vastness, etc.":
the Sanskrit term *pudgala* is translated here as "one who repeatedly undergoes rebirth" (*shuququ*). This refers to one who repeatedly creates karma and takes up various realms of existence;
it specifically denotes persons. When referring to all phenomena (*dharma*), it means thoroughly understanding the two kinds of non-existence regarding both persons and phenomena.
Because it accords with my own principle: ▲ The Commentary states that this is largely identical to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* in four respects: (1) one dharma is entirely the same;

(2) "mind" (*citta*) is equivalent to the "arousing of the mind" (*cittotpāda*) in the *Yogācāra*; (3) regarding "faith and understanding" (*adhimukti*), this text refers to both faith (*śraddhā*) and superior resolve (*adhimukti*), whereas the *Yogācāra* mentions only superior resolve without mentioning faith—this is the slight difference;
(4) "pure mind" (*viśuddha-citta*) and the "superior intention" (*adhyāśaya*) of the *Yogācāra* differ in name but are identical in meaning.

Because it is pure and exclusively wholesome, it is the pure mind (*śuddhacitta*); this mind is without regression or progression and is uninterrupted, which is precisely the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*).
The fifth and sixth names are identical in substance. The seventh, "fruition" (*phala*), refers to the perfect realization of yoga (*yoga-pariniṣpatti*).

The Commentary states that if one correlates this with the *Abhidharma* (Dharma-lakṣaṇa), it refers to the synthesis of the seven great natures from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
