The phrase "that which follows below" refers to the citation of the sutra; "should be for the sake of desire" below refers to the actual text of the sutra being cited;

"thus it is established" below refers to the terminology of the *Chao* (Excerpts); "pointing to what belongs to" (below all should be understood accordingly). If these are assigned to a single title, this corresponds to the character "Adornment" (*yan*): because giving can adorn both oneself and others; because giving fulfills the minds of others;
because the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) delight sentient beings; and because the essence of the fruit of giving is the adornment of one's own mind. Second is Precept (*śīla*).
The letter *la* and the seven stages of expedient means (*saptayogācāra*) both represent the universal character of the precepts;

because they universally cease all evil, they purify the body, and because they universally give rise to all that is wholesome, there is nothing that does not arise in accordance with the intentions of oneself and others.

Since its boundless and skillful application is universally pervasive, the form of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) cannot be perceived. The three types of patience (*kṣānti*) are the letter *bu*, which signifies "thorough investigation" (*tattvavicaya*).
Since the profound realization of the non-arising of all phenomena is not the Buddha’s bodhi, how could it be a profound realization? Furthermore, the *Fajiepin Shuchao* states:

"Patience includes both the patience [of endurance] and the patience [of insight] regarding principle; thus, through inconceivable attainment, one acquires the body of majestic power (*vīrya-bala-kāya*).

Because the virtue of patience fills the interior while majestic power manifests externally, and because they now fully accord with a single principle, it is assigned solely to the Bodhi-body. Fourth is diligence (*vīrya*).
That is to say, because the seven characters in total provide the benefit of the teachings, principles, and faculties without ceasing, their majestic power is all the more profound.
Furthermore, the *Fajiepin Sūchao* (Commentary on the Dharma-realm Chapter) states: "Because it urges forward and encourages the myriad practices, it is able to excel in accomplishing the Bodhi-body.
This is likewise another principle for the Body of Majestic Power (*vibhūti-kāya*). The five dhyānas, eight vows, and two pāramitās are all "flower" characters, and they are all [included therein].
Because the cause is dhyāna and it consists of a single mind, it is the supreme among the perfections of merit;

because the fruit of this meritorious virtue is peerless, it is called the "body without equal. Because one vows to reach the end of the future and dwell through infinite kalpas, one dwells throughout all kalpas.
The six *prajñāpāramitās* are the character "Da" (大), for they illuminate the true nature; the nine powers (*bala*) are the character "Jing" (經), for they maintain it.

Because they are not extinguished, their power cannot be shaken; they transcend all things. The ten *jñāna-pāramitās* (wisdom-perfections) take the character "fang" (方) as their nature because wisdom is the virtue of inherent quality (*svabhāva-guṇa*).
Since wisdom exhausts all phenomena and manifests according to sentient beings, the ten characters are assigned based on their meaning.
Although they do not follow a sequential order, the principle of the ten bodies of the ten Buddhas is fully visible within them. At the end of the *Chao* (Commentary), it says:
The "lower" [section] refers to the sequential arrangement (*xingbu*), wherein the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*) as causes differentiate and form the ten bodies.

This "lower" section, by contrast, refers to the perfect fusion (*yuanrong*), wherein all causes collectively constitute the Buddha-body; this is the distinction between perfect fusion and sequential arrangement. Regarding the phrase "immediately perfect and pure":

below, there is no practice that is not complete, with all myriad virtues suddenly and fully present; above, there is no fruition that is not realized. The "upper" [section] speaks in terms of manifesting characteristics, while the "lower" [section]...

The *Shizhu jingyishu* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Ten Flowers) assigns the ten flowers to the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) based on the principle of mutual manifestation through dharma and metaphor, explaining them according to the doctrine of sequential progression (*xingbu*).
However, if one considers them from the perspective of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), then each and every perfection and each and every practice fully embodies the meaning of the ten flowers;
they are harmoniously integrated and unimpeded, such that there is no need for further textual elaboration, as this can be understood through the mind alone.

The *Chao* (Commentary) cites the "flower that draws forth fruit" (*yin-kuo-hua*) as a metaphor for what follows; according to the *Shu* (Sub-commentary), the flower that draws forth fruit represents the myriad practices (*wan-xing*) that adorn the body, while the flower represents merit (*gong-de*).
The *Chao* states that it is not merely as in the *Shu*, but also takes merit to represent the two causes. Since the character "flower" (*hua*) is a metaphor for cause, it says:
the "producing cause" (*sheng-yin*) is like a seed producing a manifest sprout, while the "revealing cause" (*liao-yin*) is like a lamp illuminating an object.
These two forms of non-obstruction (*asanga*) are vastly different from other schools and serve as the causal basis for the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*).
In the *Jingxing pin* (Chapter on Pure Conduct), Part 2, it is stated that only supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and the like are cited as proof—using flowers rather than grasses or trees—as evidence.

However, in the section following "Supernatural Powers," there is an explanation that addresses a doubt: since these powers function within the prior fruit and coexist with the fruit, one might wonder: "How could supernatural powers not be pervasive? [The text clarifies that they are indeed pervasive.]

This explanation is based on that very cause. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "like the splendor of gold and jade," just as the splendor of gold and jade exists simultaneously with the body, so too do the marks such as the supernormal powers exist simultaneously with the Buddha-body.

The commentary states, "The ten flowers above collectively adorn one Buddha," which means that while the flowers that serve as the adornments are ten in number, the Buddha who is the object of adornment remains one;
because the manner in which they are adorned differs, the principle of "ten" is established. The *Xingyuan Chao* says:
"The ten flowers are the ten pāramitās; these ten pāramitās collectively adorn one Buddha."
The commentary states, "To distinguish them from those below," which clarifies this by means of an analogy.
For example, suppose one uses ten jewels to adorn a single golden Buddha, and subsequently uses ten jewels to adorn a single silver Buddha.

Although the ten jewels used as the adornments are identical, they are differentiated based on their relationship to the objects they adorn. Thus, the ten jewels that adorn the golden Buddha belong exclusively to the golden Buddha.
The ten jewels capable of adorning the Buddha who is not of silver, and so forth, are likewise applied to the ten dharmas; furthermore,
when the causes of the ten flowers equally adorn the one Dharma-realm Buddha, and subsequently the one Original-nature Buddha, and so on,
then with respect to the ten Buddhas they adorn, these causes of the ten flowers are divided into ten distinct capacities for adornment.
The causes of the flowers differ because they adorn the Dharma-realm, whereas the ten flowers of the Buddha do not adorn his original nature;

thus, the commentary states that there are ten meanings regarding their differing modes of adornment. This means that by taking the ten flowers and applying them universally across the ten Buddhas, ten meanings are established.
Here, one takes only the sense of "adornment" (zhuāngyán) and does not take the sense of "ornamentation" (yán).

The characters signify "Great Wisdom. Regarding the second section of the *Commentary* (Chao), which provides a detailed explanation: it further uses ten kinds of lotus meanings to sequentially adorn the ten Buddhas mentioned in the "Leaving the World" (*Lishi Jian*) chapter.
Specifically: first, the meaning of "containing the fruit within a single bud" adorns the Dharma-realm Buddha;

second, the meaning of "purity of light" adorns the Innate Nature Buddha; and so on, up to the tenth, the meaning of "full blossoming," which adorns the Mind Buddha. These are the words and their meanings.

The principle that those who attain Buddhahood in a single lifetime is identical to what was previously cited from the "Universal Eye" (Puyan) section of the Dharmadhātu-parivarta has already been explained.
Since the two types of ten meanings— the general and the specific—

above have already been transformed from the meaning of "flowers" into the meaning of "ornaments" and applied to the seven characters of the title to demonstrate their mutual explanation without differing from what preceded, this can be understood through reflection.

Regarding the statement in the Commentary, "Furthermore, there are ten meanings, etc.": previously, it was only held that the Buddha of the *Avataṃsaka* (Flower Ornament) is the "flower" (*huā*) which acts as the adornment, while the Buddha is the "adorned" (*suǒyán*).
Now, because cause and effect and so forth all possess mutual adornment, this is fundamentally different from what was said before. First, regarding "using the cause to adorn the fruit, etc.":
the cause acts as the adornment and the fruit acts as the adorned; this specifically reveals the nature of the adorned, and therefore [the discussion] proceeds below.

The commentary states, "It is for the purpose of completing the person. One should understand that the nine subsequent examples are likewise so. The phrase "this Flower Adornment of the Buddha" is a general designation;
therefore, the *Chao* says: "Using the cause to adorn the fruit is the Flower Adornment of the Buddha."

The *Chao* (Commentary) likewise states that this refers to the section below; that is, these ten meanings primarily take the sense of mutual adornment (*hu yan*), while also incorporating the meaning of the combined explanation found within the subsequent section on the distinct explanations of the names.
The *Shu* (Sub-commentary), fearing prolixity, has supplemented this with the *Chao*. Question:

If it is the same as the section below, how does it differ from what follows? Answer: The section below takes up the explanation of the names (*shi ming*), whereas this [section] takes up the mutual adornment; therefore, they are not the same.
It is also said that if one explains the essence [of the name] by means of the subsequent [passage], it follows the formal structure of a commentary.

In this context, the two types of analysis—*karmadhāraya* (appositional compound) and *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound)—share the same terminology as the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (characteristics of phenomena), yet their meanings are entirely different. The *karmadhāraya* analysis is based on the principle of perfect interfusion (*yuánróng*), while the *tatpuruṣa* analysis is based on the principle of sequential arrangement (*xíngbù);
these can be understood through the five pairs [of categories]. As for the first usage, "using causes to adorn the fruit," the flower is taken as the agent [of the action].
The Buddha is that which is adorned (*vyūha*), and the Buddha’s wondrous fruit is obtained through causes; therefore, this is the meaning of "adornment" (*vyūha*).

Consequently, because the fruit of Buddhahood is manifested from the cause of the flower, it is named "Flower-Buddha. Following the commentary on the *Buddhāvataṃsaka*, the term "Buddha" is applied to the Flower below, as should be understood throughout.
Regarding the two instances of "Flower-Adornment of the Buddha," there is a fundamental text, though one character is missing from the manuscript.
The *Yanjing zhiyuan shu* states that because this is the Flower Adornment (*Huayan*) of the Buddha, it is thus the fruit adorning the cause.

Third, "adorned by the person" means that having cultivated extraordinary causes in the past, one now attains the fruit-Buddha, who is then able to adorn and manifest the essence and function of the Dharma.
Fourth, "adorned by the Dharma" means [adorned] by the Dharma of the essence and function of the Great Vaipulya.

The first [aspect] adorns the cause so that it may be perfected, thereby making the fruit sublime; the fifth is the adornment of function by means of essence, and the sixth is the adornment of essence by means of function.

If the *Zhenyuan shu* states: "The fifth is the vastness of the Great, and the sixth is the Greatness of the Vast," this is because the term "Vaipulya" (方廣) has meanings that apply to both its analytical and synthetic aspects.
When spoken of simply as "Vast" (廣), it refers to function; when combined as "Vaipulya," it likewise encompasses both.

As for "function" (yòng), since it corresponds to the preceding "essence" (tǐ) as the Great Character (dàzì), one should likewise follow the previous commentary, which states that the Great Square [character] is the essence and the Broad character is the function;
thus, one should understand it accordingly. Although the wording appears or disappears [in different versions], there is no contradiction in the underlying principle.
Seventh, the essence adorns the marks (xiàng); eighth, the marks adorn the essence; ninth, the meaning adorns the teaching. This is because [it is stated] in the *Sūtra Commentary* (Shù).
That which is expressed (the signified) is inconceivable, as its reflection is beyond discussion; that which expresses it (the signifier) is beyond words, as its reflection is beyond thought.
Because they manifest one another, all the preceding points may be understood according to the commentary (*śūtra*); therefore, the sub-commentary (*chao*) does not explain them.

Regarding the tenth point, "The various causes mutually adorn one another," because there are many meanings, it is explained briefly. The commentary cites "meditation and wisdom mutually adorning one another" and so forth, encompassing what precedes.

Regarding the four instances cited in the *Zhidu chao*, where two instances each are raised before and after, and the middle two or six instances are likewise treated—just as it is here, so it is with all myriad practices.
Since these names are mutually related, they may also be explained accordingly; thus it is said that there are "many meanings.
Furthermore, these various causes adorn one another, and according to the *Zhenyuan shu*, they should properly be situated within the two characters "Huayan" (Flower Adornment).
▲ Regarding the first four items forming pairs, the subsequent section addresses a doubt. The doubt asks:

"If five items are paired with ten meanings to manifest their mutual perfection, why do the first four form pairs while the last one does not? This [section] cites that doubt and explains it; therein are two points.
First, it is not possible to use the expressive words (*vācaka*) to describe those expressed meanings (*vācya*) in such a way as to... [the text continues].
Because it elucidates that which is subtle and inconceivable, it cannot be [fully expressed] by means of teaching; thus, a doubter might object:
"If one does not elucidate and manifest the meaning through verbal teaching, how can the meaning be made fully evident? Therefore, there is also the case where the meaning is adorned by the teaching.

Regarding the second intention, the commentary states: "One should understand the meaning by taking one side as an illustration. The sub-commentary (*shu*) does not state this again because it wishes to further clarify all [points].
Because they mutually adorn one another, they are explained separately.
The commentary states: "Meditation is not wisdom," and so forth; the above is a general explanation of the broad meaning. Below this is the specific word-by-word commentary. Question:
Since there are six perfections and myriad practices, why does the *Sūtra Commentary* specifically cite meditation and wisdom as the essential form? Answer: Regarding the practice...
Because these essentials are constantly practiced and employed, they are singled out for mention: if meditation lacks wisdom, it conversely results in using wisdom to adorn meditation;
if wisdom does not attain meditation, it conversely results in using meditation to adorn wisdom.

It is said that if giving does not attain precepts, it conversely results in using precepts to adorn giving. The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "When a bodhisattva practices giving, he should exercise discernment."

If one knows that a person who does not uphold the precepts beats, tortures, imprisons, or extorts wealth through unjust laws and then uses that wealth for giving, they shall fall among horses and oxen.
Although they take the form of an animal, they carry heavy loads, are whipped and spurred, and are bound with halters;
yet they always obtain fine dwellings and good food, are held in high regard by others, and are provided for by people—just like a wicked man.
If one gives alms while harboring much anger and with a crooked, unupright mind, one shall fall among the dragons;

yet one will obtain palaces of the seven treasures, exquisite food, and beautiful forms. Furthermore, if a person full of pride and anger gives alms, they shall fall among the garuḍas, where they will always enjoy sovereignty and possess wish-fulfilling jewels as necklaces, so that all various necessities are provided.
They obtain self-mastery such that nothing happens contrary to their will; they manifest myriad transformations and accomplish every task.
Furthermore, it is like a high official who, by unjustly oppressing the people and violating the laws of governance, seizes their wealth to use for acts of giving;

such a person falls among the spirits as a *kumbhāṇḍa* ghost, able to perform various transformations to delight themselves with the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). Moreover, it is like many...
If one who is wrathful, cruel, and fond of wine and meat practices giving, they will fall among the terrestrial yakṣas,
where they constantly enjoy various kinds of music, food, and drink. Furthermore, if one who is stubborn, headstrong,
and arrogant can give away carriages and horses to serve as means of transport, they will fall among the *antarīkṣa* yakṣas, possessing great power wherever they go.
It is like the wind, or like a person who, though possessing a jealous mind and a fondness for contention, is able to give away fine dwellings, bedding, clothing, and food;
because of this, he is born among the *kinnaras* in palaces and towers where they fly, possessing various amusements and articles for bodily comfort.
Such various things can be distinguished and known [as the result of giving]. (The above cases all lack the precepts, and thus their giving is not dignified. This is called "precepts."

One must not fail to give to those of lower status; conversely, this constitutes the precept of "adorned giving. Regarding the phrase "not abandoning wealth or the Dharma," the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states:

"If one does not abandon even a single needle or a blade of grass, and when there is a seeker of the Dharma, fails to explain even a single sentence or a single verse for them, one immediately commits the grave offense of stinginess;
this is precisely the precept of 'adorned giving.'"

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "furthermore, as mentioned above," this refers to the mutual adornment of cause and effect and so forth, wherein all possess dynamic power, interpenetrate, and mutually support one another.

This involves four sets of four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) concerning the identity of existence and non-existence. As for the statement, "Now, furthermore, we shall discuss the mutual adornment of principle and practice":
there are two interpretations of principle and practice; the first is to take the two characters "Huayan" (Flower Adornment) and pair them with what precedes, beyond the five previous pairs.

The three characters *vaipulya* (fangguǎng) constitute the pair of "mutual adornment of principle and practice" (*lǐxíng hùyán*). Because this is not among the preceding five pairs, the commentary states that it is "further categorized.

Alternatively, "practice" (*xíng*) refers to the pair of "person and dharma" (*qiánrén fǎ*). Here, "Great," "Square," and "Vast" (*dà-fāng-guǎng*) represent principle, while the name *Buddhāvataṃsaka* represents practice.
One might ask: "It is acceptable to call the name *Avataṃsaka* 'practice,' but why is the character 'Buddha' (*fó*) called 'practice'? Furthermore, below...

Question: Since all phrases state that it is due to "practice" (*caryā*), why is the term "Buddha" (*buddha*) also considered a practice? Answer: The "Chapter on Manifestation" (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*) states:

"One should know that unimpeded practice is the practice of the Tathāgata; one should know that the practice of true suchness (*tathatā*) is the practice of the Tathāgata. Therefore, the Buddha also possesses practice.

Furthermore, the Buddha’s unimpeded wisdom of the provisional and the real, when viewed in relation to the principle of the integration of the ultimate and conventional truths that is realized, is also termed [practice].
It is called "cause" because one realizes the principle through the wisdom of causality by means of that which acts as a cause, rather than as a cause in its own state. Question:

Of the five pairs mentioned previously, why is it that only the pair concerning the mutual adornment of person and dharma is explained using the two sets of four propositions (catuṣkoṭi)? Answer: Because this pair is taken to manifest the most eminent [truth];

for practice (caryā) universally encompasses both cause and fruit, while principle (li) concurrently includes essence (tattva), characteristics (lakṣaṇa), and function (vṛtti). Question: Since the relationship between teaching and meaning is the broadest, why is it not addressed here?

The reason for not relying on these [two] answers is that the relationship between the signifier and the signified is not essential to the practitioner’s practice, and furthermore, they lack both scriptural authority and logical rigor;
thus, one may adopt either of the two interpretations as appropriate.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "First, by means of cultivation, the principle is manifested," this means that when practice is powerful and the principle is powerless, the principle is adorned by the flowers of the myriad practices;
thus, one realizes this Dharma-body without exception, as it subsumes the derivative back into the fundamental.
Second, when the principle is powerful and the practice is powerless, the principle... [is adorned] by its own nature.

Because the practice of the *Avataṃsaka* is cultivated through its arising, there is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm; for it arises from the source as the manifestation of the ultimate. The *Commentary* (Chao) states:

"The above is the correct explanation, etc. This means that just as the light of a pearl penetrates the substance of the pearl, and the substance of the pearl penetrates the light of the pearl—because they penetrate each other and mutually merge—they are called non-dual.
Yet, while the principle of the source and the manifestation remains undestroyed, the phenomena of the principle and the practice are distinct and clear.

Therefore, it is said that there are two. ▲ Regarding the first phrase of the *Chao* (Commentary), "the practice fuses with the principle" (*xing rong li*), this means that if one does not follow the practice that flows from the Truth (*zhen*), there is no way to accord with the true essence (*zhen ti*), as there would be no connection or involvement between them; thus, the cultivation involving activity (*you zuo*) and the ultimate essence remain distinct.
Therefore, the first phrase above—“practice fuses and returns to the principle” (*xing rong gui li*)—means that there is nothing that does not return to and realize this [Truth].
This is the Dharma-body. Next, regarding "it is not the arising of practice," this means that if it were not the true nature of the arousal of practice, it would not be manifested through practice;
because they are not unrelated, and because it is not the substance of practice, it does not allow for following conditions.

This establishes the principle of the second phrase: the fusion of its essence with practice, such that there is nothing which does not flow from this Dharma-realm. Possessing these two phrases [establishes the meaning].
To establish the third phrase: the "Commentary" (Chao) states that "correctly establishing the preceding meaning" means establishing the meaning of the third phrase.
Because the myriad practices flow from the Truth, each one accords with the Truth;

because they are the essence of the Truth, it causes all causal practices to be fully perfected, thereby correctly establishing the principle that practice and realization are fused. Because practice encompasses the essence of the Truth, it causes the fruition to be fulfilled, thereby correctly establishing [the ultimate state].

Regarding the phrase "superior practice" (*shàngxíng*) which integrates principle (*lǐ*), why does the Commentary (*Sū*) conclude the six characters of the question by referring only to the *Buddhāvatamsaka*?

Answer: This is because it follows the preceding statement regarding the perfection of cause and the fulfillment of fruit. Alternatively, while the fruit of principle is spontaneous, practice is achieved through human effort;
therefore, it is mentioned specifically. Furthermore, if a person did not attain the Dharma, how could it be called the *Buddhāvatamsaka*?
Regarding the phrase "the above [terms] are mutually fused," etc.: because the power and function of the third phrase penetrate one another, they are neither two nor destroyed;
yet, while they appear as two, their two aspects are now negated so that both are extinguished, hence it is said "two yet not two.
Thus, one knows that the expressions "not-two yet two" and "two yet not-two" merely differ in terms of their presence and extinction. Question:

Question: If the practice is thus obliterated, how can the principle be obliterated? Answer: Even if one were to say that the principle is inherently existent, it is nonetheless established only in relation to the faculties.
The Commentary states: "It transcends emotion and severs conceptualization because both are obliterated. It is not that the Adorned Dharma is devoid of causes;
for fear that one might think it is not adorned, it says "it is not unadorned," thereby eliminating even that elimination—this is the mutual adornment mentioned above.

Regarding the phrase "not adorned," the *Ji* (Commentary) states that it does not mean "not adorned" in the sense of destroying adornment; rather, it transcends both meanings of "adorned" and "not adorned.
As for the *Chao* (Sub-commentary) citing "Huayan images and so forth," the *Tanxuan ji* records that Tripitaka Master Faliang said there were [such images] in the Western Regions.
A single offering object is called a *pāṭaha*; its form consists of six tiers, being broad at the bottom and narrow at the top, adorned with flowers and jewels.
Within each tier, there are installed Buddha images, further embellished with various flowers. This is based on the meaning of mutual adornment (*anyonya-vibhūṣaṇa*);
it constitutes the metaphorical body (*dṛṣṭānta-śarīra*). As for using the metaphor to illuminate the Dharma: within the metaphor, there exist only the means of adornment.
As for the flower, it has no image that serves as its adornment; rather, the four characters "Mahāvaipulya Buddha" (Dafangguangfo) are taken from the Dharma as the metaphorical object of adornment.
To reflect the metaphor through the Dharma: within the Dharma, there are only the four characters "Mahāvaipulya Buddha" serving as the adorned, and thus there is no cause that performs the adorning.
Furthermore, taking the character "hua" (flower) from the Chinese term as the Dharma, it serves as the metaphor.
Because they are capable of adorning, it is said that "the Dharma and its metaphors reflect one another. To say that one adorns the Buddha through causal practice is still somewhat brief;
if we were to consider mutual adornment, one should further say that the fruit adorns the cause, and so forth.

Thus far, based on principle and practice, two sets of fourfold propositions have been established to exhaustively express the truth; this applies to all five pairs, which can be understood by reflecting upon them.

Regarding the statement "the first is 'Source of Birth' (*janman*) and so forth," the preceding commentary (*śāstra*) states: "The first is called 'Gushing Spring' (*utsa*), the second is called 'Source of Birth' (*janman*), and the third is called 'Manifestation' (*prakāśana*).
The preceding sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) cites the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* as saying: "The first is 'Source of Birth,' the second is 'Gushing Spring,' and the third is 'Manifestation,' etc.
The preceding sub-commentary further notes: "In the [main] commentary, because they follow the sequence of the meanings, it says: 'First, Gushing Spring; second, Source of Birth.'"
Question: Why does this present *Chao* (Excerpts) not follow the sequence of the *Śāstra*, nor the sequence of the previous *Shu* (Commentary)?
Answer: Here, we do not adopt the sequential order of the meanings, but rather cite them broadly. The *Zhenyuan Shu* states: "First, it is like a gushing spring that flows without exhaustion;
second, it is like giving birth and developing, whereby [the water] increases and spreads; third, it is 'manifestation,' which reveals both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*)."
Therefore, it is: first, the four guiding lines that establish the boundaries between the heterodox and the orthodox; second, the five penetrations that thoroughly penetrate all that is taught;

third, the comprehensive gathering that sustains the sentient beings to be transformed, causing them to return to the source and preventing them from clinging to the six sense objects or wandering through the six realms of rebirth;
fourth, the eternal and universal constant for all time; fifth, the true track of the thousand-petaled Dharma; and sixth, the canonical scripture.
Because it is correct and free from error, and because the "Ten Paths" are the path for transcending birth and death, [the author] asks:

"Of the ten meanings of the six characters above, all have been assigned to the single title according to their respective meanings to demonstrate their mutual explanation; however, the ten meanings of the character *jīng* (sūtra) have not yet been seen assigned to the seven characters.
Answer: There are many meanings here. First, the ten meanings of *jīng* are all exclusively the expressive capacity (*vācaka*).
The six characters above all signify that which is explained [by the preceding terms], and their meanings differ entirely such that they cannot be directly correlated.

However, one may correlate them by classifying them according to their respective categories as follows: first, "Gushing Spring" corresponds to the character *Da* (大), for it is called "nature" (*xing*) and is inexhaustible;

second, "Nine Classics" corresponds to the character *Fang* (方), for the principle of the True Dharma (*zhengfa*) is without error or deviation; third, "Birth and Emergence" corresponds to the character *Guang* (廣).

1. Because they unfold and multiply extensively, "three" (tri) is revealed; 2. because they interpenetrate, "five" (pañca) is threaded through—this is the character *buddha* (*bu*), for the phenomena realized manifest as the penetration of principle and fact, and of nature and characteristics;
3. because they sustain and uphold, "flower" (*puṣpa*) is the character, for those to be transformed are the cause; 4.

because they serve as a measuring line, "ornament" (*alaṃkāra*) is the character, for distinguishing between the false and the correct adorns the True Dharma; 5. permanence, 6. the Dharma, and 10. the path.
All sūtras are complete in their true nature through the Dharma-eye and serve as constant models; by following this shortcut, one swiftly transcends birth and death.

Thus, [the title] "Sūtra" (經) consists of seven or eight characters, all of which pertain to the sevenfold teaching (the character "sūtra" in the title). As for the principle (理) of the aforementioned six characters, they constitute the "constant dharma" (常法)—the "seven" and "eight"—which serves as that which is to be traversed (the "ten").
Third, the sūtra has no separate substance of its own; it is entirely comprised of the six characters, which are the conjunction of phonemes, names, phrases, and sentences.

Because it establishes the sūtra, the six characters above all possess the ten meanings of a sūtra; thus, they are collectively termed "sūtra" (*sūtra*) and serve as its gateways without any confusion.

This is because the "Great Sūtra" (*mahāsūtra*), the "Square Sūtra" (*caturasrasūtra*), and so forth differ from one another, with each being individually assigned within the ten meanings such as "Great" (*mahā*) and the rest.
This is truly because there are two kinds of categorical meanings: first, specific categorical meanings, which refer to the six characters above.

Within each individual syllable, there are two meanings that form its category, as is the case with the constant and pervasive meaning inherent in the seven syllables "Mahā" (Great), which are all termed "Mahā" and so forth;
these two general categories of meaning apply only to the syllable *sūtra*.
Generally speaking, the ten meanings constitute the category of meaning for the word *sūtra*, because the remaining six syllables possess these ten meanings and are therefore all termed *sūtra*.
Furthermore, possessing ten meanings is called the *Tijīng* (Body Sūtra), while possessing ten meanings in a square array is called the *Fǎjīng* (Dharma Sūtra);
any of these three aforementioned senses may be adopted.

Regarding the separate explanation of the names in the fourth section of the commentary, it means that the commentary text separately explains each of the seven characters so that they are individually understood.

Regarding the name, it may be interpreted separately as the distinct derivation of the seven characters; alternatively, this section may take the six types of explanation as a whole to define the title.
The first explanation of the name is an *analytic* (*nirukti*) explanation, while the subsequent explanation of the name is a *synthetic* (*samāsa*) explanation.

In Sanskrit, this is called *ṣaḍvidha-samāsa*, which is translated here as "sixfold compound. Adding the meaning to the term, it should properly be called "sixfold analytic-synthetic compound" (*ṣaḍvidha-nirukti-samāsa*). First:

The meaning of "separation" and "union" is explained as follows: because the name is formed by joining [the elements], if a single meaning were used as the name, it would be logically identical to its own essence;
thus, no further explanation is provided, as it cannot be separated or joined. Therefore, the *Shizhu chao* states: "In the Western [tradition], there are six ways of explaining names:

first, *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (locative compound); second, *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound); third, *bahuvrīhi* (possessive compound); fourth, *dvandva* (copulative compound); fifth, *tatpuruṣa* (determinative compound); and sixth, *dvigu* (numeral compound)."

The neighbors [of these terms] possess these six kinds of combinations and separations; however, if it is a single-character name, it does not constitute the six types of analysis (*ṣaḍ-vibhakti*), because the characteristics of separation and combination cannot be established therein.
Regarding the term "Great" (*mahat*), when it is named according to its own essence (*svabhāva*), whether as a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or a function (*vṛtti*), all return to the essence.

Because it is eternally pervasive and has nothing further upon which to depend, it is called the "eternal essence," and so forth. As for "Square" (*caturaśra*), this refers to dharmas such as the essence, characteristics, and so on.

Because it universally upholds all tracks and principles, "Broad" means that its characteristics encompass everything extensively; "Buddha" means that he has thoroughly investigated and exhausted the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

His brilliance illuminates the profound depths of the myriad dharmas, and his awakening penetrates the locus of the two deaths. It is said that the long darkness difficult to shatter is called "awakening from the heavy gloom of the great night.
Because his flowers of the ten thousand practices are already perfected, he is able to evoke the fruit of Buddhahood; having realized the ultimate limit of the Dharma-realm, his body [is such].
To be fully endowed with the gravity of virtue is to adorn the essence and function by means of the sublime activity, thereby causing them to manifest; this is the "adornment" (śobhā) of the Dharma.

To be majestic in the true and responsive bodies, instantly transcending all phenomenal forms, is to become a "person" (pudgala). As for the Sūtra, there is no dharma it does not elucidate and no non-arising it does not transform.
The above constitutes the explanation of the meaning derived from the preceding [text].
In this commentary, regarding the fact that each name takes the distinct meanings of the preceding seven characters:

these refer to the seven distinct meanings such as "substance" (*tattva*), "greatness" (*mahat*), "permanence" (*nitya*), and "pervasiveness" (*vyāpin*) found within the section on the "Manifestation of the Categories of Meaning.

As for the phrase "the categories can be known from the preceding," it means that the meanings can be understood from the preceding section on the "Manifestation of the Categories of Meaning," or they are abbreviated from the preceding general summary of the intent of the names.
The meaning of the title can be understood from this.
Regarding the "Explanation of the Title" (*Shiming*) at the end of the commentary: the section below should be joined to conclude the title.

The phrase "First, regarding the Dharma" refers to *Mahāvaipulya* as the object of measurement, while the six modes of explanation (*ṣaḍ-nirukti*) serve as the means of measurement. To say that "essence (*tattva*) and function (*vṛtti*) are relative" is a general statement.

The term "Mahāvaipulya" (Great Vaipulya) is analyzed as follows: "Mahā" (Great) is taken as the essence (*svabhāva*), and "Vaipulya" (Vaipulya) as the function (*karman*). This "Great Vaipulya" refers to the characteristics and functions of the Vaipulya;

it is its own name based upon the essence of "Great," which possesses a mutual relationship, and thus it receives its name from "Great. Following this combined explanation, the name "Mahāvaipulya" itself is treated as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound:
"Mahā" is the support (*āśraya*), meaning that which supports, namely the Vaipulya; and "Vaipulya" is the supported (*āśrita*), meaning that which depends [upon the Great].
The "basis" (*āśraya*) is precisely the "Great" (*mahat*). Because the dependent and sovereign dharmas are used to manifest its own name, the *Chao* (Commentary) states:

"This is according to the sequential arrangement (*vipaśyanā*), wherein the basis and that which is based upon it are each distinct. All subsequent passages follow this principle. (Regarding the *Chao*'s explanation of the "correspondence" [of the opening and closing sections], while the texts differ in their mutual presentation, the preceding *Shu* (Subcommentary) states:

"The 'Great Square' is the essence; because the Great Square has no corners, one returns the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) to the essence, and all are termed 'essence. 'Vastness' is the function (*vṛtti*); based on this, the commentary should state: 'the vastness of the Great Square. That it is not stated here serves as an implicit indication.")

Therefore, [in this context] "Greatness" (*mahā*) is taken as the essence (*tattva*) and "Vastness" (*vaipulya*) as the function (*vṛtti*). Although these were not explicitly mentioned among the five previous pairs, they are implied by way of abbreviation to clarify that there are both essence and characteristics/function.

As for the phrase "because there are characteristics and functions of that which possesses an essence," this means that apart from the essence itself of the characteristics and functions of Vastness, it is stated that within the essence of Greatness there exists the principle of "conformity" (*anuloma*) and "sequential arrangement" (*vyavasthāna*).

Question: Previously you spoke of the relative opposition between essence and function; why, then, do you now speak of "the characteristics and functions of that which possesses an essence"? Answer: [This is because]... (The answer follows).

Since both "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) and "function" (*vṛtti*) can be collectively designated as "function" when contrasted with the "essence" (*svabhāva*), it was stated above that essence and function are relative;

however, because within the category of function the characteristic and the function differ, they are discussed separately. Regarding the phrase "if [the characteristic] were identical to [the essence]," the *Shizhu chao* states:

"Function is able to manifest the essence, and the essence is able to sustain the function; this is called a 'possessive compound' (*dharmadhāraya*). Therefore, the *Chao* says: 'This is based on the principle of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), taking the essence as [the primary referent].'"

Regarding the pair [of aspects], in the explanation of the substance (*vastu*) that serves as the basis, the term "identical" (*samasama*) is used because it shares the same principle as "identity" (*tādātmya*); thus, it is said to be "perfectly interfused" (*yuanrong*).

When one asks about the dharma-characteristics, both the agent and the object of the action (*dharmalakṣaṇa-karmakartṛ*), as well as the essence and function (*svabhāva-vṛtti*), exist together, and this is universally established.

Now, since this belongs to the gate of mutual identity, when the "capable" (the agent) is identical [to the object], its own self-nature is discarded and is termed "without substance. This is like [the case where] "greatness" is identical to "square-extensiveness" (*vaihāyasatva*): once the substance of greatness is discarded, there remains only...
Question: Since there is the principle that the function and the characteristic are identical according to the Vaipulya [teachings], how can this be a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound?

Answer: This statement means that [the Great Vehicle] is "without substance" (*nirātman*) only in the sense of being able to be identified [with its cause]. Because the phenomena of dependent origination cannot establish themselves independently, and because the Vaipulya is the "establisher," it is called "having substance.
Furthermore, because the "Great" is the "established" and has no self-substance apart from the "establisher," it is called "without substance. How could this not be so?
Furthermore, if it were entirely without substance, what dharma of dependent origination could now be established?
To refute this, it is said that by abandoning its own [nature] and conforming to others, they achieve mutual identity and become a single entity. "Great" (*mahā*) refers to the "Vast" (*vaipulya*);

this is a *karmadhāraya* compound, meaning the Vast whose very essence is Greatness. Alternatively, it may be understood as a *karmadhāraya* where the essence of the Vast maintains this Great Function. Question:

"Greatness" (*mahat*) is the essence (*tattva*), and "vastness" (*vipula*) is the function (*vṛtti*). Departing from the meanings of "sustaining" (*dhāraṇa*) and "interpreting" (*vyākhyāna*), what is the essence and what is the object?
Now, in what sense is "vastness" called the essence and "greatness" the function? Answer: The terms "essence" and "function" are not restricted or limited.

For example, within the ten pairs, the pair of "essence" and "object" is termed "function" when situated within the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of power and lack of power; it is [termed essence] when situated in the absence of essence and presence of existence.
Regarding the term "substance" (*tǐ*): when all things are designated as substance based on their causal conditions, this refers to the temporal distinction between substance and function.

Now, because the capacity to establish the meaning of the Vaipulya (Extensive Teachings) is the "object of identification," it is called "substance-identification" (*tǐ-jí*). Because the meaning that is established is the "agent of identification," it is called "function-identification" (*yòng-jí*).

This is a *dharmadhāraya* (possessive) compound, which subsumes function back into substance. Between these two interpretations, if one follows the names and meanings of the three greatnesses (*san dà*), the former explanation is preferred.

Regarding the "Superior" [teaching], if one examines it according to the Dharma, there is no fixed characteristic; this will be explained later in the section on the proximate school (*upaniṣad*). (The preceding sections all explain based on the principle of dependent origination where phenomena arise through mutual dependence;

as for causes such as "mind-only," they may be understood as before. Second, regarding the "Human" [teaching], the following question is asked: Since the Buddha’s "Flower" is its own essential nature, it ought to be the practice of the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*);
why then is it said to be not the practice of the causal stage? Answer: This is the cause for attaining fruition in every moment of thought; it is not [merely] liberation.
Because it discards the practices of the causal stage following the Path, it may be considered the cause for the fruit of Buddhahood;
since it is the flower that is the cause for the fruit of a Buddha and not the cause for other fruits, it is called "the Flower of the Buddha. Now, this commentary follows one principle:
the phrase "the Buddha of the Flower" refers to the Buddha attained based on the aforementioned causal stage, and not to the Buddha of those who have not yet attained the state of a Buddha.

Based on the presiding subject and its activity, the three [categories] may be understood as above. Third, regarding the relative distinction between person (*pudgala*) and dharma, this present commentary contrasts and analyzes them with respect to what preceded;
furthermore, their inclusion and exclusion differ from one another. Previously, "Mahāvaipulya" was taken as the dharma and "Buddha" as the person, constituting a single pair of person and dharma.
Now, this commentary takes "Mahāvaipulya" as the dharma and "Buddhāvatamsaka" as the person, thus mutually reflecting upon one another.

A brief commentary explains that [the term] applies universally; it is said to be "not provisional" (non-ākṣepa) because the Buddha’s *Avataṃsaka* is named from "Great Vaipulya," and thus it is not the *Buddha-avataṃsaka* of the provisional or Lesser Vehicles.
Furthermore, since "Great Vaipulya" is named from the Buddha’s *Avataṃsaka*, it is not a dharma realized at the stage of a cause.
The above has all been a differentiation based on the *tatpuruṣa* compound. As for the question: "Since it says 'flower' (*puṣpa*)..."

Question: Why is the "Strict" (Yan) not considered a stage of the causal state (*hetu-bhūmi*)? Answer: It is because it is subsumed under the term "Buddha," and it is intended to manifest its superiority.

The *Chao* states that within the preceding section on the analysis of "opening and closing" (*kai-he*), the essence of the Dharma (*dharma-tattva*) analyzed here is precisely that which was analyzed in the preceding analysis of opening and closing;
however, while previously the essence of the Dharma was explained only in a scattered manner, now one wishes to analyze its meaning by combining [the two].

The term "bond" (*bandhana*) is merely a different name; it simply excludes the lower [stages] to manifest their completeness or deficiencies. By using the dharma and the metaphor below, the reason for the deficiency is revealed.

Within the process of distinguishing between the opening and closing through contrast, the two characters "Huayan" (*Avataṃsaka*) serve as a general metaphor for the four characters beginning with "Great" (*mahā*).

Now, within the preceding pair of dharma and metaphor, we take only the character "Buddha" to represent the fruit, while the character "flower" (*puṣpa*) serves as the metaphor for practice (*caryā*).
This differs from what preceded; it is for this reason that it is said to "exclude. Among the four pairs, the latter pair differs from the former in its structural format of opening and closing.
This has two meanings: first, distinguishing the difference based on breadth and narrowness; second, distinguishing the difference based on upper and lower [levels].

(There are further differences, as fully explained in the preceding commentary. The phrase "and yet the previous five pairs" introduces the subsequent objection. The objection states: "If the previous five..."
Regarding the explanation that proceeds from the broad toward the narrow and from the bottom upward, why is the fifth [pair] specifically designated as "cause and effect"?

It is because it is neither the most narrow nor the highest. Therefore, this answer states: from the broad toward the narrow, the meaning is fully exhausted within the "selection and retention" (jianchi) pair;
thus, one again borrows the character for "flower" (hua) from among the human beings to represent the Buddha as the cause and effect.
The pair [of terms] is explained further below.

The *Chao* (Commentary) should state: "From 'Mahāvaipulya' onwards, because one is free from the distinction between the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*), when the word 'sūtra' is used alone, what sūtra is it?
Therefore, this present sūtra receives the name *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka*, which is consistent [with that principle]."
Since the subsequent commentary specifically distinguishes this from other sutras, why does it simply refer to the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka*?

This is because the title "Sutra" (*sūtra*) is applied to the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka*; thus, it should be explained that what is elucidated here is not what is elucidated in the treatises (*śāstra*).
All such distinctions are based on the *tatpuruṣa* compound. The sequential and simultaneous modes (*anupūrva-vyūha* and *samanta-vyūha*) are as previously understood.
Regarding the statement "in the sutra there is 'lower,'" this means that "sutra" is its own name, while the six characters above it are the names of others;
taking these now as the title of the sutra constitutes a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound by taking a portion of another name. The *Shizhu chao* states:
"A *tatpuruṣa* compound means receiving a name based on what one possesses, such as *Buddha*, which here is translated as 'the Awakened One' (*jue-zhe*). This refers to...
"One who possesses awakening is called an 'awakened one' (buddha); this is an instance of taking another's name [as an attribute], just as there are those in the world who possess wealth.
This refers to the "possessive compound" (*bahuvrīhi*) as explained in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, where a subsequent example is cited.

Here, the commentary places two instances of the character "hence" (*gu*) to separate them into two distinct meanings, clarifying that these represent two different interpretations; otherwise, it would not accord with the sutra.
Within this [text], there is the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, which is already a "possessor of wealth" (*dhanavat*); how, then, could it possess the sense of being a "complete possessor of wealth"?
Therefore, the *Shizhu chao* states: "Just as the *Abhidharmakośa* is not the *Abhidharma-piṭaka-śāstra*, the *Abhidharma-piṭaka-śāstra* is the name for the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Vasubandhu relied upon that to compose the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*; for this reason, this too is called the 'Treasury of Abhidharma' (*Abhidharma-piṭaka*)."
In discussing this, the term "possessing wealth" (*sadhana*) is taken entirely from the name of another; based on this, it is used as the title for the scripture.
The character "jing" (經) is a scribal error; it should be the character "zi" (自). Alternatively, there is no harm in citing examples, as the six characters above are used as the title.
Thus, when one says that the *Buddhāvataṃsaka* possesses "Great Vaipulya," it is a case of designating a person by means of the dharmas they possess.
The name is also analyzed as a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive compound). If one were to say merely "Great Vaipulya," it would be a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive compound) referring to the whole.

Regarding the fifth section of the commentary, "unfolding without end": this means that from the beginning, starting with the Most Pure Dharma-realm (*suviśuddhadharmadhātu*), it unfolds and flows forth until it is inexhaustible.
It is called "most pure" because its self-nature is undefiled; it is not purified by the removal of obstructions.
The ultimate among purities is called "most pure" (*viśuddha*). However, the text in the lower fascicle states, "down to not even a single character or word.

Now, one should likewise develop the "single character" from the state of no-words; this is because the text briefly indicates the development of the single character into the Pure Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-viśuddhi*) and so forth.
Alternatively, it may be fully contained within the term "purity," as the *Guangchao* (Extensive Commentary) states: "Purity means the sense of transcending all marks (*lakṣaṇa*). Thus it is said.
Regarding "opening" (*kai*), it means "to unfold" or "to manifest. Thus, the Buddha is that which opens, while the *dharmadhātu* is that which is opened;

alternatively, enlightened wisdom (*jñāna*) is that which opens, or the *dharmadhātu* and so forth—considering the former in relation to the latter—are themselves that which opens, while enlightened wisdom and the like are that which is opened.
Both interpretations are valid; the subsequent sections should be understood accordingly.
[Commentary: This refers to the text that follows below the four gates. First, regarding "unfolding the dharma-realm," etc.:
this is the first layer of unfolding the dharma-realm, consisting of the six characters above.

Although there are six characters, it means that one correlates the principle and wisdom with these six characters without taking the characters themselves, but rather taking only the two dharmas of principle and wisdom. Question: [Why is this so?]
Question: It may be so for "Mahāvaipulya" (Great Vaipulya) to signify principle; however, why do the three characters of "Buddhāvataṃsaka" (Buddha-Flower-Adornment) all signify wisdom? Answer:

Because the "flower" is able to adorn the Great Vaipulya, the "adornment" is able to manifest the Great Vaipulya, and the "Buddha" is able to exhaustively realize the Great Vaipulya, they are all the Buddha-wisdom.

Regarding the phrase in the *Chao* (Commentary), "The 'Great' (*mahā*) is the essential nature (*svabhāva*), which includes [all things]," etc.: "Great" refers generally to inclusion, while its shadow-meaning implies pervasiveness;
"vast and extensive" (*vaipulya*) refers generally to pervasiveness, while its shadow-meaning implies inclusion. If this is so, how are the essence (*svabhāva*) and function (*karman*) distinguished?

The answer is that they differ only in that the essence-nature's inclusion and pervasion and the functional activity's inclusion and pervasion constitute their distinction. Regarding the statement in the *Shu* (Sub-commentary) here, "the word 'total' connects with 'conjunction,' etc.," it means:

Combining the six characters above to explain the essence and function of the fruit, this explanatory term for what is explained is collectively called a "sūtra. Question: The *Zhenyuan Shu* states that combining them to form the explanation refers to the seven characters in the title;

why does the present commentary state that combining them to form the explanation refers only to the character "sūtra" (*jing*) in the title? Answer: This involves two levels of the "explanatory" (*neng-chuan*).

First, the six characters [of the title] are combined to explain the essence and function of the fruit. Second, the character "sūtra" is combined with those six characters to explain the entire meaning of the title. Thus, there are these two layers of the explanatory.
The six characters above "one" (*yī*) constitute the essence of the signifier (*nengquan*), while the causal relationship constitutes the signified (*suquan*).
Second, the character "sūtra" (*jīng*) is the signifier, and the six characters above it are the signified. The *Zhenyuan shu* generally treats both layers as signifiers;
the present commentary, however, addresses only the latter layer of signifiers. Each relies on its own principle, and thus there is no contradiction between them.
The *Śū* (Commentary) states that because it is the general assembly of the first [section], and because it is the fundamental assembly, it is called "The Great Majestic Radiance Prince";
this refers to the "Vairocana Chapter.

The *Chāo* (Sub-commentary), however, states that from the "World Chapter" downward—that is, at the beginning of the "World-Formation Chapter"—it restates the preceding "Manifestation of Signs Chapter."
Now, regarding the question and answer within the "Exposition" (*śāstra*), the titles are already fully provided; within these titles, they are expanded to form the first assembly.
As for the term "ten oceans," because they are profound and vast, they are all collectively referred to as "oceans. Regarding the title "Small Opening and Closing" (*kṣudra-saṃkoca-vikāsa*):

herein, two [assemblies] are explained by way of combination, while the preceding two [assemblies] consist of five distinct openings; within this [assembly], ninety [subsections] are explained individually.
