'wisdom' and 'principle' constitute the dharma, while Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī are named as the persons. Alternatively, the person is the *Avataṃsaka* and the dharma is the *Mahāvaipulya*. Taking these..."

Regarding the "discrimination through the pairing of persons and dharmas," this refers to the two sages, Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī. Within the single commentary, the latter interpretation is superior.

If one follows the former interpretation, since both the person and the two sages are [identical to] Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī, how can one distinguish between the subject (the discriminator) and the object (that which is discriminated)?
One should simply say that the two sages are distinguished by way of their dharmas; why then speak of "discrimination through the pairing of persons and dharmas"?
Question: Since the *Shu* (Commentary) mentions three sages (*seng*), why does it speak of two sages? Answer: The Buddha has no separate dharma;

he is formed by the union of the preceding two [sages] into a person who possesses both wisdom and principle. Furthermore, in the latter part of the *Chao* (Sub-commentary), it states that within the categories of "person" and "dharma," there are respectively two sages each:
the Mahāvaipulya is called "person," and the Avataṃsaka is called "dharma," with two sages in each.

Regarding the assignment of the word "Buddha" (*buddha*) within the commentary, the sub-commentary states: "The Buddha is the Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī of perfect understanding and practice. This takes the character "Buddha" downward to encompass the two characters "Huayan" (*Avataṃsaka*), thereby including the two sages among humans; this is the first layer.
As for the Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī who realize the essence and function of the *dharmadhātu*, this— Please note that the provided text fragment ends abruptly.

The full passage would likely continue by explaining how these two aspects of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī correspond to the realization of the ultimate reality.The first layer is the Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī of perfect understanding and practice, who are the Buddha of the *Avataṃsaka*. The second layer is the Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī who realize the essence and function of the *dharmadhātu*. This—
The character "Buddha" (佛) is taken upward to be subsumed within the three characters "Great, Vaipulya" (大方廣); this constitutes the second layer within the Dharma section of the two sages.
Furthermore, the names Vairocana and so forth apply to both preceding layers; they are explained here according to convenience by providing both Chinese and Sanskrit terms, thereby forming the text.
Alternatively, the character "Buddha" may correspond to the term "middle" (中), thus applying generally to the explanations within the previous two sections.

Because the term "Buddha" (佛) appears within both of the preceding two sections—specifically under the "Vaipulya Dharma" (大方廣法) and above the "Avataṃsaka People" (華嚴人)—it is said that the character for Buddha occupies the center of the two layers, subsuming the preceding sections as a whole.

The commentary on the subsequent section states, "The Buddha is Vairocana, possessing both the subject and the object," while the commentary on the following section states, "The Buddha is perfect understanding and practice, etc. This refers only to these two [aspects].
The *Ke* (Commentary) considers this to constitute two layers; thus, the preceding *Chao* (Excerpts) designates two sections accordingly.

If there were not two layers, why would the text of the *Chao* not have explained the character "Buddha" from the preceding section? One may adopt either of the two interpretations, as both subsequent sections also contain two layers.

The commentary states: "The essence of mind is free from thought," and so forth; this is precisely the passage from the *Awakening of Faith* explaining the meaning of "enlightenment" (*jue*) within the section on "Revealing the Correct Meaning.
That sub-commentary explains: "The essence of mind is free from thought" means it is free from deluded thoughts, manifesting the absence of non-enlightenment.
There are two meanings of empty space used as a metaphor for original enlightenment (*benjue*): first, the meaning of pervasiveness, which refers to its horizontal pervasion.

The meaning of "no distinction between the two" refers to the fact that throughout the three periods of time—past, present, and future—the nature of those within the bonds of affliction (*saṃsāra*) and those who have emerged from them is eternally non-dual.

Regarding the phrase "Is this not the Great [Vehicle]?", this is the wording of the *Chao* (the *Dafangguangfo Huayan jing xuanzan chao*), which points out that it belongs to the discourse on the One Mind.

As for the statement that "the six perfections and myriad practices all arise," the "mind" mentioned previously—the essence, characteristics, and function of the mind—is the True Mind (*bhūtatathatā-citta*) that is the object of contemplation.

Regarding "the one mind and the six perfections" herein: the mind is that which is capable of contemplation; to contemplate the mind is to be able to [realize] that there is no difference between the subject and the object.

As for the phrase "awakening to the nature and characteristics of the mind": "awakening" (jue) refers to the aforementioned contemplation of the mind—termed "contemplation" (guan) when in the causal stage and "awakening" (jue) when in the resultant stage.

This is precisely the capacity to awaken. Regarding "the nature and characteristics of the mind": the mind is that which is capable of possessing; the essence and characteristics of true mind are what it possesses.

That which is endowed with the three greatnesses and so forth is precisely that which is to be awakened to. When it is said that awakening occurs through "a single moment of correspondence," this means awakening to the initial arising of the mind as having no initial characteristic.
Because initial awakening (śijiao) merges with original awakening (benjue), there is no further distinction between the initial and the original;

therefore, it is called "correspondence. The scriptural passage cited below is from the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottaraparivarta*). It states that the nature of awakening is without awakening.
Because the subject and object are severed below, the characteristics of awakening are distinct; because the subject and object are not destroyed below, these two are non-dual;

because existence and cessation are unimpeded below, all of these are the wisdom produced through cultivation. [The *Chao* states: "Awakening does not come from without" clarifies that it is entirely dependent on fundamental wisdom.
Being entirely identical to what is awakened to and entirely identical to fundamental wisdom, the new and the original are in dark resonance, being completely one.

"The identity of the tranquil essence means that subject and object are of one taste; even to speak of 'one' does not constitute oneness"—this is a passage from the *Dharmapada-sūtra*. To state it fully:
"Even to speak of 'one' does not constitute oneness," which is intended to shatter all numerical categories.

The following is the summary: at the beginning, one awakens to the principle through the text; at the end, through the perfection of contemplation, one enters into accord with it. If one can do so, then even while contemplating the text...
The character for "mind" (心) is without grasping or rejecting; how could it be that merely discarding written characters constitutes the true reality?

Therefore, upon encountering the text, one is able to fully expound both the words and their meaning, and in accordance with the faculties [of beings], all are skillfully subdued. Thus it is said: "There has never been a single thought-moment that was not in accord with the *Avataṃsaka*. Question:
For what reason do you say only "in accord with the *Avataṃsaka*" and not "the *Mahāvaipulya*," etc.? Answer: The *Avataṃsaka*.

When this śamatha and vipaśyanā that can observe are practiced as a unified integration and one realizes the essence and characteristics [of reality], that is precisely Mahāvaipulya (Great Extensive).
Because one realizes this, one is a Buddha. Therefore, although only the word "Avataṃsaka" is mentioned, its meaning inherently encompasses the four characters above.
Alternatively, it could have been expressed in full, but for the sake of brevity, they were not stated; however, there is further [explanation] in the commentary.
The two characters "Nature-Ocean" (*xinghai*) are the place where one returns to the ultimate.

In the tenth section of the *Shu*, "merging into equality" means that when the two dharmas of mind and object are merged into the single True Suchness (*tathatā*), then raising the mind is itself the object, and raising the object is itself the mind;
they are equal and without obstruction. Regarding the phrase "for those who have not yet understood," etc.:
First, the meaning of the merging of differences into identity and equality is explained so that those who have not yet realized their own minds may do so.
How is it realized? If one knows—as explained below—that whatever is encountered is entirely mind, then who is there to realize?

Since the "realizer" is not established, where can the "object realized" abide? Thus, as already explained in the section on the stages of practice (*bhūmi*), the words "Therefore, the holy life... are now studied.

The passage following "The Dharma" explains the purpose of this section. It states that those who "abandon the internal and seek externally" do so because they discard their own internal mind to seek external objects;

those who "delight in the cessation of conditions" abandon external conditions to internally illuminate their own minds, yet they remain attached to both mind and objects, and thus both constitute biased attachments. Now, since mind and objects are *tathatā* (suchness), they are equal.
"Unobstructed.

Regarding the phrase "the eight preceding dharma-teachers' knowledge," etc., this is an explanation of the *Śāstra* (commentary), though it refers to the section on "Dharma-learning" (*dharmaparyāya*) that follows below.
That is to say, there may be those who rely solely on the explanations of the preceding eight gates to merely seek out the text and interpret its meaning; this is what is meant by "dharma-learning."
Those who do so abandon their own minds to seek externally; they merely claim to understand the Dharma and act as models for others, yet they themselves lack correct practice.

Therefore, if one relies on the ninth [gate] to cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), delighting in the absence of external conditions and inwardly illuminating one's own mind as the object of veneration, this is to lose the true intent of the preceding nine gates. Thus, the Commentary reconciles this as a form of biased attachment.
Because both [views] stagnate in the two extremes. The *Chao* (Commentary) states that the metaphor of the "Jeweled Net" (*Indrājāla*) below is borrowed to illustrate the "Household" (*Kula*).

This means that the mirrors and lamps are the *upamāna* (the illustration), while the Jeweled Net is the *upameya* (the illustrated). Alternatively, the Jeweled Net serves as the *upamāna*, and its infinite, repeated manifestation serves as the *upameya*.
Here, it is said to be "borrowed" because that [Net] illustrates infinite repetition, whereas this [Household] illustrates equality and non-obstruction.

The term "borrowed" (*jiejǐ*) means that while the former [analogy] may generally represent all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), this particular one specifically represents the mind and its objects; therefore, it is called "borrowed.

As for the commentary’s statement, "Observe how the mind and its objects mutually reflect one another": if one understands the aforementioned analogy, then one will comprehend the seeing of the mind and its objects.

They mutually illuminate reality because the wisdom of original enlightenment enters both the mind and the objects; since the fundamental wisdom enters both simultaneously, it is said that "objects are the mind.
Because one awakens to objects within the mind, the mind is the objects;

and because the mind is realized upon the objects, the mind and objects manifest in successive layers, yet the nature of the wisdom of original enlightenment always abides within both mind and objects.
The Commentary takes only the meaning of "clarity" and uses the lamp as a metaphor; it takes only the quality of clarity within the lamp to illustrate fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Alternatively, since both mirrors and the single lamp are all clear, "clarity" itself constitutes the body of the metaphor.
Because the mind, objects, and fundamental wisdom are all the one true mind, they are distinguished according to their respective functions, yet each possesses the quality of clarity.

The commentary states: "The nature of wisdom and the nature of form" refers to the *Awakening of Faith* treatise, which uses the nature of wisdom to prove the entry into the mind above, and the nature of form to prove the entry into the realm above;
that these two are fundamentally non-dual proves the simultaneous entry into both.
This passage may also serve to prove the meaning that both mind and objects are clearly manifest. "Knowing all phenomena" and so forth is from the *Brahmacarya* chapter.
Because one enters the mind and enters the realm by means of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), all phenomena are the very nature of mind;
thus, it should be understood that both meanings are simultaneously realized. Therefore, what follows below explains the meaning of this twofold entry.
Regarding the phrase "The Honored One’s countenance is likened to the True Buddha," etc.: because one's nature is fundamentally the Buddha, it is called the "True Buddha.

Thus, the statement "Nowadays people only understand... serves to exclude misconceptions; alternatively, it raises a shallow understanding to reveal the profound meaning. The phrase "Now, to clarify... reveals the correct [view].

Although it is simply said to be "like" (tathatā), it functions as a comprehensive synthesis of all phenomena, for it is the principle that they are identical to the single mind; therefore, it is named "Suchness" (Tathatā).
It is also said that "becoming a Buddha" means, according to the principle of the mirror newly becoming bright and merging with its original brightness, it is called "becoming.

Thus, there is neither a subject that merges nor an object with which to merge. Regarding the phrase "the mind and Buddha are layered upon one another," this means that within the objective realm one perceives the layering of mind and Buddha, and within the mind and Buddha one perceives the layering of the objective realm and Buddha.
The commentary’s wording is brief, mentioning only "mind and Buddha," as it intends to complete the structure of the text and its meaning.

Because it is said that the fundamental awakened nature (*mūla-awakening*) is, from the very beginning, the single true Buddha; now, using the metaphor of an image for the true [Buddha], it is called the "dual entry into the venerable countenance.

The commentary takes both of these [meanings]: "cannot be apprehended" refers to the fact that both of the aforementioned dual dharmas—mind and object—are such that they cannot be apprehended by the mind.

To perceive its form and characteristics is the realization of *śamatha* (calm abiding). To illuminate the mental object with the mind such that it cannot be exhausted is the realization of *vipaśyanā* (insight).

The Commentary states that when these two are fused, they are like two mirrors reflecting each other; although they manifest in successive layers, they are ultimately the singular image of a single lamp.
The two entries also manifest as layered reflections; though one attempts to grasp them with the hand, they cannot be obtained. The principle of the Dharma should be understood accordingly.
Above, the two dharmas of mind and object manifest layer upon layer in mutual relation; this is called "mind and object.

Now, because these cannot be grasped, they are said to be "both lost," and thus cessation (*śamatha*) is established. Yet, the preceding mutual manifestations continue to be illuminated, such that the limits of mind and object cannot be exhausted.
They are called "contemplations" (*vipaśyanā*) because they mutually penetrate one another.

Regarding the phrase "the objects and objects facing each other": this means that by means of the wisdom of original enlightenment (*mūlapratyavekṣa-jñāna*), one simultaneously enters both this object and that object.
Thus, this object awakens to the Buddha of that object, and that object realizes the Tathāgata of this object; in this way, each and every one is identical.
The preceding instances of mind and mental factors should be understood by analogy.

Regarding the phrase "the objects are manifold," this refers to the various objects such as the defiled and the pure; each of these, when mutually compared with the fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) of the True Buddha, all enter [into it].
As stated in the *Samantabhadra-pariṇāmanā-parivarta*: "Incalculable pure light-treasures constantly emit unimpeded great wisdom."

Regarding the phrase "the light universally illuminates the dharma-realm," etc., it means that within the mind there are many minds—such as wholesome and unwholesome minds—and when each and every one is mutually compared, they both enter into the true Buddha of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
This is likewise the case for their mutual cessation and their mutual fusion;

all of these constitute *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and thus are no different from what was stated previously. Therefore, the Commentary says, "they are all of one consistency. Regarding the phrase "only through realization is there correspondence," this applies to both the preceding and the following sections.

Because this is provisionally established as a gateway for the causal stage, if practitioners are able to accord with such contemplative practice, they will become mysteriously one with the ocean of fruition.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The three wisdoms perfectly awaken to the world and so forth,” it means that the world of sentient beings refers to the faculties of those to be transformed; thus, it is said to be "equal."
Having awakened, he returns to his original state; as the Perfectly Enlightened One of the world, he is the Master capable of transformation.

This is not the same as speaking generally of the "world of the perfectly enlightened wisdom. If one were speaking generally of the world of the perfectly enlightened wisdom, it would also include Bodhisattvas from the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) downward through the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), because their sixth and seventh consciousnesses have already been transformed into the nature of untainted (*anāsrava*) perfectly enlightened wisdom. Now, [the text] refers specifically to the one who is capable...
The Master of Transformation (the Buddha) speaks with the intent of making a distinction; thus, he refers specifically to the Buddha. When speaking of "lords," there are two types:

the lords of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), such as water deities and fire deities, and the lords of the sentient world (*sattvaloka*), such as heavenly kings and dragon kings; since both are called "various kings" (*rājānaḥ*), there are only these two.
The statement "the Buddha is not of the world" serves to resolve potential objections. Question: Why is it said that the Buddha is not of the world?
Since phenomena subject to arising and ceasing cannot be called the "Wisdom-Perfectly-Awakened World," this is the answer:
because the Buddha’s own essence is not the world, and it is from the perspective of the vessel-world (the environment) and its sentient beings that the term "world" is applied;

thus, the wisdom-perfectly-awakened one who is the world is termed the "Wisdom-Perfectly-Awakened World. In this case, the "Wisdom-Perfectly-Awakened World" is the primary designation for the Wisdom-Perfectly-Awakened One.
The two explanations—*tatpuruṣa* (dependent) and *karmadhāraya* (possessive)—are applied respectively as follows:
because each of the various kings divides the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) and its sentient beings, the receptacle world is the "world," and the sentient beings are the "sentient world.
Thus, the *tatpuruṣa* and *karmadhāraya* explanations apply respectively to the "master of the receptacle world" and the "master of the sentient world."

Regarding the commentary’s statement that “the Dharma-gates, etc., are wondrous”: Question: In the previous assembly, when translating from the Sanskrit original, the word "wondrous" (miao) did not appear here in this local [Chinese] version;
why, then, is it said here that they are "wondrous"? Answer: The full term is "the majestic power (vīrya-tejas) of the Dharma-gates," which indeed possesses the meaning of "wondrous.

Because the majestic power of these Dharma-gates causes the essence and function of the three worlds to be profoundly vast and inconceivable, they are called "wondrous. This, then, is what is meant by the word.
The phrase "the translator Jianli’s skillful words" refers to that which the Lord has attained; because it is what the Lord of the Three Worlds has attained, it is said that his ground is firm.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "he attains supreme perfect enlightenment in all dharmas," this is the wording from the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* (The Sutra of Golden Light).
As for "the three karmas being all-pervasive," the aforementioned attainment of supreme perfect enlightenment refers specifically to the pervasiveness of the mental karma (*manas-karman*).
His body fills all worlds, which signifies that his physical karma (*kāyakarman*) is all-pervasive;
his voice universally accords with the lands of the ten directions, which signifies that his vocal karma (*vākkarman*) is all-encompassing.

Therefore, in the prose section below, the text generally refers to the passages from the second fascicle down to the fifth fascicle, wherein it is stated in prose that each of the kings has attained a Dharma-gate to serve as a solemn verse of praise.
The middle section praises the Buddha’s virtues, all of which manifest the adornment of the Buddha above; it says he is the "Wisely Enlightened One, the Adornment of the World.

The commentary states that the phrase "sentient beings are not adorned" below serves as a counter-manifestation (*pratiṣedha*). If explained according to the direct sequence (*anuloma*), "multitude" (*sattva*) refers to those who possess the power of the majestic adornment of the Dharma-gates;
only when such power exists can a Buddha appear. It is because the Buddha, through his three karmas, universally adorns the multitude with all virtues that he is able to [manifest].

When the principal [subject] and the transformed phenomena of the Buddha are fused such that their principles and appearances are mutually interpenetrating and without obstruction, this alone constitutes the true locus of the Buddha.

The Commentary clarifies that when one encounters those of virtue, it is the Buddha who adorns sentient beings; sentient beings obtain the adornment of the Dharma, which is subtle and wondrous, serving as an aid.
The "Wing-like" (Yìrú) Tathāgata reveals the Buddha who is transcendent and surpasses all, namely the Buddha Adorned by Sentient Beings (*yíqīngzhòng yánfó*).

There should also be the adornment of the vessel-world (*qìjiè zhuāngyán*), revealing the primary subject of transformation; the meaning of the great assembly of the ultimate ocean being capable of serving as vessels for the Dharma does not differ from what was previously mentioned.
Because the Buddha encountered possesses virtue and is supremely excellent, the commentary (*shū*) omits further mention. The topical outline (*kē*) states: "Three Adornments."
Because they are mutually constitutive, one knows it must be so.
The Commentary now clarifies that the "Introduction" (Nidāna) already encompasses the "Main Body" (Prakaraṇa) and so forth;
since the profound principle explained within the Introduction already contains the meaning of the Main Body, the extensive praise that follows returns once more to the intent of the Introduction.
The commentary states that "the dharmas obtained" and so forth means that it is by obtaining the eye of wisdom regarding profound dharmas that one is able to purify the three worlds.

Furthermore, the dharmas obtained are worthy of veneration like the eye; moreover, while dharmas are fundamentally pure like the eye, they do not merely purify themselves but are also able to purify the world.
Furthermore, "purifying" has the sense of "adorned," differing only in name. Therefore, this is now translated anew.
It is "Exquisite Adornment" (Miaoyan).
The *Chao* [commentary] integrates the majestic power of the Dharma-gate from three locations as it exists today;

that is to say, the Sanskrit original, when fully translated, is called "Majestic Power of the Dharma-gate" (*dharmaparyāyavaipulya*), the Jin translation calls it "Pure Eye" (*viśuddhacakṣus*), and the current translation calls it "Exquisite Adornment. Though the names differ, the meaning is one and the same.
Furthermore, because of the majestic power of the Dharma-gate, the Dharma-eye is purified;
since the Dharma-eye is purified, one is able to wondrously adorn the world.
*Huayan Xuantan Huixuan Ji*, Fascicle Forty (End).

*bì* (the sound of *bì*, meaning "obstinate"); *qián* (the sound of *qián*, meaning "to bind or restrain").
